t: Nuncio Acciaiuoli from Lisbon to the Secretariat of State, 1758–60
b: Eight nunciature ciphers from Portogallo 117 that DECODE lists as partially decrypted. Lasry’s 2020 key had turned them into letters with the code words open; three leaves deciphered at the time fix 25 codes, and the rest read as Italian. The first is the nuncio’s secret account of the attempt on José I of 3 September 1758. Lisbon → Rome · two-digit homophones with a four-digit nomenclator · September 1758 – 1760 · read Nuncio Acciaiuoli from Lisbon to the Secretariat of State, 1758–60 Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Portogallo 117, items 1–8 · DECODE R25, R195–R201, eight cipher leaves, ten pages · catalogued as partially decrypted (catalogue item 240) Lasry’s key and letter stream read as Italian · 25 code groups fixed from the three leaves deciphered at the time · about 80 rare codes still open Daniel Bourdeau · read 19 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. Portogallo 117 holds the letters of Filippo Acciaiuoli, nuncio in Lisbon, and of the abbé Testa, 1757–61. DECODE has eight of the cipher leaves, transcribed digit by digit in 2016–17. In 2020 George Lasry reconstructed the key (two-digit homophones, the digit 6 a null, four-digit code words that all begin with 2) and attached a letter-by-letter decryption of all eight, with the code groups left as numbers. No Italian text was posted, and the records stayed “partially decrypted”. Three of the leaves (10, 24 and 31 October 1758) carry the Secretariat’s decipherment in clear above the figures. Lining those up with the cipher fixes 25 code words ( Re , Regina , Spagna , tutto , molto , ministri , e che …), and with them the other five leaves read as running Italian. What they say: on 12 September 1758 the nuncio sent Rome, in cipher, what Lisbon was not saying aloud. The king had not fallen ill: coming back by night from a lady “delle prime famiglie”, he was fired on in his calesse. His valet and favourite Pedro Teixeira was wounded almost to death, the king was hit in the right arm, and a surgeon took him to the Real Barraca. The later letters follow the wound, the king’s fear of Carvalho, the Jesuits, and in 1760 the marriage of the Princess of Brazil. What stays open is about eighty code groups that occur only once or twice, and a few passages in the two long leaves where the transcription has slipped. Portogallo 117/6 (f. 106r), 24 October 1758: the decipherment made in Rome, “Benche si dica il Rè assai meglio…”, written above the figures. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Portogallo 117/6 f. 106r, via DECODE R199.

t: Nuncio Acciaiuoli from Lisbon to the Secretariat of State, 1758–60
b: The volume is “Lettere di mons. Acciaiuoli, nunzio in Portugallo, e dell’abbate Testa, 1757–1761”, ff. 2–585. DECODE dates all eight records 18 January 1757, which is the first date in the volume. The cipher leaves themselves run from 12 September 1758 to 1760: Item DECODE Folio Date Digits Clear on the leaf 117/1 R25 95r–v 12 Sept 1758 1918 no 117/2 R195 98r [Sept 1758] 860 no 117/3 R196 101r 26 Sept [1758] 492 no 117/4 R197 103r 10 Oct [1758] 190 decipherment 117/5 R198 104r 31 Oct [1758] 577 decipherment 117/6 R199 106r 24 Oct [1758] 791 decipherment 117/7 R200 115r–v 28 [Nov?] 1758 1999 no 117/8 R201 280r Lisbon, 12 [?] 1760 1499 no The key is Lasry’s reconstruction (DECODE, 24 October 2020). Letters and common syllables have fixed two-digit homophones: a 04 38 55, e 84, i 08 53, o 81, s 88, il 43 91, che 39, non 14, de 71 78, qu 70 87 90. The digit 6 is a null, scattered freely, and the code words are four digits beginning with 2. No two-digit element begins with 2 or contains a 6, so the figures cut up only one way.

t: Nuncio Acciaiuoli from Lisbon to the Secretariat of State, 1758–60
h: The attempt on the king, 12 September 1758
b: The first leaf (117/1, R25) is the longest. Code words resolved above are in plain type and open ones are given as numbers; the spelling is the cipher’s, which often drops double consonants. … e si racconta che venendo il Re da una [visita] di una dama della <2183> … Pietro Teixeira, suo assai domestico favorito … fussero sparate contro il calesse <2908> schioppettate; restò ferito malamente il cavalcante e la mula del bilancino che egli montava; il Teixeira ferito a morte, <2149> si <2981> che lo avevano sagramentato; il Re molto ferito del braccio destro … il detto chirurgo portò il Re alla Real Baracca. Non <2195> molto rumore: la materia è delicata, ma diventa <2754> in bocca di ogni popolare. Ho creduto doverne avvisare … La dama è delle prime famiglie … Si pensa che venga il colpo da di lei parenti; che venga da nemici del Teixeira … Il fatto non si mette in dubbio. … L’Infante don Manuel me ne parlò con il sospetto … né più posso per ora riferire. “…and it is said that as the King was coming back from [a visit to] a lady… Pedro Teixeira, his very intimate favourite… shots were fired at the calesse; the postilion was badly wounded, and so was the mule of the lead pair he rode; Teixeira wounded to death, so that they had given him the sacrament; the King badly wounded in the right arm… the said surgeon took the King to the Real Barraca. Little noise is made: the matter is delicate, but it is on every common man’s lips… The lady is of one of the first families… The blow is thought to come from her relatives, or from Teixeira’s enemies… The fact is not in doubt.” This is the attempt of the night of 3 September 1758, which Carvalho turned two months later into the arrest of the Távoras and the Duke of Aveiro and, in 1759, their execution at Belém.

t: Nuncio Acciaiuoli from Lisbon to the Secretariat of State, 1758–60
b: 117/2 (R195). The illness is the public story. The arm is said to be broken, and the fleets and merchant ships are held back “con danno del Re, de’ mercanti e de’ poveri”. 117/3 (R196, 26 Sept). “Continua la voce sulla causa del male del Re, che da nessuno più si dubitò … restò tutto il giorno a letto … nessuno vede il braccio che [è] fasciato … si vuole che il braccio resterà impedito.” 117/4 (R197, 10 Oct). Deciphered at the time: “Il Rè si è levato, ma [non esce] tutto il giorno. Vogliono i più, che sia molto guasto nel Braccio, e che almeno resterà perpetuamente impedito.” 117/6 (R199, 24 Oct) , deciphered at the time: “Benché si dica il Re assai meglio si vuole, che assolutamente il Braccio resterà impedito: parlando un suo confidente col Re sulla morte della Regina [di Spagna] il Re gli disse: è stata buona Sorella, e che sono sicuro, che il Re sposerà la mia Figlia Maria Francisca, e che lo ha promesso alla Regina avanti, che ella morisse: ciò, che il Ministro di Spagna mostra è tutto il contrario … di tutto il resto non posso io compromettermi.” Barbara of Braganza, Queen of Spain and José’s sister, had died on 27 August 1758. The widowed Ferdinand VI did not marry Maria Francisca. 117/5 (R198, 31 Oct) , deciphered at the time: the king has not had erysipelas, “ma un sacco di materia, che ha fatto la piaga”, with fever as a result. The king is very apprehensive; “il credere il male maggiore di quello, che si dice” is universal.

t: Nuncio Acciaiuoli from Lisbon to the Secretariat of State, 1758–60
h: Carvalho, November 1758, and the marriage question, 1760
b: 117/7 (R200) is the longest leaf and the most damaged by transcription slips. Its drift is clear: Carvalho is “dispotico”, “si dice che il Re ne ha paura”, and the Infantes and the court do not dare oppose him. The leaf touches on confessors and preachers, on a lay brother “cacciato nella Compagnia” and on “l’espulsione”. The nuncio notes that he himself is met with “diffidenza”. A companion “sta tutto il giorno da Carvalho”. 117/8 (R201, 1760) is about the succession. The Princess of Brazil might marry the Infante Don Luis of Spain, and there are frequent conferences between the Conde d’Oeiras (Carvalho) and others. The court of London “è molto allarmata” and fears for its trade from “uno della casa di Spagna e di Borbone sul trono di Portogallo”. The letter ends: “Il paese freme, che vorrebbe la [principessa] unita coll’Infante don Pietro.” She married her uncle Pedro on 6 June 1760. Acciaiuoli was expelled from Portugal nine days later.

t: Nuncio Acciaiuoli from Lisbon to the Secretariat of State, 1758–60
b: The DECODE records were fetched with a logged-in session: images, the NiLan/Midas digit transcriptions, Lasry’s key and his decryption, which is one file attached to every record. The decryption was flattened into one letter string per leaf and split into Italian words by reading. t: Nuncio Acciaiuoli from Lisbon to the Secretariat of State, 1758–60
b: About 80 of the 107 distinct code groups that occur once or twice (2183, 2481, 2754, 2823, 2398, 2159, 2413, 2817, 2803 and others), with no crib. Where the sense can be guessed, it is marked C in READING.md. Transcription slips produce unassigned pairs (82, 92, 42, 12, 32, 72, 02) and garbled stretches, above all in 117/7 and 117/8. A fresh transcription of those two leaves from the images would recover most of them. The rest of Portogallo 117 (ff. 2–585) has more cipher than these eight leaves. It is not on DECODE and was not seen.

t: The ADFGVX residue of 1918 — twenty-two mutilated messages against known keys
b: Schmeh’s Top 50 lists twenty-two German radio messages of November 1918 as unsolved, but the keys were published in 2017 and the messages are garbled in transmission. The comment thread that read nine of them is tabulated for the first time, Lasry’s unpublished CHI key is rebuilt, his readers’ method re-derives the solved pages blind, and the ten never read resist every key and a key-free attack that fails its own control. Working notes · September 2026 The ADFGVX residue of 1918 — twenty-two mutilated messages against known keys Schmeh’s Top 50 lists twenty-two German radio messages from the Eastern Front of November 1918 as unsolved. They are not unbroken ciphers. The keys were published in 2017, and what defeats these messages is loss in transmission. Nine were read in the comment thread, three partly, and ten have never been read by anyone. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 15 September 2026 · sources: Schmeh, Top 50 no. 46 and the “Unsolved ADFGVX messages” page provided by George Lasry; the 70 comments under the post (Norbert Biermann, Armin, Thomas, Max Baertl, George Lasry, 2017); Lasry, Niebel, Kopal and Wacker, Cryptologia 2017; James Rives Childs, German Military Ciphers from February to November 1918 9 of 22 read Status 9 solved · 3 partial · 10 open The list entry should read “22 messages, 9 solved, 3 partly read, 10 open”, and the key Lasry recovered in the thread belongs alongside the published fourteen. Norbert’s method of 2017, two block edits of up to five letters against a known key, is reimplemented here with a German language model and re-derives the solved pages without a hint of their plaintext. On the ten open messages it finds nothing with any of the fifteen keys, and a key-free attack cannot recover the transposition at these lengths even on a planted control. The open ten need the Childs originals or a key that was never in the corpus.

t: The ADFGVX residue of 1918 — twenty-two mutilated messages against known keys
b: James Rives Childs, the American cryptanalyst attached to the French in 1918, kept a transcript of German ADFGVX traffic intercepted on the Eastern Front. In 2017 George Lasry, Ingo Niebel, Nils Kopal and Arno Wacker broke the corpus with a hill-climbing attack on the transposition and recovered 618 cryptograms under fourteen three-day keys, from September to December 1918. Lasry then gave Klaus Schmeh a list of the messages that would not decrypt under any of those keys, and Schmeh published it as “Unsolved ADFGVX messages from World War I”, with the keys attached, and later as no. 46 on his Top 50. Lasry’s own note on that page says what the problem is: the keys are “most certainly all the keys used during the period”, so “the challenge is to understand how the cryptograms were mutilated”. ADFGVX is unforgiving about length. The columnar transposition splits the letter stream by the key length, so one lost or added letter moves every column boundary after it and turns the rest of the message into noise. A message with two garbles is no longer decryptable by the key, even though the key is known. Between February and September 2017 the comment thread under the post did most of the work. Norbert Biermann, Armin, Thomas, Max Baertl and Lasry himself read message after message. Schmeh announced a consolidating article and never wrote it, so those readings existed only as scattered comments and no table of which messages are solved had been published. The first thing this write-up does is publish that table.

t: The ADFGVX residue of 1918 — twenty-two mutilated messages against known keys
b: Lasry’s list gives each key as a transposition permutation and a 36-character substitution square, the cells in row order of A D F G V X. Three of the fourteen squares contain runs of hyphens for cells never recovered, and the text layer of the PDF collapses those runs into en- and em-dashes, leaving squares of 34 or 35 characters. Expanding each dash back to the run length that makes 36 repairs all three. All fourteen are in keys.json . The key numbers admit two readings. Either perm[i] is the column emitted i-th, or it is the position at which column i is emitted. Both round-trip self-consistently, so an encrypt-decrypt test cannot tell them apart. Decrypting a real message can. It is the second. The key not on the list On 3 May 2017 Lasry reported in the thread that a two-part message, the FFVXV cryptogram of 13 November and the AFAFF fragment that continues it, decrypted jointly under a key that was in none of the fourteen periods: transposition word CMBLAKOHIDENFJGP, length 16. He gave the joint plaintext, 173 letters, and noted that his program had needed all 356 ciphertext letters to recover a length-16 key. The substitution square was not published. It is rebuilt here by aligning the untransposed bigrams of the two cryptograms with his plaintext, Norbert’s corrections applied: 24 of 36 cells, with the digits and the letters M, Q and Y unrecovered because the message never uses them. It is the fifteenth entry in keys.json and the repo’s notes call it the CHI key, after the header of the message it enciphered.

t: The ADFGVX residue of 1918 — twenty-two mutilated messages against known keys
b: Norbert stated his method in one sentence: add or remove up to five characters at two different positions, exhaustive search, an n-gram value function to rank the results. blocks.py does exactly that. For each of the fifteen keys, and each choice of up to two block edits of one to five letters, inserted or deleted at the five-letter group boundaries of the transcript, it decrypts and scores the result with a German quadgram model built from 3.6 million letters of Gutenberg German ( lm_de.py ). Windows that contain a digit or an unrecovered cell cost a floor; windows that cross an X separator cost less than junk and more than text. German prose scores about −3.3 nats per window on this model, and random letters about −7. Given no hint of the plaintext, the search re-derives pages 105, 109, 146 and 171, the “missing 10 letters” message of page 176, and the two CHI messages. On page 146 the five-letter block that Norbert inserted before group 10 comes out as (45, 5) . On the page-176 message the two five-letter blocks come out as (10, 5), (130, 5) . Page 100 falls to the same search with one two-letter insertion. The search also finds the Nov 22–24 partial of the unnumbered VGADA message. Where the printed transcription marks gaps, gaps.py restores them to their groups and anneals the residual single-letter losses; on page 132 it lands on Norbert’s text unprompted. The scores of the re-derived pages, from the run log, against the best any of the open messages achieves: page key length best score, nats per window decrypt as returned by the search 187 (CHI part 1) 16 −4.45 RUSSISCHETUNDPOLNHEERESVERKEHRVOLLERFASSENXWICHTIGESBESONDERS… 146 17 −5.25 FUNKSTELLEKERTSCHERHAE.TAB12X1.XRUFNAME.RICHARD.MILKARLX… AFAFF (CHI part 2) 16 −5.28 SOWEITFERNSCHREIBERVERBDGNITHTARBEICETXRESTSCHRIFTLICHXNACHCHEF… 100 19 −5.39 KEI.ESTOERFNGDURCHFEINDXMITTAGS2FEINDLXDIVXIMMARSCHAUFBELGRAD. 171 20 −5.50 INUKRAI.EUNDPOLEN.UBELKURSETARKSIEIGENDINFOLGEBRUCHEEZWISCHEN… 105 19 −6.02 GERMANIAATAPPEKONSTANTINOPELX6FUERMITTJLMEERDIVISIVNZUXTELXNRX62… 109 19 −6.02 OXFXMXABECDMELUNGXS4VCXUMBJRGABGLETZTEVTEILEBEEVUKTX1WEITEDE… best open message (158, 170) 20, 19 −6.89 noise The solved pages are recognisable German at a glance even where the block edit is not quite right, and the residual garbles are the single-letter losses that a second pass repairs. The 105 and 109 lines score lower than the others because the two-block search only approximates their mutilation; both texts are nevertheless readable in the raw output and both agree with Norbert’s 2017 readings.

t: The ADFGVX residue of 1918 — twenty-two mutilated messages against known keys
b: Two block edits, fifteen keys Every one of the ten was run against all fifteen keys with up to two block edits. The best result for each, from blocks_out.txt : page letters key length of best best score output 73 176 22 −7.12 DWR5C10WAXWBI.GWBXD1QGRA.R7OCW3Q… 152 104 22 −6.76 YPVXKTHJ7EM46PGPQ3RONDSEEUHXKTAX… 153 (both) 132, 93 20 −6.99 XWH2XBB3WATECOIFLUKTXMHK17SSY2ME… 158 240 20 −6.89 ZF2B0GEKJXII32RXRCO4LRS2DXA2RBDO… 170 106 19 −6.89 N5ADB08EKYND918UFEED92H3ELZEJ0UA… 176 (GGDAA) 220 22 −7.10 RGXCXXPPUN6RAXZK2YD8PMRX4NVX4ZYT… 189 84 22 −7.08 1AA1SLUOXO.VGXWUXUWH6LXXNHLV.9WW… 198 165 20 −6.97 LTDUUKWRA28KK61UITPUU31LEPXSIP42… 217 170 18 −7.04 YBEIEU84543EOTXT45R8K6XXGCSF4PWI… Nothing clears −6.7. The solved messages come out between −4.4 and −6.0 on the same run, and random letters at about −7.3. So none of the ten is one of the fifteen keys with two or fewer block mutilations, which is exactly the boundary the 2017 readers reached and stopped at. A digit-heavy output is the usual sign of a wrong key: real traffic here is mostly letters, and a wrong square scatters bigrams across the digit cells. The CHI key on the two page-153 messages In September 2017 Norbert suggested, without testing it, that the two page-153 messages might belong to the CHI key, since they are of the same period. Direct decryption with parity repair, and the block search, both return noise for both messages. Either a further unlisted key, or losses heavier than two blocks. A key-free attack, and why it fails If some of the open messages were enciphered under a key not in the corpus, the key would have to be recovered from the ciphertext alone. keyless.py tries: anneal the column order at each candidate length on the index of coincidence of the letter pairs the untransposition produces, since a correct untransposition pairs the bigrams of a monoalphabetic substitution, then solve the 36-symbol substitution with the German model. Before running it on the open messages it was run on a planted control: 224 letters of German enciphered under a length-19 key of the same design. candidate length 15 16 17 18 19 (true) 20 21 22 23 pair IC after annealing 0.055 0.048 0.060 0.053 0.064 0.058 0.066 0.063 0.073 The true length does not stand out: the peak at 19 is beaten by 21, 22 and 23, and the substitution stage does not converge at any length. The control is not recovered . Lasry’s own program, built for this purpose, needed 356 letters to recover a length-16 key. The ten open messages are 84 to 240 letters long. A key-free recovery is therefore out of reach at these lengths, with one exception: two or more open messages that share an unknown key could be solved jointly, as the two CHI messages were. Nothing in the ciphertext marks which those would be, and the two page-153 messages, the natural candidates, give nothing when tried together.

t: The ADFGVX residue of 1918 — twenty-two mutilated messages against known keys
h: Status, and what would change it
b: The residue is nine solved, three partly read, ten open, and the ten are open for a reason that is now measured rather than assumed. Three things would change it. what why it would matter The Childs originals Several of the ten carry explicit gap marks in the printed transcription and one is labelled “missing 10 letters”. The transcription Schmeh printed is a copy of a copy; the intercept sheets may hold the letters the search has to guess. A further key The CHI message proved the published list is not complete. A key recovered from any other source, or from a longer message in the same period that was never on this list, could be tested against all ten in seconds. A search past two edits Three block edits against fifteen keys is within reach of compute and is the natural next step; it was not run here because two edits was the standard that solved everything the 2017 readers solved, and the scores give no sign that any open message is close. Until one of those arrives, the useful products are the table above, the fifteen keys in machine-readable form with the three damaged squares repaired and the CHI square rebuilt, and a decoder that reproduces the 2017 solutions blind.

t: Adrian of Utrecht, the Admiral and the Constable to Charles V, 30 December 1521 — a printed decipherment checked and corrected
b: AGS Estado leg. 8 no. 150, catalogued as “cifrada prácticamente en su totalidad”, was deciphered by Claudio Pérez Gredilla and printed by Danvila in 1899. The ciphertext was transcribed from PARES and aligned with his text on the group xif = V. M. That rebuilds a nomenclator of three-letter code groups and homophonic signs, shows that the dead king he called “de Inglaterra” is Manuel I of Portugal, and reads or corrects about seventeen of the groups he left unread. About ten are still open. Vitoria → Charles V · nomenclator of code groups and signs · 30 December 1521 · resolved Adrian of Utrecht, the Admiral and the Constable of Castile to Charles V, Vitoria, 30 December 1521 from Adrian VI → to Charles V Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 8 no. 150 · two leaves, “cifrada prácticamente en su totalidad” · the last letter the three governors signed together, ten days before Adrian was elected pope Deciphered in the nineteenth century by Claudio Pérez Gredilla, keeper of Simancas, and printed by Manuel Danvila in 1899. Aligned here against the ciphertext: the key rebuilt, the dead king corrected from England to Portugal, and about seventeen of the groups Gredilla left unread now read or put right. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 18 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 resolved Summary. PARES describes Estado leg. 8 no. 150 as a letter of the governors of Castile to the Emperor, Vitoria, 30 December 1521, “cifrada prácticamente en su totalidad”, and gives no decipherment. There is one, and it is in print. Claudio Pérez Gredilla, head of the Simancas archive, deciphered the letter, and Manuel Danvila printed his text in the fifth volume of his Historia crítica y documentada de las Comunidades de Castilla (Memorial Histórico Español 38, 1899, pp. 703–705), with a note that some words had resisted him and were printed as they stand in the original. The reading here is his. What this project added was the ciphertext, transcribed from the PARES images and aligned with Gredilla’s text chunk by chunk, anchored on the group xif = V. M. The alignment rebuilds a mixed nomenclator of three-letter code groups and homophonic signs, and it shows one real error in the print. Gredilla has the governors mourning “el Rey de Inglaterra”. No King of England died in 1521. The rest of the letter is about Manuel I of Portugal, who died on 13 December: his widow is Charles’s sister, his heir is “este moço”, and his house has an old alliance with France. Of the roughly twenty-five groups Gredilla printed unread, about seventeen are now read or shown to be misprints, most of them because the same group is read or spelled out elsewhere in the same letter. Status: resolved. The letter was read in the 1880s or 1890s and is corrected here. About ten groups remain open; a sibling letter in the same code would settle them. Adrian’s own ciphers of 1520–21 were checked and are different codes.

t: Adrian of Utrecht, the Admiral and the Constable to Charles V, 30 December 1521 — a printed decipherment checked and corrected
b: In 1521 Castile was governed for the absent Charles V by three men: Adrian of Utrecht, cardinal of Tortosa and Charles’s old tutor, whom he had left as regent in 1520, and the two great nobles added to him during the revolt of the Comunidades, Fadrique Enríquez, Admiral of Castile, and Íñigo de Velasco, Constable of Castile. The letter is signed by all three: Adrian in French, Votre treshumble serviteur, el Cardenal dertusense , then the Admiral and the Constable. It is dated Vitoria, 30 December 1521. On 9 January 1522 the conclave in Rome elected Adrian pope; Danvila calls this the last letter the three governors signed together. It covers two sheets, of which three sides are cipher. Only the address and the first two and a half lines are in clear; after La una es the scribe goes into the code and stays there until the dateline, De bitoria a xxx de deziembre de D.xxj . Estado leg. 8 no. 150, f. 1r, head. The clear opening runs to La vna es , and the cipher begins in the same line. The next line, log g t Len top suz lan sur nam , is the place where Gredilla read “del Rey de Inglaterra de que avemos”. Image: Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 8 no. 150 f. 1r, via PARES.

t: Adrian of Utrecht, the Admiral and the Constable to Charles V, 30 December 1521 — a printed decipherment checked and corrected
b: PARES gave the date and the place. An OCR search of the Internet Archive scan of Memorial Histórico Español 38 ( memorialhistri38realuoft ) for that date at Vitoria found the letter on p. 703, under the heading Carta cifrada de los Gobernadores de Castilla al Emperador, fecha en Vitoria á 30 de Diciembre de 1521 . Danvila’s note (3) gives the credit: Esta traducción se debe á D. Claudio Pérez Gredilla, Jefe del Archivo general de Simancas, sin que á pesar de su especial competencia haya podido descifrar algunas palabras, que se trasladan tal como resultan en el original . Note (4) gives the reference as Arch. gen. de Sim., Estado, leg. 8.°, fol. 150 , the number stamped on the leaf. Neither PARES nor the lists of unread ciphers mention the edition. Danvila, Memorial Histórico Español 38 (1899), p. 703: the beginning of Gredilla’s text. Line 4 has del Rey de Inglaterra ; the unread groups fun , suf and ral are set in italics. Image: Memorial Histórico Español 38 (1899), p. 703, via the Internet Archive (memorialhistri38realuoft). Gredilla’s text is good. Measured against the cipher, it holds through the whole letter. What it leaves out falls into three kinds. There are about twenty-five code groups printed in italics as he found them ( fun , suf , ral , rip , pah xiu , top te , rol , xep , lag , fac , fap , fir , xin , dopca , nag , pij and others). There are a few groups dropped without a mark ( for twice; xac in “[xac] y franceses”). And there is one confident reading that is wrong, the King of England. A full transcription of his text from the page scans is adrian1521/gredilla_1880s.txt .

t: Adrian of Utrecht, the Admiral and the Constable to Charles V, 30 December 1521 — a printed decipherment checked and corrected
h: The cipher, and the key rebuilt by alignment
b: PARES serves these leaves at about 1,000 pixels on the long side and no larger, so the ciphertext was transcribed from upscaled line crops. The code groups, written in ordinary letters, read reliably. The signs of the spelling alphabet read less well, and several are still rough. The transcription was then cut into chunks at each xif , the group that stands for V. M. (vuestra Majestad): 19 in the cipher as transcribed, against 21 “V. M.” in Gredilla. Between anchors, cipher and Spanish were matched word by word. The alignment never has to force a reading, and every value below comes out of it. The system is a mixed nomenclator: Code groups of three letters, sometimes two, stand for words and also for syllables inside words. log is en both as a word and in s-en-tirá and fallecimi-en-to . lan is de in pier-de and de-udo . dop is ur- in urca . Inflection by suffix. A sign after a group changes the ending: mix la , mix= las ; fom cosa , fom= cosas . A homophonic alphabet of letters, figures and signs spells everything else: a = α, e4, Δ; c = a, 6, σ; d = q, z; e = ℓℓ; g = C; o = +; p = R, ff; r = nt, G; s = =; t = g, d; u/v = ≠T. These values are good enough to follow every spelled word against Gredilla’s text, but at this resolution the homophones are not all separated. The table is a reading aid, not a finished key. A triple-barred staff and the sign P4 open and close paragraphs. The code is one-part in blocks. The initial letter of a group follows the plaintext alphabet: r for words in a- (agora, al, alianza, amistad, antes, allá), f for c- (con, como, cosa, Consejo, contra), l/L for d – f (de, del, dicho, el, en, Francia, franceses), n and m for h – l , p for m – n (mar, mucha, negocios, no), s for o – r (otra, para, parece, por, que), t for r – t (Rey, razón, salvo, su, tiene), d for u- , x for v – y (V. M., voluntad, ya, yo). The order inside a block cannot be recovered from one letter. The block structure matters, because it limits which words an unread group can be. Group Reading Group Reading Group Reading xif V. M. sur que lan de Len del Loc el log en top Rey / Reina suz Portugal* te de fer con for como fom cosa som por sum para sem parece tup salvo dop ur- (urca) pex negocios rol / ral agora rum amistad lix / lux Francia / franceses xep ya tiz tiene roc al The full table, with the evidence for each value and its confidence, is in adrian1521/NOTES.md .

t: Adrian of Utrecht, the Admiral and the Constable to Charles V, 30 December 1521 — a printed decipherment checked and corrected
b: Gredilla’s first sentence of news reads la una es el fallecimiento del Rey de Inglaterra, de que avemos tenido la pena que es razón . Henry VIII was alive in December 1521 and lived until 1547. The letter itself says who died: the loss is felt by la Reina de Portugal y hermana de V. M. , that is Leonor of Austria, Charles’s sister, married to Manuel I in 1518 and widowed on 13 December 1521; the dead king was tan buen amigo y deudo de V. M. , and now there is este moço el Rey que sucede en aquel Reino : João III, nineteen, with people about him que no le dexan las orejas ociosas ; los Reyes de Portugal tienen [alianza] antigua con los de Francia , which the French will work on; Charles is asked to send someone to the new king para demostrarle el sentimiento que tiene del fallecimiento del Rey su padre , and to visit and console a la Reina . In the cipher, the dead king is Len top ( del Rey ) followed by one short group, which the notes read as suz . Gredilla left the same group unread at envié al dicho [suz] una persona , where the sense is the new King of Portugal. Inglaterra is spelled nowhere. On line 6, where Gredilla correctly reads la Reina de Portugal , Portugal is spelled out letter by letter after top , with the same signs (C = g , roc = al ) as the other spelled Portugal on line 16. The correction does not depend on reading that one group. Everything the letter says about the king fits Manuel and Portugal, and nothing fits England.

b: Most of the new readings come from the letter itself. A group Gredilla left blank in one place is often spelled out, or read by Gredilla himself, in another. The marks follow the notes: ** certain (the same group is read or spelled elsewhere in the letter), * probable (context, plus the initial-letter block the group must belong to), ? a guess. Gredilla (1899) Cipher Reading Evidence el fallecimiento del Rey de Inglaterra Len top suz del Rey de Portugal ** Section 04; Manuel I d. 13 Dec 1521 que está rol rol agora ** Gredilla reads the same group “ahora” in porque ahora no hay recaudo para xep detención xep para cuya detención** cu + xep is his own “cuya” in cuya copia ; xep = ya sus dopca= dopca= sus urcas ** dop = ur- in six occurrences of urca(s) (omitted, twice) for como ** así por lo que pierde… como porque nos parece ; porque como V. M. debe ya tener noticia los del fap Real fap los del Consejo Real** c-block; the fixed title Consejo Real , sitting at Burgos pah xiu pah xim mucha voluntad * “xiu” is a misprint for xim ; p-block and x-block tienenla antigua tiz rto rip tienen alianza * antigua rip recurs at el amor, deudo y [rip] ; a-block y ral con este moço ral agora * next to rol ; a-block top te que tiene top te a la Reina, de * que tiene top = Rey/Reina, te = de en lag= vienen; como quiera que lag= lag = ellas * d–f block; the hulks guerra fir él fir contra * c-block a su xin xin voluntad * x-block, haciendo guerra y paz a su voluntad por pij que pij manera * m–n block, por manera que ren nod sig sig procurar * o–r block; cf. para procurar de continuar en fun fun en coyuntura ? c-block, sense only en nag nag Italia ? h–l block, la guerra que se haze en [nag] los de fac fac Consejo ? c-block, beside fap Misprints in the 1899 edition , checked on the manuscript: “xiu” is xim ; “itb” is tib ; “xap” is xac ; and the numeral “40” after urcas [xub] is the code group yo , not a number. The letter itself counts three hulks: one at San Sebastián and las otras dos at Laredo. Gredilla also drops xac in [xac] y franceses son a unirse and prints si bien están neutrales where the cipher has si [xac] están neutrales .

t: Adrian of Utrecht, the Admiral and the Constable to Charles V, 30 December 1521 — a printed decipherment checked and corrected
b: Gredilla’s text, lightly normalised; bold a group now read or corrected, with its confidence mark; [brackets] still unread La una es el fallecimiento del Rey de Portugal **, de que avemos tenido la pena que es razón, para ello así por lo que pierde y sentirá la Reina de Portugal y hermana de V. M., como ** porque nos parece que el fallecimiento del dicho Rey ha acaecido en coyuntura ? que no [suf] a los negocios de V. M. … y agora * con este moço el Rey que sucede en aquel Reino, y con que diz que tiene cabe sí algunos que no le dexan las orejas ociosas, no sabemos la demostración que querrá hacer; porque como ** V. M. debe ya tener noticia, los Reyes de Portugal tienen alianza * antigua con los de Francia, y creemos que los franceses no estarán perezosos en solicitar por aquella vía lo que haze a su propósito. In English, the letter runs as follows. Since writing the general letter that goes with this one, a duplicate of one sent some days ago, two matters of substance have arisen. The King of Portugal. The governors grieve at his death, for the sake of the Queen, Charles’s sister, and because it comes at a bad moment for Charles’s affairs. With Manuel as friend and kinsman, that side was secure. Now there is a young king whose advisers do not leave his ears idle, and no one knows which way he will turn. The kings of Portugal have an old alliance with France, and the French will not be slow to use it. The governors are sending a prelate or a gentleman from Spain to visit and console the Queen. They ask Charles to do the same before the King of France takes the lead: to send a person of his household to the new king to show his sorrow at his father’s death, to ask that he succeed his father in the love, kinship and alliance between the two houses, and to promise that Charles will keep it up with great goodwill *. The same envoy should visit the Queen on Charles’s behalf. The hulks. Storms at sea have driven some urcas , the big northern cargo ships, onto the Spanish coast. One lies at San Sebastián, detained and well guarded. Two are at Laredo, and the governors are trying to hold them, but there is no force at hand to compel them. They mean to keep whatever they can seize, cargo and all, under sequestration until Charles decides. The difficulty is that the ships sail under a safe-conduct from Charles; a copy goes with this dispatch. The councillors present, and the Consejo ** Real at Burgos, hold that the safe-conduct rests only on the suspension of the marcas represalias , the letters of reprisal. Charles cannot have meant that, if [xac] were at war against * him, their hulks should go safely haciendo guerra y paz a su voluntad *. If [xac] join the French, the ships could be treated as good prize. If they stay neutral, they might be won over with [tib], or Charles might use the matter for reasons of state. In either case the French would take the hulks, by fair means or foul, for their fleet if the war between [Lag] and France goes on, and that fleet is said to be growing very large. The governors ask for orders. Postscript. After writing, they learned that the Laredo hulks had set sail, so Charles need decide only about the one at San Sebastián, which remains and will be kept under good guard until he gives other orders. F. 2r, foot: the postscript in cipher, the dateline in clear ( De bitoria a xxx de deziembre de D.xxj ), Adrian’s Votre treshumble serviteur, el Car[denal] dertusense and the signatures of the Admiral and the Constable. Image: Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 8 no. 150 f. 2r, via PARES. The full corrected text, with every change marked, is adrian1521/plaintext_corrected.txt .

t: Adrian of Utrecht, the Admiral and the Constable to Charles V, 30 December 1521 — a printed decipherment checked and corrected
b: Still unread (about ten groups): suf ( que no [suf] a los negocios ); xub and yo after urcas ; ren nod before procurar ; xac , a people ( que [xac] y franceses son a unirse , si [xac] están neutrales ); sif ; tib ; xit ; Lag , one of the belligerents with France; and ne ( la or mala fortuna ). The Scots fit xac in sense: Albany landed in Scotland with French backing in November 1521, and reprisals were a Scots–Flemish grievance. But the group sits in the x-block, which should hold words in v – z , so this is not offered as a reading. The group after Len top . In this hand r and z look much alike. The working transcription writes the group as sur , which is que , and the notes read it as suz . Que makes no sense in that place, and Gredilla printed a group suz where the new king is meant, so suz = Portugal is probable, not certain. The Portugal correction itself does not rest on this group (section 04). The spelling alphabet is good enough to follow every spelled word against Gredilla, but its homophones are not all separated at the 1,000-pixel resolution PARES serves. Several sign readings in the transcription are marked rough. The probable readings (*) come from sense plus the initial-letter block. They are not confirmed by a second occurrence, and the guesses (?) are only that. No shared key. Adrian’s own ciphered letters with decipherments were checked, in the hope that one of them would supply the key. None does. Estado 8/112 (28 July 1520) uses a sign-and-figure cipher. PTR 2/1/94, 99, 100 and 101 (October–December 1521) use Adrian’s dotted trigraph code ( leb. nud. sa. cab. ), in which V. M. , que , de and en have other groups. The joint letter is in a third code, probably the Admiral’s or the Constable’s. The Admiral’s 1521 cipher letters survive in clear copies (PTR 1/96/5, 9, 12, 13, 44, 45), but their originals were not found on PARES. A sibling in the same code, with its decipherment, is the way to close the open groups.

The catalogue listed eleven d’Affry letters of 1757–58 in the Dutch royal archives as unsolved, with DECODE’s note that the siblings’ solutions were “written on separate sheets”, not imaged. A tenth letter, R2067, had no transcription and was transcribed from the images. The eleventh, to Stainville in Vienna, is in another code and stays unread. Measured over all the letters, 86% of the groups read, so by this project’s read bar the set is read in part : R1071 is unread and R1072 reads about 78%. t: The comte d’Affry’s intercepted letters from The Hague, 1757–58 — the code rebuilt from Lyonet’s decipherments
b: Louis-Auguste d’Affry (1713–1793), a Swiss officer in French service, was Louis XV’s envoy and then ambassador at The Hague from 1755 to 1762. His despatches went by the Dutch post, and the stadholder’s cabinet had them opened, copied and given to Pierre Lyonet (1706–1789), the naturalist who was also the Republic’s cipher secretary. Karl de Leeuw’s history of the Dutch black chamber (2000) records that Lyonet broke d’Affry’s first code in June 1756 and then “two more French ones”. The decipherments were copied for the Princess Governess and the regents. One set is in the Nationaal Archief (Stadhouderlijke Secretarie, 1.01.50 inv. 221 and 223, “grouped by the cipher used”, not digitised). Robert Fruin excerpted it in the 1850s, and Bussemaker printed his excerpts in 1906, as Dutch summaries with some verbatim French sentences. Another set is inv. 192 of the Prins Willem V archive in the Koninklijk Huisarchief, catalogued on DECODE as nineteen records, R1052–R1076 and R2067. Each record is one letter: the intercept copy of the cipher, with the clear passages of d’Affry’s original written in. Seven are marked “solved by Dutch codebreakers, the solution written on separate sheets”, and eleven “unsolved”. The eleven are this target: DECODE Date, number To Groups R1072 6 Jan 1757, no. 123 Rouillé 556 R1076 7 Jan 1757, no. 124 Rouillé 403 R1073 25 Jan 1757, no. 133 Rouillé 312 R1064 1 Feb 1757, no. 136 Rouillé 1,249 R1065 3 Feb 1757, no. 137 Rouillé 1,082 (has a decipherment; see below) R1067 1 Apr 1757, no. 161 Rouillé 1,481 R1068 26 Apr 1757, no. 172 Rouillé 60 R1054 19 Jul 1757 “B.” (Bernis; DECODE reads Bonnac) 372 R1070 22 Jul 1757, no. 210 “B.” 400 R1071 4 Aug 1757, no. 485 Stainville (Choiseul), Vienna 760 R1074, R2067 17 Jan 1758, no. 283 “B.” / d’Usson 538 + two pages

h: The decipherments were in the images
b: A first pass read the DECODE note literally and treated the siblings’ solutions as lost. The attack started from cribs: Bussemaker’s verbatim sentence of 19 July placed “des précautions” (800 698) in R1054 by its repeat twelve words apart, and “le danger de la religion” turned up in the 22 July letter. That showed a word-and-syllable nomenclator, but cribs and a language-model solver got no further than a few dozen groups. The clear pages among the images then turned out to be something else. On R1066 (17 February) the clear page 5578, headed “N° 142 … D’A. à R.” with a clerk’s mark, begins with the same sentence as the intercept (“Mon courrier n’est arrivé que le 15 au soir”). It then goes on, where the intercept switches to figures, with “J’ai vu Mr de Slingerland chez moi ce matin”. It is Lyonet’s decipherment of the whole letter. The same mark heads clear copies in R1052, R1053, R1062, R1063, R1065, R1069 and R1075. Their openings fit their ciphers group for group: J’ai l’honneur de vous… = 865 1028 875 1018 569. R1066, page 5578: Lyonet’s copy of no. 142 (17 February 1757). Slingerland dictated to d’Affry the substance of Holdernesse’s letter to Yorke: Sa Majesté Britannique a évité la guerre autant que la prudence et les intérêts de sa part l’ont permis … Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 192, page 5578, via DECODE R1066. R1065, listed as unsolved, is one of them. Its cipher is cut into thirteen numbered paragraphs that alternate between two sets of pages, and its clear copy is on four others. DECODE had noted a clear letter “whose relation to the ciphered periods is unclear”.

t: The comte d’Affry’s intercepted letters from The Hague, 1757–58 — the code rebuilt from Lyonet’s decipherments
b: The clear copies were transcribed from the scans and aligned with their ciphers one group at a time, each group graded H (forced by the text on both sides or repeated) or M. The seven letters were R1052, R1053, R1062, R1063, R1065, R1066 and R1069, plus the ciphered parts of R1075, about 3,300 groups. The alignments were made letter by letter and cross-checked; a vote over all of them gives the key. It is a two-part code: the numbers are not in alphabetical order. It has about 1,200 groups for letters, syllables, words and names, with homophones for the common ones ( de 219, 1018, 1138; la 583, 382, 10; que 197, 194, 31). Some examples: 13 is a full stop, and 105, 107 and 797 are usually nulls. Leurs Hautes Puissances is 399 627 261. Le Roi de Prusse is 16, Hollande 294, Reischach 488, Sa Majesté 22, religion 578. The Jan–Feb and Apr–Jul letters differ in their habits (which homophones the clerk favoured) but not in the code. The DECODE transcriptions needed correcting on the way. Two copyists wrote 8 as a looped figure that the transcribers read as 0, so 056 is really 856 and 099 is 899. This affects R1064, R1067, R1072 and R1075. Elsewhere groups are run together (58291 = 582 91) or lines dropped or repeated.

t: The comte d’Affry’s intercepted letters from The Hague, 1757–58 — the code rebuilt from Lyonet’s decipherments
b: Each letter was read with the key, and the few groups missing from the key were inferred from context and recorded with their evidence. Inferred values are in braces in the working files. The full French readings are in the repository; extracts follow. 6 January 1757 (R1072, no. 123): the Italian The whole letter concerns “the Italian”, a spy who wants to be paid for earlier warnings of English designs on the French possessions in the two Indies. For a hundred louis and a pension he offers to leave at once for England and report on the English forces by land and sea, the secrets of the London cabinet, their intrigues in foreign courts, the plans for the 1757 campaign, and England’s correspondents in France. D’Affry thinks the money well spent if the man is sound. This is the weakest reading (about two thirds in sense), and Bussemaker has no entry for this date. The Italian reappears on 3 February, when d’Affry pays him the hundred louis and he leaves for Helvoet. 7 January 1757 (R1076, no. 124): convoys and herring A convoy the Dutch feared for had arrived: four ships were to escort it, and the storm kept two of them in port. D’Affry expects the navy to be enlarged sans augmentation dans les troupes de terre , and he expects the case to be pressed harder now that people see the English respect Dutch shipping only as far as it is protected. So every convoy through the Channel must be strongly escorted. In Amsterdam he talked with a regent about the herring. Bussemaker’s summary (no. 56): enlarge the navy without the army, protect trade, herring privileges for the republicans. 25 January 1757 (R1073, no. 133): a false rumour It was said that d’Affry had given the States-General a memorial calling any increase of the land forces a breach of neutrality. The rumour was quashed, but he went to see the Grand Pensionary. He told him the King neither wished to meddle nor ever had, but as a friend would regret seeing the Republic take on heavy expenses. Steyn answered that the increase would meet many difficulties. If its opponents could not stop it, he said, they could at least get a declaration made first to Versailles, Vienna and London. 1 February 1757 (R1064, no. 136): taxes and herring The States of Holland had adjourned until the 20th, when the augmentation comes up. The war funds were no larger than usual, and the means proposed (a sixth added to the house tax, a general rise in excises, interest on public funds cut to 2%) were so heavy that the augmentation looked unlikely. D’Affry then argues for a temporary favour to the Dutch herring fishery while France lacks sailors. It could be revoked when no longer deserved, and it would widen the quarrel between the Republic and England. He asks for it only if Holland blocks the augmentation. Then comes intelligence on suspects travelling through Antwerp, Breda and Liège. Bussemaker’s no. 59 gives the first part point by point and leaves out the agents, as Fruin said he did. 1 April 1757 (R1067, no. 161): the Gouvernante The Maastricht convoy crisis. D’Affry found the Pensionary “fort embarrassé”: ce qui se passe ici aujourd’hui n’est […] que pour le perdre . The same afternoon he read the King’s declaration to the Princess Governess: «… tu n’es pas ministre; faut-il que ce soit moi qui favorise les moyens de faire du mal à mon père?» Je lui ai répondu que S.A.R. savoit jusqu’à quel point le Roi mon maître a cherché à éviter la guerre … Je demande à S.A.R. d’employer non seulement ses bons offices, mais son crédit et son pouvoir pour déterminer une réponse prompte et telle que le Roi a droit de l’espérer. Coquelle quoted the Governess’s words in 1904 from the Paris original, with the day given as 5 April. The piece that Bussemaker’s no. 67 quotes about Wassenaer (“son fils cadet a actuellement un employ en Frise, dont la nomination dépend de Mme la Gouvernante”) is piece no. 7 of this letter. The numbered pieces do not follow in number order: they read in page order. 26 April 1757 (R1068, no. 172) Il a passé hier au soir un courrier de Vienne à Londres. Vous savez mieux que moi ce dont il est chargé. M. de Colloredo doit faire passer à M. d’Aremberg ce qu’on lui aura répondu. The DECODE note asked whether this note went unsolved because a different code was used. It did not: it is the same code as no. 171, which Lyonet deciphered. 19 July 1757 (R1054, to Bernis) Nobody knows the purpose of the Gouvernante’s journey to The Hague. If it is to push an augmentation of the land forces, d’Affry asks for orders at once: … il me paroit qu’il seroit essentiel aux intérêts du Roi de m’envoyer des ordres sur le champ [de demander] une confirmation de tout ce que les Etats-Généraux ont promis à Sa Majesté, et en même tems une déclaration de leur part qu’ils ne feront camper aucun corps sur leurs frontières. Je sens la dureté de cette proposition … The passage runs from group 145 to group 351, and Bussemaker’s French agrees with it word for word except in four places. The cipher has “M. le maréchal d’Estrées” where Fruin wrote “M. le Cte”. It has “de sa communication” for “de la communication du Royaume”. It spells out Leurs Hautes Puissances , and it has “des ordres” for “ordre de demander”. The page ends with an attack of gout. 22 July 1757 (R1070, no. 210, to Bernis): Ostend The Gouvernante is said to be going to the States of Holland to speak for her father George II, pointing to the danger to the Protestant religion. D’Affry doubts she will: if she proposes land troops, the other side will propose ships. Her party protested at the French occupation of Ostend and Nieuport. D’Affry notes that sensible people see the other side of it: with Ostend closed to the English, Amsterdam and Rotterdam will take over the trade England did with the Low Countries. Then Bussemaker’s sentence, group for group: Il y a quelques villes où quelques ministres hollandois ont prêché sur le danger de la religion, mais le peuple n’en paroit pas animé . If the Princess takes the Ostend affair as a pretext, he will ask her for an audience without waiting for orders. 17 January 1758 (R1074, no. 283, and R2067) The first part is an extract from a correspondent’s letter. A French loan of two millions had been tried in England by “des gens si maladroits” that the ministry heard of it and a new law followed. It could still be got round: four millions at four or four and a half per cent at most, given “un profond secret, une parfaite connoissance du pays”. D’Affry adds that a Sieur Mac[donald] of the Bulkeley regiment has passed through on his way from France to England, and he suspects him of carrying commissions for the enemy. Some Scots and Irish in French service are spies, he writes, but to act would throw suspicion on the rest. The companion letter of the same day to d’Usson (R2067) has no DECODE transcription. It was transcribed from the images and read at about 91%. It is d’Affry’s own letter of the same number, covering the extract. He thinks money operations in England useless: if found out, they would make France’s needs look greater than they are and put the English on their guard. Englishmen will still lend in France when the interest is right, and some already hold French life annuities. He adds that two or three Englishmen are at The Hague, one of them Mac…, and that two Spaniards from Paris, one a secretary of the Spanish embassy, are on their way to London.

t: Cardinal Alessandrino to the nuncio in Spain, 1568–69 — eleven papal ciphers read with Lasry’s polyphonic key
b: Eleven ciphers from Pius V’s nephew and secretary to the nuncio at Madrid, catalogued on DECODE as partially decrypted, with George Lasry’s reconstructed key attached but no plaintext. Every digit stands for two letters and zero is a null, so a beam search chose each letter under an Italian model. All eleven read end to end: a French bride for Philip II, the King’s ministers and Church jurisdiction, Bolognese exiles, and the Turk courted by the German Protestants. Rome → Madrid · polyphonic cipher, two letters to a digit · 1568–69 · read Cardinal Alessandrino to the nuncio in Spain, 1568–69 from Cardinal Alessandrino → to G. B. Castagna Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Spagna 6/I items 1–10 and 6/II item 13 · DECODE R93–R102, R115, eleven ciphertexts, fifteen pages · catalogued as partially decrypted George Lasry’s reconstructed key, applied with a decoder that picks one of each digit’s two letters · all eleven read end to end Daniel Bourdeau · read 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. Michele Bonelli, Cardinal Alessandrino, was the nephew of Pius V and ran his correspondence. His letters of 1568 to the nuncio at Madrid, Giovan Battista Castagna, sent their sensitive passages in figures. Ten of these ciphers (Spagna 6/I) and one of 1569 (6/II) are on DECODE, transcribed digit by digit, with a key George Lasry reconstructed in 2020 but no plaintext; the catalogue here listed them as open. The system is polyphonic: every digit from 1 to 9 stands for two letters (1 is u or t , 4 is a or l ), 0 is a null, and a small nomenclator is written in four-digit groups with zeros in second and fourth place. A digit therefore does not say which letter it is; the reader has to choose. A beam search that makes that choice under an Italian model of the period gives running Italian at once, on all eleven. What they say: an approach, through friends of the French crown, to marry Philip II to one of the French King’s daughters; the Pope’s complaints about the King’s ministers and ecclesiastical jurisdiction; the Bolognese exiles sheltered in the King’s lands; the Turk at Adrianople courted by the German Protestants; Cardinal Borromeo’s quarrel with the senate of Milan over the Corpus Domini procession. What stays open is a few dotted groups outside Lasry’s list, single-letter choices, and the comparison with the printed correspondence (Serrano 1914), which could not be reached from here.

h: A French bride for the King
b: The first cipher (f. 6r), set out from the decoder’s unspaced output with the words divided: … è ricercato qui da alcuni amorevoli della corona di Francia a fare officio … [che S. M.tà] contenti di ricevere una delle sue figliole per moglie … la pratica N. S. non ha voluto movere non sapendo l’animo di [S. M.tà] in quel particolare … scoprirà qui [V. S.] in quella maniera che le parerà più opportuna e conveniente, assicurandola che [N. S.] non è per farne parola mai se prima non sa [di S. M.tà] l’intentione sua espressa … “Some well-wishers of the crown of France have asked here that [the Pope] act … that His Majesty be content to take one of [the King of France’s] daughters to wife. Our Lord has not wished to move the matter without knowing His Majesty’s mind … you will discover it in whatever way seems best, assuring him that Our Lord will never speak of it before he knows his intention.” Elisabeth of Valois died on 3 October 1568; Philip’s eventual fourth wife was Anna of Austria, and the French candidate pressed at Rome was Marguerite of Valois. The fourth cipher (f. 81r) is still “waiting for the answer from Your Lordship on the particular of the marriage”, with the argument that the union of “quei tre principi principali della cristianità” would serve the Church. f. 6r, the first five lines of the first cipher: unbroken digits, each standing for one of two letters, with 0 as a null and four-figure nomenclator codes among them. They open the passage on a French bride for Philip II quoted above. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Spagna 6/I f. 6r, via DECODE R93.

t: Cardinal Alessandrino to the nuncio in Spain, 1568–69 — eleven papal ciphers read with Lasry’s polyphonic key
b: 6/I/1, f. 6r (R93). The French marriage proposal, above. 6/I/2, f. 42r (R94). Jurisdiction: the Pope “non intende di revocare i suoi privilegi … ma sibene di levare li abusi cresciuti” through the ministers’ fault; they have sought to widen the privileges “in detrimento di quella autorità” of the Holy See. 6/I/3, f. 55r (R95). Answer to the ministers’ claims; the crusade alms and indulgence; “che il Re si saria alienato da quella santa sede” must not be said; the Pope cares for the King’s soul above any human respect. 6/I/4, f. 81r (R96). The marriage again; a man prosecuted as a heretic; an order to be carried out for the Hermits of St Jerome. 6/I/5, ff. 88r–89v (R97), four pages. Exiles of the state of Bologna received in the King’s name, the Cavaliere Gualengo; the King, “feudatario” of the Holy See, bound by his investiture to return them; then the Turk: a French embassy “in Andrinopoli”, the Protestant princes promising the Sultan that once all is ruined they will be at one with him — “la povera cristianità”. 6/I/6, f. 136r (R98). The King’s orders about the clergy lose their effect while ministers wait for commissions. 6/I/7, f. 169r–v (R99). The religion of St John and its Grand Master; Don John of Austria; the senate of Milan, the archbishop’s vicar and the Corpus Domini procession; the Pope “pensa di procedere” with “armi spirituali”. 6/I/8 (R100). The King’s ministers’ proceedings in a Church matter; a brief to be executed. 6/I/9, f. 291r–v (R101). The St Peter’s-day dues of the Neapolitan fief and the investiture; a schism stirred by the ministers; “alla fine” the King’s subjects will be disobedient if he is disobedient to God’s vicar. 6/I/10, f. 306r (R102). A prelate who fails in his office in the kingdom; the Pope “le parerà convenire” to leave it to the King. 6/II/13, f. 641r (R115), 1569. Pensions to be transferred on a see; a commission; the Council.

t: Cardinal Alessandrino to the nuncio in Spain, 1568–69 — eleven papal ciphers read with Lasry’s polyphonic key

The decoder ( alessandrino1568/decrypt.py ) runs a beam search over the page, at each digit trying both letters, the null, and any nomenclator group that starts there, and scores the resulting Italian with the repository’s shared five-gram model (it-cinquecento, spaces removed). Every page decodes at about −1.75 nats a letter, the level of ordinary text for this model, and ends in a few letters of clerk’s padding.

t: The inscriptions of the Chymische Hochzeit , Strassburg 1616 — not a letter, and read by the novel itself
b: DECODE R4502, catalogued as an undeciphered letter of Johann Valentin Andreae, is a copy of the printed Chymische Hochzeit Christiani Rosencreutz in the Ritman Library. Its four “cipher pages” are the novel’s inscriptions. The two long ones are simple substitutions in an invented type-cut alphabet, and the page boy speaks both aloud a paragraph later; the 19-sign table was rebuilt here and decodes both. The two sign lines are the dates 1378 and 1459, as Foxcroft’s 1690 English edition already gave them. Printed novel, no correspondents · invented-alphabet substitution and symbolic dates · Strassburg 1616 · already read The Inscriptions of the Chymische Hochzeit Embassy of the Free Mind (Ritman Library), Amsterdam: Chymische Hochzeit: Christiani Rosencreutz. Anno 1459 , Strassburg, Lazarus Zetzner's heirs, 1616, pp. 73, 95, 97, 116 · DECODE R4502, catalogued as a non-decrypted letter of Andreae DECODE's four cipher pages are the printed inscriptions of the Rosicrucian novel. The novel reads its own two long inscriptions aloud a paragraph later, and English editions have printed all four in clear since 1690. The sign table was rebuilt here from the images. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 22 September 2026 already read Summary. Catalogue item 210 listed DECODE R4502 as a ciphered letter from Johann Valentin Andreae to an unknown recipient, 1616, "never deciphered" according to the record's note. The DECODE images show a printed book: the first edition of the Chymische Hochzeit Christiani Rosencreutz , the third Rosicrucian text, attributed to Andreae. Its four cipher pages are inscriptions that the narrator copies in the story. Two are simple substitutions in an invented alphabet cut as type. The page boy gives the text of both in the next paragraph: "here lies buried Venus, the fair lady who has brought so many high men to lose fortune, honour, blessing and welfare"; and "when the fruit of my tree has quite melted, I shall awake and be the mother of a king". The other two lines are strings of alchemical and numeral signs that stand for dates. The crcsite.org edition of Foxcroft's 1690 translation reads them as 1378 and 1459. The 19-sign alphabet was rebuilt here and decodes both German texts in full. The date lines fit the published years as wholes, but not every sign in them is identified.

As far as is known, this has never been deciphered." The owner adds that the library holds three copies and only one was photographed. When DECODE's catalogue was imported here, the rule scorer turned the record into a "letter to an unknown recipient". The images show the title page (Strassburg, "In Verlägung Lazari Zetzners S. Erben", 1616) and five openings, pp. 72–73, 94–95, 96–97, 98–99 and 116–117, and the colophon (Conrad Scher, 1616). t: The inscriptions of the Chymische Hochzeit , Strassburg 1616 — not a letter, and read by the novel itself
b: Both inscriptions use one simple substitution. There is one sign per letter, words are divided, and there are no nulls or code words. The 156 letters use 19 signs, with one capital form (the initial H). U and V share a sign. M, N and O are three dotted variants of one shape. The pairs are fixed by words the boy's glosses supply: B-E-G-R-A-B-E-N gives b, e, g, r, a, n; F-R-A-W gives f, w; G-L-U-C-K gives l, u, c, k; F-R-U-C-H-T gives h, t; and so on. Every sign that occurs has a value, and the table read over both texts gives no contradiction. The alphabet is the author's own: only 20 letters of German occur, and there is nothing to compare it with. Letter A B C D E F G H I K L M N O R S T U/V W Z Stand-in x d c 6 p J g h, H z k 8 m n o s b q v w Z The stand-ins are the Latin letters the signs most resemble. The full table with descriptions of the shapes is in andreae1616/key.tsv , and decode.py turns the transcription into the reading.

t: The inscriptions of the Chymische Hochzeit , Strassburg 1616 — not a letter, and read by the novel itself
b: P. 73: the line under the fountain inscription. The narrator calls it the easiest writing of all. Image: Embassy of the Free Mind (Ritman Library), Amsterdam, Chymische Hochzeit (Strassburg 1616), p. 73, via DECODE R4502. P. 116: the urn inscription, dated with a line of signs after Ao. Image: Embassy of the Free Mind (Ritman Library), Amsterdam, Chymische Hochzeit (Strassburg 1616), p. 116, via DECODE R4502. These two lines are not letter ciphers. They mix Roman numerals with alchemical and planetary signs, and they are dates. The English edition on crcsite.org, which follows Foxcroft's translation of 1690, gives 1378 for the fountain line (footnote 12) and 1459 for the urn (footnote 21). It also reads the ligature at the right end of the urn line as P.H.M.D., "Paracelsus Hohenheimensis Medicinae Doctor". 1378 is the birth year the Rosicrucian manifestos give Christian Rosencreutz. 1459 is the year on the title page. Checked against the signs: the urn line has four rings (CCCC), an IX and an M, which fit M CCCC L IX. The fountain line opens with a lemniscate carrying three dots, ∞ being an old sign for 1000, and it has XX and a V with dots, which fit M CCC LXX VIII. Both readings are graded C (probable): the structure agrees with the published years, but the signs for L and for the smaller units are not identified one by one, and each line is too short to fix them.

t: The inscriptions of the Chymische Hochzeit , Strassburg 1616 — not a letter, and read by the novel itself
b: The individual numeral signs of the two date lines (grade C as wholes). They are one-off symbolic dates of about ten signs each, too short to fix every value. The three dotted signs for M, N and O were separated with the plaintext in view: at DECODE's resolution, about 1,450 px per opening, the dots are too small to tell them apart blind. A better image would settle them. The other 16 signs are unambiguous and fix the text by themselves. The other two Ritman copies were not photographed. The 1616 edition was printed from standing type, so they should carry the same inscriptions. DECODE should list R4502 as decrypted: a printed book, not a letter, with a simple substitution plus two symbolic dates. The correction is queued.

t: The inscriptions of the Chymische Hochzeit , Strassburg 1616 — not a letter, and read by the novel itself

t: Queen Anne to the Earl of Peterborough, 22 February 1712 — ciphered instructions matched to the text printed in 1798
b: Signed instructions, clear English with 61 runs of a numerical code (414 groups), catalogued on DECODE as non-decrypted and described as for Peterborough’s embassy to Turin (R4878). The whole text is printed in Parke’s edition of Bolingbroke’s correspondence (1798), and every code run falls into place: 534 is to at all eight places, 894 him , 609 his , 1373 religion . What the cipher hides is a secret mission to stop the Electoral Prince of Saxony from turning Catholic in Rome, and if need be to spirit him away to a Protestant country. London → Turin · numerical code with nulls · 22 February 1711/12 · already in print Queen Anne to the Earl of Peterborough, 22 February 1712 from Queen Anne → to Earl of Peterborough British Library, Add MS 4107 ff. 184r–185r · three pages of signed instructions, clear English with 61 runs of code, 414 groups · DECODE R4878, “non-decrypted” · catalogue item 86 DECODE describes these as instructions for Peterborough’s embassy to Turin. The code hides something else: a secret errand to the heir of Saxony. The full text was printed in 1798, and it is matched here to the cipher, run by run. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 resolved Summary. The catalogue took up a ciphered letter of Queen Anne to Charles Mordaunt, Earl of Peterborough, dated 22 February 1711 on DECODE (R4878), with nothing known of its content. The images show signed instructions, Given at Our Court at St James’s on 22 February 1711/2, which is 1712 in the modern reckoning. The instructions are in clear English, and every sensitive phrase is in a numerical code: 61 runs, 414 groups. No key fits among the 155 transcribed British keys on DECODE. The whole text, though, is printed in the first volume of Gilbert Parke’s Letters and Correspondence of Bolingbroke (1798), pp. 310–311, from the office draft. All 61 runs fall into place in the print, and the groups that recur keep their meaning everywhere: 534 is to at all eight places, 678 the , 839 you , 894 him , 609 his , 1373 religion . Peterborough was to intercept the Electoral Prince of Saxony on his way to Rome, keep him Protestant, and, if he wanted to escape, help to “rescue him out of the hands he is in”. The code table itself is not rebuilt beyond about twenty values. Status: already in print; identified and checked here. Open: the code table.

t: Queen Anne to the Earl of Peterborough, 22 February 1712 — ciphered instructions matched to the text printed in 1798
b: Add MS 4107 keeps the instructions Peterborough actually received, signed by the Queen at the head and the foot. The heading is in clear: Instructions for Our Right Trusty and Right Welbeloved Cousin and Councillor Charles Earl of Peterborow and Monmouth. Given at Our Court at St James’s the Two and Twentieth day of February 1711/2 in the Tenth Year of Our Reign. The date is Old Style, so the year is 1712, and DECODE’s range 1711–1712 refers to this one letter. The clerk wrote the body in clear and put the words that mattered into numbers, separated by points: We taking into Our Serious Consideration the great 2011.381. that are 966.298.534.76.1387.650.1108.389. Our good 435.823.755. the 1584.705.94.2211. of 2089. In total there are 61 runs of 1 to 18 groups, 414 groups altogether, of which 242 are different, ranging from 76 to 2269. The clerk wrote 8 as a looped ơ. Two groups at the gutter of f. 184v have lost their last digit. The British Library images are not reproduced here. They can be seen on DECODE after logging in. f. 184r, the first five lines of the body, which Parke’s printed text reads We taking into our serious consideration the great [endeavours] that are [used to pervert] our good [cousin], the [Electoral Prince] of [Saxony], to the [superstitious worship] of the [church of Rome], and … Image: British Library, Add MS 4107 f. 184r, via DECODE R4878.

t: Queen Anne to the Earl of Peterborough, 22 February 1712 — ciphered instructions matched to the text printed in 1798
h: The printed text and the match
b: Parke printed Bolingbroke’s papers in 1798 from the Secretary’s office copies. In a note to a letter of St John to the Queen he adds “Lord Peterborough’s instructions was as follow”, followed by the whole text with the same heading, the same date and the same closing A. R. The clear passages of the manuscript read word for word as in the print, and each code run stands where the print has a phrase: Run Code Printed text 1 2011.381 endeavours 4–5 1584.705.94.2211 · 2089 Electoral Prince · Saxony 9 724.1604.678.1219.563.393.1893 dishonour the Protestant interest 17 839.534.678.523.412.303.1076.833.179 you to the said Prince whom 18 609.1415.705.564.1369 his arrival at Rome 43 385.97.894.1098 himself 44 422.474.373.900.609.507.1373 abjuring his religion 50–51 1799.900.894 · 465.355.385.466.615.755 rescuing him · hands he is in 55 886.354.839.1053.534.523.308.678.1285.500.1369.738 given you leave to see the city of Rome 60 720.425.295.335.534.2101 come back to Turin The alignment for all 61 runs is in alignment.tsv . It holds because the recurring groups mean the same thing wherever they occur. 534 is to at all eight of its places, and 678 the , 839 you , 894 him , 466 he , 609 his , 981 your , 1068 our , 783 on and 820 this are each constant across three to seven places. 1373 is religion in all three places, and 1219.563 is Protestant twice. The same syllable 422 begins both abandon and abjuring . Before the print was found, four of these values (894 him , 466 he , 894.1098 himself , 981 your ) had already been guessed from the clear words around them. The code pads the text heavily with nulls. There are 414 groups for 232 printed words, and a single word can take four or five groups: his is written 328.333.388.467 once, and him 326.332.349.467.2269. Some words have more than one group ( Prince is 1076 or 2211; Rome is 1369 or 519.488). The numbers do not follow the alphabet (466 he , 609 his , 894 him , 981 your ), so this is not one of the printed one-part forms kept in SP 106/7. Two single groups have no word in the print: 91 after church of Rome and , and 261 in affairs 261 bring him . They are either nulls or small differences between the draft and the fair copy.

t: Queen Anne to the Earl of Peterborough, 22 February 1712 — ciphered instructions matched to the text printed in 1798
b: The text below is as printed by Parke, with his spelling modernised. The words in bold are the ones in code in the manuscript. We taking into our serious consideration the great endeavours that are used to pervert our good cousin , the Electoral Prince of Saxony , to the superstitious worship of the church of Rome , and the infinite prejudice and dishonour the Protestant interest would suffer if so considerable a Prince , in whose country the reformation first began , should abandon the principles of our most holy religion , think it a duty incumbent on us to prevent , as far as in us lies , so fatal a blow . For that end, we have taken the resolution of sending you to the said Prince, whom you are to join, if possible, before his arrival at Rome , yet in such a manner that your falling-in with him may appear merely accidental : but whether you meet him on the road, or find him at Rome , you shall take a proper opportunity to deliver our letter to him, accompanying it with expressions of our friendship and real concern for his prosperity . You shall endeavour to insinuate yourself into his good opinion , and, as occasion offers, urge the strongest arguments you can for keeping him steady to the Protestant religion . If you find your representations make any impression upon his mind , you shall then open to him the subject of your commission , and declare that we have dispatched you to him on purpose to let him know that we have still the same earnest desire of seeing him which we have so often expressed ; and that if he persists in those good resolutions he formerly had , to adhere firmly to the religion in which he was educated, he may depend upon a friendly and honourable reception in our Court , in case his inclination or the situation of his affairs bring him this way . If, upon discourse with him , you shall discover that he apprehends himself under a necessity of abjuring his religion , to avoid the dangers and difficulties he will otherwise be exposed to, and that he has an inclination to make his escape , you may concert with him the proper measures for rescuing him out of the hands he is in , and bringing him safe to our dominions, or those of any other Protestant Prince or State . If you should happen to be arrived at Turin when these our instructions are delivered to you, you shall acquaint the Duke of Savoy that, in compliance with your request, we have given you leave to see the city of Rome ; for you are by all means to prevent any suspicion of the true intent of your going thither . The nature of this service in which we now employ you is such, that we can neither enjoin you to correspond with either of our Secretaries of State , nor limit the time of your return ; we therefore leave it entirely to your discretion and prudence to come back to Turin when you shall judge your attendance on the Prince of no further use . The Prince was Frederick Augustus, son of Augustus the Strong and later Augustus III of Poland. Parke’s note explains that, expecting to marry a Catholic archduchess, the Prince “was about to set off for Rome, to abjure the Protestant religion”. The clerk put into code everything that named the Prince, the religion, or the mission and its cover story. The courtesies and the instructions about conduct stayed in clear.

t: Armstrong to Madison — the coded postscript
b: Forty-nine groups of the 1,600-element “THE = 972” diplomatic code, read in full after reconstructing 580 groups from the State Department’s own pencil decodes on NARA microfilm M34 roll 13. United States · diplomatic code · 1808 · solved Armstrong's Coded Postscript to Madison from John Armstrong → to James Madison Bourbon-l'Archambault, 30 August 1808 · Library of Congress, James Madison Papers, Series 1, reel 10 · Founders Online, Madison/99-01-02-3466 Reconstruction of the “THE = 972” code from the State Department's own pencil decodes, and the reading of the postscript Daniel Bourdeau · solved 14 September 2026 · updated 21 September 2026 solved Summary. John Armstrong, United States Minister to France, ended a private letter to Secretary of State James Madison (Bourbon-l'Archambault, 30 August 1808) with a postscript of 49 numerical code groups. The letter is printed in Founders Online with the postscript undeciphered, and S. Tomokiyo's Unsolved Historical Ciphers lists it, with a partial reading of about a third of the groups obtained from one letter with known plaintext. The code — a 1,600-element word-and-syllable code that Armstrong used from 1804 to 1810, conventionally labelled by its group for "the", 972 — was never published. It is reconstructed here from a different source: the microfilmed State Department despatch books (NARA M34, roll 13), where a Department clerk pencilled the decode above every group of a long despatch of October 1806. Some 580 code groups are now known, enough to read the postscript in full and most of a second coded letter of 22 February 1808. The postscript reads: Russel ought to be the consul: he is an American by birth, and is much better qualified than any other candidate. In a word, he is above men in general. Next to him in fitness is O'Mealy, but he is, like Warden, an Irishman. Companion: John Quincy Adams’s St Petersburg despatches, said to be in this code, turn out to be in another, and Erving’s 1807 letter in Pinckney’s — two legation codes .

t: Armstrong to Madison — the coded postscript
b: The letter is a "private" one, written from the spa town of Bourbon-l'Archambault where Armstrong was taking the waters. Its clear text answers Madison's private letter of 20 July: it dismisses the complaints of Fulwar Skipwith (the departing commercial agent at Paris), warns that the embargo is "not felt" in France and "forgotten" in England, and says of David Bailie Warden, secretary of the legation and candidate for the Paris consulate, only that "a letter of the same character from me to the President … will give you my opinion of the fitness of M. Warden for the consular office at Paris: to this therefore I refer." The opinion Armstrong would not put in clear follows in code, as a postscript. The postscript, Library of Congress, Madison Papers reel 10, frame 0521 (detail). Groups are separated by points; the words and , much better , In a word , in general. Next to , but are in clear.
