t: Armstrong to Madison — the coded postscript
b: Armstrong's despatches from Paris between 1804 and 1810 use a single large code in which 972 = the . Ralph Weber's survey of American diplomatic codes notes some forty letters in it among the Despatches from United States Ministers to France (DUSMF, NARA Record Group 59, microcopy M34, rolls 13–14). It is not the code of Armstrong's letter of 20 February 1808, a distinct and still unsolved system. Its structure, as recovered: Groups run from 1 to about 1600. Each stands for a whole word ( Emperor 32, Spain 326, Minister 61), a syllable ( con 470, tion 352, ness 832), or a single letter ( s 1116, n 821, d 1001). Names are spelt out in syllables: Gu-sta-va-us , Et-ru-ria , Y-ru-jo , Dan-ish , O-mea-ly . The vocabulary is laid out in many short alphabetical runs , not one alphabetical sequence. For instance 1–130 is one run of words ( circumstance, commerce, communicate, character … Minister … these, thousand, toward … week, without, yesterday ), 130–417 a second ( America, between, business, confide, contrary, country … Prince, Queen, reason, report, Russia, second, secret … which, whom, word, would, your ), and above 417 the syllables come in blocks that restart the alphabet every few dozen numbers (1201 a … 1230 c ; 1268 ed … 1298 ex ; 1302 ide … 1348 broa ; 1405 be … 1443 good ; 1500s fa … man … now ). Within a run the order is alphabetical, which is what allows unknown groups to be pinned between known neighbours. Common elements have homophones: re is 555, 561, 562, 869, 871 and 1379; on is 945 and 946; an 1210 and 1216; ing 1478 and 1594. Armstrong writes a point after each group; the clerk who decoded despatches at the Department wrote the plaintext in pencil above each group and a short dash above groups that continue a word already written out ( Et |–|–, for Etruria ).

t: Armstrong to Madison — the coded postscript
b: 3.1 The known-plaintext letter of 4 May 1806 Tomokiyo had already exploited the one letter for which both the coded original and a clear copy survive — Armstrong to Madison, 4 May 1806 (Founders 99-01-02-0393), on the Spanish minister's discovery of the confidential Florida proposals — to assign about 230 groups, with a few marked doubtful. This gave a base of 68 firm values used here, among them the, of, to, is, he, a, and, by, in, s, n , and showed the alphabetical layout. 3.2 The Department's pencil decodes (M34 roll 13) The decisive source is the microfilm itself. NARA has digitised M34 roll 13 ("Nov 12 1804 – Dec 27 1807", catalogue ID 188671172; 393 frames). Frames 0192–0201 carry a long political despatch of October 1806 (written just after Lord Lauderdale's departure from Paris, with news of "two Russian armies now entering Silesia") whose every code group has the clerk's decode written above it. A scoring pass over the roll for faint mid-grey pixels away from ink located the annotated frames; the pairs were then read off by eye, frame by frame, and recorded with a confidence grade and their frame/line reference. M34 roll 13, frame 0200, right-hand page (p. 13 of the despatch). Ink: Armstrong's code groups; pencil above: the State Department's decode — "she wears is nearly transparent — the late meeting of the Hungarian Diet & a pleasure camp in October which is to assemble a great proportion of her army under the command of Prince Charles can deceive no body … Two Russian armies are now entering Silesia and a third is destined for Moldavia …". Image: U.S. National Archives, RG 59, microcopy M34 roll 13, frame 0200, via the National Archives Catalog. About 500 pairs were harvested this way, 352 of them read with confidence. Merged with the 4 May 1806 values the table stands at 580 distinct groups (§7). Ambiguities in the pencil (the roll is a 1940s microfilm of faint graphite) were resolved by requiring each reading to sit in its alphabetical slot and to recur consistently across frames. 3.3 Interpolation Twenty groups needed for the postscript and the February letter were not in either source. Each was inferred from context and then checked against its alphabetical slot; all twenty fit. Examples: 1394 between 1393 purp and 1395 Italy must open a new run — and it reads ru in three independent places ( ru-in , Et-ru-ria , Y-ru-jo ); 250 lies between 249 other and 252 own and reads ought ; 1273 between 1272 eight and 1279 Emp reads el ; 384 between 383 w and 385 was reads ward ; 1320 between 1319 li and 1325 long reads like ; 1483 between 1482 is and 1484 it reads ish . 3.4 A control text: the letter of 22 February 1808 Armstrong's private letter of 22 February 1808 (Founders 99-01-02-2733) contains about 150 code groups embedded in a clear political survey of Europe. It shares no groups of interest with the known-plaintext letter, so it serves as an independent check. With the merged table it reads, with gaps: The ruin of Gustavus is at last resolved. Russia is to seize Finland, while France & Denmark take possession of Sweden. Denmark cannot ha[ve] very willingly … independence. And it is certainly amongst the most cruel circumstances of the British attack on her Capital that it … her … of her … and [like]wise … of conduct, and thrown her completely into the arms of France, while the Danish Minister was this morning pouring out his complaints to me upon this subject, and stating the … of his government and the means taken by it to avert the introduction into Denmark of a general army … of Hamburg waited in the antichamber, with the intelligence that the Prince of Ponte Corvo had already entered Holstein … There is no one of even tolerable knowledge and sagacity who does not see this. Yet wonderful to tell Russia not only does not … but actually assists him in accomplishing one half of the object. Can Finland compensate for a state of things which shall put it in the power of France to lock up the Baltic …? The sentences that come out whole — the ru-in of Gu-sta-va-us is at last resolve-d , the Dan-ish Minister was this morning po-ur-ing out his com-plain-t-s to me upon this sub-ject , a-ve-rt the in-t-ro-duct-ion into Denmark , as-sist-s him in ac-com-pli-sh-ing one half of the object — confirm the table and fix the values ru , ish , Russia (305, which the pencil on frame 0200 also gives) used in the postscript. One group there is anomalous: 946 is on in the 4 May 1806 letter but must be Gu in Gustavus (914 = gu elsewhere) — a homophone, or a slip in the manuscript or the transcription.

Ru-s-el ought to be the consul: he is a-n America-n by bir-th , and is much better qua-li-fi(ed) than any other can-di-da-te . In a word he is above men in general. Next to him in fit-ness is O-mea-ly , but he is like Ward-en an Ir-ish-[man] . 4.1 The people Warden. David Bailie Warden (1772–1845), born in County Down, a United Irishman exiled in 1799, naturalised American, Armstrong's private secretary and then secretary of legation. He was the front-runner for the vacant Paris consulate and got it; Armstrong removed him in 1810, and when Madison reinstated him in 1811 Armstrong protested in a letter of 3 March 1811 that Warden was "without a single grain of attachment to the U.S." and asked whether "our own country furnish[es] no native citizen willing & able to fill the consulate at Paris". The postscript shows the same animus three years earlier, and its cause: Warden was not American-born. O'Mealy. Michael O'Mealy, a Baltimore merchant resident in France since 1793 and still there in 1810 (identified in the Papers of James Madison , Secretary of State Series 10:497 n. 2). The name — of obvious Irish origin — is spelt O-mea-ly . Russel. Spelt Ru-s-el . The most probable candidate is Jonathan Russell of Providence, Rhode Island (1771–1832), a merchant in the European trade whom Madison did in fact appoint chargé d'affaires at Paris when Armstrong left in 1810; the identification is inferential, since no other document places him in France in 1808.

t: Armstrong to Madison — the coded postscript
b: Collect the ciphertext. Founders Online transcriptions of Armstrong's coded letters (4 May 1806, 22 February 1808, September 1807, 30 August 1808) were gathered, and the LOC manuscript images of the 30 August letter retrieved for collation. Locate a Rosetta stone. The NARA catalogue entry for M34 roll 13 was downloaded (393 frames). A simple image score (the proportion of mid-grey pixels not adjacent to dark ink) was used as a triage aid while browsing the roll; the annotated frames 0190 and 0192–0201 were confirmed by eye. Rerun over all 393 frames on 16 September 2026 the score does not locate them on its own: grey blank leaves outscore the annotated pages, and only the first, densest page of the October despatch ranks high (third of 392) once the score is restricted to the interlinear band near ink. See armstrong/NOTES.md. Harvest. Each annotated frame was cropped into thirds, contrast-enhanced, and read group by group; every pair was recorded with frame/line and a confidence grade (H/M). Groups seen on several frames were cross-checked. Merge and rank. A script merges the 4 May 1806 values, the harvested pairs and the inferences, ranking readings H > C > M > inferred, and renders any coded passage with unknowns and doubtful values flagged. Infer and verify. Remaining gaps were filled by context and checked against the alphabetical slot; the 22 February 1808 letter served as the independent control. Collate the manuscript. The LOC image of the postscript was enlarged to check every group against the Founders text.

t: The Cipher Atlas
b: Each arc is one document from a target's profile.json , the record kept for every cipher on this site. It is placed at the city where the letter was written and the city it was sent to, as the notes state them. A court or a person is placed where they were at that date. Letters whose sender or recipient cannot be located from the evidence are left off rather than guessed. So are the cryptograms with no route at all, such as Voynich, Scorpion and the gold bars. The coastlines are modern (Natural Earth); the map draws no frontiers, because they moved too often over five centuries. Colour gives the outcome of the write-up: read , explained or found already read , read in part , attempted .

t: “Augurellio” is the cover: Jörg Weinmeister to the Dukes of Bavaria, spring 1533
b: DECODE R9407, catalogued as a ciphered letter of “Augurellio” with unknown content, is signed in cipher, twice: Iorg Weinmaister, a Bavarian agent in Hungary. The cipher is the volume’s System A′, its key carried over from a sibling’s contemporary gloss and extended; a second pass fetched the record’s overlooked sixth image (f. 235r), transcribed all four cipher pages again and read them line by line against the scans, 96.7% of the letter’s words. It dates from spring 1533: King John’s siege of László Móré in Palota with Hungarians, Turks and Bohemians, the diet of Pressburg, Török Bálint sent away from Vienna to come back sober, Simontornya taken after Easter, copies of the dukes’ letters in Minckwitz’s hands at Kraków, and fifty thousand Turks marching from Belgrade on Buda. a Bavarian agent in Hungary → the Dukes of Bavaria · homophonic signs and numerals, no word division · late April–May 1533 · read “Augurellio” is the cover: Jörg Weinmeister to the Dukes of Bavaria, spring 1533 to Wilhelm IV, Duke of Bavaria Bayerisches Hauptstaatsarchiv, Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591 ff. 232–235 · DECODE R9407, catalogued as Augurellio to …, Partially decrypted, content unknown · Unsolved Catalogue no. 164 The letter is signed in cipher, twice. The key of the volume’s System A′ was rebuilt and extended; a second pass fetched the record’s sixth image, which the first had taken to be missing, and read all four cipher pages line by line against the scans. The letter is a report from King John’s siege of Palota in the spring of 1533, not of 1535. Daniel Bourdeau · read 22 September 2026 read Summary. The Unsolved Catalogue carried DECODE R9407 as a ciphered letter of “Augurellio”, five pages, language unknown, with nothing known of what the cipher hides. The name is only the superscription on the address leaf; the letter is signed in cipher at the foot of two leaves, Iorg Weinmaister — Jörg (Georg) Weinmeister, a Bavarian agent in Hungary, writing to Dukes Wilhelm IV and Ludwig X through his brother, a doctor and Bavarian councillor in Munich. The cipher is the volume’s System A′, the homophonic sign-and-numeral cipher of R9408–R9413 and R9427; the key was carried over from R9410’s contemporary gloss and extended by machine and by reading rounds. A first pass on 22 September 2026 read the two full pages it had and dated the letter by its docket to December 1535. A second pass the same day found that the record has seven images, not six: image P6 is a straight photograph of f. 235r , thirty-six lines, which the first pass had seen only at an angle and read at 65%. Every cipher page was transcribed again, 4,363 signs, and checked line by line at the scans. Measured over the reading, 96.7% of the letter’s 1,003 words read ; what stays open is about thirty scattered words and two name signs. The contents date it: King John has László Móré besieged in Palota by a named commander and herr Caspar with four thousand Hungarians, Turks and Bohemians — the siege that Hieronymus Łaski opened on 14 April 1533 — and “they are still before it”. The letter also tells of the diet of Pressburg, Török Bálint drunk at Vienna, the taking of Simontornya after Easter, a Munich merchant’s factor in Vienna as a safer post than the Jew who let the dukes’ letters be copied at Kraków, and fifty thousand Turks marching from Belgrade on Buda.

t: “Augurellio” is the cover: Jörg Weinmeister to the Dukes of Bavaria, spring 1533
b: DECODE R9407 is described as “Augurellio to …”, five pages, Partially decrypted , alphabet with graphic signs and numerals, language unknown; its date, 1475/1625, is the span of the whole volume, Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591, the Bavarian ducal chancery’s collection of cipher keys with ciphertexts bound in among them. The record carries seven images. In the order the letter reads: P3, f. 233r — a full page of cipher, thirty-four lines, with a contemporary interlinear gloss over the first three lines and two clear Latin phrases inside the text. P5 — the second page, thirty-one lines, with a clear Latin sentence. P6, f. 235r — the third page, thirty-six lines, with one clear Latin phrase. The first pass took this image to be absent from the record; it is there, and it is the same leaf that image P4 shows at an angle beside the slip. P4, f. 234 — the slip ( Zettel ), eight lines written across the leaf, with the news from Belgrade, Datum ut in literis and the ciphered signature. P7 , the address leaf — two cipher lines of postscript, the signature again, and the superscription le[tte]re ad Mag[nifi]co domino Augurello that gave DECODE its title. P1–P2 , the outer address, in clear: Doctor Christof [W…], Bayrisch rhat, meinem freundlichen lieben bruder , with the docket 10. Decembris 33 and München . The images are not in the public domain, so no crop of them is reproduced here.

t: “Augurellio” is the cover: Jörg Weinmeister to the Dukes of Bavaria, spring 1533
b: “Augurellio” is a name on the packet. The writer names himself inside, in cipher, at the foot of the slip and again at the foot of the address leaf, with the same fifteen signs both times: ʏ m ↓ I π ω ʏ □ 7 ϝ ʏ ʏx ÿ σ γ = I o r g W e i n m a i s t e r A faint later gloss over the second reads “… weinmeister”. The outer address sends the packet to the writer’s brother, a doctor and Bavarian councillor, for the dukes. The volume has a key made out for Augurelio — R9369, f. 172, Dno Aurelio Augurelio — and that key is not this letter’s: in it ω stands for l, here for e. The date. The first pass dated the letter from its docket, read X Decembris 35 . The figures are small and cursive, and on the second pass they read 33 ; the contents settle it. The letter reports King John’s army besieging László Móré in Palota with Hungarians, Turks and Bohemians, and says the besiegers are still before the castle. That is the siege Hieronymus Łaski opened on 14 April 1533 with Hassan Bey’s Turks and fifty Bohemian miners, and which ended when the walls were mined at the end of May, Ferdinand standing aside by agreement with his rival. The letter also mentions a castle taken the day after Easter (13 April 1533) and Ferdinand’s new peace with the Turk. It was written between late April and May 1533; the docket is a filing date, and the slip’s Datum ut in literis refers to the covering letters.

t: “Augurellio” is the cover: Jörg Weinmeister to the Dukes of Bavaria, spring 1533
b: System A′ is a homophonic cipher of invented signs, Greek-looking letters and numerals, written without word division. Letters have one to three signs each, and several signs carry two values in this hand: letters: ω e, □ n, 4 e, ч i, ʏx s, ÿ t, 3 u, x̸ u, ↓ r, γ r, 8 n, 5 a, φ a, δ l, ӏ h, I g, 7 m, 9 o, Δ f, 6 d, ⊔ c, ⊹ k, ⊕ t, Ψ ll, ⍴ rr; two-valued: ∃ d/ch, π w/b/o, o b/w, ‡‡ g/u, ʒ s/ch; ligatures: ʒo = h, ꝏ° = sp (so Caspar is c–a–[sp]–a–r); word signs: the hourglass ⧖ = “F.G.” , fürstliche Gnaden , the same sign as in the sibling key R9427, and distinct from the slashed x̸ that is u; the dotted ·ʃ· = King Ferdinand , fixed by seins herren [ʃ] … das er [ʃ] mit dem turcken ein frid gemacht ; and ∇ , the name of the man besieging Palota with herr Caspar, probably Łaski. clear figures: two numerals stand in the cipher as numerals, mit 4000 zu fuess und ross and hundert tausent und 34 tausent gulden .

t: “Augurellio” is the cover: Jörg Weinmeister to the Dukes of Bavaria, spring 1533
b: The contemporary gloss over the first lines of f. 233 reads Genedig fursten und herren … Caspar … das leger , and that is how the letter opens. The full reading, line by line, with unread words marked, is in the repository ( augurelio1535/pass2/reading.txt ). Below, the German of the main passages and what they say. f. 233r: the siege of Palota Genedig fursten und herren, … ich zu herrn Caspar in das leger fur den Palota hab geschickt … Rerum novarum autem quod hic habemus … sol ich euer F.G. wie hernach volgt verstendigen, das er durch den [∇] und herr Casparn mit 4000 zu fuess und ross, ungern, turcken und Behamen, mechtigen ungern, … het in ainem festen schloss Palota genent belegern lassen, der lange zeit grosse merderei hat getriben, und von baidern auf dem tag zu Bresburg ist ausgeschlossen, also das ieder kunig, welcher zuvor kombt, straffen mag … umb hundert tausent und 34 tausent gulden geschetzt hat; und wiewol erstlich gedachts schloss nit nach herr Casparn rat vergeblich beschossen ist worden, iedoch hofft er es mit graben und maurwerch auszerichten. Herr Caspar has been sent into the camp before Palota. King John has had the strong castle of Palota besieged by [∇] and herr Caspar with four thousand foot and horse, Hungarians, Turks and Bohemians: its holder has long carried on great murder and robbery, and at the diet of Pressburg both kings left him out of the settlement, so that whichever king comes first may punish him. The castle was valued at 134,000 gulden. It was first bombarded to no effect, against herr Caspar’s advice; now he hopes to take it by digging and undermining. The Latin Et propter illum hominem plures introduces those who have tried to get the castle relieved: this has not been permitted by [ʃ], Ferdinand, who thinks he has a peace with the Turk. So a Hungarian, Török Bálint , who one evening went drinking with [ʃ] at Vienna, was dispatched about the relief with the answer that he should come back and speak of such things in the morning, wan er nuechter sei , when he is sober. The Hungarians of his party took it as a great insult, and so the bishop of Veszprém was sent to [ʃ] with the message that everything done at Pressburg, at Constantinople and elsewhere had been done without their knowledge; they could not tell whether they had been given away or sold. P5: the truce, Katzianer, Simontornya, the post Their lord has always fed them with many words, which misled them more than it helped; now he must tell them where they stand. Before he left, [one of them] wrote to Katzianer ( Cacianer ) to ask what to expect of the truce and whether it would be extended. Katzianer answered that he had consulted his lord’s council and was to tell him, on behalf of his lord [ʃ], that [ʃ] mit dem turcken ein frid gemacht and would keep to it; he and his lord should keep the peace too and von der belegerung des More Lesl[o] abziechen — raise the siege of László Móré — or something would be undertaken against them and the castle relieved. Regardless of this threatening letter, [∇] and herr Caspar marched on the castle with many men and are still before it; they also took another castle, with much booty, the day after Easter, man heist s Simontornia, ist ser fest — Simontornya . Illud tamen summum maximum esse existimo, das euer F.G. Hansen Schetinger, burger und kaufman zu Munchen, handlen und genedigklich zusprechen, das er zu Wien seinem factor, wan er doselbs grossen handel fuert, bevelch gebe, das er alle brief, so ime von herr Caspar oder von der […] zukomen, on allen verzug euer F.G. alweg zuschicke … The main request: the dukes should have Hans Schetinger, burgher and merchant of Munich, tell his factor at Vienna, where he does a large trade, to forward at once every letter from herr Caspar; he could do it secretly. If the dukes dealt with Schetinger in this way, they would not need to use den iuden any further, dan im nit zu vertrauen ist . f. 235r: the Jew, Minckwitz, herr Caspar, the Chancellor The reason: the Jew let the letters be copied at Kraków before he delivered them, as he admitted to the writer himself, and as the dukes will learn from him. A secretary told the writer that he had seen at Kraków copies of the dukes’ letters in the hands of Minckwitz , and that they are common knowledge there. Minckwitz, the Saxon feuder, is at feud with [∇] and they have written each other letters of defiance; he has no other refuge, and no one knows what he might do with such copies: wil das als euern F.G. [un]gehorsamer undertenigkait aus schuldiger pflicht haben angezaigt, damit kain ander der hendlung wissend vertacht werde. After the Latin Quid autem actum sit : the writer has dealt with [a man whose name is not read], told him of the dukes’ good will and offer, and he thanked them warmly and is glad to serve them; he has been told to treat with the Turk on their behalf, so that if [ʃ] makes peace with the Turk, [ʃ] should have peace with all his allies too, though without naming anyone, which he is willing to do. Herr Caspar bit in aller gehorsamer undertenigkait, euer F.G. wellen ine und seine kind genedigklich bedencken : herr Caspar asks the dukes to remember him and his children. All letters should go through Schetinger. The writer encloses a copy of a letter that [ʃ]’s councillor, now in Turkey, wrote to the regents at Vienna. As far as he understands, the Chancellor is also going to Constantinople, and he will report what is negotiated there, and keep a careful watch on the news. The slip on f. 234, and the postscript [Wiss]en: heut dato ist ein Ratz komen mit briefen, der sagt, wie zu Kriechischen Weissenburg funfczig tausent turcken sind ausgezogen hieher auf Ofen zu … doch nit was fur ein frid ist, wie dan euer F.G. aus [dem] schreiben zu vernemen haben, ist zu besorgen; auch wie mir er selbs het gesagt, der [ʃ] werde mer krieg dan frid haben. Datum ut in literis. Jirg Weinmaister. Today a Rascian (a Serb) came with letters and says that fifty thousand Turks have marched out of Belgrade towards Buda ; what kind of peace this is, the dukes can judge from the letters; it is to be feared, as the man himself said, that Ferdinand will have more war than peace. The slip is dated “as in the letters”, which is also what the faint later gloss over the line says. The postscript on the address leaf commends the writer to the dukes as his most gracious lords and is signed again.

t: “Augurellio” is the cover: Jörg Weinmeister to the Dukes of Bavaria, spring 1533
b: The key of R9369, the one addressed to Augurelio, was tried first and rejected against the gloss. The letter’s system was recognised from the gloss pairs as System A′, and the key a contemporary hand had glossed over R9410 was carried across by the shapes of the signs, which gave running German at once. First pass. An EM-learned emission table over a letter-trigram model, a Viterbi decoder over per-sign candidate values and a word-aware beam with word frequencies from the Deutsches Textarchiv; reading rounds, each aligned back to the signs to re-estimate the key; about forty transcription corrections on the two main pages. Result: f. 233 and the P5 page at about 96%, the angled column 65%. Second pass. The record’s image list was taken from DECODE and P6 fetched. All pages were transcribed again, one character per sign; a homophonic annealer against the sixteenth-century German model, seeded with System A′ and pinned by the gloss, gave German on every page. A beam decoder that lets the two-valued signs choose by context then decoded each line, and every line was compared with its crop. That separated the hourglass F.G. from the slashed u, found the clear numerals, the ligature mγ , the name signs, and several dozen single misreadings. History. Hungarian accounts of the 1533 siege of Palota (Łaski, Hassan Bey, the Czech miners, Móré) confirmed the reading of More Lesl[o] and Behamen and fixed the date. The measurement is a word count over the reading: a word counts as read only when its sense is not in doubt. 1,003 words, 33 unread (30 words and three occurrences of ∇): 96.7% .

t: “Augurellio” is the cover: Jörg Weinmeister to the Dukes of Bavaria, spring 1533
b: About thirty scattered words , at most two or three on a line, whose signs are legible but give no word under the values the letter uses: among them the opening words of f. 233r line 1, a word before “turcken” (l. 5), the man before “zum [ʃ] geschickt” (l. 31), and a few words at the end of P5 (ll. 27–28). Every one was retried with the extended key and at the image. ∇ , the name sign of the man who besieges Palota with herr Caspar (four occurrences): probably Hieronymus Łaski, who led the siege (grade C). Herr Caspar himself is not identified. One name at the head of f. 235r l. 16, the man the writer dealt with on the dukes’ behalf. Grades: the passages quoted above are C (key and context agree), except Ratz on the slip and Hansen Schetinger (spelt Schotinger later), which are M ; the surname of the doctor on the outer address is not read.

t: “Augurellio” is the cover: Jörg Weinmeister to the Dukes of Bavaria, spring 1533
b: Bayerisches Hauptstaatsarchiv, Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591, ff. 232–235 — DECODE record R9407 , images P1–P7 (by login; not in the public domain, published only by permission of the archive). The sibling letters and keys of the same volume: R9408, R9409, R9410, R9413, R9427 (System A′, with the contemporary gloss that carries the key), R9369 (the key made out for Aurelio Augurelio, f. 172), R9423 (the register of 1530s keys). See the KAA 4591 write-up. The siege of Palota, 1533: “Palota ostroma (1533)”, Hungarian Wikipedia ; Rubicon, “1533. április 14.” . Language model: lang/de-1500s , built here from Deutsches Textarchiv prints of 1472–1609. No printed edition was found; the humanist Giovanni Aurelio Augurello, who died in 1524, is a different man. Transcriptions, readings, the rebuilt key and the decoders are in augurelio1535/ (first pass in work/ , second pass in pass2/ ).

t: Diego López de Ayala to Cardinal Cisneros, 30 August 1516 — a “Non-decrypted” letter read with a sibling key
b: DECODE R9954 is five pages of invented signs from Cisneros’s agent at the court of King Charles, catalogued as Non-decrypted. Tomokiyo’s key for Ayala’s letter of 12 July (R10024) reads it unchanged. Read here before the 1875 edition was found, and checked against it: the sale of vacant Castilian offices around Chièvres, Queen Germaine’s dealings with France, the peace of Noyon to be proclaimed, and the King’s departure for Spain fixed on 30 August. Brussels → Cardinal Cisneros · substitution of invented signs · 30 August 1516 · printed 1875; re-read Diego López de Ayala to Cardinal Cisneros, 30 August 1516 to Cardinal Cisneros Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 496 fol. 22 · DECODE R9954, catalogued as Non-decrypted, unknown cipher Cisneros’s agent at the court of the young King Charles writes to the regent of Castile on the day the King’s council fixed his departure for Spain. A key published by Satoshi Tomokiyo for a sibling letter reads it. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 21 September 2026 resolved Summary. The Unsolved Catalogue carried DECODE R9954 as a ciphered letter of Diego López de Ayala to Cardinal Cisneros, Brussels, 30 August 1516, with nothing known of its content. The record has eight images: a clear first page, five pages of invented signs (AGS 0002–0006), a blank and the address leaf. There is no decipherment on the record and none was found in print. Tomokiyo (cryptiana) notes that the cipher is the one of Ayala’s letter of 12 July to the “Cardenal Gobernador” (R10024), which was deciphered in the nineteenth century, and publishes the key he rebuilt from it. That key reads R9954 unchanged: the first cipher line gives cerca delos oficios que estan vacos en estos reynos . After three passes over the images the whole cipher was read but for seven words ( ayala1516/reading.txt ). Only then did the endorsement lead to the 1875 edition, which prints the Simancas decipherment of 1849: it settles the seven words, corrects about half a dozen more, and otherwise agrees. Status: already solved (printed 1875); re-read independently.

t: Diego López de Ayala to Cardinal Cisneros, 30 August 1516 — a “Non-decrypted” letter read with a sibling key
b: AGS 0001 (DECODE image 1) is Ayala’s clear opening page. The cipher runs over AGS 0002–0006, which DECODE shows in the order 8, 2, 3, 6, 4. AGS 0008 is the address leaf, endorsed 1516 and Cardenal de España . The cipher is a simple substitution of invented signs for Spanish letters. It has a few variants ( a written 9 or 6, o with or without a stroke above), a dotted sign for que and a dotted H for Xebres (Chièvres). Words are separated by small spaces or dots. The key is Tomokiyo’s, transcribed in ayala1516/KEY.md . Three signs are not in it: an arch-shaped sign (perhaps cl ), a tall I (an s variant) and Φ (= m on AGS 0004). AGS Estado leg. 496 fol. 22, image 0002: cerca delos oficios que estan vacos en estos reynos / y los inconvinientes que ay de proverse… Image: Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 496 fol. 22, image 0002, via DECODE R9954.

t: Diego López de Ayala to Cardinal Cisneros, 30 August 1516 — a “Non-decrypted” letter read with a sibling key
b: Spanish as read, with doubtful words marked [?]. The full line-by-line reading is in ayala1516/plain_0002_0003.txt and plain_0004_0006.txt . Offices (AGS 0002) cerca de los oficios que estan vacos en estos reynos y los inconvinientes que ay de proverse a personas que los venden a don Xebres … dizen que V. S. los provee todos … por tanto que haga V. S. tan bien alla lo que aconseja, cierto que verian que alla no se proveyese en ninguno, y asi lo escrive Su Alteza. Los oficios que Su Alteza a dado y prometido … al marques de Villena un regimiento de Toledo que era de Baeza, a Rodrigo Niño otro de Plasencia … el regimiento de Cuenca diz que tiene Su Alteza para Vasco de Acuña, hermano de Pedro de Acuña … crea V. S. que quanto esta vaco esta pedido y prometido para alla o hecha la provision. The King has many servants here who have served him; Cisneros should give them offices, since it is said here that he fills most of them with his own men. The Genoese are referred to him over the Cartagena galleys: provea V. S. alla como vere conviene a servicio del rey; no se altere por carta ni cedula que alla vea, que aca muchas cosas se proveen por ymportunidades. Castile and Queen Germaine (AGS 0003–0004) The King was glad of the pacification of the kingdoms and that the Constable and the Infantado stood with Cisneros. Ayala warned His Highness that Queen Germaine trae tratos con franceses , and a marriage with the house of the Duke of Alba is in hand. On AGS 0004: don García de Padilla, the cedula for the Orders, and que obedezcan primero y se castigue , for if disobedience goes unpunished it will spread through the kingdom; the people of Arévalo, and mil males del reyno . The peace and the voyage (AGS 0005) la paz se concluyo entre el rey nuestro señor y el rey de Francia, como por los capitulos della vera V. S., que aqui le enbio; manda Su Alteza que luego la haga V. S. pregonar … De la yda hago saber a V. S. que el rey … sabado treynta de agosto, y en el se acordo de partir sin falta … y se partira para Gelanda … todo estara a punto, y dandole Dios [tiempo] enbarcara, y para esto no tiene estorvo ninguno sino el tiempo. The peace is Noyon (13 August 1516). The secretary Barroso arrived six days earlier; Ayala spoke to the King before him and gave him his credence, and Cisneros’s protests have done much good. Orders and Toledo (AGS 0006) pienso que esta llevara lo de las ordenes, y no es posible; yo pido una cedula para que V. S. pueda poner presidentes cuales le pareciere que conviniente … en lo del corregidor de Toledo … V. S. provea de corregidor, que al rey le plazera. The rest of AGS 0003 and 0004 (second pass) AGS 0003 goes on to a man at court who writes mil mentiras : …ho credito a sus avisos, y yo no se por que a ese le quiso dar V. S. tanta autoridad, aviendo sido avisado de cuan mal todos estavan con el en lo de las ordenes de Calatrava y Santiago y Alcantara; por eso se enbio a V. S. el poder para que lo remedie . On AGS 0004 the Comendador mayor of Calatrava protested against Cisneros’s power; Malaga nos a puesto en mucha confusion with a commission bearing two hundred signatures; teniamos lo por acabado . The marriage is con el duque d’Alva , and some there write que V. S. dize mal de Xebres . The end of the letter (AGS 0005–0006) The King junto consejo on the Saturday; by 15 September he will be at Antwerp. Ayala gave the King his credence y requerile que por negocio ninguno cesase su partida . On AGS 0006: y respondeme a esto que pues el rey va que alla se hara, y si la yda cesare que la daran ; he has named for the posts don Alonso Tellez and a don Pedro; he gave Cisneros’s credence a solas , and was told that el y el chanciller son una persona (Chièvres and Chancellor Le Sauvage). The letter closes on the friendship to be made entre V. S. y el que la desea , y con esta amistad se hara mucho servicio a Dios y al rey . There is no signature in cipher. Third pass New on the third pass: Malága’s courier came con cinco mil y tantas firmas ; Ayala always insisted que obedezcan primero y se castigue su inobedencia, porque si no se castiga sera dar enxenplo de inobediencia a cuantos lugares ay en el reyno . From Cisneros’s own household it is written que v. s. dize mal de Xebres y que se arma contra el, y que ay en casa de v. s. se dize que el rey es inabil, y que yo e escrito mil males del reyno . At Antwerp the King will take leave of the Estates y hara la orden de la Tusion (the Golden Fleece) before Zeeland. The two nominees are don Alonso Tellez y don Pedro su sobrino ; the corregidor of Toledo is to be named at once y como sea hecho quitar se a de ynportunidades .

t: Diego López de Ayala to Cardinal Cisneros, 30 August 1516 — a “Non-decrypted” letter read with a sibling key
b: The address leaf carries, upside down, the note Copiado lo descifrado para D. … García. Simancas 14 de Ag[osto] de 1849 and a second Copiado lo descifrado p[ar]a los Sres. … . The copy went into Pascual de Gayangos and Vicente de la Fuente, Cartas de los secretarios del cardenal D. Fr. Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros durante su regencia (Madrid 1875). The edition splits the letter in two. Carta XLIX (pp. 213–219) has the clear opening and the cipher on offices, Málaga and Arévalo, and is cited as Estado 496 fol. 318. Carta LIV (pp. 238–241) runs from the peace to the end, is cited as fol. 22, and is misdated 1517. The reading here was finished before the edition was found. Checked against it: The seven open words: sábese ; the code sign after gente del is emperador ; condestable, infantadgo, Benavente ; era engañado ; diziendo en quanta perdición están ; yo ; and the dotted sign is Xebres: Mos de Xebrés oyó la creencia . Corrections to the reading here: el de Lanuça (read nu[n]ca ), solo por tocar a v. s. , después de oyda , con fe que me dio , con juramento lo comunicásemos . Everything else agrees, apart from the editors’ spelling.

t: Guidi di Bagno to the Secretariat, 5 January 1652 — the suggested key excluded
b: The reconstructed key used for the 1632 Barberini–Ceva letters in Francia 346 is a mixed-width homophonic and syllabic nomenclator. Its decisive convention is simple: the one-digit figure 6 separates groups and does not occur inside any code. Here, pairs and triples of sixes occur throughout the manuscript. Splitting at every six creates empty separators, orphan digits and groups absent from the table. A checked line passed through the Francia 346 decoder gives malformed groups and no Italian. This rules out that particular table independently of OCR quality or language-model scoring. It does not identify the actual 1652 system.

t: The marqués de los Balbases to Fuenmayor, 1677–78 — a Nijmegen plenipotentiary’s cipher rebuilt and four undeciphered letters read
b: Fourteen ciphered letters from Spain’s plenipotentiary at the Nijmegen congress to its envoy in Denmark. Ten carry a contemporary decipherment in the margin; four, of September 1677 and March 1678, carry none, and no key survives. The key was rebuilt from the ten margins by anchoring repeated words and aligning: letters and syllables in numbers, disguised letter-pair syllables, reversed vowel-first pairs and some twenty word codes. It reads all fourteen, down to the fear after the fall of Ghent. Nijmegen → Copenhagen · syllabic nomenclator · June 1677 – March 1678 · read The marqués de los Balbases to Baltasar de Fuenmayor, 1677–78 Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, Secrétairerie d’État et de Guerre, inv. nr. 2559 · DECODE R985–R998, fourteen letters, 47 pages · ten with a contemporary decipherment in the margin, four with none No key survives. It was rebuilt from the ten deciphered letters and reads all fourteen, including the four that had never been deciphered Daniel Bourdeau · solved 19 September 2026 · updated 21 September 2026 solved Summary. Pablo Spínola Doria, third marqués de los Balbases, was one of Spain’s plenipotentiaries at the Nijmegen peace congress. DECODE catalogues fourteen of his ciphered letters to Baltasar de Fuenmayor, Spain’s envoy at Copenhagen, as “partially decrypted”. It notes that the solution is written in the margin, so the file was catalogued here as a transcription job. That turned out to be true of only ten letters. The last three, of 1, 8 and 22 March 1678, and one of 19 September 1677 have no decipherment at all. No key survives. None of the eight keys of the same Brussels series (DECODE R958–R965) fits. The key was therefore rebuilt from the cipher. Every cipher line and every margin line was transcribed afresh, because DECODE’s copies miss lines and misread the margins. Anchors came from word groups that repeat across letters. A monotone aligner, seeded with those anchors, then brought the table out of the ten margins. The system has single letters and consonant-vowel syllables in numbers, letter pairs whose consonant is disguised, reversed vowel-first pairs, some twenty word codes, and nulls. It covers 97% of the 8,150 cipher groups and reads the four unread letters. They cover the Imperial protest over the dissolution of the Bremen assembly, the Brunswick dukes’ claim to ambassadorial rank, the northern princes, and the fear after the fall of Ghent: “con la pérdida de Gante estamos temiendo la de otras importantes plazas”. Still open: a handful of rare name codes, and some homophones whose values are blurred by 4/9-type slips in the transcription. R985, 3 August 1677: the cipher block, with its contemporary decipherment in the left margin (“alegrome de la buena esperança que Mons.r d’Amerong[en]…”). The key was rebuilt from ten margins like this one. Image: Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, SEG 2559, letter of 3 August 1677, via DECODE R985.

With no decipherment (four): R992 (19 September 1677), R996 (1 March 1678), R997 (8 March), R998 (22 March). Each letter opens with courtesies in clear, then gives a cipher block. t: The marqués de los Balbases to Fuenmayor, 1677–78 — a Nijmegen plenipotentiary’s cipher rebuilt and four undeciphered letters read
b: This is a syllabic nomenclator with homophones. Groups are separated by spaces. Letters. Vowels: a 21, 3+; e 2+; i 22, 67; o 18. Consonants: b 10, n; c 9; d e ; f x ; g 16; j u+; l 8, 19; n y , 24, 20; p 26; r 23, 31; s 28, B; t 27; y 25; z h. The closing consonants s, n and r are the three commonest groups. Syllables in numbers. de 46, la 55, en 76, ra 65, re 66, te 71, do 48, ta 70, lo 58, no 63, to 73, da 45, ti 72, di 47 le 56, ni 62, vi 42, ne 61, in 77, ve 41, va 40, na 60, on 78, an 75, li 57, ga 50, go 53, tu 74 vo 43, ar 80, gu 54, un 79, er 81, du 49, nu 64, ro 68, tr 188 Letter pairs: a syllable with the vowel kept and the consonant disguised. c is written x , d or l : xo , do and lo all read co; the same holds for ci, ca, ce and cu. f is written n : no fo, ni fi, ne fe, na fa, nu fu. y is written r : ro yo, ra ya. Vowel-first pairs: the syllable reversed, with the consonant disguised. s is written f : ef se, if si, af sa, of so, uf su. Also ye es, ya as, yo os. p is written d : ad pa, ed pe, od po, ud pu. m is written c : ac ma, ec me, ic mi, oc mo, uc mu. h is written q or g : aq / ag ha, eq / eg he, og ho. Others: en em, ot ch, as za. Word codes. que: d+ (struck d), b+. de: p+, g+. V.S.: H. para: 05. por: 15, is . sobre: 184. quando: 148. alguno: 100. congreso: 120. ministro: des . materia: dus . duque: ep . embax[ador]: §. -mente: dan . nuestro: fe . Flandes: ban . Francia: bef . franceses: bin . Suecia: 163. Dinamarca: or . -bourg: 105. Nulls. 13+ and most 13s, 300, 200, 700, 07, 01, 18+, 16+, 35. Many of these mark the start or end of a cipher block. A few examples: 26 67 y di ed 28 = pr·i·n·ci·pe·s xo y no 23 ic 45 e = co·n·fo·r·mi·da·d xo 20 41 62 76 = co·n·ve·ni·en[te]

t: The marqués de los Balbases to Fuenmayor, 1677–78 — a Nijmegen plenipotentiary’s cipher rebuilt and four undeciphered letters read
b: R998, 22 March 1678: the end of the clear text and the start of the cipher. The margin is empty. This letter and the three before it were never deciphered. Image: Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, SEG 2559, letter of 22 March 1678, via DECODE R998. These are machine readings from the key: the groups are decoded one by one and the text is given here in summary. The group-by-group text is in balbases1677/read/ . 19 September 1677 (R992). Balbases has seen the protest the Imperial ministers published over the dissolution of the Bremen assembly. “De nuestra parte no nos queda que hacer sino es… temer” what the confederates will do. After Charleroi they may insist at the union that the conquests be shared out before anything positive is settled. A rumour about the Danish chancellor and the Duke of Celle. He gives it no credit, “pues V.S. no lo ha penetrado ni me lo avisa”. The claim that the duke would take his share of his father’s conquests, the duchies of Bremen and Verden. 1 March 1678 (R996). Nothing in Sweden could undo “la desconfianza que arguimos hacia nuestros aliados”. What causes it is “la miserable postura en que permanecen nuestras cosas”. The Brunswicks’ proceedings rest on solid suspicions. The ministers of the northern princes had thought of writing a protest about treaties of peace that would leave out their participation. He praises Fuenmayor’s diligence in avoiding that step. Strasbourg’s lack of constancy. A French gentleman has come back from France “satisfecho del Rey Cristianísimo”. 8 March 1678 (R997). In the business of the Brunswicks’ claim to the treatment of ambassadors, the Danes have conceded nothing. No formal act was made in writing at the first step. He comments on the Duke of Hanover and his brothers: “todo me parece muy bien pesado, pero yo creo que nada de estas intrigas llegará a fin”. “Los incesantes riesgos en que estamos”, and his growing melancholy. 22 March 1678 (R998). The dependencies between the princes of the north, “de suficiente calibre para tenernos embarazados”. The evils “que nosotros estamos padeciendo”. The loss in Flanders: “con la pérdida de Gante estamos temiendo la de otras importantes plazas”. Ghent had fallen to Louis XIV on 9 March. They are still waiting on the others’ long delays while “la enfermedad” advances.

t: The marqués de los Balbases to Fuenmayor, 1677–78 — a Nijmegen plenipotentiary’s cipher rebuilt and four undeciphered letters read
b: These were read at the time. The key reproduces their margins, which recover illegible margin words and confirm the doubtful ones. Their subjects: Amerongen’s hopes for a guarantee to the town of Bremen, 3 August. The dissolution of the Bremen conference, 18 June. Villahermosa, Temple’s recall and the Danish setback at Malmö. The Bishop of Strasbourg’s minister and Orange’s journey to England, 19 October. The loss of Saint-Ghislain, December. The Brunswick claim to ambassadorial rank, which runs through the winter letters of 1678. The margin text is transcribed in balbases1677/tx/ . It is summarised here, not edited.

t: The marqués de los Balbases to Fuenmayor, 1677–78 — a Nijmegen plenipotentiary’s cipher rebuilt and four undeciphered letters read
b: The images were fetched from DECODE. Two agents transcribed every cipher line and margin line by page into tx/ . They corrected DECODE’s transcriptions, which drop lines, confuse 46/96 and 48/98, and garble the margins. Repeated n-grams across letters were set against the margin text at the same relative position to find anchors: Brunsuic , principes , conformidad , novedad , conveniente . A hard-EM monotone aligner ( align2.py ) was seeded with those anchors and ran over the ten margined letters. Each group emits a substring of the margin text, with nulls and skips allowed. Two rounds brought out the table. A frozen key then decoded all fourteen letters.

t: Johan Banér to Torsten Stålhandske, 29 December 1640 — the intercepted letter, read in part
b: A copy of an intercepted field letter from Banér at Hof, days before his winter march on Regensburg, kept in Kircher’s correspondence (APUG 568 f. 239) and posted as unsolved on Cipherbrain in 2019. No Swedish key on DECODE fits; cribs from the clear context (durch, und) let the solver write nach der Oberpfaltz und, and the key was rebuilt word by word from there. 246 of 274 cipher tokens read (89.8%); a courier’s name, one stretch corrupt in the only copy, and the fourteen code words stay open. Hof → Silesia · homophonic number cipher with a nomenclator, inside clear German · 29 December 1640 · read in part, 89.8% measured Johan Banér to Torsten Stålhandske, 29 December 1640 — the intercepted letter, read in part from Johan Banér → to Torsten Stålhandske Pontificia Università Gregoriana, APUG 568 f. 239r–v, among Athanasius Kircher’s letters · a copy of an intercepted field letter, written at Hof days before Banér’s winter march on Regensburg · posted as unsolved on Cipherbrain in June 2019; no reading since Key rebuilt here from cribs in the clear context, with a 1630s German language model · 246 of 274 cipher tokens read; a courier’s name, one corrupt stretch and all fourteen code words open Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 22 September 2026 solved in part Summary. A copy of an intercepted letter from the Swedish field marshal Johan Banér to Major General Torsten Stålhandske, dated Hof, 29 December 1640, survives in the correspondence of Athanasius Kircher at the Gregoriana (APUG 568 f. 239). Klaus Schmeh posted it on Cipherbrain in 2019 with Philip Neal’s transcription; the readers who tried it, Neal among them, did not read it. Most of the letter is in clear German; seven passages are in two-digit numbers, with fourteen three-digit code words. None of the Swedish keys on DECODE fits it, Banér’s own among them, and a language model alone cannot settle 74 homophones from 274 numbers. Two cribs from the clear context ( durch after “von zeit zu zeit”, and und ) let the solver produce nach der Oberpfaltz und , and that phrase opened the key. The letter now reads: Banér means to march “nach der Oberpfaltz und gegen die [442]” ; he expects the enemy to gather against him “und etwa auch die in Schlesien agirende [361] dazu ziehen” ; Stålhandske is to “gute acht geben” , follow the enemy “mit guten Fürsichtigkeit” , report “durch Espionen” , and tell him “wohin er seine Marche zu richten” . 246 of 274 cipher tokens read (89.8%), measured. Checked against the manuscript scans, the transcription needed four figures corrected. Open: the second courier’s name and a stretch in the fifth passage, where the figures are confirmed and every value is fixed by other words, so the only surviving copy is corrupt; and all fourteen code words, for which no key survives.

t: Johan Banér to Torsten Stålhandske, 29 December 1640 — the intercepted letter, read in part
b: The heading reads Copia Intercipirtes Schreibens General Baners an General Major Stallhausen : Stålhandske, who commanded the Swedish troops in Silesia. The letter is dated Hoff den 29 Decem. A. 1640 and signed with a flourished B. Kircher’s file calls it Copia litterarum interceptarum Generalis Baners Hoff in Silesia . The copy reached Rome, presumably so that Kircher could try the cipher; there is no decipherment on the two pages posted. The first page, upper half: the heading, the first two cipher passages (the routes of an earlier letter), and the third, which reads nach der Oberpfaltz und gegen die [442] . Image: Pontificia Università Gregoriana, APUG 568 f. 239r, via the Museo Galileo Kircher Correspondence Project. The cipher passages (S1–S7 here) hold 274 two-digit numbers with 74 distinct values from 2 to 98, and fourteen three-digit numbers: 361, 442, 464, 508, 513 and 568, which stand for names or nouns, and a cluster 766–783 in the fifth and sixth passages. The work started from Neal’s transcription and the blog’s small images; it was then checked figure by figure against the Museo Galileo’s scans of f. 239r–v (1469 × 2304 px, served openly), which correct four figures: the first figure of S4 is 86 (Neal 66), a figure in Schlesien is 86 (Neal 36), one in guten is 47 (Neal 57), and the figure Neal could not read in S7 is 92.

t: Johan Banér to Torsten Stålhandske, 29 December 1640 — the intercepted letter, read in part
b: The Swedish keys. DECODE holds the Riksarkivet’s box of Swedish chancery keys ( Chifferklaver , låda II, records R4103–R4329). Their archivists’ covers name the correspondents and give the values of a . Banér’s keys there, the Horn–Banér cipher (R4122), the code in use with Oxenstierna from late 1634 (R4123, copied in R4325 as Generalis Campi Marschalli Johan Banneris Cyffer ), and the other alphabets of the 1640 chancery register (R4325, R4266), were transcribed and tried, as they stand and at every offset from −30 to +30. None fits. Why a solver alone fails. Unconstrained homophonic annealing finds keys that score better than real German would. A control settled this: 1630s German from the Theatrum Europaeum , cut to the same segment lengths and enciphered with Banér’s 1634 key, scores −279 under the model built here ( de-1640s ), and the solver’s optima sit at −390 to −430. With eight known values the same solver, restricted to a few homophones per letter, lands on the true key. So the letter needed cribs. The cribs. The sixth passage follows mich aber von zeit zu zeit and opens 40 16 23 28 29: durch . The pair 28 29 ( ch ) comes seven times. 16 64 40 is und . With those fixed, the solver wrote nach der … pfaltz und in the third passage, the one that ends [442] loszugehen . Banér did march from Hof into the Upper Palatinate in the first days of January 1641, and surprised the Reichstag at Regensburg: … Continance erleiden will, 92 39 73 43 30 27 69 24 78 27 69 66 50 39 21 71 37 16 64 40 33 62 51 75 98 63 77 27 442 loszugehen : nach der Oberpfaltz und gegen die [442] loszugehen. Image: Pontificia Università Gregoriana, APUG 568 f. 239r, via the Museo Galileo Kircher Correspondence Project. That phrase fixes twenty values, each consistent with durch and und . From there the key was extended word by word, and no value was kept unless it read in at least two words: Schlesien agirende , dazu ziehen , gute acht geben , sobaldt , ehender , solche , Fürsichtigkeit nachvolgen , wohin er seine Marche zu richten , entgegen . The key has 70 values, one to six per letter, in no alphabetical or banded order.

t: Johan Banér to Torsten Stålhandske, 29 December 1640 — the intercepted letter, read in part
b: Clear text in roman, the deciphered passages in italics, code words in brackets, unread letters as ? . The transcription of the clear text is Neal’s. … welches ich im Duplo, als ein Exemplar Jobs [508], das andere aber in [513] n Johann ??????????? über [568] abgehen lassen … … undt gesonnen, wofern es nimmer die Ratio Belli undt des feinds … Continance erleiden will, nach der Oberpfaltz und gegen die [442] loszugehen, undt meinen aeussersten fleis anzuwenden. … es werde der feindt seine aeusserste macht von allen oertern her colligiren, undt so starck als es ihm muglig mir entgegen leitten, etwa auch die in Schlesien agirende [361] dazu ziehen. So wollt der herr General Major darau [f] gute acht geben und sobaldt (e)ich sein gegen [773] ehender [464] auf solche W ?????????????? zu [775] dem [767] ?? ein guten Fürsichtigkeit nachvolgen, mich aber von zeit zu zeit durch E(sp)ionen sie ko [m] en, dass sie mö [g] en, wie sein undt des feindes gelegenheit sey, eigentlich undt unschwierig berichten, damit ich ihm inmittelst mit seiner andeutung wohin er seine(n) Marche zu richte(n), entgegen wolten komme … In sense. Banér sent his letter of the 16th from Erfurt in duplicate, one copy by [508] , the other by a Johann by way of [568] . He has come to Hof and means, if the reason of war and the enemy’s bearing allow, to march through the Upper Palatinate and against [442] , most likely Regensburg or the Bavarians. He expects the enemy to gather every force against him, “and perhaps also draw in the [troops] acting in Silesia”. Stålhandske is therefore to keep good watch, and as soon as the enemy moves off, to follow with good caution. He is to report from time to time through spies on his own and the enemy’s situation, so that Banér, told where he means to direct his march, can come to meet him. The seventh passage, after mit seiner andeutung : 38 24 29 77 92 27 23 13 41 44 98 86 … wohin er seine(n) Marche zu richte(n), entgegen wolten . Image: Pontificia Università Gregoriana, APUG 568 f. 239v, via the Museo Galileo Kircher Correspondence Project.

t: Johan Banér to Torsten Stålhandske, 29 December 1640 — the intercepted letter, read in part
b: The second courier’s name (S2, eleven tokens after Johann , which decipher as ohrs?acbuet ). The figures are confirmed on the manuscript and all but one value is fixed by other words, so the copy itself is corrupt here. The first courier reads Jobs [508], Jobst and a surname in code (graded M). A stretch of the fifth passage ( eisen o vi rechte , fourteen tokens), two tokens before ein guten , and a stray e in sobaldt e ich (probably er sich ). The manuscript confirms every figure and every value is fixed by other words, so this copy, the only one known, is corrupt here; the sent original or a Swedish register copy would be needed. Slips of the copy (graded C): d e i n for die in ; 93 (i) for n in Schlesien ; one letter missing from Marche and one from Espionen . The fourteen code words. 442 is what Banér marches against; 361 is the force acting in Silesia; 508 and 568 are how the two copies went. The 7xx codes fall where letters are missing ( darau [778] for darauff , au [772] for auss , ko [770] en ), and five of them are letters: freed of fixed values, the solver itself returns au [772] solche [766] eise = auf solche Weise , and darau [778] = darauf , ko [770] en = kommen , dass sie mo [783] en = dass sie mögen (graded C). The other nine (361, 442, 464, 508, 513, 568, 767, 773, 775) stay open: no key survives and each occurs once. The copy is the only witness known. The sent original, or a register copy in Banér’s papers in Stockholm, would settle the corrupt stretches; neither is digitised.

t: András Bay to Ferenc Rákóczi II, Jászvásár, 8 March 1706
b: A ciphered despatch from Rákóczi’s man at the Moldavian court (DECODE R478) was catalogued as undeciphered, with no key. Scoring all 94 Rákóczi chancery keys on DECODE against it picked out R609, a Hungarian syllabic nomenclator, which reads it unchanged. The Tsar suing Charles XII for peace, the Muscovite and Polish envoys at Iaşi, a message from Pekri to the voivode, and the Swede at Vilna. Jászvásár (Iaşi) → Ferenc Rákóczi II · Hungarian syllabic nomenclator · 8 March 1706 · read András Bay to Rákóczi, from the Moldavian court, 1706 MNL OL G15 Caps. D. Fasc. 81. 5 (DECODE R478), two pages, catalogued as an undeciphered homophonic letter. It is enciphered in one of Rákóczi’s own keys, DECODE R609, which reads it unchanged. Daniel Bourdeau · read 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. DECODE lists R478 as a non-decrypted numerical letter of András Bay to Ferenc Rákóczi II, 8 March 1706, with no key attached. The ciphertext was decrypted with each of the 94 key transcriptions of Rákóczi’s chancery (G15) on DECODE and each result scored against Hungarian. One key, R609 (G15 Caps. C. Fasc. 43. 56), gave running Hungarian at once: a two-digit syllabary with a nomenclator of places and peoples and a row of nulls. DECODE’s transcription was checked line by line against the images and corrected in seven places. All 414 cipher groups then have a value, except one (50), which is missing from the key and reads ba in barát from context. The letter is a report from Jászvásár (Iaşi), where Bay was at the Moldavian voivode’s court. It covers the Muscovite and Polish envoys there, the Tsar suing Charles XII for peace, a message from Pekri to the voivode, and the Swedish army at Vilna. About ten groups in one stretch on page 2 read letter by letter but not as clear sense. No printed decipherment was found. The opening: «Valamint ez előtt negyed nappal küldött levelemben nyilván meg írtam» in clear, then the cipher (231 Mosqua, 27 és, 221 Lengiel, …). Image: Hungarian National Archives (MNL OL), G15 D 81/5, via DECODE R478.

t: András Bay to Ferenc Rákóczi II, Jászvásár, 8 March 1706
b: The letter is one sheet written on both sides. Clear Hungarian passages alternate with runs of comma-separated numbers from 1 to 300 and two signs. It is dated at the foot Jászvásár 8. Martii and signed Bay András . The key is DECODE R609, a Rákóczi chancery key of 1703–1711 in the same fonds. Its letters have homophones (A 7/70, E 8/80, I 9/90, O 6/60, U 5/59), and it has two-digit consonant–vowel syllables (30 ba to 148 vu ), short words (27 és , 28 az , 13 hogy , 14 mért ) and a nomenclator from 149 to 293 (231 Mosqua, 221 Lengyel, 270 Svéd, 285 Vajda, 252 Porta, 236 Nagyságod). The nulls are 15–19, 200, 300, Ψ and +. The letter uses the nulls 16, 18, 19, 200, 300 and Ψ. An earlier issue of the same table, R561, scored second.

t: András Bay to Ferenc Rákóczi II, Jászvásár, 8 March 1706
b: Normalised Hungarian. Clear passages are in «»; square brackets mark words supplied or doubtful. «Kegyelmes Uram! Valamint ez előtt negyed nappal küldött levelemben nyilván meg írtam,» Moszkva és lengyel követek jöttek ide; az lengyel viszont ismét [elment], a moszkva még itt vagyon. Az mint expiscálhattam, olyat mondottak mind ketten, hogy a moszkva békességet kéri a svédtől, mindenekelőtt várakat és ezen hadakozásban lött expensáit a svédnek megígérvén, «[ha oly] conditióval, hogy …» ellene a moszkva hadát declarálja-é a svéd «is» colligatióban «légyen». … Az moszkva követ «innét» Constantinápolyba «vagy» Erdélybe megyen, én nem tudhatni; mert csak maga beszéllett az vajdával, görögül. «…» Tegnapi napon az vajda tolmácsával conversatióban lévén, «… in discursu» Pekri uram által olyat izent a vajdának, hogy csak Nagyságod a magyar nemzet dolgát complanálhassa a némettel, … mindenben szándéka Nagyságodnak a török ellen való hadakozás. «…» Az tolmácsot [… ?] tudván az barát az Portának szemének és fülének lenni, még nem mondotta; «nékem is» lelkemre kötötte, hogy ki ne adjam őtet. A svéd Vilnához szállott, mely Litvánia és Moszkva-Oroszország között vagyon. «… Jászvásár 8. Martii … Bay András.» In English. As I wrote four days ago, Muscovite and Polish envoys have come here; the Pole has gone again, the Muscovite is still here. As far as I could fish it out, both said that the Tsar is asking the Swede for peace. Above all he promises him fortresses and his expenses in this war, on condition that the Swede declare [war?] against… Whether the Muscovite envoy goes on to Constantinople or to Transylvania I cannot tell, because he talked to the voivode alone, in Greek. Yesterday I talked with the voivode’s interpreter. [He told me that] Pekri had sent the voivode word that Your Highness wants only to settle the Hungarian nation’s affairs with the Germans [the Emperor], and that in everything Your Highness intends war against the Turk. Knowing the friar to be the Porte’s eyes and ears, the interpreter has not yet told him, and he made me swear on my soul not to give him away. The Swede has moved to Vilna, between Lithuania and Muscovy.

t: Gilbert Bayard to Montmorency, 5 January 1526 — three cipher lines, no key
b: A seventeenth-century copy (BnF Clairambault 325 f. 84, DECODE R2285) of a letter from one of the French negotiators at Toledo carries 56 cipher signs of 29 kinds. Champollion-Figeac printed the letter in 1847 but left the cipher out. The Calvimont and Raince keys of the same months share its shapes but not its values, and the passage is too short to solve blind. Toledo → Montmorency · graphic-sign cipher · 5 January 1526 · attempted, not solved Gilbert Bayard to Anne de Montmorency, 5 January 1526 to Anne de Montmorency BnF, Clairambault 325, f. 84 (DECODE R2285): a seventeenth-century copy of a letter from the French embassy negotiating Francis I’s release. Three lines in the middle of the letter are in cipher. The cipher was transcribed from the DECODE images and tested against the two French keys of the same months. The printed edition was checked. Nothing reads. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 22 September 2026 key not found Summary. Tomokiyo lists this passage as unsolved, and DECODE has it as non-decrypted. The writer is Gilbert Bayard, secretary of the King and élu of Bas-Auvergne. He was one of the French negotiators at Toledo, not a relative of the Chevalier Bayard. The letter was printed in 1847 by Champollion-Figeac ( Captivité du roi François Ier , no. CCXVIII), from another copy, and the cipher was simply left out. The marginal note in the Clairambault copy, which DECODE and Tomokiyo describe as irrelevant to the cipher, is a line of the letter that the copyist skipped and then restored; Champollion’s text has it in the body. The 56 cipher signs use the same pool of shapes as Raince’s 1526 key and Calvimont’s alphabet from the same volume, but neither key’s values fit. Blind annealing does not settle on one solution. Status: not solved. It needs the original letter, whose signs will be cleaner than the copyist’s and which may carry a decipherment, or another Bayard letter in the same cipher.

t: Gilbert Bayard to Montmorency, 5 January 1526 — three cipher lines, no key
b: Clairambault 325 f. 84r, lines 16–19: “…celuy de Ferrare a Calatheu”, the cipher, then “comme j’espere vous dire dimenche”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Clairambault 325 f. 84r, via DECODE R2285. The copy is headed “Lettre de M. Bayard a M. le Mal de Montmorency”, dated “5 Janvier 1526”, with the source reference “V. 41. f. 4” in the margin. It is signed “Gilbert Bayard”, “A Tollede le v e jo. de Janvier”. It reports Bayard’s talks with the viceroy Lannoy, with Lallemant and with Don Hugo de Moncada on the four points still open before the treaty of Madrid: the hostages, Fuenterrabía, and the sovereignty of the Constable of Bourbon. The cipher comes where Bayard tells how the Imperial side had asked whether he had spoken to any Italian ambassador: “…et qu’il y avoit neuf moys que je n’avoye salué celuy de Ferrare a Calatheu [ cipher ] comme j’espere vous dire dimenche.”

t: Gilbert Bayard to Montmorency, 5 January 1526 — three cipher lines, no key
b: There are 56 signs of 29 kinds (measured on signs.txt ): Greek-like letters (Φ, θ, ξ, φ, γ, ω, ∂), figures (7), Latin letters (n, o, R, b, x, k, e), triangles filled and open, a barred I, a circled m, and an m with a superscript m. With 29 kinds in 56 signs there must be homophones, nulls or code signs. Several of the shapes (7, R, n, θ, x, Δ, ε, ω, and the “ny” and K signs that are nulls in Raince’s key) belong to the pool used by French ciphers of 1525–26. The copyist drew them by imitation, so small differences between shapes may not be meaningful.

t: Gilbert Bayard to Montmorency, 5 January 1526 — three cipher lines, no key
b: Print. Champollion-Figeac, Captivité du roi François Ier (Paris 1847), no. CCXVIII, pp. 462–463, prints the letter from “copie de Bréquigny, vol. 91”. His text reads “…que j’avoye salué celui de Ferrare. A ce soir…”, with no mention of a cipher. Calvimont’s key (same volume, f. 67, solved by Norbert Biermann). Its signs were matched by shape (7 = m, 8/∂ = a, 5 = e, 6/b = t, barred I = d, ω = l) and pinned in an annealer. The result scores worse than with no pins and reads as nothing. Raince’s 1526 key (Tomokiyo, as re-measured for the Raince write-up), with the nulls removed. It gives −3.5 per sign under the 1530s French model, against −1.4 for the free solution, and the output is gibberish. The shapes are shared, but the values are not. Ciphertext only. Two homophonic annealing runs against a 5-gram model of 1530s French despatches: one free, and one allowing homophones only for common letters, with 24 restarts. The best restarts share no text. At 56 signs the problem is underdetermined.

Pozsony · Buda · Naples → Ferrara · 1482–1505 · Prior readings located Beatrice d’Aragona: four earlier readings, one plain letter from Beatrice of Naples → to Ercole I d'Este Five records in DECODE, ASMo Carteggio Principi Esteri, were grouped as partly decrypted ciphertexts. The prescribed check of printed correspondence resolves the premise of catalogue item 160. t: Beatrice d’Aragona: four earlier readings and one plain letter
b: The edition supplies the cipher text’s meaning: Matthias offers an intervention against Venice, provided the league sends money to Milan. The proposed force comprises ten thousand Swiss and six thousand cavalry; five hundred more cavalry, including a hundred hussars, also need a safe route. He does not intend to declare himself openly against Venice before his relationship with the league is settled. uno expediente optimo et necessario per lo favore et salute de tuta la lega Dece milia Svizari et sei milia cavalli del Signor Re di Hungaria. These are excerpts of the 1877 reading . The manuscript’s clear wording and cipher boundaries match the edition’s roman and italic sections. Its editorial note explicitly states that the italic words were written in secret signs. MDE III (1877), p. 13: an earlier decipherment in print. This is a crop of the public-domain edition, not an archive photograph. Image: Magyar Diplomácziai Emlékek III (1877), p. 13, via MTAK REAL-EOD.

t: Beatrice d’Aragona: four earlier readings and one plain letter
b: Beatrice relays Matthias’s criticism of the league’s reluctance to spend. The king repeats the troop offer, requires payment at Milan, and asks for decisive cooperation. The published text has the proverb: ali avari che per sparagnare uno grosso perdeno lo ducato Misers save a grosso and lose a ducat. Near the end the reading describes endless negotiations as “uno Jocare de balla cum retornare sempre ali principij” —playing ball and always returning to the starting point. Inspection of the printed page corrects the machine extraction’s holla to balla . The edition and manuscript both date the letter 8 June, despite a secondary citation giving July.

t: Beatrice d’Aragona: four earlier readings and one plain letter
h: 8 March 1486: a letter split by the editors
b: The first written page contains cipher passages about bringing Andriolo to Hungary, paying his expenses and honoring the king’s promises. They appear in MDE IV, supplement no. 45 . The editor associates the negotiation with the Djem/Cem affair; that historical identification is not a name newly recovered here. The intervening plain pages concern Ippolito’s appointment to Esztergom and opposition from Cardinal Ascanio. Berzeviczy printed them in 1914, explicitly omitting material already published in MDE III p. 67 and IV p. 367. The final paragraph of the physical letter matches MDE III no. 54: Con la cyfra havemo antiquamente con Vostra Signoria … ne li mandamo qui alligata un altra nova She is using the old cipher and sending a new one for subsequent correspondence. The printed no. 54 is therefore the closing part of this physical letter, not another ciphertext to add to the set. The related same-date letter printed as no. 53 should not be substituted for this manuscript. Limit: the 1878 reading retains Virtus , Fortis and repeated M. in awkward positions. They are visible on the printed page and are not OCR errors. Their cryptographic role remains unverified; this report does not delete them as supposed nulls or claim a flawless modern reading.

t: Beatrice d’Aragona: four earlier readings and one plain letter

A separate handwritten slip over the block begins “che don hippolyto vostro figliolo…” . The next photograph shows the same page with the slip moved aside. A later slip reads: che quello Andriolo se conferisca qua The corresponding request appears in MDE III no. 75 in the same context. t: Beatrice d’Aragona: four earlier readings and one plain letter
b: R1154 is ordinary Italian chancery writing. Beatrice asks Ippolito to send a trusted messenger with letters for the cardinal of Esztergom, giving the journey the appearance of Ippolito’s own business. She then explains why she will not write more: Et per non esser certa che le littere pervengano secure, et per non havere cifra: non ce extendemo altramente per questa “Because we are not certain the letters will arrive safely, and because we have no cipher, we do not go into further detail in this letter.” Berzeviczy prints it as no. CCCII. The manuscript’s final dating clause, M° quingentesimo quinto , agrees with its docket and photograph label: 1505, not 1504 .

R15 (ff. 7r–v) was read by George Lasry with a key he reconstructed, also printed by Meister (1906, p. 324). R16 (f. 206, dated 3 March 1586) carries a “decryption” on DECODE, but that file is byte for byte the R15 decryption, filed on the wrong record: R16 had never been read. It reads all five pages, with five groups unread: the Duke of Lorraine, the Guises, the German reiters, the Queen Mother. Two name codes of R16 are not confirmed. t: The Paris nunciature to the Secretariat, Francia 18, 1585–87
h: R16: Guise, Metz and the sale of church property, 3 March 1586
b: The despatch belongs to the quarrel over the bull of 1586 that let Henri III raise money by selling church property. The nuncio reports what the Duke of Guise has sent to tell him, what a well-placed informant heard, and the mood of the clergy’s assembly. Decoded text, word breaks added, doubled consonants as the writer spelled them: hoggi il [Duca di Guisa] mi ha mandato a dire … che egli hora tiene per fermo che il [Re Christianissimo] debba fare la […] … prima havera riscosso quanti si deve vendere per la bolla, ma che esso [Duca di Guisa] non vi acconsentira mai … che esso [Duca di Guisa] non poteva ne voleva acconsentire a detta […] … mi viene … riferito da personaggio di molta autorita havere inteso da un gentilhuomo … che egli si potrebbe contentar … si facesse quando se gli desse Metz, e una buona somma di […] … che con li […] che ricevessero hora potrebbero poi prepararsi a nuova impresa … nondimeno il cuore di […] non corrisponde all’estrinseco … li ecclesiastici della citta … restano molto mal contenti della concessione della bolla per l’alienatione … detta congregatione inclina ad appellarsi ad futurum concilium, se vedera di non potere ottenere … che essa congregatione habbia molta speranza di essere esaudita da [Nostro Signore] … In short: Guise tells the nuncio he will never consent to the King’s sale of church goods under the bull; others say he would consent if he were given Metz and a large sum, money he could turn to a new enterprise; the King shows him confidence but his heart does not match; the Paris clergy are angry at the concession and their assembly leans towards an appeal to a future council, while hoping the Pope will hear them.

b: With Meister’s key no. 40 (“Con monsig. Moresino nuntio in Francia, 8 Giugno 1587”) the transcription reads on all five pages. It is therefore a Morosini-period despatch of 1587, not a Bergamo or Nazareth letter. t: Henri IV to Béthune, 9, 10 and 22 November 1601 — two letters read, and the ceiling on the third measured
b: Three ciphered letters of the King to his ambassador in Rome, BnF fr. 3484, catalogued “avec chiffre” with no decipherment. The notice’s “copie du n° précédent” turns out to be the minute of the 10 November letter in clear, and aligning it with the cipher recovers a Villeroy-office key of the design Bazeries printed for Béthune’s brother in 1599: ten thousand écus to Cardinal Aldobrandini for the Peace of Lyon. The 22 November letter is now read too — it interleaves clear French with its cipher, and carries the Camaiano pension, Barberini’s coming and the dauphin’s baptism. The 9 November letter, a solid page of cipher, stops at about six words in ten, and an oracle bound shows why: the decoder is already past the ceiling its transcription allows. Paris → Rome · letters, dotted letters and figures · November 1601 · two of three read Henri IV to Philippe de Béthune, 9, 10 and 22 November 1601 from Henri IV → to Philippe de Béthune BnF Français 3484, nos. 7, 8 and 12 (ff. 33, 34, 46–47), the sent originals signed Henry and countersigned by Villeroy’s secretary · catalogue item 22, “avec chiffre”, no decipherment on the leaves The 10 November letter is read through its minute, which survives in clear four leaves on; the 22 November letter is read from the clear French it interleaves with its cipher. The 9 November letter, a solid page of cipher with neither minute nor gloss, stops at about six words in ten — and a measurement, not an impression, says why. Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 17 September 2026 · updated 21 September 2026 solved in part Summary. Fr. 3484 is the file of Henri IV’s letters to Philippe de Béthune, sent to Rome as ordinary ambassador in August 1601. The notice marks some twenty-five of them “avec chiffre et déchiffrement” and three, of 9, 10 and 22 November 1601, “avec chiffre” alone. The decipherments are the receiving office’s: numbered paraphrases in the margin of the cipher leaf, or, for 10 December, a verbatim footnote. The three undeciphered letters fall at the moment of the Este–Aldobrandini debt settlement, Biron’s conspiracy and the dauphin’s birth. Reading the volume on contact sheets found what the notice calls “copie du n° précédent” at f. 36 to be the minute of the 10 November letter, in clear, corrections and all: every enciphered passage of f. 34 has its text there. Aligning the two, together with the glossed passages of 8 November and 10 December, by an EM aligner seeded from hand checks at four and seven times magnification, gives the cipher’s design and its key in most letters and some twenty word signs. It is the design Bazeries printed in 1901 as the “chiffre baillé à M. de Béthune, 1599” for the elder brother, with other values: letters are figures and letter-shaped symbols with homophones, letters with a comma, one dot or two dots are common words in alphabetical series, two-digit figures are names (48 = Cardinal, 17 = Aldobrandin, 7 = le Roy d’Espagne). The 10 November letter is the King’s payment to Cardinal Aldobrandini for the Peace of Lyon: ten thousand écus paid through Sillery, ten thousand more promised for the first four months of 1602 “sans avoir esgard à l’arrest obtenu par lad. duchesse de Nemours”, to be announced through Cardinal d’Ossat with Béthune pretending not to have received the letter. The 22 November letter, four pages, turns out not to be a block of cipher at all: it interleaves clear French with eighty short ciphered runs inside the same lines, so the clear text carries the sense, and it is now read in full for the first time — the Camaiano pension paid to “relever le party françois a Rome”, Barberini’s coming, the Pope’s two audiences, and the courier sent to invite him to the dauphin’s baptism. The 9 November letter, one page entirely in cipher after “il me mande qu’il est certain que”, has neither minute nor gloss and stops at about six words in ten. An oracle bound built for this page says why, and says it as a number: the decoder already scores above the ceiling its own transcription allows, so about 29 % of the letter’s letters cannot be produced by its glyphs as anyone has read them. Ten further attempts, each measured, failed to move it. Status: 10 and 22 November read; key recovered in letters, syllable groups and common words, with the doubling sign; two-digit names open; 9 November about six words in ten, at the measured ceiling. Next is archival, not computational: Cinq cents de Colbert 346.

t: Henri IV to Béthune, 9, 10 and 22 November 1601 — two letters read, and the ceiling on the third measured
b: Philippe de Béthune, younger brother of Rosny (the future Sully), left for Rome with his instruction of 23 August 1601 (no. 2 of the volume) and served as ordinary ambassador until 1605. The letters of the King to him in fr. 3484 run from October 1601 to October 1602. They are the sent originals, signed Henry and countersigned de Neufville , that is Villeroy’s office, and the cipher is that office’s. Where the office in Rome deciphered a letter it wrote the reading in the margin, in a smaller hand, numbered 1, 2, 3 to the passages, or as a footnote keyed with a sign; the volume keeps those readings. Three letters have none.
