t: Henri IV to Béthune, 9, 10 and 22 November 1601 — two letters read, and the ceiling on the third measured
b: Bazeries ( Les chiffres secrets dévoilés , 1901, pp. 28–29) prints the “chiffre baillé à M. de Béthune” of 1599, given to Maximilien for his mission to England. Each letter has a figure (A = 3, B = 10, C = 8 …) and two or three arbitrary symbols; thirty names are figures with two dots ( Le Roy 4̈, Le Roy d’Espagne 2̈); some eighty common words are letters with a comma ( a, ayant … y, et, z, nous), with one dot (entre … mons) or with two dots (nostre … selon), each series alphabetical; the figures 2 to 11 with a comma are tout, tant, toutesfois … vivs ; a Δ doubles the preceding letter and y and $ cancel it. The 1601 cipher of the younger brother is the same office’s design two years on, with new values: f, = le, g, = la, x, = que, r, = par, q, = pour, d, = je in the comma series (the initials run l, l, q, p, p, j: alphabetical by groups, as in 1599); f: = au, s: = dit, x: = et, y: = ent in the two-dot series; t. = de, p. = ce with one dot; 61 = qui, 63 = re, 65 = si as syllable groups; 48 = Cardinal, 17 = Aldobrandin, 7 = le Roy d’Espagne as names; 68 = tout and 71 = tion are further syllable groups ( toutes = 68 ȥ g, affectionne ends 71 g ȥ). The letters: e = ȥ ‡ ε 0; a = 4 6 u; i = hooked m, v, a, 1; o = f + t; t = q 7; u/v = ꝑ, y, c; s = g, 2-shaped r, n; r = r ∂; l = h B S; m = x; g = plain m, hooked u; c = b e; p = o T; b = n; y = a. And φ is not a letter but the doubling sign Bazeries describes in the 1599 key (“Δ doublera son prochain précédent”): somme is written s-o-m-φ-e, l’année l-a-n-φ-e-φ, Sillery has h-φ for ll , occasions o-c-φ, retrouve u-φ (u and v one letter), mienne mie-n-φ-e. The “gratification” of f. 34 is written x 6 ꞔu ∂ u p ꞔm m v b 6 7 1 f : m-a-g-r-a-t-i-f-i-c-a-t-i-o(n), with the figures 6 7 1 for a t i ; the design’s figure-letters in the flesh.

t: Henri IV to Béthune, 9, 10 and 22 November 1601 — two letters read, and the ceiling on the third measured
b: The minute gives the enciphered passages word for word (differences: one word-sign where the minute has “de sorte”, “faites semblant” for the minute’s “taschez qu’il n’en soit rien dit”). In the King’s voice: after the Parlement of Paris had given judgment in the Este–Aldobrandini debt, he “fus bien aise d’avoir ce pretexte de gratifier led. Cardinal et luy tesmoigner ma bonne volonté … de sorte je luy fis payer des lors dix mil escuz par l’entremise du sieur de Sillery”; he has now ordered “qu’il face payer aud. Cardinal dedans les premiers quatre mois de l’année prochaine la somme de dix mil escuz par les mesmes mains … sans avoir esgard à l’arrest obtenu par lad. duchesse de Nemours, ny au besoing d’argent auquel je me retrouve. Car j’affectionne led. Cardinal et desire m’acquitter de lad. promesse que je luy ay faicte”; Béthune, after conferring with Cardinal d’Ossat, is to let Cardinal Aldobrandini know “de facon qu’il recoive et estime ceste grace comme elle merite”, to pretend “que vous n’aiez receu la presente”, and to be “le premier qui en avertira led. Cardinal Aldobrandin”. Pietro Aldobrandini, the Pope’s nephew, had made the Peace of Lyon in January 1601; here is the King paying for it, and managing how the gift is announced. The full text is in the repository ( bethune/reading_10nov.md ).

t: Henri IV to Béthune, 9, 10 and 22 November 1601 — two letters read, and the ceiling on the third measured
b: This letter was expected to be the harder of the two open ones: forty lines of cipher in blocks, the notice said, with no clear copy anywhere in the volume. Reading the four leaves at full resolution showed the description to be wrong in the way that mattered. The cipher is not in blocks. It is broken into eighty short runs set inside lines of ordinary clear French, so that the King’s secretary enciphered only the names, the sums and the sharpest judgements and left the grammar around them open. The clear text therefore carries most of the sense, and the letter can be read without breaking the runs at all. All four pages are transcribed in bethune/reading_22nov.md ; this is the first reading of any part of it. It answers Béthune’s despatch of 29 October, received on the 18th, and is signed Henry and countersigned de Neufville . Its core is a rebuke, in clear, of two persons the cipher names only by code group: “Il me semble que [20] [S 12], qui sont douez de toute prudence, ont faict faulte de n’avoir rompu ce coup, car ilz l’eussent faict facilement s’ilz y eussent pensé et operé d’heure, ainsi qu’ilz devoient. Mais ilz se sont contentez de … meuz d’autres considerations …” On money and discipline the King will “donner ordre que la pension que j’ay accordée au s.r Camaiano sera bien payée”, all to “relever le party françois a Rome”; but Béthune is to give no “esperances ou [fermes] des promesses a d’autres” without express command, “afin de n’abuser personne ne moy le premier”, and to act always “après toutesfois en avoir conferé avec le Card.al d’Ossat”. He acknowledges the Pope’s “bon accueil … aux deux audiences quelle vous a données”; he will receive Maffeo Barberini — the future Urban VIII, then on his way to France — “le plus favorablement que je pourray po[ur] le respect de sa S.té”; on the Jesuits he refers back to an earlier letter and will await the Pope’s answer; and he complains of an agent “qui reside en Suisse, accompagné d’un certain Julio de la Torre y Travers[i]”, whom Cardinal Aldobrandini had already reprimanded. The third leaf ends in clear on the household news that dates the whole file: “J’attends en bonne devotion le retour du courrier que je vous ay envoié pour convier sa S.té au baptesme de mon filz, lequel se faict tres bien nourrir et se fortifie a veue d’oeil” — the dauphin, born on 27 September. The letter is dated “Escrit a St Germain en Laye le xxij.e jour de 9bre 1601”, and a postscript, signed again, countermands part of what precedes it. The eighty ciphered runs are in bethune/ct_22nov.txt . Decoded with the key they give fragments only — le cardinal aldobrandin , attenter a este toute , suisses , octobre , saincteté au — which is the same ceiling the 9 November letter meets, and for the same reason. Two values are confirmed by their clear frames, 73 = vostre and the pair 48 17 = Cardinal Aldobrandin . Fifteen groups remain open; three of them have frames that constrain them, and one, 72, has a proposal against it as well as for it (see below).

t: Henri IV to Béthune, 9, 10 and 22 November 1601 — two letters read, and the ceiling on the third measured
h: The 9 November letter, and the ceiling on it
b: The corpus of known plaintext — the 10 November pair, the six glossed passages of 8 November, the footnote passage of 10 December, about 1,650 letters — was aligned by an EM procedure in which each symbol may stand for zero to twelve letters under a proper prior over strings, seeded with the values fixed by hand and allowing nulls only on the signs Bazeries’ design uses for them. The resulting P(letter | symbol) feeds the decoders. A second pass re-read the leaf symbol by symbol at four times magnification, fixed the doubling sign, the syllable groups, ꝑ = u/v and a dozen letters on words of the minute, and lifted the reading to about six words in ten: …sera la promotion au cardinalat … Alexandre … ensemble ce que vous aurez … jamais il m’avoit dit … propos de rechercher le cardinal … de vous dire la res[olution] … de telles pratiques … des advis desdits car[dinaux] . A third pass added a bigram language model built from Xivrey’s 1.43 million words, which brought in sur le revenu de Naples , le nunce resident , les cardinaux … enclins a la [26] and aux prudens advis desdits card[inaux] . The letter is about the Spanish pressure over Don Alexandre’s cardinalate and the cardinals’ advice, not the military news its clear opening suggests. What that third pass added that matters more is a way of telling when to stop. An oracle bound lets every transcribed symbol emit any value in its model’s support and asks how many of the true letters it could then possibly produce. On the known-plaintext blocks that ceiling is 71.0 %, while the decoder scores 74.5 % — it is already above its own emission bound, getting a few letters right by accident. No further work on the search or the language model can help: roughly 29 % of the true letters cannot be produced by the glyphs as transcribed at all. Ten things tried against that bound, all measured, none of which moved it. Widening each symbol’s emissions to those of its visually confusable partners raises the ceiling to 80.6 % but lowers the real decode from 74.5 % to 71.9 %: more ambiguity than the language model can resolve. Three segmentation architectures. Connected components give 1.13–1.38 components per glyph and both over- and under-cut. A forced alignment that never cuts — a dynamic program giving each token of a known sequence a variable-width slice, with templates re-estimated from the alignment — collapses to the average glyph from a uniform start. Restricting the cuts to component boundaries with a per-class width model leaves the program no freedom to recover where the components are wrong. More resolution. The second pass read from Gallica’s 2,000-pixel image; the 3,926-pixel original gives about 30 % more linear resolution, and the glyphs are visibly crisper. It does not settle them. Letting the language model re-split the figures. The re-reading did localise the disagreement — it clusters in the figure runs, not the letters, because the cipher writes figures without separators and one- and two-figure groups coexist, so “6165” reads as 61|65, 6|1|65 or 61|6|5. Offering every legal split to the decoder scores 70.8 %, and turns partant into “par [70] le roy d’Espaigne [2]”. Two independent readings, unioned. The one widening that does help, and the measurement that ends the argument. A block of 102 letters of known plaintext was read again from scratch off the full-resolution leaf without consulting the first transcription. Reader A (the second pass) scores 75.5 %, reader B (the third) 57.8 %; they agree on 50 of 72 aligned positions, and their union reaches 78.4 %. Nearly three points — and the second reading is worse than the first, despite the extra resolution. Two careful readers of the same ink agreeing on 69 % of its tokens is not carelessness. It is the statement that this hand does not carry enough information at roughly 450 dpi to fix its glyphs, which is what the 71 % bound says in another form. The confusions are sub-glyph, and one example fixes the point. In conduitte , whose reading is verified against the minute, the same m-shaped glyph stands for d in one position and i in the next, the two differing only by a hook. The three families recorded earlier — an open-tailed and a looped g (n and s), three m -shapes (g, d, f), r against the 2-shaped r (r and s) — are real, and no magnification separates them. The note in the repository that called the remainder “a day’s work, mechanical” is now corrected there, with the numbers: it was not the two-digit names that stood in the way.

t: Henri IV to Béthune, 9, 10 and 22 November 1601 — two letters read, and the ceiling on the third measured
h: The code groups, and one proposal with evidence both ways
b: The groups that carry the substance of both open letters — 2, 5, 6, 8, 9, 12, 20, 28, 31, 44, 66, 67, 69, 72, 80 — occur only where there is no decipherment. Three have clear frames that constrain them: S 12 and 20 are the two persons “douez de toute prudence”; 28 is a place, from “ce[luy] m’a escrit de [28]”; 44 follows “et par consequent”. One has a proposal, recorded here the way this project records unconfirmed things. 72 = vous : the collocation “x , 72” — que followed by 72 — occurs four times across ff. 46r, 46v, 47r and 33; 72 opens a line three times; and on f. 53r, whose marginal decipherment is verbatim rather than a paraphrase, the gloss reads “…je ne suis pas d’auis que vous pressiez sa Sain.té…” exactly where the cipher runs x , 72 , T 63 , r S Z , which with the established T = p, 63 = re, r = s, Z = e gives que · vous · p-re-s-s-e . Against it: the block on f. 49v ends … 63 72 while its footnote gloss ends “il sera meilleur de differer a luy en parler”, where a final vous is hard to place. Either the ciphered block runs on past the passage the footnote glosses, or 72 is something else. It stays unconfirmed , and is used in no reading on this page. The glossed leaves are the way to settle them, and examining ff. 53r and 56r at full resolution showed why they are tractable: their decipherments are verbatim, and whole clear phrases sit inside the ciphered blocks — “discours d’aultruy. Il fault” on f. 53r, “Mais je ne croy pas quil le face” and “si ce n’est pour” on f. 56r — each also in the gloss, in the gloss’s own order. Those are free anchors for an alignment. f. 53r contains 66 and 72; f. 56r’s margins name the King of Spain and Archduke Albert in clear. Neither block is transcribed.

t: Henri IV to Béthune, 9, 10 and 22 November 1601 — two letters read, and the ceiling on the third measured
h: What would finish the 9 November letter
b: Not more computation. The clear text of both open letters should exist in a copy, and the search for it turned up the right volume. BnF, Cinq cents de Colbert 346 is “Copies des despesches concernans l’ambassade de Messire Philippe de Bethune, conseiller du Roy en son Conseil d’Estat, à Rome, en 1601-[1605]”, whose first volume runs 23 August 1601 to 22 November 1602 and holds letters of Henri IV, Marie de Médicis, Villeroy and Béthune. That range covers both the 9 and the 22 November letters, and a copy register of this kind is made from the minutes — that is, in clear, which is exactly how the 10 November letter came to be readable here. It is not digitised: Gallica’s SRU returns no record for it. Reading it in the Salle des manuscrits, or ordering reproductions, is the single most valuable thing anyone can do to this target. Second, and independent: Eugène Halphen edited Lettres inédites du roi Henri IV à monsieur de Béthune, ambassadeur de France à Rome, du 18 octobre au 24 décembre 1601 , an edition covering precisely this stretch. It is in the HathiTrust catalogue (record 100644113) and not in Gallica, the Internet Archive or Open Library. Whether Halphen printed the ciphered passages in clear — which would have required the minutes — decides whether these letters count as already in print, as fr. 3077/3078 did for Du Bellay. Checked and excluded as sources of a clear text: Berger de Xivrey’s Recueil , vols. I–V, which prints a Béthune letter of 10 October 1601 but nothing for November; Mélanges de Colbert 17, whose first part is still running instructions at p. 179 and whose second is 1602–05; and BnF fr. 3677 and 3678, the “Registre des lettres que monseigneur de Bethune a escrites en France durant son ambassade de Rome”, which belong to the second embassy of 1624–30.

t: Ambrogio Bizozola to Maximilian Sforza, Bologna, 4 November 1529 — read with Lasry’s key
b: Catalogue item 176, BnF fr. 3034 ff. 156–157 (DECODE R4224): four pages of invented signs to the exiled Duke of Milan. George Lasry rebuilt the key in 2023 but no text was published. Read here from the Gallica scans, all four pages: written at Bologna on the eve of Charles V’s entry (5 November 1529), it reports that the Emperor’s council was discussing a partition of the Milanese state among Savoy, Monferrato, Mantua and Ferrara. The Archbishop of Bari is reported to say that Milan should rather go to Maximilian himself. 97% of the signs read; the date numerals stay open. Bologna → Maximilian Sforza in France · letter substitution with invented signs · Bologna, 4 November 1529 · read Ambrogio Bizozola to Maximilian Sforza to Maximilian Sforza BnF, Français 3034, ff. 156r–157v (no. 69 of the volume), DECODE R4224: four pages in cipher, catalogued as not deciphered. George Lasry reconstructed the key in November 2023, and Satoshi Tomokiyo shows it on his cryptiana site, but no text had been published. The letter is on Gallica. Read here with Lasry’s key, all four pages: written at Bologna on the eve of Charles V’s entry, 4 November 1529. Daniel Bourdeau · read 21 September 2026 read Summary. Catalogue item 176 is a letter from Ambrogio Bizozola to Maximilian Sforza. Maximilian was Duke of Milan until 1515 and lived in France until his death in 1530. On DECODE the letter is “Non-decrypted”, with its images behind a login. Tomokiyo’s page on the ciphers of the Montmorency volumes shows a key table for it, signed by George Lasry on 5 November 2023: one invented sign per letter, A to V, and five signs left unknown. The volume is digitised on Gallica (ark btv1b90600370, views 246–251). Every line of the first page and some later lines were cut from the full-resolution scans and transcribed, and Lasry’s table read them as Italian at once. The text itself forced a few homophones: one sign serves for a and u , and the long s serves for both f and s . The first page reports, from “a man worthy of faith”, that the Emperor’s council had several times discussed dividing the state of Milan: pieces for the Duke of Savoy, the Marquis of Monferrato, the Marquis of Mantua and the Duke of Ferrara, and Milan itself for a duke whose name is not yet clear. The second page reports that the Emperor is at the Certosa a mile outside the town, that “tomorrow is the entry”, and that the cardinals and the ambassadors of Venice and Milan went out to meet him. The date line on the last page reads “Bologna, quattro del … novembre”, and Charles V entered Bologna on 5 November 1529. The sign that Lasry left as unknown, ꝏ, turns out to be a line-end filler. A second pass at double scale settled the doubtful lines: the Archbishop of Bari’s opinion was that Milan should rather go to Duke Maximilian, “che di ragione li viene”, the recipient himself; the others named are Alessandro Attavante and Iacopo Salviati. 54 of 1907 signs stay doubtful (97% read), among them the numerals of the date line. BnF fr. 3034 f. 156r (Gallica view 246): the clear salutation Ill.mo mio sig.or sempre cordiall.mo and the first cipher lines, per le mie ultime di Cremona… intese molte cose . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3034 f. 156r, via Gallica (view 246).

t: Ambrogio Bizozola to Maximilian Sforza, Bologna, 4 November 1529 — read with Lasry’s key
b: The letter is no. 69 of fr. 3034, one of the Montmorency volumes of Italian despatches. It fills ff. 156r–157v. The salutation, the closing ( D. V. Ill.ma Ex.tia … sig.ria ) and the signature ( Humil.e Ser.or Ambrosio Bizozola ) are in clear, and everything else is in cipher. The address is on the following leaf: Allo Ill.mo et Ex.mo Principe Il S. Maximiliano Sforza … patron suo osser.mo … In Franza, Ala Corte . DECODE dates it 1520/1529. The clear parts carry no date. The cipher does: the last lines read Bologna, quattro del … novembre , and the letter describes the eve of the Emperor’s entry into the town. Charles V entered Bologna on 5 November 1529, so the letter is of 4 November 1529. The year is inferred, not written. Lasry’s table gives one sign for each letter: A ʒ, B 7, C a 9 with a tail, D 1, E ꝗ, F ʃ, G 2, H 6, I 8, L ʓ, M ε, N Γ, O 11, P a tall cross, Q Ꝗ, R a T-shaped stroke, S ɗ, T and V two further signs. Words are separated by spaces. The text adds four refinements. A long-looped sign that is not drawn in the table as published stands for t , as molte , intese and rotta require. ʒ is used for u as well as a ( aolte = volte, daca = duca). The long s is used for f and for s ( fatti , consiglio ). In the postscript a small cross stands for e . Lasry’s “unknown” ꝏ occurs only at the ends of lines, where a word runs on ( al duca ꝏ / di Savoia ), so it is a filler. Two or three other unknown signs occur only in the date line and are probably its numerals.

t: Ambrogio Bizozola to Maximilian Sforza, Bologna, 4 November 1529 — read with Lasry’s key
b: f. 156r, normalised; square brackets mark stretches not yet secure. Per le mie ultime di Cremona et far[..] [ꝏ] e de qui [..] intese molte cose de le actione de misere [..] i figli[..], come sono passato li [..] con lo imperatore, et che molte volte si è misso ogni cosa in rotta. Qua ho saputo per uno omo degno di fede che per questi rumori che il consiglio del imperatore più volte hanno fatti di grandi discorsi sopra il ducato [..], dicendo che [..] Francesco [..] uno altro [..] di fare molte parte dil stato: al duca [ꝏ] di Savoia, al marchese di Monferrato, al marchese di Mantua, al duca di Ferrara, et Milano al duca Alisandro; in questo ragionamento dise l’arciepiscopo di Baro: meglio io seria darlo al duca Maximiliano, che di ragione li viene … (f. 156v, ll. 13–17) … domane sarà l’intrata. Non di meno oggi li è andato incontra tutti li cardinali et ambassatori; quello di Venecia et de Milano hanno parlato [a] Sua Maiestà cossì a cavallo. (postscript, f. 157v) Sono molti giorni non ho vostre littere; avere il recepto di questa … The rest of f. 156v weighs whether Duke Francesco would have to be satisfied and what his brother should have, and says that the writer has written to the Pope. f. 157r concerns “misere Iulio”, a negotiation together with the Venetians, waiting to see whether the duke will come, Trivulzio, and the promise of a cardinal’s hat. f. 157v hopes that the affair of misere Iulio will pass into the Pope’s power, mentions ten thousand scudi of income a year, and ends with the date line. The decoder output, line by line, is reading_raw.txt in the repository. In English, f. 156r: “By my last from Cremona … Here I have learned from a man worthy of faith that the Emperor’s council has several times held great discussions about the duchy … of making many parts of the state: to the Duke of Savoy, to the Marquis of Monferrato, to the Marquis of Mantua, to the Duke of Ferrara, and Milan to the duke …; in this discussion the Archbishop of Bari said … I believe that if this were done, Duke Francesco would have to be satisfied …” f. 156r, lines 15–17: marchese di Mantua al duca di Ferrara / et Milano al duca … in questo / ragionamento … Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3034 f. 156r, lines 15–17, via Gallica (view 246).

Catalogue item 78 listed six DECODE records from BL Add MS 32305 under one unknown sender in Paris. The images show a working file, not a correspondence. R2963 (a German letter, 1719) and R2974 (a letter cipher, November 1749) carry full decipherments written over the figures at the time, and so do four neighbouring records outside the item. R2969, listed as the nearest key, is a frequency count headed “Carré 1742”, not a key. The open material is two codes. The Paris letters of 7 and 10 February 1719 (R2964, R2965) are clear French with runs of 3-figure code. The 7 February letter has 354 groups, 191 distinct values, 116 of them seen once, and the highest is 900. The decipherer of the time glossed about a dozen common values, and those glosses are not in alphabetical order, so the code is two-part and the known values bracket nothing. The Carré letters (R2968, R2970, R2972, the middle one catalogued separately as item 70 and now folded into item 78) are entirely in figures, with no gloss and no crib. All three were transcribed: 1,323 groups, 381 distinct values from 1 to 800, matching the decipherer’s own tally on f. 13 to within one group in 300. A letter-by-letter homophonic solution scores no better than the same groups shuffled, and the value order does not follow French alphabetical order, so this too is a two-part code of word-level entries. Neither code can be broken from this much ciphertext. Their key, a clear copy, or many more letters in the same code would be needed.

t: Paris 1719 and Carré 1742–45 code letters — two-part codes, not read
b: R2964, f. 6r: “J’avois été deja informé par” and the code, with the decipherer’s que (184), qu’il (652) and vous (243) above. Image: British Library, Add MS 32305 f. 6r, via DECODE R2964. The writer reports Lord Stair’s formal entry into Paris and his audience with the King, and tells his correspondent that he will stay in England “jusqu’au retour de S. M. Brit.” The clear text uses a family cover (“vos Parens”, “votre Cousin”, “le caractère des esprits de votre Famille”), and the second letter opens on the coming war with Spain and Cardinal Alberoni. The persons are figures marked with a cross: 27, 258, 285, 611. The decipherer glossed 36 = re, 88 = pas, 95 = le, 184 = que, 243 = vous, 347 = a, 531 = pour, 652 = qu’il and 786 = s, the same values in both letters. That is 33 of the 354 groups of the first letter. In a one-part code, where values run in alphabetical order, these would bracket the rest. Here re (36) comes before pas (88), le (95) and que (184), and a comes at 347, so the code is two-part and its order says nothing. With about 700 groups in the two letters for a code of some 900 entries, most values occur once, and the decipherer stopped where anyone would.

t: Paris 1719 and Carré 1742–45 code letters — two-part codes, not read
b: Three letters addressed to “Mr Carré in Pall Mall”, entirely in 3-figure groups, with no clear text and no gloss. All three are fair copies made by the intercepting office. R2968 (ff. 11–12) is headed “Anonyme à Monsr Carré en Pellmall à Londres”, March 1742. R2970 (ff. 14–17) is a “Copie d’une Lettre en Chiffre, sans date”, addressed with the writer’s mark ΔΔΔ to Mr Carré “en Palmal” under cover to a Mr Chevening(?), jeweller near Charing Cross, signed “Anonyme” and endorsed “R Aug. 22 1742” : it was received on 22 August 1742, five months after R2968. R2972 (ff. 22–23) is dated London, 19 January 1745. Record Groups Distinct Highest R2968 372 208 796 R2970 470 219 800 R2972 481 196 796 All three 1,323 381 800 The transcription checked against the decipherer’s tally. R2969 (f. 13, “Carré 1742”) counts the groups of the two 1742 letters together, R2968 and R2970, including a line the copyist of R2968 wrote twice and bracketed. With that line included, the transcription here gives exactly R2969’s figure for 686 (20), 212 (19), 106 (18), 121 and 12 (14), 707 (12), 781 (11), 539 and 621 (10), and fifteen more values down to 7; it differs by one for 573, 27 and 772. So the text is sound to about one group in 300. R2969’s tentative de for 686 and 106 and la for 121 are dotted guesses, not a key. Statistics. 147 of the 381 values occur once. Every hundred from 1 to 800 has 36–62 distinct values in use, so the whole range is live. The profile is flat: the commonest value, 212, is 2.3% of the text, then 12, 106 and 686 at 1.8–2.0%. Repeats are short: 94 repeated bigrams, 24 trigrams, 8 four-grams and one five-gram (151 521 330 621 212, in both 1742 letters). A run 95 57 606 451, three times in 1745 and underlined by a later hand, is probably a name spelled out. The 1745 letter uses the same code: 73% of its tokens are values seen in 1742. The intercepting clerk underlined single groups, probably proper names; 135, 204, 785 and 80 are underlined in both 1742 letters. Not a letter cipher. An assignment of one letter to each group was annealed against a French 4-gram model. It reaches −2.09 and −2.11 per character on the real text, and −2.12 and −2.17 on the same groups in shuffled order: no difference, and the output is gibberish. With 381 types for 1,323 tokens a letter homophonic would be overfitted in any case; the type–token ratio and the Zipf-like profile are a word code’s. Not a one-part code. In a one-part French code the mass of le, la, les, que, qui, et, en would pile up in their alphabetical bands. The observed token mass per band of 50 values, set against what an alphabetical list of the 700 commonest French words predicts, correlates at r = −0.26. Placing the 30 commonest values at their proportional alphabetical positions does no better than chance: 86% of 2,000 random placements do as well. The contemporary guess of de for both 686 and 106, two values far apart, points the same way. This is a two-part code of about 800 entries, like the Paris 1719 code in the same volume, whose glosses prove the two-part order. The language is assumed to be French from the headings; nothing in the figures confirms it. 1,323 tokens of a random-order code of about 800 entries allow a handful of guesses for the commonest words and no way to check them, and no crib is known. The decipherer of 1742 stopped at the frequency count and a few pencil letters under R2972. The attack is closed.

t: Bordeaux to Brienne, London, 30 May 1653 — read with the English key sheet, once the transcription was right
b: Thurloe’s intercept of the French envoy’s despatch, BL Add MS 4200 f. 88: 813 tokens (810 in the provisional transcription) of a Brienne-office cipher whose syllables run alphabetically through three marked series. A solver built on that design read its controls but not the letter. The Deciphering Branch’s own sheet for “Mr. Bordeaux”, Add MS 32263 f. 1 (DECODE R7537), is the key; checked against the page images, the transcription had merged two signs (ꝺ = u, ∂ = n), dropped tokens and lost marks. The Council heard the deputies of rebel Bordeaux before Cromwell gave the King’s envoy his audience, and Brienne is told to hold back French mediation. London → Paris · letters, syllabaries in three marked series, and a nomenclator · 30 May 1653 · read Bordeaux to Brienne, London, 30 May 1653 British Library, Add MS 4200, ff. 88–90, among Thurloe’s papers · 810 cipher tokens over 156 symbols between clear opening and close · no decipherment on the leaf, the English worksheets unfinished Read with the English Deciphering Branch’s key sheet for “Mr. Bordeaux”, BL Add MS 32263 f. 1, after the transcription was checked against the page images · the ciphertext-only attack of 16 September is explained: the design was right, the transcription was not Daniel Bourdeau · read 18 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. Antoine de Bordeaux-Neufville was Mazarin’s envoy to the English Commonwealth, and his despatches to the Secretary of State Brienne were opened in the post by Thurloe’s office. The letter of 30 May 1653 (new style) survives in Add MS 4200 with its ciphered middle unread. English frequency tables and contact counts sit beside it, but no decipherment. On 16 September this repository identified the cipher as the Brienne office’s design, in which consecutive numbers run through the syllables in alphabetical order. A solver built on that design read matched controls but not the letter. The DECODE catalogue listed a Deciphering Branch key sheet, BL Add MS 32263 f. 1, as a key of 1653 for “Mr. Bordeaux”. It is that cipher’s key, a worksheet with the syllabary series set out exactly as predicted. Applied to a transcription corrected against the page images, it reads the letter. The Council heard the deputies of rebel Bordeaux through two commissioners before Cromwell, le General , gave the French envoy his audience. The treaty agreed after the Parliament’s resolutions is still unsigned, and England is said to be helping Bordeaux indirectly. Brienne should therefore hold back the offer of French mediation. Status: read end to end. About twenty of 811 tokens stay open: six nomenclature codes (names, among them probably the Stuart king) and a dozen rare syllable numbers, each noted below.

t: Bordeaux to Brienne, London, 30 May 1653 — read with the English key sheet, once the transcription was right
b: Add MS 4200 is one of the Birch volumes of Thurloe’s state papers. Folio 88 is headed in an English hand A Letter from Bordeaux the French Amb.r in England . The letter opens in clear, Monsieur, Cellecy vous fera veoir, que la nouvelle de mon retour en France n’est pas vraye , and continues in cipher for 63 lines over five pages. It returns to clear with on n’a point icy aucune nouvelle de la flotte depuis qu’elle a paru à la hauteur d’Escosse and closes De Bordeaux, A Londres 30 May 1653 . The English made a second copy of the opening and a second copy of the ending, with a frequency count (DECODE R8393 and R8391), and started contact tables on the commonest signs (R8386, R8388, R8389). None of these reaches a reading. f. 88r, the head of the letter: the clear opening Cellecy vous fera veoir, que la nouvelle de mon retour en France n’est pas vraye , then the first five lines of cipher, which read Ce n’est pas que si nos affaires estoyent plus florissantes… Image: British Library, Add MS 4200 f. 88r, via DECODE R8390. The plaintext is not in print. Birch printed twelve of Bordeaux’s despatches of 1653 in the Thurloe State Papers and Guizot sixty more from the French foreign ministry’s archive, but neither has this one. Satoshi Tomokiyo published a provisional transcription of the cipher on cryptiana . His list gives the companion letter, Mazarin to Bordeaux of 22 June 1654, as solved by George Lasry in February 2025.

t: Bordeaux to Brienne, London, 30 May 1653 — read with the English key sheet, once the transcription was right
h: The first attempt, and why it failed
b: Tomokiyo’s transcription has 810 tokens over 156 symbols. There are 24 graphic signs ( u , x , d , ll , m , …), plain numbers, and numbers carrying a prime, two dots or an overbar. Brienne’s office used one design for its ciphers of 1651–54, known from two recovered keys: his cipher to d’Estrades of 1651, and Lasry’s key for the 1654 letter. In both, letters are signs or low numbers, and the syllables ba be bi bo bu ca ce … take consecutive numbers in alphabetical order through marked series, with a few common words filed in their alphabetical place. On 16 September a simulated-annealing solver was built with that order as a hard constraint and tested on controls: a Bordeaux despatch of 1654 enciphered with a random key of the same design and the same size. It read three of six control runs to within 1% of the key. On the letter, 21 runs over three series orders stopped at the level of the control’s failed runs. A second control, with one diacritic in ten misread, fell to 52% and 9%, and the notes concluded that a provisional transcription could explain the failure on its own. That turned out to be the case. Checked against the page images, the transcription has three kinds of fault, and together they are enough to stop a ciphertext-only attack: Two signs written as one. The transcription’s d covers two different glyphs, a looped ꝺ that is u and a backward ∂ that is n ( conte·n·te·me·∂·t , Bordea·ꝺ·x ). The English frequency count on f. 92 lists them on separate lines, so the 1653 analysts saw two signs. Dropped tokens and marks. In line 2, plus florissantes needs 76¨ ( lo ) and 27 ( n ), which the transcription leaves out. Elsewhere 96¨ na appears as 96‾, 79′ vous as 74′, 64′ ti as b 4′ , and 97¨ ne as a plain 97. Twenty-one corrections in all. One of them, the 52′ of commissaires , was omitted by the clerk himself and is restored from the duplicate R8393. The clerk’s own omissions. He often writes a syllable number without its mark: 38 for et , 43 for 43′ re , 54 for si , 97 for ne . In this design the mark is what separates re from a letter. A solver that trusts the marks puts those tokens in the wrong series.

Ce n’est pas que si nos affaires estoyent plus florissantes nous n’eussions sujet de tesmoi[g]ner quelque mescontentement de la reception qui a esté faite aux deputez de Bordeaux. Ils ont esté entendus par deux commissaires du Conseil, et l’audiance que j’avois demandée au General ne me fut donnée qu’après la leur. L’on d’y de[..]er ; ils [..]rent leurs propositions {332} au {396} [..] separées {344}, et je croy que l’on y delibere aussi bien que sur les miennes, quoy qu’après les resolutions prises dans le [Parlement] il ne restast plus qu’à signer les traitez dont nous estions demeurez d’accord. L’on m’advertist de plusieurs endroits qu’indirectement on veut y secourir Bordeaux. C’est pourquoy si vous n’avés point encores offert vostre mediation, elle se pourroit surseoir jusqu’à ce que je voye quelle sera la conduite de cet Estat. Je n’ay pas laissé dans mon dernier discours d’asseurer que Sa Majesté [s’y] employeroit avec affection ; mais s’ils prennent des mesures avec Bordeaux, ils n’auront pas grande confiance à nostre bonne volonté. La crainte que si la [France] se trouve purgée de seditions elle ne favorise le parti du {25}, et la retraite que l’on a donnée au {28}, sont capables de fort [faire] prendre au General une resolution contraire à nos interests. Si les {43} envoyent icy des deputez pour traiter de [..], comme l’on publie, il se [..]era encores plus. Ce n’est pas que son interest propre ne le deust obliger de rechercher nostre alliance, mais il croit y p[..] à temps quand mesmes il auroit delivré Bordeaux de la misere où elle se trouve. Dans peu de jours j’en seray informé avec plus de certitude. On n’a point icy aucune nouvelle de la flotte … English A paraphrase. Brackets carry over where the reading is doubtful. This will show you that the news of my return to France is not true. Even if our affairs were more flourishing, we would still have reason to show some displeasure at the reception given to the deputies of Bordeaux. They were heard by two commissioners of the Council, and the audience I had asked of the General was not given me until after theirs. [..]; they [..] their proposals [..], and I believe their proposals are being deliberated as well as mine, although after the resolutions taken in [Parliament] nothing remained but to sign the treaties we had agreed on. I am told from several quarters that they mean to help Bordeaux indirectly. So if you have not yet offered your mediation, it could be held back until I see what this State’s conduct will be. In my last speech I did not fail to assure them that His Majesty would [apply himself to it] with affection; but if they come to terms with Bordeaux, they will not have much confidence in our good will. The fear that a [France] purged of sedition would favour the party of {25}, and the refuge that has been given to {28}, could well [make] the General take a resolution against our interests. If the {43} send deputies here to treat of [..], as is said, it will be [..] still more. It is not that his own interest ought not to oblige him to seek our alliance; but he thinks he can [..] in time, even if he had freed Bordeaux from the misery it is in. In a few days I shall know more certainly. The clear close, read from the duplicate R8391, gives the other news: nothing of the fleet since it was seen off Scotland. It also reports that Cromwell aura ung corps composé de sept vingt personnes choisis par l’armée, et approuvés par les provinces , a body of seven score chosen by the army, which is the Nominated Assembly that met in July. The Swedish resident has no answer to his offer, and the Portuguese none on his peace treaty.

t: Bordeaux to Brienne, London, 30 May 1653 — read with the English key sheet, once the transcription was right
b: Bordeaux-Neufville had come to London at the end of 1652 to win recognition of the young Louis XIV’s government from the Commonwealth and to keep England out of the Fronde. The city of Bordeaux, held by the Ormée and Condé’s party against the King, had sent its own deputies to ask for English help. The letter is written four weeks after Cromwell dissolved the Rump (20 April 1653, old style). Its complaint is about order and precedence. The Council heard the rebels’ deputies through two commissioners, and only then gave the King’s envoy his audience with le General . Bordeaux reads this as a sign that the treaty, settled except for the signing, is being weighed against the rebels’ proposals. His advice is tactical. Brienne should not offer French mediation until the English position is clear, because help for the city, even indirect, would show there is no trust on the English side. The English fear, as he reports it, is that a France at peace at home would back the Stuarts. In the event the city surrendered to the royal army at the end of July 1653, and the Anglo-French treaty was not signed until 1655.

The sheet has fort ; the sense of capables de fort prendre would be better served by faire . The value is left as the sheet gives it. The key sheet’s date. Aug. 20th 1832 is how the heading reads. t: Charles I and Nicholas to Boswell — a regular key, four signs and the wrong addressee
b: Two ciphered letters of 2 November 1643 (TNA SP 84/157). The alphabet is Robert Pitt’s: a 24-letter row four times over 20–115, verified here at z = 9.6 against 20,000 permuted rows. Added here: the four graphic signs are word-signs introduced inside the spelled word (good, Cousin, Master, us), and the King’s letter is his re-credentials to the Duke of Courland’s envoy, sent through Boswell in Boswell’s cipher. Both letters read in substance. Oxford → The Hague · regular Stuart figure cipher · 1643 · read Charles I and Nicholas to Boswell from Charles I 2 November 1643 · The National Archives, SP 84/157 ff. 217 and 219 (State Papers Foreign, Holland) The alphabet is Robert Pitt’s (September 2026). Added here: the statistical control, the four signs, the addressee, and a connected reading of both letters Daniel Bourdeau · read 15 September 2026 · updated 16 September 2026 read Summary. Two ciphered letters of the same day, transcribed provisionally by S. Tomokiyo in 2021 and listed on his page of unsolved ciphers. Robert Pitt published the alphabet on 14 September 2026: a 24-letter row repeated four times over the figures 20–115, supplementary homophones in alphabetical blocks at 116–159, nulls below 20, and four word codes. That solution is not claimed here. What this page adds is verification and reading. A permutation control puts Pitt’s row 9.6 standard deviations above 20,000 random rows on the same periodic structure, with none as good. The four graphic signs that Pitt’s notes left unexplained turn out to be word-signs introduced inline — the clerk wrote the sign beside the word the first time he spelled it ( good , Cousin , Master , us ) and used it alone thereafter — which closes the three framed passages as “our good Cousin your Master”. And the King’s letter is not to Boswell at all: it is his answer and re-credentials to the Duke of Courland’s envoy, stuck at The Hague, sent through Boswell in Boswell’s own cipher, as Nicholas’s covering letter says in so many words. Simpson’s 1893 print of the King’s parallel letter to the Duke, same date, confirms the frame and gives 291 = Duke. Status: read in substance. A dozen single-occurrence word codes and some transcription slips wait on the folios, which are not online.

The Difficulty of passage {we} feare {hath} preiudiced us. Our Cousin your Master’s affeccons & offers are soe reall & acceptable to us, specially in this coniuncture of our Affaires, as we acknowledge [our] [selves] there[by] highly obliged. We [pray] you therefore to present our princely thanks [177] on this behalf, to [assure] our said Cousin your Master, & to lett him understand that we shall most [wel]comly receiue his [assistance] with in [755] [188] [musket]s, match & [powder], in {what} [pro]por[tion] it shall please him to transmit the same to us, to the [port] of Weymouth, Dartmouth, Exeter, Falmouth or [228]. Not doubting but God will shortly enable Us to recompence soe free & soe [gener]ous a c[591] & es[126]. Doe assure your self also of our fauour particular, & doe take your addres by [213] to us in very good part, as also that you haue taken care to avoyde the dangerousnes of the passage hither. And soe wishing you a safe returne back to our good Cousin your Master, to whom w[e] herewith [send] your re-credentials, Wee commit you to the Protection of the Almighty. His Majesty’s two letters herewith sent with flying Seales are put into your character, because most safe & ready; you are to decifer & interpret them. t: Charles I and Nicholas to Boswell — a regular key, four signs and the wrong addressee
b: The King’s letter is not to Boswell. It answers the envoy’s letter of 6 October, calls the Duke “your Master” three times, sends “your re-credentials”, and wishes him a safe return to his master. Simpson’s Civil War Papers (Scottish History Society Miscellany I, 1893) prints the King’s letter to Duke James of Courland of the same day, calling itself “these Our Re-credentials”, and the envoy’s later memorial: the passage was unsafe and “the ministers of their Majesties at the Hague” dissuaded him from crossing and took his letters. Nicholas tells Boswell that the King’s two letters are “put into your character” and that Boswell is to “decifer & interpret them”. Hence the catalogue’s “Charles I to Boswell”. “Monsieur F I R X S S appeares not here.” Simpson names Major Georg von Firks as the Duke’s agent. A man expected at Oxford who has not come is the envoy’s own account of himself. The arms. Muskets, match and powder to Weymouth, Dartmouth, Exeter, Falmouth or a fifth port: the Duke’s memorial says he was told their Majesties needed munitions rather than men, and Nicholas wrote to Roe in December 1643 that “arms and powder are arrived at Dartmouth for his Majesty” (CSPD). The funerals of Duke Friedrich (d. 1642) and his brother Wilhelm (d. 1640), held together in February 1643: “the Late Dukes his Father & Unkle”. Nicholas’s instruction to hinder “the coming ouer of the [181]s from the [726]”, people “understood here not to affect Monarchy”, fits the States General’s embassy of mediation resolved on in late 1643 and received at Oxford early in 1644, which the King did not want: 181+S = Ambassadors, 726 = States. That is a historical reading, not a cryptographic one.

t: Sir Ralph Boswell to his cousin William Boswell, December 1627 — already read by Mark Woodard
b: Ten lines of invented signs in TNA SP 106/5, catalogued on DECODE as King Charles I to Boswell, 1628, and undeciphered. Mark Woodard read the monoalphabetic cipher on DECODE in 2021. Here: two of his three open signs read, the sender identified from the endorsement as Sir Ralph Boswell, and the letter dated to 15 December 1627. England → William Boswell · monoalphabetic, invented signs · December 1627 · found read “Our great Duke returned from Plymouth”: Sir Ralph Boswell to his cousin, 1627 TNA State Papers 106/5 ff. 20–21 (DECODE R413), catalogued as a ciphered letter of King Charles I to William Boswell, 1628, with nothing known of its content. Mark Woodard deciphered it on DECODE in 2021. This page checks his key, fills three signs he left open, and identifies the sender and the date from the back of the letter. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 21 September 2026 Summary. The catalogue entry (no. 63) described ten lines of “esoteric symbols” from King Charles I to William Boswell. The DECODE record already holds a decipherment by Mark Woodard of Furman University, uploaded on 9 November 2021 and made with CrypTool 2’s monoalphabetic analyzer. It is a simple substitution, one invented sign per letter, and the text is English court news: Buckingham has come back from Plymouth to Whitehall, is confident of the King, and does not fear his enemies in the Commons. Aligning Woodard’s transcription with his plaintext shows every sign reading one letter without exception. Of his three open signs, one is s and one stands for a whole word, probably “part”. A pair of signs in the third line stays unread. The endorsement reads “S[i]r Ra: Boswele. 24 Jan. 1627”, so the writer is Sir Ralph Boswell, a kinsman (“my … Cosin”), not the King. “Saturday, our fifteenth of the present” then fixes the letter to 15 December 1627. Lines 1–3 of the cipher, turned to the writer’s orientation: Upon Saterday being our fifteenth of the presente… Image: The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/5 ff. 20–21, via DECODE R413.

t: Sir Ralph Boswell to his cousin William Boswell, December 1627 — already read by Mark Woodard
b: Page one has ten numbered lines of signs, written across the sheet, with no word division. Page two carries the address, To my Especiall & most Esteemed Cosin William Boswell Esq. , a seal, and the endorsement S[i]r Ra: Boswele. 24 Jan. 1627 , that is 1627/8. Below it, in the same hand, is a list of eight topics: Hopyan, Pettyt, the Court of Wards, Yorkshire lands, Sir Anthony Aucher, Morgan, one unread, and the Earl of Dorset. The same page has a tally of every cipher sign with the numbers of the lines it occurs in. That is the working sheet of whoever took the letter apart, either Boswell or a clerk. DECODE’s own note already doubted that the King wrote it; its author and 1628 date are catalogue placeholders.

t: Sir Ralph Boswell to his cousin William Boswell, December 1627 — already read by Mark Woodard
b: Upon Saterday, being our fifteenth of the presente, our[s] greate Duke returned from Plimmouth to Whitehall, contrary to the opinion of very many who conceaued he [​ w x ] would not haue appeard heere before he had heard how the pulse of the Parlamente had gone. But being confident of the King’s fauour, [f]eares not the many enemies that he hath in the Lower House, especially hauing so greate a party in the Higher House by reason of the Bishops and the new Lords, which for the most [part] are(d) of his owne makinge; and to take away the ill opini[on] of such lordes … The text breaks off mid-sentence at the end of line 10. The “new Lords” are the peers Buckingham had had created, the bishops were largely of his party, and the Parliament being discussed that winter was summoned by writs of 30 January 1628.

t: Henri IV to Savary de Brèves, 1603 — the key in fr. 3462 and the letters in print since 1853
b: Twelve royal letters of 1603 to the ambassador at the Porte, BnF fr. 3541, “avec chiffre” and listed as undeciphered, with a partial reading by Tomokiyo from a rebuilt key. The office’s own table survives as fr. 3462 f. 103, and Berger de Xivrey printed the letters in 1853 from a contemporary copy in clear: three in full, nine as summaries. Tomokiyo’s overlay of f. 60 is checked against the print ( revolteur d’Asie , protestans ). The cipher leaves are not digitised, so the letters have not been read against the key. Paris, Metz, Fontainebleau → Constantinople · homophonic alphabet with nomenclator · February–December 1603 · resolved Henri IV to Savary de Brèves, ambassador at Constantinople, 1603 from Henri IV Bibliothèque nationale de France, Français 3541 (anc. Béthune 9021) · twelve royal letters “avec chiffre”, ff. 60–104 · the year of the Celali revolt, the spahi rising at the Porte and Mehmed III’s death Listed as undeciphered (Desenclos 2018), with a partial reading by Tomokiyo from a key rebuilt from Brèves’s own letters. The original key survives in BnF fr. 3462, and the letters themselves were printed in 1853 from a contemporary copy in clear. The cipher leaves are not online, so the letters have not been read against the key here. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 18 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 resolved Summary. Two pieces of the answer were already in the BnF. First, the key: the leaf that Tomokiyo noticed after rebuilding it, fr. 3462 f. 103, is the office’s own table for Brèves’s 1602–03 cipher, with alphabet, nomenclator, persons, doubles and nulls. Second, the text: in 1853 Berger de Xivrey printed these letters in the Lettres missives de Henri IV from a copy in clear then in Monmerqué’s library, Lettres à l’ambassadeur du Levant . He gives three of them in full (18 February, 31 March, 17 April) and summarises the other nine. The volume holds twelve ciphered letters of 1603, not the two usually cited. Tomokiyo’s overlay of f. 60 matches Berger’s text closely, and Berger settles the places where the overlay went astray. Status: resolved from the printed text, not deciphered. Fr. 3541 is not digitised anywhere I could find. A second copy in clear is at the BnF: fr. 4029, a register of Henri IV’s letters to Brèves, has all twelve letters of 1603 on ff. 118–128. It is not digitised either. A reproduction of those eleven folios would give the full text of the nine summarised letters without any deciphering. A reproduction of fr. 3541 ff. 60–104 would let the letters be checked against the key.

t: Henri IV to Savary de Brèves, 1603 — the key in fr. 3462 and the letters in print since 1853
b: François Savary de Brèves was Henri IV’s ambassador at the Porte from 1591 to 1605. In 1604 he negotiated the renewal of the Capitulations. The BnF notice for fr. 3541 lists the King’s letters to him, several marked “avec chiffre”. For 1603 there are twelve. Berger de Xivrey’s source lines give the folios. 1603 Written at Fol. In Berger, Lettres missives VI 18 February Paris 60 full text, pp. 31–32 31 March Metz 63 full text, pp. 63–65 17 April Fontainebleau 66 full text, pp. 76–78 1 May Fontainebleau 69 summary, p. 668 13 May Fontainebleau 72 summary, pp. 669–70 22 June Paris 75 summary, pp. 670–71 22 July Nanteuil 78 summary, p. 672 6 August Saint-Germain 81 summary, p. 673 15 September Caen 84 summary, pp. 676–77 15 October Fontainebleau 104 summary, p. 678 (“chiffré à moitié”) 9 November Fontainebleau 87 summary, pp. 678–79 23 December Paris 90 summary, p. 680 (the BnF notice has the 24th) The letter usually cited as f. 63 of “1 March” is the Metz letter of 31 March, le dernier jour de mars . The same volume also has a fully ciphered letter of 5 January 1610 (f. 8) and a Puisieux letter with cipher (f. 39). Both date from Brèves’s later embassy in Rome and probably use another key. They were not examined.

t: Henri IV to Savary de Brèves, 1603 — the key in fr. 3462 and the letters in print since 1853
b: Tomokiyo rebuilt this cipher from Brèves’s letters to the King in BnF fr. 16144, and then noticed that the original is in fr. 3462, a volume of keys and jargons. The leaf is f. 103 (Gallica canvas 109). The next leaf, f. 104, is not the same key. It is the “Chiffre reformé pour Levant”, sent to Brèves in April 1604, after these letters. BnF fr. 3462 f. 103, the whole table: the persons on the left (from le Pape sa Saincteté to les Spahis gens de cheval ), the alphabet across the top, the nomenclator below, and the doubles and nulls at the foot of the last column. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3462 f. 103, via Gallica (btv1b9058227h). BnF fr. 3462 f. 103, the alphabet. Each letter has two to four substitutes: figures ( a = 7, 3, 5; b = 8, 9; e = 2, 3, 4), crosses and pseudo-letters. The long bar at the right end of the row belongs to the table. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3462 f. 103, via Gallica (btv1b9058227h). The table has five parts: An alphabet of homophones, figures and signs. A nomenclator in initial-letter blocks, numbered 10–99 for words in a – g ( aussi 11, avec 12, capitullations 57, Constantinople 59, corsaires 61, faire 92, fault 93, guerre 98), with signs for the rest ( le , que , qui , pour , vous , Turcs , galleres , vaisseaux , la mer ). A column of persons , each a single sign: the Pope, the King, the Emperor, the kings of Spain, Poland, Persia, Fez and Tartary, the Grand Seigneur, the Sultana his mother, the grand bassa, the viziers, the general of the sea, the aga of the janissaries, the beglerbey, the nissangi, the tesquitar and the spahis. Doubles , the figures 13, 49, 57, 30, 97, 38 and 70 marked with a caret. Two lists of nulls. Part of the nomenclator: aussi 11, avec 12, au 13 … capitulle 56, capitullations 57, Constantinople 59, corsaires 61 … faire 92, fault 93. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3462 f. 103, via Gallica (btv1b9058227h). The figures agree with the values Tomokiyo recovered from the ciphertext ( aussi 11, avec 12, faire 92, fault 93, a = 7/3/5), which confirms that this is the key of the letters. A transcription is in breves1603/key.md . Its numeric entries are firm. Its names for the signs are provisional until they can be checked against the ciphertext.

t: Henri IV to Savary de Brèves, 1603 — the key in fr. 3462 and the letters in print since 1853
b: Berger de Xivrey’s sixth volume of the Recueil des lettres missives de Henri IV (1853) cites each of these letters as “Orig. — B. N. Fonds Béthune, Ms. 9021, fol. …”, with a second source: “Cop. — Biblioth. de M. Monmerqué, Ms. intitulé Lettres à l’ambassadeur du Levant ”. That copy was in clear, and Berger printed from it. He gives the February, March and April letters whole. He lists the other nine in the table of unprinted letters at the end of the volume, each marked “(En chiffres)” and summarised. The Monmerqué manuscript has not been traced. It was probably dispersed with his library. The OCR of the 17 April letter garbles exactly those passages Berger seems to have set in italic, which may be how he marked what was in cipher. This is not checked against the printed page.

t: Henri IV to Savary de Brèves, 1603 — the key in fr. 3462 and the letters in print since 1853
b: Tomokiyo overlaid a preliminary letter-by-letter reading of f. 60 and the opening of f. 63 from his reconstructed key. Almost all of it stands. Where it does not, the cause is a sign read to the wrong homophone or a word boundary in the wrong place: Tomokiyo’s overlay Berger 1853 la juste jalousie que j’ay de mesuois*ns de mes voisins soit pour tomber et fault nau*ra *sitost que vous le ap*e soit pour tomber ou faire naufrage si tost que vous l’apprehendés ** roibuent plus craindre les armes du revolt eul dasie mais ils doivent plustost craindre les armes du revolteur d’Asie quel en sera le congres quel en sera le progrés entre les contestans et catholicques de la germanie entre les protestants et catholiques de la Germanie les armes estans ja pripes de *t et daultre les armes estans jà prestes d’une part et d’aultre (f. 63) quelle era este lissueduremument c?omance a la porte quelle aura esté l’isseue du remuement commencé à la Porte “Contestans” for protestans is probably a single sign: the key has a syllable sign for pro in the P block, and it may have been taken for con . Only the ciphertext can confirm this.

t: Henri IV to Savary de Brèves, 1603 — the key in fr. 3462 and the letters in print since 1853
b: Berger’s text of 18 February, from “que les desordres”, the stretch Tomokiyo’s overlay covers … les desordres de l’empire de ce Seigneur vont continuant et augmentant, à sa honte et au grand prejudice d’iceluy, et ay bien consideré et pris le conseil que vous me donnés sur cela, duquel je me serviray le mieux qu’il me sera possible ; mais la juste jalousie que j’ay de mes voisins ne me permet de faire pour ce regard tout ce que je desirerois et seroit necessaire. Je ne me puis persuader que cest empire soit pour tomber ou faire naufrage si tost que vous l’apprehendés, joinct que j’ay l’opinion, s’il y avoit du changement, que ce sera sur la personne du prince plustost qu’en autre chose ; car les ennemys du dict empire ne sont mieux conseillez et servys que luy, et ont des incommoditez qui les combattent, qui ne sont de petite importance ; mais ils doivent plustost craindre les armes du revolteur d’Asie que celles des autres. February. Brèves had written that the Ottoman empire might collapse. The King does not believe it: if anything changes, it will be the person of the sultan, not the empire. Its Christian enemies are no better led than it is, and the real danger is the rebel in Asia, the Celali rising. France is at peace. Bouillon has had to withdraw to Germany, finding no Protestant willing to rise for him. The King is leaving for Metz, where war threatens between the Protestants and Catholics of Germany over the bishopric of Strasbourg, disputed between Brandenburg and Lorraine. March, from Metz. He wants to know how the remuement at the Porte has ended, “car il en succedera un grand bien ou un grand mal” to the sultan and his empire. The Emperor is recruiting Frenchmen: Nevers, wounded at the assault on Buda, has vowed to go back. The King will not be drawn into mediating a peace between the Emperor and the sultan. He has ordered his subjects in the Levant to sail armed against English pirates. He reports that Elizabeth is gravely ill. April. The revolt of Mamoucte Bassa and the spahis against the sultan and his first vizier has been put down. The King regrets the fall of the mufti and his brother. Brèves is to congratulate the sultan, but not to ask for an Ottoman fleet, and to get out of the peace negotiation gently. The Emperor will not hear of peace, and the King of Spain is urging him against it so as to have a free hand at Algiers. Elizabeth is dead, and James has been proclaimed without opposition. May to December , from Berger’s summaries: the war in Hungary and Transylvania, with Moses Székely driving out Basta; the King’s wish that the Frenchmen serving the sultan withdraw, quietly and in Brèves’s own name; Spain’s enterprise on Algiers, taken up, dropped and taken up again; a treaty with James I disowning his subjects’ piracy, and Marseille ships to be armed against Barbary and English corsairs; the sultan’s chiaoux waiting at Marseille for a royal journey to Provence that did not happen that year; in August, surprise at the execution of the sultan’s son on a mere suspicion; in December, unease at “certain changement survenu à la Porte”, which the King fears favours the house of Austria. Mehmed III died on 22 December 1603, the day before the last of these letters was written. The renewal of the Capitulations in May 1604 falls after the series.

t: Henri IV to Savary de Brèves, 1603 — the key in fr. 3462 and the letters in print since 1853
b: The ciphertext. Fr. 3541 is not on Gallica: there are no records under its shelfmark or its old Béthune number, and the BnF notice has no link to a digital copy. Desenclos 2018 has no plates, and Tomokiyo does not say where his images came from. A reproduction of ff. 60–104 would let the nine summarised letters be read in full with the key. The three printed letters give about two pages of known plaintext to settle the key’s signs first. The full texts are at the BnF. Fr. 4029 (anc. 8962(3), olim Supplément français 500), a 17th-century “Recueil de copies de lettres”, holds 158 letters of Henri IV to Brèves from 1592 to 1608. Its nos. 131–142 are this series, from 18 February to 23 December 1603, one folio each on ff. 118–128. No. 130 is a letter of 6 January 1603 that has no ciphered original in fr. 3541. The volume is not on Gallica. Eleven folios of it would give the full text of the nine summarised letters, and a reproduction order for them is the cheapest way to finish this series. The Monmerqué copy that Berger used, Lettres à l’ambassadeur du Levant , is not needed. Guadet’s supplement (t. VIII–IX, 1872–76) does not print the nine in full. Checking the key’s signs. Brèves’s own letters to the King in the same cipher are online. Fr. 15578 f. 185 ( Gallica canvas 196 ) is fully ciphered, with the recipient’s decipherment written between the lines (“Je n’adjousteray a ma derniere … que la mort du grand …”). That makes it known plaintext for settling the provisional sign names in key.md before any images of fr. 3541 are obtained. It has not been transcribed yet. A loose end in Berger. His table (p. 667) also lists a “dépêche entièrement chiffrée” to Brèves of 17 April, “fol. 60”, with no copy cited. It is either a second April dispatch or a misprint. Only the manuscript can say which.

t: Maffeo da Treviglio to Ludovico Sforza, Buda 1489–1490 — the key reconstructed in 2016 had never been turned back into signs
b: Judit W. Somogyi reconstructed the cipher of Ludovico Sforza’s ambassador at the court of Matthias Corvinus in 2016, but printed it only as a table of numbers, with no image of a single sign, so nothing could be read with it. Her numbering turns out to follow the order of first appearance in the letter of 2 April 1490, which survives with its contemporary clear copy: matching the two gives the shapes back, and about twenty further signs came out of the reading. The two despatches that have no decipherment are now read, the 1489 letter in part (page 3 in patches). The four pages of 22 November 1489, of which only the first two lines had been published deciphered, cover the peace with Frederick III, the Diet, the marriage of John Corvinus against the rival Neapolitan match, the queen’s “insatiable wrath of Juno”, and a warning that intercepted cipher letters had been read; the letter of 12 January 1490 reports the king riding to Vienna on the 8th and the ambassadors following on the 15th, which its own clear second page confirms word for word. Somogyi in 2016 but printed only as numbers, with no picture of a single sign · her numbering runs in order of first appearance in a letter that survives with its clear copy, which turns the numbers back into signs · both letters now read Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 19 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read in part Summary. Maffeo da Treviglio (Maffeo de Bullis, 1430–1498) was Ludovico Sforza's man at Buda from the summer of 1489. His ciphered despatches are in the Milan state archive, some with a contemporary decipherment beside them and some without. Judit W. Somogyi reconstructed his cipher in 2016 from five cipher-and-clear pairs, but her article gives the key only in a numeric transcription: every sign appears as a two-digit number, and no image of any sign is printed, so the key could not be applied to anything. The numbers turn out to run in order of first appearance in the letter of 2 April 1490, which survives together with its contemporary clear copy in the Vestigia database. Matching the two restores the shapes behind the numbers, and about twenty further signs came out of the reading itself. With that, the two despatches that have no decipherment are now read. Buda, 12 January 1490: the king has left for Vienna and the ambassadors will follow on the 15th. Buda, 22 November 1489: four pages on the peace with the Emperor, the Diet, the marriage of John Corvinus, the rival Neapolitan match, the queen's anger, and a warning that intercepted cipher letters have been read. The 1489 letter is the oldest text this project has read; the previous mark was 1497.

b: Five letters of Maffeo survive with both a ciphered original and a contemporary clear copy; Somogyi used them to build her key. Two others are cipher with no decipherment of any kind, and those are the ones read here. Item Date, place Form Status before Vestigia 267 / 268 · Sforzesco 642, aprile nos. 6 and 6bis 2 April 1490, Vienna cipher + clear copy (“Extractus litterarum in ziffra Maphei Trivilensis”) the pair Somogyi used; the crib for this work Vestigia 276/277, 249/256, 213/214, 200/201 April–September 1490 cipher + clear copy Somogyi's other four pairs Vestigia 2831 · Sforzesco 650, 1489 no. 8 22 November 1489, Buda four pages; pp. 1–3 and the first two lines of p. 4 in cipher, the rest clear only its first two lines published deciphered (Somogyi, as a specimen) DECODE R1098 · Sforzesco 642/1, 4 12 January 1490, Buda p. 1 clear, then ten lines of cipher; p. 2 clear “Partially decrypted” in DECODE; no decipherment known Three further DECODE records from these boxes were checked and set aside: R1155 (Paolo Lanterio to Maffeo, 14 September 1492) has a seven-page contemporary clear copy in the same archive, catalogued as Vestigia 2240; R1147 (the abbot of Forlì, 18 November 1491) has its clear “Extractus Cifare Abatis Forliviensis”, printed in Dóra Labancz's edition of the 1491 letters; and R1152 (2 April 1492) is a clear draft, not a cipher at all. R1146 and R1158 are in two other ciphers, not Maffeo's. The crib. t: Maffeo da Treviglio to Ludovico Sforza, Buda 1489–1490 — the key reconstructed in 2016 had never been turned back into signs
h: Turning Somogyi's numbers back into signs
b: Somogyi's appendix prints the key as a table of numbers: a = 11, 29, 39; m = 12; b = 13; and so on through five nulls, three word signs ( et , in , che ), five doubled-letter signs, thirty-two syllable signs and six nomenclator entries (“il vescovo varadino”, “S. V.”, “ser.mo Re de Hungaria”, “madonna Bianca”, “zo. Corvino”, “la sua Maestà”). She also prints the first two lines of the 1489 letter twice, once as numbers and once deciphered. What she does not print is any image of a sign, and her numbers are her own invention, not the fifteenth-century chancery's. The way in is the sequence. Her numbers 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 read a, m, b, sa, to, re — which is “ambasatore”, the first word of the letter of 2 April 1490. 17, 18, 19 are d, e, l (“del”), 20 to 23 t, u, r, co (“turco”). The numbering simply follows that letter word by word, so the ciphered original supplies the shapes in the same order. From there the clear copy carries the reading to the end of the letter and fixes about forty signs. The rest came out of the two unread letters themselves, each fixed by a word that could be nothing else: the long 7 -shaped stroke is f (“Fedrico”, “fosse”, “satisfare”); an n with a crossed 4 is ss (“essere”, “potesse”); x with a tick is do (“quando”, “havendo”); a with a colon is gli (“meglio”); a looped b joined to o is st (“stato”, “questo”); d with a colon is fi (“figliolo”, “iustificare”); an n with a long crossbar is tt (“littere”); and a capital with a cross stands for “Ex.tia Vostra”. Numerals are written as figures, not enciphered: “ali 8 del presente”, “ali 15”, “in 20 o 25 di”. Latin words sometimes stand in the clear inside the cipher (“etiam apud”, “Sed hoc non fallet divinam sapientiam”).

t: Maffeo da Treviglio to Ludovico Sforza, Buda 1489–1490 — the key reconstructed in 2016 had never been turned back into signs
h: Buda, 12 January 1490: the king rides to Vienna
b: The ten ciphered lines of the letter of 12 January 1490, below the clear text that breaks off at “…in mane sue”. Image: Archivio di Stato di Milano, Sforzesco 642/1, 4, via DECODE R1098. The letter's clear first page is about church appointments; the cipher begins where the news turns delicate. Questo Ser.mo Re partite de qua ali 8 del presente per andare ad Vienna, non ta[nto] per che la speranza de la dieta lo tiri, quanto per proprio desiderio de andarli; et che sia el vero, questi prelati mi hano dicto che in questo camino divertira ad [Tu…] … che sono molti et gr[an]di, et non si conduc[ono] ad Vienna a piu … che in 20 o 25 di. Lo legato et li altri oratori hano, et io con loro havemo, deliberato partire ali 15 de questo … rimasti dreto, perche … and[aremo per la] recta via ad Vienna. “This Most Serene King left here on the 8th of this month to go to Vienna, not so much because the hope of the Diet draws him as from his own wish to go; and in proof of it, these prelates have told me that on this journey he will turn aside to [Tulln?] … which are many and great, and they will not reach Vienna in under 20 or 25 days. The legate and the other ambassadors have decided, and I with them, to leave on the 15th of this month … having stayed behind, because … we shall go by the direct road to Vienna.” The reading checks itself: the letter's own second page says in clear words that “lo legato et li altri oratori et io siamo insieme deliberato partire alli 15 de questo … andare per la via ad Vienna”. The cipher says the same thing in the same order, and the word “Vienna” is spelled with the same signs in lines 2, 6 and 10.

t: Maffeo da Treviglio to Ludovico Sforza, Buda 1489–1490 — the key reconstructed in 2016 had never been turned back into signs
h: Buda, 22 November 1489: peace, the Diet, and two marriages
b: Four pages. Somogyi printed the first two lines as a specimen; no reading of the rest was published. Matthias Corvinus had six months to live, his war with Frederick III was in suspense, and two marriages were in play for his illegitimate son John Corvinus: Bianca Maria Sforza, Ludovico's niece, and a daughter of don Federico of Aragon, Naples's candidate. Queen Beatrice of Aragon opposed the succession of her stepson. The reading below is close but not word-perfect: bracketed words are uncertain, ellipses mark groups not yet read. Page 1 and page 2 are read nearly throughout, page 3 in its first half and in patches thereafter. [Page 1] La Ex.tia vostra intende ad quali termine la pratica de pace et per consequente questa dieta. Questo Ser.mo Re de Hungaria e tenero del honore suo, como ho scripto altre volte; non e dubio che lui non desidera la pace, et non tanto pero che l[a] voglia receve[re] … andare ad la dieta … perche non se gli potesse imputare che per lui fosse rotta la pratica. Gli pare anche duro andarli per non cavare niente et riceverne scorno; et pero desidera havere l[ette]re da … che lo … affirmando li essere [tanto] disposto a la pace, et con questo si contenta andarli, anchora che fosse certo che niuna conclusione ne dovesse riuscire, perche gli pare … potersi sempre iustificare et satisfare ad honore suo. … Etiam che questo novo ambasiatore de Napoli [ha] tractare la reconciliatione de la [Maestà] con lo [Imperatore] per [dispo]nerla a la voglia, como lui dice, de la … per [beneficio] de suo figliolo; habia una altra volta tentate et facto mentione de la figliola de don … Fedrico, et gli ne ho facte quelle coniecture … le parole che ha dicto al Ser.mo Re, che … voglia havere rispecto al honore de la [sua Maestà]. … Liberamente questa aff[init]a essere facta in suo dispecto … al honore suo, stando questa affinita … la figliola de don Federico, che gli e dispiaciuto da morte quando fosse stato … apresso uno gentilhomo napolitano che e con lo dicto ambasiatore. [Page 2] … et, respondendoli colui parerli imposibile essendo [cocto] questo de Milano, solenemente replico essere vero, dicendo che la parentata de Milano era gia [conclusa]. Sono ancora stati de cortesani li quali, havendo inteso de la deliberatione che era facta, che messere Francisco and[a]sse ad Napoli, gli hanno dicto: “Voi andarete ad disfare quello che haveti cocto!” … Io li significo liberamente a la Ex.tia Vostra quello sento … ne pigliare[a] quella parte che gli parera … che non habia restare per lei ad [fare] omne prova se possi avertere … lo Ser.mo Re da proposito … et in questo non cedera a la insaciabile ira de Iunone … … per la experientia del passato se po iudicare del futuro. Le littere in cifra che forono intercepte, le quale duplicate sono state scoperte a[n]cora qua, hanno indicato l'animo suo … no[n] i[n]coveniente usare de quelle rotte, se co[me] usa lui … omne volta che … del adiuto de quello stato … de insolente, intolerabile … che, overo, non e da prestare fede … qua gli ne … dare … sopra la dote. [Page 3] … quando si parera, se dica qualche parola ad la sua Maestà … Francisco ad l'andare ad Napoli, e proceduto dal[la] sua Maestà … dal signore suo, de reconciliar[e] lo re con la sua Maestà … l'andar[e] ad Napoli, mando per … et gli disse che andasse con … animo … fructo de l'andar sua … habia dicto de volerlo mandare piu presto per tentarlo che per deliberatione … et dice ancora che ad … non havera ad dimorare piu che octo di, o dece al piu, et che vole affretare el camino per trovarsi presto … la singulare observantia de questo Ser.mo Re verso la … conveniente ad questo effecto, per disponer[e] la … del Turco … il Turco, dopoi … del re Ferdinando galiardamente, et co[n] tale modest[i]a che convi[e]ne … volendo la Santita sua … [Page 4, the last two ciphered lines] … quello che sapia et possi [fare]. Sed hoc non fallet divinam sapientiam de la. Ma se e dicto ancora che la … al Soldano.

t: Maffeo da Treviglio to Ludovico Sforza, Buda 1489–1490 — the key reconstructed in 2016 had never been turned back into signs
h: The clear postscript: an ambassador's expenses
b: Page 4: the cipher stops after two lines and Maffeo goes on in the clear, about money. Image: Archivio di Stato di Milano, Sforzesco 650, via Vestigia. Nothing on this page is secret, and it was never enciphered. It is also the only part of the letter that is about Maffeo himself. Credo che la Ex.tia V.ra havera facto dar quelli ducento ad m. Fran.co; che, se cosi e, la ringratio infinite volte de la clementia et bonta sua infinita. Et perche quelli denari non mi portavano fin al fine de decembre, et partendosi lui non saperia da chi imprum[ut]are uno quatrino se non dal Thexaurero Regio, che seria con graveza de la persona vostra propria … Se de questa spesa non gli ne faria honor, sonno contento che non me ne proveda; io gli posso affirmar etiam cum iuramento che, doppoi che sonno qua, ultra quello ho havuto et tolto in nome del Ill.mo S. V.ro, ho speso di mei piu de centocinquanta ducati tra mi, veste et cavalli … che la provisione che me e ordinata non mi basta, dovendo tener questo loco secundo la dignita sua. Et perche in questa novita facta de Cancelleri forse poteria esser dome[n]ticato, La supplico ordini ad chi li par che provedi sia compreso in el numero de li altri Can[cellieri] et in lassignatione facta ad la Cancellaria. A V.ra Ex. de continuo me recomando. Bude xxij Novembris 1489. E[iusdem] Ill.me D[ominationis] V[ostre] servus, Magister Trivilien[sis] . “Since I have been here, beyond what I have had in Your Lordship's name, I have spent more than a hundred and fifty ducats of my own on myself, clothes and horses … the allowance assigned me is not enough to keep this post according to its dignity. And because in this recent reshuffle of the chancery clerks I might be forgotten, I beg you to order whoever you think fit to see that I am counted among the other chancellors.” The phrase “et in lassignatione facta ad la Cancellaria” is the explicit by which the archive catalogues the letter.

t: Maffeo da Treviglio to Ludovico Sforza, Buda 1489–1490 — the key reconstructed in 2016 had never been turned back into signs
b: The images are the Vestigia plates (3240×4320, no login needed: the record page at vestigia.hu/documents/<id> carries the whole record as JSON, and the originals are served from /media/<file id>/<file name> ) and, for R1098, the DECODE scans of the same negatives. The working loop was: connected-component segmentation of each page into glyph boxes, line assignment by the peaks of the horizontal ink projection, merging of the two-stroke signs and of superscripts with the letter below them; then numbered strips, one line at a time, transcribed into values by hand against a sheet of sign exemplars cut from the letters themselves; then the values segmented into Italian, and any place where the Italian failed sent back to the image. The 2 April pair was aligned by dynamic programming against its clear copy to seed the key. Several rounds were needed: the first pass on the 1489 letter produced letter strings, the second, working from contrast-stretched crops of whole lines rather than from boxes, produced sentences. Two practical notes for anyone continuing. The automatic line segmentation misassigns glyphs in the lower half of pages 2 and 3 of the 1489 letter, where the lines converge; read those from the plate with per-row crops. And the stacked line crops drift from line 18 onward on page 3, which cost one pass its accuracy.
