t: Giuliano Caprile and Alfonso Cistarelli to Ferrara, 1519–1521 — most read at the time or since, two more read in part
b: Catalogue items 157 and 158: eight DECODE records of two agents of Cardinal Ippolito d’Este at Eger (ASMo Ambasciatori Ungheria b. 4). The 1519 letters were deciphered in 1882 and the postscript of 16 February 1521 by Judit W. Somogyi in 2025. Her texts were used as a crib to rebuild the homophonic sign cipher of 1520–21, which reads two letters with no decipherment anywhere, R1136 and R1139, in part. R1128 (a different 1519 cipher) and Cistarelli’s figure cipher R1137 stay open. Eger and Buda → Ferrara · sign cipher, homophonic; figure cipher · 1519–1521 · read in part Caprile and Cistarelli at Eger, 1519–1521 Archivio di Stato di Modena, Ambasciatori, Ungheria b. 4 (DECODE R1128–R1139): the ciphered letters of two agents of Cardinal Ippolito d’Este, bishop of Eger, to the ducal secretary Bonaventura Pistofilo and to Duke Alfonso I. Catalogue items 157 and 158. Most of the letters turned out to be read already. Two that were not are read in part here, with a key rebuilt from a decipherment printed in 2025. Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 solved in part Summary. The catalogue listed seven DECODE records for Giuliano Caprile, canon of Eger and secretary of Ippolito d’Este, and one for Alfonso Cistarelli, the cardinal’s agent at Eger in 1520, all marked partly decrypted. The Hungarian research database Vestigia holds the whole Caprile file. It shows that the 1519 letters were deciphered in 1882: the Modena inventory says the decipherments “were drawn out only in 1882”, and they are filed after each cipher original as items “b” and “c”. One letter carries the decipherment between its own lines. The postscript of 16 February 1521 (R1138) was deciphered by Judit W. Somogyi in 2025. Her two printed texts made a crib of about 700 letters for the 1520–21 sign cipher. Aligned against a transcription of the signs, they give a homophonic key, and that key reads two letters with no decipherment anywhere, R1139 (6 April 1521) and R1136 (8 March 1520), in part. Both concern the see of Eger and Ippolito’s estate: the custode , the governor, money and debts. Two items stay unread. R1128 (March 1519) is in a different cipher, about Caprile’s own lawsuit in Rome. Cistarelli’s figure cipher (R1137) gives only phrases to a ciphertext-only search. R1139, the slip of 6 April 1521: the sign cipher, read here in part for the first time. Image: Archivio di Stato di Modena, Ambasciatori, Ungheria b. 4, via DECODE R1139.

t: Giuliano Caprile and Alfonso Cistarelli to Ferrara, 1519–1521 — most read at the time or since, two more read in part
b: The 1520–21 cipher is a run of invented signs with no word division: φ, ψ, λ, ÷, ss, ff, a crossed b, m and n with a cross, an inverted T, and some forty more. There are 49 labels in all, over 2,278 signs in five texts, transcribed from the DECODE and Vestigia images. Somogyi calls it homophonic, and it is. The key was built in two steps: A ciphertext-only anneal over all five texts, scored with a sixteenth-century Italian n-gram model. It gave a rough key in which scritti , regno , signore and Ungaria could already be read. That key seeded a monotone alignment (Viterbi with gaps, re-estimated until stable) of the transcription against Somogyi’s two texts. 714 letters align, and 90% of alignments agree with the majority value of their sign. The values: a = q, T, ⊥ · c = φ, θ · d = ψ, r · e = y, ss · g = w, u · i = ƀ, ɔ, L · l = ff, n · m = z, Ħ · n = ÷, p · o = ɛ, the stacked q/b, oσo · p = & and its looped variant · r = *, x · s = m+, n+ · t = h, f · u = λ, a A lone o between letters is usually a null. So, in one place, is the figure 8.

t: Giuliano Caprile and Alfonso Cistarelli to Ferrara, 1519–1521 — most read at the time or since, two more read in part
b: The rest of R1139 and R1136. The transcription is a single reading of small, crowded signs, and misread signs leave most letters between the quoted phrases wrong. A second reading of the images against the key would go most of the way to a full text. The mechanical decrypt is in decrypt21_raw.txt . R1128 (9 March 1519). Attempted, not read. The 1519 system was worked out on R1133 against its 1882 decipherment. Each column, a small sign over a base sign, is one plaintext letter with homophones: “oratore” = L/7 -/n u/7 x/7 c/7 m/n -/a, and c/7 = o, m/n = r, x/7 = t hold across the page. Each bracket-L sign stands for a whole word: the run [d][s][&] recurs where the decipherment has “de vostra maesta”. The 1519 letters turn out to be copies of reports to the King of France on the imperial election. A fifth of R1128 is code words, and only nine letter values are secure, so a language-model search gives nothing readable. Its clear part and Caprile’s next letter (“In un’altra mia ve mandai in zifra…”) say it concerned his own lawsuit at Rome. A second, careful transcription of R1133 and another 1882-paired letter would fill the table. R1137 (Cistarelli, 25 July 1520). Two-digit groups, nearly all ending in 5 or 0, and 83 other signs, mixed with clear Italian. A ciphertext-only anneal settles part of the key (e = 0, 25; a = 86; o = 70; i = 45; t = 95; r = 85; s = 90; n = 65) and phrases such as “lettere per”, “presto”, “saria meglio”, “non se poteria” and “dua milla” (grade M). This is not a reading.

t: Cardinal Caracciolo to Charles V, 14 November 1537 — a published key, read through, past the first four lines
b: A letter from Milan catalogued on DECODE as Non-decrypted. Its eleven cipher lines are in the cipher Charles V used with Caracciolo from 1530 to 1538, reconstructed by Wanruo Luo in 2021 as Cifrario 38: a sign alphabet with homophones and a syllabary of consonant signs with superscript vowel digits. Tomokiyo had named the key and read four lines. The key reads the whole passage unchanged; about ten signs stay doubtful. Milan → Charles V · homophonic alphabet and superscript syllabary · 14 November 1537 · read Cardinal Caracciolo to Charles V, 14 November 1537 to Charles V Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 1184 fol. 110 (DECODE R9966, “Non-decrypted”). A four-page Italian letter from Milan with eleven lines of cipher, read here with a published key. Daniel Bourdeau · read 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. DECODE catalogues this letter of Cardinal Marino Ascanio Caracciolo, governor of Milan, to the Emperor as not deciphered. There is no decipherment on the leaves. Satoshi Tomokiyo noted that it can be read with Luo’s Cifrario 38 and gave a rough reading of its first four lines. Cifrario 38 is the cipher Charles V used with Caracciolo from 1530 to 1538, reconstructed by Wanruo Luo in her 2021 thesis. Applied unchanged, the key reads all eleven cipher lines and the cancelled line that continues them, 96% of the plaintext letters. Tomokiyo’s four lines are confirmed with two corrections, and the other seven are read here for the first time. The passage concerns the imperial agent Marnol’s dealings with the Swiss and the Grisons, just as the Dauphin was crossing into Italy. It covers the envoy Panizone, sent and paid in Caracciolo’s name, the Grisons to be given “la tracta del frumento gratis” as the Swiss had it, and Marnol now seeing “la malignita et perfidia” of the Swiss and their ministers. About ten signs stay doubtful, none of them in a place that changes the sense.

t: Cardinal Caracciolo to Charles V, 14 November 1537 — a published key, read through, past the first four lines
b: The four DECODE images are out of archive order. P4 is f. 110r (scan 0408) and opens “Sacra Cat. ca & Ces. a M. ta ”. It is in clear, on the Dauphin and the Grand Master crossing with munitions, the King at Briançon, and “Mons. or di Marnol” with the Colonel of the Isola working to recall the Swiss in French service. P1 is f. 110v (scan 0409), with clear text on the Grisons and then the eleven cipher lines. P3 is f. 111r (scan 0410). It has one cipher line struck through, then the clear close, dated “In M. lo ali xiiij de Nov. e M. D. xxxvij” and signed “il Car. l Caracciolo”. P2 is the address leaf, with the docket “del Cardenal Caracciolo xiiij de Nov. e 1537”. Cifrario 38 (Luo 2021, p. 657, from AGS Estado leg. 38 doc. 190) has three parts. An alphabet of invented signs with homophones. a has six signs, and e , i , l , n , o , p and u have two to four each. A syllabary. A consonant’s base sign takes a superscript digit for the vowel: 5 = a, 6 = e, 7 = i, 8 = o, 9 = u. For example, 2 is the base for s , so 2⁷ = si . Nulls, marked by the superscripts 2, 3 and 4, and a few code words. The first cipher line shows the system at work: 2⁷ a̱o⁸ 3⁶ + 9 ṉo⁵ θ 4⁷ a+⁵ ṉo⁶ = si do ve a p ra c ti ca re . F. 110v (scan 0409). The clear text ends at the struck words and the cipher begins. Image: Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 1184 f. 110v (scan 0409), via DECODE R9966.

t: Cardinal Caracciolo to Charles V, 14 November 1537 — a published key, read through, past the first four lines
b: Line by line, as the cipher spells it. [..] marks signs not resolved, and square brackets around words mark a doubtful reading. 1 solo si dovea practicare per Marno a se volevano concordarse 2 como erano Suizari, et in tal caso ho scripto piu vol- 3 te a Marno a che manda il Panizone in mio nome et pagato 4 quale a fe? resolui, perche io serria? contento 5 dare a epsi Grisoni como a[..] Elvetii la tracta 6 del frumento gratis, facendo capituli convenienti. 7 Fin qui a epso Marno a non e parso [..] dicti Griso- 8 ni; harriano 'l facto como [..] Suizari. Epso Marno a 9 se accorge hora de la malignita et perfidia de 10 Suizari et [..] et soi ministri. Se deve ne recor- 11 dare, e quante volte io ha dicto che epsi Suizari far- (f. 111r, cancelled) riano quello hora fan po[..] In substance, Caracciolo reports on Marnol’s work with the Grisons. Marnol was to find out whether they would come to terms as the Swiss had. Caracciolo had written to him several times to send Panizone in Caracciolo’s name and to pay him. The Grisons were to be given, as the Swiss had been, the tratta of grain free of duty, on suitable articles. So far it had not seemed good to them, and they would have done as the Swiss did. Marnol now saw the malice and bad faith of the Swiss and their ministers. Caracciolo reminds the Emperor how often he had said what the Swiss would do “hora”. The last words are in the line the writer cancelled.

That note was found before the work and led to the key. Here the letter was deciphered line by line from the DECODE images, and the key needed no change. t: Cardinal Caracciolo to Charles V, 14 November 1537 — a published key, read through, past the first four lines
h: The second pass, and what remains uncertain
b: The first pass left about fifteen percent open. A second pass at 4× with contrast on every line settled most of it with four rules: A superscript belongs to the sign before it. In line 5, 3⁶ 4⁷ et reads ve ti i , so the word is “Elvetii”. A bare ♀ is the letter r, and ♀ with a superscript is the p-syllable. This gives “harriano” in line 8 and “parso” in line 7. The g-shaped sign with a bar is an f homophone, which gives “frumento” in line 6. Dotted signs are nulls. About ten of roughly 330 signs (an estimate, not a sign-by-sign count) stay doubtful: Line 4: “a fe”, read letter by letter, and “serria”, where the sign read as n stands where an a is expected. Line 5: two a-homophones after “como a”. Lines 7 and 8: one sign each. Line 10: “2 a” after “et”. The cancelled line: one syllable after “po”.  id="sources"> 05 Sources Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 1184 fol. 110, scans 0408–0411: DECODE R9966 (login). Wanruo Luo, El lenguaje cifrado de Isabel de Portugal (1530–1539) , doctoral thesis, Universitat de València, 2021 (RODERIC), Cifrario 38, p. 657. Satoshi Tomokiyo, cryptiana.web.fc2.com, “Spanish ciphers during the reign of Charles V”, section on Luo (2021). Notes, reading and profile: caracciolo1537/ in the repository.

t: The Marqués del Carpio to Fuenmayor, 1677 — a Spanish ambassador’s syllabic cipher rebuilt and all ten letters read
b: Ten ciphered letters from Spain’s ambassador in Rome to its envoy in Denmark, eight deciphered in the margin without the key and two catalogued as non-decrypted. The key was rebuilt from the letters: numbers for letters and for syllables in rows of five, struck numbers for a second syllable table, and letter pairs that are syllables with a disguised consonant. It reads all ten: the French fleet at Messina and Catania, Orange raising the siege of Charleroi, Innocent XI refusing Carpio an audience, and Cardinal d’Estrées at Turin. Rome → Copenhagen · syllabic nomenclator · September–December 1677 · read The Marqués del Carpio to Baltasar de Fuenmayor, 1677 from Marqués del Carpio Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, Secrétairerie d’État et de Guerre, inv. nr. 2559 · DECODE R1002–R1011, ten letters, 29 pages · eight with a contemporary decipherment in the margin, two catalogued as non-decrypted Key rebuilt from the letters themselves: a letter table, two syllable tables and a disguised syllabary of letter pairs · all ten letters read Daniel Bourdeau · read 19 September 2026 · updated 21 September 2026 read Summary. DECODE catalogues ten ciphered letters that Gaspar Méndez de Haro, Marqués del Carpio, sent from Rome in the autumn of 1677 to Baltasar de Fuenmayor, the Spanish envoy at Copenhagen. Eight have their decipherment written in the margin, but no key. Two (13 and 20 November, R1004 and R1005) are listed as non-decrypted. The key was rebuilt here from the cipher itself. The Sept. 4 letter was lined up against its margin, and the structure then showed at once. Plain numbers 9–30 are single letters. Numbers 31–60 are consonant-vowel syllables in rows of five. Struck-through numbers are a second syllable table. Pairs of letters such as ge , bo and ma are syllables with the consonant disguised ( ge = de, bo = co, ma = la). About twenty three-letter code words stand for names. Applied to DECODE’s transcriptions, the key reads all ten letters. The two “non-decrypted” leaves turned out to carry a faint marginal decipherment too, and it agrees with the key reading. What the letters say: the French fleet leaves Messina for Catania; the Prince of Orange raises the siege of Charleroi “intempestivamente”; anti-Spanish rumours and a quarrel with Innocent XI, who refuses Carpio an audience; the loss of Freiburg; Orange’s meeting with Charles II; and fear of war in the Milanese, “pues el Cardenal de Estrées, que está en Turín, no se descuida”. What stays open is edition work: the eight margin letters are summarised here from the machine reading, not edited line by line.

t: The Marqués del Carpio to Fuenmayor, 1677 — a Spanish ambassador’s syllabic cipher rebuilt and all ten letters read
b: The file is one of several in SEG 2559 holding letters to Fuenmayor from Spanish diplomats, 1674–79. DECODE describes Carpio’s ten as partly decrypted: “the solution is written in the margin, without revealing the key.” R1004 and R1005 are “unsolved”. Each letter opens with a clear paragraph of compliments, then turns to cipher. The cipher is in one hand, in point-separated groups, with the null groups N, R, g and 4 struck through at the start and end of each block. The decipherment runs vertically in the left margin. R1005, 20 November 1677. DECODE lists this letter as non-decrypted, but a faint decipherment runs down the left margin: “mas que nos tienen con gran cuidado las apariencias y evidentes señales de que la proxima campaña havrá guerra en Milán…”. Image: Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, SEG 2559, letter of 20 November 1677, via DECODE R1005.

t: The Marqués del Carpio to Fuenmayor, 1677 — a Spanish ambassador’s syllabic cipher rebuilt and all ten letters read
b: Token Value 9–30 single letters: a 9, b 10, c 11, d 12, e 13, f 14, g 15, h 16, i 17, l 18, m 19, n 20, o 21, p 22, q 23, r 24, s 25, t 26, u 27, x 28, y 29, z 30. In practice they spell word-final consonants: n, r and s are the commonest tokens in the file. 31–60 consonant + vowel, rows of five in the order a e i o u: m 31–35, n 36–40, p 41–45, r 46–50, s 51–55, t 56–60 (33 mi, 36 na, 39 no, 48 ri, 52 se) struck numbers t row 15–19, f row 20–24, vowel + l 30–34 (31 el), vowel + s 35–39 (36 es), vowel + n 40–44 (41 en, 42 in, 43 on), vowel + r 45–49, que 50, qua 51, qui 52; struck N, R, g, 4 are nulls letter pairs a syllable with its consonant changed and its vowel kept. Cipher b → c, c → b/v, g → d, l → g, m → l, so ge de, gi di, bo co, ci vi, ma la, la ga, lu gu. Also ag ha, eg he, and a separate sign for lle 116 V.S. (Vuestra Señoría) code words sen = Rey; gin/jin/jen = S.M.; gus = Príncipe [de Orange]; quol = Inglaterra; ana = Nápoles; ten = Francia; pon = armada; san = Bruselas; gon = señor(es); ran, xan = gobernador; xon = guerra; tan = Flandes (?) R1010, 4 September 1677. Margin: “La Armada de Francia salió de Mecina y haviendo corrido voz de que se encaminava a imbadir a Brindis en el Reyno de Nápoles…”. Cipher: ma pon ga ge ten 51 mi… = la armada de Francia sali[ó]… Image: Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, SEG 2559, letter of 4 September 1677, via DECODE R1010.

t: The Marqués del Carpio to Fuenmayor, 1677 — a Spanish ambassador’s syllabic cipher rebuilt and all ten letters read
b: 13 November 1677 (R1004). Normalised; bracketed words are uncertain. … lamentarme con V.S. de lo que en todas partes nos persigue nuestra mala fortuna, pues con la llegada del Cardenal de Estrées a Turín se teme alguna gran novedad en Italia, y las cosas de [Flandes] se hallan en el estado que V.S. sabe. Si bien en las materias del Congreso parece debemos suspender el juicio hasta ver lo que resulte del abocamiento del Príncipe de Orange con el Rey de Inglaterra. En los embarazos de esta corte no se me ofrece qué añadir a lo que diré a V.S. en mis antecedentes, sino que si bien aguardaba este correo las órdenes de S.M. no las he recibido, pero no dudo las traerá el siguiente, pues de Madrid me avisan que habían llegado allá las cartas en que di los primeros avisos sobre estas dependencias. “…to lament with Your Lordship how our ill fortune pursues us everywhere: with Cardinal d’Estrées come to Turin some great novelty is feared in Italy … in the Congress [of Nijmegen] we must suspend judgement until we see what comes of the Prince of Orange’s meeting with the King of England … I expected His Majesty’s orders by this post and have not had them.” 20 November 1677 (R1005). … más de que nos tienen con gran cuidado las apariencias y evidentes señales de que la próxima campaña habrá guerra en Milán, pues el Cardenal de Estrées, que está en Turín, no se descuida. “…except that we are much concerned by the appearances and evident signs that next campaign there will be war in the Milanese, for Cardinal d’Estrées, who is at Turin, is not idle.”

t: The Marqués del Carpio to Fuenmayor, 1677 — a Spanish ambassador’s syllabic cipher rebuilt and all ten letters read
b: 4 Sept (R1010). The French fleet has left Messina. It was said to be bound for Brindisi, but its design is Catania. Carpio is dismayed by news from Brussels that Orange raised the siege of Charleroi “intempestivamente”. 18 Sept (R1011). False rumours are raised in Rome against the Spaniards after Charleroi. Carpio has had no satisfaction from the Pope or his ministers. The militia is called out and guns are mounted on Castel Sant’Angelo. 25 Sept (R1009). He got neither remedy nor inquiry. He consults the cardinals of the Spanish party, the viceroy of Naples and the governor of Milan. 2 Oct (R1006). The offences continue. The French fleet and galleys, after holding off Catania, are said to have gone back to Toulon badly battered. 9 Oct (R1007). Still no satisfaction. On the cardinals’ advice he stays away from the papal audiences while he waits for the viceroy of Naples. 16 Oct (R1008). No news. He holds firm until orders come. 4 Dec (R1002). On the King’s orders he asked for an audience of Innocent XI about the disputes. It was refused twice, and the Pope would take the King’s business only through a cardinal. Carpio will not treat the principal business until the point is settled. 11 Dec (R1003). The loss of Freiburg (taken by Créqui, 16 November) and its consequences beyond the Rhine. The Pope refused the audience again. He waits for the Marqués de los Vélez.

t: The Marqués del Carpio to Fuenmayor, 1677 — a Spanish ambassador’s syllabic cipher rebuilt and all ten letters read
b: DECODE’s ciphertext transcriptions (by RP and MEG, 2020) were parsed into tokens. The 4 September letter has a legible marginal decipherment, and lining its first lines up against the cipher showed the layout. The letter pairs looked like Spanish syllables with the wrong consonant. ca 9 [42] ca gi 24 against “va a imbadir” fixed a = 9 and r = 24, and 36 = na in both Mecina and encaminava. The rows of five followed from 33 mi, 36 na, 39 no and 48 ri. Every token of all ten letters was then tallied in context, which settled the consonant changes ( gi-os Dios, lu-ar-de guarde, ne-lo-cios negocios). The decoder ( carpio1677/dec.py ) applies the tables mechanically, and its output reads as Spanish throughout. The code words were read from context and from the historical events they fit: Charleroi, Freiburg, d’Estrées at Turin, Orange in London.

t: The Marqués del Carpio to Fuenmayor, 1677 — a Spanish ambassador’s syllabic cipher rebuilt and all ten letters read
b: The readings come from DECODE’s transcriptions. A few misread numbers show as nonsense syllables, and some tokens as unread ( {..} in the raw files). The two November letters were checked against the images; the other eight were not. Code words: tan = Flandes, cun iles = españoles and lun = cart[as] are C (conjecture from context). sen , gin , gus , quol , ana , ten , pon , san are H: each is confirmed by a marginal decipherment or by an event. Struck 14 is not fixed. It stands before -sta and -ticia, so possibly ju , which gives justa and justicia. The eight margin letters are summarised here, not edited.

t: The Marqués del Carpio to Fuenmayor, 1677 — a Spanish ambassador’s syllabic cipher rebuilt and all ten letters read
b: Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, Secrétairerie d’État et de Guerre, inv. nr. 2559. Images and transcriptions on DECODE, records R1002 – R1011 (login required). Related letters to Fuenmayor in the same file: DECODE R964–R966 (Salinas and others, 1674–76). Notes, decoder and machine readings: carpio1677/ in the repository.

t: Castelcicala to the Marchese di Circello and to Medici, 1816–1823 — the code rebuilt from four glossed letters
b: Twenty-four ciphered despatches of the Neapolitan ambassador Fabrizio Ruffo, principe di Castelcicala, in the Naples archive (DECODE R9553–R9589), all in one syllabic, homophonic code of about 2,450 groups. “Marchese di Ciscello” is the recipient, Circello, misread. Contemporary decipherments on four letters of 1816 and 1823 gave 162 values and 45% of the groups; no letter reads through yet. London, Paris → Naples · syllabic numeric code · April 1816 – October 1823 · read in part Castelcicala to the Marchese di Circello and to Medici, 1816–1823 to Luigi de' Medici Archivio di Stato di Napoli, Ministero degli affari esteri, busta 2337; DECODE R9553–R9589 (catalogue 166 and 167): twenty-four despatches in the ambassador’s code, about 9,400 groups, all transcribed here. Four letters in the same box carry contemporary decipherments between the lines. They give a key of about a hundred certain values, extended to 162. The code’s structure is now known, but most letters are still only half legible. Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 21 September 2026 solved in part Summary. The catalogue held two entries for this box: nine despatches “to the Marchese di Circello” (167), and fifteen from a “Marchese di Ciscello? Principe di Castelcicala?” to an unknown recipient (166). They are one series. The sender is always Fabrizio Ruffo, principe di Castelcicala. “Ciscello” is a misreading of the address to the recipient , the Marchese di Circello, foreign minister in Naples. The 1823 letters go to his successor, the Cavaliere de’ Medici. An earlier pass on 21 September found no key. It had taken the “decrypted” neighbours in the box for 1850s telegrams. Three of them (R9569, R9571, R9589) are in fact Castelcicala’s Paris letters of September–October 1823, in the same code, deciphered between the lines. A fourth decipherment covers the first ten lines of despatch 3874 of 1 December 1816 (R9566), and is shown below. Aligning these glosses group by group shows the system: a two-part numeric code of about 2,450 groups for syllables, words and names. It is homophonic and has short alphabetical runs. Groups written with a fifth figure are nulls. The rebuilt key gives a value to 45% of the groups in the target letters. About a third of its values are inferences, and no letter reads through yet. R9566 p. 3, despatch 3874 (Paris, 1 December 1816), with its contemporary interlinear decipherment: “questo Min.ro dell’Interno C.te di Cazes che gode sempre del più gr. favore presso del Re di Fr.a ha avuto una confer.za col Min.ro di S.M. Cattolica Sig.r Onis al suo passaggio per qui, nella quale parlandogli della cessione delle Floride, e di quella di cui si è parlato…” Image: Archivio di Stato di Napoli, Ministero degli affari esteri, busta 2337, p. 3, via DECODE R9566.

t: Castelcicala to the Marchese di Circello and to Medici, 1816–1823 — the code rebuilt from four glossed letters
b: All the documents are in busta 2337 of the Esteri series, photographed for DECODE (records R9553–R9589, access by login). The headings give the dates and places: London, 1816: 1 April (R9553, no. 2314, headed “Cifra della Segreteria di Stato”), 30 August, 6 September, 26 September, 4 October (R9556, R9557, R9579, R9558). Paris, 1816: 3 June (R9555), 17, 19 and 23 October (R9559, R9560, R9587), 30 November (R9561, seven pages), 1 December (R9566, despatch 3874, with a second fragment in another hand), 3 December (R9562). Undated, to Circello: R9554 (no. 2589), R9563 (2814), R9564 (3388 or 3588), R9565 (3721), R9567 (4086). The fragments R9582–R9585 date from 1817–1819. Paris, 1823, to the Cavaliere de’ Medici: 4, 8 and 11(?) September, 9 October (R9569, R9571, R9570, R9589). The papal conclave that followed Pius VII’s death is the theme. Another code: R9586 and R9588 (values 100–1100, faint pencil glosses), not attacked. R9590 (Paris, 12 March 1830) is also in another code. The images are not in reading order. R9579 runs P2, P3, P1, P4; R9569 P2, P1; R9561 begins at P2.

t: Castelcicala to the Marchese di Circello and to Medici, 1816–1823 — the code rebuilt from four glossed letters
b: The groups run from 1 to about 2,450, with dots between them. The same frequent groups appear in 1816 and 1823 (2201, 2211, 332, 1909, 2450, 2232, 1864, 1843), so one book served for seven years. Its units are syllables, common words and names, and a word is spelled from as many as it needs: groups reading 1708 2027 1994 · 1708 1531 1994 ele·va·zione · ele·(null)·zione 1609 2448 2221 1951 2450 · 1609 2380 2221 2076 pon·ti·fi·ca·to · pon·te·fi·ce 2009 2211 1725 2295 · 2012 2448 1535 2169 Car·di·na·le Cas·ti·gli·one 2367 2290 1404 1535 · 2367 2232 2450 par·lan·do·gli · par·la·to 2357 1758 2318 · 1919 2318 · 1739 1714 2318 li·ber·tà · No·ta · un·i·ta It is homophonic : di is 1112 and 2211, pa is 1201 and 2363, ere is 1836 and 2381. It is a two-part code with local alphabetical runs : 2201 che, 2205 ci, 2211 di, 2221 fi, 2230 l, 2231 l’, 2232 la; 2082 del, 2083 dell’, 2084 della; 2045 quella, 2049 questo; 2161 is, 2162 Isola; 1919 no, 1920 non; 2445 ter, 2448 ti, 2450 to. Between runs the order is scattered. A group written with a fifth figure (21900, 18900, 16480; about a hundred cases) always falls where the decipherer wrote nothing, so these are nulls.

t: Castelcicala to the Marchese di Circello and to Medici, 1816–1823 — the code rebuilt from four glossed letters
b: 1 December 1816 (R9566, first ten lines). Decazes, the Minister of the Interior, “who still enjoys the greatest favour with the King of France”, has met the Spanish minister Onís on his way through Paris. Speaking of the cession of the Floridas, and of the cession of Cuba to England that had been talked of, he “skilfully insinuated”… The gloss stops there. 8 September 1823 (R9571). “La Francia desidera il Cardinale Castiglione per Papa, ma si biasima di avere il Duca [di] Laval troppo fatto ciò vedere, e si teme che ciò nuoccia al suddetto porporato per la sua elevazione al Pontificato. Non esiste alcun accordo tra la Francia e l’Austria per l’elezione del Pontefice.” (France wants Cardinal Castiglioni as Pope. The Duc de Laval is blamed for making this too plain, which may harm the cardinal’s chances. France and Austria have no agreement on the election.) Castiglioni was elected as Pius VIII only in 1829; Leo XII was chosen on 28 September 1823. 9 October 1823 (R9589). Now that the King of Spain has his liberty and the orders given in Medici’s despatch no. 688 of 28 September, there can be no question of Castelcicala passing the note to the Conference. Postscript: the Duc d’Angoulême will not be back for two months. 4 September 1823 (R9569) is glossed over ten lines. It concerns the election “al Sovrano Pontificato”, France’s intentions, and whether it would use “l’esclusiva”, the veto.

t: Castelcicala to the Marchese di Circello and to Medici, 1816–1823 — the code rebuilt from four glossed letters
b: The 27 records were fetched from DECODE and transcribed from full-resolution crops by two sub-agents: 9,428 groups in the main code, 1,315 distinct. The glosses were aligned group by group, and the key was extended by hand from repeated contexts. Its 162 values are graded in key.tsv : 90 read directly from a contemporary gloss (G), 18 glossed and confirmed in a second context (X), and 54 inferred here and unconfirmed (I). With them, 45% of the groups in the target letters get a value. Scoring candidate syllables for each unknown group with an Italian 5-gram model did not separate the candidates. The known neighbours are too sparse, and the segmentation into syllables or words is unknown. So no letter reads through . The partial decode ( reading_partial.txt ) is a working file, not a reading. Some I values are surely wrong: “il Sr troppo l d’An ta” in R9579 must be a name. The next step is to read the 1816 letters one at a time, around the Floridas–Cuba–Decazes themes the gloss supplies, using the alphabetical runs to bracket unknown groups. The code book itself, if it survives in the Esteri or the Segreteria di Stato papers of the ASNa, would settle it at once. The consular keys of Borbone 1666 on DECODE (R9532–R9541) are from 1859–60 and do not apply.

t: Castelcicala to the Marchese di Circello and to Medici, 1816–1823 — the code rebuilt from four glossed letters
b: Archivio di Stato di Napoli, Ministero degli affari esteri, busta 2337, items 4–41, photographed for DECODE ( R9554 , R9566 , R9571 , R9589 and neighbours). The images are not in the public domain; only a crop is shown. Busta 2317 (DECODE R9549): a 1797–98 Vienna despatch with its decipherment, in a different code. It is not the plaintext of these letters, whatever DECODE’s note suggests. Fabrizio Ruffo, principe di Castelcicala: Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani . t: Louis XIV and Louvois to Catinat — seven Grand Chiffre despatches, and the decision to abandon Piedmont
b: The 1819 editor of Catinat’s papers printed seven court despatches of July–September 1691 in figures and could not read them; Bazeries rebuilt the code from them in 1893, printed two in clear for the Man in the Iron Mask, and stopped. His table reads all seven from the library’s OCR of the volume, 12,362 groups, checked against the page images; the two he printed agree at 98 and 99 %. The other five are read here for the first time, among them the King’s twenty-page letter of 14 September: bring the army back over the Alps, hold the passes, keep Carmagnole to cover the negotiation with the Pope, then burn it, and take Coni in the winter. Versailles and Fontainebleau → Piedmont · Grand Chiffre de 1691 · read Louis XIV and Louvois to Catinat, July–September 1691 from Louis XIV → to Catinat Mémoires et correspondance du maréchal de Catinat (Paris, 1819), t. II pp. 295–342 · seven despatches · 12,362 groups · the decision to abandon Piedmont Decoded in full with Bazeries’ table of the Grand Chiffre; two letters he printed in clear serve as controls (98 and 99 % of characters agree); the other five, about 9,700 groups, are read here for the first time in print. Daniel Bourdeau · read 16 September 2026 · updated 21 September 2026 read Summary. When Le Bouyer de Saint-Gervais published his great-uncle Catinat’s papers in 1819 he printed seven despatches from the court exactly as he found them, in three-figure groups, and admitted he could not read them. Étienne Bazeries reconstructed the code from these very pages in 1893 and used one sentence of the first letter, Louvois’ order to shut Bulonde up at Pignerol “avec un masque”, to name the Man in the Iron Mask. He printed that letter and the 19 August letter in clear, and the opening of a third, and stopped. The table he published reads all seven. Applied to the Bavarian State Library’s OCR of the 1819 volume, checked against the page images wherever the French breaks, it recovers 12,362 groups: two letters of Louvois (8 and 9 July) and five of Louis XIV (19, 24 and 29 August, 6 and 14 September 1691). The longest, twenty printed pages of figures dated Fontainebleau 14 September, is the King weighing the honourable course against the solid one and choosing the solid: bring the army of Piedmont back over the Alps at the end of the campaign, do not send it back in 1692, hold the passes, keep Carmagnole as long as possible to cover the negotiation with the Pope, then strip and burn it, and take Coni in the winter. Status: read. Six groups misprinted above the table’s range in 1819 and a residual OCR error rate near one group in seventy remain; the originals at Vincennes were not consulted.

t: Louis XIV and Louvois to Catinat — seven Grand Chiffre despatches, and the decision to abandon Piedmont
b: The 1691 campaign in Piedmont opened with the failed siege of Coni (Cuneo), abandoned by Bulonde on 28 June against orders, and closed with the French army still in the plain between Turin and Pignerol, unable to take Coni or to winter. Catinat commanded; Louvois, secretary of state for war, died on 16 July; his son Barbezieux succeeded him and the King wrote to Catinat himself. The court’s ciphered despatches to Catinat survived among the marshal’s papers and were printed in figures in the second volume of the 1819 Mémoires , pp. 295–342, with the clear passages the clerk had left in clear. Bazeries states that except for the 19 August letter, whose minute is at the Dépôt de la guerre, these despatches “n’ont pas été enregistrées”: if so, the 1819 print is the only text of the other six.* Mémoires et correspondance du maréchal de Catinat , t. II (1819), p. 320 — the end of the 6 September letter and the first lines of the King’s letter of 14 September, which runs to p. 342 (Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, bsb10720287, scan 354). Image: Mémoires et correspondance du maréchal de Catinat, t. II (1819), p. 320, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek bsb10720287 scan 354, via the MDZ. t: Louis XIV and Louvois to Catinat — seven Grand Chiffre despatches, and the decision to abandon Piedmont
b: The Grand Chiffre de 1691 is a two-part code of 587 groups: two or three homophones for each letter, consonant-vowel syllables, word stems ( Envoi , Trouv , Expliqu ), whole words ( Sa Majesté , Pignerol , Carmagnole ), a dozen nulls that mark the ends of sentences, and one group that cancels the group before it. Bazeries rebuilt it from these letters over three years and printed his table, with 91 entries left blank, at the end of Le Masque de fer ; that table, transcribed from the Gallica scan for the Feuquières letter , is used here unchanged. The figures were taken from the Bavarian State Library’s hOCR of the volume, word by word with their boxes. Specks the OCR read as a stray “1” (which would decode as Passage ) were dropped by box size, show-through glyphs stripped, the editor’s footnote markers and running heads removed, and the letters cut at their printed headers. Each group was looked up, the units concatenated between nulls, and the result word-segmented with a lexicon drawn from the three Catinat volumes, Rousset’s Louvois , Feuquières’ memoirs and Bazeries’ book, so that sa maj este vou loit sca voi r comes out as sa majesté vouloit scavoir . The segmentation is a reading aid; the group-level decode is what is checked. Controls. Bazeries printed the 8 July and 19 August letters in clear. Our reading of the OCR’d figures matches his text at 2,640 of 2,690 characters (98.1 %) and 3,204 of 3,233 (99.1 %) after normalising accents and i/j, u/v. The residue is single groups the OCR misread (26 Vous as 24 Le ), a few places where his clear text departs from the printed figures, and his free rendering of two table entries. Every stretch the segmenter could not resolve into words, 137 in all, was then cropped from the page image and read by eye: seven OCR errors were found and corrected, six groups turned out to be misprinted above 587 in the 1819 edition itself, and the rest were seventeenth-century spelling correctly transcribed.

t: Louis XIV and Louvois to Catinat — seven Grand Chiffre despatches, and the decision to abandon Piedmont
h: What the King and Louvois wrote
b: Louvois, 9 July. The more the King reflects on Coni, the more he is touched, for the reputation of his arms and for what the place will cost the winter quarters; a siege with the whole army is no longer possible. Two tasks: fortify Carmagnole so the enemy “n’osent le regarder”, and destroy every post the enemy could hold in winter against the roads to Casale and Pignerol: Villeneuve d’Ast and Quiers “vous les devriez brusler absolument”, sparing the churches, and the castles between Turin and Asti likewise, all done “de manière qu’il ne paroisse point qu’elles vous aient esté prescrites”. Seize Bene; burn Carignan if the enemy could winter in it. Seek battle before the Germans arrive and avoid it after, to let them fall sick and desert for want of pay. Oblige the peasants to bring their grain into the King’s garrisons, with commissaries to hold the governors to it. The Duke of Savoy’s talk “mériteroit bien” two thousand bombs into Turin, and the bridge of Turin would be worth breaking, “mais ce sont des vues que Sa Majesté vous met devant les yeux et non des ordres”. Louis XIV, 24 August. Chamlay carries the King’s thoughts on every course still open in the war. Will the enemy march into Savoy, or mass by Turin to eat the forage and force Catinat back over the mountains first? The negotiation at Rome makes it very desirable to stay beyond the Alps as long as possible. Casale: palisades, money for eighteen months, grain, more cavalry, gunners. Some at court think Villefranche fortified and Saluces, Savillan and Fossano garrisoned would let the army winter in Piedmont; the King does not tire of saying so, but Catinat is not to let the King’s wish override his judgement. Pignerol is “le premier objet” in any plan. And the King would greatly wish Coni taken at the close of the campaign. Louis XIV, 29 August and 6 September. A treaty offered by the people of Mondovì is good but can only serve to sound them, since the army can no longer take quarters there. The resident at Geneva reports the enemy has asked the city for passage into Savoy and would go by the Valais into the Chablais. Larray has thrown an Irish battalion into Briançon for fear the Barbets would seize it. If Catinat crosses the Po, let it be before the enemy moves. Chamlay has arrived. Louis XIV, 14 September, Fontainebleau. Chamlay has reported, and the King has seen “avec peine” that the upshot is to withdraw the army of Piedmont over the mountains at the end of the campaign and not to bring it back. He sets out both sides at length. Against withdrawal: the enemy masters of Italy, the allies and neutral princes forced to declare against him, Casale lost from view, the reputation of his arms damaged and his enemies encouraged by an appearance of weakness “quoyque fausse dans le fonds”. For it: the impossibility of subsisting in Piedmont without Turin; a country “fort estroit et extrêmement couvert”, cut by torrents that rise in hours and cannot be bridged; the distance of Casale; the sickness of the troops every campaign, with no hospitals to hold them; the enemy’s freedom to engage or refuse behind the Doire and the Po. Then Catinat’s plan for the defensive: the cols of Provence, Dauphiné and Savoy held, the heights of Saint-Pierre by Pignerol and of Suze occupied, cheaper subsistence, fewer sick, the surplus cavalry on the Saône ready to go to Germany, and the Duke of Savoy left to choose between keeping the allied army idle in his ruined country or sending it away and seeing the French return. “J’ay comparé les inconvénients et les avantages d’un parti avec ceux de l’autre … et je me suis déterminé à préférer le parti solide à l’honorable.” The orders follow. Prolong the campaign to All Saints or even Saint-Martin, and keep Carmagnole to the last, because both cover the negotiation with the Pope and the Italian princes that might extricate him from Casale “et mesme peut-estre de la guerre de Piedmont”; the enemy must not learn that he means to quit Piedmont for good, so the works at Carmagnole go on, “avec un peu moins de vivacité et de dépense”. When the order comes, carry off what can be carried, the grain on the cavalry’s cruppers to Pignerol, throw the rest in the water, tear up the works, burn palisades, gates, hay and grain. Secure Pignerol’s magazines against a bombardment, which “me donneroit beaucoup de mortification en présence de mon armée”. Hold the valleys of Pragelas and Pérouse for the Briançon road. After recrossing, take Coni in the winter; the artillery and stores are ordered to Lyon and Grenoble. Fortify Briançon and the frontier against the valleys of Luzerne, Saint-Martin and Angrogne. Winter quarters by Catinat’s memoir. And retreat with such precaution that the enemy can attempt nothing. The full segmented readings, with the groups as printed and page breaks, are in the repository under catinat1691/letters .

The catalogue listed five ciphertexts of Barberini to Ceva as a transcription job: DECODE says “deciphered in original”, so the text was taken to have been read at the time and the work to be copying a decipherment off the leaf. That was only half right. Two were left: R75 , of 25 September 1632, and R84 , of 18 December 1632. Both are read here. The system is homophonic and syllabic on two-digit figures, with every pair beginning 2 a null and the single figure 6 as word separator; because 6 occurs inside no code, word boundaries are certain and the only ambiguity is whether the next code is two digits or a three-digit nomenclator element. One hundred and seventeen nomenclator elements stay unread, and the names of both letters are inside them.

h: What was catalogued, and what was there
b: Busta 346 of the Francia series of the Segreteria di Stato holds the originals and ciphers sent from Rome to Ceva during his extraordinary nunciature, 1632 to 1634. DECODE catalogued eleven ciphertexts from it, R74 to R84. The catalogue entry here named five — R75, R77, R78, R82, R84 — and scored them by rule from the metadata, unviewed. Opening the records changed the problem. Every one of the eleven carries, as an attachment, a key marked #KEY: reconstructed , #TRANSCRIBER NAME: George Lasry , #DATE OF TRANSCRIPTION: October 24, 2020 . Every one also carries the same 29,050-byte file of aligned decipherments, covering four letters. So the state of the dossier before this session was: DECODE Item Date Pages Before R74 346-1 7 Sept 1632 1 read by Lasry R75 346-2 25 Sept 1632 2 not read R76 346-3 1632 3 marked decrypted R77 346-4 1632 2 read by Lasry R78 346-5 1632 2 read by Lasry R79–R81, R83 346-6 to -8, -10 1632–34 7 marked decrypted R82 346-9 27 [Oct] 1632 1 read by Lasry R84 346-11 18 Dec 1632 2 not read Three of the five ciphertexts the catalogue named were therefore already read, and two were not. t: Barberini to Nuncio Ceva — the two letters of ASV Francia 346 without a published reading
b: The key is Lasry’s. It was re-derived here from his four aligned readings, parsed into 104 line pairs and 179 distinct tokens, which confirms it and settles three points the key note leaves open. Token Value 6 word separator 2x null — no pair beginning 2 ever carries plaintext XY letter or syllable, 61 codes: three homophones for each vowel, two for most consonants, and groups for al, che, chi, con, da, de, di, et, il, in, io, la, ma, mi, no, per, qu, quel, se, si, st pXY nomenclator element: one prefix digit followed by an ordinary two-digit code First, the figure 6 occurs inside no code at all — not in a key pair, not in any of the ninety-five nomenclator elements. Word boundaries in this cipher are therefore certain, which is unusual and is what makes the rest tractable. Second, the DECODE key note says the nomenclator elements “have 4 digits starting with prefix 4”. They have three . Concatenating Lasry’s own token stream for 346:1 and diffing it against the original transcription of the same leaf gives a 99.7% match with no dropped prefix; the elements are three digits as they stand. The prefix is 4 in twenty-seven of the ninety-five, but it is also 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 8 or 9. Third, in ninety-one of the ninety-five the two digits after the prefix are themselves a valid key code. The element is a prefix plus an ordinary code, which is exactly why the parse is ambiguous: at most positions a two-digit and a three-digit reading are both legal. Twenty-nine of the hundred pairs are dead ( 02 05 06 12 16 32 33 36 42 46 52 56 60–69 72 76 82 86 92 96 99 ), and meeting one forces the three-digit reading, but that is not enough on its own.

b: The decoder is a position-indexed beam search over the digit stream. Every 6 is consumed as a separator; elsewhere the beam chooses between a two-digit code, a two-digit null and a three-digit element, scored by a character model. Scoring is incremental — the shared lang package’s dense model is a flat table of log P(c | previous four characters), so each emitted character costs one array lookup and a beam of several hundred is cheap. The model matters more than the search. it-cinquecento is Renaissance diplomatic Italian but stops around 1620 and knows nothing of this clerk’s hand: one sign for u and v, doubled letters dropped, word division his own. It was interpolated with a model built on 7,693 characters from the dossier itself — the passages the clerk wrote in clear, plus Lasry’s plaintext of whichever letters were not under test. Calibration is leave-one-document-out against Lasry’s four letters: the nomenclator inventory offered for a document is built from the other three only, which is the situation of R75 and R84. Agreement with his own segmentation: Model Tokens Nomenclator recall Precision it-cinquecento alone 0.945 0.52 0.70 interpolated, w = 0.6 0.958 0.70 0.79 Per letter, interpolated: 346:1 0.871, 346/4 0.928, 346/5 0.905, 346/9 0.951. The figure to keep in view is the nomenclator recall. Three elements in ten are still missed, and a missed element is not rendered as a gap — it comes out as two or three plausible Italian letters. Errors in the readings below are concentrated there. The one independent check is R75’s own leaf. A decipherer in 1632 wrote his reading between the cipher lines, and the DECODE transcriber copied what was legible of it. It was used for nothing — not the key, not the model, not the decoder. On the twenty-four lines where enough survives, 1,105 letters, 77.5% agreement , ignoring word division; the last line agrees at 100%. The residue is shared between this reading and the witness’s own illegibility, since the transcriber flagged much of the faded interlinear with ? and * . R75 (25 September 1632), f. 81r, left half of four lines in the lower part of the page: the 1632 decipherer’s interlinear, … di guerra saranno sempre in pericolo … a conoscere quanto sia pericolosa alla Francia … cominciano hormai a pensar a … , the witness this reading was checked against. t: Barberini to Nuncio Ceva — the two letters of ASV Francia 346 without a published reading
b: Two pages, 1,446 code groups. Barberini on what the Swedish victories do to the French alliance. The argument is a single one, pressed hard: the victories make l’accomodamento easier and l’unione far harder, and the nuncio is to make the French court see that the power now winning is a danger to France herself. Gaps are unresolved nomenclator elements or transcription noise; italics mark elements read here. …le vittorie di […] e quella forza renderanno per avventura più facile […] quell’accomoda mente di […], ma più difficile assai […] quell’unione… per […] interessi di Francia … è tempo che se cominci a conoscere quanto sia pericolosa alla Francia la potenza d[i …], che cominciano [hor]mai a pensar a cose [grandi] et ad indrizar la [mira] loro a […]; consideri quanto sia oportuno alli vastissimi pens[ieri] di […] natione estendere il loro dominio sino al Mediterraneo con acquisto d’una piazza , e con quanto buon fonda mente lo possono sperare in una [rivoluzione] … di Francia … hanno tanto forze marittime e terrestri; consideri… che la vittoria […] è altret anto formidabile alla Francia quanto alla […]… [non si] sarà sempre al medesimo, darà sempre orecchie a[l] torbidi, et haverà chi li suggerisca; et un successor[e]… restringer in maniera che sempre non habbi libertà di [salvarsi] in campagna… [bisogna] cercar di compor[re gli] esterni, che cagioneranno e fo[men]teranno li domestici… [è] già… arrivata a tal […] di gloria… che può con ragion temere che la […] fortuna non si rivolti; cerchi dunque d’augumentarla con l’arti… pur vuol seguitar… indrizi le cose per intraprender guerra contro… quel[li] che sola parte manca alla gloria di […]. In somma… le congiunture presenti sono più contrarie alla s[ua] […] quell’unione, tanto più deve […] pensar a ritrovar ragioni che la persuadano. The unnamed power is Sweden. The 1632 decipherer’s own interlinear supplies, where this reading has a gap, the words pensieri di goto natione — the Gothic nation — and it is the reach of that nation sino al Mediterraneo that Rome wants Paris to contemplate.

t: Barberini to Nuncio Ceva — the two letters of ASV Francia 346 without a published reading
b: Two pages, 954 code groups, written a month after Lützen (16 November 1632). The first folio is largely in clear: Barberini acknowledges Ceva’s despatch of the 8th, says he has nothing further to answer, and refers him to Mons. Bichi at court. The cipher carries the analysis, and it turns throughout on quella vittoria . ricordando a […] che si […] quella vittoria contro […] con la sua consueta prudenza , ad indur[re] […] a facilitar il […]… […] che bollivano in Francia dopo la mia partenza; pure de[…] li torbidi di […] furono cagione che li […] concludessero la […]… le gelosie [che] quella potenza di Francia cerca di […]; e li spiriti inquieti […] fanno pastura su li impegni che il […] tiene con […] potenti, e si muovono più facil mente con speranza di fo[men]to e diversione. Per stabilire et assicurar le cose […] bisogna levarsi le inimicitie esterne… nascerà l’alt[r]o in mano di Francia . Posso dire che stia […] se vo[gliono] ridur a termini ragionevoli le pretensioni… non […] entrar in […] cose, non lascierà di andar [f]acilitando le […] maniera che a lei s[i] accenna… la fuga di […] non so quanto sia a proposito con ins[o]liti rigori… [in] Francia metter in disperatione… potendo da[…] conseguenze che tengano disunita per un lungo pezzo la Francia , e sotto giogo alle esterne violenze, o almeno impotente a soccorrer li suoi alleati. That last clause is the point of the despatch and it is new. The Roman reading of Lützen, a month on, is not relief at the death of Gustavus Adolphus but apprehension about France: the danger is now a France held disunited, under external pressure, and unable to help her allies.

Deciphering R75 puts a placeholder at each element; aligning that reading against the 1632 interlinear shows which word of the contemporary decipherment stands at the placeholder. Twenty-two elements caught a witness fragment, and six survive checking against Lasry’s four letters, where they were not fitted: Code Reading Evidence 474 mente piena~, principal~, non sola~ per il solo proprio, malacomoda~; witness fragment met 495 quanto “e ~ al proporre arbitrare”; pairs with 498 498 tanto “che ~ in <347> quanto in <857> si sappia la cagione” 830 Francia four times out of four in Lasry’s letters, always after a feminine article: “render la ~ più poderosa”, “valere a danno quella ~”, “hoggi la ~ in a di dar legge” 854 guerra R75 interlinear, twice 149 piazza R75 interlinear, “acquisto d’una ~” Adding the six raised the control agreement on R75 from 0.737 to 0.775. That test is partly circular for 854 and 149 , which came from the witness itself; the independent evidence for 474 , 495 , 498 and 830 is that they fit the four letters Lasry read, which the witness never touched. The pairing of 498 and 495 as tanto…quanto around two unread place codes is the cleanest of them. One near miss is worth recording. 491 drew the fragment goto — the Gothic nation, Sweden — but it does not fit its four contexts in Lasry’s letters, where it stands before unione and after conferito con . It is left open rather than forced.

b: Six letters to the duc de Nevers catalogued as one ciphered correspondence. No. 23 is a clear copy with a nine-entry name code whose key is bound on the next leaf, and reads in full. Nos. 24, 25 and 60 share a two-digit alphabet laid out in alphabetical order, rebuilt from a few letters glossed between the lines: ten of twelve runs read. No. 78 and Laurière’s 1593 letter stay open. Paris and Champagne → the duc de Nevers · name code and two-digit alphabet inside clear French · 1590–91 · read in part Champagne news-letters to Nevers, 1590–91 to Duke of Nevers BnF français 3623 nos. 23, 24, 25, 60 and 78, and français 3625 no. 55 (Laurière, 9 July 1593), all listed “avec chiffre” and without decipherment (DECODE R9453–R9455, R9459, R9460: Non-decrypted). Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 21 September 2026 read in part Summary. The catalogue item grouped six letters to Louis de Gonzague, duc de Nevers, as one Champagne correspondence and proposed to test Tomokiyo’s seventy Nevers keys on them. They turned out to be three different things. No. 23, Bienvenut’s letter from Paris of the last day of February 1590, is a clear copy in which only nine persons and provinces are coded by small numbers, and the key is bound with it on the next leaf: it reads in full. Nos. 24, 25 and 60, news-letters of June 1590 in one hand, use a short two-digit homophonic alphabet whose values rise with the alphabet (a in the 30s, e in the 40s, n in the 60s, u in the 90s). A few letters written faintly above the figures of nos. 25 and 60 anchor it, and the order does the rest: ten of the twelve cipher passages read in whole or in part (“la rupture de l’edict [de] l’union”, “contre la ligue”, “du sieur Ludovic”). Tomokiyo’s key no. 46, the one used from Nevers’s office in 1593, does not fit. No. 78 has a single group of six signs and stays open. The Laurière letter of 9 July 1593 (fr. 3625 no. 55) is f. 66r, in a mixed syllabic code of figures and signs; the groups it shares with his 13 July letter (no. 10, f. 10r), which carries the office’s interlinear decipherment, read it in fragments (“… que le Roy soit encores …”, “… la volonté du pape …”).

The code is syllabic: most words of the decipherment sit over two to five groups whose boundaries are not marked, so only groups that fall under the same word twice, or alone under a one-word gloss, were accepted. With that table 19 of the 86 groups of no. 55 read, e.g. “come […] du que […]”, “[…] que le Roy soit encores […]”, “[…] a la volonté du pape […] aussitost”. The rest stays open; a language model has nothing to score with four groups in five unknown.

t: Charles IX to Philibert du Croc — an undated Scottish cipher already read by George Lasry
b: A two-page letter wholly in graphic cipher, addressed to Charles IX’s ambassador in Scotland and catalogued by DECODE as non-decrypted. George Lasry had already solved it and Satoshi Tomokiyo published his full-page plaintext overlays in 2022. Charles directs du Croc to shape the peace, government and council around the young James VI, prevent a marriage before France is consulted, preserve Scottish attachment to France, and stop English encroachment. The catalogue’s “1 Jan 1550” is a metadata error: Destray labels the original without place or date; it belongs to 1565–67 or 1572. French court → Scotland · homophonic nomenclator · 1565–67 or 1572 · already solved Charles IX to Philibert du Croc from Charles IX Archives départementales de la Nièvre, fonds du Bourg de Bozas, exact cote unreported · two pages, French, wholly ciphered · DECODE R2789, “Non-decrypted” · catalogue item 34 The images were behind DECODE’s login. Once opened, the cited edition led directly to the answer: George Lasry had already deciphered the letter and published full-page plaintext overlays in 2022. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 20 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 already solved Summary. DECODE R2789 describes this two-page symbol cipher as non-decrypted and the catalogue consequently ranked it as an open class-C target. It is not open. Satoshi Tomokiyo’s Cryptiana page publishes George Lasry’s red plaintext overlay on both pages, dated 25 May 2022. The authenticated DECODE images, Destray’s 1924 facsimile on Gallica, and Lasry’s overlays are the same recto and verso. Charles tells his ambassador to protect the Scottish peace, shape the young James VI’s upbringing and council, prevent him from concluding a marriage before France is consulted, preserve Scottish attachment to France, and stop English encroachment. The prior reading leaves several signs and short clauses as question marks, which are retained here. The catalogue date “1 Jan 1550” is also wrong: Destray labels the letter without place or date, and Charles was not born until June 1550. The defensible date is 1565–67 or 1572, du Croc’s Scottish missions.

t: Charles IX to Philibert du Croc — an undated Scottish cipher already read by George Lasry
h: The document and the date correction
b: Paul Destray printed the address as “A monsr du Croq, mon conseiller et me d’hostel ordinaire et mon ambassadeur en Escosse” and catalogued the item as document XLIII, S. l. n. d. : without place or date. He noted that the letter, its addition, and the King’s second signature were in cipher; Pinart countersigned it. The two following facsimile leaves are the same images now served by DECODE. DECODE’s structured date spans 1550–1574 but supplies day and month as 1 January; the catalogue flattened that into “1 Jan 1550.” That cannot be a document date: Charles IX was born on 27 June 1550. Cryptiana’s cautious “1565–1567 or 1572” follows the periods in which du Croc served in Scotland and is retained here. The contents fit the minority of James VI, but they do not distinguish those missions securely. The recto: the main letter in graphic cipher, followed lower on the leaf by Charles’s signature and the beginning of the ciphered postscript. t: Charles IX to Philibert du Croc — an undated Scottish cipher already read by George Lasry
b: Tomokiyo’s page “George Lasry’s Solutions of Unsolved Ciphers” has a section headed “Charles IX to Philibert du Croc (1565–1567 or 1572).” Beneath the manuscript it says “This is solved as follows” and reproduces Lasry’s plaintext in red directly over the signs on both pages. That is decisive prior art, not a conjectural match: page geometry, line breaks, signatures, and the postscript agree throughout. The system is a French homophonic nomenclator: several graphic signs can represent letters, while other signs stand for whole words or names. Lasry’s displayed key includes values such as de , et , que , par , pour , je , vous , la Royne d’Angleterre , la Royne d’Escosse , and royaulme . It is not the symbol system used in Catherine de Médicis’s separate letter to du Croc of 27 April 1567. Lasry’s published overlay on the verso, continuing the postscript about English encroachment. It reads the document in substance while honestly retaining several groups as question marks. Image: Overlay by George Lasry on the verso, published by Satoshi Tomokiyo on Cryptiana, 25 May 2022.

t: Charles IX to Philibert du Croc — an undated Scottish cipher already read by George Lasry
b: The opening tells du Croc that he knows both the man and those with whom he must deal, and that his demonstrated devotion makes further advice unnecessary. He is to follow the instructions already given and those now sent, especially “le bien de la paix du dict pais.” Charles then turns from what can presently be done for “ma seur” to the young King: Je desire que mon nepveu aussy sur toutes choses soit bien nourri, qu’il ait tousjours, à l’imitation de ses predecesseurs, à moi et aux miens sa principalle affection. Du Croc is to attend closely to the settlement of Scotland’s peace, government, and council. Without revealing that the direction comes from Charles, he must ensure that James neither marries nor concludes a marriage before Charles has been informed and can send his intention. Above all, he is to retain the hearts of the Scots so that their accustomed affection for the French kings does not diminish. The postscript is blunter: Ce que vous avez principalement affaire par delà est de donner ordre que les Anglois n’empiètent aucune chose en Escosse… Du Croc must act prudently, make the Scots recognize that France seeks their preservation, and avoid occasions that could obstruct the friendship. The closing lines mention the English ambassadors and a possible treaty, but the gaps in the overlay are too large for a responsible continuous translation. The repository preserves a line-by-line diplomatic transcription and a normalized summary.

t: An anonymous figure cipher of October 1586 — the “unread” two thirds were deciphered in 1586, on the next leaf and between the lines
b: A League-period letter in two-digit figures, listed with a partial key and two thirds of its first page unread. The volume holds its own decipherment: folio 168 is a clear text of the cipher down to a cross mark, and from that cross to the end the decipherer wrote the plaintext between the lines. Tomokiyo’s key agrees with the glosses ( Guienne , tres confident , Fumé ), which also give 87 = e and the King of Navarre’s sign. The letter: Fumé, vice-admiral of Guyenne and Navarre’s Catholic confidant, keeps proposing a reconciliation between Navarre and the addressee, probably Guise, while Catherine de Médicis negotiates. Angoumois → a League leader · two-digit figure cipher · 28 October 1586 · decipherment found An anonymous figure cipher of October 1586 BnF Clairambault 357 ff. 167–168 · a Catholic nobleman writes to a League leader during Catherine de Médicis’s talks with Navarre · listed as “two thirds of the first page unread” The volume holds the letter’s own 1586 decipherment: a clear text on the next leaf and plaintext between the lines of the rest · Tomokiyo’s partial key checks against it · the letter is read from it Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 18 September 2026 · updated 21 September 2026 resolved Summary. Satoshi Tomokiyo published part of the key of this letter, a homophonic two-digit figure cipher dated 28 October 1586. He noted that about two thirds of the first page was not deciphered. The volume already holds a decipherment. Folio 168 is a clear text of folio 167r, in a secretary hand, from the first words (“Jay receu voz deux lettres en ung mesme temps”) down to a cross mark (“qui passe avant ✝”). The same cross stands in the margin of f. 167r. From that cross to the end of the verso, the decipherer wrote the plaintext between the lines , word by word over the figures. Tomokiyo’s key agrees with the interlinear words wherever it was tested, so the clear text belongs to this cipher. It is not a separate letter. The letter is from a Catholic of the Angoumois. Fumé, vice-admiral of Guyenne , a Catholic and “tres confident du Roy de Navarre”, has several times proposed through him a reconciliation between Navarre and the addressee, who is probably the duke of Guise. The letter also covers Catherine de Médicis’s negotiation, what the Queen of England could procure, and Villeroy writing about Mayenne. Status: resolved from the contemporary decipherment, not by new cryptanalysis. The transcription has uncertain words, and the verso glosses were read only in part.

t: An anonymous figure cipher of October 1586 — the “unread” two thirds were deciphered in 1586, on the next leaf and between the lines
h: The interlinear decipherment, and the key check
b: About thirty lines down f. 167r, a ✝ in the left margin marks the point where f. 168 stops. From there the decipherer worked between the lines. Checking the glosses against Tomokiyo’s table is a direct test of both: F. 167r. The glosses Fumé , visadmiral , de and du Roy de Navarre stand over the figures. Then the writer continues in clear: bien qu’il soit catholique et loyal a . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Clairambault 357 f. 167r, via Gallica (btv1b9001053r). Figures Interlinear gloss Tomokiyo’s key gives 74 24 34 28 29 72 Guienne g u i e n e 26 43 28 82 tres t r e s 18 37 19 35 34 25 28 19 26 confident c o n f i d e n t 25 24 # du Roy de Navarre d u + a nomenclator sign 35 24 64 87 Fumé f u m + 87 , which is therefore e 92 81 et que et que Above the cross, the key’s reading of the figures matches f. 168 in the runs tested. For example, 25 28 88 22 20 24 26 88 72 82 70 14 | 18 28 gives de r · autres pla|ce , where f. 168 has et autres places qui vous ont esté distraictes . The check adds a few things to the published table. 87 is e and 71 is a. 22, the commonest group, reads as a null in every word checked. 66 is a null, and so are the dotted groups 45.31.73.65.21. The double-barred # is the King of Navarre, glossed three times. D is England, and && is Mayenne, as Tomokiyo had it.

t: An anonymous figure cipher of October 1586 — the “unread” two thirds were deciphered in 1586, on the next leaf and between the lines
b: From f. 168, with uncertain words marked: Jay receu voz deux lettres en ung mesme temps, dont jay faict communication a M r de la Forest et M r de Corbet … tres fasché du bon terme en quoy sont voz affaires … Indisposé d’une maladye qui m’a travaillé pres de deux moys … le commis a l’abbé de la Couronne … le voyage et negotiation qu’il entreprenoit estoit contraire a celle de l’an passé, seroit trouvé estrange non seullement de ses amys catholiques de France, mais des princes estrangers. Sur quoy il apportoit tout ce qu’il pouvoit de raisons … de la Royne mere … qui luy promettoit … de ne desirer faire la paix qu’a condition qu’il n’y auroit que la Religion catholique en France … que chascun avoit faict son affaire, et l’avoit on laissé seul abandonné. … Je croy que faisant [?] et autres places qui vous ont esté distraictes vous les pourrez avoir … la brouillerie du Roy de Navarre et de vous, que je tiens tres difficile pour la qualité que chascun de vous a prinse … qui passe avant. ✝ From the interlinear decipherment of the rest: Je vous diray que j’ay esté pressé, et la seule bonne volonté d’un que vous congnoissez … qui s’appelle Fumé, visadmiral de Guienne, tres confident du Roy de Navarre, bien qu’il soit catholique et loyal a moy … pour quelque negotiation … Il est bien adverty. Il m’a plusieurs foys proposé cette reconciliation, qu’il dict luy estre aussy aysé et facille comme je la luy fais difficille et malaisée … si vous y voullez entendre … Il m’a quasy prié de la part du Roy de Navarre … la guerre … asseurance que la Royne d’Angleterre ne pourroit procurer … and on the verso … Jay envoyé a … Villeroy, qui me manda que pour contenter Monsieur du Mayne … conclure la paix, et si l’on donne quelque advantage aux Huguenotz … The writer is a Catholic nobleman of the Angoumois or Saintonge. He mentions the abbey of La Couronne near Angoulême, M rs de la Forest and de Corbet, and Bordeaux. He writes during the autumn of 1586, while Catherine de Médicis was negotiating with Henri of Navarre (the interviews of Saint-Brice took place that December). The addressee is set against Navarre as head of the other religious party, and Mayenne is named in the third person, so the addressee is most likely Henri, duke of Guise. That identification is an inference and not a reading.

t: Lord Cobham to Walsingham, May–June 1588
b: Four letters of the English peace commissioner in the Low Countries, clear English with cipher passages in Greek-like signs (BL Harley 287, DECODE R8490–R8496). Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read in part Summary. DECODE catalogues four letters of Lord Cobham to Walsingham from the spring of 1588 as undeciphered. They are clear English with passages in Greek-like signs. The key record the catalogue suggested is Bodley’s 1590 cipher and does not fit. The right key comes from Cobham’s own April letters in the same volume, which were deciphered between the lines at the time. About sixty glossed words, aligned at full scan resolution, give a sign inventory ( signs.tsv ) and the code numbers: 7 is the Queen, 10 the Lord Admiral, 15 Parma and 16 the King of Spain. The system turns out to be polyphonic, with one sign for s, t and a, and another for r and y. So a small solver ( solve.py ) gives each sign its set of letters and matches the cipher words against a word list drawn from the Calendar of State Papers Foreign for 1588. Rereading the runs line by line against its candidates reads about a third of the cipher words: “in all armadas”, “so forwarde in the action that he promised Q[ueen]”, “have promised the haven of Rain”, “Italians arriving … Antonio”, “within France”. The consolidated reading, with a grade on every word, is in cobham1588/READING.md . The rest stays unread where signs could not be resolved from the scans.

t: Lord Cobham to Walsingham, May–June 1588
b: William Brooke, Lord Cobham, was one of Elizabeth’s commissioners sent to treat with Parma’s deputies in the spring of 1588. The talks moved from Ostend to Bourbourg while the Armada was fitting out. The Calendar of State Papers Foreign (vol. 21 pt 4) calendars his letters in SP 77, but not these Harley copies. t: Lord Cobham to Walsingham, May–June 1588
h: The sign inventory, and what reads
b: A third pass worked from the scans at full resolution (7,200 pixels wide), aligning about sixty glossed words on ff. 75, 79 and 89 sign by sign. The result is cobham1588/signs.tsv . The families that look alike at reading size separate cleanly. p is a loop with its tail swept down-left (“upon”, “popes”, “perswade”). l is a circle crossed by a straight stem (“arrival”, “holding”). h is a stem with a bowl to the right (“harken”, “thought”). m is a horizontal S with a loop (“made”, “commission”), and w a dot and stroke (“willing”, “sworne”). The glosses also show that the system is more polyphonic than any simple key allows. Λ is s and t (and probably a), γ is r and y, c is o and once a, and the l sign once stands for t. The code numbers are glossed too: 7 = her Majesty, 10 = the Lord Admiral, 15 = the Duke of Parma, 16 = the King of Spain. f. 80r: “as usuall in all armadas in numbers, that at the armada … which was the 20”. The word ΛV∽ΛŧΛ gives ARMADA with m glossed, if the wide Λ is a and ŧ is d. Also “hoping them in the □ pances ”, probably “expences”; a run with vertical word dividers ending “ to these termes ”; and “22 is … in the action … that he promised Q[ueen] ”. (M) f. 88r: “15:” is the Duke of Parma . The first cipher run probably begins “ captain …” before a name, “with 40 men of …, [who] have promised the …”. The rest turns on signs no gloss shows. (M/I) f. 92r: “4 sent by …”, perhaps “the Portugals” (I), and “of letters ” (M).

Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 resolved Summary. The Unsolved Catalogue listed DECODE R24 (item 238) as a ciphered letter from an unknown sender at Cologne to an unknown recipient, dated 1 January 1721, with what the cipher hides unknown. The date is only the year DECODE was given. The leaf is headed in clear Brusselles 9 ott.re 1721 , and it is filed in the archive of the Cologne nunciature. It is not unread. In November 2020 George Lasry attached a reconstructed key (“ASV – C15”) and a segmented decryption to the record, and Paolo Bonavoglia attached a running reading with an English translation. Checked against the image, the transcription is right. Three values are added from context: 18 is qu , not que ; 55 is gli ; 67 is probably g . With them, 182 of the 189 tokens have a value. The slip asks for news of someone at Tournai, mentions “the Cologne affair” and offers to write to a correspondent. Three short tokens and four nomenclator codes stay open. Arch. Nunz. Colonia 5, f. 26r. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Arch. Nunz. Colonia 5 f. 26r, via DECODE R24.

t: A cipher slip from Brussels to the Cologne nunciature, 9 October 1721 — already read by Lasry and Bonavoglia
b: The leaf carries a clear dateline and nine lines of figures, 189 tokens separated by commas, with no address or signature. Brussels was then the capital of the Austrian Netherlands, and ecclesiastical business there went through the nunciatures, so the slip was probably sent by someone at Brussels to the nuncio at Cologne, in whose archive it is kept. Nothing on the leaf proves this. The key, as Lasry rebuilt it, gives letters and a few syllables fixed homophones of one to three digits (a 6|77, e 04|40, i 17|71, o 16|61, r 14|41, s 01|38, che 35, di 53, ma 74). The nulls 2, 22 and 222 stand between words, and four-digit codes in the 9300s and 9400s stand for words or names. Because the groups are separated by commas, there is no parsing problem.

t: A cipher slip from Brussels to the Cologne nunciature, 9 October 1721 — already read by Lasry and Bonavoglia

Sopra l’affare di Colonia, ma egli, a quel che vedo, ne è informato. Se stima a proposito che io [76] scriva in [9356] ad un suo corrispondente, lo farò volentieri, ma attendo i suoi ordini in questo. “About the curate […] a divinis [suspended from his office?], [I would be] glad to know something of [9336 9485] of Tournai. About the Cologne affair: he, as far as I see, is informed of it. If you think it right that I write [76] in [9356] to a correspondent of yours, I will gladly do so, but I await your orders on this.” Bonavoglia’s reading is the same, except where the values below change it.
