t: “Mr. Conleys Hand”: two royalist letters in Abraham Cowley’s hand, Paris 1652–53 — clear text read, code groups open
b: DECODE R7768–R7769, catalogued under an author “Mr. Conleys Hand”, are a fair copy of two letters from the Queen’s court at Paris to a royalist in Holland; the docket reads “mr Cowleys Hand”, the poet who ciphered for Jermyn and Henrietta Maria. The letters are clear English; the cipher is 23 numbers in five runs hiding a few names and a place. Too few to break without a key; the Hyde–Barwick key does not fit, and the letters are not in Cowley’s printed correspondence. Paris → a royalist in Holland · numbers in clear English · 28 December 1652 and 3 May 1653 · attempted, not solved “Mr. Conleys Hand”: two letters in Abraham Cowley’s hand, Paris 1652–53 from Abraham Cowley British Library, Harley MS 7003 ff. 314r–315r, DECODE R7768 and R7769: a fair copy of two letters from the exiled Queen’s court at Paris, in clear English with a few code numbers. Both letters were transcribed from the DECODE images. The author on DECODE turns out to be a misread docket. The numbers were tested against the one related key in the repository, and the printed Cowley letters were searched. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 attempted Summary. DECODE lists these two records under an author called “Mr. Conleys Hand”, sending from Paris to an unknown recipient, and calls them a non-decrypted nomenclator. The images show a clean copy of two letters, dated Paris, 28 December 1652 and 3 May 1653. A docket in another hand reads “mr Cowleys Hand”: the original was written by Abraham Cowley. The poet was secretary to Lord Jermyn and, by his biographer’s account, ciphered and deciphered most of the letters between the King and Queen. The letters are almost wholly in clear English. They cover Bordeaux’s mission to England, the Dutch war, the Fronde, the King’s journey into Holland and a rumour that the Bordelais would declare a republic. The cipher is 23 numbers in five runs standing for a place and a few persons. These are not read. The numbers are too few to rebuild a key. The Hyde–Barwick key of 1659 gives nonsense, and the letters are not among Cowley’s printed letters to Henry Bennet. One reading is offered as a hypothesis only: the place is “Scotland”. Status: clear text read; code numbers not read. A Jermyn or Queen’s cipher of 1652–53 would open them.

t: “Mr. Conleys Hand”: two royalist letters in Abraham Cowley’s hand, Paris 1652–53 — clear text read, code groups open
b: Harley MS 7003 f. 314r, letter of 28 December 1652: two of the five code runs inside the clear text. Image: British Library, Harley MS 7003 f. 314r, via DECODE R7768. R7768 images f. 314r and f. 314v. R7769 images f. 314v and f. 315r, so the middle leaf appears on both records (the two files are byte-identical). The first letter runs from f. 314r to the top of f. 314v, and under it another hand has written “mr Cowleys Hand”. DECODE read that note as “Conleys” and made it the author. The second letter starts lower on f. 314v and ends on f. 315r with a postscript. Below that, f. 315r starts an unrelated letter (“My Lo:”) from a royalist waiting at the Hague. It has no numbers on the imaged part. The writer is at the Queen’s court. “She intends to write to you”, and he has promised the recipient money. That fits Jermyn’s household, where Cowley wrote. The recipient is in Holland and short of money, and has a son for whom he has asked a favour of the King and Queen. He is neither Secretary Nicholas nor the Chancellor, since both are named in the third person. He is not identified.

t: “Mr. Conleys Hand”: two royalist letters in Abraham Cowley’s hand, Paris 1652–53 — clear text read, code groups open
b: The full text is in conley1652/transcription.txt . In short: 28 December 1652. The “unlucky and unseasonable sending of Monsieur Bourdeaux into England” has not yet harmed the royalists in Holland. An outright Dutch victory at sea would have been dangerous “to us”. Mazarin has not yet returned to Paris. Cardinal de Retz is in prison. The King will go to the Parlement to register edicts worth seven or eight millions. The army is before Sainte-Menehould. Then comes the cipher: “I wish I could send you any Account of the present estate of 228:196:188 (for it is undoubtedly of great importance if you can procure any assistance to be sent thither against next spring …) but wee know nothing here that you will not be informed of by 102:43:97:133:52:180 and concerning 57:102:58:20:30 dispatch back (who was the person that came lately from 248:88:46:47:96:52:7:57 ) Mr Chanchellour has given an Account of it to Secretary Nicolas.” The letter ends with a promise of money “by the next”. 3 May 1653. The writer still believes the King ought to have gone into Holland in person, although it is now too late. The Court has gone to Fontainebleau. The Count de Brienne reports that “the Bourdelois have resolved to declare themselves a Republique” under English protection; it is certain only that they have sent a person into England. The request for the recipient’s son “receives noe difficulty either with the King or Queen”. Postscript: “You may doe well to write a word to Mr 203 .”

t: “Mr. Conleys Hand”: two royalist letters in Abraham Cowley’s hand, Paris 1652–53 — clear text read, code groups open
b: run context 228:196:188 a country or region: “the present estate of ___ … assistance to be sent thither against next spring” 102:43:97:133:52:180 a person: “informed of by ___” 57:102:58:20:30 a person: “concerning ___ dispatch back” 248:88:46:47:96:52:7:57 a place: “the person that came lately from ___” 203 a person: “write a word to Mr ___” There are 23 numbers, 20 of them distinct, running from 7 to 248. The runs of five, six and eight look like names spelled out letter by letter, and the three-number run and the single 203 look like code words. Three values repeat: 102, 52 and 57. Hypothesis (grade M). The eight-number place is “Scotland” (s c o t l a n d). In the winter of 1652–53 the Glencairn rising was being raised in the Highlands, and the court at Paris was looking for help for it by the spring. That would make 52 = a and 57 = d, and the run 57:102:58:20:30 would begin with d . The other runs share too few letters to test it, so it stays a guess from context.

Not attempted: 23 numbers cannot fix a key.

t: The prince de Conti’s ciphered mémoires, March 1649 — the Fronde’s instructions to its envoys with the Archduke
b: BnF fr. 3854 nos. 41–43. The two “undeciphered” mémoires of 26–27 March were read by Lasry in 2023; they are read again here from the leaves, with three small corrections. The third, whose decipherment was meant to be the crib, is a different number code, and its clerk never glossed the first twelve lines. A key rebuilt from about 3,300 glossed groups reads them: Conti to Laigue, 5 March 1649, explaining the Rueil conference away to Archduke Leopold Wilhelm. Paris → the Archduke’s camp · letter cipher and syllabic number code · March 1649 · read The prince de Conti’s ciphered mémoires, March 1649 from Prince de Conti → to Archduke Leopold Wilhelm BnF fr. 3854 nos. 41–43, the Frondeurs’ secret instructions to their envoys with Archduke Leopold Wilhelm during the Rueil conference · two mémoires “avec chiffre”, and a third “avec chiffre et déchiffrement” The two “undeciphered” mémoires turned out to be in print (Lasry 2023), and were read again from the leaves. The deciphered one was not finished: its first twelve lines had never been read Daniel Bourdeau · read 18 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. The catalogue of new targets listed Conti’s mémoires of 26 and 27 March 1649 as two ciphers left without a decipherment. It assumed the third mémoire, which has one, would be the crib. Nos. 41 and 42 were already read. George Lasry broke them in 2023 as a “poly-homophonic” letter cipher. They were read again here, from a fresh transcription of the Gallica images with his key, and the reading adds three small corrections to his text. No. 43 is not the same cipher. It is a number code of letters and syllables, with a contemporary decipherment between the lines. That decipherment starts only at the thirteenth line. The opening — the address to Laigue and the purpose of the whole mémoire, 264 groups — had never been read. No. 43 read in full. The key was rebuilt from about 3,300 glossed groups and used to read the opening. The whole mémoire was then edited: Conti to Laigue, 5 March 1649, the day after the Rueil conference opened, explaining the conference away to the Archduke.

t: The prince de Conti’s ciphered mémoires, March 1649 — the Fronde’s instructions to its envoys with the Archduke
b: BnF Français 3854 (Gallica btv1b52520094g ) is a recueil of Fronde papers from the prince de Conti’s side, January to April 1649. It holds his instructions to his envoys, the marquis de Noirmoutier and Geoffroy de Laigue, the Archduke’s Spanish answers, and three pieces in cipher that Omont describes as follows: No. 41 (f. 113r–v): “Mémoire, avec chiffre, du prince de Conti. A Paris, ce 26 mars 1649”. No. 42 (f. 115r): the same, “ce 27 mars 1649”, signed Armand de Bourbon . No. 43 (ff. 117r–120r): “Mémoire, avec chiffre et déchiffrement, du prince de Conti, pour un de ses envoyés auprès de l’archiduc”, undated. The catalogue’s “verify first” was to confirm that the three share one cipher. They do not. Nos. 41 and 42 are written in lower-case letters mixed with clear words. No. 43 is written in numbers, with a clerk’s letters and syllables above most of them. No. 41, f. 113r: “A Paris ce 26 Mars 1649”, then the letter cipher inline with clear words. Jcctg nle Monsieur de nrgmtild is “Affin que Monsieur de Noirmo[u]stier”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3854 f. 113r, via Gallica (btv1b52520094g).

t: The prince de Conti’s ciphered mémoires, March 1649 — the Fronde’s instructions to its envoys with the Archduke
h: Nos. 41 and 42: found already read, and read again
b: Prior art. A web search before any work found George Lasry, “Armand de Bourbon’s Poly-Homophonic Cipher – 1649”, HistoCrypt 2023 . Lasry deciphered both letters, printed their text with a translation, and described the system. How it works. Each plaintext letter is written as a cipher letter. A, L and R each have two signs. Five signs each stand for two to four letters: a = t/p/a/b, e = e/g, i = c/z, m = s/d/x, n = m/q. The key. There is no nomenclator. The key’s second row spells J’aime c’est un grand mal , a Boesset air of 1642. The catalogue entry. His paper cites the volume as “fr. 3584”, a typo, which is why the catalogue harvest did not match it. Read again here. All three pages were transcribed sign by sign from the full-resolution images. A beam search over each sign’s possible letters, scored with a French quadgram model and then a period word list, picked the readings. The text agrees with Lasry’s throughout, with three additions: f. 113r: dans lequel temps les choses ne pouvant pas . The cipher has ge = NE, which the printed text drops. No. 42: ordonne à ses députez de se joindre à ceux de son Altesse le prince de Conti pour insister à demander l’éloignement du cardinal Mazarin . The words are in the cipher ( arldtgmtmaed ) and in Lasry’s own figure, but not in his clean text. f. 113v: Bretaigne is enciphered with the L-sign in second place, a slip of the encipherer’s. “Monsieur de Tenerande ”, with whom Longueville is to treat, reads the same under the key; the person is unidentified. “Dix” or “six mil hommes” cannot be settled, because one sign serves both d and s. Depuis la lettre que je vous escrivi hier j’ay cru vous debvoir advertir qu’on a donné aujourd’huy arrest au parlement qui ordonne à ses députez de se joindre à ceux de son Altesse le prince de Conti pour insister à demander l’éloignement du cardinal Mazarin. On ne doute plus après cela de la rupture … Ne concluez rien pourtant que vous n’ayez le dernier advis, mais si elle arrive, mettez-vous en estat d’en faciliter les suittes. No. 42, 27 March 1649

t: The prince de Conti’s ciphered mémoires, March 1649 — the Fronde’s instructions to its envoys with the Archduke
h: No. 43: a number code, and twelve lines nobody read
b: No. 43, f. 117r. Twelve lines of numbers and clear words with nothing written above them; the clerk’s interlinear decipherment starts only at the foot ( po ur p r o cu , “pour procu[rer]”). Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3854 f. 117r, via Gallica (btv1b52520094g). The clerk who deciphered no. 43 wrote a letter or syllable above almost every number from f. 117r line 13 to the end of f. 120r. He wrote nothing over the first twelve lines. Those 264 groups carry the address and the purpose of the mémoire. The key, rebuilt from his glosses. Agents transcribed number/gloss pairs page by page, and the tallies ( key43.txt ) show a regular design: Four interleaved single-letter alphabets: 3–25 run a→z, 28–50 run z→a, 51–73 run a→z again, and about 80–98 run down. Syllables in blocks of five, in vowel order: ca ce ci co cu = 256–260, and so on through the consonants, with a second, homophonic series in the gaps. Underlining a number reverses its syllable: 385 = ra , underlined 385 = ar . Code words: 451 la Reyne , 457 le cardinal , 458 le parlement , 472 l’archiduc , 482 France . The 500s are dates. Nulls: the numbers from about 99 to 250, which are never glossed. The opening, decoded. Of the 264 groups: 220 take the value the same number has in the glosses. 24 follow from the alphabets or are nulls. 20 are syllables of the second series, fixed from context. The first draft was checked against the rest of the mémoire. Nine of the context and structural values were later found glossed on ff. 117r–120r, all as predicted: 279 de , 364 la , 354 ne (underlined, en ), 443 te , 445 su , 37 o , 43 h , 86 n , and 36 p . None was contradicted. Pour Monsieur de Legue. Parce que nous ne doutons que le cardinal ne donne une mauvaise interprétation à toutes ses actions, et qu’il ne face principalement ses efforts pour mettre l’archiduc dans la défiance de nos bonnes intentions sur le sujet de la conférence que [le] parlement a accordée, j’ay jugé à propos de vous en faire instruire, afin que vous puissiés destourner les mauvais effets des artifices du cardinal, et faire comprendre à l’archiduc que ce pourparler n’a esté causé et résolu que par les retardemens que l’archiduc apporte à nous secourir, et que nous sommes tousiours dans nos mesmes desseins … No. 43, f. 117r, lines 1–12, read here for the first time

t: The prince de Conti’s ciphered mémoires, March 1649 — the Fronde’s instructions to its envoys with the Archduke
b: The last line of f. 120r is glossed à Paris le 5me mars 1649 . That is the day after the Rueil conference opened between the court and the parlement. Conti writes to Laigue, who is with Archduke Leopold Wilhelm, to keep the Spanish alliance alive while the Frondeurs negotiate with Mazarin’s side. Why the conference happened. The parlement laid the Archduke’s envoy’s proposals ( dom Joseph ) before the Queen. Mazarin, who saw that real peace would ruin him, proposed a conference to drag things out and to make the Archduke believe the Frondeurs were giving way. “À quoy l’on a employé Vautorte.” Conti would have refused it if the Archduke’s help had been ready and Paris not starving. What it bought. No suspension of arms. Saint-Germain lets in a hundred muids of corn a day from Corbeil for as long as the conference lasts, which buys time, “mais fort peu, en vous attendant”. Why it cannot succeed. The deputies are “tous gens de bien, dans le zèle de la paix générale et dans une haine irréconciliable pour le ministériat du cardinal”. They cannot give way on Mazarin, whom the parlement has condemned. The generals stayed away on purpose, so as to be free to break the talks at will. The promise. “Dès le moment qu’il entrera en France, cette conférence se rompra”, and a truer one will be opened with the Archduke’s own deputies. The plea. “Il n’y a plus un seul moment à perdre pour nous secourir.” Laigue is to press for help with all the Archduke’s forces. Even if the Archduke will not march without a treaty, nothing is to stand in the way of relief. The complete edited text of the mémoire is in conti1649/READING43.md . Where it fits. The three mémoires frame the Frondeurs’ double game. On 5 March, Conti promises the Archduke that the conference is only a way to buy time. On 26–27 March, he tells Noirmoutier that the talks are about to break on Normandy and Mazarin, and that he should be ready. The Peace of Rueil was signed on 11 March, in between. The parlement’s arrest of 27 March shows the generals still pressing the Mazarin article after the peace.

t: The prince de Conti’s ciphered mémoires, March 1649 — the Fronde’s instructions to its envoys with the Archduke

t: The Copenhagen cryptogram — not a simple substitution of any language tested
b: Three lines found behind an 1835 portrait of a Danish general, 107 characters, unsolved at the American Cryptogram Association since the 1950s. Transcribed twice, attacked in ten languages under six reading conventions; the same solver recovers matched controls at 96 to 100 percent and the note never comes close. Working notes · September 2026 The Copenhagen cryptogram Three lines of strokes, dots, carets and digits found behind an 1835 portrait of a Danish general in a Copenhagen military museum, no. 23 on Klaus Schmeh’s Top 50, attacked here as a simple substitution in ten languages under two transcriptions and six conventions, with matched controls, and not read. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 15 September 2026 · Sources: Klaus Schmeh’s Cipherbrain posts of January 2015, August 2017 and October 2021 and their comments; the 614 × 147 px scan Danish-General-Cryptogram.jpg attempted Not solved — and not a simple substitution of any language tested closed from the scan Both transcriptions in circulation were attacked with a 5-gram annealer in ten languages. The best any language reached was −2.69 nats per letter , and 300 restarts did not move it. The same solver recovers twelve of fifteen random 103-letter passages enciphered the same way, and genuine text of this length scores between −1.4 and −2.1. Either the slip is not a simple substitution of a text in these languages, or both readings share a transcription error.

t: The Copenhagen cryptogram — not a simple substitution of any language tested
b: The slip carries three short lines. It was found, probably in the late 1950s, behind an 1835 portrait of a Danish general in a Copenhagen military museum, and sent to the American Cryptogram Association. The ACA never solved it and never wrote it up. The museum, the general and the finder are all unrecorded. Klaus Schmeh received a scan from ACA member Kent Ramliden, a Swede living in Florida who died in 2016. He published it three times: in German in January 2015, as no. 23 of his Top 50 unsolved messages in August 2017, and as German and English “cold case” posts in October 2021. The only image in circulation is that scan, 614 by 147 pixels. Two reader contributions from the 2021 comments matter here: a 25-symbol transcription by “ShadowWolf”, and a Danish quadgram hill-climb by Matthew Brown that found nothing.

t: The Copenhagen cryptogram — not a simple substitution of any language tested
b: Two readings were used. cipher.txt is this project’s, made from the scan upscaled four and six times, half a line at a time. cipher_sw.txt is ShadowWolf’s 25-symbol reading from the comments of the German post of 7 October 2021. This is the merged reading, one token per symbol, space separated: 7 N F n F B 3 A D B n o 3 D B P 6 3 B 3 P 8 D F 2 n 3 | 2 3 A W R F 0 3 A n 2 0 B n o 9 P n P 9 2 B 3 v v 3 D B | 0 A B v 3 D B P n o F 3 8 0 D B P X 0 3 B n o n F 9 n D B v n | 1 3 | n o n 3 F D B 3 F B A 1 2 3 A That is 107 tokens: 103 symbols of 20 kinds, plus 4 long vertical strokes written | and treated as sentence dividers. Digits 4 and 5 never occur. token mark on the slip count 3 digit 3 16 n plain n 13 B backslash with its trailing dot (\.) 14 F slash with its trailing dot (/.) 8 P plus sign 6 A caret or lambda (^) 6 D free-standing dot that precedes a stroke 8 o small round letter o 5 2 digit 2 5 0 tall zero 5 v as written 4 9 digit 9 3 1 digit 1 2 8 digit 8 2 7 6 X as written 1 each N n with two dots above 1 R small “or”-like glyph at the end of line 1 1 W caret with a double accent above 1 | long vertical stroke, sentence divider, not counted among the 103 4 Where the two readings differ The two readings agree symbol for symbol except that ShadowWolf splits what is merged here. He separates the backslash with a dot after it from the backslash with dots on both sides, which here is a free dot D followed by B . He separates the slash with a trailing dot from the slash with a leading dot, here D followed by F . He gives the small raised double tick after the first caret pair its own symbol. He distinguishes four caret shapes: a tall lambda-like one, which is the first caret of line 1 and the last symbol of line 3; a small one; one with a trailing dot opening line 2; and one after the zero in line 2. And he reads the second tall stroke around 1 3 in line 3 as the digit 1 rather than a divider. With those splits the symbol count is 25, which is Schmeh’s figure; merged it is 20. Both readings were attacked. Two internal regularities The letter o occurs five times and every time directly after n : no3 , no9 , +no , non and non3 , with non twice in line 3. The doubled pair vv occurs once, in line 2. Section 06 shows how far they go.

t: The Copenhagen cryptogram — not a simple substitution of any language tested
b: solve.py builds character 5-gram language models from Project Gutenberg texts in ten languages: Danish, Swedish, Norwegian, German, Dutch, French, English, Latin, Icelandic and Finnish, 0.6 to 2.4 million letters each. The corpus is not in the repository; it is fetched through the Gutendex API with the ids in the session log. The solver is simulated annealing over an injective symbol-to-letter map, 60 to 80 restarts per run, with the long strokes treated as sentence boundaries. The annealer optimises the 5-gram score alone; its top candidates are then re-ranked by dictionary coverage, which it does not optimise. Six token conventions were tested on the merged reading: the free dot as a letter, dropped, as a boundary, or fused to the following stroke; the long stroke as a letter; and the dotted n merged with plain n. The 25-symbol reading was run as it stands. A separate script, solve_sp.py , tests the hypothesis that the two dotted strokes are word separators, which would make the text 22 words averaging 3.7 letters, using a space-aware model and scoring whole-word hits. Nothing readable came out in any language under any convention. Best per-letter scores, with what the best key produced: language best score per letter, any convention what it looked like Latin −2.69 fxsisted tine togeteom scie ... Danish −2.77 junindel dige dskedesf ... / ... udstødes ... velsigne ... Norwegian −2.81 bærersag sena stjasatm ... Swedish −2.81 honensam sera stfasatv ... English −2.88 cydidsea sine stbesetf ... German −2.93 uchthien itze irbeierm ... French −2.97 chiailes lape ltbeletr ... Dutch, Icelandic, Finnish −3.07 to −3.30 The word-separator hypothesis scores −4.6 per letter under the spaced model, where real text scores about −2.3. It yields only isolated Danish words: er , elle , unge , død , døde . The last two are the fragment discussed in section 06.

t: The Copenhagen cryptogram — not a simple substitution of any language tested
b: A failed search proves nothing on its own, so the solver was calibrated on texts it should solve. control.py draws passages of 103 letters with three sentence breaks at random from the same corpora, enciphers each with a random simple substitution of about 20 symbols, and attacks it with the identical solver. Three trials per language, 40 restarts each; the real cryptogram got 60 to 80, then 300. Accuracy is the share of the passage recovered. language trial letters in key accuracy score found score of true text outcome Danish 1 19 0.99 −1.99 −1.85 recovered Danish 2 19 0.99 −1.93 −1.96 recovered Danish 3 18 0.99 −1.85 −1.76 recovered German 1 22 0.96 −1.88 −1.78 recovered German 2 19 0.79 −2.64 −1.75 partial German 3 22 0.14 −3.42 −1.81 search failed English 1 20 1.00 −1.44 −1.44 recovered English 2 21 0.99 −1.99 −1.85 recovered English 3 20 1.00 −1.67 −1.67 recovered Latin 1 18 1.00 −2.09 −2.09 recovered Latin 2 18 1.00 −1.74 −1.74 recovered Latin 3 19 0.99 −1.87 −1.72 recovered Swedish 1 22 1.00 −1.95 −1.95 recovered Swedish 2 22 0.05 −3.49 −1.59 search failed Swedish 3 22 1.00 −1.99 −1.99 recovered Twelve of fifteen passages are recovered essentially completely, and the true text always scores between −1.4 and −2.1 per letter. Two trials fail outright and one partly. In each case the true key would have scored far better than what the annealer found: −1.81 against −3.42, −1.59 against −3.49, −1.75 against −2.64. These are search failures at 40 restarts, most likely tied to 22-letter keys, and they mean that a single failed run on the real text would prove nothing. That is why the strongest candidate languages were rerun with 300 restarts on both readings. Against that calibration the cryptogram never scores better than −2.7 in any language or under any reading. So either it is not a simple substitution of a text in these ten languages, or the transcription conflates or splits letters in a way that both independent readings share. Danish, the default assumption since 2015, fits no better than Latin or Norwegian. Matthew Brown’s Danish quadgram hill-climb in the 2021 comments came to the same nothing.

t: The Copenhagen cryptogram — not a simple substitution of any language tested
b: non reads as død Under n = d, o = ø, 3 = e, the n-o-n pattern gives Danish død (dead, death), non3 gives døde (died, the dead), and no3 gives døe , the pre-1900 spelling of dø (to die). It is the one suggestive fragment in the whole search. It surfaced in the word-separator run, whose only other whole-word hits were er , elle and unge . The three symbols involved account for 34 of the 103 tokens, so this assignment fixes a third of the text. It does not extend. The rest of that reading is noise, and the run as a whole scores −4.6 per letter where real text under the same model scores about −2.3.

t: The Copenhagen cryptogram — not a simple substitution of any language tested
h: Status and what would reopen it
b: not solved Closed from the scan that exists. Three routes would reopen it. The original slip or a better scan. The ACA received the slip from the museum, so the ACA archive or Kent Ramliden’s papers are the places to ask. A second image would settle the split-versus-merged question in section 02. The painting. An 1835 portrait of a Danish general in a Copenhagen military museum points to the Tøjhusmuseet, now the Danish War Museum. Identifying the general would give a name, a date and a language. Shorthand or a private code. If the strokes and dots are a shorthand or a private code rather than letters, no substitution model applies, and nothing here tests that possibility.

t: The Cardinal of Como to the nuncio Dandini, 1580 — Henri III and the nun
b: Two cipher enclosures from the papal Secretariat to the nuncio in France, catalogued on DECODE as partially decrypted. George Lasry had decrypted the longer one (R73) in 2020. The other (R72) keeps his frame and nomenclator but reassigns the letter codes; the letters were rebuilt here by annealing, and the text matches the clerk’s decipherment written below the figures. Both letters tell the nuncio to stop Henri III visiting a nun, discreetly. Rome → Paris · homophonic figures with nomenclator · 1580 · read “The affair of the Most Christian King with the nun”: the Secretariat to the nuncio in France, 1580 from Cardinal Gallio Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Francia 283C, f. 52 and ff. 89–90 (DECODE R72, R73). The DECODE records call these cipher enclosures from the Cardinal of Como to Mgr Anselmo Dandini “partially decrypted”. R73 was already decrypted by George Lasry. R72 would not open with his key: it keeps the frame and the nomenclator but uses its own letter assignment. That assignment was rebuilt here and checked against the clerk’s decipherment written on the same leaf. Daniel Bourdeau · read 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 Como to Dandini, Paris (1580) — Read 22 14 50 38 18 12 62 48 22 82 40 72 36 30 38 36 12 · la voce et l’opinione · 266^ che · 966^ tanto · 366^ per Rome → Paris · homophonic figures with nomenclator · 1580 · read “The affair of the Most Christian King with the nun”: the Secretariat to the nuncio in France, 1580 from Cardinal Gallio Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Francia 283C, f. 52 and ff. 89–90 (DECODE R72, R73). The DECODE records call these cipher enclosures from the Cardinal of Como to Mgr Anselmo Dandini “partially decrypted”. R73 was already decrypted by George Lasry. R72 would not open with his key: it keeps the frame and the nomenclator but uses its own letter assignment. That assignment was rebuilt here and checked against the clerk’s decipherment written on the same leaf. Daniel Bourdeau · read 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 Summary. The catalogue entry (item 244) listed two ciphertexts from the papal Secretariat to its nuncio in France in 1580, with a note that one was “deciphered in the original”. Both are now read. R73 (ff. 89–90, about 1,080 groups) was decrypted by George Lasry in October 2020; his key and his decryption are attached to the DECODE records. R72 (f. 52, the enclosure of Como’s letter of 16 May 1580, about 520 groups) gives nonsense with that key. The groups still parse in Lasry’s frame: two-digit letter codes and three-digit nomenclator groups closed by a mark. The nomenclator is the same (266^ che , 966^ tanto , 366^ per ), but the letters are reassigned. Annealing the letter values against Italian, with the nomenclator words held fixed, gave readable text at once. The block of clear writing under the figures, which looks like a postscript, turned out to be the contemporary decipherment, and the two agree word for word. Both letters are about the rumour that Henri III was keeping company with a nun, which Gregory XIII wanted stopped. A few nomenclator groups and 32 illegible groups in R73 remain open. R72, f. 52: the figures, then the secretariat’s decipherment in clear, “La voce et l’opinione della pratica del Re Chr.mo con la monaca…”. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Francia 283C f. 52, via DECODE R72.

t: The Cardinal of Como to the nuncio Dandini, 1580 — Henri III and the nun
b: Francia 283C holds the Secretariat’s original letters and ciphers to the nuncio for 1580: “Corrispondenza fra il Cardinale di Como (Gallio) e Monsignore Dandini Nunzio a Parigi”. DECODE has two ciphertexts from it: R72 , f. 52: a single page of figures, filed with Como’s clear letter from the Villa, 16 May 1580 (ff. 50–53, attached to the record). The decipherment is written in clear below the figures. R73 , ff. 89r–90r: three pages of figures, undated, on damaged paper, with no decipherment on the leaves. Lasry’s reconstructed key (DECODE attachment D3190, 24 October 2020) is deterministic. Letters are two digits with an even second digit, vowels have one or two homophones, and there are no nulls. Nomenclator groups are three digits followed by a special mark, for pronouns, titles and common words: 124^ S.S., 824^ N.S., 822^ V.S., 224^ S.M.tà, 266^ che, 200^ non, 800^ mente, 988^ essere. His decryption of R73 (D3191) reads the whole letter apart from illegible groups. R72 fits the same frame. Parsed with a small dynamic program (two digits, or three digits plus the mark, which SofPe’s 2019 transcription gives as 7 or t/+ ), every group except 38 falls inside Lasry’s table. The nomenclator words come out right, but the letters between them are nonsense. The letter codes had been reassigned: letter R72 R73 (Lasry) a 14 52 81 50 92 c 18 83 14 e 12 62 18 52 i 30 72 (24) 26 62 l 22 28 n 36 22 o 38 82 34 72 r 44 40 t 28 48 44 u/v 50 92 46 82 The full R72 table, with the codes seen only in the anneal marked, is in the notes.

t: The Cardinal of Como to the nuncio Dandini, 1580 — Henri III and the nun
b: This is the clerk’s decipherment at the foot of f. 52. The decryption with the rebuilt key agrees with it, except that the cipher has commercio where the clerk wrote concetto : La voce et l’opinione della pratica del Re Chr.mo con la monaca è uscita tanto publica che se ne ragiona hormai per tutto, et da ogniuno è tenuta per vera: onde quando bene non fusse vero il fatto come vien detto a V.S. da chi presuppone di saperne l’intiero, è pure sì grande il scandalo che nasce dal concetto di S. M.tà in quel luogo, che per levarsi la infamia che gli ne viene, dovrebbe astenersi in tutto dall’andar più a quel monasterio: et V.S. doverà ricordar questo punto, et incaricarlo gagliardamente, già che si ha voluto persuaderle che il fatto non è vero. Quanto alla pratica scoperta per conto del credito et sforzo del denaro per la spesa, N. S.re persevera nella sua deliberatione persuaso a ciò da molte ragioni che non occorre scrivere. “Talk of the Most Christian King’s affair with the nun has become so public that it is discussed everywhere and taken as true by everyone. So even if the thing were not true, as Your Lordship is told by someone who claims to know the whole of it, the scandal it causes is so great that, to rid himself of the infamy, His Majesty ought to stop going to that monastery altogether. Your Lordship is to raise this point and press it on him hard, since they have tried to persuade you that it is not true. As for the scheme uncovered over the credit and the raising of money for the expense, His Holiness holds to his decision, for many reasons that need not be written.”

t: The Cardinal of Como to the nuncio Dandini, 1580 — Henri III and the nun
h: R73: the same affair, at more length
b: Lasry’s decryption, with its gaps, first turns to a princely marriage negotiation that “N.S. è certificato” a gentleman has raised: the Pope would take it up “con buon fondamento”. It then comes to the nun. Rome does not want Dandini to raise it with the Queen: “non lauda M.S. che V.S. tenghi proposito alcuno con la Regina nel particolare della monaca, per non pigliare occasione di far con tal coperta qualche rumore non conforme alla mente di S.S.” . The Pope has already acted through the confessor, “l’officio che N.S. ne fece con il confessore” , and the reproof is to come from him to the King, “tanto circonspettamente che non ne nasca rumore né disordine alcuno” .

t: The Cardinal of Como to the nuncio Dandini, 1580 — Henri III and the nun
b: The two records were fetched from DECODE with a session cookie: page images, the clear covering letter, SofPe’s and KaJo’s transcriptions, Lasry’s key, and his decryption of R73. Lasry’s key on R72 gave nonsense. A plain two-digit tokenisation, annealed as a free homophonic cipher, collapsed or failed to converge. R72 was parsed in Lasry’s frame instead. The letter values were annealed by swaps over a fixed letter multiset, scored with Italian 4-grams from a Renaissance corpus, with the nomenclator words kept as known plaintext. t: The Debosnys cryptograms — a French syllabary, and why it stops there
b: A convicted wife-killer’s invented script, about 1,200 glyphs, unread since he was hanged. Three passages transcribed. The cipher poem is twenty lines of rhyming couplets, and line length and rhyme both make it a syllabary too short for any crib-free attack. Working notes · September 2026 The Debosnys cryptograms Henry Deletnack Debosnys, convicted of murdering his wife Elizabeth Wells at Essex, New York, in August 1882 and hanged at Elizabethtown in April 1883. In jail he left poems, paintings and four passages in an invented script. Number 3 on Klaus Schmeh’s Top 50 . Originals: Brewster Memorial Library, Essex County Historical Society. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 15 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 attempted Not solved — and not solvable from the surviving text alone Three of the four passages were transcribed here, 969 glyphs in all. The cipher poem turns out to be twenty lines of rhyming couplets , and its line lengths and rhymes both point to a French syllabary : one glyph for one spoken syllable. That identification is also why this attempt stops. A syllabary with this many signs needs roughly 800 to 2,000 glyphs before only one key fits the text, and the whole surviving corpus is about 1,200. Every known plaintext that could be tested failed. What is left needs a source outside this project: the original Debosnys copied from, or a key sheet in his papers.

t: The Debosnys cryptograms — a French syllabary, and why it stops there
b: More than the usual summary suggests. In 2017 Brian, who writes the Sektu blog, transcribed the whole corpus — 1,188 glyphs of 425 types — decomposed the glyphs into sub-glyphs with a small grammar, and proposed that they are French syllables, the tilde marking nasalisation. That transcription was never published. An earlier version of this project’s tracker presented the glyphs’ systematic composition as a new observation; it was Sektu’s, and is credited to him here. Two further leads were public. Matthew Brown showed in 2021 that almost every clear “poem” Debosnys left is copied, mostly from Thomas Moore, which suggested the enciphered texts might be copies too. And Nick Pelling noticed in 2015 that passage No. 9 holds the clear initials H. D. D. L. M. F. with dots under each letter counting the letters left out: Henry, Deletnack, Debosnys, then three words of 7, 7 and 6 letters.

t: The Debosnys cryptograms — a French syllabary, and why it stops there
b: the cipher poem chance under 10 −5 The “monographe verse” is twenty lines of rhyming couplets Lines 1–4 of the monographe verse (detail). Lines 1 and 2 end in the same curl, lines 3 and 4 in the same dotted X. Image: Brewster Memorial Library, Essex County Historical Society, Debosnys papers, the monographe verse. The last glyph of each line repeats in pairs. It is identical within 9 of the 10 couplets , and the tenth pair shares its base and differs only in where a cross is placed. Across couplet boundaries — lines 2 and 3, 4 and 5, and so on — it matches in none of 9 . Even if any two glyphs matched a fifth of the time, nine of ten would come up by chance about four times in a million. It is the flat AABB rhyme of French couplet verse, and the rhyme of the first couplet returns in the ninth, as a sound would. the unit two independent lines One glyph is one French syllable If identical final glyphs carry the rhyme, glyphs stand for sound. Which size of sound is settled by comparing the poem with 279-unit samples of real verse: unit per line types in 279 most frequent Debosnys glyphs 13.9 111 9.0% French syllables 13.5 166 3.8% English syllables 10.2 172 4.5% French words 8.6 174 4.7% French letters 37.4 26 14.7% Only syllables fit the line length, and the rhymes decide the language. In real rhyming couplets the final syllable is spelled identically 61% of the time in French verse but only 31% in Moore’s English. Nine identical endings in ten would happen with English syllables about three times in ten thousand. So the plaintext is most likely French, although nearly everything Debosnys is known to have copied was English. The text behaves like language, not decoration: repeated glyph pairs occur at twice the rate of a shuffle of the same glyphs. Two details do not fit a plain syllabary. The dotted X is too frequent for a single syllable at 9%, and it appears doubled five times, perhaps one sign in two parts. the corpus one system Three passages, one script Transcribed glyph by glyph from the scans: the twenty-line poem (279 glyphs), the four cipher lines on page No. 10 (99) and the prose passage No. 9 (597), 969 glyphs of 333 types. The passages share their inventory — 47 of the poem’s 111 glyph types recur in No. 9, covering 58% of the poem — and the dotted X leads both at 9.0% and 8.2%. The weak point is identity: whether two similar composites are the same sign. The transcription files record each decision, and the least legible line lies under a water stain.

t: The Debosnys cryptograms — a French syllabary, and why it stops there
b: Every search here was first run on a planted text — real French encoded the same way, with noise — to prove it would find a hit if one were there. None of the real searches produced one. the poem on the same page excluded The four cipher lines of No. 10 do not encode the French poem written under them The obvious crib: about 93 glyphs above a clear poem whose first eight lines have about 93 syllables, and both end in a question mark. Aligning glyphs to syllables and scoring how consistently each glyph maps, the real pairing scores 58 — exactly what random French verse scores (median 59). A planted encoding of the same poem scores 86 to 88 against a control maximum of 80. The lines are more likely the end of No. 9. French verse excluded No match in 7,821 couplet windows of French poetry Twenty-eight volumes — Racine, Corneille, Molière, Voltaire, Boileau, Chénier, Hugo, Musset, Gautier, Baudelaire, Verlaine — cut into every 20-line window in rhyming couplets and aligned against the poem line by line. A planted encoding of one real window ranks first of 7,821 by a wide margin; the poem’s best matches form a smooth tail with no outlier. The same holds for Delille’s verse translation of the Aeneid , prompted by the lines of Virgil copied beneath the poem. what he copied excluded Not Moore, not Stoddart, not his own English copies Line-length profile and couplet structure against Moore’s complete poems, Lalla Rookh , Stoddart and Debosnys’s own clear poems: best fits at the chance level for seven thousand windows, and Moore’s couplet lines run three or four syllables short. letters, not syllables excluded The glyphs are not stacks of letters Read each glyph’s component marks as letters in some order and search for the key: the real glyph order scores no better than the same glyphs shuffled, in French or English.

t: The Debosnys cryptograms — a French syllabary, and why it stops there
b: Ciphertext-only attack needs enough text to pin the key down. For a substitution, that threshold is the unicity distance : the key’s information divided by the language’s redundancy per symbol. French verse syllables carry 7.7 bits each under a bigram model; a key for 333 glyph types, drawn from a syllable inventory of 600 to 9,000, carries 3,100 to 4,400 bits. The threshold comes out at about 800 to 2,000 glyphs — with a perfect model and a perfect transcription. The whole surviving corpus is about 1,200. The experiment agrees. Real French verse was encoded as a clean syllabary, one glyph per syllable and no noise, and attacked with a syllable language model trained on 1.15 million syllables: glyphs glyph types text recovered guessing the commonest syllable 1,000 364 0.0% 3.2% 5,000 944 5.4% 3.3% 20,000 1,810 4.3% 2.9% At the Debosnys length the solver recovers nothing. A stronger solver would do better on far longer texts, but none can beat the information limit. If Debosnys wrote a syllabary — and the rhymes say he did — this cipher falls only to a crib.

t: The Debosnys cryptograms — a French syllabary, and why it stops there
b: His papers. The Essex County Historical Society holds the originals. A clear copy of the poem, a draft, or a key sheet among them would turn this into an afternoon’s work. The source text. If the poem or No. 9 is copied like his clear poems, finding the original is the whole job. The search tool is built and tested; the likeliest ground not yet covered is popular French song and verse of the 1860s and 70s, the kind a soldier and drifter would have known by heart. Sektu’s transcription. An independent reading of the full corpus would settle the glyph-identity decisions that weaken every test. t: Van Dedem at Constantinople, 1788–1799
b: Four ciphered despatches of the Dutch ambassador to the Porte. The 1788 letter was read at the time: its decipherment is filed as DECODE R2121. The 1789 and 1793 letters use the same heavily homophonic word code, which three deciphered siblings are not enough to rebuild, and the 1799 despatch uses a different marked system. Constantinople → The Hague · numerical code · 1788–1799 · attempted, not solved Van Dedem at Constantinople, 1788–1799 Nationaal Archief, 3.01.26 (L.P. van de Spiegel) inv. 212, and 2.01.08 inv. 346 (DECODE R2120, R2122, R2131, R1895). These are ciphered despatches from the Dutch ambassador to the Porte to Grand Pensionary Van de Spiegel and, in 1799, to the Agent van Staat Van der Goes. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 21 September 2026 key not found Summary. The catalogue entry grouped four DECODE records, all marked non-decrypted. One of them, R2120, was in fact read at the time: its two cipher pages were photographed again under R2121, together with the clerk’s full clear decipherment, a despatch of 22 December 1788 (DECODE dates R2120 to 11 October). It concerns an Ottoman loan of seven or eight million, secured on the revenues of nine provinces. The letters of 15 January 1789 (R2122, 258 groups) and 9 February 1793 (R2131, 50 groups) use the same code, and it is heavily homophonic: one group stands for about one word, and a common word has several groups. No key for it survives on DECODE. The undated Fagel key series is a set of alphabetical Dutch codebooks of another size. Three deciphered siblings (R2121, R1947 and R2053, about 1,300 groups in all) were transcribed and aligned with their solutions. Only about half the target groups occur in them, and the aligners found no consistent group values, so no reading is offered. The 1799 despatch (R1895) uses a different system, with marks over the digits, and was not attacked. R2122, 15 January 1789: the opening groups 2504 2604 2704 also begin R2120 and R2053. Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 3.01.26 inv. 212, despatch of 15 January 1789, via DECODE R2122.

t: Van Dedem at Constantinople, 1788–1799
b: This is the clerk’s decipherment (R2121). Van Dedem reports a conference with the Reis Effendi, the Kaymakam and the Kâhya Bey. He told them that the States would not take on the Porte’s proposed loan directly, but might allow it to be raised quietly. The Porte then set out its security: om speciaal voor de geheele Leening en de interest tot de geheele aflossing toe te verbinden al de inkomsten van de Provincie Morea, Negropont, Salonique, Volos, Urfan en Cara Agatz, als ook die van de Landen van Damascus, Sorien en Rodosto … het geheel vast jaarlijks tribut van Jenischeher “to pledge, specially for the whole loan and the interest until full repayment, all the revenues of the provinces of Morea, Negropont, Salonica, Volos, Urfan and Cara Agatz, and those of the lands of Damascus, Sorien and Rodosto … the whole fixed yearly tribute of Jenischeher.” The Porte also offered cotton and wool from Salonica and Smyrna at preferential prices. Van Dedem suggests that the Directors of the Levant Trade, or failing them Hope & Co., should take the loan up. Some place names were left in clear inside the cipher.

t: Van Dedem at Constantinople, 1788–1799
h: What was tried on R2122 and R2131
b: Keys. DECODE’s notes link these records to fourteen others in the same code: Kroll 1784–85, Van Haeften 1776, Schenck 1777, and Van Dedem 1789 and 1809. None of them is a key. The undated Fagel series “Cijffers zonder bestemming” (R2842–R2852, before 1793) is made of large alphabetical Dutch codebooks. In R2843 the words from a to ad alone run past 670, so it is not this code. The code. It is not alphabetical. For example, welke falls near 2888, landen near 1277 and als near 17. It is also strongly homophonic: in R2121’s clear text de occurs 36 times, but no group occurs more than 11 times, and 541, 641, 841 and 941 are all frequent. The fixed opening 2504 2604 2704 and the frames 701 801 … 301 401 501 601 look like nulls. Cribs. R2121 (Dutch, 633 groups), R1947 (8 Nov 1789, French, 498) and R2053 (1 Dec 1789, French, 196) were transcribed together with their solutions. Only 58% of R2122’s groups and 52% of R2131’s occur anywhere in them. The French and Dutch cribs share only 17% of their groups. Alignment. Hard-EM and leave-one-out word aligners were run with restarts, and a variant that treats the hundreds digit as a dummy was also tried. None converged to consistent values: the same group came out as different words in different places. Without reliable values nothing in the two letters can be read.

t: Desmarets to an unnamed correspondent, 4 June 1710 — clear prose between the lines, the code unread
b: DECODE R10198: a letter of the Controller General of Finances on the Geertruidenberg talks, with French prose alternating with lines of a numerical code and 22 lines of code alone. Four alignment models show the French is not the decipherment of the figures. The 471-group code has no key on DECODE or in print. Marly → unnamed correspondent · numerical code · 4 June 1710 · attempted, not solved Desmarets to an unnamed correspondent, Marly, 4 June 1710 DECODE R10198 (“Desmaretz_1”, contributed by Alexander Pillon): three pages, signed by Nicolas Desmarets, Controller General of Finances. The holding library is not named on the record. DECODE marks it partially decrypted. The lines of French between the figure lines turn out not to be a decipherment of them. The coded part has no key anywhere online. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 key not found Summary. The letter is dated “a Marly ce 4 juin 1710” and signed Desmaretz. On its first page and a half, a line of French prose alternates with a line of dotted numbers, 34 pairs in all. Then come 22 lines of numbers with nothing between them, and a clear closing formula that runs on from the last figure line. The French reads as one continuous text about the Geertruidenberg peace talks. The powers sent are “assez estendu”, the King wants “la paix, mais seure”, and the Allies’ further demands must not reach “des demembrements entiers”. At first sight the French is an interlinear decipherment, but four independent alignment models find no consistent key between it and the numbers under it. The same group stands under unrelated words, and repeated French phrases do not repeat in the figures. The figures are nonetheless a real code: 183 distinct groups in 471, from 1 to 568, with a Zipf-shaped head and a repeated six-group sequence. The letter is therefore most likely what DECODE’s note calls it, partly clear and partly in cipher, with the secret text in the numbers. No French ministerial key of 1700–1715 is on DECODE, and no printed text was found. Status: not solved. What would open it is a clear copy in the Affaires étrangères Hollande volumes for 1710 or in Desmarets’s papers, or the recipient’s key.

t: Desmarets to an unnamed correspondent, 4 June 1710 — clear prose between the lines, the code unread
b: Read on its own, the prose is one continuous text. It opens: “On a voulu tenter un evenement, dans l’esperance qu’il pourroit estre heureux, qu’il seroit changer la face des affaires presentes. Soit prudence soit impossibilité on n’a rien fait, mais il y a grande apparence que ce qu’on n’a pas tenté volontairement deviendra forcé”. It goes on to the courier held back and the powers now sent, “assez estendu”, though “on ne s’y rendra pas absolument”. It asks for guarantees and explanations about the further demands: “on veut la paix, ou la veut seure, mais on veut encore menager l’honneur de son gouvernement”. It then states the condition. The demands must not go “a des demembrements entiers” and must be held to “peu de chose au dela des preliminaires”. It closes: this is “un relachement qui peut produire la paix, ce qui n’auroit pas esté selon toutes les apparences si l’on estoit demeuré fermes dans les premieres resolutions.” The subject is the French negotiation at Geertruidenberg, March to July 1710.

t: Desmarets to an unnamed correspondent, 4 June 1710 — clear prose between the lines, the code unread
h: Why the French is not the decipherment
b: If the French were written over the figures that encode it, each group would stand for a fixed word, syllable or letter run, apart from homophones and nulls. Four models were fitted to the 34 glossed lines: per-line EM with each group emitting 0–9 letters; one global alignment of all the text against all the groups, with a length prior; per-line soft EM with bonuses for word boundaries; word-level EM, with each group emitting zero, one or two whole words. None converges on a key. 111 falls under paix , seure , selon , on and apparence , and 231 under toutes , fermes and la . The run 209 92 85 sits under both “vostre courier” and “inevitable, peu”. “Demandes ulterieures” occurs twice, over 128 78 65 343 147 and over 209 64 321 161 27. A line-offset test finds only a weak excess of shared groups between lines that share French words (0.77 against 0.49 for any pair, on 22 pairs). The numbers themselves are not decoration. There are 183 distinct groups in 471, where a random fill of the range would give about 320. The commonest are 111 (13 times), 224 (11), 347 and 56 (10 each). The six-group run 119 101 402 49 197 424 occurs twice, first under “dans les premieres resolutions” and again in the unglossed tail. That is the one hint that the coded text may deal with the same matter.

t: De Swart to Van Bleiswijk, 8 March 1782 — the unidentified codebook was the Croiset key of 1765
b: DECODE lists two ciphered letters of the Dutch resident at St Petersburg as non-decrypted, with a codebook that “could not be identified”. The despatch of 1782 is in the Croiset codebook of 1765 for the Russia legation, whose key survives as DECODE R1038. Daniel Bourdeau · read 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. Johan Isaac de Swart was the Dutch Republic’s resident at St Petersburg. Two of his ciphered letters are on DECODE as non-decrypted: a despatch of 8 March 1782 to the Grand Pensionary Pieter van Bleiswijk (R1036) and a letter of 29 November 1787 to the States-General (R1040). Both are written in three-digit groups. A mark on one digit (two short strokes, an underline, a caret, a small circle, or a circle with a bar) makes a different group, so 340 and 340 underlined are unrelated. DECODE also holds the Croiset codebook of 1765 for the Russia legation with an authenticated partial transcription of its key (R1038). Parsed with the marks kept, that key gives 5,961 entries and reads 84.2% of the 1782 despatch as it stands. Thirty-four further values, each checked against every occurrence, and 41 entries read directly from the codebook scans bring the reading to 1,663 of 1,719 groups (96.7%). The despatch covers three matters: the French and Spanish answers to the Austro-Russian mediation, Catherine II’s “Greek project” for the young Grand Duke Constantine, and Prussia’s accession to the Armed Neutrality. The 1787 letter changes codebook part-way through, as Karl de Leeuw noted in 2000. Its second part reads with the same 1765 key. The first 1,928 groups use another codebook that is missing and remain unread.

t: De Swart to Van Bleiswijk, 8 March 1782 — the unidentified codebook was the Croiset key of 1765
b: R1036 has nine scans. Two leaves are duplicate copies of the same passages (images 5419/5421 and 5420/5422). DECODE’s transcriptions of each pair agree at 96.7% and 99.6%, and they were merged, keeping the reading that exists in the key where they differ. After merging, the despatch has 1,719 groups and 596 distinct ones. R1036, first page: the clear salutation, then the code, beginning 15, 452, 730, 833 = waar bij ingesloten . Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 3.01.25 inv. 610, first page, via DECODE R1036. The key is the codebook that Croiset prepared in 1765 for the Russia legation (DECODE R1038). Its values are words, syllables and single letters, so many words are built from pieces: Spa·nje , Dene·mar·ken , Enge·land . DECODE’s authenticated transcription of the key is partial, which is why about a sixth of the groups have no value on the first pass. The marks are part of each group. If they are dropped and the groups reduced to their three digits, unrelated entries collide and the reading fails.

t: De Swart to Van Bleiswijk, 8 March 1782 — the unidentified codebook was the Croiset key of 1765
b: The opening, normalised to modern spelling. Brackets mark a group whose value is inferred or open: Waarbij ingesloten waren de antwoorden van de hoven van Frankrijk en Spanje op de propositie, welke de beide oorlogende hoven dezelve hadden laten volgen op de bewuste preliminaire propositie […], welke de Oostenrijkse minister zondag van zijn hof ontvangen heeft … Betrekkelijk zowel op de bewuste antwoorden als op dat van Engeland … bleef even zo min als tevoren enig middel over, waardoor de voornoemde oorlogende hoven [haar] mediatie van […] enige verdere werkzaamheid zouden kunnen geven. (“Enclosed were the answers of the courts of France and Spain to the proposal that the two belligerent courts had made in reply to the preliminary proposal, received on Sunday by the Austrian minister from his court … As to those answers and to England’s, there remained no more means than before by which the belligerent courts could give her mediation any further effect.”) The despatch covers three matters: The mediation. The French and Spanish answers are unwelcome to Russia. England insists on keeping the American colonies in some form, and Spain will not negotiate while the question of Gibraltar, or an equivalent for it, is unsettled. There is doubt whether the Emperor is dealing honestly with Russia (of nu den Keizer in dezen met haar oprecht handelt) or only means to amuse her. The Greek project. The Empress has not abandoned her project. The young Grand Duke Constantine is being taught Greek and given Greek attendants, and orders have been sent for Greek youths to be brought to him. The Armed Neutrality. Prussia is acceding. The Vice-Chancellor has spoken with the Swedish and Danish ministers about the accession act. The Empress wants it signed pure et simpliciter , without the secret articles, and asks for a firm and unalterable law for the rights of neutrals. The despatch also discusses the Prussian minister’s report to Berlin and the King’s reply on the fourth and sixth articles. The full token-by-token reading is deswart1782/R1036_machine_decipherment.txt , with every group beside its value in R1036_tokens.tsv . The machine text is the authority. The normalised passages here are editorial.

Examples: 881 = nje , completing Spa·nje each time; 340 underlined = mar in Dene·mar·ken ; 311 underlined = land in Enge·land . 176 with a caret = mpli , read twice in pure et si·mpli·citer . 741 = haar , used twelve times for the Empress: met haar oprecht handelt , om haar te amuseeren , haare mediatie . 39 = hun , as in hun acte and hun onderdaan . 681 underlined = mogendheden ( de oorlogende mogendheden van Frankrijk, Spanje en Engeland ); 363 with a circle = tusschen in tusschen·komst ; 3 with a circle = stel in veronder·stel·d and vast te stel·len . t: De Swart to Van Bleiswijk, 8 March 1782 — the unidentified codebook was the Croiset key of 1765
b: Karl de Leeuw noted that the letter of 29 November 1787 is coded, “presumably by accident”, with two codebooks. The change comes at group 180 of image 5459, where the 1765 key begins to read dit alles . From that point to image 5474, the 1765 key reads 84–90% of each full page. The text reports signs of an alliance between Austria and France, close attention to it from the Prussian and British representatives, news from Berlin, Kaunitz and the Bavarian exchange, and the likely positions of the four powers: Dit alles, gepaard met vele andere omstandigheden, schijnen als indicien te zijn welke de hiervoor gedetailleerde [berichten] wegens de effectief, zo niet reeds gesloten, ten minste op het tapijt zijnde alliantie tussen de hoven van Frankrijk [en Oostenrijk] zeer waarschijnlijk maken. The first 1,928 groups are in a different codebook, probably the one used under Rechteren. It does not survive online, though the Rechteren cipher filed as Nationaal Archief inventory 158 may be it. Three plain/cipher pairs from the same legation (R2032, R2051 and R2052, from 1784 and 1786) were aligned against it. Transfers from them cover only 2–3% of the segment and give no connected prose, so no reading of it is claimed.

t: De Swart to Van Bleiswijk, 8 March 1782 — the unidentified codebook was the Croiset key of 1765
b: In R1036, 56 groups (51 distinct codes) have no value. A third pass read the entries DECODE’s transcription of the key left illegible straight from the codebook scans. The word stands to the left of its code, and the parallel columns of homophones confirm faint words. It kept the 41 readings that fit the letter, such as 781 = geheel (“het Griekse project geheel stil”), 748 with two strokes = commercie (“de vrijheid van de commercie der neutralen”), 488 underlined = Zijne Keizerlijke Majesteit , and 515 with a circle = twaalf , the twelve Greek boys. The groups still open are entries lost in the binding shadow of the scan, blank in the book, or too faint to use. Inflections are sometimes uncertain where the key gives a stem only, as in hot for hof/hoven . The first 1,928 groups of R1040 are unread, pending the Rechteren-family codebook.

t: Dinteville to the Duke of Nevers, 3 July 1592
b: DECODE lists BnF fr. 3621 f. 130 as a letter with its decipherment, but the leaf has none: two cipher passages in a clear letter, and a clear postscript. A sibling Dinteville letter on f. 128, in the same signs, carries an interlinear decipherment of about 150 signs. It does not fit a one-sign-one-letter key, and the letter stays unread. Langres → Nevers · letters, digits and signs, apparently with code signs · 3 July 1592 · not read Dinteville to the Duke of Nevers, 1592 to Duke of Nevers BnF Français 3621, no. 116, f. 130 (DECODE R9451; Gallica btv1b52524472n , view 269). A clear letter from the royalist lieutenant in Champagne with two cipher passages, about ten lines in all. The catalogue listed it as a transcription job, because DECODE says the leaf has a decipherment. It has none. The one crib, on a sibling letter at f. 128, did not give a key this session. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 not read Summary. DECODE describes R9451 as a “letter, with cipher and decryption”, and the catalogue therefore marked it as read at the time. The image shows no decipherment. f. 130r has a clear letter dated at Langres on 3 July 1592 with two passages in cipher (about 3 and 7 lines), then an autograph postscript in clear French. The volume turns out to be on Gallica in full resolution, and two leaves earlier, f. 128r is another Dinteville letter of July 1592 in the same signs, with a contemporary decipherment written above each cipher line: m’a dict avoir veu d’ascendre a Geneve deux millions d’or d’Espaigne … quarante cinq + mulets chargez … prendre le chemin de Besançon . That is a crib of about 150 signs. A test for a one-sign-one-letter key (homophones allowed, up to three null types) finds none: the same sign sits under o in auoir and under d a few signs later. The decipherer also left some signs as crosses, which suggests code signs for words. Status: not read. What would finish it is a careful sign-by-sign transcription of f. 128 against its interlinear, then of f. 130.

t: Dinteville to the Duke of Nevers, 3 July 1592
b: f. 130r, the head of the letter: clear French with the first cipher passage (lines 4–7) set inline. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3621 f. 130r, via Gallica (btv1b52524472n, view 269). The letter is in clear French, and the cipher breaks into it twice. The signs are a mixed set: digits ( 1 3 4 9 0 ), letters ( o v w m z c a ) and marks ( # ψ α Δ □ ¢ ∇ π ƒ + ), some barred or crossed, many followed by a dot. There are roughly 400 to 450 signs. The paragraph after the date, beginning Monseigneur ce matin j’ay sceu … l’armée lorraine , is Dinteville’s own clear postscript, not a decipherment. The verso carries the address. Nothing on the leaf glosses the cipher.

t: Dinteville to the Duke of Nevers, 3 July 1592
b: f. 128r, another Dinteville letter of July 1592: the cipher lines, with the contemporary decipherment written above each (“avoir veu d’ascendre a Geneve deux millions d’or d’Espaigne”). Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3621 f. 128r, via Gallica (btv1b52524472n, view 265). This leaf is probably no. 114, which the BnF notice lists as a Dinteville letter “avec chiffre et déchiffrement”. It uses the same signs as f. 130. The decipherment is written above the cipher, roughly word by word, and runs: … m’a dict / avoir veu d’ascendre a Geneve deux millions d’or d’Espaigne / … quarante cinq + mulets chargez qui doibt aussi passer dans trois / jours et prendre le chemin de Besançon … , news of Spanish money moving through Geneva and Franche-Comté towards Flanders.

t: Dinteville to the Duke of Nevers, 3 July 1592
b: I transcribed the second cipher line of f. 128 as 50 signs against its 48-letter gloss. A search for a consistent key (each sign one letter, several signs per letter, up to three sign types as nulls) finds no solution. The first five signs fit auoir cleanly, but α then has to be both o and d . Either the cipher is not a plain homophonic alphabet (code signs for words such as Geneve and Espaigne , or signs worth more than one letter), or my reading of the glyphs by eye is wrong in places. With about 150 aligned signs and no second crib, the two cannot be separated from here.

t: Charles of Egmond — a ciphered request for support in war
b: A cipher George Lasry had already solved in 2023 (key on cryptiana), solved again here independently: the French body and ciphered address read with an inferred graphic substitution key and nulls. Charles asks the grand master to support his affairs and assist the commander of Saint John. Arnhem, apparently 18 July; year unknown. Minor glyph uncertainties and literal anomalies remain explicit. Arnhem → grand master of France · graphic substitution with nulls · year unknown · read Charles of Egmond: a request for support in war from Charles of Egmond BnF français 3015 no. 8, folio 16: sixteen lines of cipher, two raised insertions and a ciphered address. The text is French. It asks the grand master of France to continue supporting Charles’s affairs and to assist his ambassador, the commander of Saint John. The date reads “dih[u]itieme de iuillet”: apparently 18 July, with one ink-heavy sign. The year and the recipient’s personal name are not supplied. Daniel Bourdeau · solved 20 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 Summary. The catalogue described an entirely ciphered letter by Charles, duke of Guelders, with its address also in cipher. George Lasry had already solved the cipher in 2023 (key on cryptiana, GL.htm §2). Here it was solved again independently: an inferred substitution key reads the body and address throughout, with minor glyph uncertainties retained. The address is “A mon bon cousin / Monsieur le grant maistre / de France”. Charles says that obeying the king’s commands caused him to enter the war, and asks for continuing support in his present necessity. His ambassador is described as the commander of Saint John. Both raised insertions are read. The place is Arnhem and the apparent date 18 July; no year has been recovered. This is an internal decipherment from the images, not a reading confirmed by an archived key or a matching clear copy.

t: Charles of Egmond — a ciphered request for support in war
b: My cousin, having been informed that you give all possible support to my affairs, I wished to write and ask you to continue in the future, considering the extreme need in which I now find myself after obeying certain commands of the king, which caused me to enter this war. You will learn more fully from the commander of Saint John, my ambassador, whom I have instructed to communicate everything to you. Please give him such assistance as he needs and believe what he tells you on my behalf. By doing this you will oblige me increasingly to you, as our Lord knows. Having commended myself to your good grace, I pray that he keep you in his protection. From Arnhem, this eighteenth day of July [year absent]. This translates the apparent sense, not every literal anomaly. “Certain” interprets the unexpanded aulc ; “eighteenth” interprets dih[u]itieme . The cipher gives titles, not the personal names of the recipient or ambassador.

t: Mr Eichel’s cipher sheet of 1758 — a page made only of nulls and blank key cells
b: TNA SP 106/7 (DECODE R595), 139 number groups docketed “Cypher from Mr Eichel 1758 / Prussia” and listed as an unsolved letter whose key was thought to be R594. R594 does not fit. The key in the same volume, R596, declares every number containing a 7 and four ranges to be nulls: that makes 117 of the 139 groups nulls, and 21 of the other 22 fall on cells the key leaves blank. The sheet hides no message. Mr Eichel (Prussia) → unknown · numerical nomenclator · 1758 · explained: no message A cipher made only of nothing: Mr Eichel's sheet of 1758 TNA State Papers 106/7 (DECODE R595) is one page of number groups, listed as an unsolved letter from “Mr Eichel” whose code “may be found” in the next record. That key does not fit. A second key in the same volume, R596, does, and under its own rules the page says nothing: every group is a null or an empty cell of the table. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 resolved Summary. The catalogue took R595 for a ciphered letter of 1 January 1758 from Mr Eichel to an unknown recipient. The DECODE note says “probably from Russia” and points to key R594. The docket actually reads “Prussia 1758”. August Friedrich Eichel was Frederick II's cabinet secretary. Key R594, a French nomenclator of about 1,100 values, gives nonsense on the letter. Of the other SP 106 and Prussian key records on DECODE, one matches the letter's odd pattern: R596, from the same volume, with 1,696 French values between 504 and 3293. Its heading declares as nulls every number containing a 7, and every number in 1–503, 1115–1198, 1483–1999 and 2600–2802. Under those rules 117 of the letter's 139 groups are nulls. Twenty-one of the remaining 22 are numbers the key leaves blank. Blank cells make up only 7% of the key's live numbers, so the writer chose them on purpose. The sheet is a dummy composed entirely of non-values: a specimen, a test or a blind, not a despatch. Still open: R596 is undated, and nothing here proves it was Eichel's own key.

t: Mr Eichel’s cipher sheet of 1758 — a page made only of nulls and blank key cells
b: DECODE R595 (“TNA_SP106/7_Anne_(0020)”) has a single image: a bifolium opened out. The upper half is blank apart from three dockets, “Cypher from Mr Eichel 1758”, “Prussia 1758” in pencil, and “Mr Eichel”. The lower half holds eighteen lines of numbers separated by points, 139 groups in all, with no decipherment above or beside them. The DECODE date, 1 January to 31 December 1758, comes from the docket. The catalogue's “1 Jan 1758” is the first day of that span. SP 106/7, image 0020: the first fifteen lines of the sheet, turned upright. Many groups end in 7, and the lower lines run through the 1900s and 2600s–2800s. These are the key's null ranges. Image: The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/7, image 0020, via DECODE R595.

t: Mr Eichel’s cipher sheet of 1758 — a page made only of nulls and blank key cells
b: R594, which the DECODE note proposes, is a French nomenclator from the same box, “Russia 1758” on DECODE. It covers only 39% of the letter's groups, and what it does cover reads province, de Prusse, Bavière, ob-, blo, des … , which is nonsense. The transcriptions of the other key records in SP 106 boxes 6–8, and of the Prussian keys on DECODE, were each scored by coverage. Coverage alone points nowhere: the large 3,000-value codes of 1750 cover almost everything and read nothing. What decides it is a rule written on the key itself. R596 (“TNA_SP106/7_Anne_(0013-0017)”, five images, undated) opens with this heading: Tous les nro où je trouve un ou plusieurs 7 sont les nonvaleurs dans le présent chiffre, de même que les nro depuis 1 jusqu'à 503 inclusivement et depuis 1115 jusqu'à 1198, tout comme aussi depuis 1483 jusqu'à 1999, depuis 2600 jusqu'à 2802. The table follows the rule: no value in it contains a 7, and the values begin at 504 ( un ). The letter fits it closely. Its groups end in 7 far more often than chance allows (2167, 3037, 2897, 3117, 3007 …). Its closing lines run through 1901–1984 and 2603–2802, exactly the reserved ranges.

h: What is left after the nulls
b: With R596's rules applied, 117 of the 139 groups are nulls. A random choice of numbers from 1 to 3299 would make only about 55% of them nulls. These 22 remain: 2512 1480 1413 2492 1434 3026 2093 3143 853 3150 3161 966 1291 1253 1311 1413 861 2853 2264 2264 863 911 Twenty-one of them are numbers that R596 lists but gives no value: 2511 montrer , 2512 — , 2513 mont ; 852 armement , 853 — , 854 arranger ; 2263 informer , 2264 — , 2265 inopinément . The key has 107 such blanks among its 1,527 live numbers, 7%. Twenty-one blanks out of twenty-two draws would happen by chance about once in 10 23 tries. The only group left with a value is 1480, écus , and the transcriber marked two of its digits as doubtful. A second reading of the hand does not change this. The DECODE transcriber read a looped figure as “8?”. In this hand it is more likely a 0: compare 2001 and 2002 on the last lines. With that reading, 27 groups survive. Twenty are blanks, and the others are isolated values that make no sentence: deu, Ci, difficile, chose, françois, Clo, difficile .

t: Mr Eichel’s cipher sheet of 1758 — a page made only of nulls and blank key cells
h: What it is, and what remains uncertain
b: No message. The sheet is written wholly in non-values of the R596 cipher, nulls by its own rule plus blank cells of its table. It needs a writer who held the key and avoided every live number. Most likely it is a specimen or trial of the cipher, or a blind meant to occupy an interceptor. It is not a despatch. Eichel and R596. The docket names Eichel and Prussia. R596 carries no name or date on DECODE, though its vocabulary includes Moravie, Mecklenbourg, Saxe and Hollande. That the Deciphering Branch had this key, and that the sheet uses its non-values so precisely, links the two. Whether R596 was Eichel's own cipher or a copy the Branch reconstructed is not settled here. Transcription. The analysis uses the DECODE transcription of the letter, checked against the image, and of the key. The key's blank cells were not each checked on the key images. The 21-in-22 coincidence does not depend on that check. DECODE. The note's “probably from Russia” is a misreading of the docket “Prussia”, and the key it names, R594, is the wrong one.
