t: Galeotto da Ricasoli to the Dieci di Balía, Urbino 1425 — Read
b: A letter of Florence’s envoy to the Count of Urbino, listed on DECODE as non-decrypted, though its interlinear decipherment makes it decrypted; what the record lacks is the key or a reference to it. The abbé Gabbrielli glossed a few of its words in 1863 and built a key from them, which Meister printed in 1902; the letter was never printed. The three long runs he left unread are decoded sign by sign with his glosses as seeds, two of his nulls resolved and four new values confirmed on the siblings. Urbino → the Signoria of Florence · homophonic letter cipher with word signs · early 1425 · read Galeotto da Ricasoli to the Dieci di Balía, Urbino, early 1425 Archivio di Stato di Firenze, Dieci di Balía, Responsive 2 no. 171 (old 168), DECODE R3754, listed as non-decrypted: a one-page letter of Florence’s envoy to Count Guidantonio da Montefeltro, in fast Florentine cursive with about twenty runs of cipher. The abbé Gabbrielli rebuilt the key in 1863 from a few words he glossed on this letter and three others; Meister printed his table in 1902. The letter itself was never printed. The three long runs Gabbrielli left unread are decoded here sign by sign, using his glosses as seeds and his key for alignment. His null list is corrected on two points, and four new sign values are confirmed on the sibling letters. Daniel Bourdeau · read 18 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. The Dieci di Balía, Florence’s war council, kept its incoming letters in filze of Responsive ; the earliest ciphered ones date from the war with Milan in 1424. Galeotto Fibindacci da Ricasoli wrote this one from Urbino, where he was Florence’s envoy to Count Guidantonio da Montefeltro, in the months after the Florentine defeat at Zagonara. In 1863 the archivist Pietro Domenico Gabbrielli glossed a few words over the cipher of this and three sibling letters and built a key from them, warning that it rested “on a few words in only four letters”. Aloys Meister printed the key in 1902. Nobody printed the letters. DECODE lists this one as non-decrypted, but the interlinear glosses are a decipherment, so the record should read decrypted. What it lacks is the key, or a reference to Gabbrielli’s key in Meister. Here the glossed runs were first checked against Gabbrielli’s table, then the three long runs he had not read were aligned sign by sign. They say that the Count calls his wife, Caterina Colonna, Martin V’s niece, “after all a woman, and suspicious”. They also say that her relatives and the citizens were to bind themselves in secret to the Count’s wishes, “whatever she says or wants to the contrary”. Checking against Gabbrielli’s null row showed one of his nulls is a variant A and confirmed another. Four new sign values hold on the siblings nos. 21 and 91. Status: read. The cipher runs are all decoded; two word signs are read from Gabbrielli’s marks and the context, five letter values rest on this letter alone, and some words of the fast clear hand are uncertain (section 05). Dieci di Balía, Responsive 2 no. 171, the whole letter (deskewed). The dark small hand between the lines is Gabbrielli’s 1863 gloss. Image: Archivio di Stato di Firenze, Dieci di Balía, Responsive 2 no. 171, via DECODE R3754.

t: Galeotto da Ricasoli to the Dieci di Balía, Urbino 1425 — Read
h: The letter, the key and the siblings
b: The letter opens “Magnifici potenti Signori miei” and is signed “Vostro servidore Galeotto de Fibindacci”. It is undated. Its siblings in the same hand, filza 3 nos. 91 and 92, are dated at Urbino on 17 and 28 February, in the Florentine year 1424, that is 1425. Guasti’s edition of the Commissioni di Rinaldo degli Albizzi shows the Dieci sending Galeotto to the Count of Urbino in September 1423, and prints a later clear letter of his from Urbino of 28 August 1425. “Madonna” is the Countess, Caterina Colonna, niece of Pope Martin V, who married Guidantonio in 1424 and reached Urbino on 4 March 1424. The key is page 1 of Gabbrielli’s volume Chiavi delle cifre delle lettere ai Dieci di Balía dal 1424 al 1530 , compiled in 1863–64. The volume is on the Ilardi microfilm at Yale, reel 58, and Meister printed page 1 in Die Anfänge der modernen diplomatischen Geheimschrift (1902), p. 50. It is headed “Cifra di Galeotto Fibindacci da Ricasoli, carteggio dei X di Balía, an. 1424”. It gives an alphabet with two or three signs for most letters, eighteen nulls, and a nomenclator of thirty word signs such as Conte d’Urbino , Duca di Milano , Malatesta , fanti and mille . It also lists six cover words written in clear: Giovanni for the Dieci, Andrea for Galeotto, trombetta for an ambassador, che for horse, con for war and tagliato for loss. Gabbrielli marked the letters he worked from in the margin: filza 1 nos. 163 and 165, filza 2 no. 72 and filza 3 nos. 21, 91 and 92. His interlinear glosses on no. 171 cover a dozen words: paolo , di madona , cintadini , il conte , sarrem andino , a laog. , ambasciatore , puro femina e sospettosa , el conte d’Urbino , cavalli , parenti and madonna . Several of these sit over runs far longer than the gloss, and two of them are misreadings.

t: Galeotto da Ricasoli to the Dieci di Balía, Urbino 1425 — Read
b: Each run was cut from the deskewed scan at four to five times magnification and transcribed sign by sign. The signs were then matched against Gabbrielli’s table and his gloss. Capitals are the decoded text. “Madonna è pure femina e sospetosa” The run after “perché dice che”, with Gabbrielli’s gloss above. It continues onto the next line. Image: Archivio di Stato di Firenze, Dieci di Balía, Responsive 2 no. 171, via DECODE R3754. The clear text runs: “… che disputa Giovanni [the Dieci] mandasse trombetta [an ambassador], perché dice che”. Twenty-six signs follow. MADONNA is seven signs, all in Gabbrielli’s table. PURE has P and R and E from his table and one new sign. FEMINA is six signs, all his. E is his. SOSPETOSA is nine signs. The two O signs in it stand exactly five places apart, as the two O’s of s-o-spet-o-sa do, and that fixes the alignment. Gabbrielli glossed the whole phrase but never tabulated the signs in it. The sentence reads: “because he [the Count] says that Madonna is, after all, a woman, and suspicious”. “Parenti e citadini” The run before “promettessono e obligassensi”, glossed parenti and cintadini . Image: Archivio di Stato di Firenze, Dieci di Balía, Responsive 2 no. 171, via DECODE R3754. The run has seven signs and then eight. With Gabbrielli’s values for P, A, R, E and I and three new ones, they read PARENTI and CITADINI, one letter per sign. The sentence reads: “et segretamente MADONNA et PARENTI [e] CITADINI promettessono e obligassensi che, non obstante [ella] dicesse e volesse el contrario, … farebbono quello volesse [il Conte]”. In English: Madonna’s relatives and the citizens should secretly promise and bind themselves that, whatever she might say or want to the contrary, they would do what the Count wished. “Acomandino a lui” Gabbrielli read this run as sarrem andino and the next word as a laog. Both are misreadings. The first sign is on his own list of nulls. The next ten are A C O M A N D I N O by his table and by values proved elsewhere on the page. The last three are A L I, with one sign doubtful, and read a lui . The clause reads: “che non li pare che [the Pope?] si[a] …; acomandino a lui”, “that they put themselves in his hands”.

t: Galeotto da Ricasoli to the Dieci di Balía, Urbino 1425 — Read
b: This is a working text. The clear hand is fast. Words marked (?) are doubtful. Cipher is given in capitals and word signs in brackets. Magnifici potenti Signori miei, io sono stato qui mostrato per lettera … fatto questa mia, sentito PAOLO, … non n’averavamo e parlato però di una cosa et dell’altra, che sterino insieme più … DI MADONNA et CITADINI [il Conte] … ma prosetto(?) che non li pare che [il Papa?] si[a] … ACOMANDINO A LUI; sono stati così parecchi … parlare, ma parebbe fusse più utile che qualunque commissione portata persona fusse et motivare de’ ragionamenti, che disputa Giovanni mandasse trombetta, perché dice che MADONNA [È] PURE FEMINA E SOSPETOSA, pure vedrendosi(?) coperto, se sapesse a fare, sapere et bene; ma non staza così coperto. Anno sospetto di questo [CONTE D’URBINO], detto non credo bisogni, ma pure delle cose … avere sospetto; o detto … el modo che li parebbe farebbe dimostrare fare … [FANTI] et guache(?); che [cavalli] e segretamente … dessi loro opera che metassono, et segretamente MADONNA et PARENTI [E] CITADINI promettessono e obligassensi che, non obstante [ella] dicesse e volesse el contrario, dico essi farebbono quello volesse [il Conte]. E ragionamenti furono assai e lunghi … ma parmi volesse andasse più segreta. Racomandomi alla Signoria vostra. Vostro servidore Galeotto de Fibindacci. In short: Galeotto reports long talks at Urbino about the Countess. Some party, probably under the Pope’s protection, should put itself in the Count’s hands. He advises the Dieci to send an ambassador, because the Count distrusts his wife: “Madonna is after all a woman, and suspicious”. Foot and horse are to be engaged quietly. Her relatives and the citizens are to bind themselves, in secret, to follow the Count whatever she says. He ends that the business should be kept more secret.

t: Galeotto da Ricasoli to the Dieci di Balía, Urbino 1425 — Read
b: Two heavy word signs before “sia” are not in Gabbrielli’s nomenclator. He wrote over them a small p with a looped flourish, the usual abbreviation for Papa . The Countess is the Pope’s niece, so “the Pope” fits. Grade M. Two single word signs are read from context alone. One, before “dicesse”, is read as ella . The other, over which Gabbrielli wrote il conte , is read as the Count. Grade M. Three signs before SOSPETOSA , after the E, are unexplained. They may be nulls or a short word Gabbrielli did not have. The word sospetosa is not affected. PAOLO reads cleanly, but who he is stays open. He may be messer Paolo da Capranica, whom a Florentine cover list of 1424 calls “Capra”. The clear text of lines 2, 4, 8, 10, 11 and 13 has doubtful words, marked (?) above. A second reader of the cursive would settle most of them. The five values graded C and M above rest on this letter alone. A systematic harvest of Gabbrielli’s glosses on nos. 21, 91 and 92 would test them and extend his table. The glossed runs there number in the hundreds. The full key. Other letters on DECODE use the same signs, among them R3755. Together they should give the complete key. That key could then be uploaded to the records, but only after checking that it is not already elsewhere in the DECODE collection. Not yet done (suggested by G. Lasry, 21 September 2026).

t: Sir Richard Forster, 13 May 1644 — verified blind, and why the first attack fails
b: Already read by Lasry, Biermann and Pitt; Tomokiyo’s page still says unsolved. Not a regular Stuart key but a mixed homophonic alphabet of 34 symbols over 207 tokens. Pitt’s key stands at z = 8.8 against 20,000 permutations, and an annealer recovers 31 of 34 symbols blind — but only after the French model writes u for v and i for j ; before that it reads five of six matched controls and still fails the target. France · mixed homophonic alphabet · 1644 · read by others, verified here Sir Richard Forster, 13 May 1644 Archives départementales du Val-d’Oise, 68.H.8, troisième liasse · published by Karen Britland (2013) · transcribed by S. Tomokiyo (2021) Read by George Lasry, Norbert Biermann and Robert Pitt before this session. Here: a permutation control, a blind recovery of 31 of 34 symbols, and the reason the obvious attack fails Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 15 September 2026 · updated 16 September 2026 resolved Summary. Tomokiyo’s page of unsolved ciphers still carries this passage, but it had been read: by Lasry after Britland’s article, independently by Biermann, and again in September 2026 by Pitt, whose key is public. Nothing about the text is new here , and no decipherment is claimed. What this page records is a verification and a lesson. The tracker had predicted a regular Stuart key of the Ormonde or Boswell type; the passage is instead a mixed homophonic alphabet of 34 symbols, 18 numbers and 16 letters, over 207 tokens in 37 comma-separated words. Pitt’s key stands 8.8 standard deviations above 20,000 permutations of the letter identities. A homophonic annealer with a French 5-gram model then recovers the key blind — 202 of 207 tokens, 31 of 34 symbols — but only once the training text writes u for v and i for j as a 1644 hand does. Before that change the same solver reads five of six matched controls and still fails the target, with a wrong key outscoring the truth: the plaintext, not the cipher, was outside the model. Status: verified. Four single slips and two one-occurrence words need the manuscript; priority is Lasry’s, Biermann’s and Pitt’s.

t: Sir Richard Forster, 13 May 1644 — verified blind, and why the first attack fails
h: Blind recovery, and what the controls say
b: A homophonic annealer (34 symbols to 26 letters, 150,000 steps, 8–12 restarts), first without and then with the word boundaries, on the target and on six matched controls: held-out French of 207 letters enciphered with a random key of exactly Pitt’s homophone multiplicities, adjacent words merged with probability 0.2 as in the target. run model controls read (of 6) target 1 5-gram, letters only, no word edges 0 (16–49 % right; the solver’s optimum beats the truth on 5 of 6) gibberish, 31 % of Pitt’s key 2 5-gram with spaces, raw corpus 3 at 99.5–100 %; 3 fall into an all- i attractor from OCR Roman numerals attractor 3 same, Roman numerals removed 5 at 99–100 %, one at 44 % −591.6 found against −602.4 for Pitt: a wrong key outscores the truth , 14.5 % agreement 4 same, training text with v → u , j → i 6 of 6 (98–100 %) 97.6 % of Pitt’s key blind : 202 of 207 tokens Run 1 is the lesson of the Moray letter at this length: 207 letters over 34 symbols with a plain letter-stream model is below the solver’s threshold even on controls, so nothing could have been read into a target failure. Run 3 is the more useful one: the controls pass and the target fails, so the plaintext was out of the model’s distribution. The letter writes uotre, uie, uos, seruices, uoyes, subiet, ie , as every 1644 hand does; a model trained on a nineteenth-century edition with v and j scores that spelling some 200 nats worse than modern French of the same length, and gibberish wins. Normalising the training text fixes it. The blind key differs from Pitt’s at three rare symbols only ( g , 14, e ), whose values n-grams cannot fix and the words do. The two 134-letter controls that were run under the same model (the tracker’s wrong length) both read at 97–99 %, so the length was never the obstacle.

t: The Chinese gold bar cryptograms — ten of everything
b: Sixteen strings on seven bars said to certify $300,000,000, unread for ninety years. They contain almost exactly ten of every letter of the alphabet: chi-squared 1.25 against uniform where chance predicts 25. No cipher can flatten a distribution past what randomness allows, so there is nothing to read. Shanghai · 1933 · famous unsolved · resolved The Chinese gold bar cryptograms Seven bars said to certify a deposit of $300,000,000, stamped with sixteen strings of Latin letters that nobody has read in ninety years They have not been read because there is nothing to read. The letters were dealt out, not enciphered. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 15 September 2026 · updated 21 September 2026 no message Summary. The sixteen inscriptions hold 263 letters between them, and they contain almost exactly ten of every letter of the alphabet — twenty-one of the twenty-six appear exactly ten times. Measured against a uniform distribution the chi-squared statistic is 1.25 on 25 degrees of freedom, where random sampling predicts 25 . That is a one-in-a-trillion level of over-uniformity, and it is not something any encryption can produce: substitution and transposition both preserve the plaintext’s frequency skew, and even a one-time pad is still random sampling and lands near 25. Somebody laid out ten of each letter and arranged them to look like cryptograms. Status: resolved as a construction, not a cipher. There is no message.

t: The Chinese gold bar cryptograms — ten of everything
b: The story, as Kevin McCurley set it down for the IACR in 1996, is that seven gold bars were issued to a “General Wang” in Shanghai in 1933, functioning as metal certificates against a deposit with an American bank. The Chinese text on them describes a transaction of more than $300,000,000 and gives the bars’ combined weight as 1.8 kilograms. A dispute over the claim was live at the time, and McCurley published the photographs in the hope that reading the cryptograms would help settle it. One of the bars (IACR, 1996). The cryptograms are stamped around the portraits, above and below the figure 300000000. Image: Kevin McCurley, “Cryptograms on Gold bars from China”, IACR (1996), iacr.org/misc/china. Elonka Dunin has carried the item on her list of famous unsolved codes ever since. In 2020 she reached the attorney named on the IACR page, who confirmed he had seen the bars, described them as about the size of a remote control, and said the banks had not treated the claim as legitimate; his file was closed. Others have noted that the aircraft depicted on the bars is a model that did not fly until 1934 or 1935, after the date the bars claim for themselves.

t: The Chinese gold bar cryptograms — ten of everything
b: Count the letters and the answer arrives immediately. Gold is the observed count for each letter; the pale red behind it is what 263 letters of English would give. English towers at E and falls away to nothing at Z. The bars do neither. Twenty-one of the twenty-six letters occur exactly ten times, and the five that do not are off by one, except I which is off by three: letter count letter count E 11 O 9 I 13 T 9 S 11 all other 21 letters 10 Ten of each would be 260 letters exactly; the transcription gives 263. Re-reading the photographs removes one letter (the fourteen-letter string is thirteen on the bars) and leaves one more in doubt, so the true total is 261 or 262. It does not remove the deviations: I is thirteen on every reading, and depending on how the two doubtful glyphs are read the letters off by one are three to seven. The bars carry about ten of each letter, not exactly ten with a noisy transcription. Under every defensible reading the chi-squared stays between 1.2 and 1.5 and the probability near one in a trillion. A person counting out ten of each letter and losing count by one or two is precisely this pattern.

t: The Chinese gold bar cryptograms — ten of everything
h: Why no cipher can do that
b: test value index of coincidence 0.0350 (English 0.0667, random 0.0385) chi-squared against uniform, 25 df 1.251 (random sampling predicts 25) P(chi-squared ≤ 1.251) 9.3 × 10 −13 about 1 in a trillion chi-squared against English letter frequencies 1488 random 263-letter strings at least this uniform, out of 200,000 0 The point that does the work is not that the distribution is flat. It is that the distribution is flat beyond what randomness allows . Take the candidates in turn: Simple substitution renames letters but cannot change how often they occur, so it preserves the plaintext’s skew. Index of coincidence stays near 0.066. Any transposition reorders letters and leaves the counts completely untouched. A short-key Vigenère flattens partway, to roughly 0.045, and leaves periodic structure behind. A long key, or a one-time pad , does reach a flat expectation — but it gets there by random sampling, and random sampling is noisy. Draw 263 letters uniformly and the counts scatter with a standard deviation near 3.1, so you expect a spread from about 4 to 16 and a chi-squared near 25. Twenty-one letters landing on exactly ten is not what randomness looks like. Only deliberate construction produces it. And once the letters were dealt out, the arrangement into sixteen strings looks unconsidered: there are 71 places where a letter repeats inside a string, against 65.6 expected when the same pool of letters is shuffled at random into the same lengths. Somebody counted out ten of each letter and distributed them.

t: The Chinese gold bar cryptograms — ten of everything
b: The inscriptions are decorative filler, made to look like cryptography on an object whose purpose was to look like a security. That sits with everything else known about the bars: an aircraft that had not yet been built on a bar dated 1933, banks that declined the claim, and a legal file closed without resolution. The honest conclusion is that the item should move off the unsolved-cipher lists, not because it has been read but because there is no message in it. Ninety years of failure to decipher these strings has a simple explanation, and it is the one the statistics force. On the transcription: the argument was first made on the IACR’s 1996 transcription alone, with its author’s warning that some letters were hard to read. The letters have since been re-read from the fifteen IACR photographs, enlarged and contrast-stretched. Fourteen of the sixteen strings are confirmed; one is a letter shorter than published and one letter in another is unresolved at the resolution available. The statistics were recomputed for every reading, and the result does not move.

t: Vincenzo Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua, to the duc de Nevers (1590)
b: A letter of 17 September 1590 from the Duke of Mantua to his uncle Nevers, with long passages in unbroken two-digit figures, catalogued as not deciphered and credited to “the duke of Nevers”. The key filed in Nevers’s papers, BnF fr. 3995 f. 64 (Tomokiyo no. 35), reads it unchanged: 878 of 923 cipher tokens, 95.1%. Mantua passes on the rumour that Sixtus V was poisoned by the Spaniards and assures Nevers, for the King, of his devotion against the common enemy. Mantua → the duc de Nevers · homophonic figures with a nomenclator · 17 September 1590 · read Vincenzo Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua, to the duc de Nevers from Vincenzo I Gonzaga → to Duke of Nevers BnF, Français 3979, ff. 92r–93r, DECODE R4176: an Italian letter of three pages, with about 930 cipher tokens written as unbroken runs of digits. DECODE lists it as not deciphered and names the sender “duke of Nevers”. He is in fact Vincenzo I Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua, writing to his uncle. The key survives in Nevers’s own papers, and with it about 93% of the cipher reads. The key survives in Nevers’s own papers, and with it about 93% of the cipher reads. Daniel Bourdeau · read 21 September 2026 read Summary. Catalogue item 188 is a letter of 17 September 1590 to Louis de Gonzague, duc de Nevers. The cipher passages are two-digit figures written without breaks. Satoshi Tomokiyo’s list of the Nevers ciphers describes no. 35 as “used by the Duke of Mantua” in 1590. That key is BnF fr. 3995 f. 64, headed Per Cavare 1590 , and it fits the letter at once, applied unchanged. Figures 11–40 are letters with homophones, 41–99 are words and names, and signs stand for titles and common words. A beam decoder with a sixteenth-century Italian language model resolved the writer’s look-alike figures (3/9, 0/8, 7/8). 878 of 923 tokens read (95.1%, measured). Mantua reports that many believe Sixtus V (d. 27 August 1590) was poisoned by the Spaniards. He says the Italian powers want nothing more than Henri IV’s conversion, and he assures Nevers, for the King, of his devotion to the French crown against the “common enemy”. Still unread are four short garbled stretches (writer’s slips and one looped code group), the same on both surviving images. Nobody had deciphered the letter before. BnF fr. 3979 f. 92r (DECODE R4176 image P2): the clear text runs to che la morte del Papa , then the figures 40 37 22 40 23 13 23 38 17 31 25 96 28 31 … = sia stata procurata con veleno da Spagnoli . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3979 f. 92r, via DECODE R4176 (image P2).

t: Vincenzo Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua, to the duc de Nevers (1590)
b: The letter is dated 17 de Sett.re 1590 and addressed Ill.mo et Ecc.mo Sig.r mio Zio Oss.mo . It answers four letters of Nevers (12, 27 and 20 July, 6 August) and runs from f. 92r to f. 93r. The clear passages deal with family and business: Giulio Capilupi chosen as the new agent in place of Malegnano, the citadel of Casale, the outlaw Piccolomini, the imprisonment of Nevers’s daughter by the League, and a lawsuit at Milan with the Duchess Dorothea of Brunswick. The politics is in figures. Near the end the writer comments on the ciphers themselves. The cipher Nevers sent is molto artificiosa but hard to use without errors, so Nevers should use “the last one I sent you, which is used in this letter too”. That last cipher is in Nevers’s key collection: BnF fr. 3995 f. 64, Per Cavare 1590 (Gallica btv1b525085665, view 131), no. 35 in Tomokiyo’s list. Its values are: Letters, with homophones: 11 m, 12 f, 13 a, 14 h, 15 e, 16 n, 17 p, 18 g, 19 b, 20 z, 21 d, 22 a, 23 t, 24 u, 25 o, 28 u, 30 l, 31 r, 32 i, 33 c, 34 t, 35 o, 36 e, 37 i, 38 a, 39 o, 40 s. An overbar on a letter figure doubles it. Words and names, 41–99: 42 Mons. di, 43 Gran Duca di, 45 Papa, 47 Re di, 55 Cardinale di, 58 Duca di, 60 Legato, 80 Francesi, 81 Spagna, 84 Francia, 96 Spagnoli, 97 Roma; 26 Inglesi, 27 Venetia and 29 Consiglio sit among the letters. t: Vincenzo Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua, to the duc de Nevers (1590)
b: Deciphered passages in bold, clear text plain; [..] is a stretch not read, [?] a doubtful word. The writer’s spelling is kept. f. 92r: the death of Sixtus V … non lasciando di dirle, che è opinione di molti, che la morte del Papa sia stata procurata con veleno da Spagnoli , non lo potendo far risolvere a favor loro contro cotesto Regno di Francia, la conservatione del quale è desiderata da tutti i buoni Italiani, conoscendosi P. che, anichilata cotesta potenza, li medesimi Spagnoli procureranno di sottoporsi a ognuno [..] S. Ecc.za, da che mi spiace per i molti buoni effetti che mi prometto che ne debbano seguire , et veram.te da tutti i Potentati Italiani non è cosa più desiderata della conversione del Rè al Catolicismo, il che seguendo, si vede chiaramente aperta alla via della grandezza [..] a questo Regno di Francia. “Many believe that the Pope’s death was procured with poison by the Spaniards, since they could not bring him to decide in their favour against this Kingdom of France, whose preservation all good Italians desire, knowing that once that power is destroyed the Spaniards will try to subject everyone …; nothing is more desired by all the Italian powers than the King’s conversion to Catholicism, if that follows, one sees the way clearly open to the greatness … of this Kingdom of France.” f. 92v: the King’s conscience … cose tutte [..] che per interesse di stato la devono far risolvere a correre la fortuna di [..] come fanno Venetia et sì tutti gli altri principi et nobiltà francese [..] dubitando stante la [..] la sua conscienza, che in così universal concorso se le possa opporre mancamento alcuno per conto della religione. Mi è piacciuto infinitam.te intender che quello che il Legato hà scritto in Italia nel partir di Monsignor [..] sia stato menzognero … Nevers, a Catholic who had joined Henri IV, should “for reasons of state resolve to share the fortune of [the King], as Venice and all the other princes and the French nobility do …, [no longer] fearing that in so universal a concurrence any fault could be laid against his conscience on account of religion.” What the Legate (Caetani) wrote to Italy has proved a lie. f. 93r: a message for the King BnF fr. 3979 f. 93r (DECODE R4176 image P10): 6 d’Agosto presupongo che questa mia la troverà , then eleven cipher lines addressed through Nevers to Henri IV. The signs are ⊕ S. M.tà, the barred θ per, ⊔ et and ● che. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3979 f. 93r, via DECODE R4176 (image P10). … presupongo che questa mia la troverà presso S. M.tà, alla quale la priego far riverenza per me, con certificarla della ottima mia volontà verso il suo Re, al servitio di che, sì come non hò mancato in quello che hò potuto sin hora di darne c[..] parte, e si stia sicura la S. M.tà per[?] oltre la mia particolar inclinatione, et verso cotesta corona, et parimente la con S. M.tà gli interessi contro il [..] comune nemico, me le renderà sempre devotissimo servitore, come a tempo et luogo conveniente conoscerà chiaramente da gli effetti. Nevers is to assure the King of Mantua’s goodwill. Mantua’s own inclination, and shared interests against the “common enemy” (Spain), will make him the King’s most devoted servant, as the King will see from the effects at the right time and place. For an Italian prince bordering Spanish Milan, this was a guarded pro-Bourbon declaration, sent under cipher in the month after Sixtus V’s death.

t: Vincenzo Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua, to the duc de Nevers (1590)
b: Prior work. DECODE (Non-decrypted, cipher type unknown) and Tomokiyo’s nevers.htm . Tomokiyo lists the key, not this letter. No earlier decipherment was found. Key. Tomokiyo’s description of no. 35 pointed to fr. 3995 f. 64, which was read from the Gallica image. Transcription. The digit runs were transcribed from the DECODE high-resolution strips: f. 92r in the main session, ff. 92v and 93r by two sub-agents. Unseparated figures lose their pairing whenever a digit is misread. Decoding. A beam decoder ( beam.py ) pairs the digits and scores readings with the project’s it-cinquecento language model. It tries the alternatives 3/9, 0/8, 7/8 and 27/28 where the hand makes them look alike. The sign values were then read from the key sheet. Retry. The doubtful lines were re-read at triple scale and decoded again. This recovered most of ff. 92v and 93r. Blind re-read. Every unread stretch was then transcribed again at four times scale by a sub-agent that had not seen the earlier digits, and the two versions compared. This read contro cotesto Regno di Francia , tutti i buoni Italiani , anichilata cotesta potenza , si vede chiaramente , far riverenza per me and in quello , and confirmed sottoporsi as written: 56 more tokens. Second image. The BnF microfilm of fr. 3979 on Gallica (btv1b9060544v, views 160–162) was used to re-read every unread stretch. On f. 93r the q-like sign is the key’s ♀ non and the next ● che , and the microfilm gives 14 35 31 38 hora : sì come non hò mancato in quello che hò potuto sin hora , 15 more tokens.

t: Vincenzo Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua, to the duc de Nevers (1590)
b: 45 of 923 tokens are unread (measured from the transcriptions; reading.md ). Each stretch was re-read independently at four times scale twice, and again on the Gallica microfilm, without a fit: f. 92r, line 5: about 10 tokens ( la nda a a di ) before S. Ecc.za . f. 92r, line 8: about 27 tokens in the middle, including 26 Inglesi. Probably the writer’s own slips; a beam search allowing any one digit to be substituted finds no Italian. f. 92v: about 6 tokens after dubitando stante la ( la mondezza a me as written). The three signs there are nulls on the key. f. 93r, line 8: a looped, dotted code group before comune nemico , perhaps [Re di] Spagna. No other letter in this cipher is on DECODE, and there is no clear copy. The key is complete. The digits there are the same on the DECODE scans and the microfilm, so these are the writer’s own enciphering slips; only a second copy of the letter would settle them.

t: Gramont, Mâcon and Langeac to Montmorency, 1529–1537 — four keys and texts Lasry solved in 2023, read again in public
b: Four ciphered letters to the grand maître from the French ambassadors at Rome and Venice, catalogued with no decipherment. Each has its own key. Lasry reconstructed all four from siblings in 2023 and decoded the texts then, but his decipherments were never posted. Read again here from the scans with his tables: Saint-Pol and the Venetians in January 1529; Clement VII on the council, his dream and his feigned illness on the road to Bologna in October 1529; the princes’ return in 1530; Paul III and the Farnese marriage in 1537. Rome, Venice → the Court · four homophonic letter ciphers · 1529–1537 · read Gramont, Mâcon and Langeac to Montmorency, 1529–1537 to Anne de Montmorency BnF Français 3083 no. 8, 3071 nos. 4 and 7, 3091 no. 23 · four letters to the grand maître from the French ambassadors at Rome and Venice · catalogued “en chiffre” with no decipherment · one of them 171 lines of solid cipher Four letters, four keys, all four reconstructed by George Lasry in 2023, who decoded the texts at the time; the decipherments were never posted · read with his tables at glyph level · six code signs his tables leave blank identified · the Mâcon letter checked against a contemporary decipherment pasted in beside it Daniel Bourdeau · read 18 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. The catalogue entry grouped four ciphered letters to Anne de Montmorency, written between 1529 and 1537 by three French diplomats in Italy, and asked first whether they share a cipher. They do not: each uses its own key. All four keys were already solved. George Lasry reconstructed them in 2023 from sibling letters, and Satoshi Tomokiyo published his tables as images on cryptiana. Lasry also decoded all four texts at the time, but Tomokiyo did not post the decipherments, probably for lack of space. So this is not a first reading. The work was a new, published reading of about 9,000 signs about 9,000 signs from the Gallica scans with the published tables. The letters are now read. Langeac, Venice, 14 January 1529: Saint-Pol wants leave to quit the army in Lombardy, and the Signoria refuses. Gramont, Rome, 11 October 1529: a five-page letter wholly in cipher, written as Clement VII left for the congress of Bologna. It covers the Pope’s dread of a general council and his plan to grant one and then stall it, his offer to feign illness on the road until the Admiral Chabot arrives, the soothsayers who foretell his deposition, a dream he had the night before he left Rome, and a Florentine deal the prince of Orange was floating. Gramont, Rome, 21 July 1530: a nuncio is to go to France to congratulate the King on the return of the Queen and the princes. Mâcon, Rome, 11 April 1537: Paul III offers the Farnese marriage and threatens to declare for the Emperor if it is refused. Status: Langeac and Gramont 1529 read in full; Gramont 1530 about 85 %; Mâcon about 90 % of the cipher, its clear text read loosely.

t: Gramont, Mâcon and Langeac to Montmorency, 1529–1537 — four keys and texts Lasry solved in 2023, read again in public
b: The catalogue guessed “four letters by three hands, probably three keys”. Opening each item on Gallica and matching it against Tomokiyo’s pages on the ciphers of François I shows four keys, each with a sibling letter from which Lasry built his table: Item Writer, place, date Key (Lasry’s name) Cipher Read fr. 3083 no. 8, ff. 20–21 Jean de Langeac, bishop of Avranches, Venice, 14 January [1529] Avranches’ cipher 1 (the sibling is fr. 3005 f. 107) 11 lines all but two short groups fr. 3091 no. 23, ff. 45–47 Gabriel de Gramont, bishop of Tarbes, Rome, 11 October [1529] Gramont’s cipher (1529) (siblings fr. 3040 f. 16, Clair. 330 f. 53) 171 lines, all cipher in full, 90–95 % of signs secure fr. 3071 no. 7, f. 17 Gramont, now cardinal, Rome, 21 July [1530] Gramont’s cipher (1530) (sibling fr. 3019 f. 20) 14 lines about 85 % fr. 3071 no. 4, ff. 9–10 Charles Hémard de Denonville, cardinal de Mâcon, Rome, 11 April 1537 Mascon’s cipher (sibling fr. 3053) about 45 lines, mixed with clear text about 90 % of the cipher Each is a monoalphabetic substitution with two to seven homophones for the common letters, signs for doubled letters, a handful of nulls, and a few code signs for persons. The Mâcon key uses numerals for its code signs. Lasry dated all four tables 5 November 2023, and Tomokiyo notes that the published images carry no plaintext. Lasry decoded all four letters in 2023 (personal communication, 21 September 2026), but his decipherments are not published; none of the letters is transcribed or printed elsewhere that we could find. Gallica has the volumes at full resolution: fr. 3083 is btv1b90601328, fr. 3071 btv1b9060315f, and fr. 3091 btv1b9060253s, the last filmed as two-page openings.

t: Gramont, Mâcon and Langeac to Montmorency, 1529–1537 — four keys and texts Lasry solved in 2023, read again in public
b: Fr. 3083 f. 21r. Above the cipher, in clear, is the news that Aquila has been taken “par le conte de Montore et Camille Pardo”. The block opens with two nulls and MONSEIGNEVR DE SAINCT POL . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3083 f. 21r, via Gallica btv1b90601328 view 36. Cipher in capitals, clear in lower case, spelling of the leaf kept MONSEIGNEVR DE SAINCT POL M’A CONMANDE RECHER[CHER] SON CONGE A CESTE SEIGNEVRIE, CE QV’ELLE N’A VOLV CONSENTIR, AINS A PROTESTE QVE S’IL SE DEPARTOIT QVE CE SEROIT LA TOTALLE RVINE DES EMPRINSES. ET ME SEMBLE QV’IL N’I A RAISON, VEV L’EMPRINSE DE MILLAN, LA VENVE DES ESPAIGNOLS AVEC ARGĒT POVR ICELLE SECOVRIR, ET LA PRIMEVERE APROCHER. IE CROY QV’IL NE DEPARTIRA SI LE FAICT […] sans LE CONSENTEMENT DE TOVS LES CONFEDERES, ET SI APORTEROIT […] VNG PREIVDICE IREPARABLE. Je luy ay escript AV MIEVLX QV’IL M’A ESTE POSSIBLE pour LE DIVERTIR DE CESTE OPINION, QVI EST PAR TROP DANGEREVSE. The comte de Saint-Pol commanded the French army in Lombardy from the autumn of 1528 until his defeat at Landriano on 21 June 1529. So five months before Landriano the commander wanted to leave. Venice, the league’s paymaster in the north, refused his leave on the ground that the Milan enterprise was in hand, Spanish money was coming to relieve Milan, and spring was near. The King’s ambassador tried to talk him round. The year is not on the leaf, but it is fixed by Saint-Pol’s command and by the Abruzzi news in the clear text.

t: Gramont, Mâcon and Langeac to Montmorency, 1529–1537 — four keys and texts Lasry solved in 2023, read again in public
h: Gramont, Rome, 11 October 1529: the Pope on the way to Bologna
b: Fr. 3091 f. 45r. After Monseigneur, je voy que tant par mes lettres du treziesme et du septiesme de septembre the letter is cipher for five pages. The heart on line 6 is the sign for the King. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3091 f. 45r, via Gallica btv1b9060253s view 49. This is the long one: 171 lines and about 7,000 signs across ff. 45r–47v, closing A Romme le xi me jour d’octobre over the signature G. de Gramont e. de Tarbe . The year is 1529. The Pope has just left Rome (Clement VII set out for Bologna on 7 October 1529), and Gramont leaves “demain” to join him at Perugia. The letter opens with the bull of the four décimes on the French clergy, raised for the princes’ ransom under the peace of Cambrai, and the prince of Orange is before Florence. In outline, modernised (the full reading, page by page, is in the repository): The council. Whatever the Emperor says or does only deepens the Pope’s distrust of that side. What won him to the King was the King’s message about the concile general , “lequel il craignoit sur toutes les choses de ce monde, combien qu’il monstrast … qu’il en ait grande envie”. Pressed, he confessed that he knew the council was being pushed to ruin him, and that he meant to grant it and then “s’arrester sur aucunes particularitez pour le differer, et que le delai lui succedast en rupture”. Into the King’s arms. He would “du tout se jecter entre ses bras et se fier en luy seul”. Because the times do not allow open trust, the King and his ministers may say publicly, whenever it helps, that they have little reason to trust the Pope, so long as the goodwill underneath stays whole. “Avec bonnes parolles vous aurez de luy ce que vous voudrez”. His one aim is to get the Emperor out of Italy. Feigning illness for the Admiral. The Emperor is bound “par ses chappitres”, the treaty of Barcelona, to bring the allies to full restitution or make war on them. Gramont has told Philippe Chabot, the Admiral, then on his embassy to Italy, to come as far forward as he can. The Pope offers to slow his journey, or to “faire le malade” in whatever town he is in, to wait for him. On 10 October he told Gramont he had already begun. Soothsayers and a dream. The Pope, though he should not believe “tout plein de gens qui se meslent de deviner”, greatly fears what they say of him. Several have foretold that he will be deposed or will die within the year, and that it will come “du costé dudict” [the Emperor]. The night before he left Rome he had a dream, which Gramont encloses, “lequel l’a mis en merveilleusement grande fantasie”, because he dreamed it at the kind of hour at which earlier dreams of his had come true. He told it to one man only, and Gramont asks that only the King, Madame and those they choose should know of it. Florence. The prince of Orange wanted to deal with [the Florentines]: restore [the Medici] to the state of Florence “comme il souloit”, in return for Pisa and Livorno being put in [the Emperor’s] hands. That is “chose grandement contraire” to what the Emperor had agreed with the Pope. Gramont’s letter adds detail to the French side of the weeks before the congress of Bologna. The council, Florence and the Venetian and Ferrarese restitutions all serve as bargaining counters in it, and the Pope keeps a private line to France through the ambassador. The enclosed dream is not in the volume.

t: Gramont, Mâcon and Langeac to Montmorency, 1529–1537 — four keys and texts Lasry solved in 2023, read again in public
h: Gramont, Rome, 21 July 1530: the princes come home
b: By July 1530 Gramont is a cardinal, and he uses a new key. The 14 cipher lines follow a clear passage on “la bonne nouvelle” and on Francisque’s coming mission: … [LE PAPE] A TROVVE BON QVE LEDICT FRANCISQVE Y AILLE … D’AVLTANT [QV’]ESTANT ICI IE POVRRAY OBVIER A TOVT CE QVE L’ON LVY POVRROIT MECTRE AVANT POVR LE DIVERTIR, A QVOY VOVS PVIS ASSEVRER QVE L’ON FAICT TOVTE LA DILLIGENCE POSSIBLE. MONSIEVR L’EVESQVE DE FAIANCE, NEPVEV DV CONTE DE CARPI, PARTIRA DEDANS TROIS OV QVATRE IOVRS POVR, DE LA PART DV [PAPE], […] CONGRATVLER AVEC LE [ROY] DE LA VENVE DE LA ROYNE ET DE MESSEIGNEVRS. The Dauphin and Henri, hostages in Spain since 1526, were handed back with Queen Eleanor on the Bidassoa on 1 July 1530. That dates the letter. The nuncio is Rodolfo Pio, bishop of Faenza, nephew of Alberto Pio, count of Carpi. Gramont had been asked to go himself, and the Pope sends “Francisque” instead because the Imperials would take Gramont’s going amiss. Two of the signs Lasry lists as unknown read out of this passage: 8Δ is pape (“de la part du 8Δ”) and the key-ring sign is roy . A third, ʃʃ on a stem at the head of a word, is a null.

t: Gramont, Mâcon and Langeac to Montmorency, 1529–1537 — four keys and texts Lasry solved in 2023, read again in public
h: Mâcon, Rome, 11 April 1537: Paul III and the Farnese marriage
b: Denonville, cardinal de Mâcon, was ambassador to Paul III during the war of 1536–38. His letter alternates clear and cipher. Its code numerals, which neither published table explains, read out of the text: 20 is the Emperor (“se precipiter a la devotion du dict 20”, “se declarer partial de 20”), 30 the Pope (a contemporary hand has written “le dict pappe” above it on f. 9r), and 40 the King . What the cipher says: Pier Luigi Farnese, the Pope’s son, has sent men to take possession of a place read as Novarre , and has approached the captain of a fortress to see whether he can be bought. (The Farnese were invested with Novara only in 1538, so the reading of the name is one of the few that needs checking.) The Pope has been offered the marriage of his granddaughter, Pier Luigi’s daughter Vittoria, with Cosimo de’ Medici. Mâcon thinks that if it goes the Pope’s way he will throw himself wholly to the Emperor. Through Latino Giovenale, the Pope sends word that if the marriages are refused “il aura occasion de se declarer partial de l’Empereur: ce qu’il vous plaira considerer”. “La confederation du Roy avec le Turc se verifie clerement.” If the Pope declares, it is “a craindre que les Venitiens le suivissent entierement”, since it is said that “le Roy avoit promis au Turc de faire passer grosse puissance en Italie, et qu’il s’amuse en Picardie”. In April 1537 François was campaigning at Hesdin. The French ambassadors at Venice, the bishops of Rodez and Lavaur, are trying to win over Alessandro Vitelli, who held the fortress of Florence and was angry with the Emperor. Mâcon holds back so as not to spoil their practique . He fears that if Cosimo marries the Pope’s granddaughter, Vitelli will follow, “car le dict pape a moyen de le contenter es terres de l’Eglise mesmes, de la ville de Castelle, dont il commance a se faire tirant”. The control. Fr. 3071 f. 9bis is a slip pasted into the volume, a contemporary decipherment of the f. 9v cipher: De quoy j’ay adverty mess rs de Rodez et de Lavaur qui m’ont escript avoir bon moyen envers luy de le practiquer … The f. 9v cipher was read glyph by glyph before the slip was compared, and the two agree almost word for word. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3071 f. 9bis, via Gallica btv1b9060315f view 18. In the clear text, the duke of Mantua will not host the council summoned to Mantua for May 1537 without a paid guard. His brother, Cardinal Ercole Gonzaga, said so “en plain consistoire” (those three words are in cipher), and the Pope is thinking of moving the council. The dispatch goes by way of Venice to save the cost of a courier.

t: Gramont, Mâcon and Langeac to Montmorency, 1529–1537 — four keys and texts Lasry solved in 2023, read again in public
b: No cryptanalysis was needed, only reading. Each key table was checked on the first line of its letter (Langeac’s block opens MONSEIGNEVR DE SAINCT POL ; Gramont 1529’s first full line decodes d r R + W C 4 # L ● T Δ K Lo ʒ r R ● to tredecime v & avltre v ). The short letters were then read by eye from line strips. For the long ones, each glyph was given a one-character ASCII alias and a script turned the alias strings back into letters, so that every reading can be checked against the transcription and re-run. The five pages of fr. 3091 and the three parts of the Mâcon letter were read separately and in parallel, each by a model instance working from the same brief, key and crops, and then joined. The joins fall mid-sentence and agree. The things the readers found that the tables do not say: In Gramont’s 1529 hand the loose ǂǂ for a and the compact # for m cannot be told apart, so # is read as a or m by context. A is the more frequent. A triangle or ring on a stem over a foot bar looks like ♀ ( o ) but is a null, Lasry’s “4 with a flag”. It occurs about twenty times. Read as o , it produces doepesche . The heart, which Lasry lists only as a person sign, is always the King (“escript au ♡ et à vous”). Three large signs outside the table stand where the Emperor, the Florentines and the Pope or the Medici are expected. Those identifications come from context and are marked as such. In the Mâcon key a dotted r is a null in most places but must be r in partant . Its R sign is easily mistaken for its C sign.

b: Langeac: a group of three or four signs before sans and two before vng . Gramont 1529: single letters on each page (listed in the transcriptions), a phrase on f. 45r ( fier ni a nui ) and one on f. 45v ( en voi[e] ), the first word of f. 47v l. 7, and the identity of four code signs, which is inferred. Prior art not yet seen: B. Wirtz-Daviau’s edition of the Admiral Chabot’s 1529 embassy to Italy, which may quote Gramont’s letters from a contemporary decipherment.

t: La Guiche from Rome, 1551, with Noailles and Seure, 1558 — a symbol cipher nobody deciphered
b: BnF français 3138 no. 22: Claude de La Guiche’s letter to Montmorency of 22 November 1551 carries 406 signs of cipher with no decipherment anywhere. The 22 invented signs are a simple substitution, broken here by permutation annealing with a French despatch model. Dom Diego and the Sienese envoy, and the Count of Santa Fiora ready to come over to the king. Noailles’s Venice letter of 1558 was deciphered in the margin at the time; Seure’s Lisbon letters are left open. Rome, Venice, Lisbon → the French court · symbol substitution · 1551–1558 · read in part La Guiche from Rome, 1551, with Noailles and Seure, 1558 to Henry II BnF français 3138 no. 22 and français 3151 nos. 33 and 39–44: three ambassadors’ letters with ciphered passages, catalogued together as item 10. The La Guiche passage had no decipherment. It was transcribed and broken here. Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 21 September 2026 solved in part Summary. The catalogue grouped three letters with cipher that had no decipherment noted. Each was checked for a court decipherment on the leaf or nearby. Claude de La Guiche , bishop of Mirepoix, wrote to Montmorency from Rome on 22 November 1551 with about thirteen lines of cipher inside the clear text, and nothing deciphers them. The 406 signs were transcribed. There are 22 distinct signs, one for each letter of the period’s 22-letter alphabet, and a permutation annealer with a French language model of the 1530–1600 despatches broke the alphabet. The passage reads in substance. Dom Diego [Hurtado de Mendoza] has had a Sienese imprisoned, and La Guiche has seen the trial papers. The Sienese envoy has left Rome for Siena with Dom Diego. The Count of Santa Fiora « est mal satisfaict » and « facilement se reduiroit au service du roy », on the conditions he would ask. One name and the two struck-through opening lines remain uncertain. François de Noailles ’s Venice letter of 13 November 1558 has the court’s decipherment in the inner margin, partly lost in the binding. The chevalier de Seure ’s letters from Lisbon, December 1558, are not one letter but six, including duplicates. They hold about 2,000 signs of a homophonic cipher with numeral codes and no decipherment, and are left open as their own target. BnF fr. 3138 f. 60v (Gallica btv1b90601662, view 65): La Guiche’s first cipher lines, the first two struck through, then clear « Informer led. S r cardinal du contenu en icelluy ». Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3138 f. 60v, via Gallica btv1b90601662 view 65.

t: La Guiche from Rome, 1551, with Noailles and Seure, 1558 — a symbol cipher nobody deciphered
b: La Guiche → the duc de Montmorency , Rome, 22 November 1551, fr. 3138 no. 22, f. 60v–61r. The clear text is about cardinals and the Pope’s intentions during the Parma war. It is interrupted by six cipher runs, 406 signs in all. There is no decipherment on the leaf, in the margin or on the following leaf. Noailles → the Cardinal de Lorraine , Venice, 13 November 1558, fr. 3151 no. 33, f. 59–60. The letter is in clear (galleys, Candia, Corfu), with two cipher blocks of three lines on f. 60r. Each has its decipherment written in the inner margin. Seure → de Fresne and Henri II , Lisbon, 12 and 27 December 1558, fr. 3151 nos. 39–44. The catalogue listed one letter, no. 39, but the volume holds six, and nos. 40/41 and 43/44 are duplicates. The cipher runs over some eight pages.

t: La Guiche from Rome, 1551, with Noailles and Seure, 1558 — a symbol cipher nobody deciphered
b: Normalised spelling. Clear words from the letter are in italics, [?] marks an uncertain reading, and … marks signs left unread. [struck through: Dom Diego … constituer prisonnier en ce … un Siennois … croy que …] le procès duquel j’ay trouvé moien de veoir, affin de informer led. S r cardinal du contenu en icelluy pour selon cela mettre tel fondement qu’il advisera . … de ceux de Sienes qui estoit icy, lequel est party pour s’en retorner a Sienes avec Dom Diego. … Le conte [de] Sainte Fiore est mal satisfaict, et que facilement se reduiroit au service du roy … Car ledict personnage qui estoit icy tractant avec moy la faire du sieur +arna+e … vous informer du … que le roy pourroit avoir du dict sieur +arna+e, et aux [?] … des conditions qu’il demanderoit. “Dom Diego” is Diego Hurtado de Mendoza, Charles V’s ambassador in Rome and the power behind Siena until the Sienese rising of July 1552. The count of Santa Fiora is the Sforza lord, whose family were the pope’s relations. The letter shows La Guiche sounding him out for the French side eight months before Siena turned to France.

t: La Guiche from Rome, 1551, with Noailles and Seure, 1558 — a symbol cipher nobody deciphered
b: The cipher was transcribed sign by sign from full-resolution crops of each line ( guiche_ct.txt ). The counts pointed to a simple substitution: 22 distinct signs, with one sign at 16%, the rate of French e . A free many-to-one annealer collapsed onto a degenerate i/x solution. A permutation annealer with swap moves, using the fr-1530-despatches 5-gram model without spaces, read le conte sainctefiore est mal satisfaict on its best restart. Four signs were then set from context (qu, p, y, v), and the rest re-annealed. Key: 3=e, t=r, #=i, θ=u, the stemmed 4=t, barred p=s, hook=a, f=d, d=n, open 4=o, curled d=o, p=c, Ⅲ=l, ff=qu, overbarred d=m, φ=y, the circle=v, hooked q=f, ∞=p.

The letter was read when it arrived. A complete text would need the volume opened flat.

t: La Guiche from Rome, 1551, with Noailles and Seure, 1558 — a symbol cipher nobody deciphered

None has a decipherment. There are roughly 2,000 signs under what looks like one key, so a solve is realistic, but the transcription alone is a job of several sessions. The letters stay in the catalogue as their own item.

t: Guise to the Duke of Mercœur, 27 May and 20 June 1587 — read with Lasry’s key
b: BnF fr. 15564 ff. 119 and 142 (DECODE R4162, R4165), two letters to Mercœur, probably from Henri, duc de Guise, catalogued as not deciphered. George Lasry broke the cipher in 2022 but published only the key. Read here with his key, extended: 95.1% of 2,477 letter signs. League levies of reiters, Swiss and Italian lances, and the Protestant army of 1587. [Guise] → the duc de Mercœur · homophonic cipher with a small nomenclator · 27 May and 20 June 1587 · read Guise to the Duke of Mercœur, May and June 1587 from Henri, duc de Guise → to Duc de Mercœur BnF français 15564 ff. 119 and 142 (DECODE R4162 and R4165): a page wholly in cipher and a slip with seven clear lines and sixteen of cipher. Both are read here with the key George Lasry rebuilt in 2022, which he published without a decipherment of either letter. Daniel Bourdeau · read 22 September 2026 read Summary. The catalogue listed two DECODE records in BnF fr. 15564 as an unknown sender to Mercœur, 27 May and 20 June 1587, both “Non-decrypted”. They are ff. 119 and 142 of the volume, two of the four letters whose cipher George Lasry broke in 2022; his key table and his decipherment of f. 27 are on Satoshi Tomokiyo’s Cryptiana, but neither letter’s text was published. The companion letter f. 78 is written up separately . Here every sign of both letters was labelled, a beam search under a French language model chose among the homophones, and about twenty passes against 2× crops of the Gallica images pinned the letters sign by sign. The key gained a dozen values in this hand. Of 2,477 letter signs, 2,356 read as sense (95.1%, measured per line); twelve name codes from Lasry’s “unknown” row stay open. The letters are League war news: two thousand Italian or Albanian lances and four thousand reiters promised for August, a secretary sent with twelve thousand écus to Colonel Pfyffer to raise nine thousand Swiss, the Protestant army “composée d’huict mil reistres, douze mil suisses, deux regimens de lansquenets, quatre mil harquebusiers pour Chastillon”, and by June a plan gone wrong: “nous sommes maintenant contraincts de donner ordre a nos affaires”. BnF fr. 15564 f. 119, the first lines (Gallica, view 132). The letter is in cipher from the first line to the closing formula. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 15564 f. 119, via Gallica btv1b9064027v view 132.

t: Guise to the Duke of Mercœur, 27 May and 20 June 1587 — read with Lasry’s key
b: DECODE folio date what it is signs read R4162 f. 119 27 May 1587 one page, 42 lines wholly in cipher 1,861 95.5% R4165 f. 142 20 June 1587 a slip: seven clear lines of news from Germany, then 16 lines of cipher 616 letter signs + 7 code groups 92.9% DECODE gives no sender. Lasry’s key calls the cipher “Guise → Mercœur” and Tomokiyo writes “probably from the Duke of Guise”. The texts fit: the writer speaks for the League’s war effort, of “la cause que nous poursuivons de mon costé” and of a meeting at Meaux, and the companion letter f. 78 names “mon frere”. The same cipher is used in ff. 27 and 78 of this volume and in fr. 15565 ff. 105 and 122.

t: Guise to the Duke of Mercœur, 27 May and 20 June 1587 — read with Lasry’s key
b: A condensed reading, in the manuscript’s spelling; the full line-by-line text with every gap is guise1587/f119_reading.txt . Nomenclator words are in small capitals in the files; [?] marks an unread sign, [21] a name code. […] receu la lettre qu’il vous a pleu m’escrire […] de son armee, qui est icy present […] vous rendre compte et mander la façon […], feray ce comme nous avons resolu de nous y gouverner […] certainement […] l’envie et pense les tiens que toute asseuree et resolue la levee des reistres; […] d’aoust nous avrons sans doubte deux mil lances italiennes ou albanoises et quatre mil reistres soubs la levee de ce […] [21], lesquels les leve pour nous. Il a envoye son secretaire vers […] le colonel Fifer avec douze mil escus pour arrester et traicter d’une levee de neuf mil suisses, auquel nous n’avons eu encore response et l’attendons a toutes heures. Et [le]dict duc [21] s’est aussi resolu a […] mil cinq cens hommes, qui […] tant […] d’España la voisins, que au sien advis nous avrons […]; que ses parans et amys vouloit que l’accompagner et servir. L’armee des heretiques de la grand […] des composee d’huict mil reistres, douze mil suisses, deux regimens de lansquenets, quatre mil harquebusiers pour Chastillon, leur doibt amener de cavallerie françoise, ce qu’ils pourront. Les vous dirons que les craignent trop plus: les traistres pour les ennemis, et le doubte […] si nous ne nous resolvons a nous en defaire, ce qu’est tant utile pour la gloire de Dieu et la cause que nous poursuivons de mon coste. Les […] espargner rien, soing ny diligence, et fault tous que nous en general et en particulier nous en cherchions les moyens. Il se faict fort et leve des gens de tous costes; il fault user de diligence […], les a traicter amitie ny reconciliation. Il ne se peult […] doibt, nous estant sa haine beau profitable, que la reputation generale et la conservation particuliere de nos amys […]. C’est un grand malheur que […] eschauffe davantage, et que sur luy l’on ne peult prendre plus ferme fondement. Toutesfois est il utile l’entretenir et entier, ce que […] […] il s’estoit employe […] mal a propos, car enfin c’estoit se rendre vangeur et […] passions qui sont ennemis des compagnons [& N], vous seul et leur respect, et peult et doit conserver. Nous avons […] deux […] [43] et de [M]ercoer […] a leur donner tout et contentement qu’il sera possible, comme […] toutes les autres villes des partisans [9b] et [71] son frere, comme je vous ay desia mande. Vous doit rendre compte […] subjects […] nule […], […]donne vous servir hors de toutes considerations […] vous une bien […] et moyens, et faictes moy […] particulierement en quoy vous voulez employer, en faisant estat certain. Les vous baise bien humblement les mains. The Protestant army described is the German and Swiss force that the Huguenot party was raising in 1587 and which crossed into Lorraine in August; Châtillon is François de Coligny, the Admiral’s son, who led its French contingent. “Colonel Fifer” is Ludwig Pfyffer of Lucerne, the Catholic Swiss colonel who raised regiments for the League. The name codes [21], [43], [71] are not in Lasry’s key and are left as numbers.

t: Guise to the Duke of Mercœur, 27 May and 20 June 1587 — read with Lasry’s key
b: BnF fr. 15564 f. 142 (Gallica, view 155): the clear news from Germany ends “… xy Suisses et xy lansquenets pour” and the cipher runs on from there. Dated below “Ce xx e Juing 1587”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 15564 f. 142, via Gallica btv1b9064027v view 155. The clear lines give news from Germany: the duke of Lunebourg with nine thousand horse will be on the Rhine by 20 July. The cipher (full text guise1587/f142_reading.txt ): […] de […] par, jusques icy a est[é] tousiours se monstre incredule. La ceste levee […] deust tant avancer, et encor […] il a este […] il n’a plus de six semaines, a asseurance que [73] […] ce, la levee [de] mil lances et quatre mil reistres, qui est ung instable secours; et a si bien faict par des resolutions precipitees, nous sommes maintenant contraincts [de] donner ordre a nos affaires, qui ne peuvent estre avec telles seuretez […] si nos premiers desseings eussent este effectuez avec ordre et mesure. […] faire ce qui […] possible, et dans cinq ou six jours j’espere avoir resolu la chose […] bon avec [73], les forces qui seront necessaires allant la trouver a Meaux, ou il m’a donn[é] […] aller veoir la cest effect. Et je ne faudray a vous en mander toutes nouvelles, et vous baise tres humblement les mains. [73] is probably a person the writer is to meet with troops at Meaux; the pronoun “la trouver” suggests a woman, perhaps the Queen Mother, who was negotiating with the League princes in the summer of 1587, but the code is not in Lasry’s key and the identification is not made here.

t: Guise to the Duke of Mercœur, 27 May and 20 June 1587 — read with Lasry’s key
b: Prior art. The DECODE records (created 2023) carry no key and no decipherment. Cryptiana’s page on Lasry’s BnF solutions lists ff. 27, 78, 119 and 142 under “Duke of Guise? in BnF fr. 15564 and fr. 15565” and gives the key table ( GL_BnFfr15564.png ) and the decipherment of f. 27 only. Transcription. Every sign labelled from Gallica full-resolution crops: 1,861 signs on f. 119, 623 on f. 142. Nomenclator groups (ff-ligatures for common words, digits for names) count as one sign. Decoding. Lasry’s key gives two to seven signs per letter, several of them near-identical shapes. A beam search over each label’s candidate letters under the fr-1600-letters 5-gram model gave a first French text (about 70% sense). Pinning. About twenty passes of three lines each at 2× zoom, comparing each sign with the key and fixing the letter where shape and word agree; a candidate-class phrase search over the French corpora for the last runs (it found arrester , cherchions , en faisant estat , jusques icy ). Key extensions in this hand, beyond Lasry’s sheet: the hooked sign = D or “de”; ✝ = Q; ɤ = D, T or X; the x-shape = Y or N; 3/ʒ = C or D; 8 = M, B, N or T; the dotted Є = R; ʃ = A; “=ʃ” = P. Measurement. Each reading file carries, per line, the number of signs and the number unread; the totals give 95.5% (f. 119) and 92.9% (f. 142), 95.1% of letter signs together.

t: Guise to the Duke of Mercœur, 27 May and 20 June 1587 — read with Lasry’s key
b: 121 letter signs of 2,477, scattered, no run longer than eight: each was retried in three or more zoomed passes and a phrase search. A few look like two-sign code groups (“98”, “89”, “z3”) rather than letters. Longest gaps: f. 142 line 1 (eight signs after “de”, including two ff-groups from Lasry’s unknown row), f. 119 line 3 (four), line 27 (“que [five] eschauffé”). Name codes: [21] (twice, a duke), [43], [71] (with “son frere”), [73] (twice, f. 142), [N], [&], [9b], and the groups ffv, ffσ, ffx, ffou. None is in Lasry’s table; each occurs once or twice. Grades: the passages quoted above are H (sign-true); words in the full files marked with ? or in brackets are C or M; the identifications of Pfyffer and Châtillon are historical, not from the cipher.

t: Cornelis Haga to the States General, February–May 1620 — the Bohemian revolt seen from the Porte
b: DECODE lists two ciphered despatches of the first Dutch ambassador at Constantinople as non-decrypted, with a note that their signs are zodiacal and alchemistic. They are not: the cipher is a letter substitution whose signs are ordinary letter shapes, with a 116-entry numeric nomenclator, and its key sits in the same archival file as DECODE R2118. The two records hold four letters, not two, and their pages are bound out of order. The cipher carries Haga’s advice on the Bohemian revolt — that the Hungarians should elect the King of Bohemia and proceed to the crowning of a new king — and the Porte’s urgent questions about the truce with Spain. The key’s cell for m falls outside the photograph and was recovered from the letters. The catalogue listed two despatches of Cornelis Haga (1578–1654), the first resident Dutch ambassador at the Ottoman court, as ciphered and unread, with a note on DECODE that their signs were zodiacal and alchemistic. They are not: the cipher is a plain letter substitution whose signs are ordinary Latin letter shapes standing for other letters, with a numeric nomenclator of 116 entries written in parentheses. The key for the series sits in the same archival file and is on DECODE as R2118, and it fits the letters at first try. What the two records hold is not two letters but four, and the scans are bound out of order: R2113 is the clear ending of 1 February 1620 plus a separate letter of 31 March whose first page is missing, and R2115 runs p.3, p.2, p.4, p.1 and covers despatches of 24 April and 4 May. The enciphered passages are all policy. In March Haga reports that the Porte would let Transylvania be resigned to Bethlen Gábor’s brother, and argues that the Turks would respect the anti-Habsburg side more if the Hungarians also elected regem Bohemiae ; in the same letter the Grand Vizier, the Capitan Bassa and the Mufti press him on whether the truce with Spain will be renewed, since the Porte would rather see it broken, “om Spangie van weder zyde te mogen infesteren”. In April and May he urges that the Hungarian Estates proceed to the election and crowning of a new king, reports that orders have gone to the Bassa of Buda to keep correspondence with them, and warns that nothing said in the name of the Emperor’s ambassador is to be believed. Status: both catalogued ciphertexts read in sense; one code and a handful of short cipher words stay open.

t: Cornelis Haga to the States General, February–May 1620 — the Bohemian revolt seen from the Porte
b: Inventory number 6894 of the archive of the States General holds Haga’s ciphered despatches from Constantinople. DECODE catalogues four items from it: R2113 (1 February 1620, 3 pp.), R2114 (11 May 1620, 6 pp., marked Decrypted ), R2115 (4 May 1620, 4 pp.) and, as a key record, R2118, dated 1620 with the note that the date is fictitious and that the key was probably handed to Haga when he left The Hague. R2113 and R2115 were the catalogue target; R2114 was left alone, being marked read already. The key is two sheets. The first carries the alphabet table and the first part of the nomenclator, the second continues the numbered list to 116. The alphabet is a simple substitution in which the cipher signs are themselves letter shapes, which is why the letters look like a strange but readable hand rather than a cipher: The key, DECODE R2118: a–l. a is written φ, b K, c an 8-like sign, d ℓ, e 7, f o, g x, h 9, i an ε-like sign, k ω, l a looped 2. Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, key sheet (alphabet a–l), via DECODE R2118. n–z: n is written like t, o as a cross, p as a u-like sign, q 6, r d, s z, t a long ʃ, u/v δ, w m, x B, y λ, z an n-like sign. The cell for m falls outside the photographed sheet. Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, key sheet (alphabet n–z), via DECODE R2118. The nomenclator numbers the Sultan and his officers (1 Sultan Osman, 2 Sultan Mustafa his uncle, 3 the Vizier Azem, 4 the Capitan Bassa, 7 the Mufti, 10 the Janitsaraga), then the provincial Bassas and Beys, the cities of the empire, the Christian and Mahometan princes with their ambassadors, the fleets, and the islands and havens of both sides (93 Cyprus to 116 “de Golff”). Part of the nomenclator: 69 the Pope, 70 the King of Spain, 71 the Grand Duke of Tuscany, 73 the Grand Master of Malta, then the Turkish fleets and the islands. Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, key sheet (nomenclator), via DECODE R2118.

t: Cornelis Haga to the States General, February–May 1620 — the Bohemian revolt seen from the Porte
h: Four letters, bound out of order
b: Neither record is one letter, and neither is in order. R2113. Page 1 is the clear close of the despatch of 1 February 1620 and carries no cipher at all. Pages 3 and 2, in that order, are a different letter: page 3 breaks off in mid-sentence and page 2 takes it up, ending “In Constant. den xxxj martij 1620”. The opening page of that 31 March letter is not among the scans. R2115. The order is p.3 (the address “Hooge Mogende ende Genadige Heeren”), p.2, p.4 — which ends a despatch dated “In Const. den xxiiii April 1620” and begins the next — then p.1, which closes at Constantinople on 4 May 1620 . So the record holds two despatches, of 24 April and 4 May .

t: Cornelis Haga to the States General, February–May 1620 — the Bohemian revolt seen from the Porte
h: 31 March 1620: Transylvania, Bohemia, and the Spanish truce
b: The ciphered spans of the March letter run inside clear Dutch. On Transylvania, Haga reports that the Porte will let the resignation be made in favour of “sijn hoocheijts broeder”, and that the province must stay in good correspondence with Hungary so that it does not fall into the hands of Homonnai “ofte anderen {dependenten van t huijs van Oostenrijck}”. Then his own advice: Ick oordeel dat het {bij de turcken} meerder reputatie ende estime soude geven {dat de Ongaren regem Bohemiae mede erweelden, ende met} (62) in stricte alliantie verbonden bleven. Hungary and Bohemia united under one head — the Elector Palatine — would, he writes, let Transylvania deal with the Turks on better terms in the treaties that must follow; a legation from Hungary, Bohemia and the incorporated provinces would be welcome at the Porte. The second half of the letter turns to Spain. A Polish envoy has refused to have his lodging prepared in the usual way, which Haga calls a {bravade}; and (44) {ende} (45) {arbeiden bij} (4) om tyt te winnen, dat hy provisie {een suspensie van wapenen tusschen de turcken}, ende de {coninckrijcken van Napels} ende {Sicilia} gepractiseert mocht worden … (3) (4) {ende} (7) {vragen mijn} curieuselijck ende ernstelijck {off} (50) geresolveert sijn {de treffves met} (70) {te verlengen}, {vrede} te maecken, ofte {de wapenen} wederom {aen te nemen}, twelck men {hier seer gaerne} soude sien, {om Spangie van weder} zyde te mogen {infesteren}. That is the Grand Vizier, the Capitan Bassa and the Mufti asking the Dutch ambassador, in the last year of the Twelve Years’ Truce, whether the Republic means to renew it — and saying plainly that the Porte would rather it were broken, so that Spain could be attacked from both sides at once.

t: Cornelis Haga to the States General, February–May 1620 — the Bohemian revolt seen from the Porte
h: 24 April and 4 May 1620: elect a new king
b: The April despatch reports the arrival of the envoys of the confederated Bohemian and Hungarian lands, sent from the Easter diet of Pressburg with its resolutions and with the intention of sending a formal legation and making a perpetual peace with the Sultan. They were received without delay, by the Grand Vizier and then by the Sultan, and at that audience the ambassador of the Hungarian Estates — kept back until then, the letter says, by the persuasion of the ambassador of the German Emperor — was admitted with them. The Porte answered that the ambassadors would be welcome and that it was resolved to treat and make friendship with the crown of Hungary, Bohemia and the confederated lands. The advice is in cipher. Nothing is more needful, Haga writes, than that {de Ungarische Stenden} proceed, at the most desperate pass, {tot de electie ende croeninge van een nieuw coninck}; order has already been given {aen (19) ordre gegeven is met haer goede correspondentie te houden} and to {assisteren, sonder andere last} from here; nothing done in the name of (43) is to be believed; and (3) and (7) are to {vermanen} Transylvania that {geen vrede gemaeckt werdt} with (43), and not to wait longer over the crown of Hungary. The closing pages of 4 May are clear: the Polish ambassador has at last had his licence, the Khan of Tartary is said to have marched into Poland in person, and Ottoman preparations go on but will be slow, since neither Sultan nor Vizier goes in person.

t: Cornelis Haga to the States General, February–May 1620 — the Bohemian revolt seen from the Porte
b: The DECODE JSON API gave the metadata for the whole run of records at inventory number 6894, which is how R2118 was found to be the key of the series and R2114 to be marked read. The fifteen page images were fetched with the account’s session cookie. They are photographed sideways, so every page was rotated and cut into strips of three lines before reading. The alphabet table was read off the key and tested on the first cipher words of R2113 p.2, which gave arbeiden , tusschen , suspensie and de turcken at once; the two letters were then deciphered in two parallel passes. The key’s cell for m lies outside the photographed sheet, so that letter was recovered from the text: the 4-shaped sign, confirmed by becomen , met , mijn , vermogen , teenemael and geconformeert . The nomenclator values were read off the key and then checked against the sense of the letters, which confirms (19) Buda, (62) Transylvania, (70) Spain, (3) the Vizier Azem, (4) the Capitan Bassa, (7) the Mufti, (58) the States General and (43) the Emperor’s ambassador.

t: Cornelis Haga to the States General, February–May 1620 — the Bohemian revolt seen from the Porte
b: Code (50). Read off the key, 50 is the French king’s ordinary ambassador, which does not fit “de treffves met (70) te verlengen”. Either the numbering of that column is off by a row or two as the sheet is photographed, or the code is used loosely for the Dutch side. Unresolved (I). Codes 37–45. Their column is cut off at the edge of the photograph of the key’s first sheet, so the headings are read but the numbers are inferred from the order of the list. That makes (44) and (45), in the March letter, conjectural (M). Short cipher words. ℓ7tδℓ7d7t (R2113 p.2, line 13) reads literally denvderen , perhaps meant for hinderen ; the opening phrase of the ciphered advice on R2115 p.3 is unread; a scatter of short words in both letters is marked with a query in the reading files (C or M). The clear Dutch was read for sense, not transcribed word for word; the quotations above are from the cipher spans and their immediate surroundings. R2114 (11 May 1620, six pages) was not re-read here: DECODE marks it Decrypted, though the record carries no plaintext file.
