t: Mary Queen of Scots to Archbishop Hamilton, 18 January 1569 — the decipherment transcribed
b: DECODE R8347 (BL Add MS 33531 ff. 73–74), catalogued with no names and dated January 1568, is Mary Queen of Scots writing from Bolton to John Hamilton, Archbishop of St Andrews, on 18 January 1569. The contemporary decipherment is bound in as f. 74, Bain calendared it and Tomokiyo published the key. The decipherment is transcribed in full: Mary refuses to hand over her son, counts on ten thousand men from France and Spain, and orders the rebels’ houses taken before an amnesty. Bolton Castle → the Archbishop of St Andrews · letter substitution with name signs · 18 January 1569 · read at the time Mary Queen of Scots to Archbishop Hamilton, 18 January 1569 — “I will not leave them that has not left me” BL Add MS 33531 ff. 73–74 (DECODE R8347; catalogue item 84). DECODE gives no sender or recipient and dates it January 1568. It is Mary Queen of Scots, a prisoner at Bolton, writing to John Hamilton, Archbishop of St Andrews, on 18 January 1569 (1568 in the Scottish reckoning of the letter). The contemporary decipherment is bound in as f. 74. Bain calendared both in 1900 and Satoshi Tomokiyo has published the key. The decipherment is transcribed here in full for the first time. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 21 September 2026 resolved Summary. Catalogue item 84 was a DECODE record with no names, the date January 1568 and the status “partially decrypted”. The letter opens in clear, “Reverend fader and traist cousigne and counsalo r ”, and is signed by Mary herself, “Zour gud Cusines and asuryd frinde, Marie R”, at “Bowtoun” in January 1568, which is 1569 by the modern reckoning. Bain’s Calendar of Scottish Papers ii, no. 966, identifies it as Mary to the Archbishop of St Andrews, 18 January, “chiefly in cipher”, with “(2) Decipher of same”. That decipherment is the next leaf, f. 74, and it covers the whole cipher body. Tomokiyo reconstructed the cipher alphabet (the “Mary–Hamilton cipher”), and his key, filed on the DECODE record, reads the first cipher line exactly as the old decipherment does. So the letter was never unread. What this session adds is the text: Bain prints a paraphrase, and the decipherment is transcribed here line by line. Mary refuses to hand her son over to Elizabeth, promises that her faithful subjects will lose nothing in any settlement, expects ten thousand men from France and Spain by March, and tells Hamilton to take the Hamiltons’ enemies’ houses before an amnesty buries all past deeds. A handful of short code signs, which the decipherer also left as signs, stay open.

t: Mary Queen of Scots to Archbishop Hamilton, 18 January 1569 — the decipherment transcribed
b: Two leaves. f. 73r opens with three lines in clear, then 36 lines of cipher. f. 73v has 26 more lines of cipher, a clear passage about the commission Hamilton wanted for Argyll, Eglinton, Cassillis and Boyd, the date and Mary’s autograph subscription. A later hand at the head of f. 73r notes “Lre Cyphered from ye Q. with the decifer”. ff. 74r–v hold the decipherment, 53 lines in Scots in a different secretary hand; the dorse is endorsed “Recept [x]xiiij Januar”. f. 73r, opening. “Reverend fader and traist cousigne and counsalo r . We greit zow weill. Having ressavit zour lettres be this beirar heirof ze sall understand That of laite”, then the cipher. Image: British Library, Add MS 33531 f. 73r, via DECODE R8347.

t: Mary Queen of Scots to Archbishop Hamilton, 18 January 1569 — the decipherment transcribed
b: A letter-for-letter substitution with invented signs, one sign for th or y (a thorn, as Tomokiyo suggests), word signs for and and to , and a few code signs for persons and states. The key is Tomokiyo’s, filed on DECODE R8347. On the first cipher line it gives “ϕf … ∂ɼϕz qesqsϕf” = it … bein proposit , word for word the start of the decipherment, “it had bein proposit to me”. Tomokiyo also found the same cipher in Cotton Caligula B IX f. 315b, Mary to a bishop, Bolton, 9 September 1568, printed by Labanoff.

t: Mary Queen of Scots to Archbishop Hamilton, 18 January 1569 — the decipherment transcribed
b: f. 74r, the contemporary decipherment: “it had bein proposit to me to consent that my sone suld be deliverit in ⟨E⟩ handis”. Image: British Library, Add MS 33531 f. 74r, via DECODE R8347. Line breaks follow f. 74; ⟨ ⟩ marks a code sign the decipherer left as a sign, [?] a doubtful word. Spelling is the decipherer’s. it had bein proposit to me to consent that my sone suld be deliverit in ⟨E⟩ handis and that it was not necessair that ye lord Heris, Kilwinning and otheris that thai cal of the Hamiltonnis faction suld mel thairwyth, and to that thai inserit name bot me, the lord Lennox ⟨¥⟩ and otheris of my name; and to draw me in that crafty snair thai mak thame to be meik in maner that thair angre war past, seikand me to apointment. In this mater was opinit to me to feil my opinioun, quhilk I wald not ansor on to the tyme the same war spokin to me in ⟨Ꝗ⟩ name; and than I am deliberat to schaw hir that I am content to put my self in hir handis without the advis of my gud subiectis, and wil not do the lyk of my sone for mony ressonis, and that the same behuvit to be spokin to thame first afoir me. I pray zow not to communicat to ony man except to thais of quhome ze ar assurit, and in the meane ze haif al reddi begun that ze mak sik demonstration as it may be knawin that ze nor the rest of my faithful subiectis wyl never condescend to the purposis. As to the appointment that thai desire, I am not of thais that forgettis not, bot I am resolut afoir the hiring of ony conditiounis thai sal find na thing in prejudice of my honour or ony of my faithful subiectis quhome thai haif trettit wyth thair braging; and to the rest thai sal find nathing bot my esteim, and trew sal likwyse remain hayl, for I wil not leif thame that hes not left me and schawis thame selfis loyal and faithful, as thai salbe knawin for the same, and the otheris as thai deserve. ⟨Mn⟩ As to the secors of ⟨B⟩ ⟨p⟩ ⟨sp⟩ I hoip to get of thaym bayth or the moneth of marche, at ye lest of ane of thame, for that hes bein offerid to me reddy ten thousand and ma gyf I haif ado. … ⟨X⟩ schawis that scho wilbe agains thame bayth, is ane interpriser amangis to empesche the support that the rebellis wald haif of hir, and I beleif be the principal occasion that thai seik appointment, … be the said queins [?] mand, quha feiris na thing sa that scho haif peace wyth my realme, or that scho may be assurit thairof in ony sort or wyse. I allow gretumly zo r proclamationis, and schawing heirof be in sik sort that thai may be na wyse witnessing that the same cummis of me, in cais that ony man wald peradventure sa[y] or cheif to do me displesour thairby, for the danger that I may fal in, beyng as I am in the [pu]issance ⟨X⟩. I pray zow to speik of hir M tie contray wyth sik respect as thai may not find mater to mak thair profyt agains ⟨Ƒ⟩. As to ⟨X⟩ I sal wryt yt delygence bayth to ⟨Fr⟩ and to Sp, and haist als weil the support of mony as victualis and of munitioun to ⟨X⟩ in abyding the supplie. ⟨Mn⟩ For sen ze ar assemblit, I wald or ze sinderit the nobles that ze did sum notable act agains the rebellis in taking sa mony housis as ze can, bot that thai haif, as the castel of Glasgow, Dunglas or sic otheris; for als gyf the materis cummis to apointment, as it is lyk to do, al bipast dedis wil cum undir oblivion. I wald that in tyme my faithful subiectis did sa mekle that thay war not behind the hand, for albeit the appointment cum not alwayis, than thay sal haif the advantage. As to the ciphre, we fear not that ony man had gottin ye copy thairof. As to the gyft of eschet that ze craif for ⟨k⟩, ze sal ressave the same in forme as ze desire. The clear close on f. 73v: “As concerning the commissioun ze desire us to send to the erlis of Argyle, Eglingtoun, Cassillis and Boyd, we knaw not in quhat maner ze desire the same, for we understand to haif alreddy ane generall Lieutenent … send us the same quhilk we sall subscryve and put ony day the dait … Off Bowtoun the [xviij] of Januar 1568. Zour gud Cusines and asuryd frinde, Marie R.” The line-by-line transcription of all four pages is in hamilton1569/reading.md .

b: ⟨E⟩ in “deliverit in ⟨E⟩ handis” is Elizabeth by Bain’s footnote and by the sense (C). ⟨Ꝗ⟩ in “spokin to me in ⟨Ꝗ⟩ name … to schaw hir” is probably Elizabeth too (M). ⟨B⟩ ⟨p⟩ ⟨sp⟩ is France and Spain, Bain’s conjecture, supported by the later “to Fr and to Sp” (C). ⟨¥⟩, ⟨Mn⟩, ⟨X⟩, ⟨n⟩, ⟨k⟩, ⟨m⟩, ⟨Ƒ⟩, ⟨Ɡ⟩ and a recurring separator-like sign are left as signs by the decipherer and are not resolved here. ⟨X⟩ recurs where a person or a place is meant (“as to ⟨X⟩ I sal wryt”, “munitioun to ⟨X⟩”). The day of the date on f. 73v is partly illegible on the image; 18 January is Bain’s reading. A few words of the decipherment are marked [?] in the transcription.

b: DECODE R8499, catalogued as “N. Wottoy ?” to an unknown recipient, is Dr Nicholas Wotton’s holograph despatch to Mary I from the French court (BL Harley MS 1582 ff. 8–10), almost wholly in cipher. Applied and corrected over eight passes, it reads 75% of 2,801 signs firmly, 89% with tentative readings: Carew and the rebels with the French king and the Constable, pensions and a band with wages, the Isle of Wight and Plymouth, and a repentant rebel met in Paris. DECODE lists R8499 as a non-decrypted English letter of “N. Wottoy ?” to an unknown recipient, June 1554. The images show a holograph despatch of Dr Nicholas Wotton, Mary I’s ambassador in France, to the Queen: it opens “Pleasing it your highness to understand that” and runs to about 118 lines of graphic-sign cipher with a few clear connectives. The BL catalogue dates it Soissons, 13 June 1554. Its key is on DECODE as R354 (TNA SP 106/2 f. 162, “France 1554”): a homophonic alphabet, a row of nulls and some 140 code signs for Carew, the rebels, the Constable, the French king, the Prince of Spain and common words. The letter was transcribed sign by sign, the key applied, and the transcription and key corrected over eight passes on the full-resolution images. 75.0% of the 2,801 non-null signs now read firmly and 89.4% counting tentative readings (measured). Wotton reports that Carew is at Compiègne with the French king and the Constable, that the king has raised the rebels’ pensions and offered them a band with wages, that they talk of taking the Isle of Wight and Plymouth, and that Wotton met a repentant rebel secretly in Paris who asks for the Queen’s pardon. The Harleian catalogue records a contemporary deciphered copy of this letter at ff. 5r–7v, which is not digitised; the remaining quarter waits on that copy and on about forty rare code signs that the only surviving copy of the key does not list. Harley MS 1582 f. 8r, first lines: “Pleasing it your highness to understand that” in clear, then the cipher: “Carew was at Compiegne and spake of … with the French king, the rebels, with the Constable …”. Image: British Library, Harley MS 1582 f. 8r, via DECODE R8499.

t: Wotton to Queen Mary, Soissons, 13 June 1554 — Read
b: R8499 has six images: ff. 8r, 8v, 9r and 10v of Harley MS 1582 and two binding views. The hand is Wotton’s, the address is to the Queen, and the close reads “And thus I beseech Jesu long to preserve your highness”. The body is cipher, about 3,200 signs, with clear-text pieces between the runs (“the king being then in his journey … the Court resting as yet nowhere”, “declaredde unto him your highness pleasure”). The letter is not in the Calendar of State Papers Foreign, Mary , which gives only Wotton to Petre, Soissons, 14 June, and later letters to the Queen from SP 69. The key is DECODE R354, a single sheet in TNA SP 106/2 f. 162 headed “France 1554”. It gives three to six homophones for each letter, a row of nulls (“Nihil significantia”), and a nomenclator whose entries fit Wotton’s embassy that spring: the Emperor, the Queen’s Highness, the French king, the Constable, Peter Carew, the rebels, my Lady Elizabeth, the Earl of Devonshire, the Prince of Spain, Strozzi, Siena, Guisnes, Calais, the Low Countries, “fair words”, and short words ( and, the, of, to, was, shall, have, hath, it, is ). The signs and nulls of R8499 are those of R354. The key, TNA SP 106/2 f. 162 (DECODE R354): the alphabet a–z with its homophones in columns, and below them the nulls, “Nihil significantia”. The nomenclator fills the rest of the sheet. Image: The National Archives, SP 106/2 f. 162, via DECODE R354.

t: Wotton to Queen Mary, Soissons, 13 June 1554 — Read
b: The text below follows the letter in order, in modern punctuation and the spelling as read. Square brackets with a number mark unread signs; words in italics are tentative (grade C or M). The line-by-line reading, with the signs, is final_v8.txt in the repository. f. 8r: Carew at Compiègne Pleasing it your highness to understand that Carew was at Compiegne and spake of with the French king, the rebels, with the Constable, and Carew. I am enformid Carew saith [1] he have had meny gentle and fair words … the Constable tooke it [4] that the French king had gyven him … and where Carew requyred that the band of the rebels should have the Emperor’s wagis … the Constable comenid with him how the ysle of Wight might be taken [7] … and how it might be kept. The rebels finallye, Carew advertisith me, they have concludid that … to attempt against your highness … the Prince of Spain’s coming … in the Low Countries … He the French king hath encreasidde the pensions of dyvers of the rebels … of the Cardinal Farnese , who shewing him much favour … two hundred … crownes and nothing other, likewise … offerid fowre hundrid and the leading of a band, yf him list, as he saithe. f. 8v: the rebels’ plans The rebels may dwel in France where they be, and the Emperor’s pensions to continew til the time the French king may restowr them to the Emperor’s countre … the Emperor’s ambassador sent me word that whereunto cam of late a servant of Carew to him out of the Low Countries, who shall that certein gentlemen home send him word that … in the west partis they … to take part with them … and that they [1] take Plymtown [5] and keep it rady … The king being then in his journey, the Court resting as yet nowhere, so as I could … I wold first make a step to Paris ere I went, to talk secretly with … and to advertys him of your highness’ mind … I found the meanes to talk with him in a [2] place and declaredde unto him your highness’ pleasure concerning him … he must first speak with Carew ere he could take [1] to him. The effect of his answer was these: first … the resolucion taken betwen the Constable and Carew [6] … the Constable, being enformedde that Carew was departid [from] Compiegne , satisfied , had sent the lord [16] to him to … meny fair words, and to shewe him that the rebels’ band shulde have theyr wagis. f. 9r: the repentant rebel … for lack of money … charges offred, and he would not entre in service to the French king … he did receve money of him, he could not find in his heart that they be untrew to him; and besides that, he doubting lest it be known that he gyveth me advertsmentes … would be gladde to depart this shortly; and although he sayde he took me to be an honest manne, and therfore did not mistrust my wordes … what kind of effect your highness wolde requyre of him to be done … that it were perceived that he wente abrode to attempt the Emperor against the French king … he came not fynde in his herte to return into England. He thinkith that your highness can not forget this offence … and in case your highness could forget it, yet he reckening assuredly that the French king will [not] forget it … so that, being persuadedde that he can not lyve in England without [pardon] of this, he entendeth not to return … that it would please your highness to give him … and suffer him to have a gentlemanes lyving in [2] countrey … He entendith not to open the circumstances of this fawte … if he must detect meny gentelmen, who, remaining unknown, may live honestly at home. f. 10v: Cornwel, the lantzknechtes, Saint-Quentin This is th’effect of … He shewed me that one Cornwel is rover to late and … I have not yet spoken with him … the said Cornwel … For he doutith whether he may trust him, for he was longing to the lord [4] … There is one who calling him self Greneberye , who hath been twyse offred … the first tyme they toke him for a spye … and besides that, this felaw who cam with him the first declared to Carew what he was and where … the Emperor’s sisters; Carew namid to be twenty enseignes, and lye abowte Laon, of new lantzknechtes … not the third part … passid within a myle of this towne fifty and nine canone. It is told me that … Paris, and it semith to take the way towardes Saint Quintin … what the Emperor’s intent is, is kept [2]. It is thought that the French king will be in the camp him[self] … whether the Emperor be strong to meete them. The Constable hath ben sike and is not yet [1] strong. The Duke of Gwyse [7] … And thus I beseech Jesu long to preserve your highness …

t: Wotton to Queen Mary, Soissons, 13 June 1554 — Read
b: Identification. The opening and close in clear name the Queen; the hand and the signature fix Wotton; the BL catalogue record and the Harleian catalogue of 1808 give Soissons, 13 June 1554. Transcription. A first sign transcription (3,212 signs, 158 types) was made before the key was found. A homophonic annealer on the en-1640s model, validated on synthetic controls, failed blind: the nulls and word codes defeat it. Key. The key sheet R354 was found on DECODE among the SP 106 keys and read ( key_R354.md ). With its nulls removed and its letter and code values pinned, the text began to read (“Compiegne and spake of … the rebels with the Constable”). Re-transcription. Several first-pass tokens merged distinct key signs (ω d and ꬯ and ; the French king and “your highness”; the barred and plain x). They were split sign by sign on the images (v2), then every page was re-read at full resolution (v5). Unified key and nomenclator. Page-by-page keys were merged into one (v6), all ~140 nomenclator entries were transcribed and tested against every unread stretch (v7), and a shape pass separated the upright and arched triangles and the barred and plain C (v8). Measure. Each pass was counted on non-null signs: 47%, 65%, 72%, 75%, 75% firm. The last two passes added no firm readings. page non-null signs firm incl. tentative f. 8r 734 66.6% 86.1% f. 8v 683 75.1% 90.0% f. 9r 709 81.8% 90.6% f. 10v 683 76.9% 91.4% all (v8) 2,801 75.0% 89.4% (The page rows are the v7 count on 2,809 signs; v8 removed two doubly transcribed signs and relabelled others without changing the totals.)

b: About a quarter of the non-null signs are unread or tentative: short runs on f. 8r (lines 13–15, 18, 24), the name after “the lord” on f. 8v (16 signs; perhaps “Brymstane”, Crichton of Brunstane, a Scot: M), the name after “the Duke of Gwyse” on f. 10v (“Gaspard”?: I), “Greneberye” (M), and the code Ie , read once as “the Emperor’s ambassador” (M). Blocker: the contemporary deciphered copy, Harley MS 1582 ff. 5r–7v, is not digitised by the BL or on DECODE and needs an imaging order. About forty rare code signs ( .I .p .d .M N. R. , the C with cedilla, the tailed Q, the tall looped f, the large circle) match no legible cell of R354, the only surviving copy of the key. The dotted N and R codes are probably names added to Wotton’s copy and missing from this one. Tested against the nomenclator and rejected: .I Therouanne, .M Trent, -P , the script y as “either”. Tentative code values: .Z = that, T. = me, L2 = Calais (C). Firm: 4 = that, B. = of, .B = not, dotted y = yet, small circle = hath. Grades of the connected passages: the Carew–Constable narrative of f. 8r, the rebels’ wages and pensions, and the repentant rebel on f. 9r are H; the Isle of Wight and Plymouth are H for the place names, C for the verbs; the Farnese and Greneberye names are M.

t: Stafford to Walsingham, Paris, 20 August 1586 — Read
b: DECODE R8500, catalogued as a non-decrypted letter of an unknown sender, London, is Sir Edward Stafford’s holograph despatch from Paris of 20 August 1586 (BL Harley MS 1582 ff. 65–66). Its five cipher runs in the postscript were never deciphered on the page. Read here with Stafford’s letter key, rebuilt from a contemporary decipherment (f. 72r) and glosses (f. 73r) on sibling letters: 6 is e , not a null. Junius’ son came from Cambrai with papers of his credit with Balagny. Paris → Walsingham · homophonic letter cipher with codes · 20 August 1586 · read Stafford to Walsingham, Paris, 20 August 1586 from Edward Stafford → to Francis Walsingham British Library, Harley MS 1582 ff. 65–66 (DECODE R8500). A clear despatch of the English ambassador in Paris with five short cipher runs in the postscript, never deciphered on the page. Read here with Stafford’s letter key, rebuilt from two sibling letters in the same volume. Daniel Bourdeau · read 22 September 2026 read Summary. DECODE lists R8500 as a non-decrypted letter of “…” to an unknown recipient, London, 20 August 1586. The images show a holograph despatch in clear English signed by Sir Edward Stafford, “Paris this xxth of August 1586”, endorsed “From Sr Edw. Stafford”; the recipient is almost certainly Sir Francis Walsingham, like the sibling letter R8503. The cipher is five short runs in the postscript on f. 65v, with no glosses. Stafford’s letter key was rebuilt from two siblings: f. 73r (R8502, September 1586), whose cipher words are glossed Junius , Cambray , Balagny , Germany ; and f. 72r (R8501), a contemporary clear decipherment of the long cipher passages on f. 71. Aligned sign by sign they give a homophonic alphabet in which 6 is e , not a null as the R8503 runs had suggested. With it the postscript reads: Junius’ son came from Cambrai with letters from his father and papers “of his credit with Balagny”; Stafford fears Balagny means them mischief. Four sign values rest on context; nothing is left unread. The letter is not calendared in CSP Foreign.

t: Stafford to Walsingham, Paris, 20 August 1586 — Read
b: Ff. 65r–65v are in Stafford’s own hand. The clear text reports on Captain Blaize, the Neapolitan with Cesar, his fortifications and dealings in Spain and Naples, on Locatello, and on a book lately printed at Rome by Dr Sanders. A note in the margin of f. 65v forwards a request from “one that was Mr Dennys man”. The address leaf, f. 66v, carries the endorsement “20 August 1586. From Sr Edw. Stafford”. The postscript below the signature holds five cipher runs, written in the same line as the clear words. The signs are a mixture of letter forms and graphic signs ( x D h II n oo O+ w 24 H λ ), the same inventory as Stafford’s other letters to Walsingham in the volume. f. 65v, the postscript: the cipher runs sit inside the clear English lines and read yesterday came hither [Junius sonne] [from Cambraye] and brought me letters from his father … of his [credit with Balagny] … but I am afraid [Balagny] dare them some mischief ; the last line opens with [mayntayne]. Image: British Library, Harley MS 1582 f. 65v, via DECODE R8500.

t: Stafford to Walsingham, Paris, 20 August 1586 — Read
b: Harley MS 1582 holds four Stafford despatches of August–November 1586 in the same cipher (DECODE R8500–R8504). Two of them carry the plaintext: f. 73r (R8502). A second hand glossed the cipher words: x D h x D II Junius , d w o o 24 Oo w H 6 Cambray , 24 w a w B h H 6 Balagny , B 6 O+ Oo o w h x 6 Germany , and a sum 10000 crownes . f. 72r (R8501). A whole page of clear text in a small hand, headed a., b. and c. to match the ciphered passages on ff. 71r–71v: the French ambassador’s wife writing to the Duchess of Nemours that the Queen of Scots “is in very ill state”; Villeroy sending the ambassador’s secretary to “make away Nau”. About 480 cipher signs on f. 71 were aligned against it. The alignment gives a letter alphabet with homophones, plus single-sign and numeric codes: letter signs letter signs a w n h b 24 o n c, l d p E e 6 q Δ f ψ r O+, Oo g B s II, #, I h λ t u, A i, y x, H u, v D, ρ k M w D d l a m oo Codes: B alone Villeroy, O+ alone the Duke or Duchess of Nemours, 120 the French ambassador, 47 the King of Navarre; 20, 22 and 54 recur. The earlier reading of 6 as a null (from the four runs of R8503) is wrong: it is the commonest letter, e .

t: Stafford to Walsingham, 9 November 1586 — Read
b: DECODE R8504, catalogued as a non-decrypted cipher letter of Sir Edward Stafford to an unknown recipient (BL Harley MS 1582 ff. 76–77), is a short holograph in clear English. t: Stafford to Walsingham, 9 November 1586 — Read
b: f. 76r: Stafford’s holograph. About sixteen lines of clear English, a subscription and the signature “E Stafford”. f. 76v/77: blank, with show-through. No address or endorsement survives on the images, so the recipient is not named. DECODE has no title, no date, no author, and gives the language as “English?”. Identified, transcribed and deciphered here. The cipher is a homophonic alphabet of about fifty graphic signs; the letter m is written as a group of two, three or four dots, and taking those for punctuation is what defeated the first attack. They are not one problem: R8501 is one of Sir Edward Stafford’s 1586 despatches, already read from the contemporary decipherment on its own f. 72r ( Stafford, 20 August 1586 ), while R8505 is a French political memoir in a cipher nobody had read. Its clear passages give it a title — L’Estat du Roy de Navarre & de son party en France — and a date after 1580. All four sides were transcribed (about 3,600 signs) and the cipher was then broken from the ciphertext alone, with no key, no crib and no decipherment anywhere. The break came out of a control experiment rather than a new idea about the manuscript: real French, enciphered with a homophonic key of the same shape, defeated the solver in exactly the same way, which located the fault in the search and not in the text. With the search corrected the key fell out at once, and the recovered alphabet then diagnosed the transcription — it had no sign for m or b , which is impossible for French. The dot groups, read as punctuation by every earlier pass, are the letter m; a closed oval pierced by a stem is b. Re-read on that basis, 95.1% of the deciphered text falls in French words: the prince of Parma, a party of malcontents, an Italian engineer at Lisbon, Beaucaire on the Rhône, Béziers, Carcassonne, Montmorency, d’Épernon. Status: key recovered, text read (95.1% measured). What is left is the ten nomenclator numbers, which are names, and about 5% of scattered characters where the ink is faint or two shapes of one family cannot be told apart.

t: “L’Estat du Roy de Navarre et de son party en France” — Read
b: The clear French, which is most of the four sides, surveys Henri de Navarre as a political asset: his two “qualitez” — first prince of the blood, so that his authority can only grow while the king has no children, and chief of the reformed churches of France — then the places he holds and their garrisons in Guyenne, Languedoc, Dauphiné and Provence, the counts and viscounts of his following, the harquebusiers each region can raise, the Catholic party, the German and Swiss alliances, and the marriage question. Internal dates run to 1576, 1577 and 1580; La Rochelle, Brouage and Saint-Jean-d’Angély are current concerns. That is the world of Navarre’s embassies to the Protestant powers in the early and middle 1580s — this repository holds the numeric cipher of one of them, recovered in Ségur 1585–86 — and it explains how the paper came to rest in an English secretary’s file.

t: “L’Estat du Roy de Navarre et de son party en France” — Read
b: The first attack failed. All four sides were transcribed (about 3,600 signs) and put through homophonic annealing against the repository’s French models. Nothing came out — and, tested under English, Spanish and Italian models too, every language scored alike, which is what no key at all looks like. A control located the fault. Real French was enciphered with a fifty-sign homophonic key of the same shape and run through the same solver ( control.py ). It failed in exactly the same way, so the obstacle was the search, not the manuscript. Two faults: a Sukhotin vowel/consonant constraint that is simply wrong for a key of this shape, and a temperature scale far too small for log-probability differences of this size. With both corrected the control recovers 100% of its key, and still 95.5% of its characters when 15% of its signs are randomly corrupted — so transcription noise at the level this manuscript produces is survivable. The real text then broke. The corrected search returned French immediately (“et qu’ils attendent”, “à l’avenir”, “duquel”), and basin-hopping with a word-segmentation objective recovered the alphabet. The key then diagnosed the transcription. A French key with no sign for m and none for b is impossible. That single observation sent the work back to the images, where the dot groups, φ and the two epsilons resolved it; ff. 263v and 264v were re-read sign by sign against the key, changing 29% and 31% of their signs.

b: 95.1% of the 3,551 deciphered characters fall inside French words , measured by Viterbi segmentation against a 37,000-word vocabulary built from the repository’s French corpora. The measure is conservative: sixteenth-century spellings and proper names the vocabulary does not hold count as unread. Two things are left. The ten nomenclator numbers are names; three have contexts that narrow them — 72 is a country and almost certainly France (“la guere contre ceus dela religion en 72 ”, “demeurera ferme en 72 ”), 81 a person and probably the King (“le 81 son frere”), 21 a feminine noun, the League or the army (“ 21 ch[ar]gee dela guere”) — but none is fixed by the text. And about 5% of the characters do not resolve into French words: faint ink, and shapes ambiguous within one family. A note on method, since it bears on the figure. ff. 263v and 264v were re-read sign by sign from the images against the recovered key. On ff. 263r and 264r the first-pass transcription was corrected only by a constrained pass: a token may be swapped solely between shapes that the second reading proved confusable — the dot groups against the f sign (a stem with a dot cluster at its upper right, so a faint stem reads as a bare cluster), φ against the long-s, the two epsilons, the two stem-loops, χ against the hourglass, the three bar-shapes, the bracket against Π — and only where the word model gains clearly. That is 77 tokens, 2% of the text, and every one is listed in emendations_all.txt so it can be checked against the manuscript.

Suffolk · private record, no recipient · D’Ewes’s invented alphabet, Latin · 1635–36 · read Sir Simonds D’Ewes’s cipher log of his son’s fits, 1635–36 British Library, Harley MS 286 f. 61 (DECODE R7759, “unknown sender to unknown recipient, 1635”): a small slip, one line for each convulsion fit of the antiquary’s infant son Clopton, written in D’Ewes’s private alphabet. No reading was known; the alphabet was rebuilt from the slip by crib and the log read. Daniel Bourdeau · solved 22 September 2026 solved Summary. DECODE lists R7759 as a one-page non-decrypted letter of 1635 from an unknown sender to an unknown recipient, cipher type unknown. The British Library’s own catalogue describes the leaf as “a short paper written by Sir Simonds D’Ewes, in his cipher”, though it files it under Harley MS 289 rather than 286; which shelfmark is right is not settled here. It is not a letter. It is D’Ewes’s private record, in Latin, of the convulsion fits of his son Clopton, born July 1634, beginning “Aprilis iii. mane circa horam nonam convulsionem habuit. die Veneris” and running, one fit to a line, into January 1636. The alphabet is a simple substitution D’Ewes invented at school; no key to it is printed, so it was rebuilt from the slip by crib on the recurring words convulsio , plena luna and difficilis . The dates check against the calendar: every weekday named matches the Julian date, most moon phases match, and D’Ewes’s Autobiography gives the same start, 3 April 1635, and a total of forty-four fits to 4 March 1636. The child died on 9 May 1636. 277 of 287 words read (96.5%, measured); open are the last line, trimmed under the mount, one word at the edge of line 13 and a faint phrase in lines 24–25.

t: Sir Simonds D’Ewes’s cipher log of his son’s fits, 1635–36
b: Sir Simonds D’Ewes (1602–1650), the parliamentary antiquary whose manuscripts make up much of the Harleian collection, wrote his private papers in an alphabet of his own. His diary of 1622–24 (Harley MS 481) is partly in it, and a 1915 University of Minnesota thesis deciphered that diary without printing the key. Folio 61 is a small slip mounted on a larger leaf, headed 1635 in ordinary figures, with the margin dates 1635/1636 in clear beside the January entry and a running count in cipher, huc usque xxxii , “thus far 32”, at the end of the August entries. A rule separates the summer entries from those of September and January. The foot of the slip runs under the mount and its last line is cut. Harley MS 286 f. 61: the whole slip, 30 lines. The margin note at the rule is huc usque xxxii ; the last line is trimmed under the mount. Image: British Library, Harley MS 286 f. 61, via DECODE R7759 (image 1).

b: Dates are Julian (Old Style), as D’Ewes wrote them; the year then began on 25 March. [?] marks a doubtful word, {?} an unread one. The heading and first four entries: “Aprilis iii. mane circa horam nonam convulsionem habuit. die Veneris.” Image: British Library, Harley MS 286 f. 61, via DECODE R7759 (image 1). Latin English Aprilis iii. mane circa horam nonam convulsionem habuit. die Veneris. 3 April [1635]: in the morning about nine o’clock he had a convulsion. Friday. Aprilis xxiii. pom. bis convulsiones habuit. die Iovis. cum plena luna. 23 April, afternoon: he had convulsions twice. Thursday. At the full moon. Maii xiiii. ad finem iterum trium septimanarum ix[?]. convulsiones. luna tum[?] mutata. 14 May: at the end of three weeks again, convulsions. The moon then changed. Maii xxiii. die Saturni fluxio aperta. 23 May, Saturday: a flux broke out. Maii xxv. inter horas xii et i convulsionem habuit. cum eo die plena luna. 25 May: between twelve and one he had a convulsion, the moon being full that day. Iunii xii. decrescente luna s[?]. primam convulsionem sensit. 12 June, the moon waning: he felt the first convulsion. Iunii xiii. successit alia mitis[?] convulsio. et Iun. xiiii. alia 13 June: another, mild convulsion followed; and 14 June another. Iul. xvii. ante lunae plenilunium quae in diem xix. sequentem incidit duae convulsiones mites. 17 July, before the full moon, which fell on the 19th following: two mild convulsions. Iul. xxiii. alia convulsio difficilis. 23 July: another convulsion, a hard one. Augusti ii. luna tum[?] nova difficilis [struck word] convulsio. 2 August, the moon then new: a hard convulsion. Augusti iii. mitis convulsio mane circa horam primam; cum inter meos fuit amplexus alia terribilis convulsio, quam a prandio non leve magno tremore vexit[?]. pomeridiano iterum {?} alia difficilis convulsio. 3 August: a mild convulsion in the morning about one o’clock; when he was in my arms, another terrible convulsion, which after dinner shook him with a great trembling, not a light one. In the afternoon again {?} another hard convulsion. Aug. xxiiii. mane alia difficilis convulsio. 24 August, morning: another hard convulsion. Aug. xx. parum post lunae plenilunium (quae in diem xviii. istius mensis incidebat) tres difficillimas convulsiones, in quorum tertia os ipsius pene ad aurem dextram convulsum, quod ante numquam observavi. eadem nocte ante horam i. duae aliae convulsiones sed mitiores. 20 August, a little after the full moon (which fell on the 18th of this month): three very hard convulsions, in the third of which his mouth was drawn almost to his right ear, which I had never seen before. The same night before one o’clock two more convulsions, but milder. Aug. xxi. post horam secundam mane et ante quintam duae aliae mites convulsiones. ante duodecimam horam alia difficilis. [margin:] huc usque xxxii. 21 August, after two in the morning and before five: two more mild convulsions. Before twelve another hard one. [margin:] Thus far 32. Aug. xxxi. absolutus[?] 31 August: free[?] (lighter ink, above the rule) Sept. xxi. die et ante horam primam noctis septima[?] agonia sed an {?} vel[?] alia praecedentia pede[?] convulsionem sed etiam epilepsia nativo[?]. 21 September, by day and before one at night, a seventh[?] fit of agony; but whether {?} or other preceding … a convulsion, but also epilepsy … (partly unread) Sept. xxvii. post horam secundam mane et ante vii. tres aliae agoniae. 27 September, after two in the morning and before seven: three more fits of agony. [margin 1635/1636] Ian. xxiiii. post xvii. septimanas liberationem nocte inter horam [nonam struck] viii et ix. convulsio difficilis. sperabam tamen quod evenerat ex coena nimia quam post convulsionem evomuit. 24 January [1636], after seventeen weeks’ freedom, at night between eight and nine: a hard convulsion. I hoped, though, that it came from too large a supper, which he vomited up after the convulsion. {?} … [hor]am nonam (last line, trimmed under the mount) The Autobiography gives the end: the fits came more thickly in the spring of 1636, twelve in one night on 8–9 May, and the child died about two in the afternoon of Monday 9 May 1636, a year and nine months old. D’Ewes blamed “a proud, fretting, ill-conditioned woman for a nurse”, an issue opened in the child’s neck and the violent remedies of Dr Despotine of Bury, and the rickets that followed.

t: Lord Cobham at Ostend, 20–22 March 1588 — the peace commissioner’s cipher, read in part
b: BL Harley MS 287 ff. 70–72, catalogued on DECODE as seven ciphertexts of an unknown sender to an unknown recipient, are two letters of Lord Cobham, Elizabeth’s peace commissioner at Ostend, of 20 and 22 March 1587/8, with a report from Middelburg. Every run is read in sense, among them Parma’s new canal from Ghent to Sluys and the prisoners Pigot and Barney; a code number, a surname and a few words stay open, and the share read is not yet measured. Ostend → Walsingham · graphic-sign substitution inline with clear English · 20–22 March 1587/8 · read Lord Cobham at Ostend, 20–22 March 1588 — the peace commissioner’s cipher, read from Lord Cobham → to Francis Walsingham British Library, Harley MS 287 ff. 70–72 (DECODE R8482–R8487), catalogued as seven ciphertexts of an unknown sender to an unknown recipient. They are two signed letters of Henry Brooke, Lord Cobham, written from Ostend during the 1588 peace talks with Parma, and a cipher enclosure from Middelburg. Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 solved in part Summary. Item 132 of the catalogue listed seven DECODE records from Harley MS 287 with no sender, recipient or reading. Six of them (ff. 70r–72v) are two letters of Lord Cobham, one of Elizabeth’s commissioners for the peace talks with the Duke of Parma, dated at Ostend on 20 and 22 March 1587/8 (Old Style) and signed “your assured loving friend H. Cobham”, with an intelligence report from Middelburg between them. The addressee is not named; the volume and the content point to Walsingham. The cipher runs sit inside clear English, and there is no decipherment on the leaves and none in print. The clear words gave the cribs (“commaunded to attend”, “that bearer hath”, “under colour thereof”), and the key turned out to be a simple substitution in graphic signs, with a few homophones and the words divided. Every run reads: Parma’s new canal from Ghent by Eeklo to Sluys “within 15 days navigable”, his build-up at Oudenburg, a garrison “too weak by the half” with five weeks’ pay left, the prisoners Pigot and Barney, Cobham’s lack of spies, and his refusal to be “a means to conclude an irreligious peace”. A few dotted numbers and a square are nomenclator signs: 15 is Parma, □ the States, .7. probably the Queen; 42 is not identified. The seventh record (f. 11) is a different letter in a different code and is not read. f. 70v, 22 March 1587/8: “This preparation, together with the reinforcing of his garrisons hereabout”. Image: British Library, Harley MS 287 f. 70v, via DECODE R8483.

The Commission (Derby, Cobham, Croft, Dale, Rogers) reached Ostend in March 1588. The letters name Mr Controller (Croft), “Mr Doctor Rogers” being sent to the Duke at Bruges, and a servant of Lord Burghley, all in clear. The Calendar of State Papers Foreign calendars Cobham’s letters of 22 and 24 March to Burghley, from the State Papers, but not these. The key on f. 187 of the same volume (R8497, Bodley, 1590) is a different system.

t: Lord Cobham at Ostend, 20–22 March 1588 — the peace commissioner’s cipher, read in part
b: Each run replaces the letters of English words with signs, one sign per letter and the words kept separate. A few letters have two signs (a: ∪ and ⊥; w: two dots and a dotted x; g: a barred x and a 3), and a colon after a letter stands for u. The signs of one family (l, p, h, m, all drawn as a crossed or looped stem) and the two carets for s and t are close on the scans; they were settled word by word. a b c d e f g h i l m n o p r s t u/v/w y ∪ ⊥ + 8 ∞ 7 H̅ Ӽ 3 ϵ ⊥ ϕ ∝ †† z ϕ V ∧ ∧ .. ẋ ɣ The key was rebuilt from the clear words on either side of each run. A session working on Cobham’s May–June letters in the same volume then found the same values in the contemporary glosses of f. 89 (R8493).

t: Lord Cobham at Ostend, 20–22 March 1588 — the peace commissioner’s cipher, read in part
b: Deciphered words in italics , modern spelling. Grades as in the README: (C) read from context, (M) uncertain; the rest is high. 22 March, ff. 70r–70v What effect this message will work I know not, but doubt the worst, and therefore do wish and think it expedient that some of .7. ships were commaunded to attend on this coast for all events , for I am persuaded 15 will never yield to send 42 hither . Some provision also for vittailes would be necessarily thought upon, for □ have no megasines here, nor mind to have any. That the same here is but from weeke to weeke as the bilanders do voluntarily bring it … there is any money stirring here. The present garrison will be found too weake for the defence of so large a circuit by the half at the least. The last supply of money will not [keep them] from the presentes wantes of the souldiers above five weeks longer, as the governour tells me. … The Duke is expected within a day or two to be at Bruges. The newe ditche from Gaunt by Eecloo unto Sluce is said to be almost ended, and will be within 15 dayes navigable for the float boates and vessels he hath ready prepared, being some of them fraught with stones and fagottes . This preparation, together with the reinforcing of his garrisons hereabout, Stanley’s repair unto Turnhout (M), make such [at] Oudenburgh with eleven companies of footmen , and the Duke’s coming to Bruges doth threaten somewhat (C). And in mine opinion this town is fit to be stopped (C) through some attempts upon the haven ; which being once stopped, the town being already abandoned of succour by land , cannot make resistance against the enemy many days (C) together. My greatest grief is that in all this town I am not furnished of any one spy to employ abroad for the more certainty of the enemy’s proceedings . And from Flushing I hear very seldom by reason that the passage is dangerous and subject to interception . … By my servant William I wrote in my private letter a special motion for our remove to Flushing (C), where we might better stand on terms for her Majesty’s honour. Middelburg report, f. 71r In my opinion the ships would be well guarded (C), and when all ships of charge as well of the [fleet] as merchants be at sea (C), there would be 2 or 3 pinnaces appointed to [watch] and direct the channel (C). [Bastune?] the Jesuite is within these fewe dayes sent post into Italy (surname M). R. tould me in talke with him that 15 ha[th] [in]sted his sonne (being under 17 years of age) in the government of his patrimony in Italy. 20 March, ff. 71v–72v There are new companies lately added to the old garrison of Oudenburgh, our near neighbours (C), which were very strong before. This drawing of his forces by land so near, and the provision of stone and fagots to come from Eecloo by water (C), make us suspect some attempts against this town and haven : we think it therefore expedient that some of the ships did continue upon this coast, to be ready for service upon occasions . Also we pray your honour (C) would remove us hence or dismiss us to some other place of more surety (C). This bearer hath laboured his own dispatch and would fain have had instructions , but I, fearing that under colour thereof he would proceed in his charge , did let him understand what we had generally written unto my Lord … As by the [words] of your own hand in your letter of the 16 March I perceive you oppose yourself still against such resolutions ; for mine own part I would think myself most unhappy to be a means to conclude an irreligious peace . Touching Pigot and Barney , if they shall be delivered over to the States , I am of another opinion … things standing as they do, □ will ranson them , and then what dishonour and disfavour will it be for her Majesty. Pigot is a martial man , and hath means and will to deserve his prise (C).

t: Robert Reade to his cousin, Paris, 19 April 1641 — Windebank’s return, in the Windebank cipher
b: DECODE R7766, a letter from Paris with writer and recipient unknown, is signed R. Reade: Secretary Windebank’s nephew and secretary, writing from the exiled household. Its two cipher passages read with the Deciphering Branch’s reconstruction of the Windebank cipher in Add MS 32256 (DECODE R9115): whether Windebank can return under a summons without losing his person or his fortune, and a warning about Sir William St Ravy. 89% read from the key, 5% from rebuilt values, 6% conjectured. Paris → his cousin in England · numerical nomenclator in a clear letter · 19 April 1641 · read in part Robert Reade to his cousin, Paris, 19 April 1641: Windebank’s return, in the Windebank cipher British Library, Harley MS 7001 ff. 148–149, DECODE R7766. The letter is in clear English with two ciphered passages, 254 groups in all. DECODE lists the writer and the recipient as unknown. The signature and the endorsement identify the writer. The key is the Deciphering Branch’s reconstruction of Secretary Windebank’s cipher, filed in Add MS 32256. Applied to the passages, it reads 89% of the cipher from the values it holds. Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 22 September 2026 read in part Summary. DECODE catalogues R7766 as a partly encrypted letter from Paris, dated 19 April 1641, with the writer and recipient unknown. The letter is signed “R. Reade”. The endorsement reads “1641: April 19: my Cousin Reade from Paris”. The writer is Robert Reade, nephew and secretary of Sir Francis Windebank. Windebank was Charles I’s Secretary of State and had fled to Paris in December 1640 to escape the Long Parliament. The clear text concerns Strafford’s trial, the King’s papers, Walter Montagu’s arrival and a slander against the writer. The two cipher passages carry the household’s private business. BL Add MS 32256, the Deciphering Branch’s volume of keys, holds a sheet headed “Windebank to his Son. Paris. March 1642” (DECODE R9115). It is a reconstruction of the same cipher: letters at 1–100 with the odd numbers below 50 as nulls, a set of symbol letters, and an alphabetical code up to about 735. With it, the first passage reads: in case a proclamation shall go out against [him] … they have not enough against him to confiscate his fortune, and they would be willing to take the advantage of his refusal to return upon a summons; so on the other side, I do not find how his person can be secure if he shall return . The second passage says that Sir William St Ravy has done Mr Forster no good offices in Paris. Of 215 significant groups, 191 are read from values on the key and 11 from values rebuilt here. The remaining 13 are code groups the reconstruction leaves blank. They are offered as conjectures. Status: read in part; 94% read, 6% conjectured.

t: Robert Reade to his cousin, Paris, 19 April 1641 — Windebank’s return, in the Windebank cipher
b: Harley MS 7001 f. 149r, the head of the page: the cipher continued from f. 148v, beginning “[as to] the one side, I am of opinion they have not enough against him to confiscate his fortune”. Image: British Library, Harley MS 7001 f. 149r, via DECODE R7766. The letter covers three pages (ff. 148r, 148v, 149r). The address leaf f. 149v carries the endorsement and “Given by Mr G. Holmes”. It answers the recipient’s letter of 1 April and follows Reade’s own letter of the 16th. The clear text covers: a malicious report that Reade had said, to two French gentlemen in a garden, that the Lords of the Parliament are fools. He denies it at length and asks the recipient to raise it with the Lord Chief Justice; the roads full of soldiers, which keep the household in its quarter of Paris for another month; “My Lo: Lieutenant”, Strafford, then on trial, “fallen into the hands of noblemen and persons of honor”; the King’s box of papers and a copy held by Mr Treasurer; the Queen’s business; Mr Montagu’s arrival, “very civilly” received; Sir William St Ravy leaving for England; a defence of Mr Forster, lodged with the household. The cipher begins where the letter turns to Windebank himself: “It is to be seriously considered what is to be done”.

t: Robert Reade to his cousin, Paris, 19 April 1641 — Windebank’s return, in the Windebank cipher
b: BL Add MS 32256, the page “Windebank’s C[ipher] continued 1640”: the reconstructed code from 551, with 572 to, 574 the, 578 that, 586 they, 587 there. Image: British Library, Add MS 32256, continuation page of the Windebank cipher (after f. 4), via DECODE R9115. DECODE R9115 is a two-page working sheet. The Deciphering Branch printed a blank grid of numbers and filled in the values as they were recovered. The first page is headed “Windebank to his Son. Paris. March 1642”, the second “Windebank’s C[ipher] continued 1640”. The cipher has four parts: 1–50: single letters. Every odd number is marked + (a null). The even numbers are letters: 2 c, 4 f, 6 n, 8 h, 10 r, 12 t, 14 a, 16 g, 18 p, 20 b, 22 u, 24 o, 26 l, 28 e, 32 k, 34 m, 36 i, 40 s, 42 x, 44 d. 51–100: more letters and syllables: 51 r, 53 c, 54 l, 55 s, 56 a, 57 d, 58 m, 59 t, 60 e, 62 n, 64 i, 66 p, 68 o, 69 h, 72 u, 73 and, 74 am, 75 as, 93 again, 97 an. Symbol letters: m n, E o, ω m, Ǝ r, ⊔ i, + l, φ s, Δ t, * y, ⊕ a, π c, ɔ d, ∪ e, C p, and others. A code in alphabetical order from 100 to about 735: 128 be, 183 can, 202 do, 276 from, 323 him, 335 his, 362 King, 457 Parliament, 533 shall, 572 to, 574 the, 578 that, 636 will, 732 England, 735 France. Reade’s letter uses the same cipher. The most frequent code groups in it are the reconstruction’s the, to and that, and its symbol letters are the key’s. Several signs first transcribed as digits turned out to be symbols once the key was read: φ looks like an 8, ɔ like a 2, and the looped n-sign like a D.

t: Robert Reade to his cousin, Paris, 19 April 1641 — Windebank’s return, in the Windebank cipher
b: Plain type is read from the key. Words in italics come from values rebuilt here. Words in [brackets] are conjectures for groups the key leaves blank (section 04). Nulls are dropped. Passage A (f. 148v foot to f. 149r), after the clear “It is to be seriously considered what is to be done”: in case a proclamation shall goe out against my [455: patron?] as against the last [673], for as to the one side, I am of opinion they have not enough against him to confiscate his fortune, and they would be willing to take the advantage of his refusall to return upon the a summons. So on the other side, I do not find how his person can be secure if he shall return . The only [way] i[s] [conceived] to be that [His Majesty] will please to prevent that cause, if they purpose to take it, bu[t pres]sing that [Mr Forster] [should] give in his [90]; but God knows why that will suit. Passage B (f. 149r), after the clear “Sir William St Ravy (as I hear) parts this day for England, but I do but hear it from others, for he comes not at us”: I am [informed] he has done [Mr Forster] no good [offices] here, and that he will not do him the best in Court; they have an eye [over] him. The clear text goes straight on: “It may be that Mr Forster may have ill offices done him in England…”. That confirms the sense of the passage and supports the conjecture that 718 is Forster.

t: Robert Reade to his cousin, Paris, 19 April 1641 — Windebank’s return, in the Windebank cipher
b: The passages have 254 groups, 215 of them after the nulls are dropped. Grades follow the README conventions: H read from the key, C a rebuilt value with firm context, M a conjecture. H, 191 groups (88.8%): read from values on the key, including 203 done and 729 “ct.” (Court), which are side notes on the sheet. C, 11 groups (5.1%): values rebuilt from the code’s alphabetical slot and the context. They are 100 advantage, 275 find, 437 one, 524 return (twice), 562 secure, 573 they/the (four times) and 660 willing. 573 fits “they” in three places. In “upon 573 a summons” it reads better as “the”, and there the 14 (a) is probably a slip. M, 13 groups (6.0%): blank on the reconstruction and conjectured. 650 way, 160 conceived, 319 His Majesty, 539 should. 718 Forster (twice), 359 informed 444 offices, 452 over. 487 (inside “bu…ing”), 90 (his answer or account), 455 (my patron?) and 673 (the last Lord Keeper? Finch fled in December 1640 as Windebank did). Only a fuller copy of the key would settle these. No other Windebank key is on DECODE, and no Windebank letter in this cipher was found there.

t: Robert Reade to his cousin, Paris, 19 April 1641 — Windebank’s return, in the Windebank cipher
b: The images were fetched from DECODE and the two passages transcribed. The signature and endorsement gave the writer. The key of “Mr Browne” (R8694, Add MS 72438) was tried first and failed. Its code stops at 371, and its alphabet gives nothing. A search of the DECODE record list for Windebank found R9115 in Add MS 32256. Both of its pages were read at full resolution and entered as a table. The table was applied to the passages, the doubtful glyphs were re-read against the key’s symbol list, and the result was measured. No printed edition or calendar of the letter was found. Harleian letters of this kind are outside the Calendars of State Papers Domestic.

t: Alchymey teuczsch, 1426 — the sign alphabets of an alchemists’ notebook (Cod. Pal. germ. 597)
b: A German recipe book of a circle of gold-makers near Passau, dated 1426 and listed on DECODE as non-decrypted, with substance names hidden in three home-made sign alphabets. The compiler wrote the key on the first leaf as one unbroken run of signs “so that no one should understand that it is an alphabet”, then struck it through. Wilhelm Wattenbach read it in 1869 and printed three facsimiles with their plaintexts. Here the struck alphabet of f. 1r and the invocation alphabet of f. 6v are recovered from the images and checked against his readings, a third set is partly fixed from the Heidelberg catalogue’s reading of f. 93r, and the book is ruled out as a record candidate. East Bavaria, near Passau · home-made sign alphabets · 1426 · found already read Alchymey teuczsch: the ciphers of an alchemists’ notebook, 1426 Heidelberg, Universitätsbibliothek, Cod. Pal. germ. 597 · paper, 95 leaves, Bavarian German · DECODE R2876, “non-decrypted” A circle of gold-makers wrote their recipes in German and hid the substance names in signs of their own. The compiler put the key on the first leaf and struck it through. Wilhelm Wattenbach read it in 1869. The alphabets are recovered here from the images and checked against his plaintexts; nothing here was deciphered that was not already in print. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 18 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read in 1869 Summary. The book came up as a candidate for the oldest cipher this project could read, on the strength of a DECODE record marked “non-decrypted” and a pointer to “ff. 70–71”. Neither holds. The “70–71” are Bernhard Bischoff’s item numbers in his 1954 survey of secret scripts, not folios, and those leaves are blank. The ciphers were broken in 1869 by Wilhelm Wattenbach, who printed three facsimiles with their readings and called them easy. Gerhard Eis printed more in 1957 and 1982, and the 2014 Heidelberg catalogue gives its quotations from the cipher passages resolved. What was done here: every leaf was surveyed for cipher; the compiler’s crossed-out alphabet on f. 1r and the second alphabet on f. 6v and f. 91v were recovered and checked against the printed plaintexts; and a third sign set, the one on f. 1r lines 1–2, ff. 5v–6r, 44v and 93r, was identified and partly fixed. Status: found already read. Open: a continuous transcription of the recipe passages, the f. 6r glossary and f. 44v has never been printed. It needs the doubtful signs of two keys settled first, and its value is for the history of alchemy, not for cryptography.

t: Alchymey teuczsch, 1426 — the sign alphabets of an alchemists’ notebook (Cod. Pal. germ. 597)
b: A small paper book, 22.5 by 15.5 cm, written in several Bavarian hands and dated on f. 9r: Das puch ist angehaben ym [tauro] xiiii und xxvj , begun with the sun in Taurus, 1426. Most of the recipes are headed with the name of Niklas Jankowitz. Other names are Michael von Pirpach, over a list of lucky and unlucky days, and Michel Wulfing, over a fever charm. A note on f. 94r records that on the Saturday of Easter week [14]23 “we” gave “our multiplication” to one Frydryce to work, weighed at four pounds less two lot. An address formula to Leonhard, bishop of Passau from 1424, places the circle. The book is sewn into an unexecuted 1413 charter of the Landgraves of Leuchtenberg, counts of Hals, taking the Jew Salman Teublin into their service and binding him to teach them three of his best arts. The cipher is not a letter but a working notebook’s protection. Recipes are in clear German, and the substance names, quantities and some whole sentences are in signs. A survey of all 85 images, covers included, finds cipher on f. 1r, ff. 5v–7r, 9r–15v, 20r–22r, 44v, 46r–v, 54r–61r, 79ar, 91v and 93r.

t: Alchymey teuczsch, 1426 — the sign alphabets of an alchemists’ notebook (Cod. Pal. germ. 597)
b: Cod. Pal. germ. 597 f. 1r. Lines 1–2 in the third sign set; line 3 the alphabet, run together, then vnd ich in clear and the signs for hab es ; line 4 the rest of the sentence. Image: Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 597 f. 1r, via Heidelberg digitised manuscripts (digi.ub.uni-heidelberg.de, Public Domain Mark). Wattenbach read the leaf in 1869: Das ist ein abc vnd das haben wir selbs neus gemacht, abcdefghiklmnopqrſstuwschch vnd ich hab es darum gar an ein ander gesetzt das man nicht sul versten das es ein alfabet sei — “This is an ABC that we made ourselves, new, and I have set it all together so that no one should understand that it is an alphabet.” The alphabet is written without a break, and the whole leaf is struck through. Wattenbach thought the strike was there because the key was too easy to guess; it is still legible. With the strike line removed from the image, the run gives twenty-four signs in the order of the alphabet the text names: a b c d e f g h i k l m ▪ o 2 ∴ ⊡ 8 Y ˥ : ɓ 4 ꝝ n o p q r ſ s t u w sch ch ϙ 88 ꝗ ꝁ × F ● ◒ • T ⊙ ♣ The signs are rendered with the nearest typographic shape. Two checks in running text: Line 3 continues after the clear vnd ich with ˥ ▪ o ⊡ ●, which is hab es , as Wattenbach printed. The recipe heading on f. 11r reads ϙ : ɓ 4 ▪ ● · Y ▪ ϙ ɓ ? : 2, niklas gank?icz , with one sign unread. A modern reader had already pencilled “= Niklas Gankwiz” beside it. f. 11r, the name in the f. 1r alphabet, with a modern pencil gloss. Image: Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 597 f. 11r, via Heidelberg digitised manuscripts (digi.ub.uni-heidelberg.de, Public Domain Mark). The first eleven values, a to l, are clear on the image, and a, b, c, e, g, h, i, k, l and s are checked in running text. The last thirteen are read from the shape of the signs under the heaviest part of the strike, and only a few of them have been met in running text; they are grade C.

t: Alchymey teuczsch, 1426 — the sign alphabets of an alchemists’ notebook (Cod. Pal. germ. 597)
h: The second alphabet: the invocation on f. 6v
b: f. 6v, the opening prayer in the second alphabet. Image: Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 597 f. 6v, via Heidelberg digitised manuscripts (digi.ub.uni-heidelberg.de, Public Domain Mark). Wattenbach printed f. 6v with its reading: In dem namen des faters vnd des suns vnd des heiligen geistes so fach ich schuldiger man dises buch an , “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost I, a guilty man, begin this book.” Segmenting the three lines and laying them against the text gives nineteen values: : i, a hooked Y n, 3 d, a trefoil on a stem e, Ω with an inner triangle m, a stroke a, a tall stroke medial s, a blob final s, a ring with a tail f, a T with a wavy top r, a ring with a dot h, T l, a looped stem g, two loops on a stem t, a ring with a 3-tail sch, an 8 with an inner loop b, a c joined to a 2 for ch, 9 o, and a cup with a 3 for the u of vnd . Every word of the prayer reads with them. f. 91v, the second alphabet written out in order and struck through. Its opening signs agree with the values from f. 6v. Image: Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 597 f. 91v, via Heidelberg digitised manuscripts (digi.ub.uni-heidelberg.de, Public Domain Mark). The same set is written out in alphabetical order on f. 91v and crossed out, like the first. Wattenbach did not reproduce that leaf, and the catalogue notes it only as an alphabet.

t: Alchymey teuczsch, 1426 — the sign alphabets of an alchemists’ notebook (Cod. Pal. germ. 597)
h: The third set: boxes, stars and T
b: f. 5v, the preface to the glossary of cover-names, clear German with runs of the third set. Image: Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 597 f. 5v, via Heidelberg digitised manuscripts (digi.ub.uni-heidelberg.de, Public Domain Mark). Wattenbach wrote that f. 1r uses “two different systems”. Lines 1–2 of that leaf are in a third set built from boxes with and without dots, stars and T-shapes, which also carries the preface and glossary on ff. 5v–6r and the notes on ff. 44v and 93r. Two printed readings fix part of it: f. 1r line 1, Das ist ein abc : Das [✱ 中 ⊡̈] [⊡ ✱ T] [▪ o 2]. f. 93r, read in the 2014 catalogue as Nota wir haben versucht das [in dem caichen] der [iuncfrawn] , “we have tried it in the sign of the Virgin”: [✱ T] [∴ ⊡ ■] [2 ▪ ✱ 2 ⊏ ⊡ T]. f. 93r, the Virgo note. Image: Universitätsbibliothek Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 597 f. 93r, via Heidelberg digitised manuscripts (digi.ub.uni-heidelberg.de, Public Domain Mark). Together they give ▪ a, o b, 2 c, ∴ d, ⊡ e, ⊏ h, ✱ i, T n, a filled box m, a box on a stem s and a box with two dots t. The a, b, c, d and e are the signs of the f. 1r alphabet. The i and n are not, and T, which is w in the f. 1r alphabet, is n here. The s and t rest on one word each. The glossary on f. 6r uses further dotted-box variants and has not been read.

t: Alchymey teuczsch, 1426 — the sign alphabets of an alchemists’ notebook (Cod. Pal. germ. 597)
b: The glossary on f. 5v was printed by Wattenbach in its resolved form: aqua fortis is called “the sharp water”, sal ammoniac “sal”, its oil “Nyczadar”, common salt “sal aller”, gold “the yellow earth”, silver “the white earth”, green oil “vitriol”. The cover-names were meant to spare the writers from enciphering every substance, and the recipes still mix them with signs. In the recipes (ff. 7r–22r, 46r–v, 54r–61r), the signs are mostly those of the f. 1r alphabet, as the name on f. 11r shows, with admixtures from the others; Bischoff noted that the sets are also used mixed. The runs are short, from one to a few words, and recur: the most frequent group appears about a dozen times on ff. 10v–15r. f. 79ar holds a struck table of sign groups, each over a pair of signs, which looks like a list of substances with their symbols.

t: Alchymey teuczsch, 1426 — the sign alphabets of an alchemists’ notebook (Cod. Pal. germ. 597)
b: The project’s oldest read cipher is from 1497, and a list of earlier candidates was drawn up to try to beat it. This book was on it at 1426 for three reasons: DECODE lists it as non-decrypted, with 85 images; the Handschriftencensus entry cites Bischoff for “S. 12 (Nr. 70–71)”, which was read as cipher on ff. 70–71; and the key was said to be on f. 1r. The first check on any target is for a prior reading. Wattenbach’s 1869 note, with its facsimiles of f. 1r, f. 5v and f. 6v and their plaintexts, settles it. The book is ruled out as a record candidate.

t: Alchymey teuczsch, 1426 — the sign alphabets of an alchemists’ notebook (Cod. Pal. germ. 597)
b: A continuous transcription of the enciphered recipe passages, f. 9r lines 7–12, the f. 6r glossary and f. 44v. Eis printed extracts only. The last thirteen signs of the f. 1r alphabet (m to ch), grade C until they are met in running text. One sign of the name on f. 11r ( o or w ). The third set beyond the eleven letters fixed above, and the table on f. 79ar.

t: Alchymey teuczsch, 1426 — the sign alphabets of an alchemists’ notebook (Cod. Pal. germ. 597)
b: Heidelberg, Universitätsbibliothek, Cod. Pal. germ. 597, digital facsimile (Public Domain Mark). DECODE record R2876 . Wilhelm Wattenbach, “Alchymey teuczsch”, Anzeiger für Kunde der deutschen Vorzeit NF 16 (1869), cols. 264–268, with facsimiles of f. 1r, f. 5v and f. 6v. Internet Archive . t: Mihály Hentér to Ferenc Rákóczi II, Constantinople, 8 July 1707 — the “non-decrypted” letter carries its decipherment between the lines
b: DECODE R496 lists a one-page cipher letter of “1 January 1707” as non-decrypted with no inline plaintext. The folio carries a contemporary Hungarian decipherment written between the cipher lines, and it is dated Constantinople, 8 July 1707. Two sibling Hentér letters (R533, R534) confirm the monoalphabetic key ( wi6xi2i4 = Felséged ). The pasha of Belgrade offers troops, powder and grain if Rákóczi sends six or seven thousand men against the Serbs, while Hentér chases an audience with the grand vizier. Constantinople → Ferenc Rákóczi II · monoalphabetic substitution, letters, digits and signs · 8 July 1707 · decipherment found Hentér to Rákóczi: the plaintext was already between the lines to Francis II Rákóczi MNL OL G 15, Caps. D, Fasc. 80, fol. 38 (DECODE R496), listed as a non-decrypted letter of “1 January 1707”. The folio carries a contemporary Hungarian decipherment written over the cipher. Two sibling letters from the same fascicle confirm the key, and the true date is 8 July 1707. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 21 September 2026 resolved Summary. DECODE lists R496 as a non-decrypted one-page letter from Mihály Hentér, Rákóczi’s agent at the Porte, dated 1 January 1707, with inline_plaintext = False . That record is wrong on two points. A decipherer wrote the Hungarian plaintext between the cipher lines on the folio itself, and the letter is dated Constantinople, 8 July 1707 ; DECODE’s 1 January–31 December range is only a placeholder for the year. The interlinear text gives the substance of the letter. The pasha of Belgrade welcomed Rákóczi’s gift and offered troops, powder and grain if Rákóczi sent six or seven thousand men against the Serbs. Hentér pressed for Rákóczi’s deputation to be heard by the grand vizier, and the audience was delayed amid confusion in the capital. The letter closes with a plea for a captive’s release. Two more Hentér letters in the fascicle (R533, R534) use the same monoalphabetic system with dense interlinear plaintext, and their closing formulae fix the key letters that the R496 reading needs. Some middle clauses, where the decipherer’s cursive runs over the cipher, still need a Hungarian palaeographer.

b: Below is a normalised reading of the interlinear Hungarian. Square brackets mark words that are still uncertain because the decipherer’s hand overlaps the cipher signs. Spelling and punctuation are lightly normalised. Az nándorfejérvári pasa Felséged ajándékát kedvesen vevé, és dicsértette; kiben mondá: ha Felséged hat vagy hét ezer hadat a rácok ellen küldene, assecurálja Felségedet, hogy Felséged hadait haddal, porral, gabonával is segítené. [A short sentence about the kuruc envoys, hard to read.] Ide érkezvén Felséged, Uram, levelét vettem. Elmentem és kértem, hogy a fővezér előtt a deputát [kihallgatást nyerjen / bővebben meghallgattassék], melyre ígérte magát. [Közvetítője] azt izené, hogy lett volna audientiája, de a magyar […]. […] Ezen leginkább [a] városban még a dolgok confusióban [vannak]. Idő folytában ismét sollicitáltuk az audientiát. […] izené, hogy ha bément […], voce […], bátor ad praesentandas literas […]. Felségednek a szegény rab uram felszabadulása iránt […]. Kérem Istent, Felségednek minden áldását […]. Felséged alázatos hű szolgája, Hentér Mihály. In English. The pasha of Belgrade received Your Majesty’s gift kindly and praised it. He said that if Your Majesty sent six or seven thousand troops against the Serbs, he assures Your Majesty that he would help Your Majesty’s forces with troops, powder and grain too. […] On arriving here I received Your Majesty’s letter, my lord. I went and asked that the deputation be [heard] before the grand vizier, which he promised. [His intermediary] sent word that there would have been an audience, but the Hungarian […]. Affairs in the city are still in confusion. In the meantime we solicited the audience again […], to present the letters […]. Concerning the release of the poor captive, my lord […]. I pray God for every blessing on Your Majesty. Your Majesty’s humble, faithful servant, Mihály Hentér.

t: Mihály Hentér to Ferenc Rákóczi II, Constantinople, 8 July 1707 — the “non-decrypted” letter carries its decipherment between the lines
b: Two other letters from Hentér in the same fascicle use the same system and carry dense interlinear plaintext: R533 (fol. 40) and R534 (fol. 46). R533’s closing formula gives a clean control. The cipher group wi6xi2i4 reads Felséged , which fixes w = f, i = e, 6 = l, x = s, 2 = g and 4 = d. Other repeated formulae give n = a, 0 = o, c = h, 9 = m and 5 = k; the other graphic signs cannot be typed in plain text. These values agree with the interlinear reading on R496, so the glosses are a decipherment of this cipher and not a paraphrase. Benedek Láng independently lists fols. 38, 40 and 46 as Hentér’s three 1707 letters (C.Hen.01–03) and describes their cipher as monoalphabetic.
