t: Herbault to Béthune, 13 February 1626 — the decipherment three folios away
b: The one letter marked “avec chiffre” and not “avec chiffre et déchiffrement” among some thirty of 1625–26 to the ambassador in Rome. It is not an undeciphered text: no. 26 is not a second letter but the same despatch, carrying the same cipher with the plaintext written between the lines in 1626. Identity fixed on the word-for-word clear text, the cipher runs falling at the same points and matching groups. The ciphered passages are the papal Legate and “le Pape pour l’acheminement de ces troupes in la Valteline”, the admission that France made peace with the Huguenots because “le faix d’une double guerre ne se pouvoit plus supporter”, the Dutch squadron sailing home with the Huguenot admiral, and Savoy’s attempt to engage France against Spain six weeks before Monzón. Contributed by Arya Sanketbhai Patel. Paris → Rome · nomenclator of figures and letter-forms · 13 February 1626 · resolved and read Herbault to Béthune, 13 February 1626 — the decipherment three folios away to Philippe de Béthune BnF Français 3669 no. 25 · the one letter of some thirty catalogued “avec chiffre” without “et déchiffrement” · no. 26 is the same despatch with the plaintext written between the lines in 1626 Read from the contemporary decipherment: the Valtelline, the reason for the Huguenot peace, the Dutch ships sailing home with the Huguenot admiral, and Piedmont’s push for war with Spain Arya Sanketbhai Patel · resolved 18 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 resolved Summary. Among some thirty letters of 1625–26 from Louis XIII and his secretary Raymond Phelipeaux d’Herbault to Philippe de Béthune, ambassador in Rome, bound in BnF Français 3669, the catalogue marks exactly one “avec chiffre” and not “avec chiffre et déchiffrement”: no. 25, of 13 February 1626. It looked like a one-letter gap in an otherwise readable series, and the obvious first question was whether the next piece in the volume might be its decipherment. It is. No. 26 is not a second letter but the same despatch , carrying the same cipher with the plaintext written between the lines by a contemporary decipherer. No. 25 was never an undeciphered text; its reading has been lying three folios away since 1626. What the cipher hides is worth the trip: the papal Legate’s mission and “le Pape pour l’acheminement de ces troupes in la Valt(eline)”, the reason the crown had just made peace with the Huguenots, the Dutch ships slipping away with the Huguenot admiral, and the prince of Piedmont in Paris trying to drag France into war with Spain six weeks before the Treaty of Monzón defeated him. Status: resolved and read. No cryptanalysis was required, and none would have been the right first move.

t: Herbault to Béthune, 13 February 1626 — the decipherment three folios away
h: A gap that was not a gap
b: Français 3669 is a recueil of originals: the King and Herbault writing to Béthune in Rome through the autumn and winter of 1625–26, most pieces catalogued “avec chiffre et déchiffrement” because the embassy’s clerk wrote the plaintext of each ciphered passage onto the sheet as he read it. One piece breaks the pattern. The volume is digitised from a black-and-white microfilm of double-page openings; canvas equals folio plus five, fixed on the foliation of ff. 70 and 73. Piece Letter Leaves Cipher 24 Herbault → Béthune, 6 February 1626 ff. 67–68 none noted 25 Herbault → Béthune, 13 February 1626 ff. 69–71 cipher, no decipherment 26 the same letter, 13 February 1626 ff. 72–74 cipher with interlinear decipherment 27 Louis XIII → Béthune f. 75– cipher and decipherment Both copies are made up for sending, each with its own address leaf, wax seal and docket. Both open on the same words under the same marginal note, “Le roy fera responce” . And their clear text runs word for word: the same paragraphs on Rambouillet’s delayed departure for Spain, the promotion of cardinals and Marquemont’s hat, the courier sent on the 6th through the Venetian ambassador Contarini, the peace with the Huguenots, the prince of Piedmont’s arrival — down to the King’s sore toe, “quelque douleur à cause d’ung ongle qui luy entre dans la chair”, which kept him in bed and delayed Herbault’s report.

t: Herbault to Béthune, 13 February 1626 — the decipherment three folios away
b: BnF Français 3669, f. 73r (no. 26) — cipher with the 1626 decipherment written under each line: “vray que les affaires de cet estat avoyent besoing de ce” / cipher / “relasche et que le faix d’une double guerre ne se pouvoit” / cipher / “plus supporter. J’advoue que les affections”…. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3669 f. 73r, via Gallica btv1b9060205q canvas 78. Three things establish that no. 26 reads no. 25 rather than merely resembling it. The clear text is identical , paragraph by paragraph, including incidental matter no second letter would repeat verbatim: the memoir of Cardinal Bevilacqua for Horatio Giraldi, the naturalisation letters obtained through Cardinal de la Valette, the sore toe. The cipher runs fall at the same points , after the same clear words — “en laquelle il aura laissé”, “dont nous esperons estre bientost esclaircis”, “au nom de ce prétendu comte de”, “besoing de ce”, “Vous scaurez maintenant que”, “Toutes ces propositions”, “il nous faut continuer ceste mesme routte jusques”. The groups match where checked. No. 25’s first run opens to 92 … 17 … 43 and no. 26’s opens to 92 g 17 … 43 … ; the third run ends … 68 93 … in both, with the same short group after it. The two clerks’ hands differ enough that individual figures read differently at this resolution, so no group-for-group identity is claimed here — only that the runs correspond. The cipher itself is a nomenclator of one- to three-character groups mixing Arabic figures with letter-forms. The opening run, to 92 g 17 ẓ 43 x cu 4 7 ẓ p x 3 3 6 x , stands for “le Pape pour l’acheminement de ces troupes in la Valt(eline)” — about eighteen groups for some forty-eight letters, so most groups carry a syllable or a whole word. The table is not reconstructed here because the reading does not need it, and roughly thirty further glossed letters of 1625–26 in the same cipher sit in the same volume for anyone who wants it.

t: Herbault to Béthune, 13 February 1626 — the decipherment three folios away
b: A secretary of state writing to his ambassador in Rome on the eve of the Treaty of Monzón, and enciphering exactly the three things that mattered. The Valtelline. Herbault waits on news of the papal Legate’s departure for Spain and of the last resolution in which he will have left “le Pape pour l’acheminement de ces troupes in la Valt(eline)” — an affair which deserves “l’envoy d’un courrier exprez” — and above all “principallement sy le Pape entroit dans la partialité” , the fear that Urban VIII would cease to mediate and take a side. Why the crown had just made peace with its Protestants. The peace “s’affermit de jour en jour” and is welcome even to those “qui ont tousjours le plus hautement conseillé le chastiment et la guerre contre les huguenots” — because, in cipher, “les affaires de cet estat avoyent besoing de ce relasche, et que le faix d’une double guerre ne se pouvoit plus supporter” , while “les affections de noz voysins qui font profession de ceste religion pretendue refformée estoyent grandement alterés” . That is the candid version: France made peace at home because it could not afford two wars, and because the Protestant powers abroad were turning. The ships. Béthune has already been told of “la conduitte des Anglois envers nous, et comme une partye des vaisseaux hollandois s’estoyent retirez” . Now he is to know that the Huguenot admiral — read as Soubise — “a suivy depuis sept ou huict jours avec le reste de sa flotte; la route des premiers par l’ordre des estatz et sans permission de Sa Ma(jes)té ny de Mons(ieu)r l’Admiral, et dans la conioncture de la conclusion de la paix” . The Dutch squadron lent to the King against La Rochelle had sailed home on its own States’ orders, at the precise moment France needed it least to be noticed. And Savoy’s push for war. The prince of Piedmont reached Paris on Monday the 9th, surprising Longueville and the maréchal de Créquy who were to have met him, and saluted the King out hunting in the warren at Saint-Germain. Once the King is back he will begin to treat, and all his propositions “tendent à engager le Roy à la guerre avec l’Espagne, (et que) la Seig(neu)rie de Venize contribue comme faict l’Angleterre et Holande” . Herbault’s answer is the whole French position in one clause: Sa Majesté “escoutera tout ce qu’il luy sera representé, et scaura bien prendre la resolution convenable au bien de ses affaires” . Six weeks later she did, settling with Spain separately at Monzón and leaving Venice and Savoy out of it. A closing practical passage, also part-ciphered, weighs keeping the ordinary courier route against going by the Grisons, rejected for “d’autres longueurs et incommoditez, outre la despense”.

t: Herbault to Béthune, 13 February 1626 — the decipherment three folios away
b: The key is not tabulated. It would need the groups aligned to the glossed words, which the decipherer’s placement only loosely indicates, and the volume’s thirty other glossed letters would do it better. Two proper names are read only from the gloss and are uncertain in the palaeography: the “S(ieu)r de Santriny” who made a proposition to Béthune, and the “prétendu comte de Montembelans” in whose name it was made. “L’admiral Soubise” is an identification from context — a Huguenot admiral with a fleet in February 1626 — rather than a confident reading of the gloss. Whether this letter or the series is in print was not checked. Unvalidated. Checked: the folio-to-canvas mapping on two foliated leaves, the piece list against the leaves, the word-for-word identity of the two copies’ clear text, the correspondence of the cipher runs and the matching of groups at two places, and the reading of every glossed passage quoted. Not checked: a group-by-group identity of the two ciphertexts, the key table, any printed edition. This is a reading of a contemporary decipherment, not an independent decryption.

t: The Hereditary Prince from Berlin, 12 March 1796 — the “non-decrypted” R2239 reads with a word list rebuilt from its sibling
b: DECODE R2239, three pages of numbers in the papers of William V, catalogued as an unsolved book cipher. Each group takes a whole entry of a numbered word list, chosen letters of it, or the entry cut at the front or back; the sibling R2237 carries its own contemporary decipherment, and aligning the two rebuilt the list. It read 70% of the letter; the body then proved to be printed by Colenbrander in 1906, and with that crib the unprinted opening was read: the conference between Haugwitz and Lord Elgin on a Prussian démarche in Paris for the Orange restoration. Berlin → Prince Frederik (DECODE: William V) · word-list code, letters cut from numbered words · 12 March 1796 · read The Hereditary Prince from Berlin, 12 March 1796: the “non-decrypted” R2239 reads with a word list rebuilt from its sibling from Hereditary Prince William → to William V Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V, inv. 337 (DECODE R2236, R2237, R2239). R2237 carries its own contemporary decipherment; aligning the two rebuilt about 110 entries of the numbered word list, and those read 70% of R2239 without help. The body of R2239 turned out to be printed in Colenbrander’s Gedenkstukken (1906), minus its first paragraph; used as a crib, the print completed the list, and the opening is read here for the first time. Daniel Bourdeau · solved 21 September 2026 solved Summary. Catalogue item 218 groups two DECODE records of the Hereditary Prince Willem Frederik in Berlin, R2236 and R2239, both “non-decrypted”; DECODE calls the system a book cipher. The third record in the file, R2237, is marked decrypted: its last three pages are two ciphered “observations” and its middle pages their decipherment in a clerk’s hand. Set side by side they show the system. Each number names an entry in a list of about 250 words and phrases, and a group takes the whole entry, chosen letters of it, or the entry cut by some letters at the front or the back. About 110 entries came out of R2237 with no conflicts; applied to R2239, with a handful of names inferred from context (Elgin, Haugwitz, Milord, Paris, Londres), they read 70% of the 769 groups. A search for “Elgin” in Colenbrander’s Gedenkstukken then found the letter’s body printed as no. 752, addressed to Prince Frederik. Aligned as a crib, the print fixed the remaining entries, and they read the opening paragraph that Colenbrander left out. One word of it (entry 244, used once) stays open. R2236, in Dutch and with numbers up to 2835, uses another list and is not read. R2239, first page of the letter (DECODE image P2). “comme devant” in clear at the end of line 1; the groups before it spell “annoncée” out of entry 115, abondance . Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, A31 Prins Willem V inv. 337, via DECODE R2239 (image P2).

t: The Hereditary Prince from Berlin, 12 March 1796 — the “non-decrypted” R2239 reads with a word list rebuilt from its sibling
b: A group refers to one entry of a numbered list: N underlined : the whole entry (58 = cour , 53 = Vienne , 162 = Elgin ). N,p,q,… : letters p, q, … of the entry, in that order (12 = certain : 12,1,3,2,4 = cret ). k/N (small number at the top left): the entry without its first k letters (127 = attachement : 4/127 = chement ). N (k (small number at the top right): the entry without its last k letters (24 = quelque : 24 (3 = quel ). Marks combine (84 = excellence : 2/84 (3 = celle ). Large parts of the list run alphabetically (10 Angleterre , 11 Berlin , 12 certain , 13 difficile , 14 engager , 15 France … 22 Orange , 23 Prusse , 24 quelque ); above 100 it holds common words and phrases (102 le cabinet , 107 le roi , 132 je compte , 133 on dit ). The same word can be spelled from many entries, so one plaintext has many encipherments.

t: The Hereditary Prince from Berlin, 12 March 1796 — the “non-decrypted” R2239 reads with a word list rebuilt from its sibling
b: The first paragraph is not in Colenbrander’s edition and is read here from the cipher alone: La conférence que j’ai annoncée comme devant avoir lieu le huit entre Haugwitz et Elgin s’est effectivement tenue, et Lord Elgin m’a déjà communiqué le résultat, dont je [vais?] rendre compte, tandis que le comte Haugwitz me dit avant-hier au bal du Roi qu’il viendroit un de ces jours chez moi pour me parler sur cet objet. The conference I announced as due to take place on the 8th between Haugwitz and Elgin was indeed held, and Lord Elgin has already told me its outcome, of which I [shall] give account, while Count Haugwitz told me the day before yesterday at the King’s ball that he would come to me one of these days to speak to me about it. The rest of the letter reads as printed, with small differences (the cipher has “sur cela” where the print has “à cette demande”, and “avoit” for “jouissait de”): Et il a fait à Elgin la communication de l’idée dont nous étions convenus ensemble, de faire une démarche en France pour déterminer cette puissance à consentir à rétablir les affaires dans la République sur l’ancien pied, ajoutant que vu le degré d’influence qu’il pensoit avoir à Paris il espéroit qu’une semblable proposition ne seroit point infructueuse … Lord Elgin lui dit n’être pas à même de pouvoir lui répondre … et qu’avant de prendre des nouvelles instructions à cet égard il désiroit savoir si au cas qu’une ouverture faite par le Roi à Paris fût infructueuse, le Roi la soutiendroit par les armes … Je convins avec Milord Elgin que quand Haugwitz me parlera sur cette matière et me rendra compte de sa conversation avec lui, je tâcherai de l’engager à faire une démarche en France sans avoir l’assurance qu’il désire avoir concernant nos colonies, puisqu’elle ne sauroit jamais nuire, et que si elle étoit de quelque fruit l’utilité seroit considérable, en quoi je me flatte de rencontrer les intentions de mon père, étant encore à remarquer que si le premier pas se fait, il est peut-être possible d’amener le second. The full text is in r2239_reading.txt in the repository. Prussia would sound out France on restoring the Stadholderate; Britain wanted Prussian arms behind it and would not promise the Dutch colonies in advance; the Prince meant to push Haugwitz to try anyway.

t: The Hereditary Prince from Berlin, 12 March 1796 — the “non-decrypted” R2239 reads with a word list rebuilt from its sibling
b: R2237’s cipher groups were aligned by hand with the clerk’s decipherment, group by group, and each group turned into constraints on its entry (a letter at a position, or a length). A small script ( wordtable.py ) holds the constraints, reports conflicts and decodes any group file. The rules were worked out from the first lines (90 = même gives 2/90 = me and 1/90 = eme ). An attempt to let a search split the plaintext among the groups failed, because a whole-word group can absorb any string; the alignment was done by hand. R2239 was transcribed from the DECODE photographs into the same notation. The R2237 entries decoded 59% of its groups, and context inference 70%. Colenbrander’s volume II was then searched on the Huygens Institute site. Its no. 752 matches R2239 from the second sentence on, and aligning it fixed the entries that only R2239 uses (208 défavorables , 209 désireroient , 219 instructions , 115 abondance , 202 avantageux , 79 cabale …). Those entries read the unprinted opening.

t: The Hereditary Prince from Berlin, 12 March 1796 — the “non-decrypted” R2239 reads with a word list rebuilt from its sibling
b: “dont je [vais] rendre compte”: entry 244 occurs only here, as 244 (5 ; the word is a guess (I). The rest of the opening is graded H: every group decodes, and the entries used there are confirmed by other occurrences. The body is H where cipher and print agree. A few groups in the transcription decode wrongly because a mark was misread (e.g. the entry 87 groups where the print has “les”); the print settles those words. Addressee: DECODE gives William V (the letter is in his papers); Colenbrander prints the text as to Prince Frederik. The phrase “les intentions de mon père” fits a letter to the brother. R2236 is not read, and neither is the line at the foot of R2237 p. 7 after “la proposition”.

t: The Conde de Hernán Núñez to Fuenmayor, 1674 — four Stockholm despatches read with the Balbases key
b: Four December 1674 despatches from Spain’s envoy in Sweden to its envoy in Denmark, clear Spanish with cipher passages deciphered in the margin at the time. Aligning the margins showed the cipher to be the one rebuilt here for Balbases 1677; that key reads all four unchanged, verifying the margins and recovering what DECODE could not read. Sweden on the eve of the Scanian War: the senate about to decide on arming for France. Stockholm → Copenhagen · syllabic nomenclator · December 1674 · read The Conde de Hernán Núñez to Baltasar de Fuenmayor, 1674 Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, Secrétairerie d’État et de Guerre, inv. nr. 2559 · DECODE R1012–R1015, four letters, 16 pages · clear Spanish with cipher passages, each deciphered in the margin at the time The key rebuilt for the Balbases letters of 1677 fits unchanged: the margins are verified and their illegible words recovered Daniel Bourdeau · read 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. The catalogue listed four letters from the Spanish envoy in Stockholm to his colleague in Copenhagen as "noted": the cipher was said to be deciphered in the margin, but nobody had checked how far. Each letter is mostly clear Spanish, with one to three cipher passages, 1,716 groups in all. A marginal decipherment accompanies every passage, but DECODE’s transcriber could not read parts of that hand. The margins were lined up against the cipher with seven anchors from one repeated phrase ( representado y representaré ). The values that emerged were those of the key rebuilt in this project two days earlier for the Marqués de los Balbases’ letters of 1677 to the same recipient, which are in the same volume. Applied unchanged to DECODE’s transcription, that key reproduces the margins of all four letters. Four values were added (167 Suecia, 161 resolución, os para, and 6+ o). The first pass left 7% of groups unread; a second pass checked each of them on the images, and one group stays unread (99.9% of 1,716 groups have a value, 99.3% without eleven uncertain ones). The content is Swedish diplomacy in the month Sweden entered the war on France’s side. R1012 p. 2, 5 December 1674: in the margin, ya tengo assegurado a VS que he representado y representaré siempre lo que importa que la Suecia tenga el freno desse reyno , and beside it the cipher it deciphers. Image: Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, SEG 2559, R1012 p. 2, via DECODE R1012.

t: The Conde de Hernán Núñez to Fuenmayor, 1674 — four Stockholm despatches read with the Balbases key
b: There are four despatches, of 5, 15, 19 and 26 December 1674 (DECODE R1012–R1015; the "1674–1677" in DECODE’s summary is a span, and the catalogue names give the dates). All are in the Brussels volume SEG 2559, Fuenmayor’s papers, which also holds the Carpio and Balbases letters of 1677. The cipher is the Balbases syllabic nomenclator: numbers for letters and consonant-vowel syllables (21 a, 28 s, 31 r, 46 de, 58 lo, 66 re, 70 ta), letter pairs with a disguised consonant ( xo co, xi ci, af sa, if si, uf su, ac ma), and word codes: struck d que, bef Francia, dan -mente. 13 is a null. The key is set out in full on the Balbases page . That it served Hernán Núñez in Stockholm in 1674 and Balbases at Nijmegen in 1677 suggests that Fuenmayor held one cipher for his correspondents among the northern Spanish envoys.

t: The Conde de Hernán Núñez to Fuenmayor, 1674 — four Stockholm despatches read with the Balbases key
b: These are the cipher passages, read from the margins and checked group by group against the key. Spelling is normalised. 5 December 1674 (R1012) …asegurándole en primer lugar que el reparo que hace del proyecto del tratado deste [reino] con esse reino es muy propio de su gran juicio y prudencia, y que creo ser cierto que estos ministros han convenido con el de Dinamarca en todos los puntos del proyecto que envié a V.S.; pero si la Dinamarca añadiese el de no oponerse a las armas que la Suecia pretenderá ahora, todos los artículos anteriores que contradijesen a esto quedarán anulados… y que las más veces no vienen a ser sino un juego de palabras con que pretextar lo que hacen y lo que no quieren hacer los príncipes. Ya tengo asegurado a V.S. que he representado y representaré siempre lo que importa que la Suecia tenga el freno desse reino. A later passage concerns the Swedish envoy at Copenhagen. Núñez has told him of his obligations to his father-in-law, the Constable. Fuenmayor should believe him only where other sources confirm it, "siendo hombre lleno de artificios, sin más fundamento a veces que su propia inquietud". 15 December (R1013) Con grandes promesas de la protección de la Suecia, que les ha costado buenos regalos, y deseando el enviado de Brandenburg enviar un gentilhombre suyo en su navío, estos diputados le respondieron no se atrevían por no dar celos a la Suecia… Hamburg, that is. The despatch goes on to hope that, frightened, the Hamburgers "quiten a los suecos mucha parte de la confianza", which would restrain Sweden and "alentará igualmente a los dinamarqueses". 19 December (R1014) …la mira principal que este reino lleva en haber enviado a esse su embajador, según tengo entendido, es el tomar tiempo con esto para satisfacer a las instancias que hace este embajador de Francia, y el de no asistirle por ahora con el socorro que pretende en virtud de su tratado último. The marriage of Charles XI to the Danish king’s sister will be raised. The Anglo-Swedish treaty is only a renewal of the one Coventry concluded. …no hay otro medio de retener a la Suecia, y si esa corona se ajustase a la neutralidad, le faltaría a esta el único pretexto con que se [excusa con] la Francia. 26 December (R1015) …antes de separarse este senado, que será dentro de muy pocos días, se tomará resolución en él sobre el asistir o no a la Francia a mano armada. Ha dos días que he cesado en el remedio de los baños… para salir cuanto antes a hacer las diligencias que me sean posibles para que dicha resolución nos sea favorable, prefiriendo la solicitud del real servicio al riesgo de la vida. The decision went against him: Swedish troops entered Brandenburg at the turn of the year, and Fehrbellin followed in June 1675.

t: The Conde de Hernán Núñez to Fuenmayor, 1674 — four Stockholm despatches read with the Balbases key
b: DECODE’s ciphertext transcriptions (by MEG, 2020) were parsed into cipher groups and margin text. DECODE reads the clerk’s "q." as "g.3", so it was normalised to que . The monotone aligner written for Balbases 1677, run image by image, failed: the margin glosses cross page breaks. Run letter by letter, with seven anchors from representado y representaré (66 re, 30 p, ef se, 24 n, 70 ta, 48 do, 22 y), it converged in four rounds. The converged values (58 lo, 28 s, y n, uf su, 21 a, 31 r, struck d que) were recognised as the Balbases key. That key was applied unchanged and read all four letters against their margins. Second pass (22 Sept 2026): the 118 groups the key left unread were each found on the sixteen DECODE images and read against the margin beside them. 62 were DECODE misreadings (this hand’s closed 4 read as 9, so “96” is 46 de and “189” is 184 sobre ; g for y ; groups split or run together), 48 were code groups the Balbases table lacks, fixed by the margin ( bof guerra, cuf Inglaterra, 187 tiempo, 149 quanto, 111 comercio, C+ ll ), 7 were nulls and 1 is illegible. Two key corrections apply throughout: 13 is e in this hand, not a null, and the underlined N is V.S. DECODE also omits two whole lines of R1012 (“…mas veces no vienen a ser sino un juego de pa-”).

t: Henri IV to Landgrave Maurice — the figures Rommel printed in 1840 and the key he printed in 1846
b: Rommel set the King’s ciphered passages to the Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel as rows of figures he could not read, then printed the key six years later with one sample and stopped. Put together, they read all seven passages, about 4,100 groups: Bouillon and the German princes, the Gunpowder Plot and Mérargues “forgés sur mesme enclume”, two million livres for the Dutch, and on 20 May 1606 the call to the princes to take counsel together against a Spanish King of the Romans, “pour la conservation de la liberté germanique”. Contributed by Arya Sanketbhai Patel. Paris → Kassel · two-digit code with word and name lists · 1602–09 · read Henri IV to Landgrave Maurice of Hesse-Kassel, seven ciphered passages from Henri IV → to Maurice of Hesse-Kassel Correspondance inédite de Henri IV avec Maurice-le-Savant (Rommel, 1840) · about 4,100 groups · decoded with the key Rommel printed in 1846; no application of it to these letters was published Arya Sanketbhai Patel · read 17 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. In 1840 Christoph von Rommel published the correspondence of Henri IV with Maurice the Learned, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel, from the originals at Marburg, and printed the King’s ciphered passages as rows of two-digit figures he could not read, “dans l’espoir qu’il est possible de retrouver la clef”. Six years later he had the key, from Groen van Prinsterer and van der Kemp, printed it in a German journal with one sample letter, and stopped. Nobody put the key and the other letters together: Tomokiyo’s page lists them as undeciphered, and so does the Lettres missives . Applied to the 1840 page images, the 1846 key reads all seven of the King’s passages, about 4,100 groups, in seven letters from 22 November 1602 to 24 January 1609. Two of them are the German policy the catalogue hoped for. On 22 December 1605 the King ties the Mérargues treason and the attempt on his life to the Gunpowder Plot, “forgés sur mesme enclume”, promises the Dutch two million livres again for 1606 and asks the Landgrave and the German princes for money and troops before spring. On 20 May 1606 he writes that the Spaniards mean to have a King of the Romans elected wholly at their devotion and to turn the Diet against the United Provinces, that all kings and princes jealous of Spain must “prendre conseil ensemble” in time, and that he will do his part “pour la conservation de la liberté germanique” when the others do theirs. Status: read. A prince’s name on p. 213, seven groups on p. 307, one unlisted name-group and a line of signs the 1840 typesetter could not set remain; the Marburg originals were not seen.

t: Henri IV to Landgrave Maurice — the figures Rommel printed in 1840 and the key he printed in 1846
b: Maurice of Hesse-Kassel (1572–1632) was the most learned and the most francophile of the Calvinist princes of the Empire, and Henri IV’s regular correspondent on German affairs from the Bongars mission of 1599 to the Jülich crisis of 1610. Rommel, the Hessian archivist and historian, printed 118 pieces of the exchange from the Marburg archive in 1840 (Paris, Renouard). The Landgrave’s letters are in clear; several of the King’s carry passages in figures, which Rommel set as he found them, and some of the King’s letters he printed from a contemporary decipherment with the figures omitted. The list below is what the volume prints in figures from the King’s side; nothing else on it was ciphered by him. Correspondance inédite de Henri IV avec Maurice-le-Savant (1840), p. 310 — the middle of the King’s letter of 20 May 1606: the Spanish design on the election of a King of the Romans and the call to “prendre conseil ensemble”. Image: Rommel (ed.), Correspondance inédite de Henri IV avec Maurice-le-Savant (1840), p. 310, via the Internet Archive (correspondancein00henr, leaf 352). Henri IV to the Landgrave Rommel pp. In figures Read before 22 November 1602 84 13 lines no 12 January 1603 99 12 lines no; Lettres missives vi p. 12 prints the figures 3 April 1604 170–175 5 pages yes, Rommel 1846 (used here as control) 27 December 1604 211–214 3 pages no 28 April 1605 230 11 lines no; Rommel’s footnote regrets it 22 December 1605 269–272 3 pages no 20 May 1606 307–314 6 pages no 24 January 1609 391 1 line no The catalogue entry that set this target (“12 Jan 1603, 28 Dec 1603, 27 Dec 1604, pp. 12, 148–189, 388–393”) came from Tomokiyo’s page and was wrong about the pages: p. 12 is the Lettres missives reference, the 28 December 1603 letter is printed from a decipherment with no figures at all, and pp. 388–393 hold a single line. The passages of 1602, 1605 and 1606 were on no list.

t: Henri IV to Landgrave Maurice — the figures Rommel printed in 1840 and the key he printed in 1846
h: The key, and what the texts corrected in it
b: Rommel, “La clef des chiffres dans la Correspondance inédite de Henri IV avec Maurice le Savant”, Allgemeine Zeitschrift für Geschichte V (1846), p. 403: the word lists (comma, two dots, overbar) and the symbols. The letter table is on p. 402. Image: Rommel, Allgemeine Zeitschrift für Geschichte V (1846), p. 403, via the Internet Archive (bub_gb_Zpc1AAAAMAAJ). The cipher is the one Tomokiyo found as an original sheet in BnF Clairambault 360 f. 168, dated October 1602, and it served the whole correspondence to 1610. Bare two-digit figures are letters, up to four homophones each; a comma after the figure sends it to a list of small words and syllables ( le, la, leur, que, qui, qu’il, pour, pro, pre, ma, me, mon, ne, ny, nous, on, où, sa, se, roy ), two dots above it to a second ( con, ca, car, don, da, di, do, de, en, eulx, faire, faict, point, elle, forces, troupes, guerre, cour impériale, diète de l’Empire ), an overbar to names and titles ( Bouillon, Comte, Conseil, Pape, Empereur, Roi d’Espagne, Roi d’Angleterre, l’Archiduc, Brandebourg, Brunswick, provinces unies, Protestant, Allemagne, Angleterre, argent, armée, alliés, ambassadeur, au, aux, afin ). A dozen drawn symbols stand for te, tion, tant, tous, tout, tre, grand, va, ville, votre, Hongrie ; one sign doubles the symbol before it, one cancels it, and a few flourishes are nulls. Rommel’s print of the key is right in every letter value, but its lists are set with fewer words than figures and its fourth row of homophones is misaligned, so the texts had to fix the rest: 70 is a fourth p missing from the table ( presse, perdra, principalement ); 85 is m and 83 is o ( maison, ensemble, favorisé ); 17, is la and 18, 19, le ; 24, lettre , 25, leur ; 65, pro ( profiter, prospèrent ), 66, pre ; 83, rompre ( cor-rompre ); 70 with dots is faict , 84 with dots forces ; 26 with overbar is Comte (Rommel’s own glossary: le comte de Solms ), which shifts the names one place so that 31 is Pape , 33 Empereur , 35 Roi d’Espagne and 37 Roi d’Angleterre , as the 24 January 1609 line “les ministres du Pape et du Roi d’Espagne” and the 1604 control both require. The group Rommel set under l’administrateur de Strasbourg as 59 is le Turc (“la paix avec [59]”, December 1605); the tall 4 is te or tion and the print does not separate them; the typesetter’s “9 +” is the doubling sign 94; and the ♀-, Ψ- and tt-like flourishes are nulls (“ayant ♀ tt sceu que le duc de Féria…”). Every one of these is recorded in key.py with the passage that fixed it. Controls. Rommel printed Groen van Prinsterer’s decipherment of the 3 April 1604 letter beside the key; the first lines of p. 171 decode here word for word to his text (“…ainsy demander la paix à leurs ennemis en leur pays, que la nécessité qui les presse est très grande…”). His footnotes to the Landgrave’s letter of 10 February 1603 gloss five groups ( diète de l’Empire, l’Archiduc, Protestants, Empereur, cour impériale ) and the key returns each; his 1840 glossary “Passages déchiffrés” agrees throughout. The strongest check is internal: every passage comes out as continuous early-seventeenth-century French that joins the clear text it interrupts.

t: Henri IV to Landgrave Maurice — the figures Rommel printed in 1840 and the key he printed in 1846
b: 22 November 1602. He holds his despatch for the advice Maurice promised on the Diet: whether it will meet, what will be treated, what proposal he should make “pour le public et le particulier de mes alliés”, and whether to send his ambassador on to Saxony and Denmark, “avec votre bon conseil sur le [mémoire] et instruction que je luy doibs donner”. 12 January 1603. Since the Emperor will not appear at the Diet nothing of weight will be treated, “et principallement de l’élection d’un roy des Romains”. Bouillon has not written a word about the Administrator of Strasbourg’s coming to France nor about the bishopric: “je ne sçay comme il aura pris ce voyage, ny de quelque sorte il embrasse la cause du dit Administrateur”. 27 December 1604. Why he has not sent the embassy to the German princes that Maurice advised: “la mauvaise intelligence que j’ay recogneue entre les [princes] protestants”, and “le mescontentement et dégoust qu’aucuns d’eulx m’ont donné … depuis qu’ils ont adjousté foy aux discours du duc de Bouillon et favorisé sa cause avec moins de respect et considération à ma personne que je n’espérois d’eulx”. The Hungarian revolt is out but “la suite et conséquence en sera grande”. James I’s courtship of Spain: “il fault qu’il en face les preuves devant qu’il le croye”. The Dutch have as much courage as ever and are provided for; a newly-visited prince has given them hope of arming for them next year, and Maurice should encourage him. The Spaniards forge new plots against him daily; the comte d’Auvergne, his father-in-law and his sister are in justice “d’avoir traité avec eulx plus avant qu’ils ne devoyent”. 28 April 1605. The lines Rommel regretted: the aid the United Provinces and Geneva continue to receive from him “justifient assez la vérité de ma conduite et volonté en tels cas, et le soin que j’ay de maintenir et soubstenir ceulx de la dite religion, pour les notables intérests que j’ay à leur conservation et de la cause publicque”. 22 December 1605. Mérargues’ treason and the attempt on the King “me sont arrivés quasi au mesme temps de la conspiration d’Angleterre. Il semble aussy qu’ils ayent esté forgés sur mesme enclume”; the Spanish ambassador’s complaint is what Spanish ministers do everywhere, “seduire et corrompre les subjects des princes auprès desquels ils résident”; James I has as much cause to complain “toutesfois il le couvre et dissimule mieulx”. He has recommended the United Provinces to James “au besoin extrême qu’elles ont à présent d’estre assistées et renforcées par leurs alliés pour relever l’année prochaine la réputation de leurs armes”, and asks Maurice, who has “notable intérest à leur conservation avec les autres princes d’Allemagne”, to see them helped “tant d’argent que de troupes” as some princes have promised. He will continue “la mesme assistance d’argent et de troupes que je leur ay départie ceste-cy; elle est très notable et non moindre de deux millions de livres; mais si avec cela ils ne sont point secourus d’ailleurs, il leur sera impossible de résister”, the enemy massing money and men “pour les assaillir plus vivement et puissamment qu’ils n’ont point faict”. Get the help to them by spring, “car celuy qui pourra prévenir sa partie en cela en sera grandement avantagé”. And what does the Emperor mean by the Diet he has summoned; the Turkish peace; the Hungarian accord; the siege of Brunswick. 20 May 1606. The Emperor “ne change point de conduite” and is ill served, above all in Hungary. “Les Espagnols feront ce qu’ils pourront pour faire eslire un roy des Romains de la maison d’Austriche qui soit entièrement à leur dévotion”, and Feria goes to the Diet to promote it and to propose the pacification of the Netherlands, failing which the Empire is to make war on the States: “deux propositions de grande conséquence et auxquelles toute la chrestienté n’a moins d’intérest que l’Allemagne mesme. C’est pourquoy j’estime estre nécessaire que tous les roys et princes qui doivent avoir jalousie de l’agrandissement et prospérité de la puissance espagnole doibvent d’heure aviser et prendre conseil ensemble de ce qu’il convient faire pour empescher que les dicts Espagnols ne fassent cadrer les affaires et résolutions de la dite diète à leur souhait. Pour mon regard, j’y contribueray tousjours très volontiers ce qui dépendra de moy et me sera bienséant de faire, principalement quand je recognoistray que les autres pourront faire le semblable … pour la conservation de la liberté germanique, sans toutesfois en attendre autre advantage que d’advancer le bien de la cause commune et la seureté publique”; Maurice is to tell those he judges worthy and to advise the King what he “puis et doibs faire maintenant”. James I will not break with Spain over Owen and Baldwin, “tant il désire vivre en neutralité et en paix”, and the Spaniards ply him with “offres et ouvertures très spécieuses”; their aim is the Netherlands, “un grand effort ceste année, principallement du costé du Rhin et de Frise”, waiting only for Spinola. The States, weaker, will be forced onto the defensive, “misérable condition … en un estat composé et gouverné par plusieurs testes”; all whose interest is joined to theirs must act “devant que leur débilité et inanition soyent plus grandes, autrement les remèdes y seront trop tardifs”. His earlier request that Maurice press the German princes has had “fort peu d’effect”. The Dutch prosper in the East Indies and off Portugal, but “je doubte que ceste bonne fortune leur dure si celle de la terre leur manque”. The Spaniards will exploit the quarrel of the Pope and Venice; he will try to compose it. 24 January 1609. “Les ministres du Pape et du Roi d’Espagne” will do everything to reconcile Matthias with the Emperor.

t: Henri IV to Landgrave Maurice — the figures Rommel printed in 1840 and the key he printed in 1846
b: Nine groups on p. 213 give the name of the prince who visited the States (“d’un nouveau …”) and do not resolve; seven groups at the top of p. 307, the unlisted name-group 98 with overbar on p. 211 (a prince whose friendship Lorraine mediated: Bavaria is a guess*), and a line of letters and signs on p. 311 that the 1840 typesetter could not set in figures. The Marburg originals would settle them. The 1840 print is a transcription, and single figures are wrong in it (a 36 for 26, an 18 for 15); the readings mark supplied words in brackets. The tall-4 symbol is te or tion by context; 55, and 56, are both used where paix or pays is wanted. Whether the Landgrave’s chancery decipherments survive at Marburg is not checked; the Lettres missives reprinted the figures without reading them.

t: Henri IV to Landgrave Maurice — the figures Rommel printed in 1840 and the key he printed in 1846
b: The Internet Archive’s hOCR of the volume located the pages with dense figures. The figures were then transcribed by eye from 900-pixel strips of the full-resolution page images, because the OCR loses exactly what matters: the comma, the two dots, the overbar and the drawn symbols. The transcriptions in hesse1603/ct/ keep Rommel’s line breaks and the clear text; key.py holds the key with each correction and its evidence; run.py decodes a transcription; the hand readings are in letters/READINGS.md . No solver was used and none was needed: with the 1846 key, the work was transcription and reading. About 4,100 groups.

Tomokiyo, “French Ciphers during the Reign of Henry IV of France”, section “Cipher between Henry IV and Maurice of Hesse-Cassel (1603–1610)”, cryptiana.web.fc2.com/code/henryiv.htm; the original key sheet BnF Clairambault 360 f. 168 (Oct 1602). t: Heusner von Wandersleben to Oxenstierna, 1637 — already read by Waldispühl and Kopal
b: A German numerical homophonic letter from Kassel, catalogued twice (DECODE R4332 “partly solved”, R3816 “not solved”). The two records carry the same three scans, and the letter was deciphered by Michelle Waldispühl and Nils Kopal (HistoCrypt 2024). Their key, applied here to a fresh transcription of one page, reproduces their reading. The letter is dated 15 May 1637, not March; the code numbers stay open. Kassel → Stockholm · numerical homophonic with codes · 15 May 1637 · read by others Heusner von Wandersleben to Axel Oxenstierna, 1637: already read by Waldispühl and Kopal to Axel Oxenstierna Riksarkivet, Stockholm: a letter of five pages from the Swedish commissary-general Sigismund Heusner von Wandersleben to the chancellor, catalogued here twice, as DECODE R4332 (“partly solved”) and R3816 (“not solved”). Both records are one letter, and it was deciphered and published in 2024. This page records that and one independent check of the key. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read by others Summary. Catalogue entries 208 and 209 were two DECODE records of ciphered letters from Heusner von Wandersleben to Oxenstierna, dated March 1637, one partly solved and one not solved. The three scans on R3816 are byte for byte the scans on R4332, with pages 2 and 3 in the other order, so there is one letter, not two. R4332 carries the key and full plaintext of Michelle Waldispühl and Nils Kopal, published in the HistoCrypt 2024 proceedings. The cipher is a numerical homophonic alphabet for words and phrases set inside clear German, with three-digit numbers for names and places. Applied here to a new transcription of one page of figures, their key gives their plaintext, except for three slips in the new transcription. The letter closes “Cassel den 15. May 1637”, so DECODE’s 15 March is a slip. The deciphered text is theirs. What stays open is what they left open: some sixteen code numbers.

t: Heusner von Wandersleben to Oxenstierna, 1637 — already read by Waldispühl and Kopal
b: DECODE R4332 image 1 (letter page 2), top: dem 503 · 67·4·96·82·30·9·30·94·7·8·13·30·70·61·20 = zuwieder gewesen , then vnd die 764 and übergeben in figures. Image: Riksarkivet, Stockholm, Heusner to Oxenstierna 1637, letter p. 2, via DECODE R4332 (image 1). The letter is written in clear German, and the sensitive words and phrases are in figures separated by points. The alphabet has 22 letters with one to eight values each: E has eight (8, 30, 31, 61, 100, 110, 120, 200) and H six, while K and P have one each. The values run from 2 to 202, and nothing marks word divisions inside a run. Three-digit numbers from 147 to 808 stand for persons and places. The key file on the record lists 47 under both O and U. Record DECODE status Images R4332 Partially decrypted, 5 pp.; key and plaintext attached P1, P2, P3 R3816 Non-decrypted, 3 pp., “not solved” P1 = R4332 P1; P2 = R4332 P3; P3 = R4332 P2 (identical MD5)

t: Heusner von Wandersleben to Oxenstierna, 1637 — already read by Waldispühl and Kopal
b: The plaintext is Waldispühl and Kopal’s. Heusner has fallen out with Field Marshal Banér and, warned about Franz Heinrich of Saxe-Lauenburg “wegen der Hamburger sache”, has withdrawn to 164. The Kassel court has turned away from Sweden: So erfahre ich aber das HERR UND KNECHT SEHR GEENDERT UND AM GANZEN HOFE AUSSER DER 503. NICHT EINER MEHR UFFRECHT SCHWEDISCH, IA DER 628. FAUORISIRET vnd CARESSIRET alzo die so in SEINEM ABWESEN dem 503. ZUWIEDER GEWESEN vnd die 764. UBERGEBEN wollen A campaign is talked of, “WOHIN IST STILL”, but the force is not there. Then comes the secret war material: Man hat hier in der aller größen geheimb etlich 385. CENTNER METALLISCHE SPEISSE ZUSAMMEN GESCHMELZET vnd solche verdecket auf 147 geführet, daselbst etliche schon hierzu gemachte STUCKE ZU TAUSCHEN Johan von Uffeln is to be commandant of 571, and Gunterot is to take the field. The letter ends “CASSEL den 15. May 1637”.

t: Heusner von Wandersleben to Oxenstierna, 1637 — already read by Waldispühl and Kopal
b: The figures on letter page 2 (259 tokens with the clear-text breaks) were transcribed from the scan without using the published plaintext. The published homophone table turns them into ZUWIEDER GEWESEN … UBERGEBEN … NEGOCIIREN … FORCE … BASTANT … AUS DEM LANDT ZU TREIBEN … BESTALLUNG … GELDER … GROSSES HERANTZ … RECHT IM DIRECTORIO FASSEN, the published reading. Three single figures differ (SOHL for SOLL, FEOD for FELD, CLAM for CLAR), and each is a slip in the new transcription.

t: Heusner von Wandersleben to Oxenstierna, 1637 — already read by Waldispühl and Kopal
b: The codes 147, 164, 184, 255, 289, 321, 384, 385, 503, 571, 617, 628, 703, 708, 747 and 764, left as numbers by the solvers. 747 is in their plaintext but not in their key file. From context alone, 503 is the one person at the court still loyal to Sweden, who “SOLL IN DAS FELD”, most likely Landgrave Wilhelm V of Hesse-Kassel (grade M). 147 is where the guns are cast, and 764 a place some wanted to surrender. The Hessian correspondence of 1637 would settle these.

t: Thirty favourites from the archive
b: Ten findings that are funny, ten that matter to history and ten that are simply ingenious, from two hundred cipher write-ups: a drunk envoy to be seen when sober, a king and a nun, the relief of Malta, the murder of the Duke of Guise, a despatch in lemon juice and a father’s coded log of his baby son’s fits. ſπϙ ✕⊢ · 1424 1112 1433 520 · prfsfns lkbfr du citron sur les quatre demi-pages blanches la monaca · Uriel · 8319 < 8340 < 8374 A survey · September 2026 Thirty favourites from the archive Ten that made us laugh, ten that matter to history, and ten that are simply ingenious, picked from two hundred cipher write-ups that run from 1425 to 1933 Daniel Bourdeau · posted 22 September 2026 Why this page exists. Most of the work on this site is slow: a key rebuilt sign by sign, a catalogue record corrected, a letter found to be in print since 1877. But reading five centuries of other people’s secret mail also turns up royal scandals, clerical blunders and some very clever tricks. Here are thirty of the best. Each card links to its full write-up, with the images, the key and the measured reading. As each quotation scrolls into view, it deciphers itself. 30 findings 1425–1933 five centuries 8 languages 6 never ciphers, or no message All thirty Funny Historic Ingenious ⚄ Surprise me

t: Thirty favourites from the archive
b: Drunk envoys, royal gossip, catalogue clerks with the best of intentions, and one minister who could not quite work his own code. 01 1533 Hungary → the Dukes of Bavaria read “To be spoken with in the morning, when he is sober” DECODE filed this letter under “Augurellio”, the name on its address leaf. At the foot of two leaves it is signed, in cipher, Iorg Weinmaister : Jörg Weinmeister, a Bavarian agent in Hungary. Most of it is grim news, including the siege of the castle of Palota and a report of fifty thousand Turks marching from Belgrade on Buda. Then the talks on relieving Palota run into a practical problem. The magnate Török Bálint was sent to discuss the relief one evening in Vienna while well drunk, and will have to be approached again the next morning. the reading, in English …one evening at Vienna well drunk, was sent to talk of the relief, and is to be spoken with in the morning when he is sober. Weinmeister 1533, read 96.7% Iorg Weinmaister · signed in cipher · 02 1580 Rome → the nuncio in Paris read The Pope, the King of France, and the nun This is a cipher enclosure from the papal Secretariat of State to the nuncio Dandini. George Lasry had broken its companion in 2020; this one keeps his frame but shuffles the letter codes, and was rebuilt here by annealing. The result matches the clerk’s decipherment under the figures word for word, except that the cipher has commercio where the clerk wrote concetto . What Rome wanted kept secret was the gossip about Henri III and a nun. Whether or not it was true, the scandal was so great that the King “should stop going to that monastery altogether”, and the nuncio is to press this on him hard. The companion letter adds that he is not to raise the matter of the nun with the Queen. Italian La voce et l’opinione della pratica del Re Chr.mo con la monaca è uscita tanto publica che se ne ragiona hormai per tutto The talk of the Most Christian King’s affair with the nun has become so public that it is discussed everywhere. Como to Dandini 1580 Francia 283C f. 52: the figures, and the clerk’s decipherment beneath. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Francia 283C f. 52, via DECODE R72. 03 17th c. Sloane MS 3188 not a cipher Twenty-five “secret letters” that are notes on John Dee’s conversations with angels DECODE lists Sloane MS 3188 ff. 109–169 as twenty-five undeciphered ciphertexts, sender and recipient unknown. They are bound straight after Dee’s own diaries of his spirit “actions”. They turn out to be a later reader’s notes on those diaries, in seventeenth-century English stroke shorthand with the names written out in longhand. The leaves hold an index of the Actions, a list of Dee’s writings, and a note on Kelley and Prague dated 1595. There is no cipher, no letter and no correspondent in them. longhand inside the shorthand 1582 … E.T. … Uriel … Reuchlin · Reconciliatio Kelliana Shippen’s notes on Dee f. 109r: shorthand strokes, with names written out in longhand. Image: British Library, Sloane MS 3188 f. 109r, via DECODE R8506. 04 1702–23 Blenheim Papers, Add MS 61575 not a cipher A “numerical cipher” with no numbers, thanking someone for cipher lessons DECODE catalogues folio 95 as a non-decrypted numerical cipher by “Frederic, Re di Prussia”. There are no numbers on the page. It is seven lines of plain French, spelled by ear and chopped into syllables, and the writer is thanking someone for showing him how to write in cipher. Judging by the spelling, the lessons went better than the dictation. French, as spelled moy en me mon trant d’es cria re …for the trouble you took with me in showing me how to write in cipher A lesson in cipher en me mon trant d’es cria re · no digits at all · 05 1659–60 Hyde ↔ Barwick explained Coded addresses that meant nothing at all, on purpose Several of the royalist letters between Edward Hyde and John Barwick carry numbered superscriptions that no key reads, including the full Hyde–Barwick key printed in 1721. The explanation had been in print for three centuries. The editor of Barwick’s Life , who had the papers, says the numbers were decoys. the 1724 edition superscribed with Numbers signifying nothing … only to puzzle the Enemy, if they should fall into their Hands Hyde Vita Johannis Barwick (1721), p. 396. Image: P. Barwick, Vita Johannis Barwick (London, 1721), p. 396, via the Internet Archive. 06 1758 “Cypher from Mr Eichel”, Prussia nulls only An unsolved cipher that is nothing but padding This sheet of figures sits in the Prussian papers at Kew. The key the catalogue proposed does not fit it. The key filed in the same volume does, and it begins by declaring every number that contains a 7, plus four whole ranges, to be a null. On that rule 117 of the 139 groups are nulls, and 21 of the remaining 22 land on cells the key leaves blank. It is a dummy sheet, and there was never a message on it. the key’s first rule Tous les nro où je trouve un ou plusieurs 7 sont les nonvaleurs Every number in which I find one or more 7s is a null. Eichel 1758 The Eichel sheet: 139 groups, 117 of them declared nulls. Image: The National Archives, Kew, via DECODE R595. 07 1524 Rome → Charles V read in part The oldest long cipher on the list, off by exactly a hundred years DECODE dated two letters from Rome to “April 1424”. That would have made them the longest ciphertext before 1450, and they were picked as a flagship target on that basis. The letter gives its own date on f. 128v: De Roma xviij de Abril 1524 . The catalogue’s “Luis Fernández” is the Duke of Sessa, Charles V’s ambassador. Eight sibling letters carry the court’s own decipherments, and they supplied the alphabet and about 110 code groups. Spanish De Roma xviij de Abril 1524 From Rome, 18 April 1524, and not 1424. Sessa 1524 1424 ↓ 1524 08 1652–53 Paris → Holland too short, no key How the poet Abraham Cowley became a correspondent called “Mr. Conley” The docket on these royalist letters reads mr Cowleys Hand . DECODE read it as “Conleys” and made that name the author. The letters are in clear English. The only cipher in them is 23 numbers in five short runs, too few to break, so the most tantalising phrase stays shut. English, with its code the person that came lately from 248:88:46:47:96:52:7:57 Cowley’s hand 1652–53 Harley MS 7003 f. 314r. Image: British Library, Harley MS 7003 f. 314r, via DECODE R7768. 09 1812 St Petersburg → Washington solved in part John Quincy Adams fumbles his own code: “impassioned” for “impaired” Despatch No. 88 of June 1812 reports that the Russian Chancellor Rumyantsev had suffered a stroke. Worthington Ford printed nine of its lines in 1914 as “not decyphered”. Adams’s code, which turns out not to be the one historians assumed, was rebuilt here from the clerk’s decodes, and the nine lines now read. The exception is four groups whose values are all certain. They spell im-pas-sion-ed where the sense wants “impaired”, most likely Adams’s own slip at the codebook. English, syllable by syllable if his ac-tive in-flu-ence had not been im-pas-ion-ed before it, it can scarcely fa-il to have been af-fect-ed Erving & Adams No. 88, 25 June 1812, in figures. Image: National Archives and Records Administration, RG 59, M35 reel 3, frame 0206. 10 1848 Rome → Innsbruck solved The Pope’s secret counter-order: intercepted, published with a prize, and a day late anyway On 15 June 1848 Cardinal Soglia sent 955 digits to the nuncio at Innsbruck, where the Emperor had fled. Mazzini’s L’Italia del Popolo intercepted the despatch, printed it, and offered “a prize of some size for the best interpreter of these figures”. Nobody claimed it, and in 2014 it was posted on Cipherbrain as unsolved. The code turned out to be alphabetical: Imperatore 8319 comes before istruzione 8340, which comes before Monsignor 8374. The order tells the nuncio to stay with the Emperor wherever he goes. According to the Dizionario Biografico , he had left Innsbruck on 14 June, the day before it was sent. the reading, in English …of the Holy Father that you remain at Innsbruck with the Emperor and wherever he may go Soglia 1848 The printed block of 955 digits. Image: Tony Gaffney, via Klaus Schmeh, Cipherbrain.

t: Thirty favourites from the archive
b: Sieges, assassinations, a bought crown and a king’s change of plan, several of them read here for the first time. 01 1425 Urbino → Florence read 1425: the oldest cipher read on this site Early in 1425, Galeotto da Ricasoli wrote from Urbino to Florence’s war magistracy. Gabbrielli glossed a few words in 1863, and Meister printed a key in 1902, but the letter itself was never printed and its three long cipher runs were never read. They have now been decoded sign by sign. Madonna is the Countess of Urbino, Caterina Colonna, niece of Pope Martin V. Italian perché dice che Madonna è pure femina e sospetosa because he says that Madonna is, after all, a woman, and suspicious Ricasoli 1425 Ricasoli to the Dieci, 1425. Image: Archivio di Stato di Firenze, via DECODE R3754. 02 1482 Pozsony → Ferrara solved in part Venice tries to buy the King of Hungary In July 1482, in the first weeks of the War of Ferrara, the Este envoy at Matthias Corvinus’s court reported in cipher what Venice was offering the king: the island of Veglia, a command at sea for his natural son, and 100,000 ducats a year. The alphabet was rebuilt from sibling letters that survive with clear copies. This letter has no clear copy and had never been printed. Italian et voleva dargli Vegla, et voleva lo figlio (e bastardo) per loco capitaneo … per mare and they wanted to give him Veglia, and wanted his son (a bastard) as their captain … at sea Sadoleto 1482 Sadoleto to Ercole d’Este. Image: Archivio di Stato di Modena, via DECODE R1102. 03 1565 Messina → Philip II solved The relief of Malta, reported in figures during the Great Siege García de Toledo, viceroy of Sicily, wrote to Philip II on 16 July 1565 with every sensitive word in two-digit figures. No decipherment survives anywhere. Two cribs gave eleven letters, and then the figures 12–43 turned out to run through the alphabet in order, so all 1,930 groups could be read. The letter tells how the small relief force got into the Borgo, and how La Valette’s fire signals turned back a second run of galleys. It also reports that Sicily could no longer pay for the war. Spanish el maestre les hizo las sennales del fuego clarissimas para que no entrassen the Grand Master made them the fire signals, very clear, so that they would not come in Toledo 1565 Estado leg. 1394 no. 247, f. 1r. Image: Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 1394 no. 247 f. 1r, via PARES. 04 1573 Warsaw → Paris solved How France bought the crown of Poland These are the French envoys’ letters to Charles IX during the election that made Henri of Anjou King of Poland. The key came from a sibling letter whose only decipherment was a set of margin notes half cut away by the binder, one of them car je n’ay pas cinquante escuz . It then opened three election letters. In them, the Poles can be won by money “as are the Germans, their neighbours”. On 9 May the election is carried against the Emperor, Spain, Muscovy and Sweden. French d’Espaigne, du Moscovite et du Roy de Suède, qui tous estoient bandez contre vostre Majesté of Spain, of the Muscovite and of the King of Sweden, who were all banded against Your Majesty Lanssac 1573 BnF fr. 4735 f. 124. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 4735 f. 124, via Gallica btv1b9060724s canvas 242. 05 1588–89 Blois → Rome read The papal legate reports the murder of the Duke of Guise Cardinal Morosini, legate in France, sent 36 cipher enclosures to Rome, all of them written as one unbroken stream of digits. They were cut apart with an Italian language model and Meister’s key of 1906, and 34 now read end to end. They cover the Estates of Blois, Saluzzo and Henri III’s march on Paris, and they report the killing of the Guises in the King’s own chamber. Italian il Duca di Guisa nela camera di S. M.tà è stato per ordine di S. M.tà amazato a colpi di pugnale the Duke of Guise has been killed with dagger blows, in His Majesty’s chamber, by His Majesty’s order Morosini 1588 Francia 22 f. 308r: one run-on stream of digits. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Francia 22 f. 308r, via DECODE R43. 06 1590 Mantua → the duc de Nevers read “The Pope’s death was procured with poison by the Spaniards” Vincenzo Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua, wrote to the duc de Nevers on 17 September 1590, three weeks after the death of Sixtus V. The key filed among Nevers’s own papers reads 95% of the cipher unchanged. Mantua passes on the rumour that the Spaniards poisoned the Pope, and welcomes Henri IV’s expected conversion. Italian che la morte del Papa sia stata procurata con veleno da Spagnoli that the Pope’s death was procured with poison by the Spaniards Mantua to Nevers 1590 BnF fr. 3979 f. 92r. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3979 f. 92r, via DECODE R4176. 07 1570 Tutbury → the Tower read Mary Queen of Scots writes to Norfolk in the Tower Mary wrote this letter weeks after the murder of the Regent Moray, and it is the only one in the series with no contemporary decipherment. Tomokiyo rebuilt the key but published only a partial overlay, and here the letter is read in full, all 23 lines. Mary reports that Elizabeth blames her for Moray’s death. Norfolk is to write only through the Bishop of Ross or Lady Scrope, and never in his own hand. English, as she spelled it I am asured that sche … sueves me the veyt of Murray death; but God knoueth I am assured that she lays on me the blame [Scots wyte ] for Moray’s death; but God knows Mary to Norfolk Cotton MS Caligula C II f. 74r. Image: British Library, Cotton MS Caligula C II f. 74r, via the BL IIIF service. 08 1602–09 Paris → Kassel read Henri IV’s secret letters to a German prince: printed, keyed, and never put together Rommel printed the ciphered passages of Henri IV’s letters to Landgrave Maurice of Hesse-Kassel in figures in 1840. Six years later he printed the key, and nobody ever applied one to the other. Doing so reads all seven passages, about 4,100 groups. They cover Bouillon and the German princes, the Gunpowder Plot, two million livres for the Dutch, and a call in 1606 to resist a Spanish King of the Romans. This reading was contributed by Arya Sanketbhai Patel. French pour la conservation de la liberté germanique for the preservation of German liberty Hesse Rommel 1840, p. 310: printed in figures, unread. Image: Rommel (ed.), Correspondance inédite de Henri IV avec Maurice-le-Savant (1840), p. 310, via the Internet Archive. 09 1691 Versailles → Piedmont read Louis XIV decides to give up Piedmont, in five despatches read for the first time The 1819 editor of Catinat’s memoirs printed seven despatches in figures and could not read them. Bazeries rebuilt the code in 1893 while hunting the Man in the Iron Mask, printed two, and stopped. His table reads all seven, 12,362 groups. They include the King’s twenty-page letter of 14 September: bring the army back over the Alps, hold Carmagnole as long as possible to cover the talks with the Pope, then strip it and burn it. French je me suis déterminé à préférer le parti solide à l’honorable I have resolved to prefer the solid course to the honourable one Catinat 1691 Mémoires de Catinat (1819), p. 320. Image: Mémoires de Catinat, t. II (1819), p. 320, Bayerische Staatsbibliothek, via the MDZ. 10 1758–60 Lisbon → Rome read The nuncio’s secret account of the attempt on the King of Portugal On the night of 3 September 1758, José I of Portugal was shot at in his carriage. The first of eight ciphers from the Lisbon nuncio Acciaiuoli is his secret account of it. They were read with George Lasry’s 2020 key, together with 25 code groups fixed from three leaves deciphered at the time. Italian il Teixeira ferito a morte … il Re molto ferito del braccio destro Teixeira mortally wounded … the King badly wounded in the right arm Acciaiuoli 1758 Portogallo 117/6 f. 106r. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Portogallo 117/6 f. 106r, via DECODE R199.

t: Thirty favourites from the archive
b: Invisible ink, decoy words, a monk’s vowel shift, and the detective work that turns a mislabelled record into a story. 01 1792 Berlin → The Hague read A cipher whose only job is to say that the real letter is in lemon juice The Dutch envoy van Reede wrote from Berlin on 4 February 1792. Read in full with the 1782 Grand Chiffre , the letter is a cover note. The four blank half-pages of its enclosure carry writing in lemon juice, the Prince of Orange is to be told, and “the following figures are nulls”. Those 21 nulls decode to a planted jumble of Conseil d’Etat , la Russie and Archiduc , which is bait for anyone who opens the letter. French il y a du citron sur les quatre demi-pages blanches de l’incluse there is lemon juice on the four blank half-pages of the enclosure Van Reede 1792 KHA, Prins Willem V inv. 205. Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 205, via DECODE R1057 (rotated here). 02 1933 Shanghai no message $300,000,000 in gold bars, and almost exactly ten of every letter Seven gold bars, said to have been issued in Shanghai in 1933 to certify a deposit of over $300,000,000, carry sixteen strings of Latin letters. For ninety years nobody read them. Their letter counts are the problem: against a flat distribution they give a chi-squared of 1.25, where honest random sampling gives about 25. No cipher can produce that. Substitution and transposition keep the skew of the plaintext, and a one-time pad lands near 25. Someone counted out the letters and arranged them to look like cryptography. the test χ² = 1.25 on 25 degrees of freedom, where chance predicts 25 Gold bars One of the bars. Image: Kevin McCurley, “Cryptograms on Gold bars from China”, IACR (1996), iacr.org/misc/china. 03 1635–36 Suffolk, a private record solved A father’s secret log of his baby son’s fits DECODE has this as a letter of 1635, “unknown sender to unknown recipient”. It is Sir Simonds D’Ewes, the antiquary, writing Latin in a private alphabet he invented at school. The page is a log, one line per convulsion, of his infant son Clopton from 3 April 1635, with the day, the hour and the phase of the moon. The alphabet was rebuilt from the cribs convulsio and plena luna , and 96.5% of the words read. The weekdays and moons all check against the calendar. Clopton died on 9 May 1636. Latin in quorum tertia os ipsius pene ad aurem dextram convulsum, quod ante numquam observavi in the third of which his mouth was drawn almost to his right ear, which I had never seen before D’Ewes’s cipher log 1635 Harley MS 286 f. 61. Image: British Library, Harley MS 286 f. 61, via DECODE R7759. 04 1548 Augsburg → Constantinople read in part Decoy words: nulls that look like Latin Ferdinand I wrote to Malvezzi, his resident at the Ottoman Porte, in a cipher of graphic signs padded with whole words that look like part of the Latin: etiam , idcirco , atque , Porro . The key was already on DECODE, filed as a separate record at the same shelfmark. The letter shows the French trying to wreck the Habsburg–Ottoman peace, and Malvezzi’s pay: 4,300 ducats at once. the decoys etiam · idcirco · atque · cum · Porro Ferdinand I to Malvezzi 1548 p. 4: the cipher hands back to clear Latin. Image: Hadtörténelmi Levéltár, Budapest, 1548/3, p. 4, via DECODE R366. 05 1517 Strängnäs colophon read A monk signs his chant book in code The scribe who copied this Dominican sequentiary in 1517 dated it in a colophon where every vowel is written as the letter after it: a becomes b, e becomes f, i becomes k, o becomes p and u becomes x. The Uppsala catalogue printed the reading in 1992. Watch the quotation below: it starts as the scribe wrote it. Latin, vowels shifted presens liber sequencionarius est scriptus in conuentu strengenensi this sequentiary was written in the convent at Strängnäs Strängnäs sequentiary 1517 C 513 f. 19v: the colophon under four staves. Image: Uppsala University Library, C 513 f. 19v, via Alvin (public domain). 06 1616 Strassburg, a printed book already read The “undeciphered letter” is a novel, and one of its characters reads the cipher aloud DECODE R4502 is a copy of the Chymische Hochzeit Christiani Rosencreutz (Strassburg, 1616). Its four “cipher pages” are inscriptions in the story, cut in an invented alphabet. A paragraph later the page boy reads both long ones aloud. The two lines of signs are the dates 1378 and 1459, which Foxcroft’s English edition of 1690 already gives. German HIE LIGT BEGRABEN VENUS DIE SCHONE FRAW SO MANCHEN HOHEN MANN UMB GLUCK EHR SEGEN UND WOLFART GEBRACHT HATT Here lies buried Venus, the fair lady who has cost many a great man his fortune, honour, blessing and welfare Chymische Hochzeit inscriptions Chymische Hochzeit (1616), p. 97. Image: Embassy of the Free Mind (Ritman Library), Amsterdam, Chymische Hochzeit (Strassburg 1616), p. 97, via DECODE R4502. 07 1664–68 a Habsburg prison → his kin not a cipher A prisoner’s plea, filed among the state ciphers because nobody could read it This letter was bound into the Vienna papers of the Hungarian magnates’ conspiracy, in a file headed Chiffres 1664–1668 . DECODE lists it as a simple substitution in graphic signs. The signs are Cyrillic letters and the language is Serbian. It was written by Stojan, in prison, who greets his Vlachs by name, asks for money to be brought, and sends greetings to his wife. The clerks who filed it, it seems, could not read it. from the Serbian brothers, have mercy on me: you can get me out of the German prison, and your souls out of hell Stojan’s letter from prison HHStA, Verschwörerakten Fasc. 327, f. 30r. Image: Österreichisches Staatsarchiv, HHStA, Verschwörerakten Fasc. 327 Konv. D f. 30r, via DECODE R688 (image 1). 08 1489–90 Buda → Milan read A key published only as numbers, turned back into signs In 2016 Judit W. Somogyi reconstructed the Milanese ambassador’s key, but printed it only as numbers, without a picture of a single sign. Her numbers run in order of first appearance in the letter of 2 April 1490, which survives with its clear copy. Matching that letter to its copy gives back every sign’s shape, and then the key works. It reads the despatch of 22 November 1489 on peace with Frederick III, the John Corvinus marriage, and Queen Beatrice’s “insatiable wrath of Juno”. The despatch also warns that intercepted cipher letters had been read. Italian Le littere in cifra che forono intercepte, le quale duplicate sono state scoperte ancora qua the cipher letters that were intercepted, whose duplicates have been uncovered here too Buda 1489 Sforzesco 650, 22 November 1489. Image: Archivio di Stato di Milano, Sforzesco 650, letter of 22 November 1489, via Vestigia. 09 1586 Angoumois → a League leader decipherment found The “unread” part was deciphered in 1586 Two thirds of this anonymous League letter of October 1586 were listed as unread. On the next leaf, f. 168, is a clear text of the cipher down to a cross mark. After the cross, the decipherer had switched to writing the plaintext between the lines of cipher. The glosses confirm Tomokiyo’s key (87 = e). The letter says that Fumé, vice-admiral of Guyenne, keeps proposing a reconciliation between Navarre and the League leader it is written to. French Fumé, visadmiral de Guienne, tres confident du Roy de Navarre, bien qu’il soit catholique Fumé, vice-admiral of Guyenne, very much in the King of Navarre’s confidence, although he is a Catholic Clairambault 357, 1586 Clairambault 357 f. 167r, with interlinear glosses. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Clairambault 357 f. 167r, via Gallica. 10 1801 Berlin → The Hague clear copy found A cipher despatch about stolen ciphers, whose own clear copy was misfiled The Batavian chargé in Berlin wrote in cipher on 31 January 1801, and DECODE lists the despatch as undeciphered. Its clear copy is the third image of the next record. The subject is ciphers going astray. Rosenkrantz blames a servant who copied his cipher, and the envoy Lusi says “much more definitely” that the desk his cipher was kept in had been forced. Dutch dat het bureau, waar in zyn Cyffer was, is geforceerd geworden that the desk in which his cipher was kept had been forced open Bourdeaux 1801 The clear copy, misfiled under the next record. Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 2.01.08 inv. 257 fol. 295, via DECODE R1946 (image 3).

t: Thirty favourites from the archive
b: The thirty come from the two hundred or so write-ups on this site and the notes behind them. They were chosen for the story, not the difficulty; the full list sorts by outcome, and the hardest breaks are ranked in the repository’s solved ranking . Each badge gives the status stated on the write-up: solved means the key was broken here, read that an existing key or decipherment was used, and read in part that some of the text is still open. Quotations keep the original spelling, and the translations follow the write-ups. Six of the thirty turned out not to be ciphers at all, or to hold no message: that is its own finding, and a common one. Every image is credited on its card to the archive or edition that holds it. Select an image to open it full size.

t: Henrietta Maria’s household to Charles I, 1645–46 — already read by George Lasry
b: Six numerical homophonic letters in TNA SP 106/10, catalogued as undeciphered and still on Tomokiyo’s unsolved list. The DECODE records carry George Lasry’s reconstructed keys and plaintexts for the whole run, ff. 207–247 (October 2020). Only the nomenclator numbers are left open. His key, applied here to the raw transcription of f. 247, reads it at once. St Germain / Paris → Charles I · numerical homophonic with nomenclator · 1645–46 · read by others Henrietta Maria’s household to Charles I, 1645–46: already read by George Lasry from Henrietta Maria → to Charles I The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 ff. 213–247: six letters from the queen’s circle in France to the King (DECODE R785, R787, R790, R923, R924, R929), catalogued here as undeciphered and still on Tomokiyo’s unsolved list. The keys and plaintexts have been on the DECODE records since October 2020. This page records that and one independent check. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 19 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read by others Summary. Catalogue entry 59 grouped six numerical ciphers from SP 106/10, written from Henrietta Maria’s household at St Germain and Paris to Charles I in the last year of the first Civil War. DECODE lists them as “partially decrypted” and dates them only by the handwriting, so they looked open. Fetching the record pages shows otherwise. Every letter in the run, ff. 207–247, carries George Lasry’s reconstructed key and his plaintext, uploaded on 23 October 2020, beside Sofia Pettersson’s 2019 transcription. Lasry reconstructed four keys, one for each period of the correspondence, and dated the letters from their content (July 1645 to January 1646). The six letters of entry 59 use three of them. “Partial” refers only to the three-digit nomenclator numbers for names and some words, which stay in brackets. Applied here to the raw transcription of f. 247, without his plaintext file, his key reads the letter at once. Nothing about the text is new here. The sister entries 54 (R752), 55 (R928, Goffe from The Hague) and 60 (R789, Digby) are covered by the same work and were removed from the catalogue with this one.
