t: Huang Xing to Lin Hu and Li Genyuan — a kana condenser
b: Listed as “solved but specific scheme unknown”: the Japanese Foreign Ministry filed a decode nobody could read, and an encipherment nobody could name. Both recovered, and then corrected from the frames: three kana carry one character deterministically from a private code, a superfluous kana had hidden the repeats, and the vowel is not free. China / Japan · romanised kana · 1916 · scheme identified Huang Xing to Lin Hu and Li Genyuan from Huang Xing Relayed through the Japanese Foreign Ministry, 25 May 1916 · Minister Ishii to Consul Ōta at Zhaoqing · JACAR B03050731500 The catalogue records it as “solved but specific scheme unknown”. Here is the filed decode, and the scheme. Daniel Bourdeau · solved 15 September 2026 · updated 21 September 2026 solved Summary. In May 1916 Huang Xing asked the Japanese Foreign Ministry to pass a telegram to Lin Hu and Li Genyuan in Guangdong. It went out in a cipher of the Chinese side's own making: 139 syllables of romanised Japanese kana, packed into ten-letter telegraph words, with no voicing marks. S. Tomokiyo later found a memo recording that the Ministry had filed a decode with the telegram, so the item is listed as solved — but he could not read the handwritten Chinese, and the encryption scheme stayed unidentified. Both are settled here. The decode and its annotated Japanese reading are on frames 0247 and 0248 of the file, and the message is a short reply about the National Protection Army and a traveller's sailing date. The scheme is a kana code of a kind not previously described for this correspondence: three kana encode one character, deterministically , from a private codebook. A first analysis read the consonant row as the digit and the vowel as a free homophone; the frames, re-read at 500 dpi, overturn that (section 03). Status: scheme identified, one transmission error located, plaintext read, 42 codebook entries recovered; the kana-to-digit table and the rest of the book need a second telegram.

t: Huang Xing to Lin Hu and Li Genyuan — a kana condenser
b: JACAR B03050731500 is a Gaimushō volume on the anti-Yuan risings (1.6.1.75-1_015, reel 1-0955, frames 0244–0302). The covering despatch, 電送第一九八〇号, cipher, sent 25 May 1916 at 4.35 p.m. from Foreign Minister Ishii to Consul Ōta at Zhaoqing, says in plain Japanese what the enclosure is: 黄興ヨリ林虎李根源宛電報依頼アリタルニ付同人ニ伝達アリタシ 内容ハ先日来電ノ挨拶ナリ（以下支那側暗号） “Huang Xing has asked that a telegram be sent to Lin Hu and Li Genyuan; please pass it to them. The content is an acknowledgement of the telegram received the other day. (The Chinese side's cipher follows.)” Three frames matter: 0246 , the telegram on an Imperial Government Telegraphs forwarded-message form; 0247 , headed 電稿, the decoded Chinese in cursive; and 0248 , a clerk's reading of it rearranged into Japanese word order on Foreign Ministry paper, with his own glosses. Frame 0246: the telegram as handed in. Five rows of ten-letter words, ending OSOYUANIRA KISU. Image: Diplomatic Archives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan, 1.6.1.75-1_015 frame 0246, via JACAR Ref. B03050731500. REKUTATA UHOYAKATE SEKANAOKU SAKEKINISE OSUKAKUCHI REUHONIUSU MAKASUSAKU FUREOHIHE YENIKIYEHI TAKASUREU SASHIKIHE WAONIAAHO SAYEHITE UHINAKUTA NEATEMUYE SUHEUHAKA YESOMIKANU TEASUUKU TSUHAKOSE KEKININAKI TEAKETASHI KONUOHIKE HIMIKANO SHIKUSAHE UHATAKASA KEKINIKA ATAREUSASU OSOYUANIRA KISU Read as kana this is 139 syllables, 36 of them distinct. There are no voiced kana at all — no ga, za, da, ba — which is normal for telegraph traffic, where the voicing marks were simply not transmitted. The syllables are Japanese (SHI, CHI, TSU, and the old YE and WA), not the consonant-vowel letters of the condenser used in the Swatow telegram to Sun Yat-sen six weeks earlier.

t: Huang Xing to Lin Hu and Li Genyuan — a kana condenser
h: What the Ministry had already read
b: Frame 0247 is the decode: a heading 電稿 and four columns of 12, 11, 12 and 11 characters — forty-six characters of message. Frame 0248 is the same text rearranged for a Japanese reader, and it is the more useful of the two, because the clerk added glosses where he was unsure. Frame 0247, 電稿 — the decoded Chinese. Image: Diplomatic Archives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan, 1.6.1.75-1_015 frame 0247, via JACAR Ref. B03050731500. Frame 0248 — the clerk's reading, with his glosses. Image: Diplomatic Archives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan, 1.6.1.75-1_015 frame 0248, via JACAR Ref. B03050731500. 隱印崧蕘邕行諸兄鑒：正發書翰之際，適接 哿 電，敬悉一切。護國軍能速入 湘贛 甚好。 章行嚴 何日東渡？速令出發，並望預電。興 徑 “To brothers Yin, Yin, Song, Yao and Yongxing: just as I was sending a letter, your telegram of the twentieth arrived, and I have respectfully noted it all. It would be excellent if the National Protection Army could move quickly into Hunan and Jiangxi. What day does Zhang Xingyan cross to Japan? Have him start at once, and please wire me in advance. — Xing, the twenty-fifth.” The clerk's glosses carry most of the identifications. Against the string of names at the head he wrote 林虎・李根源等ノ字ナラン , “probably the courtesy names of Lin Hu, Li Genyuan and others” — he was guessing too, and one of them is certainly 蔡鍔's 松坡. He glossed 湘贛 as 湖南江西 , Hunan and Jiangxi, and 東渡 as 日本ニ来ル , coming to Japan. 章行嚴 is Zhang Shizhao, Huang Xing's close associate. Two characters are dates in the 韻目代日 rhyme-code that Chinese telegraphy used for the day of the month: 哿 = the 20th and 徑 = the 25th — and 徑, the last character of the signature, matches the dispatch date on the covering despatch exactly. That agreement is the best single check that the decode belongs to this telegram. Correction, second session. The running text above is the clerk's paraphrase from frame 0248 (50 characters). The cursive on frame 0247, read at 500 dpi, has 46: 隱印崧誥邕行諸兄鑒正發書 · 間適接哿電敬悉一切護國 · 軍能速入湘贛甚好[章]行嚴何日 · 東渡望速啓行先電示興徑, with 章 an interlinear addition. That count matches the 46 kana triples exactly; see section 03. Several glyphs in the cursive remain uncertain and are given here on the balance of the two frames. The column lengths are 2 + 12 + 11 + 12 + 11; Tomokiyo's note gives the same figures but sums them as 68, where they add to 48.

t: Huang Xing to Lin Hu and Li Genyuan — a kana condenser
b: Forty-six characters against 138 usable kana is three kana to the character , with a single kana left spare at the end. That settles the rate. The question is what part of each kana does the work, and the gojūon syllabary answers it by its shape: it is a grid of ten consonant rows by five vowels. — K S T N H M Y R W A KA SA TA NA HA MA YA RA WA I KI SHI CHI NI HI MI — RI WI U KU SU TSU NU FU MU YU RU — E KE SE TE NE HE ME YE RE WE O KO SO TO NO HO MO YO RO WO If the consonant row carries a digit and the vowel is free, then a character repeated in the plaintext will repeat as a triple of rows but need not repeat as a triple of kana . That is a testable prediction, and the counts are unambiguous. Across the 46 groups: reading repeats observed expected by chance permutation test consonant row 7 1.03 p = 0.006 vowel 8 8.28 p = 0.70 literal kana 1 — — The consonant rows repeat seven times where chance predicts one. The vowels repeat eight times where chance predicts eight — they carry nothing whatever. And the surface kana, the thing an interceptor actually sees, repeats once in forty-six. The mechanism is visible in the repeated groups themselves, the same character spelled two different ways: S K N → SE - KA - NA and SHI - KO - NU R — H → RE - U - HO and RE - O - HI T — H → TA - U - HO and TE - U - HI S K H → SA - KU - FU and SHI - KI - HE That was the first reading, and the frames correct it. Re-fetched and read at 500 dpi, frame 0247 has four columns of 12, 11, 12 and 11 characters after the heading, 46 in all, the number of kana triples: 隱印崧誥邕行諸兄鑒正發書 · 間適接哿電敬悉一切護國 · 軍能速入湘贛甚好[章]行嚴何日 · 東渡望速啓行先電示興徑 The earlier 50-character plaintext above followed the clerk's Japanese paraphrase on frame 0248; the cursive has 46, and 章 is an interlinear addition. This plaintext repeats 行 three times (positions 6, 32, 41), 速 twice (26, 39) and 電 twice (17, 43). Under the grouping above only one of those pairs matched. Drop one kana at position 106 , the O of OHIKE at the start of character 36, and every triple from there on shifts by one: 行 becomes KE-KI-NI all three times, 速 HE-U-HA both times, 電 RE-U-SA both times, and the spare SU at the end completes the last character. The telegram as filed carries one superfluous kana, and the code is deterministic: the same character is always the same three kana, vowels included. The seven consonant-row collisions in the table are therefore not one character written with different vowels. After the shift they are pairs of different characters (印/護, 誥/日, 鑒/間, 書/敬, 國/嚴, 甚/何, 諸/示) that share a row triple and differ only in vowels. The vowels carry information. What survives of the first analysis is the rate, three kana to the character, and the fact that the kana's row is correlated with its code value; the excess of row collisions over chance is what that correlation looks like from outside. Three kana over a 50-kana syllabary would address 125,000 entries, far more than any private book; the natural reading is still a three-digit code with each digit written as one of a set of kana, the sets not being the rows. One test of that was run and failed. If the rows were the digits of a codebook compiled in dictionary order, some permutation of the ten rows would make the 42 distinct characters' code numbers monotone in standard telegraph-code order. Over all 3,628,800 permutations the best Spearman rho is 0.524; the same search on twelve shuffles of the plaintext gives a null of mean 0.468 and maximum 0.614. No signal.

t: Huang Xing to Lin Hu and Li Genyuan — a kana condenser
b: The kana-to-digit table. The row is not the digit, and 46 characters do not determine an assignment of 36 kana to ten values. The codebook beyond the 42 entries (character to kana triple) that this telegram fixes. A second telegram in the same code would settle both. What this one settles is the scheme, the plaintext, and the transmission error that hid the repeats.

t: Hyde’s ciphered superscriptions — not a cipher at all
b: The four “undeciphered addresses” on Hyde’s letters to Barwick decode to nothing under the full Hyde–Barwick key printed in 1721, because, as the 1724 editor states, they were numbers “signifying nothing … only to puzzle the Enemy”. Brussels · Restoration correspondence · 1659–60 · explained Hyde's Ciphered Superscriptions from Edward Hyde Sir Edward Hyde to Dr John Barwick, Brussels, 29 Sept and 17 Oct 1659, 14 and 16 Jan 1660 · printed in Peter Barwick, Vita Johannis Barwick (1721), pp. 358, 360, 389, 396 Not an address in cipher: dummy numbers "only to puzzle the Enemy" — on the word of the editor who had the papers, confirmed against the full key Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 15 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 explained Summary. Four letters written by Hyde from Brussels in the months before the Restoration carry, where an address should be, a line of cipher figures. They are catalogued as undeciphered. They were never meant to be deciphered. The letters are Hyde's to John Barwick, the royalist agent in London, and were printed from the Barwick papers in 1721 together with the very key the two men used. The English edition of 1724 adds the editor's explanation: several of the letters "were superscribed with Numbers signifying nothing … only to puzzle the Enemy", and he cites exactly these pages. Applying the full Hyde–Barwick key (transcribed here from the 1721 plate) confirms it: one superscription decodes to gibberish and the other three use numbers that do not exist in the key. The item should be removed from the "unsolved" list as a non-cipher.

t: Hyde’s ciphered superscriptions — not a cipher at all
b: Tomokiyo's page references (313, 335, 339, 441, 442 for the clear addresses; 358, 360, 389, 396 for the ciphered ones) are to the Latin Vita Johannis Barwick (London, 1721), whose appendix prints Hyde's letters to Barwick in English, with an engraved "Tabula Cryptographica" of their cipher facing p. 316. The four superscriptions, verified against the page scans (every group is followed by a full stop, so the grouping is certain): Date (Brussels) Vita 1721 Life 1724 Superscription as printed 29 September 1659 No. XVI, p. 358 No. XIII, p. 449 212. 23. 12. 7. 461. 36. / 108. 49. 498. 14. 21. 410. 17 October 1659 No. XVII, p. 360 No. XIV, p. 451 729. 549. 705. 99. 856. / 250. 245. 831. 100. 859. / 609. 858. 101. 24. 14 January 1660 No. XXIII, p. 389 No. XXI, p. 482 729. 549. 856. / 21. 245. 831. 99. 16 January 1660 No. XXVI, p. 396 No. XXIII, p. 486 729. 549. 856. 8. 245. 831. Vita Johannis Barwick (1721), p. 396 — the letter of 16 January 1660 and its superscription. Image: P. Barwick, Vita Johannis Barwick (London, 1721), p. 396, via the Internet Archive. Clear superscriptions in the same series are cover names for Barwick: "For Mr. Burden", "For Mr. Brookes", "For Mr. B.", "For Mr. Burges, these"; the editor notes that "B. or any Name beginning with B. seems to have signified Barwick".

t: Hyde’s ciphered superscriptions — not a cipher at all
b: The 1721 plate gives the complete cipher: numbers 1–692 in eleven columns. Column 1 is the alphabet, three figures per letter (two for k, w, y; none for x, z); 64–69 are skipped; columns 2–11 (70–131, 132–193, 194–254, 255–317, 318–379, 380–440, 441–503, 504–566, 567–628, 629–692) each run A to Y down the rows, three rows per letter, so syllables and words are grouped by initial letter across the columns rather than in one alphabetical list. Several slots are deliberately empty. Entries relevant here: the = 370, for = 210, from = 211, Mr. = 536, Master = 475, Barwick = 572, Hyde, Lord Chancellor = 589; there is no entry for these , Sir or London .

t: Hyde’s ciphered superscriptions — not a cipher at all
b: The unabridged English Life of Dr. John Barwick (1724, tr. Hilkiah Bedford), working from the Barwick family papers, appends this note to the letter of 12 June 1659 that enclosed the cipher (pp. 408–409): But to render the Cypher more difficult to be found out, as each Letter in the Alphabet is represented by three several Numbers, except K, W, and Y only by two, and X and Z by none: So several of the Numbers have no Letter, Syllable, or Word over against them, because they stand for nothing, and were only us'd to perplex such as should attempt to read what was written hereby, without the Help of the Cypher. So several of the Letters were superscribed with Numbers signifying nothing, some with two or three Lines of them, only to puzzle the Enemy, if they should fall into their Hands, which I the rather mention here, because some Persons, for want of examining those Superscriptions, as printed in the Appendix to the Latin Life (p. 358, 360, 389, 396, and 417.) with the Cypher also published there, have wondered what was the meaning of them: and it was for the same Reason, that several of the Chancellor's Letters, besides the Number denoting his Name, were subscribed with other Numbers, that either had nothing in the Cypher to answer them, or nothing to the Purpose. As to the Superscriptions, B. or any Name beginning with B. seems to have signified Barwick. The pages he names are the four in question. The same puzzle, it turns out, had already been raised and answered in 1724.

t: Unsolved Historical Ciphers
h: The Voynich manuscript is probably elaborate nonsense
b: It is a real book from the early 1400s, but the text is not a language in disguise. Every simple cipher of every European language we could test is ruled out: the writing is far too predictable, letter to letter, for any of them. Two explanations are left standing, a rigid glyph-by-glyph encoding with something behind it, or carefully made meaningless text, and the numbers lean toward meaningless. The write-up names the five tests that would settle it. 2.2–2.9 bits of conditional entropy, against 3.3 for language 1.7–2.3× more rigid word grammar than any language tested 0.09 bits H(language | scribe): Currier A/B is almost the hand Read the adjudication → ★ Solved · 1644

Savoy and Canisy’s letters are printed deciphered, but their manuscript ciphertext and d’Émery’s letter lie beyond the supplied Gallica scan of Français 5190. Louis XIII’s and Châtillon’s clear prose in Français 3758 is transcribed; the remaining cipher needs a key or a second witness. write-up 23 Sept 2026 Passano from London to Francis I, 15 March 1530 — attempted, not read : the nine-entry ciphered account in Clairambault 331 is transcribed (402 proposed signs) and tested with positive controls, but no sign has a verified plaintext value. The clear letter concerns Wolsey's payments and quittances. write-up 22 Sept 2026 Niccolò Guidi di Bagno to the Secretariat of State, Paris, 5 January 1652 — attempted, not read: the suggested Francia 346 key is excluded. Four cipher pages in AAV Francia 104 repeatedly write 66 and 666 , impossible under the 1632 table’s rule that 6 is a separator. No transcript, decipherment, clear copy, edition or matching key was found; automated transcription was too noisy to publish. write-up 22 Sept 2026 Georges de Selve at Venice to Francis I, 1535–1536 — read in part: two “non-decrypted” despatches read with a key published without text Satoshi Tomokiyo had reconstructed Selve’s cipher as a table. Applied sign by sign and extended here (a null between doubled letters), it reads the letter of 5 July 1536 at 99.1%: why Charles V wanted Marseille, the French galleys under the guns of La Garde, and the Pope refusing him tenths. The 1535 letter reads at 95% outside the decipherer’s strikes: an Imperial informant sent to the French court as a merchant. write-up 22 Sept 2026 Johan Banér to Torsten Stålhandske, Hof, 29 December 1640 — read in part: an unsolved Cipherbrain letter broken from context cribs A copy of an intercepted field letter kept in Kircher’s correspondence. None of the Swedish keys on DECODE fits; durch and und let the solver write nach der Oberpfaltz und gegen die [442] , and the key was rebuilt from there. Banér warns that the enemy may draw in the troops acting in Silesia and asks Stålhandske to follow with caution and report through spies. 90% of the cipher read; a name, a corrupt stretch and the code words open. write-up 22 Sept 2026 “L’Estat du Roy de Navarre et de son party en France”, after 1580 — cipher broken here, read in part : DECODE’s “unknown sender, unknown graphic signs” in Harley 1582 is a French memoir on Navarre’s party. Broken from the ciphertext alone — a homophonic alphabet of ~50 signs in which the letter m is a group of dots , read as punctuation by every earlier pass. The prince of Parme, a party of malcontents, an engineer at Lisbon, Beaucaire, Carcassonne, d’Épernon. write-up 22 Sept 2026 A Venetian ambassador at Rome to the Doge, 29 April 1628 — read in part: the key rebuilt from a sibling record’s own decipherment DECODE R1862 had no transcription and no known contents. Its cipher is R1874’s syllabary, and R1874 is imaged with the chancery’s decipherment; aligning the two rebuilt the key. Cardinal Barberini had asked twice whether Palmanova was fortified and the Pontebba pass secured; 91% of the groups read. write-up 22 Sept 2026 “Johann Arndt”, Das zweyte Silentium Dei , 1798 (Beinecke Mellon MS 136, DECODE R2873) — read with the key drawn in the book. Catalogued as a ciphered letter, it is an alchemical manuscript book about a “magical machine” of burning glasses. Its 31 passages are in a Rosicrucian pigpen script whose key is on p. 83. t: Unsolved Historical Ciphers
b: The three source lists are exhausted here: everything on them that has its text online has been attempted, read, or shown to be blocked on archive access. The queue that used to sit in this place has moved to the tracker in the repository, and the open work now comes from the catalogue : twenty-five undeciphered letters from 1497 to 1610 that are on none of the lists, found by harvesting the BnF catalogue on Gallica and by reading the fine print of the cryptiana articles. Each carries its shelfmark and ark, the prior art, a difficulty class, and the check that would confirm it is genuinely open. Four of the twenty-five have since been taken to the leaf and read, partly read or closed (Lanssac, Béthune, Nevers, du Bellay) and sit at the foot of the list with their outcome; twenty-one are open, and only one of those has been viewed on the image. t: A reply to Zorzo Maino, 4 May 1446 — Attempted
b: An undescribed DECODE slip (R7898) turns out to be, by Mazzatinti’s 1883 inventory, the Sforza side’s reply to its agent Giorgio del Maino: clear Lombard Italian with runs of invented signs. A second cipher of the same day, Vincenzo Amidani’s from Milan, was found photographed on R7899. Both were transcribed and annealed without result. Among the 208 Sforza keys on DECODE, Simonetta’s cipher with Vincentius shows the family uses syllable and word signs, but no key matches. Sforza chancery → Giorgio del Maino · graphic signs in clear Italian · 4 May 1446 · attempted, not read A reply to Zorzo Maino, 4 May 1446 from Francesco Sforza Bibliothèque nationale de France, italien 1583 f. 68 (Archivio Sforzesco), DECODE R7898: a single slip, clear Lombard Italian with runs of invented signs between the clauses. DECODE gives no sender, recipient or date. The slip was identified from Mazzatinti’s 1883 inventory, and a second cipher of the same day was found on a neighbouring DECODE record. Both were transcribed and attacked, and every Sforza key on DECODE was checked. The key was not found. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 attempted Summary. DECODE R7898 is one image of BnF italien 1583 f. 68, with no metadata. The slip is dated in clear “M°cccc°xlvj die iiij° may”, 4 May 1446. Giuseppe Mazzatinti’s inventory of the Sforza papers in Paris ( Archivio storico lombardo X, 1883) describes it as “Risposta a quanto ha riferito Zorzo Maino (4 maggio). In cifre”: a reply, from Francesco Sforza’s side, to what his agent Giorgio del Maino had reported. The clear clauses are about not seeking or asking for something that “does not touch us”, and about seeking, “in the name of God”, what is due; the substance is in the cipher. The next leaf, f. 70, is another cipher of the same day, Vincenzo Amidani to Sforza from Milan, written in the same family of signs. It was found photographed on DECODE R7899. Both slips were transcribed (404 and 390 signs) and attacked with homophonic annealing against a Renaissance Italian model: every run gave nonsense. Among the 208 Sforza key records on DECODE, an eighteenth-century copy of Angelo Simonetta’s cipher with “Vincentius” and others shows how these systems work. Each letter has several signs, there is a sign for every vowel–consonant pair, whole words have signs, and nulls are mixed in. Its signs are not the ones used here, and no key names Maino. Status: not read. What would open it is the 1446 key for Maino or Amidani, or a colour scan good enough to transcribe every sign and diacritic exactly.

t: A reply to Zorzo Maino, 4 May 1446 — Attempted
b: The Paris volumes italien 1583–1593 are part of the Archivio Sforzesco that the Bibliothèque impériale bought in 1867. Mazzatinti’s entry for f. 68 sits under 1446 among letters to Sforza from Angelo Simonetta and Giovanni Stavoli in Venice, and from Foschino degli Attendolo in Cremona and Ancona. That spring Sforza was fighting in the Marche and bargaining with Filippo Maria Visconti, whose court at Milan Maino was reporting on. The slip carries an old number (21.), the folio 68, and the clear date line centred at the head. The clear text, in Lombard spelling ( nuy , havemo , refferemo ), holds the frame of the reply: … cetera. Che nuy no sapiamo [cipher] questi, ne cerchamo ne domandamo [cipher] tocha ad nuy cerchare questo, ma solamente cerchamo con lo nome de dio [cipher] nostra … [cipher] gli havemo rechiesto siano contenti fargli quello e dicto et ad quello se refferemo. [cipher] voglia essere contento mettere per scripto [cipher] se tra loro no gli sera noma uno che no habia [cipher] debitamente lo debiamo havere [cipher]. The second paragraph asks someone to be content to put something in writing, and argues that if only one of them lacks it, “we ought rightly to have it”. Who and what are in the cipher. f. 68, the whole slip: the date M°cccc°xlvj die iiij° may at the head, a cipher line, then two paragraphs of cipher with the clear phrases ( cetera Che nuy no sapiamo … , voglia essere contento mettere per scripto … ) between the runs. The cipher is unread. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, italien 1583 f. 68, via DECODE R7898.

t: A reply to Zorzo Maino, 4 May 1446 — Attempted
b: The cipher is written in invented signs: barred strokes, a barred b, a phi, a barred yogh, a long s, figure 8, a cross-circle and others, some with dots or hooks. Dotted separators ( :: , .:. ) stand between runs, and three paragraphs open with the same three-sign group. With the diacritic variants merged, f. 68 has 404 signs of 26 kinds. Two signs are 12% each, two are 7%, and the rest trail off. Several long runs repeat: an eight-sign group twice, another eight-sign group twice, a four-sign group four times. The cross-circle stands directly before clear clauses several times. In the related key described below it is the word sign for de . F. 70, Amidani’s letter of the same day, is all cipher: 390 signs of 31 kinds in another hand. It uses the same stock of signs, the phi, the barred b, the barred stroke and the cross-circle among them, but in different proportions. It is not certain that each sign means the same in both hands.

t: A reply to Zorzo Maino, 4 May 1446 — Attempted
b: Letter substitution by annealing. Both transcriptions were run against the it-cinquecento model with the clear text as context: free homophones, capped homophones, nulls allowed, and strict one-to-one swaps. The solver was first checked on a synthetic 400-letter Italian cipher, which it solved. On the real texts every run gave nonsense or collapsed into runs of one letter. Word patterns. The repeated eight-sign group fits uisconti (Visconti), but the key that implies breaks the other repeats. It was set aside. The Sforza keys on DECODE. All 208 key records from the Archivio di Stato di Milano (Carteggio Sforzesco, cartelle 1591, 1597, 1598) were downloaded and scanned. Cartelle 1591 and 1598 are sixteenth- and seventeenth-century. At the head of 1597 are eighteenth-century copies of fifteenth-century keys, each headed with the correspondent. Number 14, “Angelus cum cifra Vincentij”, was used with “Johannes de Stavolis, Augustinus, Baptista, Matheus, et Vincentius”. It gives two to five signs per letter, a sign for every syllable from ab to uz , word signs ( che , per , quale , con , ma , quello , de , perché ), names ( la S. V. , lo Duca de Milano , la Signoria Veneta ) and nulls. That is why simple substitution cannot work here. But its letter signs are not the frequent signs of f. 68 or f. 70, so it is a relative, not the key. Number 17, the 1447 cipher of Sforza’s envoys to King Alfonso, does not match either. No key names Maino or Amidani. Print. Mazzatinti gives only the heading. No edition or decipherment of either slip was found.

t: A reply to Zorzo Maino, 4 May 1446 — Attempted
b: A system of this kind, 800 signs split across two hands and read from a binarized scan, cannot be broken from the ciphertext alone. Three things would change that. First, the key itself: the 1597 cartella should be searched at full size, and the fifteenth-century keys in Lydia Cerioni’s La diplomazia sforzesca nella seconda metà del Quattrocento e i suoi cifrari segreti (1970) should be checked. Second, a colour scan of italien 1583 ff. 68–70 from the BnF, so that every sign and diacritic can be transcribed exactly. Third, the seventeen other 1446 cipher letters from the same volume on DECODE (R7899–R7915), several from correspondents named on key 14. A reading of any of them in that key would show how far the family runs.

t: Benedetto Fantini, Buda and Eger, 1517–1518 — a two-tier syllabic cipher, not read
b: Two letters of a Ferrarese in Ippolito d’Este’s household in Hungary (ASMo Ungheria b. 4, Fantini nos. 5–6; DECODE R1126–R1127, filed as “Jantini”). The cipher is of the family of Caprile’s 1519 letters, shown here to be syllabic from a pairing with their 1882 decipherment. The 1,370 columns were transcribed; a syllabary annealer that recovers a control of the same size produces no Italian, and Caprile’s values do not fit. Buda and Eger → the Este court · two-tier sign cipher (syllabic family) · 1517–1518 · attempted, not read Benedetto Fantini, Buda and Eger, 1517–1518 Archivio di Stato di Modena, Ambasciatori, Ungheria b. 4, “Benedetto Fantini” nos. 5 and 6 (Vestigia 1849, 1851; DECODE R1126, R1127, where the writer appears as “Benedetto Jantini”). Two letters of a Ferrarese in Cardinal Ippolito d’Este’s household in Hungary, one with two full pages of cipher. The cipher was transcribed column by column and attacked from the ciphertext alone, and with the only sibling key there is. It is not read. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 22 September 2026 key not found Summary. The catalogue listed two DECODE records of “Benedetto Jantini”, Ferrara, 1517–18, “partially decrypted”. The public Vestigia database has the whole file under the right name, Benedetto Fantini, nos. 1–7 (1515–1518). Only nos. 5 and 6 carry cipher, and none of the seven has a decipherment, a clear copy or a gloss. DECODE’s “partially decrypted” reflects the clear passages. The cipher belongs to the family of Giuliano Caprile’s 1519 letters from the same household: a base stroke with a small sign above it, plus bracket-shaped signs. A pairing of Caprile’s letter of 1 May 1519 with its 1882 decipherment shows that family to be syllabic, with the small sign giving the consonant, the base the vowel, and the brackets whole syllables. Fantini’s two cipher pages (1,370 columns) were transcribed and attacked with a syllabary annealer. The same annealer recovers a control text of the same length in the same structure, even with a tenth of its signs corrupted. On Fantini it produces no Italian, and Caprile’s values make the fit far worse. Status: attempted, not read. It needs a key or a decipherment from the Este chancery, or a paired letter in Fantini’s own key.

t: Benedetto Fantini, Buda and Eger, 1517–1518 — a two-tier syllabic cipher, not read
b: R1126 p. 1: the clear opening (“Da Buda … scripsi a V. S. Ill.ma … il negotio dla restitution de Modena et Regio per la mandata dil duca Lorezo in Franza”) and the start of the cipher. Image: Archivio di Stato di Modena, Fantini letter (R1126 p. 1), via DECODE R1126. DECODE ASMo no. Date, place Cipher R1126 Fantini no. 5 (Vestigia 1849) [spring 1518?], Buda. Vestigia and DECODE give “1517”, the file year p. 1 after six clear lines (18 lines) and all of p. 2 (25 lines): 1,370 columns; pp. 3–6 clear R1127 Fantini no. 6 (Vestigia 1851) 6 March 1518, Eger (“Agria”) five short lines, about 46 columns, in a torn and faded leaf The letters are addressed to a lord styled “Vostra Signoria Illustrissima” and “Vostra Eccellenza”, most likely Duke Alfonso I. The clear opening of no. 5 asks for news of the restitution of Modena and Reggio and of Lorenzo de’ Medici’s journey to France. The clear pages 3–6 report the Hungarian diet and the governors appointed around the young Louis II. They continue the letter; they are not a decipherment. Fantini’s other letters (nos. 1–4 and 7, 1515–1518) are in clear.

t: Benedetto Fantini, Buda and Eger, 1517–1518 — a two-tier syllabic cipher, not read
b: Each unit is a base stroke written on the line (shapes like 7, m, n, g, y, 4, t, a) with a small sign written above it (o, 2, 1, b, &, c, L, s, d, 9 …), or an L-shaped bracket enclosing a small sign. The transcription ( t1126.txt ) counts 1,370 columns: 167 distinct forms, 299 of them brackets (22%) with 22 different inner signs. The commonest columns are 2/7 (77), -/7 (63), o/7 (60), -/y (47), -/g (46) and &/m (44). Caprile’s letters of 1519 use the same kind of script. His letter of 1 May 1519 (DECODE R1130) mixes clear sentences with short cipher runs, and the 1882 archivist’s decipherment (Vestigia 1860, “4c”) covers them. Aligned by hand, the runs read as syllables. intertenere is seven columns, y/7 9/7 [y] c/7 [y] z/m [m]: i, n, te, r, te, ne, re. The same opening recurs in intertenerlo and in che termine . oratore is o [ra] [to] [re], twice. In that key base 7 carries no vowel, m gives e and n gives o. Tested on stretches not used to build it, the values placed 16 of 18 letters in the true text, against 8.1 on average for shuffled text.

t: Benedetto Fantini, Buda and Eger, 1517–1518 — a two-tier syllabic cipher, not read
b: Siblings, clear pages, print. All seven Fantini letters on Vestigia. Bonzagni’s letters of 1512–14, the other Este–Hungary cipher, use a different, simple alphabet. DECODE has no key record from Modena for 1490–1540, and nothing turned up in print. Caprile’s key. Three pairings with the 1882 decipherments. R1131 is water-stained, and its alignment was no better than shuffled controls. R1134’s supposed interlinear decipherment is a second letter in clear with cipher insertions. R1130 gave the syllabic structure and about twenty values. A syllabary annealer ( syl_anneal.py : consonant for each upper sign, vowel for each base, a syllable for each bracket, scored with a sixteenth-century Italian 5-gram model). On a control of 2,200 letters from sixteenth-century Italian, enciphered in the same structure with two homophones per consonant, it recovers the text almost word for word once three base values are fixed. It still does so with 10% of the signs corrupted. On Fantini , eight restarts of 150,000 moves each, on the raw transcription and with the frequent pairs -/7 -/y and -/7 -/g merged as ligatures. The result is Italian-looking syllable salad that differs from restart to restart, scoring −2.37 per letter against −1.77 for the control’s true key. Seeding Caprile’s values drops the score from about −140 to −1,250. Because the method works on the control at this length and at this level of transcription noise, the failure lies in the model or the key family, not in the search. Fantini’s key is not Caprile’s, and it may use another division of labour between base and upper signs.

t: Benedetto Fantini, Buda and Eger, 1517–1518 — a two-tier syllabic cipher, not read
b: A key or decipherment in the Este chancery (ASMo, Cancelleria, Cifrari), or a letter to or from Fantini with its decipherment. A second, independent transcription of R1126. The present one has had a single reading, with a second pass over three lines only, and the pairing of small signs to bases is sometimes doubtful. R1127 is too short and too damaged to attack on its own.

t: Passano's ciphered account from London, 15 March 1530 — attempted
b: Catalogue item 281, BnF Clairambault 331 ff. 156–157: a clear Italian letter from Giovan Gioacchino da Passano to Francis I with an appended ciphered account. Nine entries, 402 proposed signs, were transcribed from Gallica. No value is verified; simple substitution and several alternatives failed controlled tests. The surrounding clear letter concerns payments and quittances from Cardinal Wolsey. London → Francis I · undetermined cipher · 15 March 1530 · not read Passano's ciphered account from London to Francis I BnF Clairambault 331, ff. 156–157. A mostly clear Italian diplomatic letter on English affairs ends in a ciphered account of payments. The account is newly transcribed here, but no defensible decipherment was found. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 23 September 2026 not read Summary. A copy of Giovan Gioacchino da Passano's letter to Francis I, dated 15 March 1530, survives in Clairambault 331. Its discussion of Henry VIII's divorce and dealings with Cardinal Wolsey is largely in clear Italian. An appended account occupies the next leaf, with nine enciphered entries and clear scudi amounts. Tomokiyo noted the cipher as undeciphered. The 402 proposed signs have been transcribed from Gallica images and tested against several language models and cipher hypotheses. An ordinary monoalphabetic substitution is not supported by a controlled test, but dotted and similar-looking signs may have been conflated in the provisional transcription. No sign has a verified plaintext value; the account remains unread.

t: Passano's ciphered account from London, 15 March 1530 — attempted
b: The heading calls this a copy of a letter to the king and an enclosed letter for the Grand Master, dated 15 March. Passano wrote from London. The clear text concerns the king of England, the papacy, the Emperor, and Cardinal Wolsey. Just before the cipher, Passano speaks of recovering payments and quittances, including the eight instalments and payments over four years, with May and November 1528 and May 1529 mentioned. The clear words identify the business of the account, not the wording of its entries. On the continuation the copyist writes that a page and three lines in cipher follow, then resumes clear Italian. The nine entries each end with an amount in scudi written outside the cipher. The signs themselves run without reliable word spaces. The start of the account on f. 157r. The figures at right are amounts, not a decipherment. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Clairambault 331, via Gallica. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Clairambault 331 f. 157r, via Gallica.

t: Passano's ciphered account from London, 15 March 1530 — attempted
b: The research transcription in ciphertext.txt has 402 proposed signs in 20 alias classes across both sides of f. 157. Its index of coincidence is 0.0819; 4 occurs 58 times and 3 51 times. These counts depend on visually grouping ambiguous cursive forms. Dots over some signs may be significant, and the transcription is not diplomatic. There is no reliable sign-to-letter key.

t: Passano's ciphered account from London, 15 March 1530 — attempted
b: One-to-one substitution search was run with period and modern Italian, French, Spanish, Latin, and English models; reversing and swapping adjacent signs did not help. Frequent signs were tried as spaces and nulls, and a many-to-one mapping and Italian word segmentation were tried. None produced connected language. The solver was checked on a same-length, same-entry-structure artificial Italian cryptogram: it recovered all 20 assignments, and recovered 18 and 17 with 10% and 20% random sign corruption. That comparison argues against simple substitution on the present sign inventory. It does not exclude a different cipher, systematic misclassification of glyphs, or missing key material. The neighbouring cipher in the same volume and the Passano/Sormano cipher in BnF fr. 3096 have different sign inventories. A related Passano report printed by Le Grand and calendared in Letters and Papers Henry VIII no. 6307 has a different date and cannot be used as a parallel plaintext for these entries.

t: Passano's ciphered account from London, 15 March 1530 — attempted
b: All 402 proposed signs are open. The next useful evidence would be an independent copy of this exact account, its contemporary decipherment, or Passano's matching London key. Before a new automated attack, the dotted and lookalike forms must be checked again against the full-resolution manuscript. The clear context is substantial, but it cannot justify guessed words in the cipher.

t: Schaeblin to Mr Jones, The Hague, 1753 — a letter about a cipher, not in one
b: BL Add MS 32256 f. 235 (DECODE R9218), catalogued as a ciphered numerical nomenclator letter of Mr Jones to Ben. Schaeblin. It is a clear English letter the other way round: Schaeblin, at The Hague on 16 January 1753, proposes a new French cipher of 3000 numbers on the model of the English one, and ways to disguise it by reversing or rotating the figures of each group or adding a dummy figure. The Hague → Mr Jones · clear letter about making a cipher · 16 January 1753 · not a cipher, read in full Schaeblin to Mr Jones, The Hague, 1753: a letter about a cipher, not in one British Library, Add MS 32256 f. 235 (DECODE R9218), catalogued as a two-page numerical nomenclator letter of Mr Jones to Ben. Schaeblin, not deciphered. The two pages are plain English, and the letter runs the other way: Schaeblin writes to Jones about the new French cipher he is compiling. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 21 September 2026 not a cipher Summary. DECODE lists R9218 as a ciphered letter from “Mr. Jones (Hague) to Ben. Schaeblin”, 1753, a numerical nomenclator with no decipherment. The images, fetched with the project’s DECODE login, show no cipher at all. It is a clear English letter dated at The Hague on 16 January 1753, signed “C. Ben. Schaeblin” and addressed “To Mr Jones”, so DECODE has the sender and receiver swapped. Schaeblin is compiling a new French cipher for the British service on the model of “the English Cypher”: 3000 numbers with blanks, the current ministers of every European court, and the European settlements in Asia, Africa and America. He proposes to disguise it without a second cipher by writing each number backwards, rotating its figures, or adding a dummy figure, each switch signalled by a “Change the Cypher” group. The only numbers on the page are his worked examples on 1753. Nothing is left to read; the French cipher itself was not looked for.

t: Schaeblin to Mr Jones, The Hague, 1753 — a letter about a cipher, not in one
b: Abbreviations kept (yr = your, ye = the, wch = which). Sr. — I have yr Honr of sending you inclosed a List of Names of most of the Ministers actually employed by the several Courts of Europe, in publick Affairs, which I intended to insert into the new French Cypher, and beg you will send it me back with the Additions or omissions that may be thought proper; I have added a List of names, that though in the English Cypher are either dead or no more in a publick Capacity, & in regard to wch I beg to be instructed. I did not think it necessary to send you also a List of the Places, Countries &c. I kept all those that are found in the English Cypher, & added many more, particularly ye names of most of the European Settlements in Asia, Africa, & America, as those places will chiefly be ye Subject of French Papers that may be wanted to be put into Cypher. As for ye rest, I shall make it in ye same manner as ye English, with ye same number of Cyphers, viz. 3000. and bring likewise in several Blanks. In Order to disguise it sometimes, without ye help of a Second Cypher, I propose several Methods, for Instance, by taking ye Figures of every Cypher backwards, E.G. 1753. write 3571. and vice versâ in decyphering it; Item, by putting ye first figure at ye End, E.G. 1753. write 7531. Item by putting ye last figure at ye head, as 1753 write 3175. & both vice versâ in decyphering. Item by adding any indifferent figure at ye head or end of each Cypher, wch is then only to be taken off in decyphering, E.G. 1753. write 21753, or 17536. Each of these Methods might be marked where it begins, by two or three Cyphers like the Change the Cypher in the last English Cyphers; & some other marks, where it changes again into the natural way. To avoid Confusion, I wd add a Note that these different Methods are not to be minded, or to follow one another immediately, without Changing before into ye natural way. I beg ye favour you will let me know, wch of these several Methods I may make use of, & as soon as I am honoured with yr Answer, I shall only want a week’s Time to put it entirely in order, & transmit a fair Copy of it. I shall do my Utmost Endeavours to make it as compleat as possible, & flatter myself to succeed as far as can be expected. — I have ye Honour &c. C. Ben. Schaeblin. To Mr Jones.

t: The Bavarian key volume: fourteen ciphertexts in Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591
b: Fourteen ciphertexts bound in the Munich chancery’s key volume, catalogued on DECODE as one “unknown sender” group, are letters in at least six systems. The Fulda protest of 1576 reads with the key five leaves earlier; Łaski’s letters of 1529–30 read from a key rebuilt from their glosses; seven German reports of 1534–35 on Hungary, the Turks and France are broken and read in part, one from ciphertext alone with a new sixteenth-century German model. Buda, Kraków, Rome, Pressburg → the Dukes of Bavaria · fourteen ciphertexts in at least six systems · 1529–1583 · read in part The Bavarian key volume: fourteen ciphertexts in Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591 BayHStA Munich, Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591 · DECODE R9291–R9427 · catalogue entry 161, “unknown sender to unknown recipient” Three letters read in full with keys from the same volume or rebuilt from interlinear glosses, one read at the time, eight broken and read in part; one blocked, one not a letter. Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 21 September 2026 read in part Summary. KAA 4591 is the Bavarian ducal chancery’s volume of cipher keys, with about a hundred key sheets from the 1520s to 1620 and fourteen ciphertexts bound in among them. DECODE catalogued the fourteen as one “unknown sender” group. They are separate letters in at least six systems. The Fulda note (R9325, 1576) reads in full with the key filed five leaves earlier (R9324). Three letters of Hieronymus Łaski and King John of Hungary (R9322, R9323, R9417, 1529–30) read in full or nearly from a key rebuilt from their interlinear glosses. A servant’s petition (R9416 f. 262) was deciphered at the time. Seven German reports of 1534–35 on Hungary, the Turks, Rincon and France are broken but only read in part: one (R9416 f. 263) from ciphertext alone with a new sixteenth-century German language model, five (R9408, R9409, R9410, R9413, R9427) from one faint contemporary gloss on R9427, and one (R9367) with a key in the volume’s own key register. The dot-grille of 1583 (R9319) is blocked because DECODE never imaged the cover letters it lies over, R9424 (1583) is attempted and open, and R9291 is a key fragment. No edition of the volume was found. Status: read in part. The working decrypts are machine output with gaps and are marked as such; none of the eight partial readings is yet a clean text.

t: The Bavarian key volume: fourteen ciphertexts in Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591
b: The key sheet five leaves earlier (R9324) has the same six null signs as the note, which is how the two were matched. It is a letter alphabet with doubled letters and a nomenclator of the Fulda affair: Pope, nuncio, the Abbot, Chapter and Dean of Fulda, the Bishop of Würzburg, the Emperor’s councillors, the Duke of Bavaria. Every sign resolves: Protestatus [est] abbas secreto coactum [se] ad litem acceptare Pontificis inhibitionem. Rogatus Pontifex ut contradicendo se interponat, declaret sive sponte sive vi contra canones esse. Si id fiat, Abbas agere cessat et cum Pontifice litigabit; … Consiliarii Caesaris iudicabunt, aut Pontifex tum facit quod iam voluit. Rogatus Dux Bavariae auxilio sit; Nuncius suadeat Pontifici ita ad protectionem via[m]. It is the deposed abbot Balthasar von Dernbach’s case: he protests that he was forced to accept the papal inhibition, and asks for the Pope’s declaration, the Duke’s help and the nuncio’s intercession.

t: The Bavarian key volume: fourteen ciphertexts in Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591
h: Hieronymus Łaski and King John, 1529–30 (R9322, R9323, R9417)
b: A graphic monoalphabetic cipher with three word signs. Interlinear glosses over some lines gave 153 word pairs, and the key from them reads the unglossed lines. The word signs follow from context: the Sultan “will have [†] in no other place than that of his brother” (King John); “concord between [†] and [X]” (Ferdinand). R9322 f. 121 , Buda, 24 November 1529: King John followed the dukes’ counsel; the Sultan, driven home by plague in his army, left John the kingdom of Hungary without tribute, with fifty guns and a thousand hundredweight of powder, and will return next summer against Ferdinand unless there is a concord. R9322 f. 122 : “Joannes Dei gratia rex Ungarie” to Duke Ludwig of Bavaria, sending Lazarus the Jew as envoy. R9417 , Kraków, 16 June [1530]: the siege of Buda; a concord best made through the imperial princes; Nicolaus Min… sent to the King of France; envoys to meet at Coburg. R9323 : Łaski tells the secretary of his pact with the Turk and warns the princes not to draw the Turks on themselves. Lines 4 and 8–10 are too faint to read in full.

t: The Bavarian key volume: fourteen ciphertexts in Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591
b: R9416. Folio 262 carries a contemporary German decipherment over every line. A servant asks the duke for seven years’ unpaid pension and for the office of Oberrichter at Straubing. Folio 263 has no gloss past its first lines. It was broken from ciphertext alone by annealing against a language model built for this target from the Deutsches Textarchiv’s German prints of 1472–1609. The faint gloss on its first lines agrees word for word with the solver’s text: “…von beden kunigen zu entlicher handlung gen Pressburg gesetzt…”. It reports the Pressburg negotiations between Ferdinand and John, a Turkish embassy, Imre Czibak offering tribute, and “den hern Griti abgefertigt” (Alvise Gritti, killed September 1534). One sign still has to be set by hand: it reads ch but the solver gives s . System A′. R9408, R9409, R9410, R9413 and R9427 share one sign family. R9427 has a faint gloss over ten lines. Aligned sign by sign, it shows that the commonest group w3vX is “ewr F.G.” (X is a code sign for Fürstliche Gnaden ) and gives a homophonic key: 4 and ω e , □ and 8 n (“48” = -en ), ↓ r , ÿ t , 5 a , π b/w , the slanted ‡ g , the upright H u/v , and so on. Every transcription was then re-checked sign by sign on the images, and look-alike signs that had been merged were split. A decoder applies the key and chooses d or ch for one ambiguous sign from context. R9410 (1535): “…vertragen … behandlung … sachen halben … kunig von Frankreich also gehandelt nit so vil als vor … bruederlich halten … wider den Turcken … gehorsamen underthenigen … datum”. R9413 (7 June, 11 July, 8 July 1534): with the key refitted to this letter, running German: “…genedig furst … empfangen … der orator des kunigs von Franckreich … Antonius Rincon … Constantinopel …”, with Niclas Jurisitz and “Cornelius”. R9427 (24 April 1534, postscript 25 April): “durchleuchtig hochgeborn furst gnediger … neue zeitung … underthenig”. R9408 (1534, addressed in Latin to “Sp…nio”, perhaps Cornelio Sperantio): Hungary, the Turk, Constantinople, Syria, “dreissig tausent man aus dem teutschen land gefurt”. R9409 (11,300 signs): intelligence with numbered articles and answers and a postscript “Auf den Reichstag…”; its decode is still noisy. R9367 , a son to his father, 22 March 1535, reads with block 2_4 (“H. Wilh.”) of R9423, a chancery register copying out nineteen keys of the 1520s–30s. The ciphered passages say he was questioned and denied everything, fears for his safety, and reports the Turks coming up; the postscript names a Friedrich and “Schmalcz”. Three signs are nulls. One sign and six lines remain unread.

t: Łaski, King John and a Bavarian at Wardein: three more ciphers in the Munich key volume
b: Three ciphertexts catalogued on DECODE as one “unknown recipient” entry are three letters to the Bavarian court from King John Zápolya’s circle. Łaski’s letter of September 1531 reads 99.5% in his own cipher with e and r swapped; a Latin letter of April 1533 on the diet of Pressburg and Ferdinand’s secret peace suit reads 95.3%; a German report from Wardein of March 1537 on the Turkish arming reads 91.3%, with two homophonic keys rebuilt from their glosses. Łask, Hungary, Wardein → the Dukes of Bavaria · three sign ciphers · 1531–1537 · read in part Łaski, King John and a Bavarian at Wardein: three more ciphers in the Munich key volume from John Zápolya → to Louis X, Duke of Bavaria BayHStA Munich, Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591 ff.226–228, 257–261 · DECODE R9403, R9414, R9415 · catalogue entry 162, “to unknown recipient, 3 ciphertexts” Two letters read in full, the third read to 91%. Keys: Łaski’s cipher from the same volume, and two new homophonic alphabets rebuilt from their interlinear glosses. Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 22 September 2026 solved in part Summary. DECODE lists three ciphertexts in the Bavarian ducal key volume KAA 4591 as one entry, with no sender and no recipient. They are three separate letters to the Bavarian court from the circle of King John Zápolya of Hungary, in three systems. R9403 is Hieronymus Łaski writing from Łask on 17 September 1531 to a councillor of the dukes. It is in Łaski’s own cipher, whose key was rebuilt from glossed letters in the same volume ( kaa4591 ), with the signs for e and r swapped; it reads 414 of 416 words. R9415 is a Latin letter of 18 April 1533 from King John’s side to the dukes, sent through their agent Aurelio Augurelio; its homophonic key was rebuilt from a one-word gloss by annealing and beam search, and it reads 95.3%. R9414 is a German report from Wardein (Nagyvárad) of 14 March 1537 by a Bavarian servant at King John’s court to Duke Ludwig; its key was rebuilt the same way and it reads 91.3% after three visual passes and a lexicon search. About ten words of R9414 are word signs with no key and about fifteen are blotted; the rest of its gaps are homophone ambiguities. No edition of any of the three was found. The archive’s permission is needed to publish the images, so this page shows none. Status: read in part (R9403 and R9415 read; R9414 below the 95% bar).

t: Łaski, King John and a Bavarian at Wardein: three more ciphers in the Munich key volume
b: Łaski’s graphic cipher (System B) was rebuilt from the glossed letters R9322 and R9417 in the same volume. In this letter the signs for e and r are the other way round (starred x = e, plain x = r) and some shapes differ. The sign DAG, three times, stands for King John. The docket says “anno 32”; the text is dated 1531. … cum hac hieme Turca oratoribus regis Ferdinandi hoc dederit responsum: Item ad dominum uestrum dicite illi nunquam ipsum amiciciam nostram, numquam pacem uel inducias consequuturum nisi cedat regno Hungarie amico nostro Ioanni regi serenissimo; quod nisi fecerit, ueniam ad querendum eum … Ruffus brought the dukes’ letters on the 15th, and Łaski thanks them. The Sultan told Ferdinand’s envoys this winter that there would be no friendship, peace or truce unless Hungary was given up to King John. Ships, guns and grain are being carried to the Danube and soldiers levied. The diet of Speyer will be short; Łaski is ill but will ride post to it, and the dukes and their friends should stop any decision against the king until he arrives. On the marriage he cannot yet write: within ten days he will settle it with the King of Poland, “for among the Poles, as among the French, the dowering of kings’ daughters is fixed by law.” Postscript: the councillor should put the king’s letters before the imperial estates.

t: Łaski, King John and a Bavarian at Wardein: three more ciphers in the Munich key volume
h: King John’s side to the dukes, 18 April 1533 (R9415)
b: The signs look like the System A′ set used by the dukes’ agents in the 1534–35 reports, but the A′ key does not fit, and neither does R9369, Augurelio’s own key of 1531. A gloss over part of line 3 (“incrementum”) gave the first values; annealing with a Latin model and a beam search gave the rest. Six signs after the clear passages are join nulls. … hostis noster una parte tractatum cum […] nobiscum inceperit, ex alia parte Turcarum Caesari pro pace clam supplicaverit, credimus D. vestras illud iam compertum habere. Georgius, the dukes’ servant, came back with their three reasons for urging concord at the diet of Pressburg. Ferdinand, “our enemy”, opened a treaty with King John while secretly suing the Sultan for peace; the Sultan’s own letters revealed it, so John recalled his orators and, at the Sultan’s request, sent his governor to him. Ferdinand boasts of peace but does not know its terms, and the dukes should not believe the rumour. The Turkish envoy in Vienna has made Ferdinand’s orator in Turkey “his” orator. The address on the fourth page, in clear, is to Aurelio Augurelio.

t: Łaski, King John and a Bavarian at Wardein: three more ciphers in the Munich key volume
h: From Wardein to Duke Ludwig, 14 March 1537 (R9414)
b: The opening, the date (“Datum Wardein … den vierzehenden tag Marcii anno siben und dreissigisten”) and the address (“Herzogen Ludwigen in Bayrn”) are in clear. The gloss over lines 6–8 gave the first values of a new homophonic alphabet; annealing and a beam with a sixteenth-century German model, three visual passes over every line and a one-edit lexicon search brought it to 91.3%. … dan der turkisch kaiser irn herrn befolhen hab das si in aller eil, ieder mit […] pferden gerust sein … The writer describes his journey back into Hungary and the state of Hungarian affairs; envoys of the pashas of Belgrade and Bosnia; the Turkish emperor ordering them to be ready and arming a hundred thousand men to win Hungary and then turn on Austria; Ferdinand’s party taking towns and villages. Duke Wilhelm never writes to him, so he asks Ludwig to intercede, citing his service to their father; he writes of his debts and leave, of mining and ore specimens, and of Hans Schwab of Kraków as carrier. Postscript: “der herr Camermaister hat mein ziffer”.

t: Łaski, King John and a Bavarian at Wardein: three more ciphers in the Munich key volume

About sixty-five are legible but unresolved: several homophones still have more than one value. R9415: nineteen words unread or doubtful, scattered (listed in r9415/count.txt ). t: Kauderbach’s intercepted despatches from The Hague, 1754–56 — an unseparated syllable cipher split and read
b: Ten Dutch copies of letters of the Saxon-Polish resident to Dresden, with passages in figures that DECODE says were never solved: the figures run on without separation. The digits 5 and 8 turned out to be nulls, the rest two-figure codes for letters and syllables; Kauderbach’s 1761 key in Dresden supplied the vocabulary, a one-to-one annealing search the numbers. All ten read: the Dutch quarrel over the augmentation of 1755, Yorke and the Saxon subsidy treaty, and the news of the Treaty of Versailles. The Hague → Dresden · two-figure letter-and-syllable cipher, unseparated, with nulls · December 1754 – May 1756 · read Kauderbach’s intercepted despatches from The Hague, 1754–56 Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 201: the Dutch copies of ten letters in which the Saxon-Polish resident Johann Heinrich Kauderbach put his secret passages in figures (DECODE R1043, R1044, R1954, R1958, R1959, R2078–R2082, “never solved”). The figures were split into their codes, the key found by machine against the vocabulary of Kauderbach’s 1761 cipher in Dresden, and all ten letters read. The figures were split into their codes, the key found by machine against the vocabulary of Kauderbach’s 1761 cipher in Dresden, and all ten letters read. Daniel Bourdeau · read 19 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. The Dutch opened and copied the letters of the Saxon resident at The Hague, and ten of the copies carry passages in figures. DECODE notes that none of them was ever solved there: Kauderbach wrote the figures without any separation, so that the Stadtholder’s office could not even tell where one group ended and the next began. Here the separation was recovered first. The digits 5 and 8 never occur inside a group and are nulls; with them removed the stream falls into two-figure groups (first figure 0–4, 6, 7 or 9, second 1–4, 6, 7 or 9), about sixty of them, one key for all four years. A plain homophonic solve failed. The key to the key was Kauderbach’s own cipher of 1761, kept in Dresden and imaged on DECODE (R936): two-figure numbers for letters and syllables ( ai, de, en, que, qui, pour… ), capitals for names, and a declared null. Its numbers do not fit the 1754 letters, but its vocabulary does. An annealing search for a one-to-one assignment of the 1754 codes onto it converged twice to the same key from different starts, and reading corrected the rest (01 = oi , 12 = ai , 27 = in , 66 = pour ). The ten letters now read at 65–97%. They cover the Dutch argument over the thirty-thousand-man augmentation in 1755, Colonel Yorke and the renewal of the Saxon subsidy treaty, and the news of the Treaty of Versailles of May 1756 (“une consternation extraordinaire ici”). The names stay in clear capitals ( S./. , Q./. , P./. ), whose 1754 meanings are known only from context. DECODE R2078, the copy of Kauderbach’s letter of 23 December 1754, first page: Les Etats de Holl. se separeront enfin samedi jusqu’à nouvelle convocation , then the figures, 9332131922166302… = il n’y a pas eu depuis longtems… ; the margin note reads Details relatifs a la Commission du C te d’Affry auprès de cet Etat . Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Archief Prins Willem V inv. 201, via DECODE R2078.

t: Kauderbach’s intercepted despatches from The Hague, 1754–56 — an unseparated syllable cipher split and read
b: Kauderbach (1707–1785) served the Saxon legation at The Hague from 1739 for almost thirty years; his despatches went to Count Brühl in Dresden (“Votre Excellence”). The Dutch post office copied them for the Stadtholder’s cabinet, and the copies are in the Koninklijk Huisarchief, Prins Willem V inv. 201, beside the d’Affry intercepts of inv. 192. Most are wholly in clear. DECODE catalogued the ten with figures, from photographs, and transcribed three. R1954 is a photocopy in a different hand, with letter-like figures; its transcription infers many digits from the pair rules and is the weakest.

t: Kauderbach’s intercepted despatches from The Hague, 1754–56 — an unseparated syllable cipher split and read
b: The Hague cabinet’s note on DECODE gives the reason for their failure: “the codegroups are not separated, by blanks or dots as is usually the case.” A first count showed no preferred period of two or three figures from the start of a passage, and the copyists’ spacing is not systematic. But two figures behave differently from the rest. 5 and 8 are rare (135 and 78 in the first 6,096 digits), never follow 5 or 8, and typically stand next to the clear sigla ( …254 M./. , J./. C./. 8095… ). Deleting them as single figures restores a clean two-figure phase (index of coincidence 0.027 against 0.021 for the shifted reading; for four-figure windows 0.155 and 0.161 at offsets 0 and 2, 0.103 at 1 and 3). A short Viterbi pass over the pair frequencies then repairs the places where a copyist dropped or doubled a figure. What is left is a table of about sixty two-figure groups: first figure 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 or 9, second 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 or 9, never 0, 5 or 8. Every letter shows the same frequency profile, so one key served from 1754 to 1756 at least. That table resisted a homophonic attack. A hill-climbing solver that reads synthetic French in the same form (sixty codes, two per cent noise, nulls, realignment) at 98% produced nothing on the real stream, in French, German, Dutch or Italian, with nulls or merged look-alike figures. The statistics of the stream still looked like language (entropy, vowel alternation 0.63, long exact repeats such as 19 29 14 44 nineteen times), so the units were not single letters.

t: Kauderbach’s intercepted despatches from The Hague, 1754–56 — an unseparated syllable cipher split and read
b: Hauptstaatsarchiv Dresden 10024 Loc. 08236/11 Bl. 5, the cipher for “Kauderbach in Den Haag”, 1761 (DECODE R936): pour chiffrer and pour déchiffrer , one number for each letter or syllable, the capitals A–Z for persons and states (S la Hollande , T l’Angleterre , U France ), and 6. est faux chiffre . DECODE’s transcription has “30 ni?” for 30 m . Image: Sächsisches Hauptstaatsarchiv Dresden, 10024 Geheimer Rat, Loc. 08236/11 Bl. 5, via DECODE R936. DECODE also holds the Dresden chancery’s cipher register, and one of its leaves is the key made for Kauderbach in 1761. It explains the 1754 system at once: a null figure, capitals in clear for the names, and a single number for each of about seventy letters and syllables. It is not the same key (its numbers use 5 and 8), but a successor of the same design. So the problem became an assignment: each 1754 code to a different item of the 1761 vocabulary. A simulated-annealing search over such assignments, scored by a four-letter French model built from contemporary diplomatic letters, reached the same key from two independent starts (seeds 22 and 24, −3.85 per letter, against −3.95 for true French on the same model), and it read. Reading then settled what the 1761 vocabulary lacked or the search had misplaced: 27 in (principales, provinces, interet), 91 ou , 33 qu , 79 st , 17 par , 22 pas , 46 qui , 66 pour , 23 fai , 76 ke (Yorke, Kniphausen), 77 z (treize, declarez), and the exchange of 01 oi and 12 ai , found independently by both readers (avoit, etoit, croire; raisons, mais, Pais Bas). 01 oi · 02 de · 03 re · 04 au · 06 ie · 07 le · 09 ne · 10 z? · 11 p · 12 ai · 13 y (re) · 14 i · 16 e · 17 par · 19 a · 20 fe? · 21 ce · 22 pas · 23 fai · 24 s · 26 et · 27 in · 29 t · 30 an · 31 b · 32 n · 33 qu · 34 du · 36 si · 37 en · 39 pr · 40 em? · 41 la · 42 ra · 43 c · 44 on · 46 qui · 47 f · 49 sa · 60 ent · 61 h · 62 que · 63 u/v · 64 d · 66 pour · 67 se · 69 l · 71 te · 72 g · 73 o · 74 ci · 76 ke · 77 z · 79 st · 90 k? · 91 ou · 92 r · 93 il · 94 m · 96 co · 97 x · 5, 8 nulls

t: Kauderbach’s intercepted despatches from The Hague, 1754–56 — an unseparated syllable cipher split and read
b: Word division, accents and the bracketed sigla are editorial; spelling is Kauderbach’s. […] marks an unread stretch, [?] a doubtful word. The clear passages are summarised in brackets. R2078, 23 December 1754 (about 90%) [Clear: the Estates of Holland will separate on Saturday until a new convocation.] Il n’y a pas eu depuis longtems une assemblée des etats de Holl. dont les objets de deliberations aient eté plus importans et en meme tems plus embarassans pour cet etat. D’un coté l’ouverture faite par le comte d’Affry presente mille epines, et quant au fond et quant a la forme des conferences a entamer …; de l’autre coté le colonel Yorke, qui ne s’endort pas dans ces circonstances, demande dans un memoire … des explications sur ce a quoi l’on peut se tenir relativement aux engagemens … The overture is to go through commissioners, conferences auxquelles le marquis de Bonnac agira et parlera comme chef de l’ambassade ; the opponents of England font assez connaitre que le principal but est de negocier un [traité] de neutralité . R1958, 20 June 1755 (about 90%) Le colonel Yorke m’a de nouveau assuré que sa cour est tres disposée au renouvellement du [traité] de subside, et qu’il ne doutoit pas que Mr le comte de Fleming … ne s’affectionnat a cette affaire a son arrivée a Hanovre. Yorke himself, dans des momens d’impatience, se sentoit incliné pour le sisteme des anticontinentistes ; Kauderbach thinks Hanover the right place pendant qu’on y est encore dans l’incertitude des evenemens en Amerique . R2079, 6 July 1755 (about 97%) Mr Haslang mande au resident de Baviere qu’il a la parole du duc de Newcastle que son [Y./.] sera renouvellé. Les apparences pour l’augmentation des [Z./.] diminuent de jour en jour … mais j’ai de fortes raisons de croire qu’il n’en sera que mieux pour nos affaires : Amsterdam would sooner renew the subsidies than vote an augmentation, qui dans leurs principes en est une pour le pouvoir du stadhouder . R2080, 22 July 1755 (about 97%) Les principales raisons qu’on a alleguées dans les debats qu’il y a eu sur ce sujet dans l’assemblée de [S./.] se reduisent en substance aux suivantes. Primo, que si le danger dont les Pays Bas sont menacés est tel que le lord Holderness l’a fait connaitre ici, une augmentation de trente mille hommes n’est pas suffisante pour le detourner. Secundo, qu’il faut constater avant toutes choses si le danger est reel pour la republique … Tertio, Holland cannot carry the burden alone while Zeeland, Utrecht, Friesland and Groningen plead exhaustion; quarto, dans le cas de necessité … tous les bons patriotes devroient sacrifier jusqu’au dernier sol et combattre pro aris et focis; mais qu’il faudroit auparavant s’expliquer avec [Q./.] . If it must be, new taxes and encore un cinquantieme denier . R1959, 5 August 1755 (about 95%) Le bruit que [E.M.] est en negociation avec [P.] ne paroit pas etre entierement sans fondement, et l’on assure que l’on a fait reellement quelques demarches aupres de ce prince, qui auroit promis a certaines conditions de se tenir tranquile tant que la [J./. C./.] ne remueroit pas. The ambassador of [Q./.] m’a sondé plusieurs fois sur les dispositions de [J./.] pour un [traité] de subside avec la sienne, a quoi je lui ai repondu constamment que je n’etois pas instruit, et que nous avions un [ministre] a Paris auquel il etoit plus naturel de s’adresser qu’a moi. R2081, 12 August 1755 (about 93%) Les [P.] sont aussi peu contens de [J./. C./.] que des [S./.]. Il me paroit qu’ils soupconnent [U./.] de ne vouloir pas elle meme au fond embrasser ces choses … Ils disent savoir positivement que le baron de Kniphausen declame plus fortement a Compiegne contre les [P./.] que [Q./.] meme. The rumoured negotiation with [M./.] is now denied: an attempt was made three months ago mais qu’elle n’a pas pris . R2082, 15 August 1755 (about 95%) L’ambassadeur de [Q./.] assure que [E.M./.] a ecrit au roi son maitre une lettre de sa propre main … qu’il avoit une armée de cent cinquante mille hommes a son service. [P./.] says openly that if the Dutch will not arm, [P./.] abandonnera le continent, et qu’elle ne sacrifiera pas … la seule occasion decisive d’humilier [Q./.] a la pitoyable conduite de [S./.], qui apres avoir eté assez avertie se tirera d’affaire comme elle pourra. R1044, 29 September 1755 (about 85%) L’on n’entend que des plaintes des membres contre [P.I.] de ce qu’ils font tant de prises en Europe sans en donner aucune raison au public ; England had taken pour plus de vingt millions de prises sur les sujets de l’Etat in the last war, qu’on recommençoit deja ce train . [Clear: Bolza’s power useless; Kauderbach’s arrears.] R1954, 16 March 1756 (about 65%) On the demand for a secours de six mille hommes : [S./.] ne peut refuser ce secours sans rompre entierement avec [B./.], qui prendra ce refus pour une infraction … ; if the neutrality party loses, le peuple s’animera … et entrainera l’Etat malgré lui dans la querelle . Many gaps: the transcription is weak. R1043, 25 May 1756 (about 85%) On a aujourd’hui des avis certains et positifs que le [traité] dont on parle depuis si longtems a eté signé a Versailles le deux de ce mois, et selon ce qu’on m’a [fait] conter confidemment, il a pour objet primo la neutralité des Pais Bas, secundo il doit y etre stipulé qu’aucune puissance ne donnera aucun secours a l’ennemi de l’autre … et tertio … de ne pas lui etre contraire relativement a l’election d’un Roi des Romains. Cette nouvelle a causé une consternation extraordinaire ici parce qu’on croit qu’il y a des articles secrets qui vont encore plus loin. Then Bonnac and d’Affry’s visit to an ambassador’s country house, et l’on a dit aussi beaucoup de reflexions sur cette demarche . The First Treaty of Versailles was signed on 1 May 1756.

t: Kauderbach’s intercepted despatches from The Hague, 1754–56 — an unseparated syllable cipher split and read
b: The sigla. The capitals with ./. (S, Q, P, U, J, C, M, E, Y, Z, W, B, G) are names written in clear, as in the 1761 key, but their 1754 meanings differ from it. S is almost certainly Holland (the Estates, the provinces), Y a subsidy treaty, Z troops; the rest are read from context only and marked as sigla in the readings. Rare codes. 10, 20, 40 and 90 occur twelve times in all and are guesses; 13 reads y and apparently also re (membres, reflexion); 66 may stand for er inside some words. R1954 (four pages in a letter-like hand) is read only at about 65%; a second transcription would lift it. Transcription slips. The DECODE transcriptions and the new ones both drop or double figures; the reading files list those met. The clear passages were transcribed quickly and are summarised, not edited. Shares read are the readers’ estimates of the cipher text given sense; 99.9% of the groups carry a key value.

b: Explore · the network The Key Web A cipher is rarely read on its own. A key rebuilt from one letter's margin is tried on its unread siblings. A contemporary key turns up filed under the next record number. A table published by Lasry or Tomokiyo is turned on a letter they never saw. Each gold key below is linked to the letters it read. Letters sit roughly by date from left to right. Hover to trace a key, click for the write-up, drag to rearrange. t: The Key Web
b: Every link is taken from an explicit statement in the target's notes: that a letter was read with a named key, unchanged or adapted, or that a key was rebuilt from that letter's own material. Links are not inferred from resemblance. A key that read only one letter is still shown, because where it came from is part of the story. Several of George Lasry's tables for the French correspondence of the 1520s and 1530s appear as one node. The file is keys.json .

t: Kurz von Senftenau to Trauttmansdorff, Hamburg 1639 — the vice-chancellor’s cipher rebuilt
b: Nine ciphered reports of the imperial vice-chancellor from Hamburg and Glückstadt, January to April 1639, in the Trauttmansdorff archive at Klášter (DECODE R3811–R4736). Mírka rebuilt the key in 2012 and read one letter but printed nothing. From the same interlinear glosses the key falls out as a regular table: 41–100 are consonant–vowel syllables, two consonants to each ten in reverse alphabetical order, and the low numbers are homophones. All nine letters decipher in a first pass: Banér in Lower Saxony, Arnim’s bid for pardon, the Danish mediation and its collapse. Hamburg & Glückstadt → Trauttmansdorff, Ferdinand III, Schwarzenberg · homophonic cipher with a syllable table · Jan–Apr 1639 · key rebuilt, all nine read in part Kurz von Senftenau to Trauttmansdorff, Hamburg 1639 — the vice-chancellor’s cipher rebuilt from Kurz von Senftenau → to Trauttmansdorff SOA Plzeň, pracoviště Klášter u Nepomuka, Rodinný archiv Trauttmansdorffů, inv. č. 200, kart. 9 · DECODE R3811–R3815, R4625, R4645, R4734, R4736 · 73 images, about 23,000 cipher signs A contemporary reader glossed one page; from it the whole table falls out. The other eight letters had never been deciphered. Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 19 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 solved in part Summary. Ferdinand Sigmund Kurz von Senftenau, the imperial vice-chancellor, spent the winter of 1638–39 in Hamburg, where the preliminaries of the Westphalian peace were being sounded with Sweden, France and the Danish mediator. His ciphered reports to Maximilian von Trauttmansdorff survive in the Trauttmansdorff family archive at Klášter. DECODE holds nine of them. Jakub Mírka rebuilt the key in 2012 from the interlinear decipherment on the first page of the 17 January letter and read that one letter, but he printed neither the key nor the text. Here the whole corpus was transcribed from the public DECODE images. The key was rebuilt from the same glosses, which show a regular table : numbers 41–100 stand for consonant–vowel syllables, two consonants to each ten in reverse alphabetical order, and the low numbers and signs are homophones for letters. With a German language model filling the rest, all nine letters decipher . They cover Banér’s invasion of Lower Saxony, Arnim’s bid for pardon, the Danish mediation and its collapse, and Kurz’s contempt for “universal” treaties (“ein teufflisch inventum”). The key is complete, but the reading is not: the transcription was a single pass, so 20–45 % of each letter is still garbled. A checked second transcription would close it. Status: key rebuilt; nine letters read in part.
