t: Kurz von Senftenau to Trauttmansdorff, Hamburg 1639 — the vice-chancellor’s cipher rebuilt
b: About 210 glossed signs on the first two pages of R3811 give the pattern straight away: 83 de, 82 di, 84 da; 43 re, 42 ri, 44 ra; 51 no, 52 ni; 72 hi, 74 ha; 93 be; 57 mi, 59 ma. Every ten is split into two halves of five. Each half has one consonant, and its first four places run o i e a : +1 +2 +3 +4 +5 41–45 ro ri re ra pu 46–50 po pi pe pa lu 51–55 no ni ne na mu 56–60 mo mi me ma hu 61–65 lo li le la ku 66–70 ko ki ke ka du 71–75 ho hi he ha gu 76–80 go gi ge ga bu 81–85 do di de da cu 86–90 co ci ce ca — 91–95 bo bi be ba us 96–100 — is es e? ru The consonants run backwards through the alphabet from 41: r p n m l k h g d c b. The fifth place of each half is a separate series of -u syllables, and each was fixed from words: Reputation and Graf von Puechheim (45), illustrissimi (50), unmüglich (55), Hunger and Churbrandenburg (60), Ankunft (65), durch (70), Herzog Augustus (75), Magdeburg, Meckelburg (80), pericula (85), Haus Österreich (95), zurück, darüber (100). The numbers 1–40 and some twenty letter and graphic signs are homophones for single letters. The commonest are 28 r, 31 n, 27 s, 26 t, 39 c, 35 h, 18/19/20 e, 17/15/16 i, 21/22/23 a, 10/11/25 u, 12/13/14 o, 36/38 g, π/α m, ψ/φ z, w /#z-tail n and 29 qu. A few stand for pairs: 9 te, 6 se, c si, n ve, d so, k ti and a looped ℓ tu. A handful of marks are nulls or flourishes. The full table, with counts, is in KEY.md . This is Mírka’s description (“homophonic substitution, bigrams, nulls, no codes”) written out as a table.

t: Kurz von Senftenau to Trauttmansdorff, Hamburg 1639 — the vice-chancellor’s cipher rebuilt
b: The readings below are word-divided and lightly normalised from the machine decipherment. Where the text is garbled, the summaries say so. 17 January (R3811) Nothing can be done with Duke Georg of Lüneburg: ohne Widerstand ist der Feindt über [the Elbe]. Recruits are going to Austria and money is short. France, Sweden and Holland im Werck sein, zum König eine ansehnliche Legation zu schicken [are about to send a considerable embassy to the King] of Denmark, to prevent a congress. Herzog Augustus von Sachsen-Lauenburg wolle sich in dennische Protection begeben [Duke August of Saxe-Lauenburg means to place himself under Danish protection]. Arnim, suspected over the Friedland affair, swears he plotted nothing against the Peace of Prague, and Kurz advises a Protectorium in optima forma . These are the points of Mírka’s summary, one by one. 27 January (R3813), a twenty-page memorandum Der Feindt gehet ganz unverwehrt hieher, zieht sich gegen Waltzwedel [the enemy comes on quite unhindered, heading for Salzwedel]. Kurz writes that it is besser ein ungeschlossener, durch den Feindt zertrennter Craistag als ein geschlossener mit einer expressen Neutralitet [better a Kreistag left unconcluded and broken up by the enemy than one concluded with an express neutrality]. He advises a defensive war to keep Austria, Bohemia and Silesia. He distrusts Salvius, who is “voller Gifft contra Domum Austriacam”, and weighs a secret particular treaty through Denmark or Brandenburg. He calls the universal treaties and safe-conducts “ein teufflisch inventum et ad exclusionem omnium tractatuum”. France wants Lorraine, Alsace and das Kaiserthumb ; mit Schweden ist umb ein leichters noch zu accordiren [Sweden is somewhat easier to come to terms with]. 3 and 6 February (R3812, R3815) Banér’s plundering will bring das ganze Stift of Halberstadt zu Grund . Between Denmark and Sweden there are grosse disgusti . Sweden wants half of Pomerania and an amnesty and will not come to a congress while it does not feel the war at home. Arnheim ist gestern Abent bei mir gewesen : Arnim describes Banér’s army as zehentausend Mann, ein ermattetes, armseliges, hungeriges Volck [ten thousand men, worn out, wretched and hungry]. To the Emperor, Kurz reports the King of Denmark ganz perplex and the Danish Reichsrat irresolut und pusillanimes . 10 and 13 February (R4625, R4645) A plan to keep the Lower Saxon Circle divided and to hold Halberstadt, Magdeburg, Hildesheim and Wolfenbüttel follows. It warns that the imperial army is gar ruinirt, et venter caret auribus . The King’s conditions for his mediation have proved empty, and wir wollen uns dannoch und auch allein wehren [we will defend ourselves nonetheless, even alone]. Count Pentz says the King must drop the mediation and denounce Sweden: ergo ruptura tractatuum hic est principium coniunctionis . 8 and 14 April (R4734, R4736) Die Interposition ist schon expirirt : the King says he has bound hands and will do nothing per force . From Glückstadt, Christian IV’s residence, Kurz writes von hinnen wolt man mich nit gern dimittiren . He reports the Danish complaint that war in Austria is paid for with peace in Lower Saxony while the Swedes sit in Mecklenburg and Pomerania: für solche Mauren geben wir unser Schweiss und Bluet [for such walls we give our sweat and blood]. A courtier ist der gescheideste in dissimuliren [is the cleverest at dissimulating]. R4736, Glückstadt, 14 April 1639: the letter is almost entirely in cipher. It opens Von hinnen wolt man mich nit gern dimittiren … . Image: Státní oblastní archiv v Plzni, letter from Glückstadt, 14 April 1639, via DECODE R4736.

t: Kurz von Senftenau to Trauttmansdorff, Hamburg 1639 — the vice-chancellor’s cipher rebuilt
b: Agents transcribed all 73 DECODE images token by token, two at a time. Clear text went in braces and the glosses were attached to their numbers. Plain homophonic annealing with a German 5-gram model (Grimmelshausen and Gutenberg German, early spelling) collapsed into enenen… , even with a letter-frequency penalty. The glosses turned the problem into a structured one: one consonant per half-ten and one value per single sign, seeded with seventeen glossed values. That solver produced fluent German on the first run ( ich müesse die Kranckheit beschreiben, damit man sich den remediis darnach zu richten… ). The irregular signs were then fixed by reading them in context and by ranking candidate values with the language model. Of the 22,913 transcribed cipher signs, 98.3 % then had a value. A checked second pass followed on 21 September 2026. Agents compared every line of the 73 transcriptions with crops of the images, working from a printout of each sign’s value, and changed a sign only where the image showed it. About 360 signs were corrected. The commonest slips were a plain c written for the looped sign worth tu , a bold 9 written for the hooked sign worth w , and 6 written for φ ( z ). In R3813 a crossed ƒ-like sign worth ta had been merged with another sign. A script fault had also dropped 56 cipher lines that began with a graphic sign. The language-model score of the decipherment improved on eight of the nine letters. Of 23,699 cipher signs, 99.9 % now have a value.

t: Kurz von Senftenau to Trauttmansdorff, Hamburg 1639 — the vice-chancellor’s cipher rebuilt
b: Transcription, not key. After the checked second pass, the garble that remains sits where the image itself does not decide: digits run together, blots and overwritten figures. The Latin passages are still the weakest. tr/PASS2_LOG.md lists the remaining lines file by file. α was first read as m , which gave Salv- before l . The images show two signs: the small upright α is sa ( Salvius , caesaris , universal- , Sachsen ), and a larger looped form is m . In one hand (R3813) the two shapes are hard to tell apart. 99 is uncertain ( e ?), 90 occurs once, and 96 does not occur. The signs 3, 4, 5, 7, m , #s-loop, #dot and p are read as nulls or are unassigned (grade M). The recurring group read ml in R3812–R3814 is sometimes part of universal- and sometimes a name. It is unresolved. The two Banér copies in R4645 are transcribed: to Lüneburg, 10 January 1639, and to the Lower Saxon envoys, 29 January 1639, refusing to leave the Circle. The endorsement on R4734 names the addressee as Count Schwarzenberg. Kurz’s own clear postscript on R4645 is only half legible.

t: Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573 — the Polish election embassy’s cipher
b: BnF fr. 4735 f. 124, catalogued “avec chiffre” with no decipherment. The key is a homophonic letter cipher with word signs, recovered from a sibling letter whose Court decipherment survives as gutter-cut marginal notes (“car je n’ay pas cinquante escuz”) and checked against the fragments on f. 124 itself. Both passages read, and the key then opens the three election letters whose only “decipherment” was that cut gloss: the Polish nation “autant vénale … comme sont les Allemans”, the Emperor’s three hundred thousand spent for nothing, and on 9 May the election carried against the Sultan, the Emperor, the princes of the Empire, Spain, Muscovy and Sweden, “qui tous estoient bandez contre vostre Majesté”. Tomokiyo’s published table for the cipher is corrected. Warsaw → Paris · homophonic letter cipher with word signs · 1573 · read Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573 to Charles IX BnF Français 4735, no. 51, f. 124 · 100 signs in two passages · catalogued “avec chiffre” with no decipherment · two weeks before Anjou’s election to the Polish throne Key recovered from the glossed sibling letters of 24 April (ff. 154, 156) and the decipherer’s marginal fragments on f. 124 itself; 96 of 100 signs read · the same key then reads the election letters of 1 and 9 May (ff. 160, 164, 174) Daniel Bourdeau · solved 17 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 solved Summary. Guy de Saint-Gelais, sieur de Lanssac, joined Jean de Monluc, bishop of Valence, at Warsaw in April 1573 to help elect Henri d’Anjou king of Poland. His letter to Charles IX of 26 April is in clear except for its first three lines and a clause near the end; the BnF catalogue notes “avec chiffre” and lists no decipherment, because the decipherment that follows it in the volume (no. 52, ff. 126–127) is of the mémoire on Polish affairs that the letter announces, not of the letter. The same volume holds five more Lanssac letters in the same cipher whose Court decipherments were written in the outer margin and cut by the gutter on the microfilm; enough survives of them to fix a crib (“car je n’ay pas cinquante escuz”), and f. 124 carries its own marginal fragments (“…d’Allemagne”, “qui passent”, “moins esté retenu”, “…ou oultre”). The two passages read: Sire, despuis les dangiers qu’encontrent en Allemagne les françois qui passent, et vostre ser[vice?]… and j’eusse sans doubte pour le moins esté retenu ou empesché de passer oultre . Lanssac had reached Poland only on 25 February, delayed across Thuringia, Meissen and Brandenburg, and owed his passage to the King’s Saxon pensioners Miltitz and L(u)elz, who escorted him with a strong troop of their friends. Status: read; the first word of passage one, the sign sequence for “françois” and four signs after “vostre ser” carry a query. Tomokiyo’s published table for this cipher is corrected (first row shifted by one letter from m). Section 05 carries the key into the three election letters of 1 and 9 May, whose catalogued “déchiffrement” is only the gutter-cut gloss.

t: Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573 — the Polish election embassy’s cipher
b: BnF fr. 4735 is the second of the volumes of “pièces originales et de copies concernant l’histoire de France, 1569–1588” and, from no. 5 to no. 80, the Court’s file of the Polish election embassy: Monluc’s letters from Konin and Warsaw, the Polish memoranda on St Bartholomew, the King’s replies, and the letters of Lanssac and Gilles de Noailles from Warsaw and Płock in April and May 1573. The catalogue marks “avec chiffre et déchiffrement” against Lanssac’s letters of 24 April (nos. 60–61), 1 May (63, 65) and 9 May (70), and “avec chiffre” alone against no. 51 of 26 April. Gallica has the whole volume as a microfilm scan (btv1b9060724s, 614 unlabelled canvases); the folio of no. 51 is 124, canvas 242, not the 126 the catalogue entry here first gave. Fr. 4735 f. 124, upper half: the ciphered opening after “Sire”, the clear itinerary, and the second passage after “j’eusse sans doubte”. The decipherer’s gloss sits in the left margin, cut by the gutter. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 4735 f. 124, via Gallica btv1b9060724s canvas 242. What the catalogue calls the siblings’ decipherments turns out to be this same marginal gloss, line by line beside the cipher, on ff. 154, 154v, 156 and 157. The microfilm keeps only the last centimetre or two of each gloss line, but on f. 154v the first line of cipher stands beside “Car je n’ay pas cinquante escuz”, and the cipher line is exactly long enough for it.

t: Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573 — the Polish election embassy’s cipher
b: Homophonic letters. Separate graphic signs (crosses, bars, figures, letter-like forms) written continuously, with points, commas and short bars as word separators. Common letters have two or three signs: e ✕ ✱ Γ Δ, a ⊤ π H, r ϕ ⊨, s 9 Lo IIII, i ⊢ ϙ, n ſ o-o, u/v o+ ff o+o, m 8 ᥙ, l 3 ⊥, o ꞔ L, t ʓ ттт, p y N, d ‡, c 7 ⋔, g ∞, f o-, h +, qu ꞗ. Syllable and word signs. et ♁, nt ꝸ, st 8 with a dot, de ᒐ, ou ᛏ, ns Λ, car Z, pour †, and Allemagne as a Z with a lower curl. Over the 741 signs transcribed from f. 124 and the first blocks of ff. 154 and 156, the merged frequencies are French: e-signs 17.6 %, then r, a, s, n, u, t, o. Tomokiyo’s table. His “Lansac’s Cipher” (cryptiana, French Ciphers during the Reigns of Charles IX and Henry III ) has the right signs but its first row is displaced by one letter from m onward (his ſ m, L n, б p, ⊨ q, 9 r, ʓ s, o+ t read n, o, qu, r, s, t, u ), his Γ = i is e , his ‡ = h is d , and the “pour” cross is the letter h in one of its two shapes. The corrected table with the evidence for each sign is lanssac/key.tsv .

t: Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573 — the Polish election embassy’s cipher
h: The key, and how it was found
b: The glossed crib. f. 154v line 1, Z ⊢✕ | ſπϙ | y⊤9 | 7⊢ſꞗπſʓ✕, beside “Car je n’ay pas cinquante escuz”, reads car ie nai pas cinquante and fixes eleven signs at once, including car = Z, qu = ꞗ and the shift in Tomokiyo’s row. Passage two by hand against its gloss “moins esté retenu … ou oultre”: † ⊥ ✕ · 8 ꞔ ⊢ o-o 9 · ✱ 8̣ Γ · ϕ ✕ ʓ ✱ ſ o+ = pour le moins esté retenu , then ᛏ Γ ᥙ y ✕ 9 7 + ✱ · ᒐ = ou empesché de , y π 9 Lo ✕ ϕ ꞔ ff 3 ттт ⊨ Γ = passer oultre , ᥙ · π ꟿ Lo = mais . Each new sign was checked in the siblings before it was kept. Annealer over the whole transcription (French 5-gram model, symbol to letter or short code, the crib letters pinned). The free signs come out the same across seeds and read words in the siblings that the cribs never touched and the glosses confirm: les dangiers , causé , l’autre , beaucoup , grant seigniur , du monde , changement , sur la teste , recommandé , doubte ou vous mettre . Lattice decode of f. 124 : each sign given its candidate values, beam search on the same model. Passage one falls out as despuis les dangiers qu’encontrent en Allemagne les françois qui passent et vostre ser… , matching the three marginal fragments “…es dangier”, “…d’Allemagne”, “qui passent”. Controls. The pinned key scores −2193 to −2198 on the real sign order and −2924 to −3009 on three shufflings of the same signs. A blind run with nothing pinned reaches a higher score (−2033) but recovers only 6 of the 21 crib letters: on a transcription this noisy the language model alone does not find the key; the cribs and the glosses do, and the model then fills the rest consistently.

t: Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573 — the Polish election embassy’s cipher
b: Cipher passages in brackets; sixteenth-century spelling kept; ? marks an uncertain sign, braces an unread run Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573. Sire, [despuis? les dangiers qu’encontrent en Allemagne les françois qui passent, et vostre ser{o r h e}] Les empeschementz et les plus grandes causes qui ayent esté depuis deux {ans} … toute la Turinge, Misnie et Marche de Brandebourg m’ont tellement retardé que je n’arrivay en Polongne à Mezeritz que le vingt-cinquiesme de febvrier. Et sans la faveur que j’ay receue d’aulcuns des serviteurs et pensionnaires de vostre Majesté, principalement des Sieurs Alexandre de Militiz et George Luelz(?), qui me y ont accompagné avec bonne et forte troupe de leurs amis et assisté de leurs moyens, j’eusse sans doubte [pour le moins esté retenu ou empesché de passer oultre. Mais], la grace à Dieu, je me suis rendu il y a desjà long temps avec Monsieur de Valence, lequel m’a enseigné l’estat auquel estoient les affaires qu’il a bien et dignement commencées et continuées jusques icy, et dont j’ay faict ung recueil ensemble de ce que j’ay peu juger, lequel j’envoye à vostre Majesté. Et ne sçachant à présent rien digne d’escrire oultre le contenu audict recueil, sinon que j’ay receu la lettre qu’il a pleu à vostre Majesté m’escrire du xxiii(?) de febvrier, en obéissant à laquelle je me fauldray(?) à me comporter de sorte que j’espère que le bien de vostre service et les affaires qui sont à promouvoir par deçà en demeureront advancez. Je priray le Créateur vous donner, Sire, en très parfaicte santé très contente et longue vie. De Warsauvia, le xxvi e d’avril 1573. English translation Sire, [since the dangers that the French who pass through meet in Germany, and your ser{vice?}…] The hindrances, and the greatest causes there have been these two {years} … all through Thuringia, Meissen and the Mark of Brandenburg, delayed me so much that I did not reach Poland, at Mezeritz, until the twenty-fifth of February. And without the favour I received from some of your Majesty’s servants and pensioners, chiefly the Sieurs Alexander von Miltitz and Georg Luelz(?), who accompanied me there with a good strong troop of their friends and helped me with their means, I should without doubt [at the least have been detained or prevented from passing on. But], thank God, I joined Monsieur de Valence a good while ago, who has told me the state in which the affairs stood that he has so well and worthily begun and carried on until now, and of which I have made a summary, together with what I have been able to judge, which I send to your Majesty. And knowing nothing at present worth writing beyond what that summary contains, except that I have received the letter your Majesty was pleased to write me on the 23rd(?) of February, in obedience to which I shall not fail to conduct myself so that I hope your service and the affairs to be advanced here will profit by it, I pray the Creator to give you, Sire, in most perfect health a most contented and long life. From Warsaw, the 26th of April 1573. The Miltitz were Saxon nobles in French pay; Mezeritz (Międzyrzecz) is the first Polish town on the road from Frankfurt an der Oder to Poznań. The “dangers” are the hostility to Frenchmen in Protestant Germany after St Bartholomew’s Day, which is why this passage is in cipher and the itinerary is not. Lanssac reached Monluc at Warsaw in time for the election Diet, which had opened on 5 April; Anjou was elected on 11 May. The recueil he announces is no. 52 in the volume, “Estat des affaires de Pollongne selon que le Sr de Lanssac y a peu aprendre”, in clear.

t: Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573 — the Polish election embassy’s cipher
h: The election letters, read with the same key
b: The catalogue credits Lanssac’s letters of 24 April, 1 May and 9 May with a “déchiffrement”. It is the Court decipherer’s note in the outer margin, and the microfilm keeps only the last word or two of each of its lines; the cipher passages themselves had never been readable from the scan. With the key they read in substance. Transcriptions and sign-by-sign choices are in lanssac/reading_siblings.txt ; unread runs are in braces, and words read from the gloss and the sign count rather than sign by sign carry a query. Fr. 4735 f. 174 (canvas 329): the six ciphered lines of the 9 May letter and the gloss beside them — “…la volunté et / …du Grand / …de l’Empereur / …de l’Empire / …de Spaigne / …et du / …Suède, qui tou[s] / …bandez contr[e] / …Majesté”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 4735 f. 174, via Gallica btv1b9060724s canvas 329. To Charles IX, Warsaw, 1 May 1573 (f. 160). … que pour en envoyer devant selon que les occasions des affaires premièrement surviennent. [Car je veoy que ceste nation est autant vénale et? sujette à se laisser gaigner par argent comme sont les Allemans leurs voisins.] Ce jourd’huy ilz mettent en délibération s’ilz doibvent prendre pour Roy ung Piaste ou ung prince estrangier, mais on sçait bien quelle en doibt estre la résolution. To the duc d’Anjou, Warsaw, 1 May 1573 (f. 164). … c’est de latin et d’argent, et à bonne quantité, car il y aura de quoy l’employer [à vostre désir]. … les traverses de nos contraires qui n’y espargnent rien pour nous empescher, [{5 signs} a despendu {4 signs} ensemble {7 signs}. C’est en ceste négotiation; l’Empereur en y a despendu plus de trois cens mil {3 signs}, si faict {5} {5}, riens qu’il vaille pour ser{…}. Seulement il le trouble {7 signs}, desseing faisant le pis qu’il peult contre vous.] Encores ne veulx-je faillir, Monseigneur, de vous ramentevoir … que vous fassiez donner ordre que les navires soient prestz pour l’embarquement. To Charles IX, Płock, 9 May 1573 (f. 174). … ayant esté employé en un affaire de telle importance et qui est reüssy tant heureusement [contre la volunté et menées? du Grand? Seigneur, de l’Empereur, des princes de l’Empire?, du Roy d’Espaigne, du Moscovite, {3 signs} et du Roy de Suède, qui tous estoient? bandez contre vo[st]re Majesté]. Si est-ce que j’auray encores plus d’occasion de louer Dieu si je suis tant heureux que vostre Majesté me juge digne d’estre employé en ce second … English 1 May, to the King. For I see that this nation is as venal and as ready to let itself be won by money as are the Germans, their neighbours. — 1 May, to Anjou. … has spent … together …. It is in this negotiation; the Emperor has spent more than three hundred thousand in it … and done nothing worth the name …; he can only trouble the design, doing the worst he can against you. — 9 May, to the King. … an affair of such weight, which has succeeded so happily against the will and the intrigues of the Grand Seigneur, of the Emperor, of the princes of the Empire, of the King of Spain, of the Muscovite and of the King of Sweden, who were all leagued against your Majesty. The 9 May list is the field of the 1573 election as the French embassy saw it: Archduke Ernest for the Emperor and Spain, Ivan IV, John III of Sweden, and a Habsburg-leaning party among the German princes. The “Grand Seigneur” (the Sultan) is the surprise, since the Porte was generally reckoned to favour the French candidate, and that group is read from the gloss (“du Grand”) and the sign count rather than sign by sign. The 300,000 of f. 164 is the Habsburg outlay as Lanssac reckoned it; the unit sits in an unread group. New sign values from these leaves — 4 = b, three strokes = z as well as t, the tailed 4 = p, Λ = ns, the hooked C = qu, the 6-like sign = o, Δ = g, the o with cross below = et — are listed in the notes; the last makes f. 124’s “retenu ou empesché” rather “retenu et empesché”.

t: Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573 — the Polish election embassy’s cipher
b: Despuis rests on two signs read once each (ꝛ as de , N as p ); the gloss fragment “…es dangier” is compatible with “…uis les dangiers” but the gutter takes the start of the line. François : the signs give fran-c-o-r-s ; the seventh sign must be the i sign ϙ, which this hand writes close to the r sign ϕ, or the word is another. Qui rests on the gloss; the cipher has ꟿ Γ, and ꟿ reads i in mais . Et vostre ser is followed by four signs that read o r h e under the key; service with one misread sign is the likely word and is left in braces. Two forms of the et sign ( et and nt ) and of the cross ( h and pour ) are told apart by context, not by shape, in the present transcription. The sibling readings of section 05 are first readings from the microfilm: f. 160 is sign by sign, f. 164 has four unread runs and one word-sign ( l’Empereur ) fixed only by the f. 174 gloss, and in f. 174 “Grand”, “de l’Empire”, “estoient” and “vostre” rest on the gloss and the sign count. Ff. 156v–157, the rest of f. 154 and the 9 May letters to Anjou, Catherine and Brulart (ff. 182 ff.) are not read. Tomokiyo’s “f. 331” is not a Lanssac item in the BnF notice.

t: Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573 — the Polish election embassy’s cipher
b: Folio located on the unlabelled microfilm from thumbnails of the pencil foliation (canvas ≈ 1.76 × folio); full-size pages fetched one at a time through the IIIF image API. Blocks deskewed by maximising the contrast of the row-ink profile and cut into one strip per line for transcription; 741 signs typed as glyph labels, with separators dropped. Crib letters fixed from the glossed line of f. 154v and from passage two of f. 124 against its own gloss. Simulated annealing of the remaining signs on a French 5-gram model with the crib letters pinned; blind and shuffled-order controls run on the same data. Beam-search lattice decode of the five f. 124 lines with per-sign candidate sets; readings checked against the marginal fragments and the clear text.

t: Lanssac to Charles IX, Warsaw, 26 April 1573 — the Polish election embassy’s cipher
b: BnF, Français 4735, ff. 124, 126–127, 154–157: Gallica btv1b9060724s ; notice BnF Archives et manuscrits . S. Tomokiyo, “French Ciphers during the Reigns of Charles IX and Henry III”, section “Ciphers of Monluc and Lansac, Sent to Poland (1573)” ( cryptiana ), with the table henryiii_Lansac.png. E.-H.-V. de Noailles, Henri de Valois et la Pologne en 1572 , 3 vols (Paris, 1867), vol. III for the printed embassy correspondence ( Internet Archive ); the 26 April letter is not in it. t: Lebel to Charles Emmanuel I of Savoy, 1593 — three unread letters from the Estates of the League
b: BnF fr. 3983 nos. 11, 62 and 100, January–March 1593: Tomokiyo rebuilt the key in 2017 and published these letters as images with many code groups undeciphered, but no reading. They are read here with his key, a dozen corrections to its letter signs and code values harvested from the letters deciphered at the time and from context in BnF esp. 336: about 98% of the enciphered tokens valued, all of no. 100 and 98% of no. 62’s recto. Mayenne wants the crown or the regency, Spain buys him off with 40,000 écus and offers four millions, the Cardinal de Bourbon offers a marriage, Feria’s jurist is laughed at, and Mayenne’s council prepares a truce. Open: the bled-through verso of no. 62 and a set of single-context code values. Paris → Turin · homophonic cipher with a 300-number code · January–March 1593 · read Lebel to Charles Emmanuel I of Savoy, 1593: three unread letters from the Estates of the League to Charles Emmanuel I of Savoy Bibliothèque nationale de France, Français 3983 nos. 11 (f. 26, 17 January), 62 (f. 130, 10 March) and 100 (ff. 194–195, 27 March 1593). Satoshi Tomokiyo reconstructed the key from two letters deciphered at the time and published these three as images, with “many code groups yet undeciphered”. They are read here sign by sign, in three passes. Daniel Bourdeau · read 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. The Unsolved Catalogue listed three letters from Lebel, Savoy’s agent in Paris, as having no decipherment noted. Tomokiyo’s article “Reading Undeciphered Letters to the Duke of Savoy (1593)” (cryptiana, 2017, revised 2023) gives the key he rebuilt from fr. 3983 no. 80 and fr. 3984 f. 182, and shows these three letters as images only: the key was in print, the readings were not. With his table, about a dozen corrections to its letter signs, and code values aligned from the letters deciphered in 1593 (fr. 3983 no. 80, fr. 3984 f. 182, fr. 3985 f. 23) and from context in the unglossed BnF esp. 336 nos. 79–80, all three letters now read. No. 11: about 720 letter signs, all but about 6 valued, and all 58 code tokens valued (41 H, 11 C, 6 M). No. 62: on the recto 607 of 617 enciphered tokens valued (98%) with all 62 code tokens valued (36 H, 13 C, 13 M); the three verso lines, under the recto’s bleed-through, about 70 of 101. No. 100: all 1,000 enciphered tokens valued, codes 65 H, 26 C, 19 M. Overall about 98% of the enciphered tokens have a value. The letters follow Savoy’s hope of the French crown through the first months of the Estates General: Mayenne wanting the crown or the regency, Spain paying him 40,000 écus down and assignations up to 260,000 and offering four millions, the Cardinal de Bourbon courting him with a marriage to his daughter, Mayenne’s secret council of the archbishop of Lyon, Villeroy and Jeannin, Philip II’s plans for the Infanta judged impossible, Feria’s jurist laughed at, and a truce proposed. What stays open is physical (the no. 62 verso) and a set of single-context code values graded M, listed in section 05. No. 62, f. 130r (10 March 1593): after the clear “J’ay appris dès la mienne derniere que” the cipher begins, letter signs run together, code numbers set off by dots. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3983 f. 130r (no. 62), via Gallica btv1b9059406b.

t: Lebel to Charles Emmanuel I of Savoy, 1593 — three unread letters from the Estates of the League
b: Lebel wrote to Charles Emmanuel I from Paris while the League’s Estates General met there to choose a Catholic king against Henri of Navarre. Fr. 3983 (Gallica ark btv1b9059406b) holds four of his letters in one cipher. No. 80 of 13 March was deciphered at the time on a separate sheet (f. 167); the other three are not. No. Date Leaf Gallica canvases Enciphered tokens (letter signs + codes) 11 17 Jan 1593 f. 26r–v 49–50 ~720 + 58 62 10 Mar 1593 f. 130r–v 233–234 recto 555 + 62; verso ~88 + 13 100 27 Mar 1593 ff. 194r–195r 333–335 890 + 110 (8 of the signs nulls) The system is a homophonic substitution of one or two signs per letter (a = pp or 12, e = Ɱ or g, o = # or ✱, s = ooo or 4t), three nulls (4+, X, o-f), a sign for et , and a code of about 300 numbers set off by dots, with an alphabetical addendum above 300 added later in 1593. Words are not divided. The counts come from the sign lists of the final passes. Grades as in the repository’s conventions: H a value in Tomokiyo’s key or glossed in a decipherment of 1593; C a value from alignment or several agreeing contexts; M a value inferred from grammar and sense in one context.

t: Lebel to Charles Emmanuel I of Savoy, 1593 — three unread letters from the Estates of the League
b: Clear text in roman, deciphered text in italics, code values in brackets with their number; M marks a context value. …je luy diray seullement par ceste que j’ay sceu et de bon lieu que le duc de Mayenne va de jour a aultre rentrant en opinion de [305 pretendre M] la [292 couronne M] [110 pour] [113 luy] , pource principallement a ceste fantasie [108 par] [283 lettres] de Rome, par lesquelles on luy escrit que le [21 pape] a dict qu’il seroit bien [137 mal] a(i)lles(?) si pouvant [130 avoir M] la [292 couronne] pour luy il la donneroit a un aultre . V. A. voit assez quelle apparence il y a que ce second(?) dessein, ou pour mieulx dire congé, puisse avoir effect. A faulte de ce il desireroit [178 fort] la regence de l’estat , faisant naistre plusieurs difficultés sur tous les subjects qui pourront estre proposés , esperant que le temps luy donnant moien de regagner aultant du credit entre les [83 François] par quelques heureux succès de ses actions, comme il en a perdu par le desavantage que ce party a receu dès que la charge et administration de l’estat luy a esté commise, il pourroit hors obtenir plus aisement ce en quoy il treuvera a present toutte [106 non M] pas difficulté, mais impossibilité. Le second dessein sera [178 fort] alterer par la resolution que le pape et [261 Roy d’Espaigne] ont prise de vouloir l’election d’un roy desirée avec toutte affection des bons catholiques. A quoy au(?)… il se voiroit contrainct de consentir, il taschera de favoriser celuy duquel il pourra non pas esperer mais recepvoir en effect plus de commodité: le Roy d’Espaigne luy [250 tout] presenter quatre millions; le [170 cardinal] de Bourbon le [250 tout] rechercher et solliciter, luy promettant d’espouser sa fille et tous les honneurs et biens qu’il vouldra desmander, disant que avec luy les [297 catholiques] principaulx qui suivent le party du [29 Roy de Navarre] se rangeront a l’union . Cest ouverture et proposition est favorisée a toutte reste par deux des trois que [26 le duc de Mayenne] a choisis pour son conseil secret en ce [250 tout], qui sont [64 le] de [50 Lyon M], Villeroy, et le troisiesme qu’est le [235 président] Jannin , s’y laira aisement ranger. V. A. voit assez les difficultés et contrastes esquels cest ouverture sera subjecte. Je ne perdrey temps a faire (en m’)entre(m)ettant(?) les offices requis au service de V. A., a laquelle je ne desmanderey pardon … puis que la mattiere de laquelle il se traitte et l’humeur de ceste nation l’ont … comme je m’asseure desia obtenu pour moy de V. A. Mayenne, lieutenant-general of the League, wants the crown; failing it, the regency; failing that, he will back whichever candidate pays best. Spain offers four millions, the Cardinal de Bourbon a marriage with Mayenne’s daughter. His secret council is “le de [50]”, the usual ellipsis for Monsieur de Lyon , Pierre d’Épinac, archbishop of Lyon (the digits re-read at full resolution; 50 = Lyon is M), Villeroy and the président Jeannin.

t: Lebel to Charles Emmanuel I of Savoy, 1593 — three unread letters from the Estates of the League
b: J’ay appris dès la mienne derniere que le mescontantemant qu’avoit [26 le duc de Mayenne] de [85 Monsieur] a esté remedié, luy ayant [251 faict] [129 donner] contantemant de ce que luy estoit deu, et estoit la somme plus grande que je n’ay escrit cy devant; il luy ont faict [275 offre M] quarante mille escus et donner assignation tant en [69 Flandres M] que Espagne, jusques au comptant de deux cents soixante mille escus. L’on estimoit que sur tant et tant de remonstrances qu’ont esté faittes aux [142 serviteurs] du [261 Roy d’Espaigne] de l’impossibilité de ses pretantions sur ces[te couronne?] … le [292 royaume M] soit [110 pour] luy [24 l’Infante] et le [163 prince] qu’il se seroit resolu d’y [105 faire] [257 parvenir] a quelque aultre de ses proches; mays ses ministres continuent plus que jamais en leur opinion, conduysant le duc de Feria ung docteur [109 qui M] veult disputter la [292 couronne] par poincts de droict, dont l’on se mocque [250 tout] ouvertemant pardessa, ou l’on remarque aussy que le Roy d’Espaigne est tres [137 mal M] conseillé de faire en ce tenps et en la face des estatz voir une armée moindre qu’aulcune qui soit encores venue, et l’[190 argent] plus court que jamays. [278 J’ay M] sceu que les [236 capitaines] de Mayenne voiant peu de jour de pouvoir faire donner la couronne au dict duc de Mayenne ny la faire tumber en la [240 maison M] de Borbon, tascheront de faire proposer une [255 tresve]; [ⅅX quelqu’un M] partira [136 bien] [134 tost] [100 pour M] [102 aller] [253 trouver M] a [23 V.re Alt.e] de la part de Mayenne . Je croy que ce sera le service de V.re Alt.e de luy donner tout contantemant et le caresser. Et a la verité sans son assistance je me fusse treuvé empesché [30 en ceste M] [94 negotiation] plus que jamais. Le duc de Mayenne et luy [251 faict] faire de grandes offres. Verso, after the clear news that Gondi, the Grand Duke of Tuscany’s envoy, is with the King of Navarre: … [252 dict] [191 le juriste] … [221 mariage] … de la niece du duc de Florance … [46 Lorraine] … [223] … [45 le duc de Lorraine] avec [29 le Roy de Navarre] … il se [251 faict] [247] . Je suis attendant … The three lines lie under the recto’s ink; after registering and subtracting the mirrored recto, about 70 of their ~101 tokens carry a value.

t: Lebel to Charles Emmanuel I of Savoy, 1593 — three unread letters from the Estates of the League
b: The cipher passages, in order (the clear news of Provence, the blockade of Paris and the siege of Noyon is summarised after). … Et par lesquelles je luy disois aussi que le [227 seigneur] n’a pardessa faict de credit comm’il a voulu faire croire. Il est [178 fort] en arriere de moiens. Il a, a la verité, des [227 seigneurs] et [150 amis M] parmy [114 eulx] . Et marche come je croy de bon pied, s’estant adressé a [23 votre altesse] pour avoir preveu que si les premiers desseins de [261 le Roy d’Espaigne] ne pouvoient reuscir, votre altesse pourroit avec plus de raison que aultre [163 prince] beaucoup esperer de cest’occasion, et que se rendant comme principal conducteur de ce [84 negotiation], il ne pourroit sinon en [274 recevoir M] beaucoup de [230 commodité M] des apresant et a l’advenir, [250 tout] [136 bien] et avancemant pour luy et les siens, que j’estimois ce que votre altesse luy vouldroit faire donner des apresant pour bien employé. Je luy en disois de mesmes pour le regard de son compagnon et du [235 président M] Jannin, mays que de luy remettre de grandes sommes entre [161 ses mains M] . Je n’estois pas de cest advis, bien ay je tousiours estimé comme je fais encores estre tres requis que votre altesse doibt faire [103 venir] [133 incontinant] a [49 Paris M] [190 argent] pour en faire son service au besoin, sans que toutesfoys ledict [227 seigneur] le sache, [109 qui] ne cesseroit d’en [305 avancer M] le desboursemant. Le [154 sieur M] Zamet seroit tres propre s’il en voulloit prendre la charge. … Je diray au reste a V.re Alt.e qu’il semble que [260 Dieu M] va conduisant les [98 affaires] au but que [250 tout] [115 bon] [142 serviteur] de votre altesse desire. Les desseins du Roy d’Espaigne pour [24 l’Infante], [163 prince(s)] et luy sont pleins de toutte impossibilité. Les [257 faveurs] que je reçois du duc de Feria et du [164 filz?] Tassis me font esperer que, ne pouvant reuscir les dicts desseins du Roy d’Espaigne, elle soit resolue de faire [257 faveur] a votre altesse . Et mesmes j’ay sceu que ledict [104 Commandeur M] Tassis a dict a un personnage qu’il croit qu’il en faudra [103 venir] la. [64 le] [170 Cardinal] [71 Pelvé] a aussi tiré quelque mot en passant qui approche de cella, et m’asseure que V.e A. n’a oublié de faire faire les offices requis vers le pape et [22 le Legat? M], pouvant asseurer votre altesse que si le pape, voyant les desseins du Roy d’Espaigne ne pouvoir reuscir, inclinoit de faire [257 faveur] a votre altesse, elle ne pourroit desirer d’avoir pardessa un meilleur [227 seigneur] que luy sera ledict Cardinal Pelvé, [278 comme j’ay M] par mes aultres [283 lettres] faict sçavoir a votre altesse , comme les procureurs du pais de Provence … Il passe tousiours par [50 Lyon M]; si [27 Mr de Nemours M] voulloit, en faire un presant a votre altesse. Il me semble qu’il seroit fort bien logé au [241 chasteau M] de Myollans. … [109 qui] est [178 fort] estonné de ne treuver icy personne [302 affectionné M] a la [153 grandeur M] du Roy d’Espaigne. [258 Aussitost M] que [26 Mr du Mayne] sera venu, il depeschera [XC quelqu’un M] a votre altesse. Lebel has worked on a man of Mayenne’s circle who is short of money but has friends, and proposes money for him, his “compagnon” and Jeannin, sent to Paris without his knowledge and paid through the financier Sébastien Zamet. The favours of Feria and the Commandeur J. B. de Tassis let him hope that Spain, if its Infanta fails, will turn to Savoy; the Pope might do the same, and Cardinal Pelvé would be the best friend Savoy could have in Paris. The clear part adds the Provence governorship wanted for Vaudémont, Navarre’s blockade of Paris and Mayenne at the siege of Noyon; the last cipher lines say Feria is astonished to find no one in Paris devoted to the King of Spain, and that Mayenne, once back, will send someone to the Duke.

t: Lebel to Charles Emmanuel I of Savoy, 1593 — three unread letters from the Estates of the League
b: Each cipher line was cut from the Gallica images and transcribed sign by sign against Tomokiyo’s table, then read ( reading11_full.md , reading62_full.md , reading100_full.md ); a third pass applied every harvested code value and re-read doubtful digits at native resolution ( reading11_final.md , reading62_final.md , reading100_final.md ). Corrections to the letter key found on the way: ∇ is also y; δ with a cross is d and also i/j; X is not always a null (it is an i in remedié ); o→ is sometimes h; the long h stands for both n and l; ∠ and a barred λ are further s forms; an α-like sign is z ( Zamet ); a barred T is b; □ is u or v; “bm/vm” is d. Code values came from the three letters deciphered in 1593 ( codes_harvest.tsv ): glossed (H) 24 l’Infante, 64 le, 71 Pelvé, 84 negotiation, 85 Monsieur, 98 affaires, 113 luy/celuy, 114 eulx, 250 tout, 255 tresve, 297 catholiques and others; by alignment (C) 94, 102 aller, 129 donner, 133 incontinant, 134 tost, 190 argent, 191 the jurist, 221 mariage, 236 capitaines. The last pass added, from context in BnF esp. 336 nos. 79–80 (ark btv1b100325613, canvases 268–273) and across the three letters: 283 lettres, 163 prince(s), 227 seigneur(s) (C); 103 venir, 257 faveur(s), 142 serviteur, 115 bon, 404 puis, 344 dire, 439 besoing, 24 l’Infante; and 100 = pour in no. 62 (Tomokiyo’s “condescendre” fits elsewhere). What stays open. No. 11: about 6 letter signs in four short spans: l. 4 a(i)lles(?) , probably ailleurs ; l. 6 second(?) , three signs under a smudge; l. 20 au(?)… , one sign; v10 (en m’)entre(m)ettant , two doubtful. M codes: 305 pretendre, 130 avoir (310 is avoir in the key; 130 may be a slip), 292 couronne (twice; the harvest gives promesse ), 106 non, 50 Lyon. 250 tout (H) reads awkwardly in two of its three places. No. 62 recto: 10 letter signs open (four after the clear “que” at the head, one or two in l. 8 sur ces[te] … , a stray “11” in l. 3). M codes: 275 offre, 69 Flandres, 292 couronne/royaume (×4), 109 qui (×2, harvest “promettoit”), 137 mal, 278 J’ay, 240 maison, 100 pour, 253 trouver, 30 en ceste, and the ⅅX sign (an envoy). No. 62 verso: about 6 signs physically under the recto’s ink before 46; one blot = one sign (probably i); codes 223 and 247 open; an 8-sign run on line 1 ( a e n l/s t s o o m a ) that does not segment into French. About 70 of ~101 tokens valued. No. 100: every token has a value; 19 code tokens are M. Forced by the phrase: 154 sieur, 161 ses mains, 235 président, 241 chasteau; near-forced 260 Dieu, 258 aussitost. Sense only: 22 (Legate or Cardinals), 27 (Nemours?), 49 (Paris?), 50 (Lyon?), 104 (Commandeur; the key’s “dire” does not fit, so the digits may be misread), 150 amis, 153 grandeur, 230 commodité, 274 recevoir, 278 comme j’ay, 302 affectionné, 305 avancer, XC (a sign outside the key: the person Mayenne will send). 164 “filz” before Tassis is odd. Three code digits are blotted (108/105 before 257, 278, 108); six letter signs are settled by sense, not shape. Why these stay open: every surviving decipherment in this key has been harvested (fr. 3983 f. 167, fr. 3984 f. 182r–v, fr. 3985 f. 23, esp. 336 no. 81), and the unglossed esp. 336 nos. 79–80 have been read for context. None of the M-grade numbers occurs under a gloss; only the office’s own nomenclator, not known to survive, would confirm them. The verso gaps are physical.

t: Erving at Madrid (1807) and Adams at St Petersburg (1812) — Erving completed, Adams solved
b: Two American diplomatic-code results from the State Department’s microfilmed despatch books. Erving’s private letter of 24 March 1807, printed from Madison’s own decode with the key “not found”: every hole closes from both received copies and Pinckney’s decoded despatches, and the holes turn out to be Madison’s slips. John Quincy Adams’s despatches are not in Armstrong’s code; his own (the = 1385) is rebuilt to 1,166 numbers from the clerk’s decodes on NARA M35 reel 3 and Ford’s printed decipherments of 1811–12. Despatch No. 88, which Ford printed with nine lines and the remainder not decyphered, is read: 380 of 390 groups as sense (0.974, measured; the nine lines 0.970, the remainder 0.961). Count Rumyantsev’s strokes at Wilna, Kurakin’s note, a proposal France never made “even after the battle of Friedland”, Napoleon’s expected thrust at the centre of the empire. United States · diplomatic codes · Madrid 1807, St Petersburg 1812 · read Erving at Madrid and Adams at St Petersburg: Two Legation Codes from John Quincy Adams George W. Erving to Madison, Madrid, 24 March 1807, Founders Madison/02-13-02-0559 · John Quincy Adams to the Secretary of State, St Petersburg, No. 88, 25 June 1812 · NARA microfilm M31 reel 12 and M35 reel 3 The holes in Madison’s own decode of Erving’s letter closed from the two received copies and Pinckney’s despatches; Adams’s code shown not to be Armstrong’s and rebuilt to 1,166 numbers from the clerk’s decodes and Ford’s printed decipherments; No. 88, which Ford printed with nine lines and the remainder “not decyphered”, read: 380 of 390 groups as sense (0.974, measured), the nine lines in full Daniel Bourdeau · solved 18 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 solved Summary. Two results from the same kind of source as the Armstrong postscript : the State Department’s despatch books on National Archives microfilm, where a reader in Washington sometimes wrote the decode between the lines. Adams. The Madison editors say that the Armstrong code ( the = 972) was also used by John Quincy Adams at St Petersburg. His despatches to Washington are not in it. Every coded despatch checked on NARA M35 reel 3 uses a different code in which the is 1385 and of is 1576; Adams held a copy of Armstrong’s cipher, but for corresponding with Armstrong at Paris. That code is rebuilt here to 1,166 numbers: 431 from the Department clerk’s interlinear decodes on fourteen frames, 312 fixed by aligning coded blocks of 1811 and 1812 with the Department’s decipherments that Ford prints, 307 uncertain and 20 inferred. With it, despatch No. 88 (25 June 1812, the day after Napoleon crossed the Niemen), which Ford’s Writings of John Quincy Adams prints with “[Nine lines of this paragraph not decyphered.]” and the remainder “undecyphered”, reads 380 of its 390 groups as sense (0.974, measured): the nine lines all 133, the remainder 247 of 257 (0.961). The nine lines are about Count Rumyantsev, the Chancellor: the journey to Wilna went against his advice, he had an apoplectic stroke soon after arriving there and a second, worse one since, the German papers wrongly reported him dead, and he cannot stay much longer at the foreign ministry. The remainder is on Kurakin’s note, which the French ambassador called a proposal France “had never thought of making to Russia even after the battle of Friedland”, and on Napoleon’s expected thrust at the centre of the empire rather than along the Baltic. Erving. Erving’s private letter of 24 March 1807 is printed from Madison’s own decode, with the note that the key has not been found. Madison had the key; the holes in his decode are his own slips. With both received copies and Pinckney’s decoded despatches every hole closes ( Hanover , in the scale , see that he was , Gibraltar ), and the one real loss is a syllable Erving himself left out. Status: Erving’s letter complete, a small completion of a text already in print. Adams: No. 88 read (above the 95% bar; 0.928 without the inferred values), key rebuilt here. Open: seven groups cut by the binding gutter on the film, which need the original, and three single groups (1508, 1185, 570).

t: Erving at Madrid (1807) and Adams at St Petersburg (1812) — Erving completed, Adams solved
b: The starting point was a note the Madison editors attach to Armstrong’s letters (Founders Madison/02-10-02-0369 and 02-12-02-0197): the code was “also used by John Quincy Adams at St. Petersburg and by Jacob Lewis at Saint-Domingue; key not found but substantially reconstructed by the editors”. On Adams to Madison, 7 January 1811 (03-03-02-0121), the editors speak of “a code provided by the State Department to John Armstrong in France and to both William Short and Adams”, citing Ford 3:328. If that held, the 580-group Armstrong table already rebuilt on this site would read Adams’s coded despatches. It does not. What Ford’s own text says. Secretary Smith’s instructions of 1809 (Ford 3:327–28) say that “the cypher with which you are furnished” is “the same with that of our minister at London” (William Pinkney), and tell Adams to “obtain at Paris, a copy of General Armstrong’s cypher also, for the like purpose”, that is, to correspond with Armstrong. In 1810 Adams acknowledges “the copy of General Armstrong’s cypher” (Ford 3:370). He held both. The despatches to Washington use the other one. What the microfilm shows. Every coded despatch checked on M35 reel 3 (1811 and 1812) uses a code in which 1385 = the , 1576 = of , 1384 = that , 668 = and , 1401 = I . In Armstrong’s code the is 972 and of is 1354 . Run through the Armstrong table (592 entries as it now stands), these pages come out as noise. Reel 2 frame 0155, of 1810, is in the same Adams code. So the table already held cannot read Adams’s despatches. The editors’ note on the 7 January 1811 letter concerns a private letter to Madison, not a despatch, and was not checked against its manuscript, which is in the Forbes collection and not online; it may be right for that letter.

t: Erving at Madrid (1807) and Adams at St Petersburg (1812) — Erving completed, Adams solved
b: The method is the one used for Armstrong on M34 roll 13, with a second source added. On M35 reel 3 the Department clerk wrote the decode above the groups of several despatches; every pair on frames 0047, 0048 (1811), 0182 (No. 80, 29 February 1812), 0183, 0184, 0185, 0189, 0190, 0194, 0198, 0206 (No. 88), 0210–0211 and 0247 was recorded with frame, page side and line. For most pages there is no interlinear decode, but Ford printed the Department’s decipherments. Coded blocks were transcribed from the film and aligned with Ford’s plaintext, group against syllable, and checked by eye: 39 blocks of 1811, and then eight despatches of October 1811 to September 1812, No. 95 against the Department’s own clear copy on frames 0230–0232. All the pairs, 3,127 from the clerk (with the earlier pair list) and 2,785 from Ford, were merged into one table of 1,166 numbers, each with a grade: Grade Meaning Numbers H the clerk’s interlinear decode over the group 431 C fixed by Ford’s printed decipherment between known neighbours 312 M the split of the syllables or the digit is a judgement 307 I inferred from the alphabetical slot and the sense only 20 The code is a numbered syllabary of about 1,600 numbers: syllables, word-parts and common words, with 1–100 mostly whole words (13 observation , 16 Emperor , 29 United States , 44 negotiation , 78 President ). An earlier version of this page described it as alphabetical blocks of fifty; the larger table does not bear that out. Values climb alphabetically only inside short runs, such as 1384 that , 1385 the , 1387 them , 1388 then , 1391 there , 1392 these , 1393 they , 1394 think , 1399 this , or 1592 on , 1594 one , 1595 ong , 1597 only , and then the run breaks (1304 tain and 1312 form sit among 1305 Bal , 1310 be , 1317 been ). The alphabetical slot therefore brackets a value only where the neighbours on both sides are in order, and inference from it is kept to grade I. A superscript o after a group adds -s ; a mark under a group changes it (a doubled letter, -ed , or another word: 1107 paper , 1107 with the mark well ; 1457 last , with the mark ll ; 1535 al , with the mark all ). A few groups carry two values in the sources (508 rect and ear ; 1570 of and occurr ; 1173 when and would ). In this hand 5 and 6, 7 and 9, and 0, 6 and 8 are easily confused. Re-reading No. 88 from zoomed crops corrected seven groups over two passes (168, not 158; 1426, not 1425; 302, not 502; 792, not 492; 1061, not 1081; 588, not 888; 1384, not 1385), showed that two groups of the last line are digits Adams himself overwrote (1383 than and 1097 sho , each with its last digit written over another), and showed that the underlined 1102 at the foot of the left page of frame 0206 is a catchword repeating the first group of the next page, not a group of the text. The table, its sources and the conflicts are in the repository ( jqa/code_table.tsv , jqa/consolidate.py , jqa/code_conflicts.txt , jqa/overrides.tsv , where every hand decision carries its reason).

t: Erving at Madrid (1807) and Adams at St Petersburg (1812) — Erving completed, Adams solved
b: No. 88 was written at St Petersburg on 25 June 1812, the day after the Grande Armée crossed the Niemen, when that news had not yet reached the capital. Ford prints it at 4:355–58, addressed to James Monroe. After Adams’s account of Prince Kurakin’s passports and the French ambassador’s demand for his, the paragraph ends: “On the other side I have reported to you what Count Romanzoff said to me the day before his departure for Wilna. Certainly negotiation then was his wish and expectation. [Nine lines of this paragraph not decyphered.]” The microfilm has the triplicate (M35 reel 3, frame 0206), and on it the clerk’s pencil stops exactly where Ford’s gap begins. M35 reel 3, frame 0206, foot of the left page. The clerk’s faint pencil runs above the groups down to 668. 295. 818. 864 (“and expectation”); from the dash and 790. 1385. 1434. 168… (“But the …”) there is none. Ford’s “nine lines not decyphered” begin here and run to the top of the right page. Image: National Archives and Records Administration, RG 59, M35 reel 3, frame 0206, via the National Archives Catalog (NAID 188725601). The block runs from the last four decoded groups to the end of the paragraph: 133 groups, 129 of them in Ford’s gap, with the clear words scarcely (twice), undoubtedly and In the German Gazettes written in the line. The rebuilt table gives every group a value ( python render.py gap88.txt ), and all 133 read as sense in the running text ( python measure.py ): 106 on clerk-attested values, 10 on Ford-fixed, 13 on uncertain and 4 on inferred ones; without the inferred values, 129 (0.970). In the reading below, words in square brackets rest on grade-I values; groups in braces have a value that does not make sense in the sentence. The opening words in brackets are the clerk-decoded close of the sentence that Ford prints. [Certainly negotiation then was his wish] and ex-pect-ation. But the [journ-ey] it-self of the Emperor Alex-an-der to Wil-na was in opposition to the Chan-ce-ll-or and adv-ice, and if his ac-tive in-flu-ence had not been im-pa-ir-ed before it, it can scarcely fa-il to have been af-fect-ed by his ill-ness im-medi-ate-ly after his ar-[riv]-al [thither], which was undoubtedly an a-po-ple-ct-ic str-oke. Since then he has had a second and a more sever-e one. In the German Gazettes even his de-a-[th] has been an-no-un-ced; but that was a mis-take. At all events it is scarcely pos-sible that he should rem-ain much long-er in the depart-ment of foreign affairs. im-pa-ir-ed : the groups on the page are 1424, then the catchword 1102 at the foot of the left leaf, then 1112 1433 520 at the top of the right leaf. The catchword is the group Adams meant to begin the page with, 1102 pa (Ford-fixed nine times), and in No. 83 (frame 0190) he codes un-im-pa-ir-ed as 1477 1424 1102 1435 520 (1435 ir , Ford-fixed three times). The 1112 1433 on the new page are his own copying slips, one digit each, for 1102 1435: read as he intended, impaired . Chan-ce-ll-or is 1385 1025 1016 1457 908 with the doubling mark under 1457, the same five groups Adams wrote for “the Chancellor” in No. 73 (frame 0165, Ford 4:256). The group before his illness is 792 by : the earlier reading 492 use took an open hook for this hand’s looped 4. Most of what the first reading of 18 September inferred is now attested: itself (1081 self , clerk 0184, 0185, 0190), advice (1575 adv , Ford 0132; 1405 ice , Ford 0036 and clerk 0190), apoplectic (1141 ple ; 1060 ct , clerk 0182), stroke (1586 oke ), second (1077), severe (1091 sever ), remain much longer (743 rem , 162 much , 888 long ), mistake (134 mis , clerk 0182), announced (479 un ), At all events (283 event , clerk 0048), foreign affairs (68, 1517), and 1186 is attested as will and Wil- (clerk 0182, 0184). Opposition (83), the key word of the first sentence, is now grade C from No. 73. Five groups of the passage remain inferred: 1434 journ and 168 ey , 1479 riv , 1398 thither and 1382 th . 3.1 What it says “He” is Count Nikolai Rumyantsev (Adams’s Romanzoff), Chancellor and minister for foreign affairs, who had gone to Wilna with Alexander. Adams reports that the Emperor’s journey to Wilna itself went against the Chancellor’s advice; that whatever influence he still had would in any case have been affected by his illness, an apoplectic stroke soon after his arrival there; that since then he has had a second and worse one; that the German gazettes had reported him dead, wrongly; and that he can hardly remain much longer at the head of foreign affairs. This fits what is known: Rumyantsev had a stroke in 1812 that cost him his hearing, and he left office in 1814. Adams’s own diary for September 1812 records Romanzoff speaking of two strokes of apoplexy suffered with the Emperor at Wilna. It differs on the timing from standard accounts (Britannica, Wikipedia), which tie the stroke to the news of the crossing of the Niemen on 24 June. Adams, writing at St Petersburg on 25 June before that news could have reached him, places the first stroke soon after Rumyantsev reached Wilna and a second, worse one before the 25th. Ford printed none of this. t: Erving at Madrid (1807) and Adams at St Petersburg (1812) — Erving completed, Adams solved
h: Erving 1807: the holes in Madison’s decode
b: George W. Erving, chargé at Madrid, wrote privately to Madison on 24 March 1807 (No. 21) “In the Cypher of the Legation”, the code Charles Pinckney had used in Spain. He reports a secret conversation between the Prince of the Peace (Godoy) and the Prussian chargé Henry: Bonaparte has offered the Prince the Electorate of Hanover for himself, and the Prince hopes by holding Hanover to make a separate peace with England and exchange it for Gibraltar. The Madison editors (PJM-SS 13:529–31) print the letter from Madison’s interlinear decode on the first received copy and state that the key has not been found (Weber, pp. 152–53). The decode has holes: “Haweder”, “Ha——er”, “Giblartar [sic]”, “see the he was more so”, “sp[eak]”, and at note 8 “to the […]” where Madison wrote “se al e”. Three sources were read: the first received copy with Madison’s decode (NARA RG 59, Despatches from Spain vol. 10, microfilm M31 reel 12, frames 0283–0286); the “Duplicate” in the Madison Papers at the Library of Congress (mjm014714), coded throughout and not decoded; and Pinckney’s own despatches in the same code (M31 reel 7 frames 0346–0352, 22 February 1803, one copy decoded by Jacob Wagner on frame 0348; reel 8 frames 0083–0084, January 1804). Pinckney’s pages confirm the common values: 1651 the , 133 of , 1343 and , 244 to , 1578 that , 69 in (Wagner: “the In-tend-ant” = 1651.69.1586.103), 1515 late . M31 reel 12, frame 0285 (detail): “he thinks having Ha—er to be able to make a separate peace with England & to exchange Hanover for Giblartar ”. The same three groups 724. 529. 934 that Madison decoded “Hanover” on the fourth line he left as “Ha — er” on the second. Image: National Archives and Records Administration, RG 59, M31 reel 12, frame 0285, via the National Archives Catalog (NAID 188605361). Founders prints Groups (both copies agree) Reading Evidence “to the […]” (n. 8; Madison “se al e”) 69.1651.1183.1497.1298 in the scale 69 is in : Madison himself so decodes it (“his retreat in Ha—er”, “went in -cog”), as does Wagner in 1803; his “to the” is a slip. 1497 is al (Madison, and in Gibraltar). Madison reads 1183 as se ( se-em-ed ), and se-al-e can only be scale : “might be of importance in the scale; again, to raise up an insuperable obstacle … & lastly to get the Prince within his grasp”, the second of Erving’s three objects. Either the key’s 1183 is sc or Erving took the neighbouring group. “Haweder”, “Ha——er” (n. 5) 724.529.934 (five times) Hanover 724 Ha and 934 er in all five; Madison left 529 blank or guessed “wed”, but decoded the same three groups “Hanover” himself at “exchange Hanover for Gibraltar”. 529 = nov . “see the he was more so” (n. 6) 1578.926.390.720.1219 see that he was more so 1578 is that everywhere else, as the editors note; the code is right and Madison’s “the” is a slip. “Giblartar [sic]” 1619.1508.1497.1594 (twice) Gibraltar At the second occurrence Madison wrote “Gibraltar”; with 1497 = al the groups spell the name correctly. The [sic] belongs to Madison’s decode, not to Erving. “sp[eak]” (n. 4) 244.1212.133 to sp[eak] of 1212 is sp ( gra-sp , 408.1013.1212). The rest of the word is missing in both copies, so the omission is Erving’s. It stays as the editors print it. “been lately doing” (n. 7, coded only in the Duplicate) …1164.1515.38.769.66… been late-ly do-ing 1515 late (Pinckney 1803), 38 ly , 66 ing : the Duplicate’s coding agrees with the clear text of the first copy. So every hole in the printed text closes, and the only real loss is Erving’s own dropped -eak . Madison had the key: the holes are his slips, not missing entries. The scale of this should be clear. The letter was already in print and legible; two of the corrections ( that , speak ) the editors had themselves suggested in their notes, and Hanover they had nearly established. What is new is in the scale , the proof that the “Haweder” and “Giblartar” forms are Madison’s and not Erving’s, and the demonstration that the Pinckney code is recoverable from the microfilm by the same method as Armstrong’s.

t: Loeschner, Vienna 1816 — a memorandum on the Staatskanzlei cipher instruction, not a cipher
b: DECODE R2227 was catalogued as a ciphered letter of “W. Loeschnen?” of 1 July 1816. It is W. Loeschner’s clear German memorandum proposing additions and changes to the instruction for using the Staatskanzlei’s cipher keys. Its only figures are worked examples with the plaintext written above them. Nothing is hidden. Vienna · Staatskanzlei cipher office · clear German memorandum · 1 July 1816 · not a cipher Loeschner's Cipher Memorandum ÖStA, Haus-, Hof- und Staatsarchiv, Staatskanzlei Interiora, Chiffrenschlüssel Kt. 20, alt. Fasc. ad 27, ff. 30–40 · DECODE R2227, catalogued as a non-decrypted letter "with short encrypted parts" from "W. Loeschnen?" to an unknown recipient It is not a ciphered letter. It is a memorandum about how the ministry's cipher keys should be used, and every figure in it is a worked example with its plaintext written above it. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 21 September 2026 not a cipher Summary. DECODE R2227 (20 pages, "Non-decrypted", numerical, "Letter with short encrypted parts") entered the Unsolved Catalogue as a ciphered letter of "W. Loeschnen?" to an unknown recipient, dated 1 July 1816. All eleven openings were viewed here. The document is written in clear German Kurrent. Its heading reads Zusätze und Abänderungen, welche in der Instruktion zum richtigen und zweckmäßigen Gebrauch der in der offiziellen Korrespondenz zwischen den k.k. Missionen und der geheimen Hof- und Staatskanzlei üblichen Ziffernschlüssel gemacht werden dürften . It is signed "Wien am 1ten Julius 1816. W. Loeschner". It comments on a cipher instruction page by page and line by line. The number groups in it are demonstrations, and each one has the French plaintext written over it, for example the announcement that the King of Spain has named the Duke of San Carlos ambassador. Nothing is hidden, so there is nothing to decipher. The target is closed as explained, and a DECODE correction (name, record type and status) is queued. Opening 9: a worked example, with the plaintext above the figures and the Parenthesis and Claudatur signs marked. t: Loeschner, Vienna 1816 — a memorandum on the Staatskanzlei cipher instruction, not a cipher
b: The eleven openings contain one continuous memorandum in a single clerical hand. After the heading, each paragraph cites a place in the instruction it amends: "Seite 2, Spalte 2, Zeile 3 von Unten", "Seite 9, Spalte 2, Zeile 5", "Seite 10, Spalte 2", "Seite 23, nach der Zahl 1918", "Seite 32", "Seite 33, Linie 2 von Unten". It closes with an appendix, Beilage: Ueber den Gebrauch der Doppel- (Supplementar-) Zahlen . The last page carries the date and the signature, W. Loeschner . DECODE's "Loeschnen?" misreads the final letter. Among the topics: the misleading name "Ziffernkabinett", which the author wants dropped from an instruction meant for Austria's diplomats; entering new words in the Déchiffrant (the deciphering half of the key) as well as the Chiffrant. The author cites a despatch of Prince Kaunitz that added supplements 16–17 to a key; the range of numbers from 3 to 6000, and the supplementary figures ( Ergänzungszahlen ); how to cipher proper names, the envelope of a ciphered despatch, and the Parenthesis and Claudatur signs.

t: Lope Hurtado de Mendoza at Rome, 1522 — an unpublished cipher broken, four letters read
b: Nine records in RAH Salazar 9/26, catalogued as part of Alonso Sánchez’s Venice correspondence among which they are bound. They are in a different cipher, and nobody had published it: Tomokiyo’s 2025 article covers Sánchez’s and Juan Manuel’s and not this. The crib was in the volume — R9644 and R9650 each carry the clerk’s own full contemporary clear version beside the cipher, keyed by marginal letters. Fifty-seven values fixed against that plaintext; the key then reads two thirds of the tokens in records DECODE calls non-decrypted, and reads el papa unaided in a letter with no crib at all. Four of the nine are read complete as to content: Adrian VI temporising between Charles V and Francis I, the French coming into Italy with a great sum of money to Lyon, a Pope too parsimonious to pay his own household. Rome → Charles V · three-letter nomenclator with a substitution alphabet, inline with clear Spanish · Sept–Nov 1522 · cipher unpublished, key rebuilt, four letters read Lope Hurtado de Mendoza at Rome, 1522 — an unpublished cipher broken, four letters read to Charles V Real Academia de la Historia, Salazar 9/26 · DECODE R9634, R9644–R9646, R9648–R9650, R9652, R9656 · the imperial agent in Rome reporting to the Emperor on Adrian VI, in the months before the French came back into Italy Catalogued with Alonso Sánchez's Venice letters, among which they are bound. They are in a different cipher, and nobody had published it · two of the nine carry the clerk's own full clear version, which cribs the key · fifty-seven values fixed against that plaintext; the key then reads in records DECODE calls non-decrypted Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 20 September 2026 · updated 21 September 2026 solved in part Summary. Nine records in RAH Salazar 9/26 were catalogued as part of Alonso Sánchez's Venice correspondence, among which they are bound. They are not Sánchez's: they are Lope Hurtado de Mendoza's, written from Rome, and in a different cipher . The point is decidable, not a guess — Sánchez's code groups end strictly in b c d f g h l m n , Hurtado's take finals p and z , and the same group xul means despues in Sánchez's key and lo in this one. Nobody had published this key. Tomokiyo's 2025 article reconstructs Sánchez's cipher and Juan Manuel's; it does not mention Hurtado, and his records fall outside both ranges it lists. The way in was already in the volume. R9644 carries both the ciphered letter and the clerk's full clear version of it (ff. 241–242), written in lettered sections A , B , C keyed to the same letters in the margin of the cipher; R9650 has its own clear too (f. 272). Aligning cipher against plaintext fixes forty-seven code values , with twenty-nine more carried separately as probable — among them all ten substitution-alphabet signs, downgraded after an 8× zoom showed signs that must be different letters looking near-identical at the magnification they were read at. The key then works where it was not built: two thirds of the tokens resolve on sight in R9648 and R9650, and in R9656 — a letter three weeks later with no clear version and no duplicate — it reads el papa unaided . Four of the nine letters are read complete as to content , from the two clear versions and a fifth record that turns out to carry no cipher at all. They show Adrian VI temporising between Charles V and Francis I: the French resolved to come into Italy with a great sum of money to Lyon, the Pope tan escasso que nunca hombre lo fue mas and his household unpaid, the peace track running through the archbishop of Bari. Status: cipher broken and the key rebuilt from contemporary plaintext; four letters read complete as to content, the ciphered leaves read in part. The five records with no clear version read in substance and not word for word, because the substitution alphabet is still thin.

t: Lope Hurtado de Mendoza at Rome, 1522 — an unpublished cipher broken, four letters read
b: These nine records sit in Salazar 9/26 among Alonso Sánchez's despatches from Venice, were catalogued with them, and look at first like more of the same: the same months, the same recipient, cipher mixed with clear inside the sentence, code groups of the same shape and the same three-letter build. The catalogue treated them as one target. Two things separate them, and neither is a matter of impression. Sánchez's nomenclator uses a strict third-position inventory — every code group ends in b c d f g h l m n — while Hurtado's groups take finals p and z ( tep , tap , groups ending -z ), which Sánchez's key does not contain. And where the two keys use the same group they disagree: xul is despues in Sánchez and lo here , ho is que in Sánchez where this cipher uses ton . Same design, same chancery tradition, different key. Nor is it Juan Manuel's, the third imperial cipher of 1522 Rome: none of the values fixed here appears in Tomokiyo's 173-code table for it. That table is itself a partial recovery, so this is consistent rather than conclusive, and it is recorded that way.

t: Lope Hurtado de Mendoza at Rome, 1522 — an unpublished cipher broken, four letters read
b: The clear at the foot of section A reads … porque esta tan escasso que nunca hombre lo fue mas ; hasta que el arçobispo venga creo que sera mejor no apretallo mucho . On the cipher page the middle clause stands in the clear, bracketing the run exactly — six tokens for six words, with no room for slippage: ton tab xud xul ɣm xon que nunca hombre lo fue mas and tu = no from no apretallo mucho . From there the alignment walks: zun top at da por , ᵇʒ7 and teɡ at era and para , zil ɣub zed zar at con el arçobispo de Cosenza, ɣub taf at el papa , rab at v. ma .

t: Lope Hurtado de Mendoza at Rome, 1522 — an unpublished cipher broken, four letters read
b: Three-letter code groups carry most of the text and are written as plain latin trigrams; spelled runs between them use a substitution alphabet. Three features matter for anyone reading it, and none is in the published account of the sibling ciphers: Homophones at code level. ta and tu both mean no , and both occur in the same line. The alphabet has them too: the single spelled word perdida writes d with two different signs. Codes carry syllables, not only words. xur + zun = na + da ; ton + ℓ∞74 = que + rian ; zil + a spelled ocia = conocia ; nul + vuc +s = obligados . zun is da the whole word in da por , the second syllable of na·da , and the middle of que·da·rian . And codes run together to make one word. lu + ho = porque , lul + ta = quales , ton +d+o = quedo . Taken together: word boundaries in this cipher go both ways , and any tokeniser that treats one group as one word will mis-read these letters in both directions. The foot of f. 237. After the clear contento : xul ton tu ton ·d·o zar d·o·n — lo que no quedo de don [Joan]. A code finished with two alphabet signs, then a name spelled outright. Image: Real Academia de la Historia, Colección Salazar y Castro 9/26 f. 237, via DECODE R9644.

t: Lope Hurtado de Mendoza at Rome, 1522 — an unpublished cipher broken, four letters read
h: The key works where it was not built
b: A key fitted to its own evidence will read the evidence and nothing else. This one does not stop there. R9648 , which DECODE calls Non-decrypted , gives nine tokens against nine words with nothing left over — ʋ ton ɣub taf tu ɣof ɣuc ton + spelled venga = «y que el papa no esta en que venga» — and further down la paz por los infieles y por la necessidad . Its spelled perdido decodes letter by letter from six signs won on the other record, in a word not looked for. R9656 is the real test: a despatch of 20 November with no clear version and no duplicate anywhere . The key reads there unaided — after the clear words las cartas traxo don Correo q vino con la valante , ɣub taf stands at el papa . Measured with a resolver that applies confirmed values only: 70% of tokens on R9648 f. 262, 62% on R9650 f. 270, 57% on R9645 f. 243, which has no crib of any kind. Those figures are unchanged by the alphabet downgrade below, because they were carried almost entirely by the code groups — which is itself the evidence that the reading rests on the safe half of the key.

t: Lope Hurtado de Mendoza at Rome, 1522 — an unpublished cipher broken, four letters read
b: Four of the nine are read complete as to content: R9644 and R9650 from their clear versions, R9648 as R9644's duplicate, and R9652 , which DECODE records as Partially decrypted but which carries no cipher at all — the leaf is written entirely in the clear and signed Lope Hurtado . R9644, 1 November. Managing a Pope who will not move. Charles V had written to warn Adrian VI directly; Hurtado approves, because if the Pope will not do his duty he should at least not be able to plead that nobody told him — no se disculpe despues con dezir que v. magestad no le mando prevenir . The Pope's voluntad is good and his obras satisfy nobody; he pleads the Turks and the Emperor's need, and is tan escasso que nunca hombre lo fue mas . Hurtado presses for the papal household to be paid before the other side buys them: si no los corrompiessen dandoles . The King of France asks a safe-conduct to send an ambassador and the Pope will not have him come. R9650, November. The intelligence that mattered: los franceses son determinados de venir en Italia, y enbian gran suma de dinero a Leon , brought by post from the archbishop of Bari, with Hieronymo Adorno 's intercepted letters behind it. Adrian is urged to act sin dilatar mas , and takes it tan tibiamente que no se espera de todo bien . R9652, November. A licenciado Bernardino , «gran bellaco», is in Rome; the Duke of Sessa wants him seized; the Pope will order it if the man is inside Rome, declines a night arrest when he is found lodging with his brother in the city ( aqui no seria bien ), and offers a formal suplicacion instead. It closes with las nuevas de Rodas que escrive el visorrey — the viceroy of Naples on the siege of Rhodes. That last line joins the two halves of this archive. Sánchez's R9653 of 20 November carries the Rhodes news from the other direction, out of Candia and the Signoria. Rome and Venice were reporting the same disaster to the Emperor in the same fortnight, in two different ciphers, bound now in the same volume.

t: Lope Hurtado de Mendoza at Rome, 1522 — an unpublished cipher broken, four letters read
h: What is open, and how good the reading is
b: Five records have no clear version — R9634, R9645, R9646, R9649, R9656 — and there the key works alone. Measured, it resolves 42% of tokens on R9656 and 57% on R9645 , concentrated in the function words and the names, with the spelled content words as the misses. R9645 comes out as … se si no con […] con vuestra magestad, que no […] en […] esta[do] […] de vuestra magestad … ; R9656 as … no […] el papa […] la […] que […] su el papa . That is fragments, not a reading. An earlier draft of this page said these five read “in substance”; measured, they do not, and the claim is corrected here. Enough survives to identify what a passage is about when the surrounding clear text helps, and not enough to read the letter. The substitution alphabet is the limit. Nine signs are fixed and cross-checked — ⋃ =p, 8 =e, ʒ =r, x / 6 =d, L =i, 7 =a, 4 =n, m / ᶻ =o. Beyond that, transcriptions of the spelled words contradict each other at DECODE's resolution. One of those contradictions turned out to be a missing homophone rather than a bad reading, so the rest may resolve the same way; unassigned signs are left unassigned rather than guessed. Confidence is tracked, not assumed. The key file carries a confidence column; the resolver applies confirmed values only and shows probables in angle brackets. An audit for two codes claiming the same plaintext produced four retractions , kept in the file as commented RETRACTED lines — among them an early guess that zar meant Bari , when it means de . Nothing probable was used to derive anything else, so nothing downstream needed unwinding. A correction to DECODE. R9652's status should be not enciphered , not partially decrypted .

t: Lope Hurtado de Mendoza at Rome, 1522 — an unpublished cipher broken, four letters read
h: The one thing that would finish it
b: The blocker is measured, not guessed. DECODE serves these leaves at 3440×2465 for a two-page opening — about 1700 px across a folio, which is enough for the latin trigrams and not enough to tell two similar cursive signs apart. That is the cause of the alphabet limit, and no amount of further crib-walking changes it. DECODE has been checked with a logged-in cookie and has nothing better. The full-size file filesrv returns is that 3440×2465 opening; MASTER_ , MS_ , ORIG_ and .tif variants all come back as the server’s not-found placeholder, and the Image Manager answers “You do not have permission to access” to a viewer session, so its zoom view is unreachable too. The ceiling is DECODE’s stored derivative. The volume belongs to the Colección Salazar y Castro , which the Real Academia de la Historia has been digitising at its own Biblioteca Digital . If Salazar 9/26 is there, those images will be far better than DECODE’s derivative copies, and the substitution alphabet becomes ordinary work. That would in turn give a word-perfect edition of the ciphered leaves and lift the five records with no clear version out of fragments and into a reading. It could not be done from here: bibliotecadigital.rah.es returns HTTP 403 to automated requests and puts a bot check in front of its search, in the same way DECODE’s image server needs a logged-in session. The search term is the old signature, Salazar y Castro, A-26 , and the leaves wanted are ff. 237–243, 260–272 and 334–335.
