t: The Marburg cipher report — a Hesse-Kassel letter’s digit cipher rebuilt and read
b: DECODE R4500, a German report in Hesse-Kassel’s cipher files at Marburg, ends in fourteen lines of digits and signs, with a contemporary gloss over the first four. No key sheet in the volume fits; the key was rebuilt by annealing against a sixteenth-century German model and checked against the gloss. The passage reads: the writer has reported to the Emperor and the Elector of Bavaria and asks to be held excused. Nine signs stay open. Unknown writer → Hesse-Kassel · digit-and-sign substitution · Thirty Years’ War (volume 1635–52) · read The Marburg cipher report: “damit ich aus allen fall entschuldigt sein” Hessisches Staatsarchiv Marburg, HStAM 4 d Nr. 1218, no. 49 (DECODE R4500, “partially decrypted”). A German letter in clear text that switches to fourteen lines of digits and signs. The key was rebuilt from the cipher itself, and the reading was checked against a contemporary decipherment written over the first four lines. Daniel Bourdeau · solved 22 September 2026 solved Summary. Volume 4 d Nr. 1218 at Marburg is Hesse-Kassel’s file of ciphers for officers and officials in the Thirty Years’ War. DECODE has put it online as about 120 key sheets and a few letters. R4500 is one of the letters. It reports troop movements (Rostock, companies on the march) in clear text, then continues for fourteen lines in digits 0–9 and a few signs. A contemporary hand wrote a decipherment over the first four cipher lines, which is why DECODE lists it as partly decrypted. None of the sign alphabets in the same volume fits. The key was rebuilt instead, by annealing against a sixteenth-century German language model and then fixing letters by hand from the words that came out: “damit ich”, “entschuldigt”, “underthenigst”. The contemporary gloss is the control. Its phrases “zumahl nicht”, “etwas tentiret werden” and “dieses orths halber” come out of the cipher with the rebuilt key. The whole passage reads except nine signs at the end of the first line. The writer has laid the matter before the Emperor and the Elector of Bavaria and asks to be held excused. About 97% of the signs read as sense. The start of the cipher passage. The contemporary decipherment runs between the first four lines. Image: Hessisches Staatsarchiv Marburg, HStAM 4 d Nr. 1218, via DECODE R4500.

t: The Marburg cipher report — a Hesse-Kassel letter’s digit cipher rebuilt and read
b: One page. The letter has lost its date and signature, and DECODE gives only the volume’s span, 1635–1652. The cipher starts in the middle of a sentence (“noch nicht zu vernehmen,”) and runs until a clear closing that points to a “beygefügter Extract”. Words are separated by spaces. The system is a letter substitution with a few homophones, written mostly in digits: sign letter sign letter sign letter 5, A, 8 a (8 also o) 6 e 0 n 1 d 12 (written together) r 2, d-shaped sign s 3 g 4 h 7 i 9 u w-sign t θ c (θ4 = ch) triangle l 4 with cross stroke m crossed t b superscript w w j d

t: The Marburg cipher report — a Hesse-Kassel letter’s digit cipher rebuilt and read
b: Normalised. Square brackets mark conjecture; … marks the unread lines. … noch nicht zu vernehmen, die landts[…] …, wir dennoch nur seit ihr endes halber … ursach; das kann dieses orths halber observiren, dagegen den selben etwas tentiret werden solte, zumahl nicht unbewandt […] gebührend zur manutenirung dero Kays. Maj. und des Reichs wie auch [bey diesen …] ungelegen; dahero ich nicht unterlassen sollen, die notturft dieser [sachen] so wol allerhöchst ihrer Kays. Maiestet als auch ihrer Churf. Durchl. in Bayern ohnlängst nochmals … underthenigst und underthenigst anzudeuten, damit ich aus allen fall entschuldigt sein und dessen, meinem gebührenden bericht an gehörigen ort, nicht ermangeln möchte. In English: this can be watched from here, and something should be attempted against them, especially since … the maintenance of His Imperial Majesty and the Empire …; I therefore could not fail to report the matter most humbly to His Imperial Majesty and to His Electoral Highness of Bavaria, so that I may be excused in any event, and not fall short of my duty to report to the proper place.

t: The Marburg cipher report — a Hesse-Kassel letter’s digit cipher rebuilt and read
b: Annealing without word spaces gave only frequency noise. After a second transcription that kept the word gaps and treated the joined “12” as one sign, a homophonic annealer on the de-1500s model produced recognisable words. Those words fixed the key. The gloss over lines 1–4 then settled the superscript sign (w) and 8 (o). At first it did not seem to follow the cipher line by line, but its phrases occur in cipher lines 3–5 in order. All 126 records of the volume (R4452–R4577) were downloaded to look for the key or a clear copy; none was found.

t: The Marburg cipher report — a Hesse-Kassel letter’s digit cipher rebuilt and read
b: The last nine signs of cipher line 1, cramped under the faded gloss: unread. Line 2 reads after restoring an initial sign dropped in transcription on two words (graded C). Single signs in lines 7 and 9 (“[bey diesen]”, “[sachen]”): conjectural, graded M. Writer, recipient and date are unknown. The deferential tone toward the Emperor and Bavaria makes him an officer or agent reporting to Kassel from the imperial side.

t: Cardinal Campeggio’s conclave articles for Francis I, c. 1534
b: Catalogued as a letter of the French marshals to the King dated 1520 (BnF fr. 3081 f. 41, DECODE R2322), the two cipher pages are a copy of the articles Cardinal Campeggio swore to the cardinals Bourbon, Lorraine and Tournon: if elected pope, he would work for the return of Milan, Asti and Genoa to Francis I. George Lasry read the first page in 2022; the second, unpublished, is read here with his key and a few sign corrections. Rome → Francis I · homophonic graphic signs · c. October 1534 · read (f. 41r by Lasry, f. 41v here) Cardinal Campeggio’s articles for the French crown, c. 1534 from Lorenzo Campeggio → to Francis I BnF Français 3081 ff. 41–42 (DECODE R2322), catalogued as “French marshals to the French King, 1 Jan 1520”. Two pages wholly in cipher. George Lasry broke the cipher and read the first page in 2022. The second page had no published reading and is read here with his key. Daniel Bourdeau · read 21 September 2026 Summary. The catalogue entry took its sender and date from the endorsement, “Dupplicata des articles envoyez par messrs les marechaulx françoys au roy”, and from the volume’s other letters of the 1520s. Shinsuke Tomokiyo’s cryptiana page on the ciphers of Francis I reports that George Lasry solved it in 2022. His key table and three overlay crops (dated 24 May 2022) read f. 41r: “Articles iurés par monsieur le cardinal Campege es mains de messeigneurs les cardinaulx de Bourbon, Lorraine et Tornon”. They do not cover f. 41v, a second full page of about 37 lines. Applied to that page, Lasry’s key reads it in full but for one sign and one code group. Francis I refuses to join a crusade against the Turk until Milan, Asti and Genoa are restored to him. The cardinal then swears that, “s’il plaist a Dieu me donner grace d’estre pape”, he will press the Emperor and the holders of Milan to return them. Tournon became a cardinal in 1530 and Campeggio died in 1539, so these are articles for the conclave of October 1534, not a letter of 1520 from the marshals. The page breaks off mid-sentence. One sign and one code group are open: 99.9% of the page’s letters have a value. BnF fr. 3081 f. 41v, the head of the page: “…stien et serenissime seigneur Francois roy de France, la Maieste duquel a esté souventefois recherchée…” Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3081 f. 41v, via DECODE R2322.

t: Cardinal Campeggio’s conclave articles for Francis I, c. 1534
b: DECODE R2322 carries four images from Gallica: f. 41r and f. 41v in cipher, f. 42r blank, and on f. 42v the endorsement. The cipher is a homophonic substitution with invented signs and no word division. It has 20 letters with one to four signs each, plus signs for CON and ET. Lasry found that the same key reads BnF Dupuy 265 f. 132, a letter of the bishop of Mâcon to the King of 29 May 1535. Mâcon was then ambassador in Rome. On f. 41v the key needed a few adjustments: The three-stroke sign that Lasry lists third under H reads Y : roy, iceluy, quoy, veoyant, moyennant. The “Rg” sign is P , not T: penser, pourveoir, pouvoir, partie, persuasion. A looped “4” acts as R : pour, pourveoir. Lasry’s first “unknown” sign, a bold ʃ, is probably S : “par [s]es dictes persuasions”. His second “unknown”, a cluster of strokes, occurs once, in “devers [·] et ses successeurs”. It is probably a code for the Emperor (grade M).

t: Cardinal Campeggio’s conclave articles for Francis I, c. 1534
b: The text is normalised: words divided, accents added. [brackets] are restorations, [?] marks signs not understood and … marks short gaps. … [tres chre]stien et serenissime seigneur Francois roy de France, la Maiesté duquel a esté souventefois recherchée de contribuer a l’entreprinse de l’expedition contre iceluy grant Turc, qu’il a tousiours niée, le pouvant faire, sinon que premier sa Maiesté feust reintegrée et restituée en la duché de Milan, conté d’Ast et seigneurie de Gennes, desquels en avoit esté spoliée violentement et par force. Et pendant que sa Maiesté n’estoit reintegrée en ses seigneuries, ne povoit pencer a une expedition si loingtaine ne aux chouses oc[c]upées d’iceluy grant Thurc. Par quoy, veoyant la volunté et grande envie dudit treschrestien roy n’estre si loing des armes qu’il ne les puisse reprendre, en maniere que la paix, qui n’a aucun lien ferme, … soit pour engendrer bien toust et prestement en Italie aultre plus grande fla[m]e de guerre que devant, si moyennant l[e]s … l’on ne vient a penser d’y pourveoir, ce que par grande experience se cognoist ne pouvoir faire sans contenter en quelque partie le dit tres crestien roi. Et pour ce, s’il plaist a Dieu me donner grace d’estre pape, suis venu avecques les negotiateurs de Sa Maiesté aux articles ci souscripts et aux conventions par moy iurées. Et premierement i’[es]saierai avecques toute demonstration, persuasion et exhortation que l’on pourroit user, ainsi devers [the Emperor?] et ses successeurs comme vers les detenteurs du duché de Milan et tout l’estat du dit duché, conté d’Ast et seigneurie de Gennes, que les dicts estatz et seigneuries soient rendus et restitués es mains du dit seigneur roi tres crestien ou des illustrissimes seigneurs ses enfans et successeurs. Et quant par ses dictes persuasions et voie … Translation. The Most Christian King has often been asked to join the expedition against the Turk. He has always refused unless he were first restored to the duchy of Milan, the county of Asti and the lordship of Genoa, which were taken from him by force. Unless that is provided for, the peace, which has no firm bond, will soon kindle a greater war in Italy than before. So the cardinal, if God gives him the grace to become pope, has agreed with the King’s negotiators to the articles below and sworn to them. First, he will use every persuasion with the Emperor(?) and with the holders of Milan to have Milan, Asti and Genoa returned to the King or to his sons. The page ends in the middle of the second clause.

t: Cardinal Campeggio’s conclave articles for Francis I, c. 1534
b: The DECODE images were fetched with the project’s login. Two Claude subagents transcribed f. 41v sign by sign, one taking lines 1–19 and the other lines 20–37. They used Lasry’s key table and his red overlays on f. 41r as a training sheet for this scribe’s hand, then read the letters through the key. The adjustments in section 01 came from words that repeat across the page. The line-by-line transcriptions are in the repository folder.

t: Cardinal Campeggio’s conclave articles for Francis I, c. 1534
b: Two further passes settled every doubtful place but two. In l. 12 the group after “chouses” is OCVPEES, “oc[c]upées” (C). In l. 15 a sign first taken for E is Lasry’s second M sign: “des armes” (C). Counted on the transcription, 1,339 of the page’s 1,341 letter tokens have a value (99.9%). One sign in l. 19 is outside the key. “fla[m]e” is from context (grade C). The code cluster read as the Emperor rests on context only (grade M). The value S for Lasry’s ʃ sign is grade C. The scribe wrote one A twice in l. 16. The rest of the articles are missing: f. 41v breaks off and f. 42 is blank but for the endorsement. The endorsement’s “marechaulx” does not fit the content, and the date of 1534 rests on the three cardinals named. Neither has been checked against a history of the 1534 conclave.

t: Cardinal Campeggio’s conclave articles for Francis I, c. 1534

t: Queen María to Alfonso V, Valencia 1435 — Attempted
b: The oldest unread ciphertext on DECODE with a public image: 42 signs inside a Catalan letter of Queen María to Alfonso V, written in Valencia on the day of Ponza, about something “continued until All Saints”, almost certainly the truce with Castile. Both printed Aragonese keys of the decade were tested: the 1437 alphabet is unrelated, and the 1429 nomenclator seems to match the word signs while its alphabet does not. Four neighbouring registers, 1,414 images, hold no cipher at all; the king’s own register shows his letter to her of 27 July 1435 was sent in ciffra . Valencia → Alfonso V at Gaeta · signs in a clear Catalan letter · 5 August 1435 · attempted, not read Queen María to Alfonso V, Valencia, 5 August 1435 from María of Castile → to Alfonso V Arxiu de la Corona d’Aragó, Cancillería, reg. 3225 f. 59r (DECODE R10171, public): the register copy of a short letter from the queen, lieutenant-general of the Crown, to her husband, written on the day he was defeated and captured at Ponza. Forty-two cipher signs in three runs sit inside the clear Catalan. Both printed Aragonese keys of the decade were obtained and tested, the queen’s and the king’s registers for 1421–39 were swept page by page on PARES, and the signs were attacked with a Catalan language model. Nothing reads. The text is too short on its own, and every online source that could hold more of this cipher is now exhausted. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 18 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 attempted Summary. This is the oldest ciphertext on DECODE with a public image that nobody has read: a letter of Queen María of Castile to Alfonso V, Valencia, 5 August 1435. The clear text says that, at the instance of certain parties and of “those of this kingdom”, she has worked so that something “is continued from now until All Saints”. That is almost certainly the truce of Majano with Castile, which expired on 16 July 1435 and which the queens of Aragon and Navarre had extended. The cipher itself is 42 signs in three runs. The Castile-war key of 1429 (Cortès & Pons 1986) and the Montcada–Amat key of 1437 (Aragó 1968) were both obtained. The 1437 alphabet is unrelated. The 1429 alphabet does not fit either, but its nomenclator appears to: the letter’s dotted and odd signs match its word signs for the kingdom of Aragon, Catalonia, the king of Castile and Navarre, which would make the first run a list of the parties to the truce. That is a hypothesis from four or five sign matches, not a reading. The sibling letters that would settle it are not online: reg. 3225 itself is not digitised, and four neighbouring registers (3226, 3224, 3113, and the king’s 2693), 1,414 images, contain no cipher sign at all. The king’s register does show why: his chancery registered ciphered letters in clear, among them his letter to the queen of 27 July 1435, marked in ciffra . Status: attempted, not read. What would finish it is in three archives: the other 1435 folios of ACA reg. 3225, the second key in Valencia, B.A.H.M. ms. 677 ff. 160–161, and any key of the queen’s side at the Arxiu del Regne de València.

t: Queen María to Alfonso V, Valencia 1435 — Attempted
b: Folio 59r (“LVIIII”) of reg. 3225 carries three items, all dated Valencia, 5 August 1435: a letter to the queen’s procurator at the Roman curia, one to the vice-chancellor and ambassador Jacme Pelegrí, and one to the king. Only the last contains cipher. By the numbering of the series, reg. 3225 is Secretorum locumtenentiae reginae Mariae 4, the queen’s secret register for late 1423 to early 1437. PARES has neither a description nor images of it; DECODE holds this one page, uploaded in February 2026. ACA, Cancillería, reg. 3225 f. 59r, the letter to the king: three runs of signs in the first four lines of the text, then the clear close, Scripta en Valencia a v dagost 1435 , and the subscription Senyor, vostra humil muller la Reyna d’Aragó e de Sicília . Image: Arxiu de la Corona d’Aragó, Cancillería, reg. 3225 f. 59r, via DECODE R10171. Working reading of the clear text, with the runs in brackets: Molt alt e molt excellent Senyor. Apres humil recomendacio, a [gran?] instancia dels [run 1] los daquest Regne, veents la gran necessitat, he treballat que [run 2] es continuada daci a tots sants. E [run 3] / stat exseguit e complit tot quant per vostra senyoria es stat manat, segons per mossen Matheu Pujades … daco e dels altres fets ha avisada vostra excellencia, la qual me mane lo que li sia plasent, e la qual nostre Senyor exalte longament. Scripta en Valencia a v dagost 1435. — Senyor, vostra humil muller la Reyna d’Aragó e de Sicília, qui humilment se recomana en vostra gracia e merce. La Reyna. “Most high and excellent lord. After humble recommendation: at the [great] instance of [run 1] and those of this kingdom, seeing the great need, I have worked so that [run 2] is continued from now until All Saints. And [run 3] has been carried out and fulfilled, everything your lordship ordered, as mossèn Mateu Pujades has informed your excellency of this and the other matters.”

t: Queen María to Alfonso V, Valencia 1435 — Attempted
b: Transcribed sign by sign from 5× to 7× crops. The runs mix digit-like forms (2, 3, 6, 8, 9), letter-like forms (a, d, n, v, M, ȝ, a doubled f with a bar) and figures: a triangle, a square hook, a b in a bracket, a circle with a dot, a cross on a curved foot, two E-shapes. Three of them (the hook, the bracketed b and the dotted circle) are flanked by dots, the usual mark of a nomenclator word. The 8 comes in three forms: plain, with a stroke at the top right, and with a tail at the lower left, and the tailed form follows every 6. Run Clear before Signs Clear after 1 instancia dels ff 6 8̣ △ 8 ·⌜· ·b)· 8ʹ 6 † 8ʹ los daquest Regne 2 he treballat que ȝ a ff 8ʹ 9 d 3 8ʹ v 8ʹ 6 8̣ 2 ·⊙· es continuada daci a tots sants 3 E E n 8ʹ a 8 3 2 8ʹ d ff 8 6 8̣ ∃ 8ʹ M ȝ / stat exseguit e complit 8ʹ = 8 with a top-right stroke; 8̣ = 8 with a lower-left tail. DECODE’s description counts four runs because run 3 breaks across a line end.

t: Queen María to Alfonso V, Valencia 1435 — Attempted
b: 1437, Montcada and Amat. The key of the embassy of Guillem Ramon de Montcada and Antoni Amat to Charles VII, dated 18 March 1437 (ACA, Cartas Reales Alfonso IV, Varios 69; Aragó, Cuadernos de Arqueología e Historia de la Ciudad 12, 1968; DECODE R10183, public; PARES 3205682). Its alphabet is dots, strokes and small hooks, one sign per letter; its nomenclator of about ninety entries uses a triangle for treva and a circle for naus . The alphabet shares nothing with the letter. 1429, the Castile war. The key published by Josepa Cortès Escrivà and Vicent Pons Alós, “Una clau criptogràfica d’Alfons el Magnànim per a la guerra amb Castella (1429)”, Saitabi 36 (1986), pp. 25–36: Biblioteca-Arxiu Històric Maiansià (Col·legi del Corpus Christi, València), ms. 677 f. 435v, headed cum baiulo generali Valencie , the king’s key with his batle general Joan Mercader. It has seventeen consonant signs, three signs for each vowel, nine nulls ( nichil importantes ), and a nomenclator of persons, places and terms of war drawn for the conflict with Castile. Alphabet: no fit. A few shapes recur (a crossed triple stroke for f, 8-like forms among the homophones of a and u, a 2-shaped q, a 3-shaped y), but a reading built on them gives nothing. Nomenclator: a plausible fit. The letter’s triangle matches the key’s regne d’Aragó (a triangle on a base); its dotted square hook, the key’s Catalunya (a barred hook); its dotted bracketed b, the key’s rei de Castella (a looped b set between dots); its 6 with a top stroke, the key’s curl for Navarra or naus ; and a plain 3 is one of the key’s nulls. On that reading run 1 would say, roughly, “at the instance of […] Navarre, Aragon and Catalonia, the king of Castile […] and those of this kingdom”, with the plain 8 as e , “and”. That suits a letter about extending a truce among Aragon, Navarre and Castile. It rests on four or five sign matches, and the alphabet signs between the word signs stay unassigned, so it is recorded here as a hypothesis, not a reading. The article also notes a second alphabet in the same volume, “aliud abecedarium in libro intitulato Segon d’estols e armades, cartes CLX–CLXI”, which has not been published.

t: Queen María to Alfonso V, Valencia 1435 — Attempted
b: Forty-two signs cannot fix a homophonic alphabet, so the plan was to find more text in the same key. Reg. 3225 is not on PARES (only 460 of the 866 registers of Alfonso IV are described there), so five neighbours were fetched in full and read page by page: Register Series Span Images Cipher 3226 Secretorum loc. reginae Mariae 5 Mar 1437 – Apr 1438 264 none 3224 Secretorum loc. reginae Mariae 3 Aug 1421 – Nov 1423 286 none 3113 Comune Sigilli Secreti loc. 6 June 1432 – 21 June 1435 472 none 2693 Secretorum 3 (the king) 1431 – July 1435 392 none The queen’s letters to the king in these registers, and her instructions to envoys in Castile, are all in clear. Reg. 3113 stops on 21 June 1435, before the truce expired. The Cartas Reales of Alfonso IV on PARES (3,055 items with images) hold thirteen pieces of 1435, none from the king to the queen and none in cipher. The king’s register explains the silence. His chancery copied ciphered despatches in clear and marked them fuit expedita in cifra : to his envoys at Rome in 1434, to the bishop of Lleida, to his almoner at Basel, to the archbishop of Zaragoza on 26 July 1435 (“the peace with Castile is signed and to be kept secret”), and to the queen herself on 27 July 1435. ACA, Cancillería, reg. 2693 f. 187r: Alfonso to the queen, Reyna molt cara e molt amada muller , from the siege of Gaeta, 27 July 1435, registered in clear and marked In ciffra at the foot. The letter itself explains: les vies d’aqui no son prou segures, conve scriure ab ciffra , “the roads from here are not safe enough; one must write in cipher”. The ciphered original, received in Valencia, has not been found. Image: Arxiu de la Corona d’Aragó, Cancillería, reg. 2693 f. 187r, via PARES (image 374). So a king–queen cipher was in use in the very week before her letter. The queen’s secretary copied cipher into the register; the king’s did not. The only place more of her side can survive is reg. 3225 itself, and the only place his ciphered originals can survive is among the letters she received, which on PARES do not include them.

t: Queen María to Alfonso V, Valencia 1435 — Attempted
b: A Catalan letter-quadgram model was built from about three million characters of Catalan text, and a simulated annealer searched one-sign-one-letter keys over the three runs, each scored with its clear context on both sides and the dotted signs treated as word boundaries. Without cribs it returns fluent-looking nonsense, as 42 signs must. Every crib is penalised heavily: la treua at the head of run 2 costs 63 log-units against the free optimum, treua at any offset 35 to 90, tregua 61 or more, castella anywhere in run 3 between 50 and 128, and most other offsets are impossible because a repeated sign would have to stand for two letters. With the 1429 nomenclator applied the result is the same. A plain substitution does not carry the expected words, which points to homophones, nulls and word signs, and those cannot be recovered from this little text.

t: Queen María to Alfonso V, Valencia 1435 — Attempted
h: What remains open, and what would finish it
b: All 42 signs are unread. The nomenclator identifications above are graded M (possible) in the README’s scale; the reading of run 2 as the truce, and of the plain 8 as e , as C (likely) and M. ACA reg. 3225, the other folios of 1435 (roughly ff. 50–80), for more letters in the same cipher. It is not digitised; a reproduction request to the ACA is the direct route. The second alphabet of B.A.H.M. ms. 677, ff. 160–161, in the Col·legi del Corpus Christi, València, the likeliest printed-adjacent source for a Valencian key of these years. A key of the queen’s side at the Arxiu del Regne de València, where the batle general’s papers are kept.

t: Matthias Corvinus to Ercole I d’Este, Pozsony 1 June 1482 — DECODE R1156
b: The King of Hungary answers Ferrara’s call for help in the first weeks of the War of Ferrara, with troops, route, names and plan in a sign cipher. DECODE lists it as partly decrypted, but it was printed in 1877 and again by Fraknói in 1895. The runs are read here from the image and a working key rebuilt; four garbled places in the printed text are corrected, among them the closing sentence the edition prints as nonsense. Pozsony → Ferrara · letter substitution with homophones and three name signs · 1 June 1482 · found already read Matthias Corvinus to Ercole I d’Este, 1 June 1482 from Matthias Corvinus → to Ercole I d'Este Modena, Archivio di Stato, Carteggio principi esteri 1622, b. 1/3, nos. 2, 2a · one page, Latin, with about fifteen runs in cipher · DECODE R1156, “partially decrypted” The King of Hungary tells his brother-in-law, whom Venice had just attacked, what help he can send and why it cannot yet get through. The cipher was read in the nineteenth century and the letter is in print. The runs are read again here from the image, and four places where the printed text went wrong are put right. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 19 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read in 1877 Summary. The letter came up as a pre-1497 candidate in the catalogue: a King of Hungary writing in cipher in 1482, marked on DECODE as only partly decrypted. It is not unread. Magyar diplomácziai emlékek III (1877) printed it from the Modena original, and Vilmos Fraknói reprinted it in Mátyás király levelei II (1895), no. 131, noting that the original is “partly written in secret signs”. The cipher is a simple one: invented signs for the letters, two to four signs for the common vowels, doubled letters marked by dots, and three signs for names (Venice, King Ferdinand of Naples, Matthias himself). Aligning the runs with the printed text rebuilds most of the key. The key then shows the edition wrong in four places. The hussars are the ones “who are worth more than the rest” ( valent , printed “valoris (sic)”). Balázs Magyar leaves with troops ( gentibus ), not servants. The closing sentence, printed as nonsense, reads Speramus cito nos res nostras ita disposituros, ut meliori postea modo vos iuvare possemus . And the “contemporary regest” Fraknói prints at the foot is the letter’s own last sentence, half in cipher. Status: found already read; corrected here. Open: one run after faciet and the clear verb before it, and the two name signs after regina .

t: Matthias Corvinus to Ercole I d’Este, Pozsony 1 June 1482 — DECODE R1156
b: Venice declared war on Ferrara in May 1482. Duke Ercole I d’Este was married to Eleonora of Aragon, daughter of King Ferdinand of Naples and sister of Beatrix, Queen of Hungary since 1476. Eleonora wrote to her sister and brother-in-law for help. Matthias answered from Pozsony (Pressburg, Bratislava) on the first of June. He was himself at war with the Emperor Frederick III, whose lands lay between Hungary and Italy. The letter is one page of Latin in a chancery hand, with the address and a red seal on the verso. The courtesies and the reasoning are in clear. The numbers, the troops, the route, the names and the plan are in cipher, set into the clear lines as short runs. DECODE holds two images (I5815, I5816). The archive keeps the rights, and the images are not reproduced here.

t: Matthias Corvinus to Ercole I d’Este, Pozsony 1 June 1482 — DECODE R1156
b: Each letter of the Latin is replaced by an invented sign. Many signs look like numerals or letters turned about (5, 4, 9, 2, 3, 7, 8, a reversed C, L, T and its inversion ⊥, Ŧ, Π, Λ, ⊏, ⊐, ∃, ∅), which makes the runs look like a string of figures at first sight. Vowels and the commonest consonants have two to four signs each. A doubled letter is one sign between dots, ·ıı· for tt in mittere and mitteremus . There are no word breaks inside a run, but the runs themselves are mostly single words or short phrases, spaced like the clear text. Lines 9–13 of the letter: statim cum d. regina consorte nostra statuimus [mittere] in [subsidium vestrum quingentos equites], inter [quos] essent [centum usarones], idest [homines] levis [armature], qui plus [ceteris valent] … Image: Archivio di Stato di Modena, Cancelleria, Carteggio principi esteri 1622, b. 1/3, no. 2, via DECODE R1156. The working key below comes from lining up each run with the printed text and keeping only values that recur in at least two words: letter signs letter signs a 8, V n ⊏, ϲ b d o 7, Π, Λ, + c Ͻ (reversed C) p ⊔ d 2, ᑐ q = e 5, 4, 9, ς r Ŧ f ϵ (once) s L, Γ, S g ᒪ (hooked L) t ⊥, + h 6 u / v ⊤, ∃ i 2, 3, ∅ tt ·ıı· l σ, ᒧ m ⊐, ᑐ Name signs: a looped ampersand for Veneti (and Venetorum ), a crossed square for regi Ferdinando , and a q with a looped tail for Rex Hungarie , the King referring to himself. Some signs seem to serve two letters (+ for o, t and e; 2 for i and d). With about 330 signs of cipher in all, the sample is too short to tell whether these are true homophones shared between letters or two similar shapes that a transcription from the image cannot separate.

t: Matthias Corvinus to Ercole I d’Este, Pozsony 1 June 1482 — DECODE R1156
b: Clear text in roman, the cipher runs in brackets, corrections to the printed text in bold. The first lines of the letter, all in clear, are as Fraknói prints them. … statim cum domina regina consorte nostra statuimus [mittere] in [subsidium] [vestrum] [quingentos] [equites], inter [quos] essent [centum] [usarones], idest [homines] levis [armature], qui plus [ceteris] [valent] . Sed cum examinaremus cum domina regina ‹two signs› et [aliis] nostris, per [quam] [viam] possemus [eos] [mittere], non invenimus aliquam [tutam]. … In crastinum hinc recedet [Mager] [Balas] [capitaneus] [noster] cum [pluribus] [gentibus] , iturus in [Croatiam] versus [confinia] [Venetorum], ubi [plures] etiam [congregabit]; et quotienscunque inventa erit [tuta] [transeundi] [via], statim significet [Regi Hungarie] et illic faciet [?] [venient]. Speramus cito nos [res] [nostras] ita [disposituros], ut meliori postea modo [vos] [iuvare] possemus. [Rex Hungarie] [scripsit] [regi Ferdinando] quomodo possent [diverti] [Veneti] et [confundere] [eos] et cum paucis [pecuniis]. Dat. Posonii, primo Junii 1482. “… at once, with our lady the queen, we decided to send five hundred horse to your aid, among them a hundred hussars, that is light horse, who are worth more than the rest. But when we considered with the queen and our other counsellors by what road we could send them, we found none safe. … Tomorrow our captain Balázs Magyar leaves here with a large force for Croatia, towards the Venetian border, where he will gather more; and whenever a safe way through is found, he is to tell the King of Hungary at once, and they will come there. We hope soon to have our own affairs so arranged that afterwards we can help you better. The King of Hungary has written to King Ferdinand how the Venetians might be drawn off and thrown into confusion, and at small cost.”

t: Matthias Corvinus to Ercole I d’Este, Pozsony 1 June 1482 — DECODE R1156
h: What the printed text got wrong
b: “qui plus ceteris valoris (így)”. The run is v-a-l-e-n-t. The hussars are the ones “who are worth more than the others”. The editor printed a non-word and marked it sic . “cum pluribus servis”. The run is g-e-n-t-i-b-u-s, with the same hooked-L g as congregabit . Balázs leaves with troops, which suits a captain sent to gather more on the Venetian border. “Speramus nos eos nostris contra dispositiones ut meliori postea modo possemus (így)”. The edition skipped the clear word cito , took r-e-s for eos and n-o-s-t-r-a-s for nostris , turned d-i-s-p-o-s-i-t-u-r-o-s into “contra dispositiones”, and left out v-o-s i-u-v-a-r-e, the verb the sentence needs. Read from the signs, the sentence is sound Latin: Speramus cito nos res nostras ita disposituros, ut meliori postea modo vos iuvare possemus. The “regest”. Fraknói ends the letter with the date and gives, as a regest written “at the end of the letter in a contemporary hand”, the words Rex Hungarie scripsit regi Ferdinando, quomodo possent diverti Veneti et confundere eos et cum paucis pecuniis . That is the letter’s own last sentence, in the same hand, before the date, with the three name signs and s-c-r-i-p-s-i-t, d-i-v-e-r-t-i, c-o-n-f-u-n-d-e-r-e, e-o-s and p-e-c-u-n-i-i-s in cipher. His words are right, but he placed the sentence outside the letter. The verso carries only the address and the seal, so if a separate decipherment exists it is on leaf 2a, which DECODE did not image.

t: Matthias Corvinus to Ercole I d’Este, Pozsony 1 June 1482 — DECODE R1156
b: statim significet [Regi Hungarie] et illic faciet [?] [venient] . The printed text has convenire . The run after faciet is the looped-q name sign followed by v-e-n-i-e-n-t (grade C). The same sign may stand here for quod or for the syllable con- . The clear verb before the first q-sign looks more like sufficietur than significet on the image (grade M). The sense is not in doubt. Two name signs after cum domina regina are not in the printed text and are not read (grade I). Signs that serve two letters (+, 2) and the single f are grade C. The rest of the key is grade H, confirmed on two or more words. The two lines Fraknói gives about the letter to King Ferdinand (“Scripsimus regi Ferdinando, ut rex ipse vel dux Ferrarie possent aliquem excogitare modum…”) were checked only where they are in cipher ( modum , tuto , mitteremus ). His “libenter mitteremus (így)” stands as printed: the run does spell m-i-tt-e-r-e-m-u-s.

t: The Silentium Dei ’s secret script, 1798 — a Rosicrucian machine book read with its own key
b: DECODE R2873, catalogued as a ciphered letter of Johann Arndt, is a 129-page alchemical manuscript copied in 1798. It describes a “magical machine” of three burning glasses. Its pigpen-type “secret script” has its key drawn on p. 83. Page 24 was read online in 2022 by Lasry and Kopal; here all 31 passages are read with the book’s key, 1,545 signs with two unread, and five passages read for the first time. Glücksbrunn, Germany · pigpen-type “secret script” with ligatures · 18–25 September 1798 · read The Silentium Dei ’s secret script, 1798 Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Mellon MS 136 (DECODE R2873). DECODE and the Unsolved Catalogue list it as a ciphered letter from Johann Arndt to an unknown recipient. It is actually an alchemical manuscript book, Das zweyte Silentium Dei in Königs Salomonis des Weisen paradiessischen Lustgarten . It describes a “magical machine” of three burning glasses, and hides its working details in a Rosicrucian cipher. The key is drawn in the book. The long passage on p. 24 was read online in 2022. Here all 31 passages are transcribed and read with the book’s key. Daniel Bourdeau · read 22 September 2026 read Summary. The catalogue entry is a DECODE record: a 1798 “letter” by Johann Arndt, who died in 1621. The Yale images show a 129-page alchemical manuscript copied in September 1798. It is a Rosicrucian-Paracelsian compilation that names Arndt as its author and gives a preface signed “Joh. Arndt 1599”. It describes a “magische Machine”: three burning glasses that focus sunlight onto glass dishes and capels to calcine, distil and “tinge” metals, minerals and plants. The cipher, “unsere geheime Schrift”, is a pigpen-type alphabet with ligature signs, and its key is drawn on p. 83. It hides one whole page (p. 24, the legend to the plates of the machine) and 30 short phrases inside clear sentences on pp. 25–76. The key reads all of them unchanged: 1,545 signs, of which two are unread. One is a sign outside the key; the other is a word that runs into the gutter. Klaus Schmeh’s Cipherbrain post of March 2022 already printed the p. 24 plaintext, from George Lasry’s transcription and Nils Kopal’s decryption. A reader’s comment there gave most of the short passages, with gaps and misreadings. This page gives the full reading, corrects both, and adds five passages not read before. Section 04 translates into English the thirteen recipes that carry the cipher: the spirit of mercury, the improvement of ores, drinkable gold, oil of talc, the “Star of the World” drawn from saltpetre, the flower distillation, the wine stone and the seven-metal mirror.

t: The Silentium Dei ’s secret script, 1798 — a Rosicrucian machine book read with its own key
b: The title page reads Das zweyte Silentium Dei in Königs Salomonis des Weisen paradiessischen Lustgarten … des Theophrasti Paracelsi Himmels Schlüssels 2ter Theil . It says the text came “von dem Patriarchen und grossen R. Rosen” out of Arabic and Spanish into High German, with its secret script, “durch Johann Arndt”. Arndt is the Lutheran author of Wahres Christentum , and here his name is a borrowed authority. The Yale record dates the copy 18–25 September 1798 at Glücksbrunn, “by Gottfried Klaussen(?)”. DECODE turned that into a sender, a date and a place for a letter, and gave it an “unknown recipient”. The book has 129 numbered pages. The plates on pp. 21–23 show the machine: a stand with three conical glasses aimed at the sun, a sand-capel, a glass globe of water, a distilling flask. The text runs from the mineral kingdom (calcination, the “Aurum potabile”, the “Alumen plumosum”) through the vegetable (distilling plants and wine) to the animal, the seven metals and a “Secretum secretorum”. Page 16 says the use of the machine is written “in unserer geheimen Sprache, so Crucis Rosen[kreuzer]”. Page 83 prints “Die Figur unserer geheimen Schrift”, under a verse: “Wer allhier diese Figur recht versteht, der sieht, wie unsre Schrift darinnen steht”.

t: The Silentium Dei ’s secret script, 1798 — a Rosicrucian machine book read with its own key
b: Page 83: “Die Figur unserer geheimen Schrift”. Each cell’s walls are its sign. The second letter of a cell is the same sign with a dot. On the right is the table of ligature signs (ae, oe, ui, ch, ck, sch, ss, st, th, und, ll, lich, nn, tz). The last five triangle signs, for v, w, y, x and z, are a later pencil addition. Image: Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Mellon MS 136 p. 83, via Yale Digital Collections (image 45). The figure is a circle crossed by two diagonals and a noughts-and-crosses grid. That makes nine square cells and four triangles where the diagonals cross the centre. Each cell holds two letters in alphabetical order, and the second is marked by a dot: sign ┘ ⊔ └ ⊐ □ ⊏ ┐ ⊓ ┌ V > < Λ plain a c e g i l n p r t v z dotted b d f h (k) m o q s u w y (x) The table beside it adds single signs for common German letter groups. A double stroke over any sign doubles it ( ll , tt , nn ). It is a textbook pigpen, the kind the eighteenth-century Rosicrucian and masonic societies used. The key has the same shape as their alphabets. It hides nothing from anyone holding the book, and the key fits every passage without a single change.

t: The Silentium Dei ’s secret script, 1798 — a Rosicrucian machine book read with its own key
b: Page 24, “Beschreibung der magischen Machine No. 1 Fig. Olis”, the only page wholly in cipher. The Latin capitals A–S, numerals and planet signs are in clear. A modern reader has pencilled some values above the signs. Image: Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Mellon MS 136 p. 24, via Yale Digital Collections (image 16). Page 24 , the legend to the plates (German as written; ☿ Mercury, ∇ water, ∴ sand): No. A. B. C. zeigen die hohlgeschliffene Gläsern, deren das erste in seiner Circumferenz M 6 oder 12 Zoll, das andere O. 12 oder 14, das dritte Q 18 oder 16 Zoll hält, wie dieselben in gleich weiter Distanz gestellet werden müssen, auf das ein Focus den andern erreichen könne bis auf das Centrum. No. D. wo der ☿ ist in. No. E. steig der Spiritus ☿ii. No. F. ist eine gläserne Kugel mit frischen gemeinen ∇ angefüllt. No. G. sey von eichenen oder andern harten Holz Aufsäz Stöcke. No. H. ist eine ∴ Capelle. No. I. ist ein Zoll dickes Brett oder Drehstock, darein die Gläser gestellet werden. No. K. ist d[ie] gläserne offene Schaalen. No. L. ist der Stock, worauf die Schaale gestellt wird. No. M. ist ein gläserner [?]. No. N. das ist eine gläserne Capelle. No. O. ist das Glas mit denen Blumen. No. P. ist das Glas, so zu lit. b. muss lutirt werden. No. Q. ist der Stöpsel. No. R. ist das runde Glas mit kleinen Löchlein, gehören zu lit. a. No. S. Renien seyn die grünen Augen-Brillen, so man in Edel-Gestein arbeitet. In English: A, B and C are the ground concave glasses. The first is 6 or 12 inches round, the second 12 or 14, the third 18 or 16. They must stand at equal distances so that one focus reaches the next, down to the centre. D is where the mercury goes, and at E its spirit rises. F is a glass globe filled with fresh common water. G are stands of oak or other hard wood, H a sand-capel, and I an inch-thick board or turntable that holds the glasses. K is the open glass dishes and L the stand the dish sits on. M is a glass [vessel, sign not read] and N a glass capel. O is the glass with the flowers, P the glass to be luted at b, and Q the stopper. R is the round glass with small holes, which belongs to a. S, “Renien”, are the green spectacles used when working gemstones. The short passages. Elsewhere the cipher hides only the working words of a recipe: vessel, material, dose or procedure. The sentence around it is in clear German, as below. The cipher words are in bold. The recipes are translated in full in section 04 . p. in context 25 set behind the receiver die ∇-Kugel No. F. ; NB diese Kugel must stand fast 29 spread the ore-slime on einen breiten glatten Reibe- oder Marmor-Stein 31, 32 a dish shaped like einer Capellen ; … gläsernen Capellen 43 a ducat of fine gold in einer gläsernen Schalen ; then a piece of gemeinen 🜍 [sulphur] 45, 47 in einer solchen Glas Schaalen ; bring it in Glas Schaalen before the machine, nach und nach 53 take rein ausgelassenen nitrum in the Glas-Schale nach K. ; der Salpeter turns yellow and reddish, nach und nach 54, 55 so that it has ein wenig dig[…] heat; näher zu unsern magischen Feuer nach und nach einkoche einen hochrothen Pulver ; gelben ; a small part dieses Pulvers in fresh water 56 the Astrum Mundi obtained durch den Salpeter 60 then lutire das Glas No. S. unten 61, 62 your spirit with its oil in die offene Glas Schaalen ; offene Glas Schaalen 70 the seven metals, one on the other, in einen weiten und starcken gläsernen Tiegel zur Zeit ihrer Regierung und eigenen Planeten Stunde 75 wie grösser die vorgebildete Brenn-Gläser sein, die bessern Gewalt haben sie, einige sta-cken zu enden; aber zu unsern hier beschriebenen Wercken seyn sie mit M. O. und Q. Zollen, endlich biss 7 Zollen gross genug . For melting, da sollst das grösste Glas vornen gegen der Sonne stehend machen , so that the rays fall together in eine Fuge ; to distil, wende deine Machine um, dass das kleinste Glas gegen der Sonne zu stehe ; … Machine mit dem Spiritu Mercurii 76 for a gentler heat so ziehe entweder die Machine oder deine vorgesezte Materiam etwas weiteres von einander, oder setze eine grosse mit frischen ∇ angefüllte gläserne Kugel darzwischen ; so that the fire casts seine centralische Strahlen justo auf die Materie werffe Page 76, the fourth cipher passage (“so ziehe entweder die Machine … darzwischen”) and, below it, “seine centralische Strahlen … auf die Materie werffe”. Image: Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Mellon MS 136 p. 76, via Yale Digital Collections.

t: The Silentium Dei ’s secret script, 1798 — a Rosicrucian machine book read with its own key
b: These are the recipes that carry the deciphered passages, translated whole from the clear German around them. Words written in the secret script are in bold . Pious asides and the attacks on apothecaries are cut to […]. (?) marks an uncertain reading of the clear hand. The German transcription is in mellon136/clear/ . The figures of the machine are on pp. 21–23, and p. 24 above gives the letters used for them. 1. The spirit of mercury (pp. 25–26) To begin using the machine, make the spirit of common mercury, which cannot otherwise be brought into its prima ens . Put common mercury into a cucurbit, as the machine shows. Set a still-head on it and attach a receiver. Behind the receiver place the water-globe No. F. NB this globe must stay there the whole time. It must not be closed, and if the water runs low it must be topped up. Then point the machine exactly at the sun, so that the third focus reaches the mercury in the flask. Its heat drives the mercury over the still-head as a spirit. NB: too quick and sudden a fire does harm. Set the stand with the machine somewhat farther off than the focus reaches, and move it up to the focus little by little. The mercury then rises with force into the receiver and turns into a spirit or aqua viscosa . This spirit leads all metallic bodies back into their prima materia , making a spiritual thing out of a bodily one. 2. The philosophical glass stone: silver, gold and a medicine (pp. 26–28) Coagulate the spirit of mercury again in an open glass dish before the machine into a metallic stone. Then melt it with the same fire into a glass, a “salamander”: this is the philosophical glass stone. Silver. Melt 1 part of the ground glass with 100 parts of fine silver. This gives a white, brittle matter that grinds easily to powder. Add 1 part of this to 1,000 parts of common mercury in open glass dishes, once the fire has taken hold and the mercury begins to smoke, and it is fixed into the best silver. This silver is too compact, as heavy as gold, so alloy each Mark of it with 4 Loth of raw copper. The copper’s sulphur “opens its pores”, and it stays good silver. Gold. Done the same way with gold, “the profit could well run higher, for it is one and the same work”. Medicine. The stone must never be taken raw. Put a small piece into a glass of wine for 12 hours, drink the wine and wait for the sweat. It purges by stool and urine, and in plague time it is “a universal medicine”. 3. Improving ores and minerals, in four operations (pp. 28–32) The book says this works for all tame and wild ores (gold, silver, iron, mercury, tin, copper and lead ores) and for the wild minerals: pyrites, blende, bismuth, glance, cobalt, marcasite, spar, vitriol earth, calamine, ochre, feather alum, tin-stone, sands and coloured mineral earths. The main rule. Take a tame or wild mineral and assay it on the mine hundredweight. Stamp it crude, as it comes from the mine, and wash off as much of the rock as you can. Set up the machine. Dry the slimes and spread them, not too thick, on a broad smooth grinding- or marble-stone . Let the machine calcine them, stirring all the time with a piece of wood, or better a glass rod, so that they take the heat evenly. Weigh the calcined mineral again and you will find “a rich increase”. The book's explanation is that the spiritus mundi gathers in it, and the wild ores ripen and fix themselves without any addition. Second operation. Put the calcined mineral into a wide, strong glass dish and let the fire work into its middle at full strength. It soon melts without any flux. Take the machine away and let it cool. Third operation, refining. Take a strong, thick glass dish of suitable size, shaped like a capel but hollowed deeper. Lay the melted metal in it and add lead, as in ordinary cupelling. Set the fire on it: the lead fumes away and leaves the finest bead, “far higher than on a capel”. An ordinary bone-ash capel will not do, because the spiritus mundi would sink into it and spoil the work. Fourth operation, parting. If the bead holds gold and silver together, lay it in a glass dish, moderately deep and not too wide, and melt it before the machine. Throw a little powdered glass on it bit by bit. The gold separates, and the silver goes with the glass into a slag. Then cupel the slag with lead in the glass capel described above. You now have the silver and the gold, each refined separately. 4. Aurum potabile, drinkable gold (pp. 43–44) Melt a ducat’s weight of fine gold in a glass dish before the machine and keep it molten until it begins to smoke. Then draw it quickly away from the machine, so that it has only a calcining heat. Throw a small piece of common sulphur on it and let it burn off, and the gold turns brittle and quite red. Stir it round with a glass rod and calcine it until it no longer smokes. Turn the machine away and let it cool. The gold is now a brittle matter, “spread with many thousand beautiful colours”, and the text claims it has gained half its weight in “astral salt”. It dissolves in wine at once, tinges it deep red and rises with it over the still-head, so it can never be turned back into gold. Boil it all down before the machine into a sweet salt. The dose is one drop, or half a Gran by weight, in wine. It works by sweating, and the book says it cures every disease and keeps a man healthy to the term God has set. 5. Feather alum (p. 45) Take feather alum ( alumen plumosum ) crude, as it comes from the mine, and treat it before the machine in such a glass dish , the same way as the pearls earlier in the book. It gives “a very noble stone” of many colours, “our true electrum”. This is the root of the tincture that raises lesser gemstones to perfection. The next page claims the same treatment makes talc, “invincible in fire”, fluid and turns it into a like tincture. 6. Oil of talc (pp. 47–48) Put common talc in the glass dish before the machine. Bring it up little by little , so that the heat only calcines it. Calcine it until it falls into a blue powder and no longer smokes. Then draw the machine back gently, little by little, so that for about 13 (?) hours it gives only a digesting heat. The calcined talc then draws the spiritus mundi to itself and dissolves into a flesh-coloured oil and spirit. Every metal, mineral, stone, coral and pearl is brought to spirit and oil the same way. The more a mineral has been calcined, the more strongly it draws the world-spirit. In a stronger fire the solution coagulates again and fixes itself “in the very highest degree”, for health and for improving metals and gemstones. 7. Drawing down the Star of the World, and a water that multiplies seed (pp. 53–55) The vegetable tinctures are of two kinds, one for multiplying plants and one for health. The multiplying tincture needs the Astrum Mundi first. Attractio Astri Mundi. Take purely melted-down nitre , spread it thinly in the glass dish, as at K. , and calcine it very gently before the machine until all its moisture has fumed off and the saltpetre turns yellow and reddish. Then draw it little by little away from the machine until it has only a little digesting [?] heat. It now draws the spiritus mundi to itself, “its very nearest blood-relation”. In a few hours one can collect “many measures” of the world-spirit. Set the collected spirit nearer to our magical fire , so that it little by little boils down into a bright-red powder , or one of the yellow kind. The author breaks off here: three words more, he says, would show the philosophers’ stone to the whole world. Throw a small part of this powder into a great deal of fresh water. It rises and ferments, and the froth is skimmed off. Sprinkle grains of wheat or any other seed with this tinging water before sowing: the book promises a thousandfold increase and fruit of unheard-of size. For plants, trees and shrubs, wet their roots with it a little. 8. The vitrified stone of the Astrum Mundi (p. 56) Take the Astrum Mundi caught by means of the saltpetre . After calcining it, melt it before the machine into a vitrified stone, which takes 4 to 5 (?) hours. “All the forces of nature” are said to be in this stone, for wonders “in all three kingdoms”. A curse on anyone who misuses it (Deuteronomy 28:59) runs on to p. 59. 9. Distilling flowers downwards (pp. 59–61) What the machine drives up over a still-head is only a clear spirit, though it is “a thousand times better” than what a coal fire gives. With plants, what is driven down ( per descensum ) is far finer. Fill glass No. O (the glass for the flowers) heaped full with rose petals or other flowers, and close the stopper on top. Lute the glass No. S. underneath , set the whole in a ring on a stand before the machine, and let the fire work very gently. It drives first the spirit, then the oil, down into glass No. P. One drop of it is worth more than a thousand of waters distilled the common way. The cipher reads “No. S.”, but on p. 24 the glass to be luted is P, and the clear text on p. 61 calls it P. 10. The “cure” of all flowers and herbs (pp. 61–62) Put the spirit and oil driven down above into the open glass dishes and let the fire shine on them gently. They draw the Astra Mundi to themselves and boil down to a very fine powder of the same colour as the flowers. Of this, 1 grain to 1 Maas of fresh water tinges it all into the best rose water, or the water of whichever flower it came from. 11. Concentration of wine: the stone that turns water into wine (pp. 62–63) The vegetable universal is made from the noblest wine. It lets a person “carry about with him two hundred and more Ohm of wine”. Choose the wine you find best to drink. Fill the open glass dishes with it and set the machine so that the rays strike down on it steadily. It begins to simmer. Do not let it boil hard, but let it boil down to half and keep adding more, or let it drip in from another vessel, no faster than it boils away. Go on until three or four Maas or more have been boiled down to dryness. Then strengthen the fire and hold what is left in fusion for an hour, which increases it by a third. Turn the machine aside and let it cool: “you then have a stone that turns water into wine”. To raise it higher, crush the stone, calcine it and melt it in an open glass dish over a very gentle fire into a liquor. 12. The electrum of the seven metals and the magic mirror (pp. 69–71) No one can work wonders with characters, sigils or electrum amulets without first making an electrum with this fire, in the right conjunction and course of the planets. Take all seven metals in equal weight, fine and refined, and melt them one after another in a wide and strong glass crucible, each at the time of its rule and in its own planetary hour . Gold goes on Sunday in the hour of the Sun, silver on Monday, iron on Tuesday, mercury on Wednesday, tin on Thursday, copper on Friday and lead on Saturday. Each will be found heavier. Then melt all seven together on a Sunday in the hour of the Sun into an electrum metallicum . Cast it in a mirror mould and have it polished. The polisher must never look into the mirror with bare eyes, but always through spectacles (“Renien”, the green glasses of p. 24): whoever first looks into it is its master. It then shows whatever is asked of it. A little bell cast from the same electrum is said to put a whole army to flight. 13. How to set the machine for each fire (pp. 75–76) The larger the burning glasses, the greater their power […] but for the works described here, glasses of M., O. and Q. inches, up to 7 inches, are large enough. Too much power overdrives the work. Each operation needs its own fire: Melting: make the largest glass stand in front, facing the sun . It throws the rays together onto the matter into one joint . Distilling: turn the machine round so that the smallest glass faces the sun . The rays spread and warm the whole glass, as in the machine with the Spiritus Mercurii (recipe 1). Digesting, or a still weaker fire: either draw the machine and the matter set before it somewhat further apart, or set a large glass globe filled with fresh water between them . Melting, calcining and fixing: set it so that the fire casts its central rays exactly onto the matter . “This is, NB NB, the chief rule in all the works.” The book then turns to the “receptacle No. 2” for catching the Astrum Mundi (pp. 76–78): a helm and counter-flask made in one piece, pierced with sixteen holes the width of a little finger, four to each quarter of the sky. The world-spirit is driven through them into a round receiver.

t: The Silentium Dei ’s secret script, 1798 — a Rosicrucian machine book read with its own key
b: Nils Kopal told Klaus Schmeh about the book, and Schmeh put it on his Encrypted Book List as no. 00114. His post on Cipherbrain (4 March 2022) links a video by Kopal. In it Kopal decrypts page 24 from a transcription by George Lasry and shows how CrypTool would break it without the key. The post prints the p. 24 plaintext and points to the key on p. 83. On 10 March 2022 a reader, Christof Rieber, commented with readings of most of the short passages. The search that found these came after the key had been read here, but before any passage was transcribed. They were then used as a check. Page 24 agrees with the published text except for small points: Stöpsel (not “Stopfel”), Löchlein , zu lit. b. muss lutirt werden , arbeitet , and the unread sign after “No. M. ist ein gläserner”, which the published text passes over. Rieber’s list has gaps and some misreadings. He gives “rotiere das Glass noch unten” for lutire das Glas No. S. unten (p. 60) and “noch” for the cipher No. (pp. 25, 60). He gives “nachtnach” for nach und nach and “einige raschen” for einige sta-cken (p. 75). The p. 75 word is still doubtful. Rieber does not have the second passage on p. 47 ( nach und nach ), the third on p. 53, the one on p. 56 ( durch den Salpeter ), or seine centralische Strahlen … auf die Materie werffe on p. 76.

t: The Silentium Dei ’s secret script, 1798 — a Rosicrucian machine book read with its own key
b: The Yale Digital Collections site blocks scripted requests, so the manifest was read in a browser and the 69 images were then fetched from the IIIF server. Contact sheets of every opening located the cipher: p. 24 and pp. 25–76. No page before 24 or after 76 has cipher, except the key on p. 83. Pages 84–87 give a cabbalistic letter-number table in clear. Each passage was cut from the full-resolution image and read sign by sign with the p. 83 key. The transcription is kept as key values with ligature signs bracketed, and a short script maps it back to signs and counts it: 1,545 signs, 345 words, two unread.

t: The Silentium Dei ’s secret script, 1798 — a Rosicrucian machine book read with its own key
b: Unread (2 signs). p. 24, No. M.: one sign after “ein gläserner” that is not in the key, probably a pictogram of the vessel. p. 54: the word after “ein wenig dig” runs into the gutter, probably digerirende (Hitze). Yale’s image is the only one available. Doubtful (C). p. 24 “steig der Spiritus” (or steigen ); p. 24 “No. K. ist d gläserne” (one sign, perhaps short for die ); p. 53 “nach K.” (a clear capital after the cipher; sense unclear); p. 75 “einige sta-cken zu enden”, read letter by letter but obscure. “Renien” (p. 24, No. S.) reads cleanly but is an obscure word. On p. 60 the cipher reads “lutire das Glas No. S.”, but the glass to be luted is P on p. 24 and on p. 61. The copyist probably slipped, or the S is an unusual P; the reading keeps the S. Everything else is H: read sign by sign with the book’s key, in sense, and consistent with the clear text and the plates.

t: Frater Elias’s secret names, c. 1525 — an alchemical cipher that will not read
b: DECODE R2877, catalogued as a letter of Elias of Cortona, is the Beinecke’s pseudo-Elian Lumen luminum , an alchemical codex of about 1525. Its Italian prologue gives, in about 234 letters of cipher, what each of the twelve zodiac “spirits” is called and the ingredients of a recipe for gold and one for silver. Simple substitution (with a control that shows it would have worked), homophonic, progressive, Vigenère and Alberti-disk attacks all failed; the strings may be invented secret names. Pseudo-Elias of Cortona · alchemical codex, North Italy · letter cipher of an unknown kind · c. 1525 · attempted, not read The secret names in Frater Elias’s Lumen luminum Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Mellon MS 29 (DECODE R2877). This is not a letter. It is a small Venetian (?) alchemical book, ascribed to Brother Elias, St Francis’s successor, and falsely dated 1315. In its Italian prologue the twelve zodiac signs stand for twelve “spirits”, and what each of them “is called” is written in cipher. So are the ingredients of a recipe for gold and one for silver. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 22 September 2026 not read Summary. The catalogue entry, taken from DECODE, described a ciphered letter from Elias of Cortona (d. 1253) to an unknown recipient, dated 1525, in “graphic signs”. The images show something else: a paper codex of the Lumen luminum , copied in North Italy about 1525, with the cipher confined to the Italian prologue on ff. 1v–2v. A late sixteenth-century owner recopied it on the front pastedown. The cipher is about 234 lower-case letters with three scribal signs. It fills a twelve-line table giving what each zodiac sign “se chiama” (is called), and the ingredient lists of a Sol recipe and a Luna recipe. The recipes use the zodiac names in clear, so the table should be the key to the cover names. The letter statistics look language-like (IC 0.075), but no simple system produces Italian or Latin. Monoalphabetic, homophonic, Caesar and Trithemius shifts, Vigenère, an Alberti cipher disk with an unknown ring, and a word-pattern solver over some 170 substance names were all tried. A control shows that the substitution solver would have broken a real Italian ingredient list of this size. The text stays unread. The shapes of its words suggest invented “secret names” as much as a cipher. The Beinecke catalogue already suspected charlatanism.

t: Frater Elias’s secret names, c. 1525 — an alchemical cipher that will not read
h: The book and where the cipher is
b: Mellon MS 29 has 33 leaves, written in red and black in an italic hand. It opens with an Italian prologue (ff. 1r–2v). Then comes Liber alkimistalis quem frater Elia edidit apud Imperatorem federicum … Incipit liber lumen luminum traslatus de sarracenico ac hebraico in latinum (ff. 3r–36r). Last are a Latin–Arabic synonym list and some Italian recipes (ff. 36r–37v). Every leaf was checked. The Latin treatise and the recipes are in clear, with only the usual ʒ and ℔ weight signs. The cipher is on four pages only. f. 1r , clear: the book was “experimentado nel 1315”. Its medicine serves the Sun and the Moon, whose names the author has hidden in two figures, a star and a reversed C with a p. Five bodies make sun and moon: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus and Mercury. f. 1v , clear: the medicines, “ouer nomi deli spiriti che lauano purgano et mondificano li corpi”, are Aries, Taurus, Gemini and the rest of the twelve signs. Then comes the Sol recipe : “Primo nel nome de dio piglierai:” followed by three lines of cipher, then in clear “Dapoi pista in mortaro et tritale in poluere minutissima … agiongerai ʒ che dir onze de leone”. f. 2r : the Luna recipe , “piglia i nomi del signor.”, followed by three lines of cipher that contain the clear words in and cioe . It goes on in clear: “… et scorpio et tauro et gemini piglia ʒ cioe drama 1”. f. 2v : the zodiac table , “Ariete se chiama …” for all twelve signs. Front pastedown , a later hand: the Luna recipe and the table copied again, with many variants, among clear notes in Italian and Latin. The notes gloss the planets (“sol significa oro, luna significa argento, saturno significa piombo … mercurio significa argento vivo”) but not the cipher. f. 2v, the table: “Ariete se chiama srcon pggy”, “Taurus se chiama lrqrlrpnqsr7g” and so on to “Pissis se chiama 7 t by hqph yv”. t: Frater Elias’s secret names, c. 1525 — an alchemical cipher that will not read
b: The transcription is in mellon29/transcription.txt . It uses 3 for ʒ, 7 for the et-sign, 9 for the con-sign and B for ß. Q with a straight tail is kept apart from looped g. Agnieszka Rec (2014) quotes Cancer and Scorpio as “irgp∫hk∫cel” and “prk∫yq∫7gp”, which agrees on the long s and the et-sign. The q/g split is not certain, so every test was run with and without it. f. 1v, the Sol recipe: “piglierai: o∫or · Rerpij leor sglgrʒ · hshr hyor larohgt gsg yhʒy solir tʒs · noyp. Dapoi pista im mortaro …” Image: Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Mellon MS 29 f. 1v, via Yale Digital Collections. f. 2r, the Luna recipe: “piglia i nomi del signor. ylior. lay. gnotrh. ghplr. agksro. in ʒshuk∫∫. cioe gpr. ∫grghs. hr. hqihʒ. yʒ. set. Vʒ Vs. sn. qrpt.” Image: Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Mellon MS 29 f. 2r, via Yale Digital Collections. Sign “se chiama” Sign “se chiama” Ariete srcon pggy Libra 9 qsgqxqkb3 Taurus lrqrlrpnqsr7g̃ Scorpio prk syqs7qp Gemini qrqrsipqsop 3g Sagitarius xi n ak 7 sqol Cancer irqpshkscel Capricorno 7 n qqpypt7r Leo rqlpsonspyh B Aquario qk sqrongya Virgo pqyqpqs. q. st Pissis 7 t by hqph yv The index of coincidence is 0.075 in the table and 0.075 in the recipe lists, a language-like value. The two parts differ, however. q is 17% of the table and under 2% of the lists, and h 3% against 10%. Sukhotin’s vowel test picks q as the main vowel in one part and r in the other. Some shapes are very hard to get from real words under a fixed substitution: Virgo’s pqyqpqsqst has q in every second place, and Taurus and Gemini both begin ?r?r ( lrqrlr , qrqr ). Front pastedown, late sixteenth century: “Se tu vorai far argento perfettissimo … di al nome di iddio ylior lay girrt h g kyli gixkso vshu Rs si aptrugr sgaghs hr hy yhʒ yʒsot aʒ vssugint”. It is a looser copy of f. 2r, not a decipherment. Image: Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Mellon MS 29, front pastedown, via Yale Digital Collections.

t: Frater Elias’s secret names, c. 1525 — an alchemical cipher that will not read
b: Simple substitution by annealing with the lang/ 4-gram models (Italian 1490–1620, modern Italian, Latin). Runs were made with and without word division, with q and g split and merged, and with the table and lists together and apart. The best was −4.0 per letter, which is gibberish. Control: a 206-letter Italian ingredient list (“sale armoniaco onze una, argento vivo …”) under a random key comes out at −2.6 and nearly word-perfect. A simple substitution of Italian would have been found. Homophonic (many letters for one): gibberish. Caesar and Trithemius progressive shifts for each entry, over five alphabets (with ʒ = z and 7 = &), steps 0, ±1 and ±2: nothing. Vigenère , periods 2–7, with the key running or restarting at each entry: nothing beyond overfitting. Reversed words; every other letter a null : nothing. Alberti’s cipher disk. The cipher letters include k , y , h and an et-sign, and two capitals ( R , V ) sit inside the runs. That is how Alberti’s movable lower-case ring and index capitals look. His published ring was tried on each segment. Then an unknown ring was annealed together with a separate setting for each of 19 segments. Nothing read, even with that much freedom. A sibling manuscript. Sarah Lang’s survey of alchemical cipher manuscripts lists one Italian codex with the Elian texts: Manchester, John Rylands Latin MS 65 (15th century). All 449 images were checked. It has the Latin Lumen luminum but not the Italian prologue. Its “cipher table” is a pseudo-Lullian Tabula alphabetorum Raymundi , in which single letters stand for substances (E vitriol, F saltpetre, G cinnabar). Read that way, the Mellon strings become formulas of ten or more ingredients with letters repeated inside one name, which gives no sense. Word patterns against about 170 Italian names of salts, metals, minerals, numbers and weights, with a consistent key required across the table: no fit. Only one name, cristallo , even matches Ariete’s letter pattern.

t: Frater Elias’s secret names, c. 1525 — an alchemical cipher that will not read
h: What it probably is, and what would finish it
b: If the strings are a real cipher, it is a private system with changing alphabets or whole-name code words. About 234 letters in fourteen short units are too few to rebuild such a system without a clear copy. The alternative fits the book as well. The strings may be invented “names” that look like a secret to a buyer: the book is credited to the Franciscan general, backdated by two centuries, bound under an IHS stamp, and says it hides even the names of Sun and Moon in “figures”. The Beinecke catalogue description already suggests “the intention to deceive a pious but gullible devotee”. Rec (2014) called the table a code and left it aside. The later owner who copied it onto the pastedown could not read it either. Another manuscript of this Italian Elias prologue with the recipes in clear would settle it. None was found.

t: Philip II to Mendoza, 7 September 1589 — the “second undeciphered letter” is the decipherer’s copy
b: BnF fr. 3641 holds both of Philip II’s letters of that day twice: the originals in the general cipher Cg.13 and the 1589 decipherer’s fair copies, laid out like the originals with the unread code words in the margin, one of them miscatalogued as a second cipher letter. Aligning the pairs rebuilds some seventy syllables and fifty code groups of Cg.13, reads groups the decipherers left blank (respeto, vuestro, negocio) and corrects their “Francia” to England. Fourteen groups open. Spain → Paris · general cipher Cg.13 · 7 September 1589 · resolved Philip II to Bernardino de Mendoza, 7 September 1589 — the two letters of Français 3641 from Philip II BnF Français 3641 ff. 10, 12, 14, 76 · catalogue item 32 · “second letter, avec chiffre, no decipherment in the volume” The “second letter” is the 1589 decipherer’s fair copy of the first. Both 7 September letters exist as Cg.13 originals and as copies with the unread code words listed in the margin; aligning the pairs rebuilds some seventy syllables and fifty nomenclator groups of Philip II’s general cipher and reads several of the groups the decipherers gave up on. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 17 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 resolved Summary. Omont’s catalogue of Français 3641 lists two letters of Philip II to his ambassador in France dated San Lorenzo, 7 September 1589 (nos. 5 and 6), and a decipherment of only one of them (no. 7). The Gallica harvest therefore put no. 6 (f. 14) on the catalogue of new targets as a same-day sibling with a key in reach. On the image, f. 14 is not a cipher letter. It is the 1589 decipherer’s copy of the letter on f. 10, written in clear except for the nomenclator groups he could not read, which he underlined in the text and listed in the margin, and laid out like the original down to Yo el Rey , the countersignature and the address. Its twin is f. 76, the same treatment of the other 7 September letter (f. 12), which Omont catalogued as “déchiffrement de la lettre portée au n° 6” and which is in fact the decipherment of no. 5. Omont’s no. 7 (f. 15) is a third letter, of 8 September, in another cipher. Aligning each original against its copy, group by group, agrees with the published fragment of the Cg.13 table at every syllable it covers and extends it; cross-reading the two letters then reads code groups the decipherers left blank ( pur = respeto, mes = vuestro, san = negocio), corrects two of their readings (their “Francia” for dun , which the second letter shows to be England; “si se hiziesse” for the King’s si yo hiziesse ) and leaves fourteen groups open with contextual proposals. Status: resolved; the letters were read in 1589, the catalogue was wrong, and the general cipher is partly rebuilt. Fourteen nomenclator groups in the two letters remain unread; the Simancas table (Devos 1950) would close them.

t: Philip II to Mendoza, 7 September 1589 — the “second undeciphered letter” is the decipherer’s copy
b: Cg.13 is the general cipher Devos dates 1587 and Tomokiyo found in use by Philip II, Parma and Mendoza in 1588–89; Viète broke it in France and Phelippes in England, and the copies in this volume are Phelippes’s file. Its letters are single figures or letters ( n = a, b = u, m and 9 = e, 1 = o, 7 = y, g = el), its syllables two-figure groups in rows of five in the order a e i o u (ta–tu 10–14, sa–su 20–24, na–nu 40–44, ra– 50–, va–vo 55–58, ma–mu 60–64, pa–pu 65–69, ca–cu 70–74, ga–gu 75–79, ha 80, la–lo 85–88), some rows reversed (bu–ba 95–99, fu–fa 90–94, du–de 36–39), with the qu-row at 45–49 so that 46 is simply que . Three marks after a group add a letter: a colon adds n (10: = tan, 73: = con, 9: = en), a point adds s (85. = las, 37. = dos, 7. = ys), a cross adds r (68+ = por, 56+ = ver); a stroke above inserts r after the consonant (30ʹ = dra) and a bar doubles an l . Words of the nomenclator are two- or three-letter groups ( na carta, yu cosa, quer Rey, quor Reyno, Zan para, he aviso), with the same marks for plural and changed endings ( na. cartas, he+ avisar, yenc otra). The full table as recovered, with the evidence for each value, is mendoza1589/key_cg13_partial.tsv .

t: Philip II to Mendoza, 7 September 1589 — the “second undeciphered letter” is the decipherer’s copy
b: Letter A (f. 10, copy f. 14). Dos papeles que se han escapado de [Inglaterra*] refieren que salieron de alli en compañia de Manuel de Andrada, [portugués*], que segun les dixo, pasados a [Francia*], y va a llevar dos cartas, una al Reyno de [Francia*] y otra al principe de Bearne; de [quien] entendieron juntamente que las copias desta carta vernian a parar a vuestras manos; y que Antonio de Goda, [portugués*], que es castellano y governador de un castillo y ysleta que esta a la boca del puerto de Premua, seria [fru] que quisiesse hazerme algun servicio con entregarme lo que tiene a su cargo si yo hiziesse alguna negociacion con el. Y pues el Manuel Andrada va con pensamiento de veros, ya avreys entendido el [tum] que esto puede tener, y a haver alguno para encaminar el negocio, que seria tan a proposito, no dudo que avreys procurado ponerlo en [cor], porque por todo buen respeto me ha parescido avisaros desta particularidad que se me ha dado, y encargaros que me aviseys si aveys entendido algo del [tum] que tuviere. Two papers smuggled out of England report that their writers left in company with Manuel de Andrada, a Portuguese (Dom António’s agent, Walsingham’s informant “David”), who said he had crossed to France carrying letters for the French court and for Navarre, and who expected copies of the present letter to reach Mendoza; and that a Portuguese castellan of an island fort at a harbour mouth might hand it over if the King dealt with him. Andrada means to see Mendoza; the King wants the matter followed and reported. Letter B (f. 12, copy f. 76). Receipt of Mendoza’s letters of 27 July, 2 and 8 August; the death of el Rey mi hermano (Henry III, 2 August) ha sido cosa de gran lastima ... por todos los respetos que se pueden considerar ; with France in such confusion Mendoza is to suspend the leave he has to quit the kingdom, porque siendo tan importante vuestra [gu] en el [bu] para el buen assiento de las cosas , and in no way absent himself without a new order, but attend to los negocios con el cuydado que soleys , steering towards el bien publico, que es solo el fin que yo tengo ; news of England is badly wanted, en lo que toca a sus [designios*] y lo que traman y traçan , since the route by which their fleet came home is known from prisoners; Mendoza is to keep his sources going and write often, y de creer es que entre ellos y el de Bearne se deven andar urdiendo malas cosas ... todo importa entenderlo, y en particular sus armaçones .

t: Philip II to Mendoza, 7 September 1589 — the “second undeciphered letter” is the decipherer’s copy
b: Read from the other letter. pur = respeto ( por todos los respetos que se pueden considerar ; the copyist of A wrote “puerto” for por todo buen respeto ). bor , which the copyist of A rendered “porque”, is not: Phelippes reads porque as dur on f. 5, and pero fits both letters. mes = vuestro (A: a vuestras manos ; B: glossed vro ). san = negocio: B has a la forma que el negocio pidiere and, where the copyist wrote “a lo necessario”, the cipher has a los with a plural mark before san ; in A it gives para encaminar el negocio, que seria tan a proposito . A miscopy. The copyist’s tur in A does not exist; the cipher has tum in both places ( el tum que esto puede tener ... algo del tum que tuviere ): one word, perhaps fundamento . Two wrong readings. The copyist wrote francia for dun in A and glossed tam as francia in the same letter; two groups cannot both be France. In B, dun is the power whose fleet came back by a route known from prisoners, whose plots run entre ellos y el de Bearne , and whose armaçones matter: England, in the summer the Drake–Norris expedition returned. So dun = Inglaterra* and tam = Francia*, which is where Andrada went and where Mendoza was. The copyist’s struck Inglaterra on f. 14 shows him weighing exactly this. And si se hiziesse alguna negociacion con el stands where the cipher has 18 = yo : the King wrote si yo hiziesse . From Phelippes’s own hand. His interlinear decipherment of Parma’s letter of 30 December 1588 (f. 5, same cipher) confirms the syllable values at every overlap and supplies bur persona, dom dicho, dur porque, pen mucho, mis V. M., and the x-row at 25–29. From Viète’s papers. fer , qualifying Manuel de Andrada and Antonio de Goda , is the group in the heading of a spy report copied in Cinq Cents de Colbert 33 (f. 113), Avisos que ha venido a dar David, traducidos de [fer] : Portugués*. Still open (contextual proposals only, asterisked in the key file): tum , fru , cor in A; hon (copyist: diligencia ; the sense wants licencia ), bor ( pero ?), gu , bu , com , ga ( armada ?), Jam , lo , bem , par in B; and a sixteen-group passage of B that the encipherer struck out and the copyist skipped.

b: Item 32 traced to the leaf through the BnF Archives et manuscrits notice (folios for Omont’s numbers) and the Gallica IIIF manifest (folio labels); ff. 10–15 and 76–77 fetched at native resolution, with the pacing the server enforces (30 s between requests, two-minute back-offs after 429).
