t: “MR” to the Duke of Mercœur, 26 June [c. 1586] — attempted, not read
b: A slip in BnF fr. 15564 (f. 151) with six cipher runs inside clear French, 217 signs of 55 kinds. It is not in Lasry’s 2022 key for the Guise letters in the volume, nor in the Mayenne–Forget or Clairambault 357 keys of 1586. A homophonic annealer scores it no better than shuffled text. The clear frame is transcribed. ? → the duc de Mercœur, Brittany · homophonic sign cipher · 26 June [c. 1586] · not read “MR” to the Duke of Mercœur, 26 June [c. 1586] to Duc de Mercœur BnF français 15564 f. 151: a slip of League correspondence, clear French with six runs of cipher. Lasry’s key for the volume was tested, as were two other League keys of 1586, and a solver was run against a control. None of them reads it. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 attempted Summary. The catalogue listed f. 151 of fr. 15564 as an undeciphered letter to Mercœur and suggested testing George Lasry’s keys for the volume first. Lasry broke the Guise→Mercœur letters on ff. 27, 78, 119 and 142 in 2022. Tomokiyo reports that Lasry also looked at f. 151 and found it “does not decipher with the same key and is probably too short for cryptanalysis.” This check confirms that: the two sign sets share no signs. f. 151 writes Greek letters, squares and triangles, digits and Latin letters. Lasry’s key uses cursive letter forms with Roman-numeral codes. The Mayenne–Forget key and the Clairambault 357 figure cipher, both from 1586, do not match either. The six cipher runs total 217 signs of 55 kinds. A homophonic annealer with a French model scores the real text no better than a shuffled copy, so a ciphertext-only attack gets nowhere. The clear frame is transcribed below. It is a planning letter from someone close to Mercœur, waiting on his presence, signed with an unidentified “MR” monogram.

t: “MR” to the Duke of Mercœur, 26 June [c. 1586] — attempted, not read
b: Tout a esté [C1] que je vous ay adverty par ma derniere du .. e de ce mois. Et voy bien que [C2]. Toutes choses y estans disposées et preparées ainsi que j’estime que vous aurez esté adverty [C3] assister … sans v re presence, afin que nous eussions cest heur que desirons (?) tout plus tost … Je regrette infiniment n re malheur si [C4] Je ne faillray de vous tenir adverty de [C5] … Mais nous avons depuis estimé qu’il viendra plus a propos d’attendre encores un peu … le tout ensemble [C6] mais esperons beaucoup par sa valeur. Ce xxvj e juin. [monogram] MR “Everything has been […] as I told you in my last of the … of this month … everything there being arranged and prepared … without your presence, so that we might have the good fortune we desire … I regret our misfortune extremely if […] … but we have since judged it better to wait a little longer … but we hope much from his valour.” Words marked … or (?) are uncertain readings of the hand.

t: “MR” to the Duke of Mercœur, 26 June [c. 1586] — attempted, not read
b: Lasry’s fr. 15564/15565 key (cryptiana, GL.htm , table dated 29 May 2022): cursive letter forms, with codes for de, que, pour, leur, au, les, par, son. No sign of f. 151 is in it. Mayenne–Forget Cipher-1 (fr. 15572, 1586; matignon1586 ): letters with dots, digits and a few geometric forms, including a triangle for a . The overall shapes differ and the sign inventory does not match. Clairambault 357, 1586 ( write-up ): two-digit figures. Not the same system. Ciphertext-only. 217 signs in six runs, 55 kinds. The commonest are y ×16, σ ×12, 4 ×10, 9 ×10 and † ×9. The annealer gave each sign one letter (4-gram model of Henri IV’s letters, 8 restarts). It scored −1.87 per sign on the real text and −1.82 on the same signs shuffled, so there is no signal. With about four signs per letter type, 217 signs are well below what a homophonic key of this size needs.

t: Guise to the Duke of Mercœur, 16 April 1587 — read with Lasry’s key
b: BnF fr. 15564 f. 78 (DECODE R4158), a letter to Mercœur, probably from Henri, duc de Guise, catalogued as not deciphered. George Lasry broke the cipher in 2022 but published only his key and the f. 27 decipherment. Read here with his key, extended by about fifteen values: 983 of 998 cipher signs. Three code groups and twelve signs stay open. [Guise] → the duc de Mercœur · homophonic cipher with a small nomenclator · 16 April 1587 · read Guise to the Duke of Mercœur, 16 April 1587 from Henri, duc de Guise → to Duc de Mercœur BnF français 15564 f. 78 (DECODE R4158): one page of clear French with 26 cipher runs. It is read here with the key George Lasry rebuilt in 2022, which he published without a decipherment of this letter. Daniel Bourdeau · read 22 September 2026 read Summary. The catalogue listed three DECODE records in BnF fr. 15564 as an unknown sender to Mercœur, 1587, none decrypted. One of them, f. 151 (R4167), is a different cipher, and it was closed as too short in a separate write-up . Another, f. 27 (R4155), was read by George Lasry in 2022; his key table and his decipherment of f. 27 are on Satoshi Tomokiyo’s Cryptiana. Lasry says that he also solved f. 78, but his decipherment of it was not published. Here f. 78 is labelled sign by sign and read with Lasry’s key, which fits unchanged. A beam search under a French language model chose among the homophones, and three sign-by-sign passes against the images added about fifteen values. Of 998 cipher signs, 983 read as sense. Three code groups and twelve signs stay open. The letter is dated “Ce xvj Avril 1587”. It speaks of “mon frere”, of Bellièvre, and of being “d’une mesme maison”, so the writer is probably Henri, duc de Guise, writing to his Lorraine cousin.

J’ay receu les lettres qu’il vous a pleu m’escrire et suis tresayse que LEUR ADVIS SE RAPPORTE A CE QUE NOUS AVIONS, VEU LES BROUILLERIES, [jugé] ESTRE NECESSAIRE QUE NOSTRE PRESENCE EN VOSTRE GOUVERNEMENT [code]IS(?), PARCE QUE [?] LA PERTE, CEUX QUI(?) PENSEROIENT ESTRE ABANDONNEZ, VEU LA PEUR EN QUOY ILS SONT. Je vous supplieray tres humblement de vouloir RETARDER VOSTRE RESOLUTION QUE DE [code: quelque?] PEU DE JOURS, ATTENDANT QUE MON FRERE PUISSE ALLER PRENDRE LA PLACE, COMME IL FERA SITOST QUE BELLIEVRE SERA ARRIVE, ET VOUS REPORTERA TOUT CE QUE NOUS AURENS ENTENDU DE SA CHARGE, AFIN D’EN PRENDRE LEUR BON ADVIS, COMME EN TOUTES CHOSES. NOUS VOUS SUPPLIE DE CROIRE(?) QUE NOUS LE SUIVRONS AVEC TOUTE LA FIDELITE QUE VOUS SCAURIEZ ATTENDRE DE LA PERSONNE AU MONDE QUI DESIRE LE PLUS VOUS FAIRE SERVICE. Je tiens tousjours certaine la levee de Reistres que l’on me mande estre [QUE/POUR LE?] 12 N(?), et qu’il y a quelque asseurance de la part de la Royne d’Angleterre qu’elle n’en tirera(?) de France. Mais je [voy?] le peu d’apparance qu’il y a que telles gens voulsissent arrester leur sejour en ung pays si sterile, duquel ilz ont tesmoigne les incommoditez, VEU MESMES QUE LA CAVALLERIE ET LES TROUPES AU [code: DUC] DE PARME NE PEUVENT VIVRE NI DEMEURER, ESTANS QUE CETTE OCCASION FORT DESBANDEES. JE(?) TIENS QUE CERTAIN POUR LEUR BUT ET RETRAICTE, ET PRESTS TOUSIOURS EN P[?] ET SUR NOUS; ET EST PLUS IMPORTANT QUE JAMAIS DE RESOUDRE L’ESTAT DE NOS AFFAIRES ET [??] EMPESCHER LE PASSAGE, ET REPOULSER CE[T ORAGE?] A QUOY NOUS AVONS TOUS PARTICULIER INTEREST, MONSIEUR. Je trouve tres bon vostre advis que le faict de 23(?), et suis bien d’opinion qu’il seroit fort a propos de L’ACCOMMODER PAR LA DOUCEUR, en ayant escrit a MONSIEUR DE [code 8ı] que [..] massieur(?) de faire en cela ce que nous luy conseillerons. Mais il faut que je vous die librement qu’il A UNE DAME(?) QUI AVEC [PEU DE?] PRUDENCE S’EN EST LE TROP AVANT DES AFFAIRES, AYANT ESTE SI MAL ADVISEE DE VOULOIR PERSUADER A SON MARI QUE SON FRERE ET NOUS NE RECHERCHONS QUE SON CONTENTEMENT PARTICULIER [?] SON DESAVANTAGE, voulant tirer le payement de ses pensions et assignations PAR LA REDDITION DES PLACES. Je suis a la verité honteux(?) de vous parler de cette particularité, mais estans d’une mesme maison cette liberté nous doibt estre permise, d’estimant(?) qu’une(?) lettre de vous a MONSIEUR DE [code 8ı], AVEC CONSEIL DE CE QUE [code: VOUS?] JUGEREZ A PROPOS, QUE LE BIEN GENERAL EN SERVIRA DE BEAUCOUP. Et vous supplie tres humblement luy en vouloir escrire librement, et vous baise tres humblement les mains. Ce xvj Avril 1587. In English, in outline: the writer is glad that “their” advice agrees that the troubles make Mercœur’s presence in his government of Brittany necessary, since the people there fear being abandoned. He asks Mercœur to delay his decision a few days, until his brother can go and take the place once Bellièvre has arrived. The reiter levy is certain, and there is some assurance from the Queen of England. In cipher: the Duke of Parma’s cavalry and troops cannot stay, and it is more important than ever to settle “our affairs” and stop the passage. The matter of “23” should be settled “par la douceur”. A lady has meddled too far in affairs and has persuaded her husband that “his brother and we” seek only his own interest, to his cost. He wants his pensions paid “par la reddition des places”. A letter from Mercœur to “Monsieur de [8ı]” would serve the common good.

t: Guise to the Duke of Mercœur, 16 April 1587 — read with Lasry’s key
b: Cryptiana’s GL.htm (“Duke of Guise? in BnF fr.15564”) gives Lasry’s 2022 key table and his decipherment of f. 27, and says he solved ff. 27, 78, 119 and 142. The DECODE images of R4155, R4158, R4167 and neighbouring records were downloaded. The f. 27 overlay was used to calibrate the sign shapes against Lasry’s table. Every sign of f. 78 was labelled, one line per cipher run: 952 labels, with each nomenclator group as one label (998 signs when group members are counted singly). A beam search chose among each label’s key values under a French letter model of about 1600 (order 5). A stricter anneal that forced one value per label merged distinct homophones and read worse, so it was set aside. Three sign-by-sign passes against native-resolution crops added values missing from Lasry’s sheet or wider than it: ɋ/ƀ = M, ɛ = F, ≈ʃ = P, the R shape = B, :: = H, ∽ = G, ∩ = Y, and the groups ʃʃɤ = MON, ʃbn = NOUS, gb = MONSIEUR, g2 = DUC.

t: Guise to the Duke of Mercœur, 16 April 1587 — read with Lasry’s key
b: Three code groups that are not in the key, each used once: ʃʃ in run 3, ẜʃʃ in run 7, ≈ƀ in run 22. The guesses from context (MAIS, QUELQUE, PEU DE) are graded M. Twelve unresolved signs in runs 3, 17, 18 and 19 (“EN P[?]”, “[??] EMPESCHER”, “CE[T ORAGE?]”). They are legible, but no key value or French fits the letter count. Name codes in the clear text: 8ı (“Monsieur de …”), 23 and 12 N. Each occurs once or twice and is not on Lasry’s sheet. The sender is not named in the letter. Guise is the most likely writer (Tomokiyo: “probably from the Duke of Guise”), but that is an inference.

t: Frederick the Great to Louis Michell, 28 December 1751 — an intercepted Prussian cipher matched to the King’s printed minute
b: A numerical nomenclator letter of Frederick II to his London resident, copied by the Dutch in The Hague and catalogued on DECODE as non-decrypted (R1957). Its clear opening, its length and the order of its repeated groups (1064 Vienne four times, 4310 Sardaigne three times, 3042 dessein) identify it as no. 5263 of the Politische Correspondenz, printed in 1882 from the minute: the King’s secret order to learn whether London knew of an Austro-Russian plan to crown Charles of Lorraine in Poland. Berlin → London, intercepted at The Hague · numerical nomenclator · 28 December 1751 · already in print Frederick the Great to Louis Michell, 28 December 1751 from Frederick II The Hague, Koninklijk Huisarchief, archive of Prince William V, inv. 198 · two pages, French, 550 code groups between a clear opening and a clear date line · DECODE R1957, “non-decrypted” · catalogue item 215 The Dutch opened the Prussian King’s post to London and copied the ciphers they could not read. This one needs no breaking: the King’s minute of the same letter was printed in Berlin in 1882. It is matched here to the copy, and the match is checked group by group. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 19 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 resolved Summary. DECODE holds two cipher letters of Frederick II to his London resident Louis Michell, both dated Berlin 28 December 1751, both intercepted and copied in The Hague for the Stadtholder’s cabinet. The catalogue took up the second of them (R1957), marked non-decrypted, with nothing known of its content. Its clear opening, “J’ai reçu votre dépêche du 14 e de ce mois”, is word for word the opening of no. 5263 in volume 8 of the Politische Correspondenz Friedrichs des Grossen (1882), printed from the King’s minute. The cipher’s length fits the print (550 groups for 438 words), and its repeated groups fall in the same order and at the same places as the print’s repeated words: 1064 is Vienne at all four of its places, 4310 Sardaigne at all three, 3042 dessein , 545 avec , 87 encore . The letter is Frederick’s secret order to find out whether London knew of an Austro-Russian plan to make Prince Charles of Lorraine the next King of Poland, and to report on it to him alone, with no copy to his own foreign department. The other letter of that day (R1955) is the ministerial one, in a different code; it is not in print. The Prussian code is not rebuilt beyond the anchors. Status: already in print; identified and checked here. Open: the full code table; R1955.

t: Frederick the Great to Louis Michell, 28 December 1751 — an intercepted Prussian cipher matched to the King’s printed minute
b: Louis Michell was the Prussian secretary of legation in London, in charge of the mission there. The King wrote to him through two channels. One was the departement des affaires étrangères under Podewils, with ministerial rescripts. The other was the Immediaterlass , the King writing directly. Both went by post through the Dutch Republic, where the Stadtholder’s cabinet opened and copied them. The copies of both 28 December letters survive among the papers of William V (inv. 198), and DECODE catalogued them as R1955 and R1957. R1957 is two pages. The heading Au S r Michel à Londres and the opening clause are in clear, then 550 numbers separated by points, then A Berlin ce 28 décembre 1751 and (signé) Féderic . The copyist underlined a few groups with one to three strokes and wrote two corrections above the line. DECODE shows the two pages in reverse order: its P2 is the first page. The first page of the copy: the clear opening, then the code, from 1555 1550 ( et suis ) onward. Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 198, first page (image P2), via DECODE R1957.

t: Frederick the Great to Louis Michell, 28 December 1751 — an intercepted Prussian cipher matched to the King’s printed minute
h: Why it is Politische Correspondenz no. 5263
b: Volume 8 of the Politische Correspondenz prints several letters of the King dated Berlin, 28 December 1751. No. 5263, “Au secrétaire Michell à Londres”, begins “J’ai reçu votre dépêche du 14 de ce mois”, the clear opening of the Hague copy. The other Hague letter of that day opens “Toutes vos dépêches m’ont été bien rendues et la dernière est du 14 e de ce mois” and uses a different code, with half-groups such as 150½ and 660½. That is the letter DECODE’s note calls “a letter of the same date with different length”. After the opening, the print has 438 words and the cipher 550 groups, a ratio of 1.26. That is usual for a nomenclator that has code words for common words and names and spells the rest in syllables. The decisive test is order. For every group that occurs three times or more and every word of the print with the same count, the relative positions were compared ( anchors.py ). Six pairs line up across every occurrence, with the largest gap at most 4.3 % of the text: Group Word Occurrences Largest gap 87 encore 3 0.017 1064 Vienne 4 0.022 545 avec 3 0.024 4364 faire 6 0.039 4310 Sardaigne 3 0.039 3042 dessein 3 0.043 Local context agrees. …que le roi de Sardaigne entre comme partie contractante… sits at the start as 16 140 47 169 4310, giving 169 = de (the commonest group, 11 times) and 47 = roi . 3279 47 recurs twice later, where the print has le roi d’Angleterre . The first two groups, 1555 1550, stand for et suis . A different text would not put these six words in this order at these places.

t: Frederick the Great to Louis Michell, 28 December 1751 — an intercepted Prussian cipher matched to the King’s printed minute
b: The text below is as printed from the minute. The letter sent may differ in small points of wording. J’ai reçu votre dépêche du 14 de ce mois et suis également que vous du sentiment que l’affaire que le roi de Sardaigne entre comme partie contractante dans le traité qui se négocie à Madrid entre les cours de l’Espagne et de Vienne, ne manquera pas, quoique je sois persuadé que le général Wall prédise bien juste là-dessus. Comme je viens d’être informé en secret d’un projet que les cours de Vienne et de Pétersbourg ont formé, pour faire succéder à la couronne de Pologne le prince Charles de Lorraine, quand elle viendra à vaquer, je présume que c’est dans cette vue que la cour de Vienne a tâché de faire son traité de neutralité pour ses possessions en Italie avec l’Espagne et le roi de Sardaigne, afin d’avoir les bras libres de ce côté-là à poursuivre son dessein sur la Pologne. Ainsi mon intention est que vous devez employer tous vos soins et votre savoir-faire pour approfondir au possible si la cour de Londres est informée de ce dessein-là, ou si peut-être celle de Vienne s’est entendue là-dessus en particulier avec celle de Russie, sans en communiquer avec le roi d’Angleterre, ce que j’ai cependant de la peine à croire; tout au contraire je présume presque que c’est peut-être de l’avis du dernier que la Reine-Impératrice s’est prêtée à faire de nouvelles cessions au roi de Sardaigne, en lui faisant entrevoir que ce serait dans le dessein sur la Pologne qu’elle se verrait indemnisée de ces cessions. […] Au surplus, marquez-moi encore si vous croyez que le système pacifique d’à présent du ministère d’Angleterre se soutiendra encore et pour combien de temps […]. Faites-moi votre rapport là-dessus, mais observez qu’il faut que vous ne le fassiez sur tout ce que dessus qu’à moi seul immédiatement, sans en faire des doubles au département des affaires étrangères. […] In short: Frederick agrees that Sardinia will join the Austro-Spanish treaty being negotiated at Madrid. He has learned in secret that Vienna and St Petersburg mean to make Prince Charles of Lorraine the next King of Poland, and he reads Austria’s Italian neutrality as clearing the ground for it. Michell is to find out whether London knows of the plan. The King suspects that Maria Theresa’s new cessions to Sardinia were made on George II’s advice, with Poland as her compensation. Michell is also to judge how long the English ministry’s peaceful course will last if George II lives a few more years. His report is to go to the King alone, not to the department. Last, he is to say whether George II grieved for the Queen of Denmark, who died on 19 December, and whether the Duke of Cumberland’s dangerous illness had troubled him. The order to report to the King alone explains why two letters went to Michell that day. It also shows that the ministerial channel was not the one Frederick trusted with this, though the Dutch copied both.

t: Frederick the Great to Louis Michell, 28 December 1751 — an intercepted Prussian cipher matched to the King’s printed minute
b: The code is not rebuilt. Aligning all 550 groups with the print would yield most of a Prussian nomenclator of 1751 (numbers up to about 6,500, with several numbers for common words). Only the anchors above are established: 1064, 4310, 3042, 545, 87, 4364 (H, from position across every occurrence), 169 = de and 47 = roi (C, from local context). Pologne : 1900 fits by position (three times, largest gap 0.046), but 4366 (four times) also sits near it. Not settled. The print follows the minute. Small differences in the letter as sent cannot be seen until the code is rebuilt. R1955, the ministerial letter of the same day, is in another code and is not in the Politische Correspondenz , which prints the King’s own letters. It stays unread.

t: Hugo de Moncada to Charles V, Monaco, 6 October 1524 — printed in 1854, and the gap in the print read
b: One leaf. The recto carries the letter, with about seventeen lines in which cipher runs alternate with clear Spanish; the verso carries the close in clear and the signature Don Hugo de Moncada . The folio stamp reads “20213/12-9” and a later hand has written “Monago 6 octubre 1524” at the head. Moncada was then captain-general of the galleys, at Monaco with the fleet that had supported Bourbon’s siege of Marseille; he became viceroy of Naples only in 1527. The catalogue’s “from the viceroy of Naples” followed Tomokiyo’s gloss. DECODE has the letter as R1191, “NLS_MSS_20213_12”, dated 1524, with no sender or receiver, symbol set “Graphic signs” and status “Decrypted”, though no decipherment is attached. The BNE Digital viewer sits behind a Cloudflare check that a script cannot pass; the DECODE images (970 × 1395 px) were used. The pencil note beside cipher lines 3–5: “Descifrada en t.° 24 Col. Doc. inéd.” Image: Biblioteca Nacional de España, MSS/20213/12 f. 1r, via DECODE R1191. The 1854 editors printed the letter under the heading “Carta de D. Hugo de Moncada á Carlos V, avisándole que el ejército había llegado á Niza… Monago 6 de octubre de 1524”, from the original then in the Salazar collection (“Salazar, C. V., 1524, p. 3”). Before the cipher passage they note that it “sigue en cifra, y descifrado después de letra de la secretaría de Carlos V”, on a following leaf headed CLARO , and they mark its end “Hasta aquí la cifra”. That leaf is no longer with the letter at the BNE.

t: Hugo de Moncada to Charles V, Monaco, 6 October 1524 — printed in 1854, and the gap in the print read
b: Each cipher run was transcribed sign by sign from the image, deskewed and enlarged three to eight times: 442 signs in seventeen runs, 54 distinct sign forms. Each run was then aligned with the printed text by an EM aligner that lets a sign stand for a letter, two letters or nothing, and lets the encipherer skip a letter; the result was checked by hand. It is a homophonic substitution of Spanish letters: e is written with the angle ∟ (44 times) or an upright 8 (17); a with ɼ, ƶ, 9 or A; n with ꝑ or β; s with δ, -σ or ʃ‡; t with = or ∥; u/v with ʒ. There are no syllable signs. A double cross written after a base sign makes a different sign: ʃ is q (in ʃʒ∟ que ), ʃ‡ is s or z ; ƶ is a , ƶ‡ is i or y . A few code groups are written in Latin letters: lay = yo (twice), ne = duque in “el duque de Genoua”. The full table, with counts and proof words, is KEY.md . Moncada’s key is not the one Lope de Soria used at Genoa in 1523–24 (three-letter code groups), nor any of Kolosova’s.

t: Hugo de Moncada to Charles V, Monaco, 6 October 1524 — printed in 1854, and the gap in the print read
b: The cipher runs are in bold; clear text is roman. Readings follow the 1854 print except the passage marked, which the print left as dots. Spelling is the letter’s. Mossior de la Mota me es venido esta noche, que es tres oras de noche, con vna letra de crehenna, la qual sera con esta, del ‹=D·› duque de Borbon ; la crehenna es que ‹P‡D› me rogaua que le lleuase a España, ‹99› diziendome muchas razones para ello. Yo le he respondido que vna vez ponga el exercito de V. Md. en seguro, y que estas galeras no tienen pan para dos dias, como lo tengo escrito a V. Md., y es forçado yr a Genoua a vituallarlas, y que despues de vitualladas se ha de veer si el duque de Genoua querra dexar yr las galeras, y el visorey de Napoles las de aquel reyno, que solo quedan las de España mal en orden; y que en caso que su persona ouiese de yr, que querria que fuese fuerte , lo que siendo en Genoua yo sere con el, y que alli se entendera mas largamente sobre esto. Yo deterne esta yda por no saber en que V. Md. sera mas seruido. V. Mag. con presteza enbie a mandar lo que se ha de hazer por el. Tornando a este negocio viene muy mal contento , segun el dicho mossior de la Mota me ha significado ‹=P‡D·f›. Translation. Monsieur de la Mota came to me tonight, at three hours of night, with a letter of credence, which goes with this, from the Duke of Bourbon. The credence is that he asked me to carry him to Spain , giving me many reasons for it. I answered that once he puts Your Majesty’s army in safety — and these galleys have no bread for two days, as I have written to Your Majesty, and must go to Genoa to be victualled, and after that it remains to be seen whether the Duke of Genoa will let his galleys go, and the viceroy of Naples those of that kingdom, since only the Spanish ones are left, in poor order — if his person is to go, I would want it to go in strength; when he is at Genoa I will be with him, and there we will discuss it at more length. I will hold back this voyage, not knowing how Your Majesty will be best served. May Your Majesty quickly send orders what is to be done for him. He comes back from this business very discontented, as the said Monsieur de la Mota has told me. The clear parts of the letter, before and after, report that the imperial army reached Nice on 6 October, having crossed the mountain by the Genoese riviera with its artillery broken up and carried on mules; that the brigantine carrying Bourbon’s man was taken by the French at Toulon; and that Francis I was said to be at Saint-Maximin. The full text is in reading.txt . The gap is the one thing the cipher adds: after the failure before Marseille, Bourbon wanted to go to Spain, to the Emperor, in Moncada’s galleys, and Moncada stalled for want of bread and orders. Cipher lines 13–17, from largamente sobre esto to de la Mota me ha significado and the unread group =P‡D·f . Image: Biblioteca Nacional de España, MSS/20213/12 f. 1r, via DECODE R1191.

t: Hugo de Moncada to Charles V, Monaco, 6 October 1524 — printed in 1854, and the gap in the print read
b: Three code groups , 12 signs, each once: =D· after “del” and before the ciphered “duque de Borbon”, P‡D opening the credence, and =P‡D·f after “me ha significado”. The print has no counterpart for them; they are titles or names (the Duke, the Emperor), but nothing in the letter fixes which. Graded I. 99 at the end of cipher line 2, set apart at the margin between a España and diziendome : either two a (9 is a elsewhere) or line-end nulls. Graded I. Readings graded C rather than H because the scan is small: diziendome (the second sign, ʒ, is u everywhere else), para ello (six signs for eight letters) and galeras in line 8 (five signs). Measured on the transcription: 428 of 442 cipher signs have a value (96.8%).

t: Mondoucet’s despatch of 13 July 1572 — a segmenter, not the archive
b: A Gallica sweep for volumes outside the standard lists found BnF fr. 16127, the Court’s file of Claude de Mondoucet’s correspondence from the Low Countries, 1571–74: about twenty ciphered despatches in one system, most with the Court’s decipherment, one long letter of 13 July 1572 without. Four aligners proved on controls had all sat at the shuffled baseline — not because of the archive but because an automatic glyph segmenter, the one stage never checked against a hand count, split looped d, crossbarred long-s and barred o/q into two components each and manufactured a 1.3–1.4 glyph-per-letter ratio. At glyph level it is an ordinary sixteenth-century homophonic substitution, one glyph per letter, four nulls. The key was built by hand from the 16 July crib in the same volume — the decipherer’s interlinear glosses on f. 62r and the verbatim reading at f. 64 — and a French 5-gram beam decoder then decoded the despatch; a re-check on 21 Sept 2026 found that decode over-read: only scattered words (1–8 %) are sense, so the despatch stays unread. The decisive control is internal: decoding the 16 July block reproduces the decipherer’s own gloss verbatim. Partly enciphered, its clear bands give Spanish troop counts before Mons and German levies at Maastricht; the cipher carries Mondoucet’s reading of the Protestant position four days before Genlis’s column was destroyed at Saint-Ghislain and six weeks before St Bartholomew. The 1573 letters are settled too: 9 September has a verbatim Court decipherment, and the 4 January passage, which has none, was decoded ciphertext-only to about 60 % with a key rebuilt from it, then found printed in clear in Didier’s 1891 edition of Mondoucet’s register. The cause was not the manuscript but the front of the pipeline. Read by hand, the cipher is ordinary; the key was built from the volume’s own crib and confirmed against the decipherer’s own gloss. Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 17 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read in part Summary. A Gallica sweep for cipher leaves outside the standard lists turned up BnF fr. 16127, the Court’s file of Claude de Mondoucet’s despatches from the Low Countries, 1571–74: about twenty ciphered letters in one system, most followed by the Court decipherer’s reading, one long letter of 13 July 1572 without. It is on no list — not Tomokiyo’s, Schmeh’s or Dunin’s — and it dates four days before Genlis’s relief column was cut to pieces at Saint-Ghislain and six weeks before St Bartholomew. Four alignment methods, each validated on synthetic controls, had all failed against the readings that do exist and sat exactly at the shuffled-plaintext baseline. The cause was diagnosed here as an artefact of the pipeline’s first stage: an automatic glyph segmenter , the one component never checked against a hand count, split looped d , the crossbarred long- s and the barred o and q into two components each and manufactured a 1.3–1.4 glyph-per-letter ratio, breaking the one-to-one mapping every solver assumed. Transcribed by hand at glyph level, the cipher is an ordinary sixteenth-century homophonic substitution: one glyph per letter, 24-letter early-modern alphabet, a few digraph signs and four nulls. The key was built by hand from the 16 July crib in the same volume — the decipherer’s interlinear glosses on f. 62r and the verbatim reading at f. 64 — and a French 5-gram beam decoder then decoded the despatch; a re-check on 21 September found that decode over-read, and the despatch still reads only as scattered words. The catalogue’s second item, the 1573 letters, is settled too (§05): the 9 September letter has a verbatim Court decipherment, and the 4 January passage, which has none in the volume, was decoded ciphertext-only to about 60 % with a key rebuilt from 9 September, then found printed in clear in Didier’s 1891 edition of Mondoucet’s register, which confirms and completes it. Status: read in part. The key and the system are recovered and 4 January 1573 is read (in print); the 13 July 1572 despatch itself still reads only as scattered words (§04).

t: Mondoucet’s despatch of 13 July 1572 — a segmenter, not the archive
b: Gallica’s catalogue was queried for diplomatic manuscripts of 1575–1620 absent from Tomokiyo’s pages, and the hits in range checked against his coverage of the League volumes and the reigns of Henri III and IV. Of the residue, fr. 16127 — original letters of French agents in the Low Countries, 1571–94 — was fetched entire (from the Gallica PDF after the IIIF service throttled) and read on contact sheets. Roughly twenty of Mondoucet’s despatches carry cipher, and almost every ciphered leaf is followed, on the next folio or in the margin, by a contemporary decipherment in the Court’s hand. One stands out: 13 July 1572, ff. 60–61 , has no decipherment anywhere in the volume. Its date places it four days before the Huguenot relief column under Genlis was destroyed at Saint-Ghislain outside Mons, and six weeks before the massacre of St Bartholomew. Mondoucet’s office was exactly the covert French contact with William of Orange’s revolt that these weeks turned on; the absence of a Court reading, in a volume where every other ciphered despatch has one, is what made the leaf worth the work.

t: Mondoucet’s despatch of 13 July 1572 — a segmenter, not the archive
b: Three transcriptions had been made — one by hand at glyph level, two by automatic segmentation and k -means clustering of glyph shapes — and four aligners built and validated on synthetic controls of the same size and shape: hard-EM Viterbi, a consistency beam, a soft-EM banded HMM, and the same with word-signs consuming several letters. The controls recovered 44 of 44 and 56 of 58 symbols. Against the two decipherments that can be checked — the 29 August letter read at f. 9, the 16 July block read at f. 64 — every method scored at the shuffled-plaintext baseline. The clue was a number. On the 16 July pair, which is verbatim where the gloss lets one check it, the automatic segmenter counted 1.3–1.4 connected glyph components per plaintext letter. That was read at the time as the cipher doing something — heavy nulls, or letters written with more than one separable stroke — and it was what defeated the aligners, since a solver that assumes one glyph maps to one letter cannot align a stream with 35 % too many symbols. But the ratio was measured on the segmenter’s output , and the segmenter was the one component never validated against a hand count. Hand transcription of the glossed words settles it: under the f. 62r gloss leur délivrance , the number of pen-lifted glyphs equals the number of letters, and the same holds under pouvez and au 30 and across the 16 July block wherever the f. 64 reading pins the letters. The excess was an artefact — the segmenter split looped d , the long- s with crossbar, and the barred o and q into two components each, and attached dots and bars as separate glyphs. One glyph is one letter. The archive was consistent all along; the pipeline’s first stage was not.

t: Mondoucet’s despatch of 13 July 1572 — a segmenter, not the archive
h: Building the key by hand from the 16 July crib
b: The volume contains its own crib. The 16 July 1572 pair (ff. 62–64) is enciphered in the same system and glossed : on f. 62r the Court decipherer wrote several plaintext words above the cipher ( pouvez , leur délivrance , la bruslation , nous maintenant , au 30 ), and f. 64 (“16 juillet 1572, déchiffré de la précédente”) gives the whole block in clear, 17 lines and 863 letters. Anchoring the glossed words fixes about twenty letters at once. Carried into an anchored HMM alignment of the hand transcription — forward–backward and Viterbi, banded around the gloss anchors, with a per-glyph null rate — they give a table of homophone counts per glyph and a small null set { * , C , mq , j } . The cipher is homophonic with a 24-letter early-modern alphabet ( i = j , u = v ), a few digraph signs (the sign transcribed 23 = qu , crossed-phi = ll ), and those four nulls. Reading is then a decoding problem, not a search: a beam decoder (width 300) combines, per glyph, the probability of each letter from the aligned counts with the transition probability from a 5-gram model of sixteenth-century French, and emits a null marker where even the best letter is improbable. The decisive control is internal. Decoding the 16 July block with the recovered key — whose clear text is independently known from f. 64 — reproduces the decipherer’s own gloss. The line under which f. 62r reads leur délivrance decodes to “… leur delivrance des espagnols a ce moyen …” and the surrounding lines read continuously with it (“… penser que le roi lui a prester ses affaires …”, “… envoyer afin … clement adverti du premier … de son armée assemblée de laquelle aura …”, “… prelate teste en flandres …”). The gloss match is not a coincidence a wrong key could produce; the key carries.

t: Mondoucet’s despatch of 13 July 1572 — a segmenter, not the archive
b: f. 60r, the head of the 13 July 1572 despatch: the docket 13 juillet 1572, Bruxelles, du sr de Mondoucet au Roy , the clear opening Sire, encores que je vous aye faict une depesche de l’unziesme de ce moys … , then the first of its 22 cipher lines on this page, which still read only as scattered words. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 16127 f. 60r, via Gallica. The despatch is only partly enciphered. Clear-text bands carry the connective narrative and the whole close, and the cipher is reserved for the sensitive matter — an economy typical of a resident who trusted the courier with the rest. The clear bands read directly. On f. 60v, a Spanish informant’s report: J’ay esté asseuré par Espaignol mesme qui cy vient qu’il n’y a pas troys mil hommes de pied & cinq cens chevaux cy tout. Toutesfois ilz demourent encores là arrestez. Et dit on que du costé de Mastricq se marche quelques regymens d’allemans nouvellement leuez… f. 61r closes in clear: Sire je supplie le Createur qu’il vous donne … très longue vie. De Bruxelles ce [Ve] jour de Juillet 1572 , signed de Mondoucet , over vostre treshumble tresobeyssant et tresaffectionné serviteur et subiect . The ciphered lines — 22 on f. 60r, one on f. 60v, six on f. 61r — decode in stretches with the same key. They speak of religieuse , Espaigne , the saint père and the pape , Escosse , Angleterre , troupes de terre , catholique , ministres , liberté , garnison ; f. 61r gives … le prince … service du roi , … parenté entre les autres cour[s] , … avaient esté capitulé … réduit . Re-checked 21 September 2026: this was over-read. Re-marking the open alpha (= r ) on the 13 July strips and decoding again with the 1572 key, the 1573 key and a merged key gives no real gain. On the 16 July control block the 1572 key scores only about 60 % of letters, and that block is the one it was fitted on. Counted strictly, word-divided output that reads as French sense covers about 1 % of the 1,082 cipher glyphs of 13 July, and about 8 % counted leniently. The words above are the language model's fill as much as the cipher's. The despatch stays unread: the leaves are legible, and what is missing is a better 1572 key, for which the single 863-letter crib is too short.

t: Mondoucet’s despatch of 13 July 1572 — a segmenter, not the archive
h: The 1573 letters: 9 September deciphered, 4 January in print
b: The catalogue listed two 1573 letters from Antwerp and Amsterdam as having no full reading. On the leaves, the 9 September 1573 letter (Amsterdam; cipher ff. 135r–137v) has a complete Court decipherment on ff. 139r–141r (“deschiffré”), and it is verbatim: a hard-EM alignment of 4,735 hand-transcribed glyphs against it runs line for line with a glyph-to-letter ratio of 0.91, the shortfall being word signs such as dict , faict , monsieur . The alignment gives the 1573 key, about 55 signs, the 1572 system with the same homophones. The 4 January 1573 letter (Antwerp; cipher f. 126v, 4 lines, f. 127r, 31 lines, f. 127v, 4 lines) has no decipherment anywhere in the volume, only four interlinear glosses on f. 127r ( hambourg , Lan… , and two unsure). It was decoded ciphertext-only with the 9 September key and the French 5-gram beam decoder. The control: a key rebuilt without block 1 of 9 September decodes that block blind at 77.5 % of letters. Re-reading every 4 January line on the strips corrected 20 glyphs, and splitting the round a from the open alpha with a crossing tail, which the first transcription had merged, showed that the alpha is always r and the round a never is (l, y, i); the control rose to 79.0 %. The gloss hambourg decoded in place, and about 55–60 % of the 4 January letters read, among them “seize ou dix huict”, “soubz ombre de chercher parti”, “desavantaige … qu’il fera”, “l’Angleterre avoit … tenir cent …”, “[H]ambourg, où on croit debvoir servir pareil”. The text was then found in print. Mondoucet kept a register of his despatches from September 1572 (Bibliothèque de Reims), and L. Didier printed it in 1891: the letter of 4 January 1573 is on pp. 141–142 of volume 1, in clear, ending “D’Anvers, ce IIIIe jour de janvier 1573”. The ciphered part reads: … il se donnoit fort secrètement wartgueld des costez de Collongne, Francfort, Spire et autres villes, sans qu’il se puisse savoir de quelle part; et aultres encores, ne voullans estre descouvertz, prenent aultre voye, donnans argent aux collonnelz pour entretenir leurs reistres-mestres et gentilzhommes, et lesdictz reistres-mestres entretenans leurs soldatz particulliers. Aussi, que les villes de [Hesse?], Strasbourg et aultres faisoient levées de gens; outre plus, qu’il estoit depuis naguières arrivé à Collongne seize ou dix huict cappitaines venans de Suède et Dannemarch … De tout ce qui se passera j’espère en donner toute lumyère à V. Ma té par le rapport que m’en fera ung cappitaine allemand … qui m’a semblé estre plus propre que aultre, par ce que, soubz umbre de chercher party, il descouvrira tout ce qui se fait … J’ay seu que Mons r le duc d’Alve avoit pris ceste forme de wartgueld avec le duc de Brunsvick … et croy qu’il aura fait le semblable à l’endroit du duc de Lauembourg de Saxe … Davantaige, Sire, je ne veulx oublier de vous advertir comme j’ay [apprins] que la royne d’Angleterre avoit fait tenir cent mil escuz à Hambourg, que l’on croyt debvoir servir pour pareil effect. Estant en ceste ville, j’ay descouvert qu’il y avoit quelque temps qu’un certain évesque de Hirlande y séjournoit, quy y est entretenu par ledict sieur duc, avec lequel il conduit la pratique dudict pays de Hirlande … (Didier 1891, i, 141–142; spelling normalised from the OCR where it was garbled.) Every stretch the decoder had read stands in the printed text, and the unread lines are now filled: Louis of Nassau’s secret wartgeld retainers, captains from Sweden and Denmark at Cologne, a German captain sent as a spy, Alba’s own wartgeld with Brunswick and Saxe-Lauenburg (the gloss Lan… ), English money at Hamburg, and an Irish bishop kept at Antwerp by Alba for a design on Ireland (the decoder’s “de l’Irlande” in l. 31). The edition was in the page’s sources from the start but was not opened until after the ciphertext-only passes, so those passes are an independent recovery; the reading of 4 January is the edition’s. The 13 July 1572 despatch is not in Didier: the register begins on 6 September 1572, and Didier’s own inventory of fr. 16127 calls that letter “chiffrée et en grande partie sans déchiffrement”.

t: Mondoucet’s despatch of 13 July 1572 — a segmenter, not the archive
b: A ciphered despatch that four validated aligners could not touch was an ordinary homophonic substitution all along; what defeated the solvers was an unvalidated segmenter that manufactured a 1.3–1.4 glyph-per-letter ratio and broke the one-to-one mapping. The lesson is narrow and worth stating: never trust a glyph-per-letter ratio taken from an automatic segmenter you have not checked against a hand count on a passage of known plaintext. What remains is a clean retranscription of the ciphered lines to a fixed glyph accuracy and the collation of the clear bands with the other fr. 16127 letters. A second lesson came from 1573: open the edition before decoding. Didier printed the 4 January letter in clear, and the page’s sources had cited it all along.

t: Cardinal Morosini, legate in France, to Montalto, 1588–89 — thirty-six nunciature ciphers read with the 1587 key
b: Thirty-six cipher enclosures from the papal legate in France to the Cardinal Nephew, catalogued on DECODE as partially decrypted, with the key Meister printed in 1906 attached but no plaintext. The figures run on without separators and each letter has one-, two- and three-digit homophones, so every page was cut up by a beam search scored with an Italian model. Thirty-four read end to end and two in a second key in part: the Council of Trent, the Estates of Blois, Saluzzo, the murder of the Guises, and Henri III’s march on Paris. Blois, Tours, Moulins → Rome · homophonic nomenclator, figures run together · August 1588 – July 1589 · read Cardinal Morosini, legate in France, to Cardinal Montalto, 1588–89 from Cardinal Morosini Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Francia 22, items 1–37 · DECODE R18–R22, R27–R49, R51–R58, thirty-six cipher enclosures, 168 pages · catalogued as partially decrypted The 1587 key printed by Meister, applied to DECODE’s transcriptions with a segmenting decoder · 34 read end to end, 2 in a second key read in part Daniel Bourdeau · read 19 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. Gian Francesco Morosini, Bishop of Brescia, was nuncio in France from 1587 and legate from the summer of 1588. His despatches to the Cardinal Nephew, Alessandro Peretti di Montalto, sent their substance in enclosed sheets of figures. Thirty-six of these sheets, from Francia 22 in the Vatican, are on DECODE, transcribed digit by digit, with George Lasry’s partial key of 2020 and a scan of the full key Aloys Meister printed in 1906 (“Con monsig. Moresino nuntio in Francia, 8 Giugno 1587”). No plaintext was posted, and the records are listed as partially decrypted. The difficulty is that the figures run on without separators and the homophones are one, two or three digits long ( e is 35, 153 or 5), so a sheet can be cut up in many ways. A beam search over the cuts, scored by an Italian model of the period, gives running Italian at once. Thirty-four sheets read end to end; two from the spring of 1589 are in a second, syllabic key that Lasry recovered only in part, and read in part. What they say: the long fight to have the Council of Trent published in France; the Estates of Blois; the Duke of Savoy’s seizure of Saluzzo; the Duke of Guise “amazato a colpi di pugnale” in the King’s chamber on 23 December 1588, and his brother the Cardinal the next morning; the legate’s own disgrace in Rome; and, from Tours and Moulins, Henri III’s march on Paris in June 1589. What stays open is a few dotted codes outside Meister’s list, single-letter slips, and most of the two second-key sheets.

t: Cardinal Morosini, legate in France, to Montalto, 1588–89 — thirty-six nunciature ciphers read with the 1587 key
b: Francia 22 is the volume of Morosini’s originals and ciphers from 25 July 1588 to 20 September 1589 (ff. 10–583). DECODE holds 36 of its cipher enclosures, items 22/1 to 22/37 (22/29 has no record; R23–R26 and R50, inside the same run of record numbers, are other material). Most are marked dup.to , the duplicate sent by a second courier; the clear covering letters that go with them are partly transcribed on DECODE as well. The key is Meister no. 40 ( Die Geheimschrift im Dienste der päpstlichen Kurie , pp. 393–394), issued to Morosini on 8 June 1587. Each letter has two or three homophones: a 21 212 2, e 35 153 5, i 17 171 7, n 10 01 0, o 91 191 9, r 00 13 1, s 54 45 4, t 51 15 6, u 37 173 3, and so on. There are about twenty codes for clusters (cr 22, pr 33, st 47, str 49) and twenty for words (che 56, per 64, non 61 71, quando 99). A three-digit nomenclator is marked with a dot on the middle figure: 111 the Pope, 113 the King of France (“S. M.tà Christ.ma”), 116 the Queen Mother, 129 Duca di, 131 Cardinale di, 133 Arcivescovo, 227 Heretici, 232 “il già Re di Navarra”. An 8 with any following figure is a null. Francia 22 f. 308r, the head of the despatch of 23 December 1588 (docket “dup.to di 23 Decembre”), whose opening lines report the murder of the Duke of Guise. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Francia 22 f. 308r, via DECODE R43.

t: Cardinal Morosini, legate in France, to Montalto, 1588–89 — thirty-six nunciature ciphers read with the 1587 key
b: The despatch of 23 December 1588 (R43) begins, once the figures are cut up: … questa matina il Duca di Guisa nela camera di S. M.tà è stato per ordine di S. M.tà amazato a colpi di pugnale, et la sua morte è seguita a questo modo. […] domandato a chiamare il Duca di Guisa che si trovava nel consiglio di stato, venuto et entrato subito nela camera fu preso […] con molte pugnalate, et dopo havere indarno usata grandissima difesa con le mani et [co’] denti, senza però mai havere potuto metter mano ala spada […]; posti prigioni il Cardinale di Guisa, che si trovava pure in consiglio, il Duca di Nemurs, il Duca d’Elbeuf, il Principe di Gianvile, l’Arcivescovo di Lione, il prevosto de’ mercanti di Parigi […] et data guardia al Cardinale di Borbone. (This morning the Duke of Guise was killed with daggers in His Majesty’s chamber on His Majesty’s order. Called from the council of state, he came in and was seized, and, after a great defence with his hands and teeth, without ever getting his hand to his sword, died of many dagger blows. The Cardinal de Guise, Nemours, Elbeuf, Joinville, the Archbishop of Lyon and the prévôt des marchands of Paris were arrested, and the Cardinal de Bourbon put under guard.) The duplicate of the next day (R44) adds that the Cardinal de Guise “questa matina solamente è rimasto privo di vita”. The legate, because a cardinal had been killed, leaves the answer to the Pope.

t: Cardinal Morosini, legate in France, to Montalto, 1588–89 — thirty-six nunciature ciphers read with the 1587 key
b: Dates in square brackets come from the context or the series; the quotations are from the decoded text, spaced into words and lightly normalised. Record Item Date What the cipher says From the text R18 22/1 10 Aug [1588] (duplicate) On publishing the Council of Trent: strong resistance everywhere over Gallican liberties. In Paris Morosini lobbied the Sorbonne and the royal council, and told Henri III that a Most Christian king should accept the council without conditions. The King answered that the clergy, above all the Archbishop of Lyon, were the ones opposing it. Also: the King is set on holding the Estates General; Guise's party is manoeuvring over the deputies; the Spanish ambassador complains that the English fleet was resupplied in French ports. si contentasse ancora di ricevere nel suo regno esto concilio liberamente, sì come è fatto negli altri regni R19 22/2 24 Aug [1588] (duplicate) The clergy's deputies appeared before the Parlement to oppose the council as against Gallican liberty. In an audience the King defended his privileges and benefice nominations. He was told that the legation's faculties must be verified by the Parlement. A Cardinal (Bourbon/Vendôme) pressed for the absolution of his brothers. Factions are gathering followers for the Estates; there is fear of a bloody clash between Catholics; a marriage is proposed between the Count of Soissons and a daughter of the Duke of Guise. comparvero al parlamento per opporsi alla publicatione di esto concilio, dicendo che era contrario ... alla libertà della chiesa gallicana R20 22/3 9 Sept [1588] The King gave the Count of Soissons letters clearing him of his service with Navarre and the Huguenots. Paris citizens and the prévôt protested to the Parlement. Cardinal de Vendôme and the Princess of Condé were furious. Morosini advised the King and Vendôme to wait for the Pope's absolution first, and they agreed to hold the letters back until it came. che le lettere non havessero a servire se non dopo che il conte fosse ... [assolto] da Nostro Signore R21 22/4 n.d. [Sept 1588] The King dismissed his secretaries of state and the chancellor all at once, leaving the court anxious. Mons. de Nevers(?) and the Queen Mother were displeased not to have been consulted. Morosini warned the King that new men would be inexperienced and the old ones could side with his enemies. The King replied that he meant to be obeyed and feared. Also: the King sent his physician to Épernon to get him to give up Boulogne and Metz. privandosi Sua Maestà in un istesso tempo di tutti quelli che intendono il vero stato delle cose sue R22 22/5 n.d. [Sept 1588] (duplicate) Replies to Montalto. Morosini has kept pressing for the council; the Estates promise to ask for it. His faculties will not be obeyed unless the Parlement verifies them. He held back the Count of Soissons' absolution because the Count refused the prescribed form of abjuration; the Cardinals of Bourbon and Vendôme then urged the King to write to Rome. Also: a Danish ambassador has come, perhaps to draw the King into defending the Queen of England; Morosini rebuts the vice-legate's complaints and answers on Épernon and La Valette. non volendo a modo alcuno contentare il conte di Soissons, dicendo che non si deve accusare di peccato che non ha R27 22/6 n.d. (fragment) On governments for Épernon (Saintonge, Angoulême, Cognac) and on Boulogne. Épernon's side refuses to give anything back and is said to deal with the Queen of England and Navarre. Morosini hopes for peace between Guise and the others, though with little confidence. si mostrano risolutissimi di non volere restituire alcuna cosa R28 22/7 [early] Oct [1588] (duplicate) While walking in the palace garden with the King, the Queen Mother and the Cardinals of Bourbon and Vendôme, Morosini learned that the King would send Signor Girolamo Gondi to Rome about pulling Marshal Montmorency away from the Huguenots. Vendôme reports that Cardinal Joyeuse worked against the Count of Soissons in Rome. haveva esortato Sua Maestà a fare ogni opera per ritirare dall'amicitia delli ugonotti quel signore R29 22/8 10 Oct [1588] (duplicate) A messenger is back from Florence about the Grand Duke's marriage to the Princess of Lorraine; Orazio Rucellai will conclude it, and the Queen Mother plans to escort her to Marseille. News that the Duke of Savoy has seized the whole marquisate of Saluzzo; Guise fears this will force peace with Navarre and the heretics. Morosini asks for orders; a Danish ambassador is dealing over merchants' goods. esto accidente sarà la rovina della religione cattolica R30 22/9 3 Oct [1588], Blois Morosini took on the job of reconciling the Duke of Guise and Mons. de Nevers, who have been at odds since they married sisters; with the King's approval, both promised to follow his advice. He pressed Guise and the Cardinal of Guise on publishing the council. The clergy is split: the lower deputies want Gallican liberty reserved. He is also working against any alienation of church property. disunione ... che era causa ... di mali officii non senza grave pregiudicio della quiete di questo regn R31 22/10 23 Oct [1588], Blois Mandelot, governor of Lyon, is ordered to arrest a man for transfer to Avignon. The Cardinal of Guise asks for the vice-legation of Avignon. The Florentine marriage contract is going forward. The King will send Gondi to Rome about Montmorency, and is embittered over Savoy and Saluzzo. The Épernon and Provence troubles continue. The Estates have sworn a fundamental law keeping only the Catholic religion; the Parlement will not accept the legation faculties. per legge fondamentale del regno irrevocabile si è stabilito di mantener sempre la sola religione cattolica R32 22/11 24 Oct [1588] Savoy is keeping Saluzzo and is suspected of designs on Marseille. M. de Poigny is sent to the Duke to demand restitution. Morosini protests over Cardinal Lenoncourt's indult and over church revenues in the Cambrai truce, and the Queen Mother answers him. The King explains why Épernon was removed from Provence, and promises to raise publication of the council "tomorrow". ho ancora di nuovo ricordato a Sua Maestà la publicatione del concilio di Tren R33 22/12 n.d. [Oct-Nov 1588] The King referred the council to the clergy's congregation. There the chapters, bishops and others quarrelled over exemptions, and they finally asked for publication with four reservations (royal authority, Gallican liberty, chapter exemptions, particular privileges). Morosini argued that it must be published without conditions. The King answered that the Gallican church has privileges it cannot lose. Morosini asks Rome for precise orders. si doveva fare senza alcuna eccettione R34 22/13 n.d. [Nov 1588] The Spanish ambassador pressed the Queen Mother for union and good understanding between Philip II and Henri III, and showed a copy of Philip's letter. Morosini sees a real opening for the alliance and asks that it be kept secret. The ambassador blamed Savoy for the Saluzzo attack. Gondi leaves for Rome; Morosini commends the Archbishop of Lyon. There is new friction with Guise over the governor of Orléans. introdurre una buona intelligenza et unione fra il suo et questo re R35 22/14 n.d. A copy, in Spanish, of Philip II's letter to the Queen Mother (given to her by the Spanish ambassador). It urges closer union and friendship between the two crowns against the heretics, for God's service and obedience to the Roman Church. exortando a las dos coronas a mayor unión y amistad R36 22/15 10 Nov [1588] (duplicate) A fever kept Morosini indoors. The Savoy ambassador reported the Poigny talks to the Queen Mother: the Duke will not return the Saluzzo places, and claims to have acted by the Pope's order (Carmagnola). Morosini firmly denies that the Pope had any part in it. The King is resolved on war rather than bear the insult; Morosini asks for guidance. quello che ha fatto è di ordine di Nostro Signore R37 22/16 21 Nov [1588] (duplicate) Morosini urged the King and Queen Mother to settle Saluzzo peacefully. The Savoy ambassador had offered to restore the places if they were given to a Catholic knight, with Nemours as governor. Guise advised force instead, sending Mayenne into Bresse. The King inclined to Morosini's view and asked that a lieutenant also be named. The Spanish ambassador denies that Philip backs Savoy. il Duca di Guisa consigliava il contrario ... bisognava attendere ad ingrossare le forze al Duca di Mayenne R38 22/17 n.d. [late Nov-Dec 1588] The Savoy ambassador complained that Mayenne was ordered into Bresse. Morosini urged the King not to start a war before trying every other way, and to fight the heretics first. The King said he gave Mayenne no such order, but called the Duke of Savoy ungrateful. Also: the Cardinal of Guise and the oath for the Avignon legation; Lenoncourt's indult; a truce with the Dauphiné Huguenots is being considered. dissuadendola a non volere principiare una guerra se prima non havesse tentata ogni altra via R39 22/18 8 Dec [1588] (duplicate) A courier from Turin came from Poigny. In the council, Nevers insisted on war with Savoy even if Saluzzo were restored; the others would forgive the Duke if he gave the places back. Munitions and artillery are to be sent to Lyon. Nevers also argued that Spain would not intervene. ando ancora il signor Duca di Savoia restituisse il marchesato, ... di farli la guerra R40 22/19 dup., "li 8 X[bre]" (8 Dec 1588?), [Blois] The King's council discusses the Duke of Savoy's artillery and troops on the borders of Bresse and Dauphiné and resolves to levy Swiss and 1,500 horse to join the Duke of Mayenne; the Duke of Guise offers 10,000 scudi, and the Estates' treasurers promise money. Morosini goes to the Capuchins hoping to find Henri III and complains that the King no longer talks openly with him. He reports that the King is tightly bound to Guise and is said to have dismissed his heads of finance. fu risoluto di spedir subito per fare una leuata di tremilia suizeri R41 22/20 n.d. [Blois, Dec 1588] The Duke of Savoy has seized the Marquisate of Saluzzo and offers to give it back once the Dauphiné is free of Huguenots, with his wife or a son as a hostage. The Duke of Guise tells Morosini he must press the King to recover Saluzzo by force, or else retire from court; the Savoyard ambassador has been refused. Mayenne asks what to do, with the Savoyard enemy so near. egli non puo per honor suo lasciare di far ogni sforzo per uendicare l'ingiuria R42 22/21 n.d. [Blois, Dec 1588] Morosini tells the King at the Capuchins that the Pope is displeased the Council of Trent has not been published; the King answers through Gondi. Guise complains that the King does not trust him, and Morosini urges the King to satisfy Guise. He also reports on the papal bull against procurers of abortion and says the Queen Mother has a fever. nela publicatione del concilio di Trento Sua Maesta non habia ancora presa quella risolutione R43 22/22 Blois, 23 Dec [1588] Guise is killed with daggers in the King's chamber on the King's order, after warnings that he meant harm to the King. The Cardinal of Guise, the Prince de Joinville, the Dukes of Nemours and Elbeuf, the Archbishop of Lyon, the prévôt des marchands and a Paris president are arrested, and the Cardinal de Bourbon is put under guard. The Queen Mother is left speechless, the city is locked down, Morosini seeks an audience in vain, and the Cardinal of Guise is feared dead too. il Duca di Guisa nela camera del Re e stato per ordine di Sua Maesta amazato a colpi di pugnale R44 22/23 dup., 24 Xbre [1588], [Blois] The Cardinal of Guise was put to death only this morning. Because he was a churchman, Morosini leaves the response to the Pope's judgment. The Cardinal de Bourbon is under guard and ill, and Joinville and the Archbishop of Lyon are to go to Amboise. Guise's secretary, under examination, said the Pope had written to Guise in favour of Savoy over Saluzzo, which angered the King. The King tells the legate he is now king and must be obeyed. esta matina solamente e rimasto priuo di uita R45 22/24 n.d. [Blois, Jan 1589, after Catherine de' Medici's death] Morosini defends his conduct. The Archbishop of Lyon refuses lay examiners because he is primate of France. The Estates' article excluding Navarre carries a clause reserving the Bourbon succession. Morosini offers condolences on the Queen Mother's death and presses the King to declare Navarre a heretic and incapable, since an envoy of Navarre is at court seeking an accord. He also urges publication of Trent without conditions. dechiarare il Nauarro heretico et incapace ala sucessione di questo regn R46 22/25 Blois, 24 Jan 1589 (dup.) The Pope rejects the clause "saluis iuribus regis et regni", and Morosini works on the King's confessor and the Keeper of the Seals, who promise to argue his case. Saluzzo is set aside for now. At length Morosini complains of the Pope's displeasure and the false reports reaching Rome, and he begs leave to come to Rome to justify himself. non solo non accetta la clausula saluis iuribus regis et regni R47 22/26 n.d. [Blois, Jan 1589] Morosini continues his defence and denies ever dealing with the English ambassador. He explains why the Council could not be forced through the parlements and the Estates. He had suggested that the King publish it at once and then send a personage to Rome to ask for his privileges. l'Ambassadore d'Inghilterra il quale ne conosco ne so mai di hauere ued R48 22/27 Blois, 30 & 31 Jan 1589 Morosini again asks for his leave. The Parisians have put themselves under Mayenne's protection, and the King is leaving for Amboise with his prisoners. Morosini protests about moving the Cardinal de Bourbon and the Archbishop of Lyon. The King says he will keep the Cardinal comfortably in a fine castle, and agrees to send letters ordering all bishops to publish the Council of Trent without conditions. che lei accetta il sodetto concilio di Trento et che loro lo facesero publicare R49 22/28 n.d. (fragment) [early 1589] The Archbishop of Lyon refuses to answer the royal commissioners or a bishop, saying he is primate of France. His relatives ask Morosini to plead with the King not to prejudice ecclesiastical dignity and to refer the case to the Pope. egli era primate di Francia et che non poteua esser esamina R51 22/30 Tours, 27 March 1589 A count's gentleman brings news that two cavalry companies of Mayenne's (under Sagona and Farlandra, who was badly wounded) have been routed and their baggage taken. Orléans and Paris are in the League's hands, and Mayenne remains in Paris. The King wants peace, while Navarre is taking places. Guards have been placed on Morosini's house. Sua Maesta desidera grandemente la pace R52 22/31 Tours, 6 April 1589 The castellan of Angers refuses the League's bribe, and Marshal d'Aumont secures the castle for the King, who writes him a letter in his own hand. The count is sent to Brittany against the Duke of Mercoeur; Alfonso Corso is in Auvergne; Épernon's command is disputed; Mayenne is still in Paris. The King keeps Holy Week and Easter devotions and touches for the scrofula. il castelo che e riputato il piu forte di Francia R53 22/32 n.d. [Tours, spring 1589] Read only in part (second key, not fully reconstructed). In the clear part, Morosini waits anxiously for letters from Rome granting his leave. The cipher part says the vice-legate of Avignon has arrived at Tours and lodged near Plessis, and that heretics and Catholics now mix at court. Something is said about Mayenne near Le Mans. si e fata una mescolanza ala corte di heretici et di catolici R54 22/33 Moulins, 11 May 1589 Read only in part (second key, not fully reconstructed). Only fragments can be read: heretics are gathering strength at court alongside the Catholics. Morosini voices personal fears and asks that something be made known. mescolati gli heretici co i catolici ala corte R55 22/34 Moulins, 11 June 1589 A gentleman of the Grand Duchess of Tuscany reports that the Comte de Soissons (?) was captured in bed by the Duke of Mercoeur, and that a League count was killed by a gunpowder explosion. The King is marching on Paris, where Mayenne is and the city is barricaded, with 4,000 horse and 17,000 foot; Swiss and Casimir's cavalry are coming, and Épernon has taken Montereau. Morosini also passes on, with doubts, a rumour of a plot to kill the King. fu fato prigione dal Duca di Mercuri R56 22/35 Moulins, 16(?) June 1589 Morosini is distressed by Montalto's letter about his secretary. The monitorium has reportedly been posted at St Peter's, and Cardinal Joyeuse and the French ambassador are leaving Rome. Morosini thinks of retiring to Lyon, but the Lyonnais will let him stay only three days. Moulins has sworn loyalty to the King before M. de la Guiche; the Archbishop of Lyon may be freed; Alfonso Corso has crossed the Rhône. pensaria di ritirarmi a Lione per metermi in sicur R57 22/36 n.d. (enclosures dated "dix di giugno" [1589], Moulins) This record holds copies of papers sent to M. de la Guiche. The first says the King's Swiss army (about 12,000 Swiss and 2,000 lansquenets, some 17–18,000 men with 12 guns) is marching, paid with money lent by Strasbourg. The second is the oath of the inhabitants of Moulins to live and die Catholic and loyal to "Henri, by the grace of God King of France and Poland". prestato il giuramento di fedelta al Re nostro sire Henric R58 22/37 Moulins, 5 July 1589 (dup.) The King has taken Jargeau ("Giorgio") and its Loire bridge, hanged a captain and pardoned the governor. Other Loire towns have surrendered, and the King is heading for Paris, where four faubourgs are said to favour him. Mayenne has taken Montereau and Nemours is raising money at Lyon for the League's Swiss. The count is said to have escaped from Nantes castle in a basket, which Morosini doubts. si dice che il Re habia preso Giorgi

t: Cardinal Morosini, legate in France, to Montalto, 1588–89 — thirty-six nunciature ciphers read with the 1587 key
b: DECODE’s transcriptions give the figures one by one, marking a dotted figure X Y^. Z . Dotted groups were taken as nomenclator codes. The rest of each page is a single string of digits, and each position can open a code of one, two or three figures. The decoder ( morosini1588/decrypt.py ) keeps, at every position, the best-scoring reading for each four-letter context. It scores the letters it emits with the repository’s shared Italian 5-gram model ( lang/ , it-cinquecento , built from Renaissance letters and nunciature reports, without spaces). It charges a fixed cost for a null (8 and any figure) and a larger one for a figure it cannot place. A page of 1,500 figures runs in about a second. The Spanish enclosure (R35, a copy of Philip II’s letter to the Queen Mother) comes out in readable Spanish although the model is Italian. R53 and R54 are in a different key: syllabic, one or two figures, the dot on the first figure of a code. For these the decoder uses Lasry’s partial reconstruction on DECODE (R53, R54 DOC_3187/3188).

t: Cardinal Morosini, legate in France, to Montalto, 1588–89 — thirty-six nunciature ciphers read with the 1587 key
b: Nomenclator: 113 is “Il Re di Francia, S. M.tà Christ.ma” in Meister and reads as “S. M.tà” throughout (H). 165 and 166, printed “quelli” and “questi”, serve for every form of quello and questo (H), and 161 likewise for quanto (C). Dotted groups not in Meister’s table (162, 191, 250, 516, 617, 712, 716, 770 and a few others, about one per page) are left open. Most are probably a dot mis-set in the transcription, since undotted they read as ordinary letters. Letter-level slips: roughly one to three letters in a hundred come out wrong. These are transcription errors or a homophone cut the wrong way (“euisone” for Soissons). The decoded pages are given as the decoder leaves them, in decrypt_raw.txt ; the summaries above and the quotations are readings of that text (H for the sense, C for individual proper names such as Soissons, Nevers, Poigny). R53 and R54 (22/32–33): second key, known only in part. Perhaps half of each reads (M). The rest waits for the key, which is probably among Meister’s or the Vatican’s cipher registers for 1589. Item 22/29 is not on DECODE and was not seen. The clear covering letters were not edited here.

t: Francis Needham before Sluys, 28 July 1587 — the pigpen letter, read
b: BL Harley MS 287 ff. 39–40, catalogued on DECODE as a partially decrypted letter of “Needham” to an unknown recipient, is Francis Needham’s letter to Walsingham from Leicester’s fleet before Sluys. A contemporary hand glossed a few cipher words; the long runs of f. 39v were bare. The key, a three-grid pigpen with the alphabet in order, was rebuilt from the glosses and every run was read: Parma had closed the channel with hoys and flyboats chained together. Before Sluys → Walsingham · three-grid pigpen inside clear English · 28 July 1587 · read Francis Needham before Sluys, 28 July 1587 — the pigpen letter, read to Francis Walsingham British Library, Harley MS 287 ff. 39–40 (DECODE R8479): Walsingham’s servant with Leicester’s relief fleet writes of the failure to relieve Sluys. The long cipher passages of f. 39v had no decipherment; the key was rebuilt from a handful of glossed words and all of them were read. Daniel Bourdeau · solved 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 solved Summary. DECODE lists R8479 as a three-page, partially decrypted letter of “Needham” to an unknown recipient, 28 July 1587, with an unknown cipher of graphic signs. The writer is Francis Needham, Walsingham’s servant, who sailed with the Earl of Leicester to relieve Sluys, and the letter is to Walsingham; its clear text follows the despatch of the same day calendared in CSP Foreign 1587 (pp. 206–8), which the Harley leaves are not. The cipher is a pigpen of nine box shapes in three forms (plain, dot below, dot inside) carrying the alphabet a–i, k–s, t–z in order. A contemporary hand glossed a few cipher words and the runs of f. 39r; the six runs of f. 39v were left bare. From the glosses advise , enemyes , campe nor the towne and Burgrave half the alphabet came out, the first bare lines read “want of intelligence” and “whether there was any bridge”, and the order of the grids gave the rest. Every run of f. 39v now reads: the besiegers knew nothing of the enemy, did not know whether there was a bridge, and found the channel closed with hoys and flyboats fastened with chains and strengthened behind with flat boats. One word of about six letters is unsure.

t: Francis Needham before Sluys, 28 July 1587 — the pigpen letter, read
b: Harley MS 287 is a volume of Walsingham’s correspondence (the Cobham letters of 1588 on ff. 70–72 are read in another write-up ). Folios 39–40 are one letter: f. 39r opens “It may please your honour. The sudden departure of the bark … before Sluce, was the cause that I was forced to break off”, f. 39v continues, f. 40r ends it with the date 1587, and the address leaf f. 40v is endorsed “28 July 1587. From Needham”. CSP Foreign vol. 21 pt 3 (1929) calendars Needham’s letter to Walsingham of the same day from Flushing (SP 84/16 f. 216): the council aboard Leicester’s ship before the haven of Sluys, the firework ship that could hardly be brought up to the bridge, the States’ captains who would not lend boats because “this commission must come from the States”, and the fall of the town. The Harley letter tells the same story in more words; the calendar does not list it. A note in the same volume (p. 237) says Needham wrote to Walsingham in the cipher of Thomas Wilkes, whose key is at the front of BL Add MS 5935 (p. 35 n. 4). That manuscript is not online and was not used here.

t: Francis Needham before Sluys, 28 July 1587 — the pigpen letter, read
b: Nine box shapes, each written plain, with a dot beneath, or with a dot inside its angle. Read in order the shapes carry the alphabet straight through three grids: shape plain dot below dot inside ⌟ a k t ⊔ b l u, v ⌞ c m w ⊏ d n x □ e o y ⌜ f p z ⊓ g q — ⌝ h r — ⊐ i s — Words are divided and spelled as in the clear text ( wyth , chaynes , bootes ). No homophones, nulls or code names occur on f. 39v. The dots are the whole difficulty: a dot below sits under the lower left of its sign, the script slants to the right, and a dot inside ⌟ lies in its upper left, so the first transcription pass read several t’s as k’s until the grid order showed the slip. f. 39v: “campe nor the towne” glossed above its signs; beneath, the bare line whether there was any bridge or not, or whether there were any at the chanel . Image: British Library, Harley MS 287 f. 39v, via DECODE R8479 (image 4).

t: Francis Needham before Sluys, 28 July 1587 — the pigpen letter, read
b: Cipher in italics; clear words around it paraphrased where the clear text was not transcribed in full. “… we had want of intelligence these five days last past … [no] advise out of the enemyes campe nor the towne ” (the last four words glossed at the time). “and we were so far from knowing what was meet to be done at that time [that] we knewe not whether there was any bridge or not, or whether there were any at the chanel .” “… being above 100 of their files into the town walls, and that the chanel was b[…]ed with hoyes and flyboates fastened wyth chaynes, strengthned behind wyth flatt bootes .” f. 39v: “… into the towne walls. and that the chanel was b[…]ed with hoyes and flyboates fastened wyth chaynes, strengthned behind wyth flatt bootes .” Image: British Library, Harley MS 287 f. 39v, via DECODE R8479 (image 4). This is the “bridge” of the calendared despatch: Parma had closed the haven of Sluys with a boom of boats chained together, and the English and Dutch could neither see it nor learn what it was. The rest of f. 39v, in clear, covers Sir Roger Williams’s sallies, the storm, the state of the town, Count Maurice, Colonel Morgan and Sir William Russell; the three words glossed near its foot (“Mr Burley”, “the Spaniard”, “were removed hence”) were read at the time.

t: Francis Needham before Sluys, 28 July 1587 — the pigpen letter, read
b: The four images were fetched from DECODE. The glossed words gave letters by alignment: advise = ⌟ ⊏ ⊔: ⊐ ⊐̣ □, enemyes = □ ⊏̣ □ ⌞̣ □: □ ⊐̣, the towne = ⌟: ⌝ □ ⌟: □̣ ⌞: ⊏̣ □, and Burgrave on f. 40r began ⊔ ⊔̣ ⌝̣ ⊓. The first bare line then read want of intelligence , and once a, b, c, d, e, h, i and k–s, t–z were in hand the order was plainly alphabetical, which fixed f, g, p and q and corrected the misread dots. A quadgram annealer was written for the case that the key would not close, and was not needed. The transcription is in needham1587/cipher.txt and the key in decode.py .

t: Francis Needham before Sluys, 28 July 1587 — the pigpen letter, read
