t: A correspondent at Randan to the Duke of Nevers, 27 March and 4 April 1587 — read
b: BnF fr. 3975 ff. 28 and 30 (DECODE R4285, R4286), two clear letters to Nevers with seven cipher items, catalogued as from an unknown sender at Rome. Key no. 11 of the Nevers key book (fr. 3995 f. 23) reads them, once a glossed letter by the same hand from Clermont (fr. 3413 f. 102, assigned by Tomokiyo to the cardinal de Guise) shows how the writer draws its signs. The first letter is dated in cipher De Randan, in Auvergne; Épernon took alarm passing near Lyon; 94, 6, 23 are the marquis, Entragues and the queen of Navarre. 26 of 27 cipher units accounted for. Randan (Auvergne) → the duc de Nevers · letter-figure-symbol substitution with word capitals and name codes · 27 March and 4 April 1587 · read A correspondent at Randan to the Duke of Nevers, spring 1587 to Duke of Nevers BnF Français 3975 ff. 28 and 30 (DECODE R4285 and R4286, “non-decrypted”, sender unknown, origin given as Rome). Two letters in clear French with seven cipher items between them. All seven read with a key from the Nevers key book. The key only works once you know how this writer draws its signs, and a third letter in his hand, glossed at the time, shows that. Daniel Bourdeau · read 22 September 2026 read Summary. The catalogue entry was two DECODE records: letters to Nevers of 27 March and 4 April 1587 from an unknown sender, said to be at Rome, with “what the cipher hides not known”. On the leaves they turn out to be letters in clear French. The cipher is four code numbers, a ten-sign place name in the dateline of the first letter, and one thirteen-sign run in the second. Two words of the second were glossed at the time (“Le duc d’Espernon” over 45, “Lyon” under the run). Those glosses matched key no. 11 of Nevers’s key book (BnF fr. 3995 f. 23), and that key reads every code: 94 the marquis, 6 M. d’Entragues, 23 the queen of Navarre, 45 the duc d’Épernon. Straight from the key table, the rest of the run and the dateline would not read. The breakthrough was a third letter: Tomokiyo notes that key no. 11 is used in a letter in fr. 3413, which he assigns to the cardinal de Guise. It is in fact this correspondent’s, from Clermont, with five cipher lines and an interlinear decipherment, and it shows how this writer draws the key (Ŧ for p, the capital F for “et”, a dotted 1 for d). With that, the run reads “passant pres Lyon et ce pais ” and the first letter is dated “De Randan” , in Auvergne, not Rome. 26 of the 27 cipher units are accounted for: letters, words, codes, three nulls, and two signs of a false start the writer struck out. One sign, between a null and “et”, is taken as a null against its key value.

t: A correspondent at Randan to the Duke of Nevers, 27 March and 4 April 1587 — read
h: The two letters and the key
b: Fr. 3975 is a volume of the Nevers papers for 1587 in the Collection Mémoires de la Ligue , on Gallica as btv1b90605473 . The BnF’s piece-by-piece notice lists f. 28 as no. 7, “Lettre avec chiffrement et déchiffrement adressée à M. le duc de Nevers pour lui rendre compte d’un voyage à Lyon. Ce XXVII mars 1587” , and f. 30 as no. 8, “Lettre adressée par le même correspondant et sur le même sujet” , 4 April. Both are signed with the same monogram and written in a hand that fills its line ends with a long s. Nothing on the leaves says where the writer was. DECODE’s “Rome” seems to be borrowed from a neighbouring piece (no. 13, the marquis Malatesta, Di Roma ). f. 28r–v, 27 March (R4285): code numbers 94, 6 and 23, each followed by the key’s virgule, and a ten-sign place name before the clear “ce xxvij Mars”. f. 30r, 4 April (R4286): code 45 and one run of thirteen signs. A contemporary hand glossed the code and the first four signs of the run. F. 30r. “45, a esté en tres grande alarme, passant pres”, then the run. The gloss Le duc d’Espernon is over 45, and Lyon is written small under the first four signs. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3975 f. 30r, via Gallica (btv1b90605473). The key is no. 11 in Tomokiyo’s catalogue of the Nevers key book, BnF fr. 3995 f. 23 (Gallica btv1b525085665 , view 52). It has an alphabet of two to four signs per letter, capitals for twenty-two small words (C = de, F = et, K = me, M = avec…), and some hundred names and words written as a figure or letter followed by a virgule. The instruction on the sheet: “L’on pourra se servir de toutes sortes de caractaires que l’on voudra faire a plaisir avec ceulx qui sont dans ce chiffre, lesquelz serviront de nulles” , so invented signs are nulls. The name list leans south and to Auvergne: St Vidal, Mandelot, Maugiron, Randan, the grand prieur, the comte de Sault, the bishop of Clermont. The full table is in nevers1587/key.md . BnF fr. 3995 f. 23, the alphabet of key no. 11 (turned). Under l: m and π; under y: ^ and <; under o: n, u and an underlined ꭓ; under p: a script l and a script F. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3995 f. 23, via Gallica (btv1b525085665, view 52).

t: A correspondent at Randan to the Duke of Nevers, 27 March and 4 April 1587 — read
h: The letter from Clermont that taught the hand
b: Straight from the table, the codes read at once and so did the glossed Lyon (π ^ ꭓ é = l y o n). The rest did not: “… a p c e t a i s”, and a dateline of “r a q …”. Enumerating every value and null against a French language model, and allowing one or two scribal slips, produced nothing convincing. Tomokiyo notes that key no. 11 “is used in a letter of Cardinal of Guise to the Duke of Nevers, Clairmont, 25 February”, BnF fr. 3413 f. 102 (Gallica btv1b52510705j , view 213). It is not the cardinal’s. It has the same hand, the same long-s line fillers and the same monogram as the two letters in fr. 3975, and it is dated in clear “De Clairmont ce xxv feb” . It reports the Gevaudan Huguenots’ raids and the King’s order to St Vidal to prepare the sieges of Marvejols and Le Malzieu (Joyeuse took both in August 1586, so the letter is of February 1586). It has five lines of cipher with a decipherment written between them: “Mr du Mayne m’a mandé qu’il desire que je l’aille trouver avec ma compagnie, deux mille hommes de pied et bon nombre de ma cavalerie … si je l’abandonnois” . BnF fr. 3413 f. 102r, the same correspondent from Clermont, February [1586]: the cipher lines with their contemporary decipherment, from Mr du Mayne m’a mandé to si je l’abandonnois . t: A correspondent at Randan to the Duke of Nevers, 27 March and 4 April 1587 — read
b: 4 April, f. 30r. The run divides π ^ ꭓ é | ∞ ƥ | F | ƨ h | Ŧ ◊ 7 o = Lyon · two nulls · et · ce · pais : “ 45 [le duc d’Espernon] a esté en tres grande alarme, passant pres Lyon et ce pais , et sans aucun subject, car je vous puis asseurer qu’on n’a jamais songé de luy faire desplaisir; ce sont les charités qu’on preste en ce temps cy, lesquelles, je m’asseure, tomberont sur les inventeurs, car la verité, si elle ne l’est desja, sera bien tost cogneue.” (“The duc d’Épernon was in very great alarm passing near Lyon and this country, and without any cause, for I can assure you no one ever thought of doing him harm; these are the charities people lend one another these days, which will fall on their inventors.”) The letter opens with Nevers’s laquais sent back, the duke having gone to Chenonceau “jusqu’apres de Pasques” and now happily returned to Paris. 27 March, f. 28. The writer answers Nevers’s question about a journey he made to Lyon. He went on private business. Tournon and St Vidal were there with the bishop of Le Puy to settle the war in the Vivarais with Mandelot, and “en ce temps mesme 94 [le marquis] y arriva, qui vendit une terre a 6 [M. d’Entragues], dont ils s’estoient remis a mons. de Lyon pour le marché … Pour ce qui est de 23 [la reine de Navarre], je ne m’en suis voulu jamais mesler … je sçay combien je doibs de respect en ces lieux la.” The dateline, C | ∞ | 6 ƥ z ι ◊ é | ι ⊕ , reads C = “de”, ∞ a null, then r a n d a n: “De Randan, ce xxvij Mars” . The last two signs would read “de”, but they are a false start: the ⊕ is a pale blot with a double stroke through it. The writer began the date in cipher, cancelled it, and wrote “ce xxvij Mars” in clear. Randan, north-east of Clermont, was the seat of Jean-Louis de La Rochefoucauld, comte de Randan, governor of Auvergne. Marguerite de Valois, the “23” of the letter, was then held at Usson, in the same province. The end of the ciphered place, enlarged: … a n (the diamond and the looped é), then the struck-out false start (ι and a pale ⊕ with a double stroke through it), then ce xxvij in clear. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3975 f. 28v, via Gallica (btv1b90605473). F. 28v, the foot: the ciphered place, C ∞ 6 ƥ z ι ◊ é ι ⊕ = de [·] Randan and a struck-out false start, then ce xxvij Mars in clear. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3975 f. 28v, via Gallica (btv1b90605473). Both letters in full, with the cipher resolved, are in nevers1587/reading.md . t: A correspondent at Randan to the Duke of Nevers, 27 March and 4 April 1587 — read
b: No name appears on the leaves. The three letters show a man who writes from Clermont and from Randan. He keeps a company and cavalry of his own, and Mayenne asks him to bring two thousand foot. He had asked the King for leave to keep horse against the Gevaudan Huguenots. He stays well clear of the queen of Navarre’s affairs, and he hopes to wait on Nevers at Nevers. That fits the comte de Randan, the League governor of Auvergne (killed before Issoire in 1590), and he is the obvious candidate. The key lists “Mr de Randan” as 8, though, and nothing on the leaves names him, so the page calls him a correspondent at Randan. “94, le marquis” in Auvergne that spring is probably the marquis de Canillac, Marguerite’s keeper at Usson, who had gone over to her that winter. That is context, not proof.

t: A correspondent at Randan to the Duke of Nevers, 27 March and 4 April 1587 — read

It is taken as a null (M). Randan (6 signs): H for the letters. z is the key’s q, but this writer’s z and 2 (n) are one shape. t: A court informant to the Duke of Nevers, 29 April 1588 — read
b: BnF fr. 3976 f. 62 (DECODE R3705), a Paris news letter to Louis de Gonzague, duc de Nevers, with nineteen cipher runs and no decipherment. No known Nevers key fitted; the key was rebuilt from the interlinear glosses of the same informant’s letter of 4 June 1588 and every run read. Henri III nearly had five or six Paris ligueurs drowned; Guise answered that he had forty thousand men. Paris → the duc de Nevers · letter-and-figure homophonic cipher with code numbers · 29 April 1588 · read A court informant to the Duke of Nevers, 29 April 1588 to Duke of Nevers BnF Français 3976 f. 62 (DECODE R3705, catalogued as “1 Jan 1588”, not deciphered). One page of Paris news in clear French with nineteen cipher runs and ten code numbers, and no decipherment. The key was rebuilt from a later letter by the same informant that does carry glosses, and all nineteen runs were read. Daniel Bourdeau · solved 22 September 2026 solved Summary. DECODE catalogues this leaf as a non-deciphered letter from an unknown sender to Nevers, dated 1 January 1588. The date is a placeholder. The letter is dated 29 April 1588, and the BnF notice describes it as news that includes the lifting of the sieges of Sedan and Jametz. The writer, an informant at court whose monogram also closes ff. 131 and 133 of the volume, spelled some names and words in a cipher of letters and figures. He also used bare code numbers, and he explains in his last lines that he spelled the words out because Nevers might not remember the numbers. None of Tomokiyo’s Nevers keys in fr. 3995 fitted, and a ciphertext-only anneal found nothing. The key came from f. 131, the same informant’s letter of 4 June 1588, where a secretary wrote the plaintext over each run: “conte de Brissac” over 7 i7 id i2 t 6 s 8 g p i3 f 2 X showed that a sign is one character, or the figure 1 plus a character. From there the runs of f. 62 were read one at a time against their clear context, and each run added to the key. 350 of the 353 letters read. The letter reports that Henri III was nearly resolved in council to have five or six of the leading Paris ligueurs thrown in the river, a fortnight before the Day of the Barricades, and gives Guise’s answer. One name, one word and four code numbers stay open.

t: A court informant to the Duke of Nevers, 29 April 1588 — read
b: Fr. 3976 is a volume of Nevers’s papers for 1588, on Gallica as btv1b9060548h ; f. 62 is view 111. The BnF’s piece-by-piece notice lists it as no. 30: “Lettre, avec chiffre, adressée au duc de Nevers, contenant entre autres nouvelles, celle de la levée du siège de Sedan et de Jametz. Ce 29 avril 1588.” The neighbouring pieces at ff. 56 and 60 are symbol ciphers from the cardinals of Bourbon and Guise, each with its decipherment. They use a different system. F. 62, the first lines. Run 1 ( 4kd3si4ti3 ) follows “si”; the second line ends in the run for “leur entreprise a failly”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3976 f. 62r, via Gallica (btv1b9060548h, view 111). The last lines explain the method: “Il y a quelques motz au chiffre cy dessus que j’eusse plus aisement et briefvement mis par nombres, mais craignant que ne feussiez memoratif d’iceulx n’ayant ce chiffre, j’ay mieulx aymé estre plus long.”

t: A court informant to the Duke of Nevers, 29 April 1588 — read
h: The key, from the informant’s June letter
b: The same hand, cipher and monogram appear on f. 131 (4 June 1588) and f. 133 (6 June 1588). On f. 131 someone wrote the plaintext above the runs: “quelques mutins d’entr’eux”, “conte de Brissac”, “que s’il pouvoit”, “Roy”, and over the numbers 24 “nevers” and 11 “le Roy”. (The gloss over 24 was first read here as “Navarre”; the letter of 6 June, read later the same day , showed that 24 is Nevers.) F. 131 (4 June 1588): “conte de Brissac” and “est tué et que d’Elbeuf est au fort Ste Catherine” written over the runs. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3976 f. 131, via Gallica (btv1b9060548h, view 221). The Brissac gloss fixed the unit. 7 · i7 · id · i2 · t · 6 · s · 8 · g · p · i3 · f · 2 · X is fourteen signs for the fourteen letters of contedebrissac , where the i-like character is the figure 1 and pairs with the sign after it. With some fifteen values from f. 131, the runs of f. 62 began to read. Each run then added values to the key: 11 p n o t 14 17 ϙ after “les grosses larmes de 12 et” gave Villeroy ; the next person named gave Bellièvre ; …n ce royaume gave 9 = a; “chancellier et d’O” gave v = d. The alphabet is homophonic, and some signs stand for two letters: the curly 8 is b, u or v, 9 is a, h or r, and 3 is g or j. The hand’s 2 looks like a z, its 8 like a curly d and its 9 like a g, and the first transcription fell into all three traps. The key is in key.md .

t: A court informant to the Duke of Nevers, 29 April 1588 — read
b: The deciphered runs are in bold. Numbers are the writer’s code numbers. J’ay communiqué a 28 la lettre de [monogram]. Suivant laquelle je diz qu’il ne faudra pas, si Fougères(?) est encore icy, de luy representer les pertinentes raisons contenues en icelles, par lesquelles se congnoist assez que les advertissements de 24 ne peuvent avoir esté cause de leur ruyne comme ilz disent, ny de quoy leur entreprise a failly . Aussi la pluspart de ceulx qui en ont parlé n’entendoyent pas que celle de 24 feust semblable a l’autre, ny que ce que 24 feust venu eust esté a l’appetit de 9, ains seulement a la ruyne de 10, assistée de plusieurs gens de bien et d’autorité qui y estoyent fort disposez et s’i disposent encore tous les jours. Mais 28 et 70 estiment bien que 24 a assez de jugement pour n’embrasser telle entreprise que bien a propos. J’ay sceu que led. 28 a prié 70 d’advertir icelluy 24 […]. Il cuyda estre resolu au conseil de prendre et jetter en l’eau cinq ou six des plus grans ligueurs de 102, a quoy poussoyent fort a la Royne, chancellier et d’O . Et 11 n’en fut desmeu sinon par les remonstrances et grosses larmes de 12 et Villeroy , qui saigement remonstrerent que tout aussi tost que cela seroit executé, non seulement l’on perdroit entierement 102, mais encore 20 des plus belles et fortes villes du royaume . De cela 9 fut incontinent adverty, qui appela Bellièvre pour le luy dire, jurant et reniant que si le moindre de la ville l’avoit mal , il feroit aud. 49 pareil traitement, et qu’il le mandast hardiment a 11, et que si telle affaire s’entreprenoit et executoit, luy avoit a son commandement 40 mil hommes , avec lesquels il remueroit tant de messages(?) en ce royaume que led. 11 en auroit la plus petite part . Voila tout ce que j’ay peu scavoir de nouveau. The second line from the top is the run de prendre et jetter en l’eau cinq ou six des plus grans ligueurs de , followed by the code 102 (Paris). Below it: chancellier et d’O , Villeroy , des plus belles et fortes villes , du royaume and Bellièvre . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3976 f. 62r, via Gallica (btv1b9060548h, view 111). Translation of the core. The King was nearly resolved in council to seize and throw into the river five or six of the chief ligueurs of Paris, pressed to it by the Queen, the chancellor and d’O. Only the remonstrances and tears of 12 and of Villeroy stopped him: they argued that once it was done he would lose Paris and twenty of the finest towns of the kingdom as well. Guise (9) heard of it at once and sent for Bellièvre to tell him, swearing that if the least man of the town came to harm he would deal with 49 the same way. Bellièvre could tell the King so plainly. If the thing were attempted, Guise had forty thousand men at his command, and with them he would stir up so much in the kingdom that the King would be left with the smallest share. Guise’s answer. The overlined 40 with m above it is 40 mil , forty thousand. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3976 f. 62r, via Gallica (btv1b9060548h, view 111). Code numbers: 11 = the King and 24 = the duc de Nevers are glossed on f. 131, and 10 = the duc d’Épernon on f. 139 ( see the June letters ). 102 = Paris and 9 = the duc de Guise follow from the context. 12, who wept with Villeroy, is probably Catherine de Médicis.

t: The intercepts summarised for Nevers, 1589 — the ciphertext is not there, and eleven deciphered ones are
b: BnF fr. 3977 no. 96 digests several letters written in cipher by the King’s enemies in September and October 1589 and sent to the duc de Nevers to be interpreted. The catalogue could not say whether the ciphered originals survive beside it. They do not: every September–October piece in the volume is in clear, and the digest itself is clear French — Mercœur asking Spain for help, powder carried to Nantes “avec le chiffre général d’Espagne”, Mendoza at Bayonne on Arques and Dieppe, Spain pressing the Pope to renew the excommunication. The sweep turned up something better: eleven other intercepted ciphered letters in the same volume, February to August 1589, each carrying its contemporary decipherment written word by word above the cipher — three of them from Mendoza to the duke of Parma, hidden in a multi-folio catalogue entry. intercepted League and Spanish traffic → the duc de Nevers · September–October 1589 · nothing to read under no. 96 The intercepts summarised for Nevers, 1589 to Duke of Nevers BnF Français 3977 no. 96 · a digest of “plusieurs lettres escriptes en chiffre par les ennemis du Roy” , sent to Nevers “pour estre interpretées” · catalogued with the ciphertext’s survival unknown The intercepts are not in the volume and the summary is in clear French — but eleven other intercepted ciphered letters are, each with its 1589 decipherment written between the lines Arya Sanketbhai Patel · resolved 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 resolved Summary. Catalogue item 31 is a single piece: a Recueil sommaire of the principal points of several letters written in cipher by the King’s enemies in September and October 1589, sent to the duc de Nevers to be interpreted . The entry could not say whether the ciphered originals survive alongside it, and scored the target “unknown whether there is any ciphertext to attack” . They do not survive. Every piece in fr. 3977 dated September or October 1589 is in clear, and the summary itself is a clear-French digest in fifteen numbered points, read here: Mercœur asking Spain for help, powder and money carried to Nantes by Diego Maldonado “avec le chiffre général d’Espagne” , Mendoza at Bayonne writing on Arques and Dieppe, and Spain pressing the Pope to renew the excommunication. That is a negative result. The useful part is what the sweep turned up instead: eleven other intercepted ciphered letters in the same volume, February to August 1589, every one carrying its contemporary decipherment written word by word above the cipher — including three from Mendoza to the duke of Parma that the catalogue’s own piece list hides in a multi-folio entry. Status: closed from the evidence. No ciphertext under no. 96; the summary is read; the eleven deciphered intercepts are located but not transcribed.

t: The intercepts summarised for Nevers, 1589 — the ciphertext is not there, and eleven deciphered ones are
b: The catalogue entry is unusually candid about its own ignorance: “Only the ‘Recueil sommaire’ of the interpreted letters is described; whether the intercepts survive in the volume is unknown” , scored “unknown whether there is any ciphertext to attack” , with the instruction “sweep fr. 3977 around no. 96 for cipher leaves” . So the target is really a question, and the work is to answer it either way. BnF fr. 3977 is btv1b9060546p , 715 canvases, a volume of the Collection Mémoires de la Ligue . Its catalogue notice carries a piece-by-piece dépouillement : 138 pieces, nos. 2–143, folios 3–423. Canvas labels are all NP , and the folio offset drifts — f. 125 is canvas 229, f. 318 is canvas 520.

t: The intercepts summarised for Nevers, 1589 — the ciphertext is not there, and eleven deciphered ones are
b: Folio 318 is canvas 520. The piece is headed, in a large chancery hand: Recueil sommaire des principaux poincts contenuz en plusieurs lettres escriptes en chiffre par les ennemis du Roy — En Septembre et Octobre 1589 — et envoyées à S.A. pour estre interpretées en decembre aud. an. fr. 3977 f. 318 (canvas 520): the digest and its first points. It is in clear French throughout — the cipher it describes is elsewhere. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3977 f. 318, via Gallica (btv1b9060546p, canvas 520). It is in clear French, not cipher : a digest in fifteen numbered points running fol. 318r–319r. The first nine: The duc de Mercœur has asked Spain for help; the King of Spain has sent powder and money by Diego Maldonado , despatched to Nantes “avec le chiffre g[e]n[er]al d’Espagne” , who arrived on 18 October 1589. Mendoza has lent the Prévôt des marchands a sum, to his master’s satisfaction; the Prévôt has since repaid it, and Mendoza is cautioned against gratifying him too promptly “à cause des envieux et calumniateurs” . The sieur de Mauléon is aggrieved at not being employed by Spain; Mendoza renews the signal agreed with him, “par tant la lettre escripte du chiffre qu’ilz ont ensemble” . The master of the posts of Bordeaux passes Spain’s advices, and what Matignon orders him for the King’s service. Villeroy has complained to Mendoza that the help the League expected never came. Mendoza writes repeatedly from Bayonne on what passed at Arques and Dieppe , “jusques a dementir les advis et les memoires du Roy” ; the sornettes Madame de Montpensier tells him; and the King reproves him for not reporting particularly enough on the Cardinal de Bourbon , the duc de Guise , d’Elbeuf and the archevêque de Lyon . The commandeur de Diou presses his suit at Rome, and what the consistory means to allow him. The King of Spain presses the Pope , and has his adherents press him, to renew the excommunication against subjects who obey the King. Spain resolves to maintain the war in France , to continue the Leaguers’ agreed annual payments and to have them paid in full; Parma to send his forces into France; Moro , captain of light horse; Balagny . fol. 318v, points 7–9: the commandeur de Diou at Rome, Spain pressing the Pope to renew the excommunication, and the resolution to maintain the war in France. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3977 f. 318v, via Gallica (btv1b9060546p).

t: The intercepts summarised for Nevers, 1589 — the ciphertext is not there, and eleven deciphered ones are
b: Every piece in fr. 3977 dated September or October 1589 — nos. 81, 84, 85, 89, 90, 91, 92, 94, 95, 96, 97 — is in clear . Not one is ciphered. The letters behind the digest were sent to Nevers to be interpreted and are not bound in this volume; what was kept is the interpretation. So for catalogue item 31 there is no ciphertext to attack , and the item should be scored as answered rather than open. The scoring note “unknown whether there is any ciphertext” can be retired.

t: The intercepts summarised for Nevers, 1589 — the ciphertext is not there, and eleven deciphered ones are
b: The sweep the entry asked for turned up something better than the thing it was looking for. The same volume holds eleven intercepted ciphered letters, each with a contemporary decipherment — the working papers of the same royalist codebreaking effort, three to seven months earlier: piece folio letter no. 29 79 Governor of Milan → Bernardino de Mendoza, Milan, 16 Feb 1589 no. 31 83 P. de Acuña → Mendoza, Turin, 28 Feb 1589 no. 38 115 Governor of Milan → Mendoza, Milan, 4 Mar 1589 no. 39 117 Bernardino de Yssunça → Martin de Yssunça, Brussels, 18 Mar 1589 nos. 43–45 126, 128, 130 three letters, Mendoza → the duke of Parma, April 1589 no. 47 135 news of the duc de Mayenne → Claude Maumarché, for Pierre Letelier, 21 Apr 1589 no. 48 137 a Leaguer to a royalist he is trying to win for the Union, Paris, 21 Apr 1589 no. 49 139 Mendoza → Juan de Moreo, Paris, 21 Apr 1589 no. 71 191 Robert, marquis de La Vieuville → the duc de Nevers, 13 Aug 1589 A parsing trap worth recording. The three Mendoza–Parma letters are the richest of the group and the easiest to miss: the dépouillement files them in a single multi-folio entry, “Fol. 126, 128 et 130 • 43 à 45” , which a regex written for “Fol. N • M” drops in silence. They are not described as ciphered in any single-folio line, and folio 125 shows no cipher in the catalogue at all. fr. 3977 f. 126 (canvas 229), “Copia de la carta escrita al Duque de Parma por Don Bernardino” : the cipher runs in continuous strings mixing figures and letters, and the French decipherer has written his plaintext word by word above every group . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3977 f. 126, via Gallica (btv1b9060546p, canvas 229). What he read there: El Vizeseneschal de Montelimart, que V.A. conoce … aqui me escriva … un billete de Monsieur de Vienna en su creancia … y lo que por [Ma…] me ha dicho es el yr a dar intelligencia a V.A. de los abisos que tienen del Coronal Fifer … la leva que el haze por los de la Liga, y la que el Rey levanta de los 12.000 que los Cantones hereies le han acordado … puntos en que no me alargare, pues ellos … ha de referir a V.A. That is eleven complete cipher-and-plaintext pairs for Spanish ciphers of 1589 — the material from which the keys themselves could be rebuilt. It is unexploited, and it is the real find of this item.

t: The intercepts summarised for Nevers, 1589 — the ciphertext is not there, and eleven deciphered ones are
b: Points 10–15 of the digest, on fol. 318v–319r, are not transcribed. None of the eleven deciphered intercepts has been transcribed, and no key has been reconstructed from them. They are located and one is photographed; that is all. It is a separate piece of work and a promising one, since each leaf carries its own plaintext. Whether the September–October 1589 originals survive elsewhere — in another Mémoires de la Ligue volume, or among the Nevers papers — was not pursued. The digest says they were sent to Nevers in December to be interpreted, so they were in his office at some point.

t: Nevers to Pisany, 1593 — the numerical key reads two letters, and the other five were never in it
b: Seven ciphered copies of the duc de Nevers’ letters from the road to Rome, catalogued as one office’s key. They are two. Tomokiyo’s Nevers cipher no. 46, read from the full-resolution table in fr. 3995 and checked against the office’s own decipherment of a Gondi letter, resolves every figure of the two letters to Pisany: the 8 September letter whole, the 14 October one in long stretches. The five letters to Revol are in the Court’s symbol cipher no. 60; one copy is in clear, one carries ninety symbols, three were not reached. Nevers, Edolo → Rome · two-digit figures with bars and dots · 1593 · two of seven read Nevers to Pisany, 1593: the numerical key reads two letters, and the other five were never in it from Duke of Nevers BnF Français 3985 nos. 66, 88, 116 and Français 3986 nos. 68, 75, 81, 101 · Louis de Gonzague, duc de Nevers, to Louis de Revol, secretary of state, and to Jean de Vivonne, marquis de Pisany · copies, August–October 1593 Catalogue entry 21. The task was to apply Tomokiyo’s Nevers cipher no. 46 to all seven and measure coverage. It covers the two letters to Pisany; the five to Revol use the Court’s symbol cipher no. 60. Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 17 September 2026 · updated 21 September 2026 2 of 7 read Summary. In the autumn of 1593 Nevers travelled to Rome to ask Clement VIII to absolve the newly converted Henri IV; the Pope refused to receive him as ambassador. The BnF catalogue lists seven of his letters from the road as “avec chiffre”, three to Revol and one to Pisany in fr. 3985, three to Revol and one to Pisany in fr. 3986, and the new catalogue scored them as one office’s key with one passage already read. They are two keys. The letters to Pisany are in the numerical cipher that Tomokiyo catalogued from fr. 3995 as no. 46 (“Chelles, October 1592”): a two-digit alphabet with homophones, barred figures for common words, plain figures for a second word list, double-dotted figures for names, and the digit 1 dropped in as a null. Read from the full-resolution table and checked against the office’s own decipherment of a Gondi letter in the same key, it resolves every figure of both Pisany letters. The 8 September letter reads whole: l’on dissuadoit [le Roy] de rechercher [que le Pape] luy donnast l’absolution … [le duc de Nevers] alléguoit qu’il n’estoyt besoin qu’il allast sans cela, parce qu’il ne feroit rien … l’on n’a volonté de contanter le Pape, que l’on n’y aille poynt . The 14 October letter, written the day after Possevino told him at Poschiavo that he would not be received, reads in long stretches: [le duc de Nevers] ne sera receu come [ambassadeur] pour pluseurs resons … n’avoir autre charge … [le cardinal Gondi, le duc de Mantoue] … m’avancer de plus pour faire ce que m’a esté escrit … tenir secret . The letters to Revol were written in the Court’s symbol cipher: the 27 August copy is in clear throughout, the 9 October copy carries two and a half lines of symbols, and three were not reached on the image. Status: two of seven read, one of them with residual garbles; the Revol passages need the symbol key, for which the deciphered siblings in the same volumes are the route.

t: Nevers to Pisany, 1593 — the numerical key reads two letters, and the other five were never in it
h: The letters to Revol and key no. 60
b: The five letters to Revol are in the Court’s symbol cipher, Tomokiyo’s no. 60, endorsed “Chiffre baillé à Monsieur de Nevers, Montereau, aoust 1593”. Its enciphering sheet (fr. 3995 f. 109) gives four or five symbols for each letter, a syllabary ba … vu , word signs, Roman numerals for provinces, towns and persons ( iiij xx for 80), and a row of nulls; Nevers’s secretary added a deciphering table sorted by the shape of the symbols (ff. 110v–111). Both tables were read from the full-resolution images on 17 September 2026 and are transcribed in key60.txt ; the deciphering table is complete and legible, and it settles the values Tomokiyo found doubtful (the y-shaped sign is s , the 4-shaped sign is x , the crossed η is the doubling sign). The deciphering table, fr. 3995 f. 110v: Roman numerals, Arabic figures, letter-shapes. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3995 f. 110v, via Gallica (btv1b525085665). The cursive forms the copyist uses in the letters differ from the Court hand of the table, so the values were checked on Henri IV’s letter to Nevers of 7 October 1593 (fr. 3986 f. 151), a page in the same cipher with the office’s interlinear decipherment: plusieurs , contre , de la , promesse , respondre , Bellièvre , Villeroy , Zamet pin down thirty of the commonest signs. The Instruction of 31 August turned out to be the richer crib: part 2 of the Mémoires de Nevers is on Gallica after all (ark bpt6k64451005, reached through the catalogue notice rather than search), and its pp. 492–499 print the Instruction in clear; better, the cipher pages of the manuscript Instruction itself (fr. 3985, canvases 264–268) carry the office’s interlinear decipherment in the same copyist’s hand as the Revol letters, matching the print word for word. That gives three full pages of symbol–plaintext pairs in the target hand, on top of the King’s letter of 7 October. The crib: Henri IV to Nevers, Chartres, 7 October 1593, with the decipherment between the lines. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3986 f. 151, via Gallica (btv1b9060631k). The second crib: the Instruction of 31 August 1593 (fr. 3985), interlined by the office; the same text is printed in the Mémoires de Nevers , ii, 492–498. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3985, Instruction of 31 August 1593, via Gallica (btv1b90606498, canvases 264–268). Where the cipher sits in the copies, from the full-resolution pages: 21 August, fr. 3985 f. 88–88v, six lines; 27 August, f. 115, one line (the earlier pages of that letter are in clear); 2 September, f. 176, about ten lines with the sign lxxix for Rome; 7 October, fr. 3986 f. 146v, nine lines; 9 October, f. 157v, four lines; 23 October, f. 198, five lines. The f. 146v and f. 157v passages are transcribed symbol by symbol ( ct_3986_f146v.txt , ct_3986_f157v.txt ) and run through the decoder; a second pass at higher magnification then showed that both pages, like the interlined Instruction, mix short cipher stretches into faded clear cursive, so those transcriptions over-read cipher and carry a revision note. Tomokiyo’s three anchors on f. 146v fall out of the table at once, l’absolution (λ 14 ꝑ 4 20 xx ‡ π ⊥ = la·b·so·l·u·t·i·o·n), à la vérité and intérêt , with qu’il , bien , et , que , nous , si around them; but between the anchors the output is still letter salad, because the copyist runs the small symbols together ( ue , ur , ıı , v ) and the same stroke stands for two or three table entries. The next pass is a glyph-level alignment of the copyist’s forms against the crib page in the same hand, then the other four letters. fr. 3986 f. 146v, the block of cipher in the letter from Vese, 7 October 1593. t: The duc de Nevers to Villeroy, 16 August 1595 — seventeen runs in a key Nevers did not keep
b: Nevers’s file copy of a letter written from Saint-Quentin during the siege of Cambrai (BnF fr. 3993 no. 102) carries 753 signs of figures and Greek-like signs, listed by Tomokiyo as undeciphered. The closest key in Nevers’s own collection, fr. 3995 no. 76, was read in full: the same family of signs and the same design, but other values. A solver that reads a matched control letter for letter finds no French under six ways of cutting the figures, so this is a nomenclator, not a plain homophonic cipher, and without its key it stays unread. Saint-Quentin → Villeroy · figures and signs, nomenclator · 16 August 1595 · attempted, not solved The duc de Nevers to Villeroy, 16 August 1595 from Duke of Nevers → to Nicolas de Neufville, seigneur de Villeroy BnF, français 3993, no. 102, ff. 148r–149r: Nevers’s file copy of a letter written from Saint-Quentin while Fuentes besieged Cambrai. Seventeen passages, 753 signs, are in a cipher of figures and other signs. The runs were transcribed from the Gallica scans, tested against every Nevers key of 1594–95 that survives, and attacked ciphertext-only with a solver checked on a matched control. The control reads; the letter does not. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 22 September 2026 key not found Summary. The catalogue carried this letter as a solve candidate with no known key: Tomokiyo’s League page lists it as undeciphered, noting that none of the ciphers in the Nevers collection (BnF fr. 3995) decodes it. The copy is in clear French with seventeen inserted runs: 753 signs, dominated by the figures 1 and 2, with about forty-five other signs (λ, π, θ, Δ, ∞, ‡, ϖ, a reversed c, a tau…). Nevers explains at the outset why he enciphers: what is most pressing should go in cipher “affin que 72 ne puissent prendre cognoissance de noz affaires”, with the enemy written as the code number 72. The closest key in the collection, no. 76 (fr. 3995 ff. 142v–143r), was read in full here: same family of signs, same design of figures, letters, Greek capitals and a numbered word list, but different values, and no French comes out. Nos. 65, 66 and 68–75 do not fit either. A fast homophonic annealer reads a control of the same length and shape letter for letter, and fails on the letter under six ways of cutting the figures into units. So this is not a plain homophonic cipher. It is most likely a nomenclator with syllables and word codes whose distinguishing marks the copyist dropped, and 753 signs are too few to break that without the key. The next letter in the series, of 18 August, is all in clear. Status: not solved. It needs the key (not in fr. 3995) or the letter as Villeroy received it, which may carry his secretary’s decipherment.

t: The duc de Nevers to Villeroy, 16 August 1595 — seventeen runs in a key Nevers did not keep
b: f. 148r, the long run: “Or j’ay bien ce mauvais augure…”, three lines of cipher, “par ce qu’il faut necessairement que nous”, three more. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, français 3993 f. 148r, via Gallica (btv1b9059229n, view 161). The copy (BnF notice: “Lettre, avec chiffre, de Louis de Gonzague, duc de Nevers, à monseigneur de Villeroy… De St Quentin, ce 16 aoust 1595. Copie”) runs over three pages in a secretary’s hand. Nevers was commanding in Picardy after the fall of Doullens (31 July); Fuentes had opened the siege of Cambrai, held by Balagny, a few days before. The letter is about the relief of Cambrai: a convoy that must risk “ung grand combat”, the people of the town who will not hold, the need to assemble the council. Nevers opens with a reproach that explains the cipher: Vous faictes beaucoup pour le service du Roy a escrire assez intelligiblement … mais il me semble que ce qui est de plus pregnant seroit bon d’estre en chiffre, par ce que s’il se perdoit des lettres … pour le regard du [ cipher ] affin que 72 ne puissent prendre cognoissance de noz affaires. f. 148r l. 7, the first run, between “pour le regard du” and “affin que 72 ne”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, français 3993 f. 148r, via Gallica (btv1b9059229n, view 161). The other runs sit in the same way inside clear sentences: “dans lequel temps il faut se resoudre de […] contre […]” (f. 148v), “et croy que […], pour faire donc telle chose il faut assembler le conseil” (f. 148v), “aussy tost que […]. Et a moy advis” and “et si luy ne parle […], je le doibs declarer” (f. 149r). The copy ends “De St Quentin ce 16. Aoust 1595”.

t: The duc de Nevers to Villeroy, 16 August 1595 — seventeen runs in a key Nevers did not keep
b: The 753 signs (measured on the transcription, ct_f148r.txt and ct_f148v_149r.txt ) are 54 kinds. Figures make up more than half: 1 occurs 112 times, 2 92 times, a small circle (letter o or figure 0; the copy does not distinguish them) 74 times. The figure 1 is followed by another figure 87% of the time and “20” occurs 33 times, so the figures are mostly written in pairs. Cut into pairs wherever a figure is followed by another, only about 45 figures are left over. The other signs are Greek letters (λ, π, θ, Δ, χ, ϖ), ∞, a crossed dagger, a reversed c, a tau, an arch, a u with two bars, and italic letters. There are few repeats longer than four signs; the longest, “41 0 3 1 2”, occurs twice.

t: The duc de Nevers to Villeroy, 16 August 1595 — seventeen runs in a key Nevers did not keep
h: The keys of the Nevers collection
b: The alphabet of fr. 3995 no. 76 (rotated): a = 8, y, +; b = 7, x; c = 9, z; d = 5, K; e = 3, t, ϖ; … p = λ, h; r = ∂, ƒ, θ; s = □, e, π; nulls at the right. The same family of signs as the letter, with other values. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, français 3995 ff. 142v–143r, via Gallica (btv1b525085665, view 274). BnF fr. 3995 is Nevers’s own collection of keys, catalogued by Tomokiyo as nos. 1–76. Those of 1594–95 were opened on the Gallica images: No. 76 (ff. 142v–143r) was read in full. Its alphabet gives each letter a figure, a letter and sometimes a Greek sign (λ, π, θ, Δ, #, ϖ all occur in the letter), eight nulls, and a numbered list of common words in two cycles, dotted numbers 12–99 for A–L and barred 1–100 for M–V, followed by titles, persons, ladies, provinces and towns up to 181. This is the letter’s design. But its values give no French on the runs (1 would be g, 112 times), and 72 is not a party in any of its lists. No. 75 (f. 140v), the “Chiffre commun entre messieurs les secretaires d’estat et messieurs du conseil” given to Nevers, is all figures (A 90–99, E 70–79, I 50–59, O 30–39, U 20–29…), with no signs. No. 66 (ff. 122v–123r) uses λ, π, θ and T, but as n, o, l and r; no. 65 (Lesdiguières, ff. 120v–121r) gives each letter a sign and two numbers between 12 and 64, with 10, 20…100 as nulls. Neither reads. Nos. 68–74 are Italian ciphers or figures only; no. 70 is the Balagny–Charles de Gonzague cipher used at Cambrai in the same weeks, all figures. Balagny’s own letters to Nevers (fr. 3993 ff. 130–134, 245, 255) use another alphabet, reconstructed by Tomokiyo. The key the letter used belonged to the Nevers–Villeroy correspondence and is not among the keys Nevers kept. A “clef d’un chiffre employé par le duc de Nevers” in BnF fr. 3618 ff. 3–4 dates from 1591 and is not digitised.

t: The duc de Nevers to Villeroy, 16 August 1595 — seventeen runs in a key Nevers did not keep
b: A homophonic annealer (one plaintext letter per unit, five-gram model of Henri IV’s letters, incremental rescoring, 600 000 moves, four restarts) was first checked on a control: 753 letters of French in the letter’s seventeen run lengths, enciphered with a random key of 49 homophones and three nulls. It reads the control letter for letter, and all restarts agree. On the letter it was run under six ways of cutting the figures into units: every sign alone; pairs of figures after 1 or 2; every pair of figures; 1 joined to the following sign (the unit of the 1588 informant’s cipher in the same archive); pairs collapsed to their decade; and no. 65’s design, with 10, 20… as nulls and numbers above 64 as codes. None gives French; the restarts do not agree with one another. A second solver that lets a unit stand for a consonant-and-vowel syllable, as the figures do in the Court key no. 57, fails on its own control of that design, so that hypothesis cannot be tested at this length.

t: The duc de Nevers to Villeroy, 16 August 1595 — seventeen runs in a key Nevers did not keep
b: All seventeen runs, 753 signs. The key is not in fr. 3995. The letter as sent, in Villeroy’s papers, has not been located; it may carry a decipherment. The transcription is a first pass: the circle is not split into o and 0, and dots over figures (which mark the word cycles in no. 76) are not all recorded. With a key in hand these would be settled on the image. The next letter to Villeroy, from Saint-Quentin on 18 August (fr. 3993 no. 133, ff. 173–174), is all in clear and gives no crib.

t: Mary Queen of Scots to the Duke of Norfolk, “the 20th”, February or March 1570 — the one letter of the series with no contemporary decipherment
b: BL Cotton MS Caligula C II f. 74r is the only letter of Mary’s ciphered correspondence with Norfolk in the Tower with no contemporary decipherment, dated only “the tventi of this instant”. Tomokiyo rebuilt the key from the three deciphered siblings and overlaid a partial letter-by-letter decode. Undeciphered did not mean unsolved: the key was available, and the contribution here is the transcription and the reading. The key is checked on f. 66r, and the letter is read in 23 lines from the new British Library IIIF images, stitched from tiles. Written weeks after the Regent Moray’s murder: Elizabeth blames Mary for the harquebus shot, Morton is rumoured on the move, and Norfolk is to write through the Bishop of Ross or Lady Scrope, never in his own hand. Tutbury → the Tower · letter cipher with word signs and a nomenclator · February or March 1570 · read Mary Queen of Scots to the Duke of Norfolk, “the 20th”, 1570 from Mary Queen of Scots → to Duke of Norfolk British Library, Cotton MS Caligula C II, f. 74r · 23 lines, all in cipher · the one letter of the series with no contemporary decipherment · listed undeciphered (not unsolved) by Tomokiyo, who reconstructed the key and overlaid a partial decode Tomokiyo’s key checked on the deciphered sibling f. 66r and applied to new images stitched from the BL’s IIIF tiles · the letter read line by line, with a handful of signs and spots still open · written within two months of the Regent Moray’s murder Daniel Bourdeau · read 18 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. Between October 1569 and August 1570 Thomas Howard, 4th Duke of Norfolk, was a prisoner in the Tower for his plan to marry Mary Queen of Scots, and Mary, at Tutbury in the Earl of Shrewsbury’s keeping, wrote to him in a private cipher. Cotton MS Caligula C II keeps four of those letters. Three have a decipherment made at the time and are in print; the fourth, f. 74r, is dated only the tventi of this instant and has no contemporary decipherment. Satoshi Tomokiyo rebuilt the key from the other three and published a decode of f. 74 as a letter-by-letter overlay on the image, with gaps, and a continuous transcript of about the first half in the source of his page. This page gives the whole letter as text, using his key and new images from the British Library’s IIIF service. Mary tells Norfolk to write to the B[ishop of Ross] of your part , or through your sister Scrup , and not to put anything in his own hand. She thanks God for delyvring us of our [enemy] Murray . Elizabeth sueves me the veyt of Murray death : she lays the blame for the harquebus shot at Linlithgow on Mary. There is a rumour that Morton is on the move, and news has come from York. She ends yours feithful til death . Status: read in 23 lines. Five nomenclator signs have no value in the key, and a few words are still unread: two groups in line 1, the end of line 4 under a stain, and a few single words. Much of the letter-level decoding is Tomokiyo’s. What is new here is the transcription and the continuous reading, the fill of his gaps, the sense and the names, and the date. No key was recovered here.

t: Mary Queen of Scots to the Duke of Norfolk, “the 20th”, February or March 1570 — the one letter of the series with no contemporary decipherment
b: Cotton MS Caligula C II is a volume of Scottish state papers from Burghley’s circle. Folios 66 to 75 hold Mary’s ciphered letters to Norfolk that were intercepted or surrendered, with deciphered copies. Tomokiyo’s cryptiana page on Mary’s ciphers ( mary.htm ) lists them this way: Folio Date on the letter Decipherment In print f. 66r “last of Januarie” [31 Jan 1570] transcription f. 67, decipherment f. 72 Labanoff iii p. 19 f. 69 “the xv of this instant” [15 Jan 1570] f. 70 Labanoff iii p. 11 f. 74r “the tventi of this instant” none none found f. 75 [18 Apr 1570] clear text f. 73, roughly corresponding Labanoff iii p. 35 Tomokiyo marks f. 74 “undeciphered”, meaning it has no contemporary decipherment; it is not on his unsolved page. He found no matching letter in Labanoff’s Lettres de Marie Stuart , vol. 3, or in Froude, and took the address my oun good lord as a sign that it too is from Mary to Norfolk. He then reconstructed the key from the deciphered letters (“Mary-Norfolk Cipher (1570)”, corrected 16 July 2023). With it he printed the first two lines as a paraphrase, “I have, my own good lord, your friendly [letter??] [with??] no [g?]entle satisfaction and for * I will never [do??] anything in hand …”, and left two further pieces of work that are not on the visible page. One is an HTML comment in the page source: a continuous transcript as far as about line 11 ( … in? deliveri[n]g us of our * the Queen of England … ). The other is an image, mary_CottonCaligulaCII_f74.png , with his decode written in magenta over each of the 23 lines, letter by letter. Unkeyed signs are shown as asterisks, doubtful letters as queries, and words are not divided. That overlay is the starting point, and it has to be credited. For most lines it already has the letters, including murton is gon to , Talbo and herkebus . This page adds the reading. The letters are divided into words and made into sentences, and many of his asterisks and queries are filled. Line 8, which the comment leaves out when it runs and I shall be your sister scrup from the end of line 7 into line 9, is restored. The names are identified and the letter is dated. The verso, f. 74v, has no address. It carries only a short note written upside down relative to the text, with a mark above it; the note reads Norffolke (or Northfolke ).

t: Mary Queen of Scots to the Duke of Norfolk, “the 20th”, February or March 1570 — the one letter of the series with no contemporary decipherment
b: The cipher is a simple substitution of one sign for each letter, with no homophones except f . Nulls are scattered through the text, even inside words. About twenty word signs and a handful of name signs complete it. This is Tomokiyo’s reconstruction. Before it was applied to f. 74, it was checked against f. 66r, whose contemporary transcription and decipherment survive (ff. 67, 72). The opening of f. 66r, My oun lord, I vret to you befor to knou your pleasur if I schould sik to mak an entrepryse , reads correctly with it. The control, f. 66r, lines 1–3: the letter of the last of January 1570, whose decipherment (f. 72) is printed by Labanoff. The same signs and word signs as f. 74r. Image: British Library, Cotton MS Caligula C II f. 66r, via the BL IIIF service. a b c d e f g h i k l m ω φ Ш ∠ 8 6, б A 3 Π ǂ 4 + n o p r s t u/v x y nulls a □ 2 ⊏ H (#) X ρ Φ 7 g-like, m, small s, ῶ, Σ̃, ɓ, ₱ Word signs Names and ⊧ · but λ · for ⊞ · friend ♁ · have o (round) · I 9o · in ④ · is ᵻ · not ∥ · our ε · that ᵹ · the X slashed · to Z · will 4 barred · with δ · would ƀ · you ʃ · your ∂; also signs for me and my Queen of England V · Bishop of Ross IV · Murray L · Norfolk Rp F. 74 adds three uses the table does not state. ǂ standing alone is and ; inside a word it is still k ( kan , spok , lyk , York ). The pair εʃ is me . A б with a bar through it is friend , besides the ♁ form. There are no signs for j , q , w or z . The writer uses v for w ( vreit , veil , vel or vo ), which is Scots spelling, not a gap in the cipher.

t: Mary Queen of Scots to the Duke of Norfolk, “the 20th”, February or March 1570 — the one letter of the series with no contemporary decipherment
b: Line by line as on the leaf; the writer’s spelling kept; [..] a word not read, [word] supplied or uncertain; {sign} a nomenclator sign with no value in the key, with a guess where the sense allows one 1 I have, my oun good lord, [..] your friendl[y] [..] no [g]entle satisfaction, and fore 2 I will never take anithing in hand {⊕: unless?} some ver good mey come of it to me, anithing ex- 3 -ept I var sur it var to your veil as for myn; and if I mocht be so to us both, I would be sur 4 al schould not be in denger. For I have experiance [..] that [f]avour that me oune f[riend]s [… stain …] but no[t], 5 my oun lord, that your {a—} and myn friend[s] would not believe so to use a way can nothing content 6 the Queen of England. I find be that the cardinal is with that is veil mynded to help me; [..] for find meanes that 7 our caus[e] be not [lost] for falt of solisitation: vreit to the B[ishop of Ross] of your part, and I schal 8 be the nixt to [..] friendes, would al[so], as I kan, to persuad {⊘: a person} to hest [to] find meanes. 9 Be your sister Scrup or uther to caus [..] knou your mynd, for I have no meanes that he mey be 10 sur of forces, and had al friends in hand. [..] I trust God he will help us, as he be[gan] al- 11 -redy in delyvring us of our {o—} Murray. The Queen of England hes spok[en] courtusli to the B. of Ross of 12 you [..] schued, as if I would caus schut her friend a harkebus-schut. [It] would not hurt me, God be juge, 13 betvix us. I am asured that sche [..] sueves me the veyt of Murray death {ø}; but God knoueth if 14 [..] her mynd would [..] at le[a]st you knou the treuth of this. God will, I trust, prosper us both, the 15 better that ve have som[e] [..] [..]les. That brut is that Murton is gon to[..]; but not for treuth it 16 I vreit [ane?] this: nicht to me Lord Talbot [..], not for treuth, it cometh from York. [..] 17 [..] I will end, and prey you not to constren you or hasard you to vreyt your self, but caus {⊗} but vreyt t- 18 -o ani uther in your nem, but you ar vel; and remembers your oune. I desyr no mor, for and I hear 19 nothing, I fear ever that som teales mak you ofendet at me. I schal, God veling, 20 never mak caus, but sens the last [lie?] I ever am in doubt of the lyk. I 21 prey him to preserve you from feynit friends, and send us mor confort, [and] 22 yet vi have had in this meantym in vel or vo, I schal ever remen yours feithful 23 til death. {Mary}. The tventi of this instant. F. 74r, lines 21–23: … and send us mor confort / yet vi have had in this meantym in vel or vo, I schal ever remen yours feithful / til death. {Mary}. The tventi of this instant. The folio number 74 is in a later hand. Image: British Library, Cotton MS Caligula C II f. 74r, via the BL IIIF service. English A paraphrase in modern English. Where the leaf is doubtful the paraphrase is too, and the brackets carry over. I have, my own good lord, [..] your friendly [..], to my small satisfaction. I will never take anything in hand [unless?] some real good may come of it to me, and nothing at all unless I were sure it was for your good as much as mine; if it could be so for both of us, I would be sure that not everything would be put in danger. For I have learnt by experience [..] the favour that my own friends […] but not, my own lord, that your [friends?] and mine would believe it right to go a way that cannot please the Queen of England in anything. I find by this that the cardinal is among those who are well minded to help me; [..] to find means so that our cause is not [lost] for want of pressing it. Write to the Bishop of Ross on your side, and I shall be next to [..] friends, and would also, as far as I can, persuade {someone} to hurry to find means. Through your sister Scrope or someone else, let [..] know your mind. I have no means of making him sure of forces, [though] he had all his friends in hand. [..] I trust God will help us, as he has begun already by delivering us from our [enemy] Murray. The Queen of England has spoken courteously to the Bishop of Ross about you [..] showed, as if I would have her friend shot with a harquebus. [It] would not hurt me, God be judge between us. I am assured that she [..] lays the blame for Murray’s death on me; but God knows whether [..] her mind would [..]; at least you know the truth of this. God will, I trust, prosper us both, the better because we have some [..]. The rumour is that Morton has gone to [..], but it is not to be taken for truth. As I write this, [news came] to me tonight [from?] Lord Talbot [..], not for truth; it comes from York. [..] I will end, and beg you not to press yourself or risk writing in your own hand, but have [someone] write to anyone else in your name, only that you are well, and remember your own. I ask no more, for if I hear nothing I always fear that some tales have turned you against me. God willing, I shall never give cause; but since the last [lie?] I am always afraid of the like. I pray him to keep you from false friends and send us more comfort than we have had in this meantime, in good or ill. I shall ever remain yours, faithful till death. [Mary.] The twentieth of this month. The names. The B. of Ross is John Leslie, bishop of Ross, Mary’s ambassador in London. Your sister Scrup is Norfolk’s sister Margaret Howard, wife of Henry, Lord Scrope of Bolton, who had been Mary’s keeper at Bolton in 1568. Murray is James Stewart, Earl of Moray, Regent of Scotland, and Murton is James Douglas, 4th Earl of Morton, the leading man of the King’s party after him. Lord Talbot is the courtesy title of the Earl of Shrewsbury’s eldest son, and Shrewsbury was Mary’s keeper. The cardinal is not named; her uncle Charles, Cardinal of Lorraine, is the obvious candidate but the leaf does not say so. Veyt is Scots wyte , blame, and brut is bruit , a rumour. In line 18, and means if .

t: Mary Queen of Scots to the Duke of Norfolk, “the 20th”, February or March 1570 — the one letter of the series with no contemporary decipherment
b: The letter gives only the day, the tventi of this instant , without a month or place. The content fixes it closely enough: After Moray’s murder. The Regent was shot with a harquebus at Linlithgow on 23 January 1570 by James Hamilton of Bothwellhaugh and died the same night. The letter thanks God for delyvring us of our {o—} Murray , speaks of Murray death , and has Elizabeth talking as if I would caus schut her friend a harkebus-schut . So the 20th is not 20 January. Elizabeth already knows, and blames Mary. Labanoff’s chronology puts Elizabeth’s receipt of the news, and her placing of the Bishop of Ross in the Bishop of London’s custody, on 10 February. Norfolk in the Tower. He was there from October 1569 to August 1570, which fits the warnings about writing and the talk of forces and meanes . Mary’s letters of January to April 1570 printed by Labanoff are dated from Tutbury. That leaves 20 February or 20 March 1570. One point leans towards February without settling it. Labanoff prints (iii, pp. 31–33) a decipherment of Mary to Norfolk dated the 19th of march which opens I have forborn this long time to write to you, in respect of the dangers of writing and grieves for Pembroke, who died on 17 March. A letter written the next day that says nothing of Pembroke would be odd. So would one written a day after she said she had not written for a long time. F. 74 says neither.

t: Mary Queen of Scots to the Duke of Norfolk, “the 20th”, February or March 1570 — the one letter of the series with no contemporary decipherment
b: Five unkeyed signs. ⊕ in line 2 (read from the sense as unless ), a circle with a b inside (⊘) in line 8 (a person, perhaps a nomenclator for a name), ø after Murray death in line 13, ⊗ in line 17 (someone Norfolk might have write for him), and the two dash signs in lines 5 and 11 ({a—}, {o—}). The {o—} before Murray is read as enemy in the paraphrase only from the sense. None of these occurs on the three deciphered leaves often enough to fix it. Unread spots. In line 1, the two groups after your friendl[y] and the group ∠ s 3 ɹ after lord ; the end of line 4 under a stain; single words in lines 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 15, 16 and 17, marked [..] above. Line 16 is the weakest line: [ane?] this: nicht to me Lord Talbot is read letter by letter, but how it hangs together is a guess. Word division and sense. The signs run on without spaces and nulls stand inside words, so the division into words is an editorial choice. In lines 5–6 and 9–10 the sentences are read as closely as the words allow, and the paraphrase should be taken as one reading of them. The month. February or March 1570, as set out above. Nothing on the leaf decides between them. The hand. Tomokiyo remarks that the hand of the Norfolk ciphers looks like Mary’s own but differs in the h and in spelling from her autograph letters, and suggests comparing it with her secretary Raulet’s. That was not attempted here.

t: Sir Henry Norreys to Cecil, 1567–68 — DECODE R9251
b: DECODE R9251 is Patrick Forbes’s copy of only the ciphered words of seven letters of Elizabeth’s ambassador in France. No key is on DECODE, but the Cecil–Norris cipher that Tomokiyo reconstructed from a decipherment printed by mistake in Cabala (1663) reads the siblings: demaund, reason, ruin, remain, Master Stewarde, as the Calendar of State Papers summarises them. A shuffle control (8 word hits against at most 3 in 1,000 shuffles) confirms the table is Norris’s. The target letter of 9 March 1568 has three items: the French King’s name sign, a name sign probably for the Queen of Scots, and a four-sign word not read. Paris → Sir William Cecil · homophonic symbol cipher with name signs · June 1567 – March 1568 · read in part Sir Henry Norreys to Cecil, 1567–68 — the ciphered words of seven despatches from Henry Norris → to William Cecil BL Add MS 4136 ff. 160–161 (DECODE R9251, and the foot of R9250) · Patrick Forbes’s 1730s copy of only the enciphered words, numbered · catalogue 90 No key survives on DECODE · the Cecil–Norris cipher, reconstructed by Satoshi Tomokiyo from a decipherment printed by mistake in Cabala (1663), reads the sibling letters against the Calendar of State Papers · the target letter’s three items read in part Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 21 September 2026 solved in part Summary. DECODE lists R9251 as a non-decrypted letter of Sir Henry Norreys (Norris), Elizabeth’s ambassador in France, to Cecil, “9 Mar 1567”. It is three pages of Patrick Forbes’s deciphering file. Only the top of the first page is Norreys’s, and there Forbes copied just the ciphered words of three letters, 9 Feb, 24 Feb and 9 Mar 1567/8. The date is Old Style: the letter is of 9 March 1568 . Four more Norreys letters (June–July 1567 and 6 Feb 1568) are on the page before. None of the keys filed in the volume fits, but Tomokiyo’s partial table of the Cecil–Norris cipher does. Under it the groups come out as demaund , reason , ruin , remain and Master Stewarde , words the Calendar’s summaries of the same letters contain (“Stewart’s name in cipher”). The same table reads the lord of Murrei (10 July 1567), Savoia … intend to ouerthrou … and England (4 June 1567) and Rothes , papystes , reaums , stayid (6 Feb 1568). With the letters shuffled among the same signs (1,000 trials) the groups give on average 0.2 dictionary words and at most 3, against 8 for the real table. The target letter has only three ciphered items. The first is the French King’s name sign, turned (H: the same sign stands for the French King on 6 and 9 February); the third, a closed-loop name sign, is probably the Queen of Scots (I, by position). The middle one, four signs, reads a t ? l and is not read: “Pope” and “Catholic” were both tested against the cipher passages printed in Cabala and rejected. The originals in TNA SP 70, which may carry the clerks’ decipherments, were not seen. Add MS 4136 f. 161 (DECODE R9251 p. 1): the end of the 6 February list, then the ciphered words of 9 February, 24 February and 9 March 1567/8, numbered by Forbes. Image: British Library, Add MS 4136 f. 161, via DECODE R9251 (p. 1).

The Norreys section is: Letter Folio Items CSP Foreign viii 4 June 1567 160 7 (two long) no. 1265 6 July 1567 160 1 no. 1405 10 July 1567 160 1 no. 1427 6 Feb 1567/8 160–161 23 no. 1987 9 Feb 1567/8 161 11 no. 1998 24 Feb 1567/8 161 8 no. 2025 9 Mar 1567/8 161 3 no. 2054 The rest of R9251 is Throckmorton (27 Aug 1562), Middlemore (8 Apr 1563) and Smith (7 Mar 1562/3), in other ciphers.

t: Sir Henry Norreys to Cecil, 1567–68 — DECODE R9251
b: The key records in the volume (R9257 Percy, R9260 Throckmorton’s first and second ciphers, R9261 Smith and Croft, R9262 Throckmorton’s third) do not match Norreys’s signs. A crib search against the Calendar’s wording was inconclusive: the groups are too short and too many words fit. The name signs did give three identifications, because they recur in the same order in the 9 and 24 February letters, and both Calendar entries run “the Protestants … the Prince [of Condé] … the Admiral”. The break came from Tomokiyo’s page on Elizabethan ciphers. Cabala (1663) prints Cecil’s cipher letters to Norris, and its “Postscript” to 27 September 1568 is really the decipherment of that letter’s cipher passages. From it Tomokiyo rebuilt a partial table. Signs may be turned in any orientation (⊏ = ⊔ = e, Γ = L = d), and single signs stand for persons. Applied to Norreys’s groups: Letter, item Reading Calendar 6 July 1567 (1) Master Stewarde “Signed: Stewart’s name in cipher” 4 June 1567 (6) #… Savoia … the in[t]e[n]d to ouerthrou # # a[nd] Engla[n]d “the King of Spain, the Emperor, with the Duke of Savoy intend to overthrow the Protestants of France, Flanders, and England” 10 July 1567 (2) the lord of Murrei … (rest garbled) “the Earl of Murray” 6 Feb 1568 (1)–(4), (7), (16) Leisly; [the] earl; Rothes ; papystes ; reaums (realms); stayid “one Lesley, brother to the Earl of Rothes, who came from the Papists of Scotland” 9 Feb 1568 (1), (3), (4) demaund ; reason ; peac[e] “whether now the demand of Calais were not very expedient … a mean to make peace” 9 Feb 1568 (5)–(9) the French King, the Protestants; ruin ; the Prince, the Admiral “peace betwixt the French King and the Protestants, otherwise Norris much doubts the ruin of the Prince of Condé and the Admiral” 24 Feb 1568 (2)–(4), (6), (8) the Protestants, the Prince, the Admiral; money; remain “the Prince and the Admiral … that they may have money to pay the Almains, whom otherwise he much fears will not long remain with them” Control. The script work/tomokiyo_apply.py counts dictionary words (the, and, lord, papists, realms, Rothes, earl, stayed, reason, ruin, master, steward…) in the decrypted groups. The real table gives 8 hits. With its letter values shuffled among the same signs (1,000 seeded trials) the mean is 0.22 and the maximum 3, and no shuffle produces a whole cribbed word such as Rothes, papystes, Steuarde, Murrei or Savoia. The table is Norris’s cipher, used from 1567 and not only in 1568.

Montmorency’s first return from the treaty holden at Longjumeau the King despatched four gentlemen, viz., to the Pope, the Emperor, the King Catholic, and the Swiss … Thinks if peace be concluded some attempt will be made into Scotland for the delivery of the Queen.” Forbes copied three items: Item Signs Reading Grade (1) ꝺ (turned) the [French] King H: the same name sign as in 6 Feb (5), (13) and 9 Feb (5), where it matches the Calendar’s “the French King” (2) crossed arrowhead, o, loop, ∞ not read: a t ? l open. t: Cardinal Alessandrino to the nuncio in Spain, 1567 — six “unknown sender” ciphers read with Lasry’s key
b: Six DECODE records catalogued with no sender, no recipient and the date 1566. The archive’s description of the volume puts them among Cardinal Alessandrino’s letters to the nuncio of 1567, and the key George Lasry reconstructed for the 1568 letters reads all six unchanged. Philip II’s journey to Flanders, Borromeo against the Milan senate, the unconfirmed archbishop of Cologne, and advice to imprison the Constable Montmorency during the second French civil war. Rome → Madrid · polyphonic cipher, two letters to a digit · 1567 · read Cardinal Alessandrino to the nuncio in Spain, 1567 from Cardinal Alessandrino → to G. B. Castagna Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Spagna 1, ff. 165–324 · DECODE R85–R90, six ciphertexts, ten pages · catalogued as “unknown sender to unknown recipient, 1566” Sender and year identified from the archive’s description of the volume · George Lasry’s key for the 1568 letters reads all six unchanged Daniel Bourdeau · read 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. Catalogue item 261 was six DECODE records from the Vatican’s Spanish nunciature papers with no sender, no recipient and the volume’s opening date, 1 January 1566. The archive’s own description of the volume, copied onto every record, puts folios 146–338 under “original letters and ciphers of Cardinal Alessandrino to the nuncio, 2 January – 29 December 1567”, and all six ciphers fall there; the clear openings of the letters are addressed “Molto Rev.do Mons.r come fratello”, the cardinal nephew’s form to the nuncio, Giovan Battista Castagna. George Lasry reconstructed a polyphonic key for these papers in 2020 and attached it to the records, but posted no plaintext. It is the same key, byte for byte, that read Alessandrino’s 1568 letters ( write-up ), and the same decoder, run unchanged, reads all six as running Italian. What they say: the Pope wants Philip II to make his journey to Flanders and would meet him on the way; the senate of Milan’s officers must be punished for their attack on Borromeo’s jurisdiction; the archbishop of Cologne, years in his see without confirmation, is to be deprived, and the King should keep the chapter from electing a heretic’s man; and, in the autumn of the second French civil war, the King of France should imprison the Constable Montmorency and his son until Condé and Coligny lay down their arms. Two records are copies of that last letter and a third repeats its close. Open: one recurring word, some dotted groups outside Lasry’s list, single-letter choices, and the printed correspondence (Serrano 1914), which could not be reached.

t: Cardinal Alessandrino to the nuncio in Spain, 1567 — six “unknown sender” ciphers read with Lasry’s key
b: DECODE lists the six as “ASV i. 1025, Segretario di Stato, doss. I”, records ASV_i1025_SdS_Spain_I-1 to I-6, with the archive’s list of the volume’s units in the comments. Their folios are 165r (R85), 236r (R86), 249r–250r (R87), 301r–v (R88), 314r–v (R89) and 324r (R90): 7,817 digits in all, transcribed for DECODE by RebAn in 2016. Each cipher is the enciphered part of a letter that opens in clear: f. 163r, before R85, is about hurrying the archbishop of Toledo, Bartolomé Carranza, to Rome; f. 299r, before R88, is about “il negotio di Milano”. t: Cardinal Alessandrino to the nuncio in Spain, 1567 — six “unknown sender” ciphers read with Lasry’s key
h: “Put the Constable in a secure prison”
b: R88 and R89 are two copies of one cipher; where one copy’s transcription is damaged the other fills it. Words divided from the decoder’s output (R89, f. 314r–v, with R88 where R89 is damaged): … il [Re di Francia] … da credere tanto al cancelliere, la Mortiglier[i], … l’Albaspi[na], suoi {consi}glieri, che non si sa risolvere a far cosa buona, sempre medicando il male col peggio … tanta ambitione di dominare … credo bene che sia una mala cristiana … In tanto vi dirò [quel] solo, [che] se [S. M.] facesse [me]tter[e] in una prigione sicura il conestabile Memoransi [e] suo figliolo, protestandoli [che] se in termine di tre giorni [non] facessero deponere le armi al Amiraglio al Principe, … tagliare il capo, vedereste [che] si … fine a tanti tumulti … presto, [per]ché si crede [che quel] tratta[to] sia fatta tuta con saputa del [con]estabile e del figliolo … si trova da un giorno ingannata, si pentirà tardi di [non] … voluto credere [a]li buoni … The text is set out from the decoder’s unspaced output with the words divided; letters in square brackets are supplied from the sense, … marks a stretch left out or not clear. “The King of France is so taken with the Chancellor, Morvilliers and l’Aubespine, his counsellors, that he cannot bring himself to do any good, but always doctors the evil with worse … [the Queen Mother’s] ambition to rule … I truly believe she is a bad Christian … Meanwhile I will tell you only this: if His Majesty had the Constable Montmorency and his son put in a secure prison, warning them that unless within three days they made the Admiral and the Prince lay down their arms he would have their heads cut off, you would see an end to these troubles, and soon, for it is believed the whole plot was laid with the knowledge of the Constable and his son … she will find herself deceived one day, and repent too late of not having believed the good.” The Prince is Condé and the Admiral Coligny, in arms after the Surprise of Meaux (28 September 1567); the Constable died of his wounds at Saint-Denis on 12 November. The letter therefore belongs to October or early November 1567. It goes on that the Catholic King should be “well instructed of that court and of the nature of its principal persons”. R90 (f. 324r) carries that close once more. f. 301r (R88), the first four lines, with the reverse bleeding through: the opening on the troubles of France, which the decoder reads as … tumulti di Francia … il Re di Francia … da credere tanto al cancelliere, la Mortiglier[i] … Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Spagna 1 f. 301r, via DECODE R88.

t: Cardinal Alessandrino to the nuncio in Spain, 1567 — six “unknown sender” ciphers read with Lasry’s key
b: R85, f. 165r. The Pope wants to be sure whether the King’s journey will take place, because if so he wants an abboccamento with him “in quel loco che li sia più comodo”; the nuncio is to find out and tell him. Words alone are no foundation; the King should be urged, since the meeting would bring “gran frutto alla [religione] cattolica”. R86, f. 236r. Milan: the authors of the attack on the archbishop’s jurisdiction; the senate “with its arms”, the Pope with “armi spirituali” and a monitory; “the dignity of this Holy See” requires proceeding at least against the Capitano di giustizia and the fiscal, “il peggio di tutti”, and some of the senate; the King should deprive the ministers concerned. R87, ff. 249r–250r. The Pope wants the King’s journey to Flanders, for religion there and in Germany. Then: “[N. S.] vuole ancora che [V. S.] faccia intendere al [Re] che l’arcivescovo di Colonia, [el]etto già sono molti anni, [non] li ha mo[sso] … la [con]firmatione da [quella] santa sede”, nor made the profession of faith in the form “che ordina il [concilio] di Trento”; he is treating with the Duke of Cleves; the Pope means to proceed to his deprivation, and the King should see that the chapter of Cologne, “[non] tutto cattolico”, does not designate a suspect person who could attack “lo stato ecclesiastico di [quello] arcivescovado”. Friedrich von Wied resigned in 1567. R88, f. 301r–v; R89, f. 314r–v. France, above. R90, f. 324r. The close of the France letter again: the King “instructed of the nature of that court”; the Queen Mother trusts men who are unfaithful.

t: The Secretariat of State to the Nuncio in Spain, 1718–1720 — already read by George Lasry, and 61 more nomenclator groups recovered
b: Twenty-four ciphered despatches of Clement XI’s Secretariat to the nuncio at Madrid (ASV Segr. Stato Spagna 364D, DECODE R154–R177), catalogued here as an unread transcription job behind a login. They were neither. George Lasry reconstructed the key in October 2020 and filed his segmented decipherment of the whole Spagna 364 corpus on every one of the records; measured token by token it reads 97.6 per cent of the 34,243 cipher groups. The gap was the nomenclator, where 189 of the 399 four-digit groups in use carried no value. Because the key is alphabetical in runs, 61 of them are recovered from the brackets and the corpus contexts — promozione, aggiustamento, giurisdizione, tribunale, vascelli, Vicerè, corriere — and the calendar block resolves into two parallel Gennaio–Dicembre runs, with 4538 Luglio confirmed by the date of Alberoni’s promotion. Rome → the nuncio at Madrid · homophonic cipher with a nomenclator · 1718–1720 · already solved; key extended The Secretariat of State to the Nuncio in Spain, 1718–1720 Archivio Segreto Vaticano, i. 1025, Segretario di Stato, Spagna, dossier 364D · twenty-four ciphered despatches, 4 January 1718 to 6 January 1720 · DECODE R154–R177, 90 pages · catalogue item 249, rated “noted”: a transcription job behind a login Not a transcription job and not unread · George Lasry reconstructed the key in October 2020 and his decipherment of the whole corpus sits on every record · measured here at 97.6 % read · the real gap was the nomenclator, and 61 of its 189 valueless groups are recovered Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 20 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 resolved Summary. The catalogue listed this dossier as a job of transcription: DECODE calls the records “partially decrypted” and notes a contemporary decipherment written into the letters, so the text was presumed read at the time and merely unpublished. Both halves of that were wrong. The contemporary marginal decipherment is a few words a page and several of them are mistakes. What is actually on the records is much better: each of the twenty-four carries, as an attachment, a reconstructed key signed George Lasry, 24 October 2020 , and an 800 KB file holding his segmented decipherment of the whole Spagna 364 corpus — volume 364C items 1–32 and 364D items 1–24, the digit stream cut into groups with the plaintext aligned underneath. The cipher was solved six years ago and the letters have been readable ever since. Measured token by token, Lasry’s reading gives a value to 33,408 of the 34,243 cipher tokens in 364D, 97.6 per cent . The one real gap is in the nomenclator: his filed key lists 268 four-digit groups, the corpus uses 399, so 189 groups — 11.0 per cent of all nomenclator tokens — stood without a value . Those do not need cryptanalysis, because the key is alphabetical in runs and the corpus is 85,000 tokens long: each unvalued group has a bracket from its lettered neighbours and a dozen contexts to read it in. Sixty-one groups are recovered here , among them promozione , aggiustamento , giurisdizione , tribunale , vascelli , Vicerè , corriere , cifra and negoziato , together with the entire calendar block, which resolves into two parallel Gennaio–Dicembre runs. Unknown nomenclator usage falls from 11.0 to 3.4 per cent across the corpus. Status: already solved by others; nothing about the system was open. What is new is the measurement and the key extension.
