t: The Secretariat of State to the Nuncio in Spain, 1718–1720 — already read by George Lasry, and 61 more nomenclator groups recovered
b: From Lasry’s key sheet, whose editorial notes state the design outright: The despatch is an undivided stream of digits, with no word division and no group separation. Ordinary elements are two digits ; nomenclator elements are four digits beginning with 4 . Reading is therefore deterministic: a 4 opens a four-digit group, anything else is a pair. The single digit 3 is a null — except when it falls among the three digits after a 4 prefix, where it belongs to the nomenclator group and is not a null. This is the one place the scheme is not context-free, and Lasry flags it. Homophony is modest for letters and heavy for punctuation: 50 alone for a , 17|71 for i , 12|21 for c , but six variants for the full stop ( 303|323|343|363|373|393 ). A few two-digit groups are syllables or short words rather than letters — 91|94 = che , 55 = con , 78|88 = del , 01 = al . The nomenclator is where the design shows. It is not one alphabet but a series of runs, each ordered alphabetically within itself, and this is what makes the missing values recoverable: range contents 4001–4078 particles, pronouns and word endings, loosely alphabetical ( ancora, ben, come, essere, fare, molto, quando, quanto, questo, tutto, -zione ) 4079–4296 nouns, titles and names, A–R ( Arcivescovo, Armi, Auditore, Camera, Capitolo, Chiesa, Concistoro, Corte, Ecclesiastica, Guerra, Imperatore, Italia, Napoli, Pace, Regni, Religione ) 4401–4479 the same alphabet continued, S–V ( risoluzione, Roma, S. Sede, scrittura, sempre, Sig.re, Spagna, spedizione, subito, tempo, troppo, Turco, Ungheria, Vienna ) 4485–4531 calendar words and the day numbers, 4501–4531 = 01–31 in plain order 4532–4543, 4552–4563 two parallel month runs, Gennaio to Dicembre (see below) 4564–4619 a second alphabetical run, A–T ( aggiustamento, alcun, altro, attenzione, Breve, conforme, costì, dispaccio, giustizia, parola, possibile, pubblico, riflessione, stesso, tempi ) 4681, 4706, 4870+ scattered later blocks ( Cristian-, contro, espulsione, present- )

t: The Secretariat of State to the Nuncio in Spain, 1718–1720 — already read by George Lasry, and 61 more nomenclator groups recovered
b: No cryptanalysis was needed and none was done. The method has two halves, and a value was only accepted when both agreed, or when one of them was overwhelming on its own. The bracket. Because each run is alphabetical, an unvalued group is pinned between its nearest valued neighbours. 4467 sits between 4466 troppo and 4468 Turco , so it begins tr… to tu… . 4198 sits between 4197 maggior and 4200 necessari . 4233 sits between 4231 occasione and the opportun­ recovered at 4236, so it is of… . The contexts. The corpus is 84,961 tokens with everything else already read, so each unvalued group comes with its sentences. 4467 appears in “far retrocedere le numerose — che si dicono già incamminate” and “presi nelle proprie case con — di fanteria”. Both halves give truppe . The agreement of the two is the check. 4469 lies between Turco and Vescovo , so it is va–ve ; its contexts are “li — di Spagna hanno preso camino”, “il soccorso de’ — da mandarsi in Levante” and a list of “due palandre et undici barche”. Vascelli satisfies both and nothing else does. The calendar block, and the control it supplies. The month codes fell out as a structure rather than one at a time. Lasry’s sheet has only three of them: 4535 “Apte” , 4539 Agosto , 4562 Novembre . The corpus uses 4533 to 4539 contiguously and 4560 to 4562, always after a day number and before passato or corrente . Two parallel Gennaio–Dicembre runs at 4532–4543 and 4552–4563 place Agosto at 4539 and Novembre at 4562 exactly, and make Lasry’s puzzling “Apte” simply Aprile , the fourth slot. That scheme puts Luglio at 4538, and 4538 then supplies its own proof. The corpus has “in data delli 4499 4538 passato, qual appunto fu il giorno della promozione del Sig. Card.” Giulio Alberoni was created cardinal by Clement XI on 12 July 1717 . The month run, derived from an offset, lands on Luglio; the day code beside it is 12; and the sentence names the day of the promotion. Three independent things agree, and 4499 = 12 comes free.

t: The Secretariat of State to the Nuncio in Spain, 1718–1720 — already read by George Lasry, and 61 more nomenclator groups recovered
b: These are Clement XI’s Secretariat writing to the nuncio at Madrid in the two years when relations with Philip V collapsed: Alberoni’s Sardinian and Sicilian expeditions, the Quadruple Alliance, and Spain’s retaliation against the Roman jurisdiction. Two words run through everything and both of them were among the unvalued groups, which is a fair measure of what the gap in the key was costing. The first is promozione , the 45-token group: whether Rome would make the promotion Alberoni wanted, and whether it should be held back as leverage. The second is aggiustamento , the settlement of the “note pendenze” — the giurisdizione , the tribunale of the nunciature in Spain, the abolition of the Nunziatura at Naples, the espulsione of the nuncio. Around them run the vascelli of Spain taking their course for the Levante, the Emperor’s truppe in the Ferrarese, the Turco , and the Trattato of the neutrality of Italy. A specimen of the text as it now reads, from 364D/3, where the transcription is clean and no group in the span is unvalued — the Secretariat on the Spanish ambassador at Rome, Cardinal Acquaviva: … Card. e Acquaviva, a cui non solo per mezzo mio ma da sé stesso ha procurato N.S. di fare conoscere l’indispensabile necessità di tal sospensione. Non mostrando d’appagarsene, pretese di rimuoverne N.S. con dedurre le sue ragioni compilate nella scrittura, di cui, non con altra mira, se le manda copia che per fare vedere costì la loro insussistenza et la stranezza delle [ragioni] con le quali si sostengono…

b: 135 nomenclator groups still without a value , in 221 tokens — 3.4 per cent of nomenclator usage across the corpus. Almost all occur once to four times, which is why they resisted: a single context, often in a badly transcribed line, does not settle a value against a bracket several letters wide. The frequent ones among them are 4434 (13 tokens, somewhere in the S run), 4130 (10, a person named “il Sig. e —” who carries news to N.S., bracketed D–E), 4795, 4340, 4213 and 4063, all in passages the transcribers left half-legible. 722 tokens unvalued in 364D overall (2.1 per cent), the great majority of them two-digit groups the 2016–17 transcribers could not read. These are an image problem, not a cipher problem, and the images are behind the DECODE login. Volume 364C (items 1–32) is covered by the same key and the same corpus file and was used here only as context for the key extension. It has not been read through on its own account. Three of the twenty-four items (R172, R174, R176) are dated 1717 and fall outside the dossier’s stated span; they are in the same cipher and were measured with the rest.

t: The Secretariat of State to the Nunciature in Spain, 1736 — already read by George Lasry, and 46 of its code words recovered
b: Eleven ciphered despatches of Clement XII’s Secretariat to Abate Guiccioli at Madrid, July to December 1736, during the rupture over Spanish recruiting in Rome (ASV Segr. Stato Spagna 423, DECODE R179–R188), catalogued as unread. George Lasry reconstructed the key in 2020 and filed his decipherment on every record, but his key gives no value to any of the 166 four-digit nomenclator groups. The nomenclator is not alphabetical, so 46 groups were recovered from context alone, among them N.S., V.S., S. Sede, Corte, Spagna, Napoli, Brevi, -mente and -zione, taking the text from 90.6 to 95.3 per cent read. Rome → the nunciature at Madrid · homophonic cipher with a nomenclator · July–December 1736 · already solved; nomenclator recovered The Secretariat of State to the Nunciature in Spain, 1736 Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Spagna 423: eleven ciphered despatches to Abate Guiccioli at Madrid during the rupture over Spanish recruiting in Rome (DECODE R26, R179–R188). They had already been read by George Lasry in 2020, except for the code words. His key leaves all 166 of them without a value. Here 46 are recovered from context. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 resolved Summary. The catalogue listed ten DECODE records of 1736 papal despatches to Madrid as unread: “what the cipher hides is not known.” Every record carries George Lasry’s reconstructed key “ASV - S423” (24 October 2020) and his segmented decipherment of all eleven items, 14 July to 22 December 1736. So the cipher was solved and the letters read before this project looked at them. His key covers only the two-digit elements, the letters and syllables. The 166 distinct four-digit nomenclator groups, 708 tokens and 7.9 per cent of the text, are printed in his decipherment as bare numbers, and they carry the names and most of the key words. Unlike the Spagna 364D key of 1718, this nomenclator is not alphabetical, so values were fixed from context alone. A value was kept only when every occurrence reads with it. 46 groups were recovered, covering 424 of the 708 tokens; the text goes from 90.6 to 95.3 per cent read. 120 groups remain open, most of them seen once or twice.

h: The dossier and what was on the records
b: Spagna 423 is described in the Vatican index (i. 1025) as “Lett. originale e ciffre della Segretaria alla nunziatura, dal 7 gennaio 1736 al 29 dicembre 1736”. The catalogue took its “7 Jan 1736” from that heading, but the ciphered items run from 14 July to 22 December 1736 . The clear dates on the transcriptions are 14 and 21 July, 4 August, September, 29 September (two), 6 October, 15 and 22 December. The dockets name the addressee as “Sig. Ab. Guiccioli, Madrid”. There are eleven items (423/1–11) across ten DECODE records. Each record carries three attachments: the item’s raw digit transcription (Matt F and NiLan, 2015–17); Lasry’s key, “#KEY: reconstructed · ASV - S423 · George Lasry · October 24, 2020”; and a single file holding his decipherment of the whole dossier, the ciphertext split into elements with the plaintext aligned underneath.

t: The Secretariat of State to the Nunciature in Spain, 1736 — already read by George Lasry, and 46 of its code words recovered
b: In spring 1736 Spanish recruiters took men by force in Rome and the Papal State (“arrolamenti”, “ingaggiature”, “arrolatori”), which set off riots in Trastevere and at Velletri. Spain and Naples broke with Rome. The despatches deal with the tumults “contro la S. Sede”, Cardinal Acquaviva, the Duke of Montemar, Bishop Molina, the expulsion of the nuncio and the pensions at the Court of Naples. From October they turn to the Dataria, the padronato reale over benefices, the “Regalista” doctrines of the Madrid junta, Briefs to the King and Queen, and the nomination to cardinals’ hats (“col maggior numero di cappelli”).

t: A letter from Rome to the abbé d’Orbais, 23 August 1589 — read in part with the Nevers–Piles alphabet
b: BnF fr. 3413 no. 62 was catalogued with three cipher keys bound in the same volume that might read it. None does. The letter, from a secretary of Cardinal Pellevé in Rome to Jean de Piles of the League’s council in Paris, is almost all in clear and carries the news of Henri III’s murder as it reached Rome. Its 91 cipher signs are in the Nevers–Piles alphabet that Tomokiyo identified; his partial table was filled out from fr. 4715 f. 2, a letter of 1586 in the same cipher with its decipherment written above the lines. 75 signs read (82%, measured): depeschera … le doien , la protection , Cassin , vostre , Mr le […] mon maistre a esté retiré, j’ay veu ung advis qui confirme , and the signature Baron . Three code signs and two short runs, 16 signs, stay open. Rome → the League council in Paris · symbol cipher inside a clear letter · 23 August 1589 · read in part A letter from Rome to the abbé d’Orbais, 23 August 1589 BnF fr. 3413 no. 62 · a secretary of Cardinal Pellevé writes to Jean de Piles, of the League’s council in Paris, as the news of Henri III’s murder reaches Rome · catalogued with three cipher keys bound in the same volume None of the three keys fits · the cipher is the Nevers–Piles alphabet, filled out from a deciphered letter of 1586 · 75 of the 91 cipher signs read (82%, measured); three code signs and two short runs, 16 signs, are still open Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 18 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read in part Summary. The catalogue entry supposed that one of three keys bound in BnF fr. 3413, nos. 53, 61 and 69, might read the letter at no. 62. None of them does. No. 53 is a numerical key and the letter has no figures. No. 61 is an Italian key with a different set of signs. No. 69 is a League key in which the square sign is e , where the letter needs n . The letter is almost all in clear . It comes from a secretary of Cardinal Pellevé in Rome, dated 23 August [1589], and carries the news of Henri III’s death. It has 91 signs of cipher, in fourteen short runs. Satoshi Tomokiyo identified the cipher as the Nevers–Piles alphabet and read one name in it. His table comes from BnF fr. 3612, which is not digitised, and it is partial. It was filled out here from BnF fr. 4715 f. 2 , a letter of 1586 in the same cipher whose decipherer wrote the plaintext above each line: about fifty of its words were aligned sign by sign. The readings: depeschera … dedans deux jours le doien ; la protection ; Mons. Cassin ; vostre ; Mr le […] mon maistre a esté retiré, j’ay veu ung advis qui confirme plus particulierement que nul aultre ; and the signature, Baron . Status: read in part, 75 of 91 signs (82%, measured). Open: three single code signs (the first and last signs of the depeschera run, and the one after Mr le ) and two short runs of six and seven signs, 16 signs in all.

t: A letter from Rome to the abbé d’Orbais, 23 August 1589 — read in part with the Nevers–Piles alphabet
b: Fr. 3413 is a Nevers-collection volume of League papers, on Gallica as btv1b52510705j . No. 62 is ff. 126r–127r (views 259–261), and the address is on f. 127v: A Monsieur, Monsieur l’Abbé d’Orbais, Con er au Conseil estably a Paris pour la S te Union, A Paris . The abbé d’Orbais is Jean de Piles. He was the League’s envoy to Rome earlier in 1589 and later a deputy of the clergy at the Estates of 1593. The letter is dated only “du lieu que vous sçavez ce xxiij e d’Aoust”, but its content fixes the year. It reports how the news of the King’s death came to Rome. A courier from Spain had passed through Lyon on the 12th. The Grand Duke of Tuscany sent an express, which reached Rome on the 20th. It carried the Duke of Lorraine’s copy of a letter of 8 August from his agent in Paris, the s r Bardin: le Roy a esté tué, et c’est le Roy de Navarre qui l’a faict faire, l’on a proclamé Roy a Paris Mons. le Cardinal de Bourbon, et au mesme temps le Roy de Navarre s’est aussi faict appeller Roy par ceux de sa secte The writer apologises that his senior colleague, “son aisné de mesme charge”, has been kept from writing by a fever for a fortnight. He asks Piles to keep him in mind, and he signs in cipher.

Tomokiyo identifies it as Nevers collection no. 42. Does not apply: the letter has no figures. 61 f. 125 (257) An Italian key for the Savoy–Piedmont theatre (Birago, Saluzzo, Carmagnola…): a symbol alphabet, doubles, nulls, word signs, and a nomenclator 80–204. Different signs. It cannot give Cassin or protection . 69 ff. 137–138 (281–284) A French League key: a place-name nomenclator, boxed numbers, and a symbol alphabet written sideways on f. 138. Here the square is e and there is no W, so Cassin does not come out. Key no. 69, f. 138, the alphabet turned upright. It is a League key of the same period, but its square is e and its signs are not the letter’s. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3413 f. 138, via Gallica (btv1b52510705j).

t: A letter from Rome to the abbé d’Orbais, 23 August 1589 — read in part with the Nevers–Piles alphabet
h: The cipher, and a key from 1586
b: Tomokiyo, cataloguing the Nevers ciphers, noted that no. 62 “appears to employ the Nevers–Piles Cipher” and read Mons. Cassin in it. Cassin appears as Pellevé’s secretary in the proceedings of the Estates of 1593. His table for that cipher was rebuilt from Piles’s own letters to Nevers of 1586 in BnF fr. 3612. That volume is not on Gallica, and the table has gaps. It does list word signs, among them ⌘ for Mr and n for et . The same cipher is used in BnF fr. 4715 f. 2 ( btv1b52509819x , view 17), the Cardinal de Guise to Nevers from Soissons, 6 October 1586. That letter is a full page of cipher, 29 lines, and the decipherer wrote the plaintext loosely above each line. Fr. 4715 f. 2r. Over the second cipher line the decipherer wrote encores … nouvelles de … qui s’est . Over the third, … vous aurez subiect d’estre satisfaict de nous … Je loue Dieu … aultant de content[ement] . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 4715 f. 2r, via Gallica (btv1b52509819x, view 17). The whole page was viewed at full resolution, line by line, and about fifty words were aligned sign by sign with the writing above them (the rest of the interlinear is too cursive and abbreviated to align letter for letter). They give values the table lacks and confirm the ones it has: Plaintext above Signs Values gained or confirmed Jay receu vre ʃ · ⊡ θ 8 y ɔ · b ⊡ æ ʃ jay (word sign), ⊡ r, θ e, 8 c, y e, ɔ u, b v, æ e encores θ H W ce m x ÷ H n, W c, ce o, ÷ s nouveles ◻ ce ◻′ φ x + y ÷ ◻ n, φ v, + l subiect d’estre ÷ b z g θ W ꝏ · 7 θ q δ m æ z b, g i, ꝏ t, 7 d, q s, δ t de nous 1 ⋕ ce ɔ ÷ ⋕ (H with two bars) Je loue Dieu ẋ y · + ce ɔ θ · 3 ẋ θ ɔ 3 d , dotted x i monde, home, chacun ∇ ce ◻ 7 θ · 4 ce ÿ y · W 4 v 8 ɔ ◻ 4 h , ∇ m pour le bien; le monde e ʃ̄ z 9 θ ◻ · ʃ̄ ∇ m ◻ 7 θ barred ʃ le (word sign) qui monstrent ε x m ◻ q … x m , tailed m o ou nous ferons; et a mon avis … a θ m ce ◻ ÷ · n − ∇ ce ◻ v 9 ÷ a f , n et de, qui 1 · ε word signs, as in Tomokiyo’s table A key was assembled from these values, Tomokiyo’s table and cribs from the clear context of no. 62, with the source of each value recorded ( orbais/decode62.py ). A run counts as read only when it reads as French sense; letter values that give no sense are counted unread.

t: A letter from Rome to the abbé d’Orbais, 23 August 1589 — read in part with the Nevers–Piles alphabet
b: F. 126v. “… et inscrutables. Ƃ 1 6 θ ÷ W 4 æ ⊡ − ʃ dedans deux jours Ƒ 3 tt ħ θ ◻ . Devant cette …” The first run is […] depeschera […] , where 1 is the sign for de ; the second is le doien . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3413 f. 126v, via Gallica (btv1b52510705j, view 260). Context in clear Signs Reading Grade … inscrutables. … dedans deux jours Ƃ 1 6 θ ÷ W 4 æ ⊡ − ʃ [Ƃ] depeschera [ʃ] C dedans deux jours … Ƒ 3 tt ħ θ ◻ le doien C Il ne vous fault rien dire pour ce qui touche … φ tt o V æ ʃ° ÷ open – Il ne fault oublier … que vous sçavez ꝥ V 6 ⊡ m ooo θ W 8 · ɸ tt ◻ la protection H Mons. … detenu d’une fiebvre W V ÷ 9 ◻ Cassin (Tomokiyo) H Maintenant que vous serez a … si l’histoire est vraye ɔ tt ÷ ooo ⊡ θ · n a æ η ◻ θ vostre [open] H Depuis que … a esté retiré ⌘ Ƒ τ x ⋕ ◻ ∇ V 9 · ÷ ooo ⊡ θ Mr le [τ] mon maistre C a esté retiré … qui ʃ ɔ θ φ ɔ ◻ η − 7 b ɸ q j’ay veu ung advis C qui … plus particulierement que nul aultre W ⋕ ◻ Ⱥ 9 ⊡ x æ confirme C vostre tres humble servit r … p nte ses tres humbles recommandations 2 V ⊡ m Ħ Baron H F. 127r. “Depuis que ⌘ Ƒ τ x ⋕ ◻ ∇ V 9 / ÷ ooo ⊡ θ a esté retiré ʃ ɔ θ φ ɔ ◻ η − 7 b ɸ q qui W ⋕ ◻ Ⱥ 9 ⊡ x æ plus particulierement que nul aultre.” That is: Mr le […] mon maistre , j’ay veu ung advis , confirme . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3413 f. 127r, via Gallica (btv1b52510705j, view 261). The passage on f. 127r now reads: “Depuis que Mr le […] mon maistre a esté retiré, j’ay veu ung advis qui confirme plus particulierement que nul aultre”: since his master withdrew, the writer has seen a notice that confirms the news of the King’s death more precisely than any other. ⌘ is Mr in Tomokiyo’s list of word signs and Ƒ is le , as the barred ʃ is in fr. 4715 ( pour le bien , le monde ). The sign between them, τ, has no entry anywhere; “Cardinal”, for Pellevé, is the likely sense, but it is not counted. The run begins with ʃ, which fr. 4715 gives as jay (“ʃ receu”, Jay receu ), and the next three signs give ung as in the 1586 letter. A constrained word search over a period French lexicon ranked confirme first among the readings that make sense. After dedans deux jours , Ƒ = le and ħ = i (Tomokiyo’s second form of i) give le doien , the dean. The signature is the writer’s own name. In the key, 2 is b , and protection fixes the tailed m as o . The last sign is the H-form that is n in fr. 4715, so the name reads Baron , not Barot. A “S r Baron” writes in the same League dossier of 1593 as Piles (Gallica btv1b9059406b , piece u, “Du S r Baron, du 7 aoust”). That identification is circumstantial. The run after vostre is not regne or Champaigne , as was guessed earlier. Fr. 4715 gives n = et and a = f , which make it et f e g n e , not sense. It stays open.

t: A letter from Rome to the abbé d’Orbais, 23 August 1589 — read in part with the Nevers–Piles alphabet
b: Measured over the fourteen runs: 91 cipher signs, 75 read as sense, 82.4% (before the second pass with fr. 4715, the same count gave 47 of 91, 51.6%). Grades as in the table above: H for la protection , Cassin , vostre , maistre and Baron , C for the rest. Open, 16 signs: Ƃ , the first sign of the depeschera run: the subject of the verb ( Sa Sainteté ? il ?). A single code sign with no entry in Tomokiyo’s table and none on the aligned part of fr. 4715. ʃ , the last sign of the same run. It is jay elsewhere, which does not fit here. τ , after Mr le : probably “Cardinal”, with no key entry. “pour ce qui touche φ tt o V æ ʃ° ÷ ”: the known values give v o p a e ? s , not sense. Vos amis and vos gens each need a value to break. “a vostre n a æ η ◻ θ ”: et f e g n e with the fr. 4715 values, not sense. Some sign values differ between the two letters. In fr. 4715, 8 is c and the plain m is r ; in no. 62, protection needs 8 = t , and the tailed m is o in both. Two squares ( n and u ) are told apart only by small differences of form. The rest of fr. 4715 f. 2 (lines 7, 9–11, 13, 16, 18 and 21–29) is not aligned sign by sign and might still give τ, ʃ°, Ƃ or the n–a pair. The real key source is Tomokiyo’s, BnF fr. 3612, six letters of Piles with interlinear decipherments. A new search of Gallica confirms it is not digitised; it has to be seen at the BnF.

t: Philip II’s letter to the nuncio Ormanetto, 1573 — two cipher passages not read
b: Catalogued as Ormanetto to the Secretariat, 7 January 1573, DECODE R116 is the nuncio’s copy for the Cardinal of Como of a letter from Philip II: the King’s recovery, jurisdiction, the Turkish slaves, the bishop of Liège in clear, and two passages in dotted and marked figures. Lasry’s 1568 Spain key and four keys printed by Meister do not read them, and annealers that read matched controls find nothing. Madrid → Rome (Cardinal of Como) · numeric cipher with dotted and marked digits · spring 1573 · attempted, not read Philip II’s letter to the nuncio Ormanetto, 1573 — two cipher passages not read from Philip II Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Spagna 7, ff. 303r–304r and address leaf (DECODE R116; catalogue item 259). The record is catalogued as “Ormanetto to the nuncio of the Secretariat, 7 January 1573”. It is in fact the nuncio’s copy of a letter from the King, sent to Rome with two passages in figures. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 21 September 2026 Summary. The catalogue’s date and correspondents come from the volume heading. The item is a copy, headed Copia della lettera di S. M.tà al Nuntio , of Philip II’s letter to “el obispo de Padua”, Niccolò Ormanetto. The King says he has been ill and is up again, and answers in clear on jurisdiction, the Turkish slaves in Rome and the bishop of Liège. Two passages, 13 and 10 lines of figures, are in cipher. The address leaf sends the packet to the Cardinal of Como, Gregory XIII’s secretary of state, and is docketed 17 June 1573. The figures are digits with dots, a cross-stroke joined to some digits, and later underlining. The same system appears on the nunciature’s R118 of 1576–77. Five keys were tried and none reads it: Lasry’s 1568 Spain nunciature key, Meister’s 1561 Crivelli key, and his three Como-era keys (one with a Spain nomenclator). Homophonic and polyphonic annealers that read controls of the same length produce nothing here. The passages stay unread until the Rome decifrato or the nunciature’s ordinary key is found.

t: Philip II’s letter to the nuncio Ormanetto, 1573 — two cipher passages not read
b: f. 303r: the end of the King’s clear text (“… los puntos que de parte de Su S. en ellas me escrivis”) and the start of passage A, marked “A.” in the margin. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Spagna 7 f. 303r, via DECODE R116. f. 303r gives the King’s titles and the address to the bishop of Padua. He has received the nuncio’s letters but could not answer them sooner “por mi indispusicion, de que al presente (gracias á Dios) quedo bueno y levantado”. The nuncio may write this to His Holiness by the courier now leaving for Italy, and thank God for him. The King will answer the points raised on the Pope’s behalf. Passage A follows. An Italian slip pasted over the heading reads Della sanità ragguagliata del Re . f. 304r has three numbered clear answers. (1) Jurisdiction: the King has written to Don Juan de Zúñiga, his ambassador in Rome, and refers to that. (2) The order for dividing the Turkish slaves held in Rome has been sent. (3) He will look into the affairs of the bishop of Liège that the Pope recommends. Passage B follows, marked “B.”. The Roman summary at the head lists only the three clear points. The address leaf reads All’Ill.mo et R.mo S.r mio Col.mo Mons.r Ill.mo Cardinal di Como · à Roma · Per servitio di N. S.re , with the docket 73 / a 17 Junii . The ciphered passages are what the King or the nuncio kept out of the clear copy.

t: Philip II’s letter to the nuncio Ormanetto, 1573 — two cipher passages not read
b: Line 1 of A: 8̇222t 40 2̇4t 0̇6 4084t 975t 32t 2̇0̇… . The cross-stroke (DECODE’s “1”) is joined to the digit before it. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Spagna 7 f. 303r, via DECODE R116. 1,098 digits in 23 lines, from DECODE’s 2020 transcription, spot-checked against the images: A 756 signs, B 568. Dots over digits are frequent: 0̇ 148 times, 4̇ 46, 5̇ 36. A cross-stroke follows 2 (74 times), 4 (59) and 5 (51), rarely anything else. There is no word division and no pair structure: the parity of every second digit is 60/40 at both offsets, line by line. Over 31 working signs the index of coincidence is 0.055. That is too low for plain substitution into Italian or Spanish.

t: Philip II’s letter to the nuncio Ormanetto, 1573 — two cipher passages not read
b: Spain nunciature 1568 , Lasry’s polyphonic key (one digit stands for two letters, 0 null), which reads the Alessandrino letters. It gives nonsense here. Crivelli, nuncio in Spain 1561 (Meister, p. 259): polyphonic, with codes ending in 9, 3 or 5. Nonsense. “Cifra col cardinal di Como” (Meister VI.1, pp. 262–264, from Ottob. 3208–09). Its Spain nomenclator includes secretaries Zayas and Idiáquez, Cardinal Deza, Antonio Pérez and the Cruzada, and it marks codes by crossing or hooking the second digit, much like the stroke here. Letters with an odd second digit do not parse. Idiáquez and Deza date it to Sega’s nunciature after 1578. Meister VI.2 and VI.3 . VI.2 comes with the rules of “la cifra ordinaria di mons. nuntio di Spagna”: null 8 at the end of every word, a dot over the codes for che, chi, qua, que, qui, et, mente . Its letters do not parse. VI.3 (nuncio in Spain to nuncio in Flanders) uses only even digits, and this text has 330 odd ones.

t: Philip II’s letter to the nuncio Ormanetto, 1573 — two cipher passages not read
b: Homophonic substitution over three sign sets (digit; digit with dot and underline; dotted 0 and the stroke joined to the digit), annealed against Italian and Spanish 4-gram models with a letter-frequency penalty. The same annealer largely reads an Italian control of the same length with 28 signs. On R116 nothing readable comes out in any setting. Polyphonic “one digit, two letters”, the 1568 family, with the pairs annealed through a Viterbi pass. On 1,100 digits of an Alessandrino letter it recovers 7 of Lasry’s 9 pairs at −2.18 per letter. On R116 it scores −2.30 to −2.47, and five restarts give five different keys, in either language, and again with 1 as a null. A first quadgram solver failed its own control (it preferred repetitive strings to the true text), so its results were discarded. Only runs whose control reads are counted above.

Madrid → Rome · numeric cipher · 1576–77 · not read Ormanetto and Clementino, Spain nunciature, 1576–77 to Tolomeo Gallio ASV Segretario di Stato, Spagna 10 (DECODE R117, R118). The catalogue listed two ciphertexts, one of them “possibly already deciphered on the same page”. One is not a cipher, and the other has no decipherment or key. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 attempted Summary. The Unsolved Catalogue (no. 239) carried these two DECODE records as nunciature ciphers of 1576 with a contemporary decipherment on the leaf. The images tell a different story. R117 (ff. 245–246) is a clear Spanish memorial about the fruits of the see of Pamplona during its vacancy of 1573–75. Its only figures are sums of ducats in Roman numerals, so there is no cipher. R118 (f. 365) holds six lines of contiguous figures, 389 digits with dotted digits and a barred 4. Below them, in another hand, is a clear Italian note: the nuncio has taken up with Antonio Pérez everything in Rome’s cipher of 19 September. The note was tested as the plaintext of the figures and does not fit: a crib aligner scores it barely better than shuffled copies of the same letters. No key for the Spain nunciature of the 1570s is on DECODE, and the 1580 Como key read elsewhere on this site has a different structure. The cipher stays unread.

t: Ormanetto and Clementino, Spain nunciature, 1576–77 — one record not a cipher, the other not read
b: R117 ( ASV_i1025_SdS_Spain_10-1 , two pages). Copia del Memorial dado por parte del obispo de Pamplona : the see fell vacant on 27 January 1573 at the death of Diego Ramírez. The Pope held back the bulls of the new bishop, Antonio Manrique, for nine months, and the memorial argues that those months’ fruits belong to the bishop. The right-hand column repeats the sums in Roman numerals with the Spanish thousands sign ( xbnUdn L-ix , xxxbjUdn — m ). Those sums are what DECODE catalogued as “ciphers within cleartext”. R118, f. 365: the figures, and below them the Italian note in another hand. Image: Archivio Apostolico Vaticano, Segreteria di Stato, Spagna 10 f. 365, via DECODE R118. R118 ( ASV_i1025_SdS_Spain_10-2 , one page). The figures are undated on the leaf. The note reads: Il Nuntio ha trattato col Sig.r Perez tutto quello che V.S. Ill.ma scrive con la cifra di 19 di sett.re, il qual Sig.r ha promesso di buoni uffici al Re, et di procurare risposta, de la quale V.S. Ill.ma sarà poi sabbato avvisata. The nuncio has discussed with Signor Pérez everything Your Most Illustrious Lordship writes in the cipher of 19 September. He has promised his good offices with the King and to obtain an answer, of which Your Lordship will be told on Saturday. The letter therefore dates from the autumn of 1576 or 1577, not from 9 January 1576, which is only the start of the volume’s date range.

t: Ormanetto and Clementino, Spain nunciature, 1576–77 — one record not a cipher, the other not read
b: It could have been. It is about as long as the cipher (some 200 letters written out, against about 190 digit pairs), and 20 70 53 both opens line 1 and returns at the end of line 2. A beam search tokenised the first two lines into one- to three-symbol tokens aligned letter by letter with the note. It kept the token→letter map consistent and minimised the number of distinct tokens. The note needs 43 tokens for 60 letters, and three shuffles of the same letters need 47, 51 and 48. The best alignment is also incoherent, mixing token lengths with no stable pair structure. The note is the nuncio’s clear message, written in the third person under the cipher. It is not the Rome decifrato. The one nearby key on this site is Lasry’s reconstruction of the Cardinal of Como’s 1580 cipher to Dandini ( Dandini 1580 ). It writes letters as two digits with an even second digit. This text has odd second digits throughout (53, 07, 03, 05), so it is not that system.

t: Maltravers to Ormonde — a regular block cipher
b: Doubled letters written with consecutive figures betray a regular key (consonants three figures each from 7, vowels from 64, nulls 91–111). Every spelled word reads, and the nomenclator is then confirmed clause for clause against Wentworth’s own dispatches in Knowler’s Strafforde’s Letters (1739): the King refusing Kildare, and Ormonde moved for the Council “in exchange” for Sir Piers Crosby. Ireland / England · nomenclator · 1634–35 · solved Lord Maltravers to the Earl of Ormonde from Lord Maltravers → to Earl of Ormonde Dorking, 13 September 1634 and Whitehall, 22 January 1634/5 · HMC, Calendar of the Manuscripts of the Marquess of Ormonde , i (1895), pp. 28–29 The letter alphabet, its nulls and the layout of the key recovered from 59 printed figures; the nomenclator then confirmed clause for clause against Wentworth’s own dispatches Daniel Bourdeau · solved 15 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 solved Summary. Two letters from Henry Frederick Howard, Lord Maltravers, to James Butler, Earl (later Duke) of Ormonde, contain 59 figures of a numerical cipher, printed undeciphered by the Historical Manuscripts Commission in 1895 and listed as unsolved by S. Tomokiyo. The figures divide cleanly into letters (below 91), nulls (91–111) and a small nomenclator (112 and above). The doubled letters in letters and councellor are written with consecutive figures, which betrays a regular key: consonants in alphabetical order, three figures each from 7, vowels from 64. With it every spelled word reads — angry , letters , Crosby , a councellor — and the nomenclator falls into place from the history of the 1634 Irish Parliament: Kildare came to England "because he was angry [with] the Lord Deputy, [and the King] refused to see him because he brought no letters from the Lord Deputy"; and in January 1635 "the Lord Deputy hath written … much in praise of Ormonde … for his good carriage in Parliament, and upon his motion Ormonde is to be a councellor" — Ormonde was sworn of the Irish Privy Council that month. Wentworth’s own dispatches, printed by Knowler in 1739, describe both events in the same terms: the King “refuseth to admit” Kildare, and Ormonde is moved for the Council “in exchange” for Sir Piers Crosby, with the warrant to swear him sent back in the margin. Status: solved. Seven of the nine nomenclator codes are fixed by the documents; the two parties in one clause about Crosby (185, 149) are not.

t: Maltravers to Ormonde — a regular block cipher
b: Maltravers (1608–1652), heir of the Earl of Arundel, sat in the Irish Parliament of 1634 and was a friend and correspondent of the young Earl of Ormonde. His letters from England report court news; the sensitive parts — the quarrel between the Earl of Kildare and the Lord Deputy, Wentworth, and what was being written about Ormonde himself — are in figures. The originals are in the Ormonde papers (now National Library of Ireland); the only witness online is the HMC calendar, whose figures were checked against the page scans. HMC Ormonde MSS, old series i (1895), p. 28 — the letter of 13 September 1634. t: Maltravers to Ormonde — a regular block cipher
b: Nulls, 91–111. Nine values (93 95 97 98 99 100 103 108 111); seventeen of their eighteen occurrences stand at the edge of a cipher run or beside a code number — 93 185 95 , 99 149 , 95 186 98 , 98 218 97 , 100 174 103 , 111 95 221 . Tomokiyo's guess is confirmed: they pad the names. Nomenclator, 112 and above. 113 143 149 174 185 186 218 221 270, each standing alone; 270 is a code being assigned ("for whom 270 thus hereafter"). t: Maltravers to Ormonde — a regular block cipher
b: Red = spelled in cipher · blue = nomenclator code, value from the documents in §05 · nulls dropped 13 September 1634. My lord of Kildare is long ago in England though I have not seen him; it is said he came over because he was angry [113 = with] [186 = the Lord Deputy] ; [143 = the King] refused to see him because he brought no letters from [186 = the Lord Deputy] . 22 January 1634/5. You desire to know what [185] hath written unto [149] concerning Crosby , for whom 270 thus hereafter; of which I can give you no account at all, only by what I hear it is like to go worser with him rather than better. [186 = the Lord Deputy] hath written unto [218 = Secretary Coke] much in praise of [174 = Ormonde] in general, and particularly for his good carriage in [221 = Parliament] , and upon his motion [174 = Ormonde] is to be a councellor , in which courses [174 = Ormonde] shall do well to continue. The history confirms the reading. George FitzGerald, 16th Earl of Kildare, fell out with Wentworth over the Kildare estates during the 1634 Parliament and crossed to England that summer; Sir Piers Crosby, having opposed the Lord Deputy in the same Parliament, was removed from the Irish Council early in 1635; and Ormonde, who had backed Wentworth in the Commons debates, was sworn of the Irish Privy Council in January 1635 — the very month of the second letter. 186 as the Lord Deputy is used three times consistently; 174 as Ormonde ("your lordship") three times; 221 as Parliament follows "his good carriage in". The next section fixes 143, 218 and 113 from Wentworth’s own letters; 185 and 149 remain open.

t: Maltravers to Ormonde — a regular block cipher
b: Wentworth’s dispatches were printed in 1739 by William Knowler as The Earl of Strafforde’s Letters and Dispatches . Volume I covers 1634–35, and the events behind both cipher passages are in it, in Wentworth’s own words, with Secretary Coke’s answers in the margin. Wentworth to Coke, October 1634 (i. 309). “The Earl of Kildare went away from hence without the privity of this State, and in seeming displeasure against me … within an hour after, he put to sea for England. Indeed I should not have mentioned thus much, but that I hear his Majesty refuseth to admit him to kiss his hand , which I acknowledge as a respect to me.” Margin: “The Earl of Kildare shall be sent back as is advised.” That is Maltravers’s sentence of 13 September: Kildare angry [113] the Lord Deputy ; the King refused to see him because he brought no letters from the Lord Deputy. So 143 = the King , and 113 is the connective between “angry” and the Lord Deputy (“with”; Wentworth’s word is “against”). Wentworth to Coke, Dublin 22 December 1634 (i. 352–3). “In the Higher House, there is my Lord of Ormond, that hath as much advantage of the rest in judgment and parts, as he hath in estate and blood; and one, who upon my observation since I came hither, expresseth very good affections to the Crown and Government; so as I hold him a person of consequence, and fit to receive some mark of his Majesty’s favour, and humbly offer it to his Majesty’s wisdom, whether it were not seasonable to make him a Counsellor … so as I should think we had got much the better by the exchange of the Earl of Ormond for Sir Piers Crosby .” Margin: “for the Earl of Ormond, your Lordship shall receive herewith his Majesty’s warrant to swear him Counsellor, according to your advice.” Maltravers, a month later: the Lord Deputy hath written unto [218] much in praise of [Ormonde] in general, and particularly for his good carriage in [Parliament], and upon his motion [Ormonde] is to be a councellor . The match is clause for clause: 186 = the Lord Deputy , 174 = Ormonde , 221 = Parliament (Wentworth’s “Higher House”), and 218 = Mr Secretary Coke , the addressee of the dispatch. The dispatch was for the King and Coke’s marginalia are the King’s answers, so “the King” is the alternative for 218, but the King already has 143. 270 is the code Maltravers assigns to Crosby after spelling the name once. James Howell, writing to Wentworth from Westminster on 1 January 1635, has Crosby in England and “in a bravery resolved never to see Ireland while your Lordship governs”: the court gossip behind “like to go worser with him”. code value evidence 186 the Lord Deputy (Wentworth) three consistent uses; Knowler i. 309, 352–3 174 the Earl of Ormonde three uses; Knowler i. 352–3 and Coke’s marginal 221 the Parliament “good carriage in” ↔ “in the Higher House” 143 the King “refused to see him” ↔ “his Majesty refuseth to admit him to kiss his hand” 218 Mr Secretary Coke (or the King, through Coke) addressee of the 22 December dispatch 270 Sir Piers Crosby assigned in the text 113 with / against connective between “angry” and the Lord Deputy 185 unidentified party “what 185 hath written unto 149 concerning Crosby”; not the Lord Deputy 149 unidentified party same clause; not the King or the Lord Deputy

t: Maltravers to Ormonde — a regular block cipher
b: 185 and 149. Ormonde had asked what one party had written to another about Crosby, and Maltravers “can give you no account at all”. Since the Lord Deputy and the King have their own codes in the same letters, these are other parties unless the key carried homophones: the adjacent numbering of 185 and 186 suggests a grouped list of officers (Lord Treasurer beside Lord Deputy), and 149 beside 143 the royal or Council group. Only the key sheet, or Ormonde’s letter asking the question, would settle it. The fourth figure of angry is printed 26 , which the grid makes k ; r is 43–45. The scan confirms the print, so either Maltravers slipped or the 1895 transcriber misread 44/45. "Angry" is the only word that fits a n g ? y . 89 at the end of letter is either u (a slip for s , if the vowel blocks are six wide) or a null/plural sign (if they are five wide). 31 (= m ) before 174 in "upon his motion 31 174 is to be" is unexplained — perhaps "m[y lord]" begun and abandoned. A key sheet, if one survives, would be among the Ormonde papers (NLI) or the Arundel papers; neither is online. The Bodleian’s online Carte Calendar begins at 1660, so the 1630s Carte letters to Ormonde cannot be checked for more of this cipher from here.

t: German police double-box radiograms, 1942 — one key, not broken
b: Six Ordnungspolizei radio messages from the Eastern Front in the Army’s double-box cipher, published by Frode Weierud and posted by Klaus Schmeh in 2020 as unsolved. One has a Bletchley decrypt: sixteen police killed on the Bobruisk–Mogilev road and the village of Borki razed. The five of 27 February 1942 turn out to share one key, 970 letters. Every ciphertext-only attack fails, on the real text and on a synthetic control of the same size, because the second pass through the same boxes leaves no gradient. A known-plaintext solver needs about 80 pairs, and the Borki decrypt does not align with its ciphertext. Mogilev, Rovno, Proskurov → Berlin · Doppelkastenschlüssel, two boxes, two passes · February and June 1942 · not solved German police double-box radiograms, 1942 Six radio messages of the Ordnungspolizei on the Eastern Front, intercepted at Beaumanor, kept in NSA’s Historic Cryptographic Collection at NARA, and published by Frode Weierud (CryptoCellar, 5 August 2020); Klaus Schmeh posted them as unsolved on 30 August 2020. One of them has a Bletchley decrypt; the other five do not. The five messages of 27 February 1942 are one key, 970 letters. No ciphertext-only attack tried here breaks them, and none breaks synthetic text of the same size either. A known-plaintext solver would, from about 80 pairs. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 18 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 attempted Summary. In 1942 the German Order Police enciphered their radio traffic in the Army’s double-box system: two 5×5 boxes, each letter pair enciphered twice through the same boxes. Weierud published six intercepts. The message of 16 June 1942 from Mogilev has a plaintext, the Bletchley decrypt reproduced by Hanyok in Eavesdropping on Hell : sixteen men of Police Battalion 51 killed on the Bobruisk–Mogilev road, and the village of Borki razed and its inhabitants “liquidated”. The five messages of 27 February 1942 have none. Their discriminator groups show that all five, seven parts and 970 letters, are enciphered in one daily key. Every ciphertext-only attack tried here fails on them: single encipherment is excluded outright, and for the double encipherment annealing, staged scoring, tempering, relaxation and EM all fail on a synthetic 970-letter text with a known key as well, so the failure on the real text says nothing about the plaintext. The failure is measured: the true key sits in a basin eight to ten swaps wide, and the second pass leaves the search nothing to climb outside it. A known-plaintext solver recovers the boxes from about 80 plaintext–ciphertext pairs. The obvious source of pairs, Bletchley’s text of the June message, does not align with its ciphertext under any spelling, layout or length tried, so the words enciphered were not the words in the decrypt. Status: not solved. What would finish it is about 80 known pairs for one key: Bletchley’s decrypts of the 27 February traffic (TNA HW 16/17, not online), or the exact German wording of the June message.

t: German police double-box radiograms, 1942 — one key, not broken
b: A115 is Nr. 14 from Mogilev, callsign SQF, the station at the headquarters of the Higher SS and Police Leader Russia Centre, handed in at 2325 on 16 June 1942 by its preamble and taken down at Beaumanor on 3742 kHz; stations 51 and 43 both copied it. Hanyok’s Eavesdropping on Hell (NSA, 2005) follows this one message from intercept to decrypt, and reproduces Bletchley’s decrypt as entry 21 of that day’s German police decrypts: Bletchley’s decrypt of A115, entry 21. Image: NARA, RG 457, HCC, Box 1386, as reproduced in R. J. Hanyok, Eavesdropping on Hell (NSA, 2005). An Rf SS und Chef Orpo. An Strasse BOBRUISK–MOGILEW, Partisanenkampf: 16 Mann von Pol. Batl. 51 gefallen. Das Dorf BORKI, in dem Waffen und Munition gefunden wurden, wurde dem Erdboden gleichgemacht. Die Einwohnerschaft liquidiert. Von Höheren SS und Pol.führer Russland Mitte. To the Reichsführer SS and the Chief of the Order Police: in a fight with partisans on the Bobruisk–Mogilev road, sixteen men of Police Battalion 51 were killed; the village of Borki, where weapons and ammunition had been found, was levelled; the inhabitants were liquidated. From the Higher SS and Police Leader Russia Centre. Hanyok notes that several villages named Borki exist in present-day Belarus and does not locate this one, but the place is well known: it is Borki in the Kirovsk district of Mogilev region, destroyed on 15 June 1942 together with the settlements around it (Zakrinichye, Krasny Pakhar, Dzerzhinsky, Proletary, Dolgoe Pole, Khvatovka). The operation was carried out by the Dirlewanger SS special battalion with Einsatzkommando 8 and police units after partisan attacks on the Mogilev–Bobruisk road; Dirlewanger’s own report counts 2,027 dead, and a memorial now stands on the site. Zhukov’s history of the Dirlewanger unit cites the same sixteen dead of Police Battalion 51 as the decrypt, so the message of 16 June is the Higher SS and Police Leader’s report of the Borki massacre. (Identification by Ilya, a reader, September 2026: Zhukov , Mogilev regional executive committee , partizany.by .) The decrypt is what makes this group of messages “partially solved” in Schmeh’s 2021 list of unsolved Second World War ciphers. An odd count The message is 228 letters in both intercepts and in the German preamble. Without the discriminator that leaves 223, but the cipher works on pairs and every enciphered text has an even length. The German clerk therefore added or dropped a letter, or a letter was lost in transmission. Where it went can be measured. A double-box cipher is deterministic on pairs, so a repeated plaintext pair in the same position of the layout gives a repeated cipher pair, and the pairs only show their repeats when they are counted from the right starting point. Counted from the end, A115 has 25 repeated digraphs of 19 types. Counted from the start it has 8, which is chance level. So the stray letter lies among the first nine or so, and the rest of the text pairs up normally.

t: German police double-box radiograms, 1942 — one key, not broken
b: Weierud reads the discriminator as the last three letters of the group, in any order, and cites the Bletchley note that four discriminators were issued with each daily key. Read that way, with the O/Q confusion allowed for in one group, the seven parts of 27 February use exactly four: discriminator parts WOJ D33 ( KFWOJ ); D67 part 1 ( OWQWJ , read OWOWJ ) OSX D34 part 1 ( DNOSX ); D67 part 2 ( WNSXO ) ANR D34 part 2 ( DRANR ); E72 part 2 ( LENRA ) WYY E72 part 1 ( SBWYY ) Two parts of one message carry different discriminators, and the Mogilev and Proskurov traffic shares them. The four are therefore four names for one key, and all seven parts, 970 letters, can be attacked together. C43’s XOS is also OSX , which suggests either that it is misdated by a year or that a key ran for more than one day; Weierud already noticed the shared indicator. C43 was kept out of the pooled text.

t: German police double-box radiograms, 1942 — one key, not broken
b: Two manuals survive and both were read here: the OKH draft Schlüsselanleitung zum Doppelkastenschlüssel of 2 December 1940 and the OKW issue of December 1941. They agree. There are two 5×5 boxes. The plaintext is written in double lines of 17 letters, and the pairs are the letters that stand one under the other; a remainder too short for a double line is split in half. Each pair is enciphered twice with the same boxes. When the two letters of a pair fall in the same row, each cipher letter is taken from the right. The spelling rules are CH → Q, ß → SZ, and the hyphen written STRIQ. The reference implementation, dk.py , enciphers both manuals’ worked examples letter for letter (the 1941 manual prints tylhu on p. 5 for the tvlhu it has correctly on p. 6). The Army’s “NI” field cipher, as NSA’s Cryptologic Quarterly describes it, is the same scheme with 21 -letter lines and the left neighbour for same-row pairs; its worked examples (EU → VR → QZ, en → FL → NC, ea → HK → TT) also reproduce exactly. Which variant the police used is not documented, so every attack here was run under both. That February 1942 is the double-box period at all rests on Hanyok: the police changed from double transposition to double Playfair between September and early November 1941, and Bletchley found the new system easier to read. The cross-row identity The double pass is what matters. After the first pass the first letter of a pair has been taken from box B, but the second pass looks it up in box A. So each letter is used by its position in both boxes. Write each letter as four coordinates: its row and column in A and its row and column in B. Deciphering a cipher pair (c1, c2) in the cross-row case gives the intermediate pair v1 = A[ B-row of c1 ][ A-col of c2 ] v2 = B[ A-row of c2 ][ B-col of c1 ] and the plaintext pair p1 = A[ B-row of v1 ][ A-col of v2 ] p2 = B[ A-row of v2 ][ B-col of v1 ] Every step mixes an A-coordinate with a B-coordinate. Between the two passes sits the map from each letter’s cell in box A to its cell in box B, a random permutation of the 25 cells. Section 06 shows why that permutation, rather than the size of the key, is what stops the attacks.

b: A failed search proves nothing without a control, so each attack on the double encipherment was first run on synthetic text: 970 letters of German text enciphered twice with random boxes by mksyn.py and dk.py , in parts of the same lengths as the real ones. Scores are quadgram log-probabilities per letter from 25-letter German tables ( build_lm.py ); German text scores about −3.9 and random letters about −6. hypothesis or method result verdict Single encipherment, all seven parts pooled, line length 1–30, pairs in written and reversed order best −5.91 per letter against about −3.9 for German excluded Single encipherment per part and per discriminator group, line lengths 1, 17 and 21, both pair orders −5.0 to −5.6, the level at which short texts overfit noise excluded Double encipherment, simulated annealing on quadgrams ( dksolve2.cs ) on the synthetic 970-letter text it never leaves noise (−6.0); started four swaps from the true key, it does not climb back fails on its control Staged unigram → bigram → quadgram scoring; steepest-ascent iterated local search; parallel tempering; relabelling moves; a row/column product score; Sinkhorn relaxation on GPU ( relax.py ); hard EM with the plaintext as a variable ( emsolve.cs ) all fail on the synthetic text. The same search recovers a synthetic spelling in 35 seconds no alignment The single-encipherment results exclude that hypothesis: the pooled text is 970 letters, far more than a single-pass double box needs, and the best key found is nowhere near German. The double-encipherment results exclude nothing about the plaintext, because the same methods fail on text where the answer is known. They measure the attacks, not the messages. The alignment result does say something. A115’s repeated cipher pairs are real (section 02), and the aligner, given a synthetic text spelled in one of the ways it tries, finds it. On A115 no combination of spellings, separators, numbers, layout and length makes every repeated cipher pair fall on a repeated plaintext pair. Either the words enciphered differ from Bletchley’s rendering, through abbreviation, order or extra matter such as a longer address, or the police layout differs from both manuals.

t: German police double-box radiograms, 1942 — one key, not broken
h: Why the second pass defeats local search
b: This matches the public record. Hill-climbing solvers by Lasry, Norbert and others break single-pass double-box texts of 100 to 150 letters, and the Army’s Truppenschlüssel, a simplified one-pass relative, has been broken ciphertext-only from surviving messages. No published attack breaks a double pass through the same boxes. The synthetic runs here show where the difficulty lies. The true key is the optimum, but a narrow one. Under the unigram score the true key is the best key (−1.221). Its basin is only about eight to ten swaps wide. Under the quadgram score it is narrower still: annealing started four swaps from the true key does not climb back. Outside the basin there is nothing to climb. Random starts stall at −1.39 to −1.42. The local optima they reach share no row or column structure with the true boxes: measured as the precision of their row and column groupings against the key, they score about one in six, which is chance. Size is not the problem. Giving the solver the true permutation of cells between box A and box B, which leaves only the labelling of the letters to find, does not help: it still stalls at −1.42. The difficulty is the conjugation through a random cell permutation (section 04). The likely mechanism: a key that is partly right gives intermediate letters that are wrong, and the second pass sends those to unrelated cells, so partial correctness earns no score. Known plaintext changes this, because it removes the second pass from the scoring. kpsolve.cs enciphers each known plaintext pair once forward, deciphers its cipher pair once backward, and asks the two intermediates to agree row by row and column by column. Each half is a single pass, which gives the local search a gradient; on the synthetic controls about 80 pairs are enough.

t: Pallotto to Barberini — the ciphers of BAV Barb.lat. 6960, printed in 1897, key found in 2018
b: Twenty-eight ciphered sheets in the register of the nuncio to the Emperor, catalogued as undeciphered with their contents unknown. The contents have been in print since 1897: Kiewning’s volume of the Nuntiaturberichte prints these despatches from the Roman office’s own decipherments, and the register’s clear pages confirm the identification. The key had also been found, though not by this project. George Lasry pointed out that 6960 uses the key Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach recovered in 2018 for the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, which is filed on DECODE but was never linked to these records. Applied here, it reads all twenty-eight sheets, apart from about 1,750 name groups missing from the 1628 key. The system is two-digit homophones and syllable groups, three-digit nomenclator groups and one-digit nulls in a single digit stream. That mix of widths is why every fixed-width attack made here failed, though the controls had correctly shown that the cipher used fixed groups of varying length. Vienna → Rome · homophonic cipher with nomenclator and nulls · August–November 1629 · contents in print, key found by others Pallotto to Barberini, 1629 from Giovanni Battista Pallotta → to Francesco Barberini Twenty-eight ciphered passages in the register of Monsignor Giovanni Battista Pallotto, archbishop of Thessalonica and nuncio to the Emperor: Vatican City, BAV, Barb.lat. 6960, digitised in full on DigiVatLib. DECODE carries them as R286–R313, all “Non-decrypted”, and the catalogue entry said that what the cipher hides is not known. It is known. Hans Kiewning printed these despatches in 1897 from the Roman office’s own decipherments, and the register’s clear pages confirm the identification word for word. The cipher was broken too, though not here. George Lasry had found that it uses the key Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach recovered in 2018 for the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, and that key reads it.
