DECODE carries them as R286–R313, all “Non-decrypted”, and the catalogue entry said that what the cipher hides is not known. It is known. Hans Kiewning printed these despatches in 1897 from the Roman office’s own decipherments, and the register’s clear pages confirm the identification word for word. The cipher was broken too, though not here. George Lasry had found that it uses the key Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach recovered in 2018 for the sibling volume Barb.lat. 6956, and that key reads it. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 20 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 · key identified 21 September 2026 resolved Update, 21 September 2026. George Lasry wrote: “Barberiniani Latini 6960 uses the same key as Barberiniani Latini 6956 (which was found by Norbert Biermann and Thomas Bosbach). I found this years ago, but the DECODE DB was never updated.” He is right. That key reads these ciphertexts, as section 00 shows. So the analysis below documents attacks that failed on a cipher someone else had already broken. Its measurements stand. Its one positive finding was half right: the cipher does use fixed groups of varying length, but it concluded from them that the cipher could not be homophonic, and the letters are in fact homophonic. Its conclusion that the key was not known is superseded. Summary (20 September 2026). Barb.lat. 6960 is the Barberini register of Pallotto’s nunciature at the imperial court in the second half of 1629, the months when the Mantuan succession was pushing the Emperor and France towards war. Its 194 pages interleave sheets written entirely in figures with pages of clear Italian. DECODE catalogued twenty-eight of the ciphered sheets as undeciphered, with no indication of their contents. Their contents have been published since 1897: Hans Kiewning’s volume of the Nuntiaturberichte aus Deutschland for 1629 prints some forty of Pallotto’s despatches under the heading dechiffr. , taken from the copies received and deciphered in Rome, now ASV, Nunz. di Germania 119. The first ciphered sheet, pp. 5–6, is headed in clear Di Vienna 4 di Agosto and is Kiewning’s Nr. 153; the register’s clear pages on either side of it run straight through the cipher sheet and carry that document’s wording exactly, and p. 13 is its second enclosure, again verbatim. So the historical question the catalogue asked is closed. The cryptanalytic one is not. The cipher is numeric and written without separation, and its code width could not be established: there is no phase preference for two-digit or three-digit codes anywhere in the 112,805 digits. The opening twenty-seven letters of the 4 August despatch do align as two-digit codes, and then the alignment breaks and never recovers — but a control shows twenty-seven is below the chance baseline for this material, so that match is not evidence of anything. No partial key is claimed : a held-out test shows that the table learned from one part of the despatch predicts the rest no better than the same table with its letters shuffled (0.355 confirmations per letter against a control mean of 0.359), so the 55 per cent consistency an aligner reports is the aligner fitting the crib. What the failure does have is a measured cause. On synthetic ciphertext — the same plaintext under a random two-digit key — the identical pipeline recovers the whole key from a clean transcription, 87 codes of 100 at a 0.5 per cent digit error rate, and 7 of 100 at 1.7 per cent, because each inserted or dropped digit flips the code phase for everything after it. So the method is sound. A third test then went further: the longest provably consistent two-digit alignment between the cipher and the known plaintext is 39 letters, and controls that shuffle the plaintext or reverse the cipher give 36 to 39 — while the synthetic cipher at the same noise gives 207. The real material sits exactly on its chance baseline. Transcription noise is therefore not a sufficient explanation. A fourth test then searched the whole printed volume — 1,161,303 letters — for the plaintext of any window of four of the ciphertexts, at code widths two, three and four, by a method calibrated to find a planted encipherment in 16 windows out of 254 even at the real noise level, with no false positives. It found nothing. So these ciphertexts are not fixed-width substitutions of any text printed in the edition . One test came back positive, and it says what the cipher is: the digit stream holds thirty-nine repeated twenty-four-digit strings where chance gives none, which no well-made homophonic cipher can produce — homophones exist to destroy exactly that. This is a code or nomenclator writing each word or syllable the same way every time, in groups of varying length. And a late find reframes the whole target: DECODE’s own transcriptions carry some 640 clear-text annotations, and in five records a decipherment written on the page itself. Most of these despatches are mixed letters — short ciphered clauses embedded in clear Italian, not wholly enciphered texts — which is why a crib drawn from the printed edition could never have matched them. That is where the next attempt should start. Status on 20 September, superseded by the update above: contents already in print; key not recovered, no partial key claimed, and every fixed-width hypothesis ruled out by calibrated controls. Exactly two possibilities survive, and they are the whole remaining question: a variable-length nomenclator, or ciphered passages whose Italian is nowhere in print because the edition summarises them in German.

t: Pallotto to Barberini — the ciphers of BAV Barb.lat. 6960, printed in 1897, key found in 2018
b: The sibling volume, Barb.lat. 6956, holds seventy ciphered sheets of the same nunciature for May to August 1628 (DECODE R215–R285 and R318). Its key was broken in March 2018 by Norbert Biermann and, independently, Thomas Bosbach . Their two keys, a merged key and a sample decryption are filed on DECODE as documents attached to the first ciphertext record, R215, not as a key record. That is why this project's metadata harvest never saw them. DECODE still lists all twenty-eight 6960 records as “Non-decrypted”. The system: Two-digit homophones for the letters: a = 00, 02, 20; e = 09, 30, 90; i = 05, 40, 50; o = 03, 07, 70; and so on. Two-digit groups for syllables and short words: 47 che , 52 con , 57 per , 69 di , 73 la , 93 to . Three-digit nomenclator groups from 200 to 999 for names and titles: 360 Duca di Mantova , 460 Imperatore , 670 Sua Maestà , 925 Spagna . The single digits 1 and 8 as nulls , mostly at word boundaries. Doubled letters are often written once, so 33 can stand for d or dd . Applied to DECODE’s transcriptions of all twenty-eight 6960 records, by a dynamic-programming segmentation over those three widths, the key yields running Italian in every record. R286 opens ho riceuto la risposta datami in scritto , the first words of Kiewning’s Nr. 153. About 2,000 nomenclator groups resolve from the 6956 key. About 1,750 three-digit groups do not appear in it ; they are presumably names and titles particular to 1629, and they stay open. Some 200 digits fit no code, which is consistent with slips in the volunteer transcription. The unedited output is in the repository ( pallotto1629/key6956/decrypt_6960.txt ). The key also explains why every attack below failed. A null or a three-digit group shifts the phase of every two-digit code after it, so no fixed-width alignment can survive more than a few words. That is where the first-pass crib match stopped: the 8 after ho had been read as the first digit of a two-digit code. The long repeated digit strings that section 04 reports are the nomenclator and syllable groups, written the same way every time.

t: Pallotto to Barberini — the ciphers of BAV Barb.lat. 6960, printed in 1897, key found in 2018
h: The volume and the twenty-eight ciphertexts
b: Barb.lat. 6960 is on DigiVatLib at digi.vatlib.it/view/MSS_Barb.lat.6960 , 194 pages, with an IIIF manifest. It is an old bitonal microfilm scan and the image service’s own info.json gives a maximum of 748 × 1088 pixels per page; anything larger the server returns is an upscale of that. At that size a figure is about ten pixels wide. DECODE, however, holds its own scans of the same leaves at 1491 × 2066 — four times the pixel area — behind its login. Anyone transcribing this manuscript should work from those, not from DigiVatLib’s. DECODE’s records R286–R313 are the twenty-eight ciphered passages; R315 is the volume as a whole, described there as “mixed ciphertext and cleartext”. Each record’s note gives its page range in the same DigiVatLib pagination, so DECODE page n is canvas n . The ranges run from pp. 5–6 to pp. 192–193, and the volume’s own title describes the ciphers of Pallotto dal 4 agosto al 29 settembre 1629 , though the records carry dates as late as 29 November. The cipher sheets are written across the full width of the page in a dense unbroken stream of figures, about thirty lines to the page and some sixty-six figures to the line. The clear pages are written quite differently, in a narrow column on the right of the leaf with a wide margin. The two alternate through the volume. Barb.lat. 6960, p. 5: the first ciphered sheet, headed in clear Di Vienna 4 di Agosto · Ill. mo et R. mo Sig. r Card. le P. rone , with a struck-out opening line of plaintext above the figures. Image: © Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Barb.lat. 6960 p. 5. Transcriptions of all twenty-eight were made for DECODE by volunteers in 2019 and 2020 and are downloadable as DOC_R*.txt . They record the figures one digit at a time, so the manuscript’s (decorative and irregular) grouping is lost. Measured, they come to 112,805 digits; the shortest is R308 at 854, the longest R306 at 9,332, and R286 — the one worked in detail here — has 3,573.

t: Pallotto to Barberini — the ciphers of BAV Barb.lat. 6960, printed in 1897, key found in 2018
b: The relevant edition is Hans Kiewning (ed.), Nuntiaturberichte aus Deutschland nebst ergänzenden Aktenstücken. Vierte Abteilung: 17. Jahrhundert , Band 2: Nuntiatur des Pallotto 1628–1630 , 2: 1629 (Berlin 1897). It is on archive.org as item 4-2_20200807 , in full text. Kiewning works from the copies received in Rome, ASV, Nunz. di Germania 119, and heads each ciphered despatch dechiffr. with the date the Roman office deciphered it — Nr. 153 is “Pallotto an Barberini, 1629 August 4, dechiffr. 22. August”. What he prints is therefore the contemporary decipherment. He gives the substantive passages in Italian verbatim and summarises the rest in German regesta, so the coverage is close to complete but not literally complete. Two checks tie the register to the edition. The 4 August despatch. The cipher on pp. 5–6 is headed Di Vienna 4 di Agosto , which is Nr. 153. The clear pages around it are not a decipherment written against the cipher but the register’s own fair copy, and they run straight through the cipher sheet: p. 4 ends … non haver facoltà di accettar altro partito, che’l proposto in and p. 7 resumes nome del suo Rè . That sentence is Kiewning’s Nr. 153 word for word. The enclosure. Page 13 is the paper Kiewning prints as Nr. 153, Beilage II, Propositione P. Valeriano per Sabran (his source: Bibl. Barber. LXIX 60 fol. 122). The manuscript reads, and the edition prints: … il quale aggiunse di più, che fatta la pace, quando S. S. tà , come padre comune, proponga una lega et unione di questi eserciti, affine di abbatter il Turco commune nemico del nome christiano, che S. M. tà mandaria plenipotentiarii in Italia, acciò N. S. re potesse concludere così gran negotio, con che il demonio resteria ingannato e burlato. Barb.lat. 6960, p. 13: the enclosure to the despatch of 4 August 1629, printed by Kiewning as Nr. 153 Beilage II — P. Valeriano Magno’s proposal for Sabran, ending con che il demonio resteria ingannato e burlato . Image: © Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, Barb.lat. 6960 p. 13. What the ciphers hide, then, is the business of the Mantuan succession crisis in the second half of 1629: Pallotto’s attempts, working through the Capuchin P. Valeriano Magno and the imperial minister Eggenberg ( Echembergh in the despatches), to mediate between the Emperor and the French envoy Sabran over Casale and Monferrato, the civil rather than armed possession of the duchies, the withdrawal of the French from Susa and the imperial troops from the Grisons, and, behind it, the fear that the real object was to humble Venice and restore imperial authority in Italy.

t: Pallotto to Barberini — the ciphers of BAV Barb.lat. 6960, printed in 1897, key found in 2018
h: The cipher, and why it is not broken here
b: The figures are numeric only, written without separators. Across all twenty-eight ciphertexts the digit frequencies are markedly uneven — 0 at 16.1 per cent, 4 at 4.8 per cent — and adjacent digits carry about 0.18 bits of mutual information, so the stream is structured rather than random. Beyond that the structure would not resolve. The code width does not show. For a fixed-width numeric code one phase should stand out from the others. None does. Taking the twenty-eight ciphertexts together, the index of coincidence of two-digit codes is 0.01462 at phase 0 and 0.01466 at phase 1, and the digit distributions at even and odd positions agree to within 0.2 per cent at every digit. Three-digit codes behave the same way at all three phases. The crib takes hold and then lets go. With the plaintext of Nr. 153 in hand, the opening of R286 aligns exactly, as two-digit codes, for twenty-seven letters: 55 70 83 65 03 29 00 69 38 73 11 36 50 23 22 07 92 20 86 72 52 06 38 97 12 33 23 H O R I C E V U T A L A R I S P O S T A D A T A M I I That is not merely a fresh assignment at every step: 38 occurs twice and is T both times, 23 occurs twice and is I both times, which by chance would happen about once in 180 tries. The twenty-eighth code conflicts, and from there nothing is consistent. A banded dynamic-programming aligner over the whole despatch, allowing two-digit codes plus one- and three-digit resynchronisation for transcription slips, and iterating the code table to convergence against a hand-corrected 3,359-letter crib, reached about 55 per cent code-to-letter consistency — well above the 20 per cent a wrong alignment gives, well below what a recovered key looks like. Ciphertext-only search fails. Fixed-multiset simulated annealing over the hundred two-digit codes, on 5,000 codes of text, scored by a space-free Italian five-gram model built for this from the repository’s clean Italian corpora (12.0 million characters), settles at −3.54 log-probability per character where real Italian of the period scores about −1.5. A syllabic reading of the same codes — each two-digit group standing for one to four letters — was tested against the known plaintext and collapsed back to single letters for every well-attested code, so there is no syllable table to find. The 55 per cent is not a partial key. A held-out test settles it. Learn the table on the first 55 per cent of R286 against the crib, freeze it, then align the remaining digits to the remaining crib and count confirmations — cases where the code was already in the table and agrees. Against eight controls that keep the table but shuffle the letters among the codes: confirmations per letter DP score key learned from the first half 0.355 −3266 shuffled controls (mean of eight) 0.359 −3313 No separation at all. The same test on a “two-digit codes plus nulls, no digit slips” model gives 0.440 against a control mean of 0.431 — again nothing. The consistency figure is the aligner fitting the crib, and any partial key read off it would have been an artefact. The positive control, which is where the useful number is. Encipher the same crib with a random two-digit homophonic key, damage the digit stream with single-digit insertions and deletions at a chosen rate, and run the identical learner. The fraction of the true key it recovers: digit error rate key recovered 0 % 100 / 100 0.5 % 87 / 100 1.7 % 7 / 100 4 % 19 / 100 The method is sound; it simply needs a transcription accurate to better than about half a per cent of digits. Above roughly one per cent a two-digit key cannot be recovered from this much text even with the plaintext in hand, because every inserted or dropped digit flips the code phase for everything after it. That also explains why no phase preference shows in the statistics above: slips scattered through thirty lines randomise the phase across the corpus. The run-length test, which settles it. A crib aligner can fake a fit, because a fresh code may always be given a fresh letter. What cannot be faked is a long consistent run: inside one window a repeated code must carry the same letter and the mapping must stay a function, so a false run dies at its first repeat conflict. Scanning every pairing of digit offset against crib offset and extending each run while it stays consistent: longest consistent run real cipher against the plaintext of Nr. 153 39 letters control: plaintext letters shuffled (five runs) 39, 39, 36, 38, 36 control: cipher reversed 39 synthetic two-digit cipher, same text, 1.7 % digit noise 207 letters synthetic two-digit cipher, clean transcription 2705 letters The real material sits exactly on its own chance baseline, while a genuine two-digit cipher at the same transcription noise runs five times further. The tool is not the weak point either: on that noisy synthetic text this method recovers 81 of 100 key codes, where the dynamic-programming learner managed 7. And because chance runs here reach 36 to 39 letters, the twenty-seven-letter opening match quoted at the top of this page is below the baseline — it is not evidence, and I was wrong to present it as a one-in-180 coincidence. So transcription noise is no longer a sufficient explanation. On this evidence the cipher sheet is not a two-digit homophonic encipherment of the text Kiewning prints as Nr. 153 . The next test widened that to the whole volume. The corpus search. The run-length test compares one ciphertext with one crib. This compares four ciphertexts with the entire edition at once, and exactly. For a substitution, equal codes force equal letters — so take a window of the cipher, list every pair of positions inside it holding the same code, and require the plaintext to repeat at precisely those offsets. That condition is checked across all 1,161,303 letters of Kiewning in one pass, with a bitmask per gap. Calibrated by planting the true plaintext in the corpus and enciphering it with a random key: windows hitting the true position false positives synthetic, clean transcription 253 / 254 0 synthetic, 1.7 % digit noise 16 / 254 0 So even at the real noise level about six per cent of windows still give an exact hit, and the method never fires falsely. Applied to four of the ciphertexts at three code widths: record width 2 width 3 width 4 R286 0 / 266 1 / 261 0 / 256 R292 0 / 460 0 / 456 0 / 452 R306 0 / 710 2 / 705 0 / 700 R311 0 / 510 1 / 505 0 / 500 The four apparent width-three hits are artefacts: every one lands in the edition’s index of Roman numerals ( XIUXXUXXUIXXUIIXXUIII… ), a degenerate stretch of corpus where any repeat pattern matches. Genuine hits: none, anywhere. Under the hypothesis, R286 alone should have produced of the order of eight — so the probability of seeing none is around e −8 . What survives. The ciphertexts are not fixed-width substitutions of anything printed in the volume — not of Nr. 153, not of any other despatch. Two possibilities remain, and they are now the whole question. Either the system is not fixed-width , a nomenclator with variable-length groups, which no fixed-width alignment can ever match however good the transcription — the complete absence of phase preference points the same way. Or the sheets encipher text that is not in the edition : Kiewning prints the substance in Italian but renders the rest as German regesta, and that Italian exists nowhere in print. Both are testable, the first with a variable-length version of the same tool, the second by weighing a ciphertext’s length against the part of its despatch the edition only summarises. How good is the transcription, then? Re-read on DECODE’s larger scan, line 1 of p. 5 differs from DECODE’s transcription in two digits out of seventy-four — both substitutions, with no length difference (they read 93 where the scan shows 73, and 30 where it shows 38). Line 2 differs by a digit or two and possibly in length. So the transcription is close, no length error is demonstrated at the point where the alignment breaks, and the break there is not a transcription artefact. Two explanations therefore remain open and cannot be separated from this material: the transcription carries enough length errors elsewhere to defeat recovery, or the cipher is not a fixed-width substitution of this plaintext at all.

t: Pallotto to Barberini — the ciphers of BAV Barb.lat. 6960, printed in 1897, key found in 2018
b: Every test above is negative. This one is not, and it constrains the system. Count repeated digit substrings across all twenty-eight ciphertexts — 112,805 digits — against an independent control with the same digit frequencies: substring length repeats in the cipher independent control ratio 4 105,170 102,865 1.0× 6 64,083 9,590 6.7× 8 28,519 91 313× 10 12,109 1 12,000× 16 966 0 — 24 39 0 — Thirty-nine repeated twenty-four-digit strings where chance gives none. A well-made homophonic cipher cannot do that : homophones exist precisely to break repetition, and this hand is repeating long runs constantly. What repeats like this is a code — a nomenclator in which a given word or syllable is written the same way every time. That also explains, at a stroke, why every homophonic attack above failed. Segmenting the corpus by BPE gives 266 token types over 44,816 tokens, averaging 2.5 digits and spread over lengths one to seven: syllable-scale, and not a fixed width. Two further hypotheses were tested and fail. The repeat spectrum of the first despatch matches its crib’s at roughly one digit per letter (3,570 digits against 3,359 letters), which for twenty-one letters over ten digits would mean a polyphonic cipher — and there the constraint reverses, equal letters forcing equal digits. Longest consistent letter-to-digit run: 17 letters, against shuffled controls of 18, 19 and 18. Chance. And since encipherment preserves order, a repeated BPE token should land on the same plaintext word each time; 16 token types of 74 do, against controls of 13, 12 and 13. Not significant. One correction. Section 03 above reports no phase preference at widths two and three. I first offered that as evidence against fixed-width codes, and that was too strong: at the observed digit error rate a single despatch carries some sixty slips, each flipping the phase for the rest of its line, which would wash out a real phase signal by itself. The phase test is inconclusive. The calibrated corpus search is the sound version of the claim, and it stands.

t: Pallotto to Barberini — the ciphers of BAV Barb.lat. 6960, printed in 1897, key found in 2018
h: The crib source I should have found first
b: DECODE’s transcriptions are annotated, and I had only skimmed the head of the first one. Across the twenty-eight files there are about 640 <CLEARTEXT> marks, and in five records <PLAINTEXT> lines — DECODE’s notation for a decipherment written on the document itself . record clear-text marks decipherment on the page R298 68 R296 63 R305 54 In un lungo discorso R307 53 R292 51 R309 35 Con l’ord(ina)rio passato intendo che fu scritto da S. M. tà à… R308 22 restati più contenti della risolutione R313 14 Nel particolare This reframes the target. Most of these despatches are mixed letters : short ciphered runs set inside clear Italian, clause by clause. R308 reads, on the leaf: Non sono · 369092022550852359029255082700852173166 2 8 · circa il particolare de · 6680650… with, written above the figures: restati più contenti della risolutione That is an exact crib with known boundaries, in the right register, and it is nowhere in Kiewning. It also explains why a crib from the printed edition could never have matched a record like this one: the ciphered passage is a clause, not a despatch, and the edition prints the sense of the whole letter rather than the ciphered fragment. And yet it does not fit either. Forty-one digits for thirty-four letters, with the figures and the gloss both checked against DECODE’s 1523 × 2088 scan. Searched exhaustively, under the deterministic constraint that section 04 implies and again allowing homophones: model result fixed width 1, 2 or 3 no fit (41 is not divisible by 2) deterministic letter code, groups of 1–2 digits 0 solutions (exact) deterministic letter code, groups of 1–3 digits 0 solutions (exact) 2-digit groups, syllables of 1–3 letters 0 solutions (exhaustive, 4.0 M nodes) the same, homophones allowed 0 solutions (exhaustive, 7.3 M nodes) So either the decipherer’s gloss does not align exactly to that run — he may have glossed only part of it, or run on into the next — or the system is more complex than any of these. That is where the work stands.

t: Pallotto to Barberini — the ciphers of BAV Barb.lat. 6960, printed in 1897, key found in 2018
b: The key is Biermann and Bosbach’s (2018), identified for 6960 by George Lasry. This project did not recover it. What remains open is the ~1,750 three-digit groups of 6960 that are missing from the 6956 key. Kiewning’s printed Italian could fill most of them by alignment, but that has not been done. The twenty-seven-letter alignment at the head of R286 is not suggestive: the chance baseline for consistent runs on this material is 36 to 39 letters, so it is a run of luck shorter than average. Kiewning’s coverage is close to complete but not literal: where he gives a German regest rather than the Italian, the exact wording is still only in the cipher. This may be the whole difficulty. The volume’s clear pages do not contain the ciphered passage — pp. 3–4 and 7–9 run continuously through the cipher sheet — so the Italian of what pp. 5–6 encipher may survive only in ASV, Nunz. di Germania 119, which is not digitised. If that is so, no crib drawn from the printed edition can ever match, however good the transcription or the solver. The sibling volume, catalogue entry 236 (BAV Barb.lat. 6956, DECODE R215–R285 and R318), is solved by others and has been removed from the catalogue. Where the next attempt should start: extract every clear-text and decipherment annotation with the digit runs on either side, across all twenty-eight records. That yields hundreds of short ciphered clauses with their Italian context, and five with a contemporary decipherment attached. Check each gloss against the image before trusting its extent — the R308 gloss is the best-documented one and it still does not fit, which most likely means its extent is not what it looks like.

t: Palm to Starhemberg and Visconti, 1727 — German letter with ciphered passages, not read
b: DECODE R7927 is a German letter of the Emperor’s London resident, mostly clear, with fourteen passages in a homophonic cipher with a small nomenclator; the Deciphering Branch glossed only a handful of groups. R7930 holds only a cover and a worksheet for a different code. The adjacent Windischgrätz key does not fit, and 162 letter tokens are too few to break the cipher without Palm’s key. London → Starhemberg / Visconti · homophonic cipher with nomenclator · March 1727 · attempted, not solved Palm to Starhemberg and Visconti, 1727 to Gundaker Starhemberg British Library, Add MS 32270 ff. 16–18 and 41 (DECODE R7927–R7930). The two records behind the catalogue entry turn out to hold one German letter with ciphered passages and one decipherer’s worksheet for another letter that is not imaged. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 key not found Summary. The catalogue listed two ciphertexts of Palm, the Emperor Charles VI’s resident in London, to Visconti and Starhemberg, 1727. DECODE R7927 (ff. 16–17) is a German letter fragment to Starhemberg, written mostly in clear. Fourteen passages are in a cipher that uses numbers 2–79 for letters, about two per letter, and three-figure groups for words and syllables. The Deciphering Branch glossed only a handful of the groups. R7930 (f. 41) holds only the cover of a Palm–Visconti letter and, on its verso, a codebreaker’s 1–500 grid for a French or Italian nomenclator. The letter itself is not on DECODE. The key filed between them, R7928, belongs to Windischgrätz and Starhemberg and contradicts the glosses. Simulated annealing with a German 5-gram model, with the gloss values fixed, did not converge on 162 letter tokens. The letter stays unread until Palm’s key or the contemporary clear copy is found. f. 16v (DECODE R7927, image 2): the clear text “So sehen sie doch den ihrer Meinung nach bevorstehenden Krieg …”, then the first ciphered passage with the decipherer’s glosses. Image: British Library, Add MS 32270 f. 16v, via DECODE R7927 (image 2).

t: Palm to Starhemberg and Visconti, 1727 — German letter with ciphered passages, not read
b: The R7928 key applied to the passages: it gives 40 = r and 23 = u where the glosses have ſ and n. Ruled out. Simulated annealing on the letter values (the project’s de-modern 5-gram model), with the codes drawn from a list of German words and syllables and the clear context kept for scoring. With and without the gloss values fixed, the output stayed word salad. A control on synthetic German of the same shape (162 letter tokens over 47 values), with the true values of the six commonest symbols fixed, recovered only 44–50% of the tokens. That is unreadable, so this length is out of reach without the key. A web search for a printed decipherment of Palm’s 1727 intercepts found nothing.

t: János Pápai to Ferenc Rákóczi II, 1706–1710 — the envoy’s own key
b: Twelve ciphered despatches of Rákóczi’s envoy at the Porte (DECODE R731–R823, filed under three catalogue entries, one as from an ‘unknown sender’) were catalogued as undeciphered. The key issued to Pápai survives as DECODE R580, a Hungarian syllabic nomenclator, and nothing linked the two. Applied unchanged, it gives values for 16,346 of 16,861 groups in eleven letters, the rest mostly nulls: Imperial troops crossing Ottoman ground, audiences before the internuncio, the French ambassador failing to bring the Porte to war, the French and Muscovite ambassadors, money. The twelfth letter (Belgrade, 1710) uses a graphic-sign alphabet and stays unread. Constantinople → Ferenc Rákóczi II · Hungarian syllabic nomenclator · 1706–1710 · read in part The envoy’s own key was in the same archive to Francis II Rákóczi Seven despatches of János Pápai to Rákóczi, MNL OL G15 (DECODE R731–R823), catalogued as not or partly decrypted. The key table issued to Pápai survives as DECODE R580. It reads six of the letters almost without residue. The seventh uses a separate graphic-sign alphabet and stays unread. Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 21 September 2026 read in part Summary. János Pápai served as Ferenc Rákóczi II’s envoy at the Ottoman Porte, at first together with Ferenc Horváth. DECODE holds seven of his ciphered despatches, dated 1 May 1706 to 8 May 1710, an eighth filed as from an unknown sender (R784, 1707), and four more of January–March 1706 filed as from “Constantinople envoys” (R793–R796). The Hungarian National Archives also keep the key issued to him: DECODE R580, headed Nemzetes Vitézlő Pápai Jánosnak adott Clavis , with two further copies (R581, R452). Nothing on DECODE connected the key to the letters. Applied unchanged, it gives values for 16,346 of 16,861 groups in eleven letters: R795, R796, R793, R794, R805, R823, R765, R784, R757, R741, and the cipher passage of R740, which was transcribed here from the image; 306 further groups in R793–R796, above the table’s range, are nulls that the contemporary interlinear decipherer passed over. The text is continuous Hungarian, with Latin in the audience report of December 1706. The letters deal with Imperial troops crossing Ottoman ground, audiences with the Vezír in the presence of the Imperial internuncio, the French ambassador’s failure to bring the Porte to war, the French and Muscovite ambassadors, and money. A second pass splits run-together groups, re-joins split ones, treats every 3-digit group above 322 as a null and reads the unlisted 220 as a . That brings the numeric letters to 16,641 of 16,698 groups (99.7%) ; the 57 left are digit fragments no key value fits. The twelfth letter, R731 (Belgrade, 6 March 1710), hides six short passages in a graphic alphabet. They were transcribed tentatively and attacked with a substitution solver that reads a control exactly, and they gave no Hungarian. Benda’s 1963 edition of Pápai’s Turkish diaries is not online.

t: János Pápai to Ferenc Rákóczi II, 1706–1710 — the envoy’s own key
b: The key gives a continuous reading. Word breaks and accents below are editorial, and every reading is grade H (a direct table value). The full decoded text of each letter is in the repository. R805, 1 May 1706. The Porte should refuse the Germans passage across Ottoman ground: az németnek szabados általmenetelt ne engedgye … az Aradi Bassának ordere nélkül meg ne engedgye az németnek Szeged felé való általmenetelt . The envoys have also spoken to the Vezír about Muscovy. R823, 19 Dec 1706. An audience in the presence of the Imperial internuncio, reported partly in Latin: praesentia autem vestra non est ingrata Portae . The hereditary-kingship argument follows: legibus imperatoris hereditarii regis sunt Angliae, Daniae, Sveciae, et tamen legibus subsunt , with the envoys’ answer that Hungary will not give up its old laws. R765, 5 Jan 1707. Submission to the Prince’s will and the state of Poland. On the Prince’s order the envoys went to the French ambassador: a Francia Ország orátorához elmentünk . R795, R796, R793, R794, January–March 1706 (added 21 Sept 2026). Catalogued as two ciphertexts of “Constantinople envoys”, partly deciphered interlinear at the time; they are four despatches of Pápai, read in full with his key. R795, signed Constancz die prima Januarii Ezer het szaz hat, Pápai János , written with Ferenc Horváth, reports the Prince’s discretion money handed to the Vezír’s Kiaya, the Tatar Khan, the Pasha of Temesvár and a new route for letters through Moldavia. R796 (20 February) answers the Prince’s letter from the Tisza: the Germans spread false news, the confederates are scorned, the Muscovite envoy is at the Porte and nothing is resolved on the propositions. R793 (March) reports secret talks with the Porte’s chancellor on the Muscovite quarrel, the King of Sweden and a Hungarian confederation with the Porte certis conditionibus , and the Prince’s manifesto translated and given to the Vezír. R794 (undated) concerns recruiting horse in Wallachia and the French King’s money, which the ambassador will not pay without the King’s order. In R795 every group above 322 is a null. R784, 1707 (added 21 Sept 2026). Catalogued as “unknown sender to Rákóczi”. Unsigned and undated, but in Pápai’s key, which reads it unchanged. A Francia Ország orátora jelentette … hogy semmi ratiókkal nem inducálhatta a Fényes Portát az hadakozásra : the French ambassador reported that no arguments could bring the Porte to war. The grandees of the last war have sworn to see that the Sultan resolves on it, and the whole Turkish nation leans that way. France means to turn Turkey wholly against the Germans ( ezt a Török Országot egészen a német ellen fordítsa ), from which Hungary would draw harm rather than profit. The ambassador has written the same to the Tatar Khan, and if Muscovy and Poland do not second it, the Germans will overrun Hungary. A note on p. 2 in another hand asks the Prince to keep the letter secret and decipher it himself ( … titokban tartani s maga decifrálni ). R757, 16 May 1708. A message from the Muscovite ambassador, and Pápai explains why he cannot send money from Constantinople. R740, 2 Jan 1710. The Kiaya’s answer, which is the only enciphered passage: legyen patientia, [ne] siessen, várakozzék … ha a Fényes Porta szívére nem veszi … ne kellyen illy haszontalan költeni s alkalmatlankodni Felségednek a Fényes Portán . In short, the Prince should be patient and stop spending money and effort at the Porte to no purpose. R741, 8 May 1710. A visit to the Defterdar. The Pasha of Belgrade’s letter had concerned only the merchants’ business.

t: János Pápai to Ferenc Rákóczi II, 1706–1710 — the envoy’s own key
b: R731 is signed Pápai János at Belgrade, 6 March 1710. It is in clear apart from six short passages in a graphic alphabet: three on p. 1 and three on pp. 2–3, about 330 signs. They were transcribed here at 1.8× zoom ( R731_signs.txt ). The transcription is tentative: the low swash stroke may be a pen link rather than a sign, and the dots above and below the bars may be vowel marks. A swap-annealing solver with a 4-gram model of Pápai’s own Hungarian recovers a same-length control exactly, but on R731 it finds no Hungarian under any reading tried. So either the transcription merges signs or the dots carry letters, and the camera images cannot settle which. The row of signs in the corner of the key copy R581 is ciphertext of the same kind, not an alphabet. 57 groups in the eleven numeric letters still have no value ( decode2.py , retry_groups.tsv ). Scored in context against every key value, none wins clearly. About 41 more tokens are marked “?” in DECODE’s transcriptions. Prior print. Kálmán Benda’s edition of Pápai’s Turkish diaries (1963) was not checked for these despatches. Image rights. No manuscript image is reproduced. DECODE states: “The image is not in the public domain. Publishing it is only possible with the permission of the archive.”

t: Pelissier to Jeannin, Burgos, 13 September 1592 — the League’s agent at Philip II’s court
b: Nine pages, mostly in cipher, that Tomokiyo lists as only partially deciphered: the League’s agent in Spain reporting to Mayenne’s councillor four months before the Estates of 1593. Tomokiyo’s key for Pelissier’s later letters fits; calibrated on 1,764 signs of those letters aligned with their clear text, it reads 93 % of the plaintext words, about 250 gaps marked. Philip grants 500 ducats, Pelissier argues against holding the Estates now and for two armies at 300,000 écus a month, and reports the case being made in France for Navarre. Burgos → France · homophonic letter cipher with nulls and code groups · 1592 · read in part, gaps marked A. Pelissier to Pierre Jeannin, Burgos, 13 September 1592 to Pierre Jeannin BnF Français 3982 no. 22, ff. 46r–50r · nine pages, 377 cipher runs, about 18,400 signs · listed by Tomokiyo as “mostly in cipher, only partially deciphered” · the League’s agent at Philip II’s court, four months before the Estates of 1593 Tomokiyo’s key for Pelissier’s cipher fits. It was calibrated sign by sign on 1,764 signs of Pelissier’s October letters aligned with their clear decipherment, and the whole letter was then re-read with the split sign classes: 94 % of the ciphered words now read (90 % firmly), and every gap is listed Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 18 September 2026 · updated 21 September 2026 read in part Summary. Pelissier was the Catholic League’s agent in Spain, and this is his long report of September 1592 to Pierre Jeannin, the duc de Mayenne’s councillor. The clear-text passages had been legible all along. The ciphered ones, most of the letter, carry the negotiation itself, and the letter survives with only a few scattered interlinear glosses by a contemporary decipherer. Satoshi Tomokiyo reconstructed Pelissier’s key from two later letters in the same volume that have a clean decipherment (nos. 45 and 46, 27 October 1592), but he did not read no. 22. His key reads it. What the cipher says: Philip grants Pelissier 500 ducats to stay and wait for news. Pelissier argues against holding the Estates now and for two armies in the field, one to push Henri IV back from the Seine to the Loire, the other to free Paris and Rouen, at about 300,000 écus a month . He reports what people in France were saying for recognising Navarre, and the suspicion that Philip wanted France kept divided. He warns that Mayenne’s authority is being undermined, and he is still waiting on the 50,000 écus the Idiáquez keep promising. A first reading got about half to two-thirds of the cipher. The residue was not in the key but in look-alike signs merged in transcription, so the key was then calibrated on Pelissier’s own October letters , 1,764 signs aligned with their clear decipherment, and every page re-read with the split sign classes. 94 % of the ciphered words now read , 90 % firmly; the 256 remaining gaps are single hard signs, holes in the paper and a few names, and they are marked as unread rather than guessed. Two new code groups are identified from context: 310, probably the Duke of Savoy, and 441, probably France. Measured as a share of plaintext words, 93 % read, below this project’s 95 % read bar, so the letter stands as read in part ; the gaps, 310, 441 and the confessor’s name stay open.

t: Pelissier to Jeannin, Burgos, 13 September 1592 — the League’s agent at Philip II’s court
b: BnF fr. 3982 is one of the Mémoires de la Ligue volumes (fr. 3974–3995), which gather League correspondence, much of it ciphered, from the 1580s and 1590s. No. 22 runs from f. 46r to f. 50r with the address on f. 50v: nine close-written pages, about fifty lines each, dated “A Burgos le xiij septembre 1592”, signed “Vre bien humble et obeissant serviteur Pelissier”, and marked Tripta (the third copy sent). Clear French and cipher alternate within the same lines, and the cipher is written with a small repertory of letter-like signs, figures and marks. f. 46r: “Monsieur J’entreprins mon voyage de la court si a contre temps que arrivant a Valladolid ou le Roy avoit sejourné deulx moys…”, and then the first cipher. The small writing between the cipher rows is the contemporary decipherer’s. His glosses are few and scattered, and they are the letter’s whole “partial decipherment”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3982 f. 46r, via Gallica (btv1b9060543f, canvas 100).

t: Pelissier to Jeannin, Burgos, 13 September 1592 — the League’s agent at Philip II’s court
b: Tomokiyo’s League page reconstructs the cipher Pelissier used in nos. 45 and 46 (Madrid, 27 October 1592) from their clean decipherment on f. 115. It is a homophonic alphabet with one to seven signs per letter. Some signs are two-digit numbers (24, 26, 28, 30, 33, 36, 44, 56, 60, 80). There is a sign for et , signs for the doubled letters rr , ss and uu , and six nulls. His table is not reproduced here; it is on his page. No. 22 is six weeks older and on the same key, with two additions: Code group 315 is the Béarnais , Henri IV: “le [315] ayant incontinant tourné la teste et s’estant campé pres l’armée catholique”, “les forces d’Allemaigne … iointes au [315]”. It occurs on four of the nine pages. Code group 310 occurs once, on f. 50r: “ne correspondront pas a ce que pretend [310], et l’ambassadeur … a esté renvoyé sans aultre esclaircissement sur ses demandes”, next to a passage on the governor of Milan. A claimant with an ambassador at Philip’s court and a Milanese connection is most likely the Duke of Savoy , Philip’s son-in-law, who had his own pretensions in France; the Duke of Lorraine is the alternative. Context only. Code group 441 occurs once, on f. 49v: “non seulement en [441] mais en toutes aultres regions de la Chrestienté”, which asks for France . Context only. The decipherer’s glosses check the key wherever they are legible. They agree on de , auisa , meschans , roy , les tirer , Noyon , a la main qu , n’auoit , en atendant , quar la bataille , mais le retour , de crainte , langaiges , Valentia , a gens matez des and (qu’ay)ant pleu a Dieu , among others. One gloss disagrees in an instructive way. Over “nos forces” the glosser wrote os a orc : he applied the table’s ϝ = a literally where the sense needs f . The hand that deciphered this letter in 1592 was working from the same table, and it slipped on the same sign. Calibration. Tomokiyo’s table gives each sign a letter; it does not say how to tell apart signs that look alike on a fast page, and that is where the first reading stalled. The two letters he built the key from were therefore aligned with their clear text on f. 115, sign by sign: 835 signs of no. 45 (f. 111r) and 929 of no. 46 (ff. 113r–v). That settles the look-alikes with known plaintext: 4 : the plain closed 4 is n (and often m ), never t ; t is the 4 with a hooked lead-in off the crossbar, or with a curl. The first transcription had written both as 4, and a decode that let every sign take any letter wanted that 4 to be t 355 times. ⊤ : flat-topped is a ; with a hooked top and a descender, p ; with a tail, s . The lone hooked τ is g . δ : with a straight ascender o ; curling over into a long hook, c ; with a big open loop over a closed bowl, r . 56 : compact, y ; with the long hooked 5 and the 6 set high, c . 8 : plain, n ; crossed at the waist, q . + is h and ∐ is l , never e ; π is i , never s (the tailed ϖ is s ); the barred ӿ is u and the large plain ✗ a null; 7 is b , or h . The October letters and no. 22 were written by the same hand six weeks apart, and the page readers found a few further habits in no. 22 alone: an alpha-shaped sign and a barred 5 for g , a small box-shaped ∐ for e , the tall double long-s for rr , and a looped ℓ that stands for u or e by context. The whole guide, with exemplar crops of every form, is pelissier1592/GLYPHS.md and cal/atlas/ . f. 46v. Clear text (“a l’arrivee du Roy en ce dict lieu de Burgos Je retornay treuver le seigneur Don Joan, lequel m’ayant donné une heure particulliere”) runs straight into cipher. The cipher opens “i’exposay pour fondement de mon discours qu’il n’est rien plus requis en un estat que la conservation de la reputation”. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3982 f. 46v, via Gallica (btv1b9060543f, canvas 101).

t: Pelissier to Jeannin, Burgos, 13 September 1592 — the League’s agent at Philip II’s court
b: Deciphered words are in the reading as written, with the letter’s spelling. The page summaries below are in English. The full text, page by page, with gaps marked, is in pelissier1592/READING.md . f. 46r. Pelissier reached Valladolid just as the court was leaving, and Don Juan de Idiáquez put business off to Palencia. In cipher, he says his credit is gone, “le credit m’est[oit] failly pour n’avoir satisfaict au payement des sommes qui m’ont esté prestées a Madrid”. He takes the King’s long silence for a refusal and asks leave to go home. He is told Philip has his own ministers in France. Philip’s answer to the rest is “yo lo creo”. Then comes the grant: “elle m’avoit ordonné cinq cens ducats, qui valent environ quatre cens cinquante escus, ou plus”, payable in Madrid, “ou je me pouvois retirer avec les ambassadeurs et aultres estans par deça de la part de princes estrangiers”, so that he can wait for news. f. 46v. At Burgos, Don Juan gives him a private hour. Pelissier’s theme is reputation, and his example is Parma’s army of 1592. While it flourished, “la plus part de la noblesse catholique qui suit ce party se retira chacun en sa maison” and towns began to treat. If it had wintered in France, the Béarnais would have been brought to “une ruine tres certaine”, and the Germans “n’eussent eu l’audace de sortir de leur pays pour l’assister”. Its return to the Low Countries undid everything: League towns afraid of being exposed if the enemy returned began their own dealings, and La Fère, Soissons and the places of Picardy, perhaps Corbie “pres d’Amiens” (a doubtful reading), were left in danger. ff. 47r–47v. The French “aymeroient mieux mourir touts l’un après l’aultre” than be forced, as the rising against “le dernier Roy” showed; mildness and benefits would win them to anything. The King asks whether Pelissier speaks on Mayenne’s orders. He has had no word since the armies faced each other at Caudebec. The Spanish answer is that no king had ever given such help, and any failure lay with those who received it. Pelissier’s reasons for putting off the Estates are taken for a trick. The minister recalls that Mayenne, in the time of the Cardinal de Bourbon, had pressed for everything else to be set aside for the Cardinal’s “deliurance”, and Pelissier is heard to say it would be “necessaire que l’on mist sus deux armées”. Yet the minister concedes that the League’s French would take it very badly if Spain delayed “la nomination d’un roy legitime pour l’opposer a l’heretique et tyran”. Of the Spanish ministers, Pelissier writes: “ilz ont les oreilles delicates”. f. 48r. He calls for a “troisiesme moyen”. This is the wrong time to hold the Estates: the people are exhausted, the clergy intimidated, and the nobility held only by its interests, and they would sooner accept “un accord qui creera un Roy pour l’opposer a celuy qui se pretend”. He foresees a war that may end only “par l’extermination de la race de l’un desditz deux Roys”. His remedy is the plan already put to Philip “de tenir deux armees en pied”. One army would drive the enemy from the Seine to the Loire. The other would take the Seine towns and free Paris and Rouen. He answers the cost, “pres de trois cens mil escus par mois”, by saying the effort need last only a few months. A war left to drag on would be “si sanglante” that, driven to despair, it would spare neither age nor sex: “ne pardonnant a aage ni sexe”. f. 48v. The army should be mostly French, “tant a pied qu’a cheval”, stiffened by “un corps de sept ou huit mil Alemans” and some Spaniards and Walloons “assistés de bons capitaines”. A victory would ruin the enemy. After a defeat, an army of Philip’s own nations “seroit preste pour recueillir les reliques de ceste deffaicte”. Piecemeal aid only ruins the provinces. And if Philip showed “quelque affection particuliere en la nomination du roy”, everyone would follow. f. 49r. The campaigns of 1591–92: Chartres, Noyon, the Prince of Ascoli’s relief, Caudebec, Henri’s daily offer of battle, and the retreat towards Château-Thierry. The clear text blames Parma for letting chances go by, which gave the enemy room to spread the rumour that Philip fights only to keep the French busy while he subdues his Low Countries rebels. f. 49v. What Frenchmen were saying: that Philip wanted France kept “en telle balance” so that he could take his share of a divided crown. Then the case for Navarre. God called him “comme par miracle a la succession”. He has lived “en perpetuelle peine et travail, pauvre et miserable”, and so he will want peace. If he turned on the Catholics, they would be “libres du serment de fidelite”. Such talk works on “gens matez des maux soufferts et plains de desespoir de mieux”. Philip alone can cure the malady, and would add to “Catholique” the names “tres chrestien” and “liberateur de la Chrestienté”. f. 50r. “Ilz vont minant l’authorité” of Mayenne: finances first, then command, then credit: “ilz luy diminuent le credit … l’abaisser le plus qu’ilz pourront. Dieu veulle que je me trompe”. Whatever [310] pretends to, its ambassador has been sent home without an answer, and Pelissier pleads for a union among the League so close that an offence to one would be felt by all. In clear, Pelissier stays “pour essayer de tirer une derniere resolution sur la partie de cinquante mil escutz”. A postscript describes a visitor sent to Palencia, whom the King received well enough to send him horses for his audiences.

t: Pelissier to Jeannin, Burgos, 13 September 1592 — the League’s agent at Philip II’s court
b: Transcription by sign. Each page was cut into third-width bands at 1.5× from the full-resolution Gallica scan. Every sign was written as a token (a name for its shape) and every clear passage in full. Seven parallel agents did ff. 47r–50r; ff. 46r–46v were done here and served as the worked example. A beam decoder, not a solver. Each token carries the letter the key gives it, plus cheap alternatives where two signs look alike. A beam search over a conditional quadgram model of period French picks the reading, and word breaks come out of the model. Second pass. For every row that did not decode to French, the signs were re-read at 2.5× and genuine misreadings were corrected on every page. A change was made only when the sign was visibly different on the leaf, never just because French would then appear. Each page’s reading lists the glosses and whether they agree. Calibration and third pass. The key’s own source letters were aligned with their clear text (section 02), the look-alike families were split into separate tokens, and every row of all nine pages was re-read against the scans with them. Unread words fell from 413 to 256 and doubtful ones from 278 to 158. What went wrong, usefully. Twice, once per page and once over the whole letter, the sign-to-letter map was hill-climbed against the language model from the key as a start. Both times it drifted to the degenerate “every frequent sign is e ” attractor, which a noisy transcription always rewards. The key was right. The errors were in the tokens, which had merged signs the key keeps apart: 56 with a flourish is c , and plain 56 is y . The plain δ is o , the δ with a long curling hook is c , and the closed-loop ∂ with a curled top is r . The flat-topped ⊤ is a , the hooked τ is p , and the small curled “Tz” is g . Among the barred I forms, the plain one is l , the bold-footed one is o , and the double-barred one is o as well (Ƒ). vv is et , and also ff . ϝ is a in the table and f in dozens of words. That diagnosis was right, and the calibration in section 02 is the remedy: most of these splits are now tokens in their own right, confirmed on known plaintext.

t: Pelissier to Jeannin, Burgos, 13 September 1592 — the League’s agent at Philip II’s court
b: 256 words unread , marked [?] , against 3,734 read inside the ciphered stretches (94 %), and 158 more read but doubtful, marked (?) . Every page’s reading lists its open rows with their tokens. They are single signs the eye cannot settle, a hole in f. 50r, and names. Nothing is supplied by conjecture. Grades. The key is H (in print, and confirmed on 1,764 signs of known plaintext and by the glosses). The reading of the firm stretches is H; the (?) words are C. 315 = the Béarnais is H (it recurs, and “appeler [315] comme par miracle a la succession” fixes it); 310 = Savoy and 441 = France are M, one occurrence each; Corbie and Amiens on f. 46v are I. Names. The Dominican confessor on f. 50r reads c-o-r-n-e | n-t-(u/e) across a line break, “Cornente” or “Cornete” if a heavily inked 4 is cancelled; not identified. A “don …” beside the governor of Milan, the visitor of the postscript, and a place in the 1592 campaign (f. 49r) are unread. Everything is in the repository under pelissier1592/ : the account in NOTES.md , the reading in READING.md and reading_46r.md … reading_50r.md , the token transcriptions t46r.txt … t50r.txt , the decoder beam.py with cands.txt , the sign vocabulary in TOKENS.md , the calibrated guide in GLYPHS.md , and the alignments of nos. 45 and 46 with their exemplar crops in cal/ .

t: Sir Henry Percy to Cecil, Norham, 23 July 1559 — attempted, not read
b: DECODE R9256 is a Forbes Papers tracing of the four cipher passages in Percy’s letter of 23 July 1559: 63 signs in a box script with dot and underline marks. Cecil deciphered them at the time and the letter is calendared, but which words were in cipher is not printed. No single letter substitution fits the four passages, and the text is too short to break without the key. Norham Castle → Sir William Cecil · box script with dot and underline marks · 23 July 1559 · not read Sir Henry Percy to Cecil, Norham, 23 July 1559 from Henry Percy → to William Cecil British Library, Add MS 4136 f. 172 (DECODE R9256): a page of the Forbes Papers with a tracing of the four cipher passages of Percy’s letter, numbered (1) to (4), and his signature. The original, with Cecil’s decipherment, is at The National Archives in SP 52/1. Transcribed and attacked as a substitution cipher. No single alphabet fits the four passages; 63 signs are too few to break without the key. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 attempted Summary. DECODE catalogues R9256 as a ciphered letter of Henry Percy to Secretary Cecil, 23 July 1559, not deciphered. The one image is a page of the Forbes Papers volume (BL Add MS 4136), not the letter. It carries an eighteenth-century tracing of four short cipher passages and Percy’s signature. The lower half is an unrelated key, Sturmius’s cipher of 1562, which DECODE files separately as R9257. The letter is calendared twice: Calendar of State Papers Foreign I no. 1051 and Bain, Calendar of State Papers Scotland I no. 501. Bain describes it as having “a few words in cipher, deciphered by Cecill”. The calendared text names Knox, Whytlaw, the Lord Prior, Lord Hume, the Merse and Teviotdale, the Dowager, the Congregation and Haddington, but does not say which of them were in cipher. The four passages have 63 signs: box shapes like pigpen, with an underline, one dot or two dots beneath, and five other signs. No key in the same volume uses this script. The attack failed: no single letter-for-letter alphabet makes sense of all four passages, whether the marks are counted as separate letters or ignored, and either way round. Status: attempted, not read. What would finish it is the TNA original with Cecil’s interlined decipherment, or the ciphered original of Percy’s 1 July postscript, whose plaintext Laing prints.

t: Sir Henry Percy to Cecil, Norham, 23 July 1559 — attempted, not read
b: BL Add MS 4136 f. 172, upper half: the Forbes tracing of the four cipher passages of Percy’s letter of 23 July 1559, with his signature. Image: British Library, Add MS 4136 f. 172, via DECODE R9256. The heading reads “Sr Hen: Percy to Sr Wm Cecill from Norham 23 July 1559”. A second heading on the same page, “from Norham 22 July 1559 · A”, has only the signature under it. Below a rule is “Sturmius’s Cipher, 4 March 1562”, an alphabet with name codes and nulls. Its signs are Greek-like letters, not boxes, so it is not Percy’s key. The passages are transcribed one sign at a time. Each sign is a box shape (⅃ ⊔ L □ ⊏ 7 ⊓ Γ, and a barred I) with or without a mark beneath: an underline, one dot or two dots. Five other signs appear: a crossed 4, a boxed cross, a trident, a tailed 6 and a house. In all there are 13 words, 63 signs and 19 distinct sign-and-mark combinations. The transcription is in percy1559/transcription.txt . Passages (3) and (4), on either side of the signature, begin with the same five signs and share their second word’s first three signs.

t: Sir Henry Percy to Cecil, Norham, 23 July 1559 — attempted, not read
h: What the letter says, and what was in cipher
b: Bain’s calendar (no. 501) summarises the letter. Percy has had Knox’s answer by word of mouth. Whytlaw is fully instructed, so his journey is at an end. Percy has conveyed a letter to the Lord Prior and encloses the Prior’s unsigned answer. Lord Hume has put off the border meeting at Lady Kirk. The Merse and Teviotdale go to the Dowager tomorrow, and the Congregation towards Haddington. The note on the manuscript is “A few words in cipher, deciphered by Cecill”. On 22 July Percy had written Knox’s name as a cipher sign (CSP Foreign I no. 1045). On 4 August he told Cecil he had sent the Lord Prior “a cipher” (Laing, Works of John Knox VI, p. 61). Percy’s cipher could spell out whole sentences as well as names. Bain (no. 480) records a postscript Percy added in cipher to Kirkcaldy’s letter of 1 July and deciphered himself. Laing (VI, pp. 33–35) prints it in clear: “The letter that Knoxe wrythe to you is by the meanes of the hole Congregatione, the names of whome I sende yowe here inclosed.” Its ciphered form is on the original only.

t: Sir Henry Percy to Cecil, Norham, 23 July 1559 — attempted, not read
b: Word patterns. Each cipher word was matched against a vocabulary from Sadler’s State Papers and the Forbes volumes, with the calendar’s names added. Many words fit on their own. The repeated five-sign word fits prior or merse , for example. Rosicrucian pigpen. This tested each box shape as a cell of three consecutive letters, with the mark choosing among them. Every cell layout and mark order was tried, with 24- and 26-letter alphabets. None produces a single dictionary word, so this system is ruled out. One alphabet for all thirteen words. A constraint search looked for one alphabet that makes all thirteen words real words. It was run with the marks counted as distinct letters, with dots ignored, with underlines ignored, with all marks ignored, and with homophones allowed. It found no solution. The same search on the words read right to left also found none. A version that left up to six words free as name codes timed out without producing a candidate. Statistical search. The search scored letter triples, and then whole words from a vocabulary of the period. It gave only fluent-looking nonsense, as expected for 63 signs. Guessed names. Prior , Lord Prior , Knox , Whytlaw and Norham Castle were placed on the repeated words. None gives an alphabet that holds across all four passages.

t: Sir Henry Percy to Cecil, Norham, 23 July 1559 — attempted, not read
b: All four passages are unread. They may be name signs rather than spelled-out words, or the tracing may have miscopied some marks; a tracing cannot settle either question. Two documents would: the original of 23 July in TNA SP 52/1 with Cecil’s interlined decipherment, or the ciphered original of the 1 July postscript, which would give a sentence of known plaintext. Neither is online.

t: Sir Henry Percy to Cecil, Norham, 23 July 1559 — attempted, not read

t: La Chaulx to Charles V, Vitoria 1522 — read at the time
b: DECODE R1187, catalogued as an unread Spanish cipher letter of 1 January 1522, is a French despatch of Charles de Poupet, sieur de La Chaulx, envoy to Adrian VI, dated Vitoria 28 May 1522. Its five homophonic cipher passages, marked A to E, are read in the contemporary decipherment bound in as MSS/20212/39/2; the first line was checked against it. The cipher covers the Pope’s sailing: plague at Barcelona, the galleys of Naples, 4,000 men rumoured as 20,000. Vitoria → Charles V · homophonic substitution, French · 28 May 1522 · read at the time; decipherment bound in La Chaulx to Charles V, Vitoria 1522 — read at the time to Charles V Biblioteca Nacional de España, MSS/20212/39/1–2; DECODE R1187. The catalogue listed a Spanish cipher letter of 1 January 1522 whose content was unknown. It is a French despatch from the Emperor’s envoy to Adrian VI, written at Vitoria on 28 May 1522. The decipherment made when it arrived is filed as 39/2. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 21 September 2026 resolved Summary. Charles de Poupet, sieur de La Chaulx, was sent to Spain early in 1522 to the newly elected Pope Adrian VI, who was still in the Peninsula. The 18 pages of R1187 are two items. Item 39/1 is his signed letter to the Emperor in French, dated “en vostre ville de Victoire le xxviij me de may 1522”. It has five cipher passages, marked in the margin A, b, C, D and E. Item 39/2 is a contemporary decipherment in another hand, keyed by the same letters. DECODE’s “Inline Plaintext: Yes” refers to it. The first cipher line was aligned with it here. The sign counts fit combien que je word for word, and e takes three different signs, so the cipher is homophonic and 39/2 is its reading. Nothing in the letter is unread. The key was not rebuilt, and no printed edition of this letter was found. Above: passage A in cipher (39/1, image 2). Below: the same passage in the 1522 decipherment (39/2, image 9), “A — Combien que je vouldroie mectre mon ame en gaige que vous estes la personne de ce monde quil ayme le plus…”. Image: Biblioteca Nacional de España, MSS/20212/39/1 (image 2) and 39/2 (image 9), via DECODE R1187.

t: La Chaulx to Charles V, Vitoria 1522 — read at the time
b: 39/1 (DECODE images 1–8): the original, in French, signed Lachaulx . The five cipher passages are A (end of f. 3v), b (f. 5r to 5v, a full page), C (f. 6r), D (f. 7v to 8r) and E (f. 9r). Some signs carry interlinear glosses, for example “que sont quatre mille hommes” on f. 6r. The address and endorsement read “A l’empereur” and “1522, de Victoria, de la Chaulx”. 39/2 (images 9–11): the decipherment, in the same A–E order. DECODE records the language as Spanish and gives 1 January 1522, the first day of its 1522 date range. Both are wrong.

t: La Chaulx to Charles V, Vitoria 1522 — read at the time
b: The cipher is a substitution in cursive signs and digits, with no word division. Passage A opens E o+ o φ 2 ꝑ 3 m4 7 o ꝝ ꝭ o+ ▷ c ɗo ʆ ɗ ꝑ… . Against the decipherment that is c-o-m-b-i-e-n q-u-e j-e v-o-u-l-d-r-o-i-e . Every word gets one sign per letter, and e is written with three different signs ( ꝑ , o , ꝭ ). The key was not rebuilt. That would mean transcribing some 1,500 signs from 1024-pixel scans for a text that was read in 1522.

t: La Chaulx to Charles V, Vitoria 1522 — read at the time
b: From the 1522 decipherment. Grade M (moderate): read from the scan, abbreviations expanded. Doubtful words are in brackets. A. Combien que je vouldroie mectre mon ame en gaige que vous estes la personne de ce monde quil ayme le plus, mais ne doubtez que luy estre a Rome il sera sollicite et practique de tant de costez que lon luy pourroit [desmouvoir] quelque chose dont il ne se [retireroit]… b. Sire, entant que touche le partement du pape… le lieu de Barcelone ou il entendoit assembler son armee, la peste sest mise de sorte quil fauldra quil aille a Tarragone ou a Cartagena… Il actend davoir deux caracques qui sont en ung havre vers Landelousye… et ma dit que sy voz galleres de Naples venoient, il est du tout delibere avec icelles et les nefz de dela soy [embarquer] et passer… mais il le fault tenir secret… Je suis tousjours de loppinion que vous ay escript quil ne partira de tout le mois de juing… le nombre de gens quil a entreprins de mener, que sont quatre mille hommes… il fait courre le bruit quil emmenera vingt mille… In passage A, La Chaulx would stake his soul that the Pope loves the Emperor above anyone. He warns that at Rome Adrian will be pressed from so many sides that he may commit himself to something he cannot undo. Passage b is about the Pope’s sailing. Plague at Barcelona moves the muster to Tarragona or Cartagena. Adrian is waiting for two carracks in an Andalusian port and for the galleys of Naples, and La Chaulx does not expect him to leave before July. He will take 4,000 men and let it be rumoured that he takes 20,000. Adrian in fact sailed from Tarragona in August. Passages C–E, on money and the Cortes, the Infanta Catherine and Portugal, and the news from France, England and the Swiss, are read in 39/2 and summarised in the notes.

t: Ghinucci, Lee and Poyntz to Wolsey, Valladolid 1527 — read at the time
b: DECODE R8565, catalogued as a ciphered letter of Francis Poyntz to an unknown recipient, is the separated second part of the joint despatch of Ghinucci, Lee and Poyntz to Cardinal Wolsey, Valladolid 17 July 1527 ( Letters and Papers IV no. 3271). The folio offset from its neighbour R8566 places it, and the public thumbnails fit. Its short passages in the Lee–Worcester sign cipher are deciphered between the lines, and Tuke’s decipherment is in print: Milan and the daughter of Portugal for the duke of Richmond, and the French envoy’s secret fourth instruction. Valladolid → Cardinal Wolsey · Lee–Worcester sign cipher, English · 17 July 1527 · read at the time; decipherment in print Ghinucci, Lee and Poyntz to Wolsey, Valladolid 1527 — read at the time to Cardinal Wolsey British Library, Cotton MS Vespasian C IV ff. 174–177; DECODE R8565. The catalogue listed a ciphered letter of “Fran. Poynts” to an unknown recipient, content unknown. It is the second part of the three English ambassadors’ report to Wolsey on their audiences with Charles V. Its few cipher passages were deciphered in 1527, and the decipherment is in print. Arya Sanketbhai Patel · resolved 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 resolved Summary. In July 1527 Henry VIII had three men at the Emperor’s court at Valladolid: Edward Lee, the King’s almoner; Girolamo Ghinucci, bishop of Worcester; and Sir Francis Poyntz, newly arrived with the French envoy, the bishop of Tarbes, to mediate a peace between Charles V and Francis I. Their joint report to Cardinal Wolsey of 17 July 1527 is calendared in Letters and Papers of Henry VIII , vol. IV, as no. 3271: “Pp. 23. The cipher deciphered by Tuke … One part of this despatch is separated from the other.” DECODE R8565 is that separated part. The folio numbers place it: the calendar puts the second part at old f. 166, and old ff. 166–169 are DECODE’s new ff. 174–177. The pages are English in clear, with about five short passages in the Lee–Worcester sign cipher, each deciphered between the lines. The calendar prints what they say: Charles’s professions of goodwill to Henry, the idea of giving Milan with the daughter of Portugal to Henry’s son the duke of Richmond, and the French envoy’s secret fourth instruction. Nothing here is unread. This was identified from the calendar and DECODE’s public thumbnails. The full images are behind the DECODE login and were not viewed, so one check on the first page remains.

t: Ghinucci, Lee and Poyntz to Wolsey, Valladolid 1527 — read at the time
b: DECODE R8565 has eight images, 7 pages of text, status “Partially decrypted”, with inline cleartext and inline plaintext both marked “Yes”. The key linked to it is “Lee–Worcester Cipher (1526–1529)”. The public thumbnails (200 pixels wide) show: seven written pages under the Cotton running head “Hispania 1527”, mostly English in clear; about five short bands in which a line of cipher carries a line of decipherment above it (images 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7), which is DECODE’s “Partially decrypted” and “inline plaintext”; three signatures at the foot of image 7, as expected for Ghinucci, Lee and Poyntz; image 8, the address leaf with its endorsement. So the catalogue entry is wrong on two counts. The letter is not from Poyntz alone but from all three ambassadors, and the recipient is Wolsey.

t: Ghinucci, Lee and Poyntz to Wolsey, Valladolid 1527 — read at the time
b: The calendar prints the deciphered passages in italics. For this part of no. 3271 they are the following. The words are the calendar’s summary of Tuke’s decipherment, not the letter’s own spelling, except where the calendar quotes. … Perceive the French would not have brought him to show any demands. He professes willingness to do everything for the King , and we avoid giving him any token but that the King and your Grace are still wholly his . … Buclans asked if they restored Sforza, what security they should have that he would not give up the duchy to France, and suggested that the Emperor might give it along with the daughter of Portugal to the duke of Richmond . De Tarbes has now shown us the fourth instruction. Perceive well why he withheld it; for he is to say to the Emperor, before the English ambassadors, that they desire his amity more than that of any other prince . 17 July 1527. Signed. So the ambassadors kept three things out of reach of anyone who opened the packet. First, they were privately reassuring Charles that Henry and Wolsey were still “wholly his”, while they mediated alongside the French. Second, the Emperor’s side had floated a marriage: Milan and Maria, daughter of Manuel I of Portugal (the Emperor’s niece), for Henry Fitzroy, duke of Richmond, Henry’s illegitimate son. Third, the French envoy had been told to court Charles in front of the English. The companion letter no. 3272, from the same three men and “chiefly cipher, deciphered by Tuke”, continues in the same vein. It reports an intercepted despatch from Charles’s ambassador in France: De Tarbes could offer the Viceroy’s conditions undiminished; Lautrec had authority to conclude in Italy; Wolsey had pressed Francis to marry the Princess Mary. It also names a portion of 400,000 ducats for the Portuguese match.

t: Ghinucci, Lee and Poyntz to Wolsey, Valladolid 1527 — read at the time
b: This is the sign cipher Lee and Ghinucci used with Wolsey from 1526 to 1529: graphic signs for letters, with signs for words and names. Satoshi Tomokiyo reconstructed it, and his table is attached on DECODE to R8566. It has already been checked against the interlinear decipherments of two sibling records. On R8566, the signs under “possibilite” and “good” read p-o-ss-i-b-i-l-i-t-e and g-o-o-d. On R8567, the run under “can not” reads c-a-n-n-o. The key was not applied to R8565, because its signs could not be seen at thumbnail size and the reading exists. R8565, f. 177r, the last cipher passage of the despatch: each line of Lee–Worcester signs has the contemporary decipherment written above it, that De Tarbes has now shown them the fourth instruction, which he is to use before the English ambassadors: that they desire the Emperor’s amity more than that of any other prince. t: “Frederic, Re di Prussia” to an unknown recipient — a thank-you for lessons in cipher, not a cipher
b: Blenheim Papers Add MS 61575 f. 95 is catalogued on DECODE (R8774) as a non-decrypted numerical cipher. The page has no numbers: it is seven lines of plain French, spelled by ear and split into syllables, thanking someone for teaching the writer to write in cipher and wishing them a good journey. Writer and recipient are unidentified. Blenheim Papers · to an unknown teacher · plain French · date unknown (volume 1702–1723) · not a cipher A Lesson in Cipher British Library, Add MS 61575 f. 95 · DECODE R8774, catalogued as a non-decrypted numerical cipher of "Frederic, Re di Prussia", 1702 There is no cipher on the leaf. It is a short thank-you note, in French, for lessons in writing in cipher. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 21 September 2026 not a cipher Summary. Add MS 61575 is the Blenheim volume of the Marlboroughs' cipher material. Its folio 95 is on DECODE as R8774: "Non-decrypted", symbol set numerical, cipher type unknown, author "Frederic, Re di Prussia", dated 1702–1723 (the span of the volume). It entered the Unsolved Catalogue as item 98 on those metadata alone. The page image shows no numbers and no signs. It holds seven lines of French in a large, careful hand, spelled by ear and set out syllable by syllable in spaced columns. Read aloud, it is a thank-you note: the writer thanks someone for the trouble they took in showing me how to write in cipher , and wishes them a good journey. That subject explains why it was filed with the ciphers. Nothing on it is enciphered. The writer and the recipient are not identified. No signature survives under the ink blot below the text, and DECODE's attribution to a Prussian king cannot be checked from the leaf.

t: “Frederic, Re di Prussia” to an unknown recipient — a thank-you for lessons in cipher, not a cipher
b: One page, written in brown ink across the top half of the leaf, with a long rule below and an ink blot at the left where a signature could have been. The folio number 95 is at top right. The words are broken into syllables and spaced out in rough columns, as in a writing exercise. Spelling follows sound: eun for une , Payne for peine , d'es cria re for d'écrire , sif fer for chiffre , as seu re for assurer . The s for ch is what a German speaker would write, which fits a Prussian writer, but proves nothing about which one.

t: “Frederic, Re di Prussia” to an unknown recipient — a thank-you for lessons in cipher, not a cipher
b: Line for line, as written: par cel le cy je vient vous re mer cier en cor eun ne foy de la Pay ne que vous aves eue avec moy en me mon trant d'es cria re en sif fer et vous as seu re que je se roys tous jours re cog naissent vous sou haytant eun bon voya ge. In standard French: Par celle-ci je viens vous remercier encore une fois de la peine que vous avez eue avec moi en me montrant d'écrire en chiffre, et vous assurer que je serai toujours reconnaissant, vous souhaitant un bon voyage. "By this I come to thank you once more for the trouble you took with me in showing me how to write in cipher, and to assure you that I shall always be grateful, wishing you a good journey." Every word reads; the only doubt is the letter shapes of eun in the last line, which could be un with a flourish.
