t: Bornemisza on the Kendi treason, Transylvania c. 1556 — read at the time
b: DECODE R1212, catalogued as a Latin letter from an unknown sender to “Paulo Borne?” (HHStA Vienna, Chiffrenschlüssel Kt. 13 Fasc. 20 ff. 38–39), is a report in the cipher of Pál Bornemisza, Bishop of Transylvania, written in his own voice to Ferdinand I: Ferenc Kendi, “ter perfidus”, has lost Transylvania to the king. A contemporary hand deciphered it between the lines; its key is the next DECODE record, R1211. Every run was re-read from the signs with that key, correcting the gloss in a dozen places; 276 of 288 cipher tokens read, nine number codes stay open. Transylvania → King Ferdinand I · homophonic sign cipher, Latin · c. 1556 · read at the time; decipherment interlined, key R1211 Bornemisza on the Kendi treason, Transylvania c. 1556 — read at the time to Ferdinand I Österreichisches Staatsarchiv, HHStA, Staatskanzlei Interiora, Chiffrenschlüssel Kt. 13, Fasc. 20, ff. 38–39; DECODE R1212. Catalogued as a Latin letter from an unknown sender to “Paulo Borne?”. It is a report written in the cipher of Pál Bornemisza, Bishop of Transylvania, and in his own voice, to “Your Sacred Majesty”, King Ferdinand I: Ferenc Kendi, “three times a traitor”, has lost the kingdom of Transylvania to the king. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 22 September 2026 resolved Summary. The four pages of R1212 mix clear Latin with runs of graphic signs, and a contemporary hand has written the Latin over almost every run. The docket on p. 4 reads “Sibenbürgische Ziffern(?) das ist mit dem Bischof daselbst dno Paulo Bornemißa”: the Transylvanian cipher used with the bishop there, Pál Bornemisza (bishop 1553–1556). The key is the next leaf of the volume, DECODE R1211 (f. 37): a homophonic alphabet of 21 letters in signs and digits, with two name codes, 34 Transsylvania and 27 Petrovics. With that key every cipher run was deciphered afresh from the signs and compared with the old gloss. The gloss holds; the signs correct it in a dozen places ( ipse , nisi , maledictum , inflammavit , vexillum , in celo ) and supply the few words left unglossed. Pages 3–4 are in the first person of the bishop: Kendi urged him to give up Alba and live in the castle of Gyalu, and “these are the words of Ferenc Kendi to me at Vásárhely at the diet”. So the sender is Bornemisza himself, not his correspondent. Of 288 cipher tokens, 276 read as sense (95.8%). Open are nine number codes that the key does not contain (24, 15, 10; 41·70·55·78·18; 52) and three signs that are illegible.

t: Bornemisza on the Kendi treason, Transylvania c. 1556 — read at the time
b: R1212 is two leaves, ff. 38–39, in the Vienna collection of cipher keys, a volume whose DECODE dates (1540–1774) are the span of the whole box. Pages 1–2 and 3–4 are two reports under the same head, “D[omi]no … Thur. Prim.” and “Practica Thur. Prim.”, each opening with the enciphered words horum omnium motuum , “of all these disturbances”. The foot of p. 4 carries two rows of signs with faint pencil letters over them: an inventory of the signs in the order they first occur in that heading, not the key. The key is R1211, f. 37, the leaf filed just before the letter: A = Δ 3 5, B = L, C = 9, D = ꝛ, E = y M 2, F = o, G = B, H = #, I = Π Ꝛ ~ k, K = β, L = L 4, M = Ϙ Λ, N = P, O = φ x v, P = A, Q = Ҁ, R = Ɔ, S = σ, T = Ω, U = C Λ ɧ, X = π, and the codes 34 Transsylvania and 27 Petrovics. R1210 (f. 36), also labelled for Bornemisza, is an older numerical key of about 1540 (Rex Joannes, Frater Georgius, Verbőczy) and does not read this letter. The writer is loose with the key: x and v stand for u as well as o, ~ for u and o as well as i, 9 (c) for t in prodicionem , nacionum , comiciis ; the barred Π is his h, and β serves for c and h as well as k. A pair of digits in a run is usually two letters (34 in alias , aliquando , alliciebat ), not a code.

t: Bornemisza on the Kendi treason, Transylvania c. 1556 — read at the time
b: Clear words as written, deciphered words in italics, codes in braces. Spelling as enciphered. Pages 1–2 [ horum omnium motuum ]. Commendavi hactenus semper Vestrae Sacratissimae Maiestati hominem de bonis omnibus … perfidia acusare debeo merito . Nullus enim alius causa est istius tumultus nisi Franciscus Kendi, ter perfidus; ipse ad hoc induxit Antonium Kendi et Melchiorem Balassa aliosque non multos ex nobilibus … fecit autem perfidus homo hanc prodicionem ex pusillanimitate … et desperacione nimia . Terra caelumque obruant hunc maledictum proditorem Copiae, qui perdidit hoc Regnum a Maiestate Vestra sacra; nemo alius . {24} {15} et {10} ultra portam solicitantur ut in hoc regnum veniant , porro proh dolor. Haec Vestrae Sacratissimae Maiestati brevibus perscripsi sed vere, in qua re nullum est dubium. {41}.{70}.{55}.{78}.{18} interfecti sunt; adhuc ad Sacram Maiestatem Vestram expectant … auxilium a sacra Maiestate … sed non diu ; si gentes plures nunc adessent cum bono Capitaneo , vulnus adhuc sanabile esset . … feliciter Regia Maiestas: dicam iterum quod solus Franciscus Kendi perdidit regnum a Maiestate Vestra , nemo alius . Profligati sunt hostes. Hoc ita verum est sicut Evangelium Christi . Sine ordine nequaquam; absque eius consilio nihil fit in hoc regno ; ergo ipse alios hos tumultus excitare inflammavit , alias non evenisset manifestum excidium. Quamvis horribiles querelae contra insolenciam militum Transflumen Vaiuodarum passim fuere de virginum tenerarum defloracionibus, et hoc in publica trium nacionum presente conventu … multae coniugatarum violaciones . Profligati sunt hostes; ultra alia spolia multa , proh dolor, quae enumerare homo non possit Transflumen. “No one else is the cause of this revolt but Ferenc Kendi, three times a traitor; he drew Antal Kendi and Menyhért Balassa and some others of the nobles into it … out of cowardice and too much despair. May earth and heaven overwhelm this cursed traitor, who has lost this kingdom to Your Sacred Majesty … I say again: Ferenc Kendi alone lost the kingdom; nothing is done in this realm without his counsel … horrible complaints of the voivodes’ soldiers beyond the river, of young virgins deflowered, and that in public before the assembly of the three nations.” Pages 3–4 [ horum omnium motuum et perniciosarum factionum ] feudatarius unicus author … Buda et certissimus est … Franciscus Hungarus Kendi … pro certo desperatus de defensione … posteaquam intellexerunt terra recursiones arces Babolchia et alias amissas esse , qui nunc sperat ab {27} … pro principatu Transsylvaniae excursiones habiturum … et me sub quodam praetextu insidiose {34} alliciebat blandiciis suis … Episcopatu debere permanere uno tantum defectu, sed quod Albam cederem … filio {52} multa milia, et ego in arce Gialu residerem … et aliquando Albae in domo Prepositi … Hec sunt verba Francisci Kendi ad me in Vasarhel sub comiciis , trans flumen ultra pontem, in conclavi ambobus tantum existentibus … si non constasset hanc defeccionem regni a Maiestate vestra Franciscus Kendi {34}. Proh dolor, nullus motus talis in hoc regno nunc fuisset ; porro non est dubium … propterea est hoc ita verum sicut Deus in celo . “… and he enticed me with his flatteries, under some pretext, to remain in the bishopric with one condition only, that I give up Alba … and that I live in the castle of Gyalu … These are the words of Ferenc Kendi to me at Vásárhely during the diet, the two of us alone in a room … Had Ferenc Kendi not stood for this defection of the realm from Your Majesty, there would be no such movement in this kingdom now; this is as true as God is in heaven.”

t: Bornemisza on the Kendi treason, Transylvania c. 1556 — read at the time
b: The four DECODE images were read in horizontal bands, first at half and then at full resolution, one pass per pair of pages. Each cipher run was deciphered from its signs with the R1211 key before the gloss was consulted, and every disagreement was settled on the image. The gloss is right in substance throughout; where the signs differ they give the better text ( ipse for the gloss’s apparent esse , nisi for nostri , maledictum for maledicti , evenisset for evenissent , inflammavit for inflamare , intellexerunt for intellexerat , perniciosarum for perniciosam , in celo for in celis , vexillum (?) for auxilium ). Apparent codes 0399, 134 and several 34s dissolved into letters. Counts: 288 cipher tokens (274 words and 14 codes); 257 words read securely, 14 uncertain but in sense, 3 unread; 5 codes keyed, 9 not.

t: Bornemisza on the Kendi treason, Transylvania c. 1556 — read at the time
b: Number codes not in the key : {24} {15} {10} (“are solicited beyond the gate to come into this kingdom”), {41}·{70}·{55}·{78}·{18} (“have been killed”; five persons) and {52} (“to the son … many thousands”). The contemporary decipherer could not read them either: he copied them into the margin and guessed “Siculi vel Saxones” for a 44 in the margin. R1211 lists only 34 and 27; R1210’s name codes (2–20, 80, 90) belong to a different cipher of about 1540 and give no sense here. Illegible : two signs on p. 1 l. 9 half covered by a struck gloss, and the run R Ɔ C on p. 3 l. 5 (gloss “-ias”?). Uncertain (grade M) : vexillum (p. 3 l. 12, gloss auxilium ), habiturum , residerem , constasset , vestras , and about ten clear words at the damaged top of p. 1 and on p. 3 (the heading “Thur. Prim.”, “tehem…”, the closing phrase of p. 4). Date : not on the letter. Kendi’s turn to Queen Isabella and Bornemisza’s loss of Alba point to 1556, before Kendi’s own murder in 1558.

t: Cipher letters to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, 1428–1430 — Read
b: DECODE R1854, catalogued as one letter from an unknown sender, is four cipher letters to the lord of Mantua: Pandolfo Malatesta (Rome, April 1428), an unnamed agent (Rome, August 1428), an informant at Forlì (November 1428) and Francesco de’ Cattanei (Rome, February 1430). Two keys were rebuilt from the ciphertext alone and one taken from a contemporary interlinear gloss; three letters read (96.6–100%): a Gonzaga marriage, the Malatesta and the count of Urbino, and the archbishop of Patras offering his see to Venice. Pandolfo Malatesta’s own runs stay unread. Rome and Forlì → Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, Mantua · homophonic sign ciphers, Latin and Italian · 1428–1430 · three of four letters read Cipher letters to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, 1428–1430 — Read in part to Gianfrancesco I Gonzaga Archivio di Stato di Mantova, Archivio Gonzaga; DECODE R1854 “Mantova enciphered letters” (5 images), catalogued as a single letter from an unknown sender to an unknown recipient, status “partially decrypted”. The five images are four letters of 1428–1430 to the lord of Mantua, in four different ciphers. Three were read here, two of them from the ciphertext alone. Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 22 September 2026 solved in part Summary. R1854 carried no sender, date, language or shelfmark on DECODE. Each of its five images has an archivist’s date and place at the top, and together they are four letters to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga (lord of Mantua, marquess from 1433): Pandolfo Malatesta, archbishop of Patras and brother of Gianfrancesco’s wife Paola, from Rome on 22 April 1428; an unnamed Gonzaga agent in Rome, 9 August 1428; an informant at Forlì, “Ricc. de Mutiliana”, 6 November 1428; and Francesco de’ Cattanei in Rome, 13 and 21 February 1430 (the last image is the verso of the second, photographed upside down). The key record next to it, R1853, is the Gonzaga cipher register of about 1401–1420, and none of its alphabets fits these letters. The Rome letter of August 1428 (1,802 signs) and Cattanei’s two letters (1,736 signs) are homophonic substitutions with nulls and syllable signs; their keys were rebuilt from the ciphertext with an annealer on a Latin language model, and then every sign was checked on the image. The Forlì letter carries a faint contemporary letter-by-letter decipherment, from which its key was taken to decipher all 894 signs. These three letters read at 96.6–100%. They cover a Gonzaga marriage negotiation in Rome (“Carolus est nimis iuvenis ad talia”), Romagna intrigue around the Malatesta, the count of Urbino and the pope, and Roman news of 1430, including the archbishop of Patras offering his see’s temporal lordship to Venice. Pandolfo Malatesta’s three runs (262 signs) are not a simple or homophonic substitution in Latin or Italian and stay unread. At 1428 these are among the oldest cipher letters read in this project.

t: Cipher letters to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, 1428–1430 — Read
h: Rome, 9 August 1428: a marriage for the Gonzaga
b: The whole letter is in cipher: 37 lines of graphic signs and digits, dated in clear “Rome die viiii augusti”. It uses about forty letter signs, a dozen nulls, syllable signs for con , et and -rum , and two word codes, one of them twice in “in domo [·] Senensis” and “cum prefato [·]”, that is, the cardinal of Siena. The opening, as deciphered: Heri Iohannes de Orlandis, quam primum me vidit, dixit michi quod ser Victorius eomet die venit ad ipsum dicens dominam comitissam velle facere id totum quod placet et Iohanni predicto. Verum quia ipse incipiebat tunc prandere, dixit se ad eum reversurum et dicturum latius de ista materia. Postea cum heri sero plures essemus congregati in domo [cardinalis] Senensis pro quodam actu scolastico et cenaturi cum prefato [cardinali] … Ser Vittorio goes on to report the countess’s answer: as far as she is concerned she agrees to the match of her daughter, but her subjects are not content, “quia dominatio vestra nimium distat, si ibi contingeret aliquod sinistrum; et quod Carolus est nimis iuvenis ad talia”. The bridegroom under discussion is Gianfrancesco’s son Carlo, then eleven. The cousins of domina Palma and Antonio Colonna, the pope’s nephew, appear as parties to the negotiation. The full text, with the doubtful spans marked, is in reading_p2.md .

t: Cipher letters to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, 1428–1430 — Read
h: Forlì, 6 November 1428: the Malatesta, Urbino and the pope
b: This letter is in Italian, clear text interrupted by cipher runs. Over every sign a contemporary hand has written the plaintext letter in small faint script, and three word signs are glossed as names: el signor Malatesta , li fioli del signor marchese and el papa . About two-thirds of the gloss is legible. Thirty sign values attested in it (each two to fifty-six times), plus a handful of rare signs fixed from context, decipher all 894 signs: … a ciascuno pare che questo acto sia molto dannoso a le signor Malatesta et cusì, perché [el] dà ad intendare a molti che el papa fia cum loro. Se la S.V. havesse da papa fare questa impresa insieme cum lo signor Malatesta [e] conte d’Urbino, la S.V. se faria una grande signore in pocho tempo. Bene che el signor Malatesta è riputato così povaro, molti se copriano per lui … The informant reports that the governor secretly favours the marquess’s sons, and that Guidantonio da Montefeltro, count of Urbino, is in secret contact with Giovanni de Ramberto, which has aroused suspicion. Full text: reading_p3.md .

t: Cipher letters to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, 1428–1430 — Read
h: Rome, February 1430: Francesco de’ Cattanei’s news
b: Cattanei’s letter of 13 February is again wholly in cipher, a third homophonic system with signs for et , con and -rum ; he writes x as “cx” ( dicxit , reducxit ). It is a newsletter. The magnificent lord Carlo speaks of a marriage alliance with King Louis. A galley of Giovanni de Orlandis (the man in the 1428 letter) took a Catalan ship and was itself taken at Gaeta, a loss of five thousand ducats. The king of Castile presses Aragon. An envoy of the lords of Rimini left without obtaining anything. Then: dominus a[rchi]episcopus de Patras … cum licencia domini nostri dare volebat temporale dominium dominio Venetorum, et illud defenderet ab infidelibus. Dominus noster fecit proponere cardinalibus. Responderunt melius est perdere quam Venetis tradere, quia una vice recuperabitur; set si Veneti haberent, recuperare nunquam esset possibile. The archbishop is Pandolfo Malatesta, the sender of the first letter. Patras fell to the Palaiologoi in 1430. The rest of the letter concerns the chancellor of Niccolò da Tolentino, an abbot freed from excommunication, and six citizens of Bologna expected in Rome, “duos de maioribus, duos de mediocris, et duos de diminutivis”. The three cipher lines on the verso of the second letter (21 February) report the Rimini envoys: “dominus Astorgius et dominus Bartolomeus anbasiatores dominorum de Arimino die lune comparuerunt coram comisariis et producxerunt mandatum et certas copias bullarum auctenticatas … credo parum iuvabit”, and in clear, “denarios non habeo pro expensis”. Full text: reading_p4.md .

t: Cipher letters to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, 1428–1430 — Read
b: The first letter opens in clear with the news, just arrived in Rome, of the peace between the duke of Milan and the league (the peace of Ferrara, 19 April 1428), “licet nondum publicatam”. Pandolfo writes that he has conceived plans “valde utilia” for his brother-in-law, and the secret parts follow in three runs: after “decrevi ne” (58 signs), after “quo modo valeat” (70) and after “nolit rem ipsam negligere” (134). The signs are letter-like (ſſ, η, ʒ, H, cc, ∩, I, ƀʒ, v, ꭏ), with separators strewn between them at random. They would not decipher. The index of coincidence is 0.056 with 29 sign types and about 44% vowel-like signs, which points to a near-monoalphabetic system. Yet annealing in Latin and in Italian (fifteenth- and sixteenth-century and modern models), with and without word spaces, with costed nulls, with vowel and consonant classes, reversed by line, by word and globally, and with digraph signs split or merged, gave nothing. The same solver reads a synthetic 266-letter Latin text in a monoalphabetic cipher even with 12% of its signs corrupted. A second, sign-by-sign transcription corrected three misreadings and made no difference. The register’s Malatesta keys share several shapes with these signs (ſt, H, Λ, v, ꭏ, ƀʒ) but not their values. The best lead is Pandolfo’s letter of 1 March 1438, nearly all in cipher (ASMn, AG, b. 1081, c. 159–160), whose contemporary Italian translation survives (b. 840, c. 95) and is printed by Anna Falcioni. If its cipher is the same family, that pair would give the key. Its images are not online.

t: Cipher letters to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, 1428–1430 — Read
b: All transcriptions were made from the DECODE images, in crops at 4–13×. For the August 1428 letter the triangle sign is followed by sign 17 in 21 of its 29 occurrences, which fixed q and u. A homophonic annealer on the project’s shared Latin model then produced Latin words, and per-sign and per-occurrence rescoring separated nulls and look-alike glyphs, confirmed on the image: a bold ∇ is s while a thin dotted ∇ is a null, and a tailed circle is p while a plain circle is h. Cattanei’s letters were broken the same way. A second transcription pass checked every sign against the image with the key in hand and made 209 corrections, splitting look-alikes (a slanted and a rounded b, i and o; η and 9). For the Forlì letter the key comes from the contemporary gloss, and every run was deciphered from its signs rather than from the faint gloss.

t: Cipher letters to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, 1428–1430 — Read
b: Pandolfo Malatesta, 22 April 1428 : 262 signs in three runs, not read (no key; see above). Rome, 9 August 1428 : the word code in “in filium [·]” (once), and about 60 signs in doubtful spans on lines 15, 19, 26, 28 and 31–35 (for example “habet [in] num[ero] de ve[..]”); grades M–I. Forlì, 6 November 1428 : two unglossed signs (one of them twice) and about 25 signs in doubtful words (“de Ianus(?) ubi(?)”, “dice cavad(?)”). Rome, 13 February 1430 : “leonebi … re[∂]bs” (l. 4), “a-mhi episcopus” (l. 14, expected archiepiscopus ), “debert onorio” (l. 20), “domicus” (l. 22); names read letter by letter but not identified: Trrusius(?), Berardelus, Bonifacius de Meana(?), Canedulum(?).

t: A Venetian ambassador at Rome to the Doge, 29 April 1628 — read in part
b: DECODE R1862 (ASVe Busta 27 f. 354), catalogued as an anonymous ciphered letter from Rome with no transcription and nothing known of its contents. Its cipher is the one in the sibling record R1874, which is imaged together with the chancery’s own decipherment; aligning that decipherment to its cipher by soft-EM rebuilt the key — a syllabary grid in which the prefix gives the vowel and the last two digits the consonant — and it reads this despatch unchanged. Cardinal Barberini had asked twice whether Palmanova was fortified and the Pontebba pass secured; the ambassador pressed that the Pope go in person as legate to settle Mantua and Savoy. 98.8% of the groups have a value and 91% stand in lines that read; thirteen word codes of the nomenclator band, and the four lines that turn on them, are still open. Rome → the Doge and Senate of Venice · numerical syllabary with word codes · 29 April 1628 · key rebuilt from a sibling, read in part A Venetian ambassador at Rome to the Doge, 29 April 1628 Archivio di Stato di Venezia, IT ASVe 0045 010 (Serie) Busta 27 f. 354 · DECODE R1862, four pages, catalogued Non-decrypted , with no transcription on the record and no sender, receiver or reading recorded The key was rebuilt from the sibling record R1874, whose contemporary decipherment is imaged beside its cipher, and applied here unchanged · the despatch reports an audience with Cardinal Barberini in the first weeks of the War of the Mantuan Succession Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 22 September 2026 solved in part Summary. The catalogue listed this as an anonymous ciphered letter from Rome, 29 April 1628, with nothing known about what it hides: DECODE holds four images, no transcription, and no sender or recipient. The address “Ser.mo Principe” makes it a Venetian ambassador’s despatch to the Doge. Its cipher is the same one used in another ASVe record, R1874 (Alvise Mocenigo from Madrid, 26 October 1628), and that record is imaged together with the chancery’s own decipherment of it. Transcribing that decipherment as known plaintext and aligning it to the cipher by a soft-EM forward–backward pass recovered the key: a syllabary grid in which the prefix gives the vowel and the last two digits the consonant, with single letters, a small word list and paragraph marks beside it. Applied to R1862 unchanged, it reads. The ambassador had spoken with Cardinal Barberini , who had twice asked him whether Palma (Palmanova) was well fortified, what garrison it had, and whether the pass of the Pontebba was secured — questions the ambassador answered by asking, “con intiera confidenza”, to what end they were put. The rest relays the Cardinal on the Emperor, on Wallenstein’s price for coming into Italy, and on the imperial aulic council; and the ambassador pressing that the Pope go in person as legate to settle Mantua and Savoy together. Status: cipher broken, key rebuilt and extended, 98.8% of the code groups given a value, and 91% of them standing in lines that read as continuous Italian. What is still open is thirteen word codes of the nomenclator band and the four lines that turn on them.

t: A Venetian ambassador at Rome to the Doge, 29 April 1628 — read in part
h: The record, and the sibling that carried the key
b: DECODE R1862 is four images of a despatch at ASVe, Busta 27 f. 354, dated 29 April 1628 and placed at Rome. The record carries no transcription, no sender and no receiver, and the archive’s images are not in the public domain, so nothing of them is reproduced here. Cipher and clear text alternate on the page: page 1 and page 2 are almost entirely in figures, page 3 runs clear for eleven lines and then ciphers again, page 4 opens and closes in the clear with two ciphered blocks between. The way in was a sibling. DECODE R1874 (ASVe Busta 30 f. 174) is a despatch of Alvise Mocenigo from Madrid, 26 October 1628, in the same cipher; its sixteen images hold the ciphered despatch, a second enciphered copy of it, and — on images 8955–8959 — the chancery’s own decipherment , paragraph by numbered paragraph. That decipherment had never been used to recover the key: an earlier attempt on R1874 had read the letter from the decipherment and left the key unrebuilt.

t: A Venetian ambassador at Rome to the Doge, 29 April 1628 — read in part
b: The decipherment of R1874’s paragraphs 5 to 16 was transcribed here, about 4,800 letters of plaintext. DECODE’s transcription of R1874’s cipher was then split into five stretches matching those paragraphs — the ratio is a steady 1.84 letters per group — and each stretch aligned to its plaintext by a soft-EM forward–backward pass over monotone segmentations, sharpened each round until every group settled on one value. The solver was checked first on a synthetic syllabic cipher built over the same text, which it recovered exactly (97 of 97 groups). The first run on the real data collapsed, because a group was allowed to stand for nothing and the frequent groups went null; capping values at four letters and forbidding nulls fixed it. One detail decided the shape of the answer. DECODE’s transcriber wrote the figure 5 in two forms, as “13” and as “21”. Folding both to a single 5 gave a muddled key; keeping them apart — they are 51 and 53 in R1862’s clearer hand — made the table regular at once, because they are two different rows of it.

t: A Venetian ambassador at Rome to the Doge, 29 April 1628 — read in part
b: The cipher is a syllabary laid out as a grid . The prefix gives the vowel and the last two digits the consonant: vowels: 6 = a, 51 = e, 62 = i, 53 = o, 64 = u (61 is a second i/e row) consonants: 07 b, 08 c, 09 l, 10 d, 11 f, 13 g, 14 gn, 17 gr, 19 l, 20 m, 21 n, 22 p, 23 pr, 24 qu, 26 ss, 27 r, 28 s, 31 st, 33 t, 34 tr, 37 v, 38 z — so 6210 di , 5133 te , 5333 to , 6433 tu , 5308 co , 6220 mi single letters: 680 a, 6280 e, 6480 i, 5190 o, 6490 u, 692 n, 6292 r, 6482 l, 5390 s word codes: 670 che , 672 con , 6270 in , 6249 il , 5102 del , 5302 nel , 5124 and 5387 quel , 5384 qual ( che ), 5374 per , 5142 duca , 6440 sua , 6442 suo , 6240 ave , 5373 part , 6477 poc , 6287 non , 5347 papa , 6247 Cesare paragraph marks: 698, 5198, 5199 stand at the edges of the ciphered passages, as 6499 does in R1874 The word band is alphabetical. Above column 39 the codes of each prefix row run in alphabetical blocks — row 53 gives papa 47, part 73, per 74, piu 77, qual 84, quel 87, ques 88; row 64 gives signor 39, sua 40, suo 42. That brackets every code that is still open, and it is how several were read: 6274 falls just after in and is “molto” (“star molto oculati et avvertiti”), 5140 falls just below duca and is “dov” (“dovrian star”). It also caught three values inherited from the R1874 alignment that were wrong: 628 is sa , not “n” (“non sarian giamai”, “fatto sapere”); 6439 is signor , not “mini” (“Sua Signoria Illustrissima”, “il Signor Cardinal Barberino”); 6481 is a second i . The grid cells that R1874’s decipherment never reached were filled by the structure itself (a cell’s value is its column’s consonant plus its row’s vowel), and the word codes were read from context in this letter: 5384 by “cavar anche qualche intimo particolare”, 5347 by “a fin che il Papa deliberasse”, 6240 by “ ave ndomi ricercato”.

t: A Venetian ambassador at Rome to the Doge, 29 April 1628 — read in part
b: It opens in the clear and turns to cipher in the middle of the first line: Opportunissima occ.ne ho io havuta hieri col Cardinal Barberino di parlargli di quel negotio che lei mi si è commesso con cotesto Eccelso Conseglio, et di cavar anche qualche intimo particolare desiderato da lei… What the ambassador had been asked to find out, and what the Cardinal had asked him, are the heart of it. Twice the Cardinal had wanted to know …se Palma si era ben fortificava, […] o presidio aveva, se il passo della Pontebba si era ben assicurato… — that is, whether the Republic’s great fortress of Palmanova and the Alpine pass above Venice were ready. Hearing from other quarters that “Imperiali uniti con Spagna parlavano con molto sprezzo” of the Republic, the ambassador answered by asking, “con intiera confidenza”, whether the questions had been put “a qualche fine”, and begged that anything of the kind be told him, so that the Serenissima might know in time “perché da lei fossero trovati i rimedii oportuni” — but without naming “quelli che trattassero simili” matters. The rest of page 2 is the substance of the audience, and it turns on secrecy: such dealings “non sarian giamai […] palesi, ma ben sotto profondissima segretezza”, and the Cardinal spoke “aprendosi in co[nfidenti]ssima confidenza”. He had come by “particolar notitia de pensieri vasti”; of arms and men “che si trovavano in piedi nella Germania”, which left him “dubitando avessero qualche pensiero di molestare la Republica”; and he told the Cardinal that “quelli Signori dovrian star molto oculati et avvertiti”, so that he “non potei far di meno di non dimandarle” more. The Cardinal “interrogavami per dir il vero”, and the ambassador “mi sono andato certificando” that even if Spaniards and Imperialists had set “l’animo contro la Republica”, they “non sono in tu[tto]… effettuar i loro… disegni”. The clear paragraph at the foot of page 2 and the top of page 3 carries the Cardinal’s argument that Venice need not fear an imperial descent: the Emperor ha pur troppo che fare in casa propria , having to watch the King of Denmark, Bethlen Gabor, the Dutch and perhaps the Turk; Wallenstein would not come into Italy without his whole army, and quartering it would take gran summa d’oro, di che l’Imp.re n’ha gran carestia . The ciphered part of page 3 reports the Cardinal on the imperial aulic council , “nel qual, se ben la maggior parte de’ consiglieri sia aderente al Re di Spagna”, and that he shows himself “più tosto amorevole che difidente”. It ends with the Cardinal offering “un particolare da esserne gran ri[f]lesso” and asking, in the line that had been missed out of the transcription altogether, “la prego non nominarme” — do not name me as the source. Page 4, in the clear, lays the attempt on Genoa at the Duke of Savoy’s door, and argues that Spaniards and Imperialists, ill satisfied with him, will trust him less. Then, in cipher, the ambassador’s own move: …ringratiai il cardinale di co[sì] confidenti communicatione, et sopra […] l’ultimo del Duca di Sivoia presi ocasione di caricar la mano a fin che il Papa deliberasse mandar la sua persona legato […] per acomodar gli interessi di Mantova e di Savoia insieme… — pressing “la facilità che già si averia trovata nel Duca di Savoia di ridursi”, and the glory for His Holiness of “questa opportunità di dar pace”. The last ciphered lines return to the Cardinal, who “have dato il sudetto aviso… di Genova”. All of this is late April 1628: Vincenzo II Gonzaga was dead, Nevers was in Mantua, Spain and Savoy had agreed to partition Monferrato, and Urban VIII’s nephew was running a papal policy of professed neutrality.

t: A Venetian ambassador at Rome to the Doge, 29 April 1628 — read in part
h: How the transcription was made, and what is still open
b: The record has no transcription, so the 1,274 code groups were read off the images here and then checked, line by line, with the key in hand: a line that does not decipher into Italian is a line to look at again. Five passes of that kind were run. Two traps in this hand mattered: a final n-shape is a 2 , not a 1, and a 7 is a “>” with a long open tail while an 8 is a hook plus a closed loop. Page 2’s lines bow by up to 35 px, and two of its transcribed rows turned out to have been blended from the head of one physical line and the tail of another, with a third row belonging to no line at all; tracking the baselines and re-splitting fixed the alignment, and the join it produced — “andavo dubitando avessero qualche pi | nsiero” across two lines — is its own confirmation. Eleven passes of that kind were run in all, and two of them changed the shape of the text: one manuscript line on page 3 had never been transcribed at all (it reads “la prego non nominarme” — I beg you not to name me ), and the lines slope enough that a fixed horizontal band picks up the neighbour’s ink on the right-hand side, which is what produced the blends. What remains: fifteen group tokens (1.2%) have no value — 6478 and 5386 twice each, and 5349, 5389, 5370, 51708, 683, 5378, 5379, 6279, 5189, 699, 6241 once each. All of them sit in the word and name band, the part R1874’s decipherment does not cover, so only another letter in this cipher will settle them; none is digitised on DECODE, and the Venetian key registers that are (the Codice Amadi and the Busta 4 registers) are all of the previous century. Four lines — P1 L17, P2 L17, P2 L22, P2 L26 — are image-true after three independent readings each and still give no sense: they turn on those codes, or on the clerk’s own slips, for he writes sivoia for Savoia, germinia for Germania, dovore for dovere. The ambassador himself is still anonymous: he does not name himself, and the Calendar of State Papers Venetian, which calendars only the England-related despatches, has nothing from Rome for 29 April 1628. The reading was measured, not asserted: each line’s decipherment is scored against an Italian character model of the period, calibrated on genuine Italian of the same length taken from R1874’s decipherment (real text of this length falls below −2.25 per character only 5% of the time), and scored with the edges of its neighbours so that a word split across a line end is not counted against it. By that measure 91% of the code groups stand in lines that read ; a stricter 25-character sliding window gives 86%, the difference being the clerk’s own spelling.

Madrid → Doge and Senate of Venice · numerical syllabic cipher, Italian · 26 October 1628 · read at the time; decipherment in the same record Mocenigo to the Doge, Madrid 1628 — read at the time to Doge Giovanni Cornaro Archivio di Stato di Venezia, IT ASVe 0045 010 Busta 30 f. 174; DECODE R1874. Catalogued as an undated ciphered letter from an unknown sender to an unknown recipient. It is a despatch of Alvise Mocenigo, Venetian ambassador in Spain, dated Madrid, 26 October 1628. The Venetian chancery’s decipherment of it is imaged in the same record. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 21 September 2026 resolved Summary. The 16 images of R1874 hold four things. The first is the despatch, clear paragraphs alternating with paragraphs in a numerical cipher (images 8951–8954). The second is a clerk’s decipherment of the whole letter, with paragraphs numbered 6 to 9 in the margin (8955–8959). The third is a second copy of the despatch, enciphered separately and dated “Madrid li 26 Ott:re 1628” (8960–8964). The last is the address leaf, followed by a deciphered page of the next despatch, of 29 October. The clear text names the sender and date: Spinola lodging with his son-in-law Leganés, the English beaten off La Rochelle, Monterrey at Genoa. So does the Calendar of State Papers, Venice , vol. 21, no. 515, whose clear opening is the same sentence. Its “italics deciphered” passage (Cottington’s journey to Madrid dropped after Buckingham’s death, Endymion Porter waiting for orders, Rubens negotiating a truce with the Dutch) is on the decipherment page 8958. The decipherment was checked against the cipher in two ways. The cipher’s paragraph mark 6499 splits it into the decipherment’s paragraphs 6 and 7 at a steady two letters per group. And the one run of groups that occurs three times, 672 2133 6210 2190 62x9 637 2127, falls where “conte di Olivares” falls, at 26, 71 and 92 per cent of the paragraph against 25, 70 and 91 per cent. The key, a syllabic nomenclator, was not rebuilt.

It gives the whole letter in clear, clear passages included, with the ciphered paragraphs numbered 6, 7, 8 and 9. 8960–8964 : a second copy, enciphered with different groups (1,405 against 840 for the same text), dated “Madrid li 26 Ott:re 1628”. t: Mocenigo to the Doge, Madrid 1628 — read at the time
b: The groups are numbers written as clusters. The looped sign that looks like b is the period’s 6, and the s -like sign is a 5, which DECODE’s transcription renders as “13” or “21”. Every group has the form 5 or 6, then an optional 1–4, then two digits. After the first digit only 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8 and 9 occur. The two copies have about 2,245 groups of 355 kinds. The group 6499 marks the edges of the numbered paragraphs. Each group stands for about two letters of plaintext: paragraph 6 (“Et già si è publicato… di ogni gran Casa di Spagna”) has 386 groups for about 760 letters, and paragraph 7 (“Continuo io… in alcun tempo”) has 245 for about 445. That makes it a syllabic cipher or nomenclator, not a simple homophonic alphabet. Solving it from the ciphertext alone failed. Letter-by-letter homophonic annealing against a Renaissance Italian model gave gibberish, although the same solver reads a synthetic Italian homophonic cipher of the same size without error. Treating whole prefix classes as nulls did not help either. A monotone alignment of the groups against the decipherment, seeded with the Olivares runs, settled into even two-letter splits and taught nothing. Rebuilding the key would need a fresh, group-exact transcription and more anchors.

t: Mocenigo to the Doge, Madrid 1628 — read at the time
b: The two ciphered paragraphs checked against the cipher, from the decipherment (8955–8956): [6] Et già si è publicato, che seguirà anco il Re alla giornata, persistendo l’Ecc.mo nelle prime risolutioni, che il Re ò abbracci le tregue, overo le faccia assignam.ti pronti, effettivi, et sufficienti per le imprese necessarie. Il Conte di Olivares ha desiderato con buone parole, et promesse condurlo à risolutione di ritornar in Fiandra; anco con qualche violente termine lo hà procurato, ma il Marchese constantem.te è stato ne’ primi propositi, nè hà potuto non ricever molti disgusti. Continuano quelli delli conti, che le sono dimandati, et quello che più lo affligge è haver dato sua figlia in moglie à Don Diego Messia, il quale è mantenuto dal Conte di Olivares nel posto di auttorità et gratia che haveva prima, se le diminuisse la speranza del titolo di Grande, et resta la figliola con minor fortuna di quella che senza il favore del Conte di Olivares poteva conseguire con il parentado di ogni gran Casa di Spagna. [7] Continuo io nelli affari propri con molti soldati di S. M.tà, li quali si offerseno di nuovo al servitio della Ser.ma; alcuni sono officiali di molta esperienza, et con tanto maggior affetto le corrispondo; sono la maggior parte Napolitani de’ terzi reformati… et però certa cosa, che il Re non può render tutti contenti, et molti con ragione si vegono abbandonati, et altri senza le sodisfattioni de’ proprij crediti, et desperati di poter li conseguire in alcun tempo. That is: it is given out that the King will go on campaign. Spinola holds to his first position, that the King must either accept the truce with the Dutch or give him ready and sufficient funds for the campaign. Olivares has tried fair words and harsher means to send him back to Flanders, and has failed. Spinola is also harried over his accounts, and grieved that he married his daughter to Diego Mesía, whom Olivares keeps in favour while holding back the grandeeship. Paragraph 7 reports Mocenigo’s recruiting of officers left unpaid by Philip IV, most of them Neapolitans from disbanded tercios , for the service of the Republic. Paragraphs 8 and 9 (8957–8959) cover Savoy’s campaign against Genoa over Oneglia and Ormea, Cottington’s cancelled journey, Rubens, Catalonia and Valencia, and Savoy’s bid for the government of Milan. Grades: the decipherment is contemporary (H). The transcription above is a first reading from the scans. Two words are doubtful (M): “prime risolutioni” and “terzi reformati”.

t: Foscarini to the Doge, Escorial 1761 — read at the time
b: DECODE R1875, catalogued as a ciphered letter from an unnamed sender in Spain to an unknown recipient, is despatch no. 178 of Sebastiano Foscarini, Venetian ambassador at the court of Charles III, written at the Escorial on 13 October 1761. The chancery deciphered it on the despatch itself, between the lines and on the facing pages, and barred out every cipher line. The letter reads in full: Madrid’s view of the broken-off Anglo-French peace talks, and a union with “another court” — the secret Family Compact. Escorial → Doge and Senate of Venice · numerical cipher, Italian · 13 October 1761 · read at the time; decipherment on the despatch Foscarini to the Doge, Escorial 1761 — read at the time Archivio di Stato di Venezia, IT ASVe 0045 010 (Serie) Busta 30 f. 178; DECODE R1875. Catalogued as a ciphered letter from “…” in Spain to an unknown recipient, 13 October 1761. It is despatch no. 178 of Sebastiano Foscarini, Venetian ambassador at the court of Charles III, written at the Escorial. The Venetian chancery deciphered it on the despatch itself and struck the cipher through. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 21 September 2026 resolved Summary. The six images of R1875 show a despatch enciphered almost from its first line. Every cipher line is struck through with a heavy ink bar. On page 1 the chancery clerk wrote the decipherment between the barred lines. For the cipher at the foot of page 1 and on pages 2 and 5 he wrote it on the facing pages 3 and 4, which begin with the catch-words “dell’Ecc.mo Senato” and end with “Sono per ogni conto”. The clear close on page 5 picks up from those words, and the letter is signed “Dall’Escoriale 13. Ottobre 1761. Sebastian Foscarini Amb.r”. The address leaf is docketed as received on 2 November. Foscarini’s cipher practice is described on crittologia.eu: the decipherment written on the despatch, and the cipher barred so that no one could rebuild the key by comparing the two. The letter reports Madrid’s reading of the broken-off Anglo-French peace talks. Spain, the best-informed said, could no longer stand aside while France lost America, and a union with “another court” was in view. This was the Family Compact with France, signed in secret that August. The whole letter reads (312 words in cipher). The key was not rebuilt.

t: Foscarini to the Doge, Escorial 1761 — read at the time
b: From the chancery decipherment, with abbreviations as written: Com’ebbi l’onore di rassegnare a VV. EE. mercordì S. M.a e tutta la Reale famiglia si sono trasferiti in questo soggiorno. La poca distanza di ove io pure mi sono condotto, animato dal mio rispettosissimo desiderio di manifestare a V.a Ser.tà in ogni miglior guisa il vero impegno della mia buona volontà, e mosso dalla torbida configurazione de’ tempi presenti, i quali esigono tutta la maggior vigilanza, come avrebbero bisogno di una mente illuminata ed attiva per agevolarsi il camino al conoscim.to di quei maneggi, i quali per tutti i riguardi possono interessare la sapienza dell’Ecc.mo Senato. Le sciolte negoziazioni fra le Corti di Londra e di Versaglies sono la fonte da cui scaturiscono infinite congietture e sistemi politici. Li soggetti più sensati e meglio conoscitori delle massime de’ Principi e del vero interesse di questa Corona sono nella ferma persuasione che ella non potrà più oltre riguardare con indifferenza nell’intiera sconfitta del Christianissimo nell’America negli immensi acquisti che avevano fatti, e che vie più possono aggiungersi all’Inghilterra nelle sue poderose forze del mare. Questi raggionam.ti trovano molti seguaci ma non sono atti ad estinguere il peso di quelli i quali esaminando diligentem.te lo stato militare e maritimo e la forza dell’erario di questo Monarca, le pacifiche disposizioni del suo animo e il genio de’ suoi Ministri, credono difficile il caso che possa uscire dalla massima sin ad ora professata. Quindi questi due ultimi obbietti vengono distrutti con la risoluzione che non sempre i Principi e i Ministri loro possono servire al proprio piacere, ma che la necessità impone bene spesso la legge e abbatte tutti li più opposti dissegni, e passando con ciò a dimostrare l’urgenza e la copia dei mali giungono perfino a riflettere sulla costituzione di alcuna altra Corte, e credono agevole il caso di una congiunzione atta a sostenere li vicendevoli interessi. [clear:] Sono per ogni conto rispettabili li autori di questi pensamenti, ma io non posso produrli all’Ecc.mo Sen.to che spogli di qualunque autorità, quanto mi sembrano degni di tutta quell’attenzione ch’io prometto a VV. EE. anche in questo grave proposito. Grazie. Dall’Escoriale 13. Ottobre 1761. Sebastian Foscarini Amb.r In English: the King and the royal family moved to the Escorial on Wednesday, and Foscarini has followed them, the better to follow events in troubled times. The broken-off negotiations between London and Versailles give rise to endless conjecture. The most judicious observers think Spain can no longer look on with indifference at France’s complete defeat in America, at the vast conquests England has made there, and at the further gains its sea power may bring. Others, weighing the King’s army, navy and treasury, his peaceable nature and the temper of his ministers, doubt that he will depart from the policy he has followed so far. The first group answers that necessity often overrides the wishes of princes and ministers, and after setting out the urgency of the danger they go so far as to consider the position of another court, expecting a union to defend common interests. Foscarini passes these views on “stripped of any authority”, but worth the Senate’s attention. Grades: the decipherment is contemporary (H). Two words struck out by the clerk on page 3 and replaced between the lines by “nel” and “negli” are his corrections, not text.

t: Foscarini to the Doge, Escorial 1761 — read at the time
b: The cipher is written as runs of digits, with groups separated by points and many of them ending in 6, 7 or 9. It has nothing in common with the 1628 syllabic cipher of R1874 in the same busta. According to crittologia.eu, eighteenth-century Venetian ciphers had dropped the old code dictionary and kept only an alphabet and an orderly syllabary. About 37 barred lines carry 1,565 letters of plaintext. The bars cover much of each digit, so a group-exact transcription, and with it the key, was not attempted: the reading does not depend on it.

Germany → an officer of the Orange troops · 6×6 digit square with word signs · c. 1795 · read in part A son of William V on the rassemblement: the “non-decrypted” letter of R1892 Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V, inv. 339 (DECODE R1892), two pages catalogued as an unsolved letter of “1 January 1795” from an unknown writer. Each letter is a pair of digits 1–6 written one above the other. The square was recovered from the ciphertext alone and reads both pages, the first in French, the second a Dutch postscript. Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 21 September 2026 solved in part Summary. DECODE lists R1892 as a non-decrypted two-page letter to Prince William V, in “graphic signs, numerical”, and an archivist’s note on the photocopy says no nomenclator was found. The figures are a 6×6 square: every letter is a vertical pair of digits from 1 to 6, top over bottom. Both pages were transcribed from the DECODE images (1,829 pairs). A quadgram annealer on the Dutch page recovered the square without a crib, and the same square then read the French page straight off. The writer is a son of the Stadholder (“mon père”, “mon frère”), instructing the officer in charge of the Dutch émigré troops gathered in Germany: if General Dundas stops their pay or orders them to embark, accept it and ask only for a gratuity for those who will not submit; tell the troops on what footing they will enter the service of His Britannic Majesty. The most frequent sign is de ; three more are probably zich , te and ik ; about twenty rare signs and one faded line stay unread.

t: A son of William V on the émigré rassemblement, c. 1795 — the “non-decrypted” R1892 is a 6×6 digit square
b: Page 1 (French) Decipherment, word-divided and lightly normalised; [·] marks a graphic sign. … écrit en cognito … du … en date du … décembre. Mon père chargeant Nagel d’aller [·] nouveau chez les ministres pour insister sur une réponse quelconque aux différentes représentations qui leur ont été faites touchant … du rassemblement, je me flatte qu’enfin … en viendra une; mais comme il pourroit arriver entretemps que le général Dundas vous déclarât qu’il cesseroit le payement, ou bien que les troupes devroient se laisser embarquer, il faudroit y souscrire et vous borner uniquement à tâcher d’obtenir [·] pouvoir donner une gratification à ceux qui ne voudroient se soumettre dans ce cas … Je vous prie cependant [·] donner connaissance aux troupes du pied sur lequel elles entreront au service [·] S.M.B., et vous pourrez leur donner à cet effet une pièce à peu près semblable à celle qui étoit destinée à leur être donnée dans le premier moment où il étoit question [·] leur embarquement. Vous pourrez trouver cette pièce parmi mes papiers, et vous pourrez y faire les changements que vous jugerez convenables vu les circonstances présentes. Ayez la bonté [·] ne point mettre sur le compte … la dépense pour mon logement, ne voulant pas … être dans le cas d’avoir la moindre obligation, mais [·] le payer [·] l’argent que vous avez à moi appartenant. “Nagel” is A. W. C. van Nagell, the Orange envoy in London; the cipher spells the general’s name Vundas , a slip for Dundas; S.M.B. is Sa Majesté Britannique. Page 2 (Dutch postscript) … in het geval … het rassemblement te zamen te houden … die vrijwillig … te laten … de officieren … en benoemen die … het zelve … willen aangesteld … alle heeren officieren … kunnen weten … geene die hier … willen geëmployeerd … en geeven tegen … bepaalde dagen … dan zelve keus maken in … nemen … het mogelijk is alleen … die hun in zedert het intrekken der Fransche niet geboden hebben; indien zich hoofdofficieren genoeg bij … ieder [1000] man kunnen plaatsen … wat in cijffer schrijf … naam … mijn nader … ons tot nog toe niet tegenstaan alle stellingen die gedaan … antwoord te … reeds weken … mijn eerste … toen zou … mij zeker niet gesteld hebben; tegenwoordig nog hier te … op antwoord te wachten … welverzekerd … mij niets … engageeren … veel liever … gebleven was … mijn gesteld is geweest had willen mededeelen. Le prince [·] me marque en outre … vous aurez la bonté de communiquer le contenu de ce chiffre à mon frère. The postscript opens with “den generaal Bertincy” (probably Bentinck). The postscript deals with keeping the corps together, naming and placing the officers, giving those who will not serve a fixed number of days to choose, and the writer’s weeks without an answer to his first letter.

t: A son of William V on the émigré rassemblement, c. 1795 — the “non-decrypted” R1892 is a 6×6 digit square
b: The writer calls William V “mon père” and asks that the cipher be shown to “mon frère”, so he is one of the Stadholder’s two sons, the Hereditary Prince or Prince Frederick. The addressee is an officer managing the rassemblement , the Dutch troops who followed the House of Orange into Germany in British pay after the French conquest of January 1795. DECODE’s “1 January 1795” is the file’s date; the letter cites a despatch “en date du … décembre” and discusses the corps’ transfer to British service and embarkation, which fits the winter of 1795–96. “To William V” in the record reflects where the letter is kept, not its addressee.

t: A son of William V on the émigré rassemblement, c. 1795 — the “non-decrypted” R1892 is a 6×6 digit square

J. A. Sillem’s biography of Dirk van Hogendorp describes how the envoy, dissatisfied with Chancellor Alexander Vorontsov’s response, sought another channel to place Batavian interests before Emperor Alexander I. He approached General Jan Pieter van Suchtelen, a Dutch-born officer who commanded the Russian engineers, enjoyed the emperor’s confidence and saw him daily. Authenticated DECODE access also found the matching 1803 codebook, R1035, whose marked three-digit groups have the same form as the letter. Status: the subject and argument are identified with high confidence from print, but no exact code-group alignment or diplomatic plaintext is claimed.

t: Hogendorp to Van der Goes, 5 July 1803 — the Van Suchtelen channel identified from print
b: J. A. Sillem narrates Hogendorp’s first approaches in St Petersburg on pp. 151–153 of his biography. Dispatch no. 10 of 5 July supplied the argument for a Russo-Batavian commercial treaty: Russia should have an immediate interest in the Batavian Republic’s continued existence as an independent state, and concluding the treaty would demonstrate that interest. Vorontsov was not persuaded. Sillem continues: Hogendorp vond zijne houding althans “zo wonderlijk” dat hij naar andere kanalen zocht om den Keizer onze belangen voor te dragen. Hij meende een gelukkigen greep gedaan te hebben door de tusschenkomst in te roepen van den Generaal van Suchtelen, Nederlander van geboorte, die in russischen dienst tot Opperbevelhebber der genie was opgeklommen, en het volste vertrouwen genoot van Czaar Alexander, met wien hij dagelijks omging. The footnote attached to that passage reads: “Rijksarchief. Dep. van denzelfden dag No. 12 gecijferd.” In English: “National Archives. Dispatch of the same day, no. 12, ciphered.” The manuscript supplies No. 12 ; Sillem supplies the content; and his preceding note fixes “the same day” as 5 July 1803.

t: Hogendorp to Van der Goes, 5 July 1803 — the Van Suchtelen channel identified from print
b: The secure reading is at the level of subject and argument. Vorontsov’s attitude and answer struck Hogendorp as so strange that he sought another route to the emperor. He chose Van Suchtelen because the general’s Dutch origin, senior position and daily access to Alexander made him a plausible intermediary. The object was to place the Batavian Republic’s interests—and in context its independent survival and the desired commercial treaty—before the emperor by a channel outside the chancellor. A concise English reconstruction is: Chancellor Vorontsov’s attitude and answer appeared so strange to me that I sought another way to bring our interests to the emperor’s attention. I believe I have found it in General Van Suchtelen, Dutch by birth, commander of the engineers in Russian service, who enjoys Emperor Alexander’s full confidence and sees him daily. This is an editorial paraphrase of Sillem’s account, not a quotation from a deciphered text. Connectives, spelling, the exact request made of Van Suchtelen and any material Sillem omitted remain unknown.

R1944 is the Batavian chargé d’affaires Etienne Bourdeaux’s dispatch no. 16 from Berlin, 31 January 1801, set almost entirely in three-digit groups with superposed marks. The authenticated DECODE scans of R1944 show only the cipher. The third image of the neighbouring record R1946 (Bourdeaux, 7 February 1801) is a clear sheet headed N°. 16 , dated Berlyn 31 January 1801 and signed “(get.) Bourdeaux”. The archive’s stamped folio numbers run on: 294 on the cipher and 295 on the clear sheet. The clear text is about 90 words against about 110 code groups, which fits a codebook with whole-word entries. It reports that Rosenkrantz, sent away from St Petersburg, says he does not know why; he supposes a servant took and copied his cipher. The Prussian envoy Lusi says more definitely that the desk holding it had been forced. That is why a Mr Schuer was to have carried a new cipher to Petersburg. The code groups have not been aligned to the text, and the key has not been identified.

t: Bourdeaux to Van der Goes, 31 January 1801 — the clear copy, misfiled under another record
b: N°. 16. Berlyn 31 January 1801. De Heer van Rosencrantz verzekert de eigentlyke oorzaak van zyn renvoy te ignoreeren. Hy veronderstelt dat zyn Cyffer door middel van een bediende is genomen, en gecopieerd geworden, waar door dan zyne Gevoelens zyn bekend geworden. — Vry positiever meldt Lusy, dat het bureau, waar in zyn Cyffer was, is geforceerd geworden. — Het is om die reden, dat men den Heer Schuer, in N°. 13 gementionneerd, heeft willen naar Petersburg zenden om een nieuw Cyffer over te brengen. (get.) Bourdeaux Translation. Mr van Rosencrantz assures us that he does not know the real cause of his dismissal. He supposes that his cipher was taken by a servant and copied, and that his views became known that way. Lusi reports, much more definitely, that the desk in which his cipher was kept had been forced open. That is why they had wanted to send Mr Schuer, mentioned in no. 13, to Petersburg to carry a new cipher. The people are identified from context, not from print (grade C). Rosencrantz is most likely the Danish diplomat Niels Rosenkrantz, whom Paul I sent away from St Petersburg at the end of 1800. Lusy is Count Spiridon Lusi, the Prussian envoy there. Schuer is not identified.

Daniel Bourdeau · read 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. DECODE lists R2232 as an unread homophonic cipher letter from an unidentified Wolff at The Hague to Wilhelmina of Prussia, wife of the exiled Stadholder William V. The next record, R2233, is Wolff’s covering letter of 8 September 1801 with “la clef ci-jointe”: 45 numbered rows, each holding four consecutive values of one running sequence of fractions, digits and letters. A group is a row number with a superscript 1–4, so every letter has up to four homophones. Applied as it stands, the key reads the whole letter at the first attempt. Wolff says he wrote a plan, sent to the Princess and to the King of Prussia in the spring of 1798, for a landing at Le Havre with a bombardment of Paris and a second landing in Holland. He had offered the late Prince Frederick several thousand men of the Swiss brigade in a letter sent the morning of 14 September 1795, the day he was arrested, and spent 39 months and 5 days in prison. He now offers his services again and asks her to obtain British half-pay for him from the day of his arrest. A few groups are one place off from slips, and a few words of the clear text were not transcribed.

t: Wolff to Princess Wilhelmina, 25 July 1801 — the “non-decrypted” R2232 reads with the key he sent after it
b: The opening of R2232 (rotated): the clear “j’ai l’honneur de LUI exposer ce qui suit”, then the cipher, which starts “je suis l’auteur d’un plan”. Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Wilhelmina Prinses van Pruisen (A32) inv. 192, first page (image P2), via DECODE R2232. The three DECODE images are out of order. The letter begins on image 2 (“Madame! Je demande Grace à Votre Altesse Royale, du mystérieux que je mets dans cette Correspondance”), continues on image 3 and ends on image 1 with the date “La Haye ce 25 juillet 1801” and a ciphered signature. The clear framing sentences, the forms of address and some whole sentences are in clear; the substance is in numbers. DECODE R2233, the key sent with Wolff’s letter of 8 September 1801. Row 1 = 0 ⅛ ¼ ½, row 5 = 1 2 3 4, row 15 = a b c d, row 45 = i o u a. Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Wilhelmina Prinses van Pruisen (A32) inv. 192, via DECODE R2233. The key lists one sequence, 0 ⅛ ¼ ½ 1 2 … 9 à a b c … n ô o p q r s t û u v w x y z a e i o u a , in overlapping windows of four: row N holds values N to N +3. The writer picks a row and marks the place in it with a superscript; a bare number means the first place. So a can be written 15, 14², 13³ or 12⁴, and the vowels at the end of the sequence give a, e, i, o more choices still. DECODE’s note on R2233 describes the system correctly, but neither record gives a reading.

t: Wolff to Princess Wilhelmina, 25 July 1801 — the “non-decrypted” R2232 reads with the key he sent after it
b: Ciphered passages in brackets; spelling lightly modernised. Madame! Je demande grâce à Votre Altesse Royale du mystérieux que je mets dans cette correspondance; l’importance de sa matière m’y contraint. Je crois être sûr que ma lettre du 1er de juin est bien parvenue, et j’ai l’honneur de lui exposer ce qui suit. [Je suis l’auteur d’un plan qui a été envoyé à] Votre Altesse Royale et [au roi à Berlin en mars ou avril 1798, lorsque j’étais dans les villes anséatiques, d’un rassemblement … une descente au Havre de Grâce, et fait le bombardement de Paris; une autre en Hollande; un corps attaque l’Yssel et le reste opère sur le continent; de la pacification de ce pays-ci; d’un nouveau genre de commander des armées combinées], et d’autres choses trop longues pour être transcrites ici, et qui finit par le vœu de pouvoir faire comme [Coriolan]. Puisque cette pièce a été faite après [la paix] de [Campo Formio], et que les circonstances se ressemblent, je n’ai pas voulu manquer de me faire connaître, pour offrir très-humblement mes faibles services, pour co-opérer à son exécution en général, et spécialement dans l’endroit où j’aurais déjà alors voulu me voir employé … Outre cela j’ai [offert à feu le prince Frédéric de lui amener quelques milles hommes de la brigade suisse avec l’élite des officiers, par une lettre que j’ai expédiée le matin du 14 septembre 1795, jour que je fus arrêté; sans cet accident je serais entré alors à la solde de l’Angleterre, je n’aurais point soupiré 39 mois et 5 jours dans la prison, et je ne serais pas dans le besoin où je me trouve à présent. Je ne veux pas offusquer le mérite des autres]; mais s’il m’est permis de le dire, je crois pouvoir me flatter d’avoir aussi mérité en quelque façon [pour la bonne cause], que je ne suis pas indigne pour implorer la [générosité bienfaisante du gouvernement britannique] pour en obtenir la [demi-paye] depuis le jour de [mon arrestation; j’avais comme quartier-maître 50 florins] par [mois] courant, [ou un secours] conforme à sa [magnanimité] … … Daignez, Madame, m’accorder cette grâce avec la même bienveillance qu’il a plu à Votre Altesse Royale de s’intercéder pour moi, lorsque j’ai eu l’honneur de m’adresser à Elle en [1791, à Berlin] … et agréez [de disposer de moi …, lui fournir des occasions où je puisse donner des preuves de ma reconnaissance], ainsi que de [mon adhérence à la bonne cause], et de [mon attachement] aussi [sincère] que très [profondément respectueux à la personne et à la maison] de Votre Altesse Royale, dont [les ordres pourront me parvenir] par cette [même voie sans adresse], avec [3 marques ▽] … [Wolff]. La Haye ce 25 juillet 1801. In short: a royalist who had been in the Hanseatic towns in 1798 claims authorship of a two-pronged invasion plan against France and the Batavian Republic sent to the Princess and to Frederick William III. With peace in the air again in 1801, he offers to help carry it out. He recalls an offer of Swiss troops to Prince Frederick of Orange (d. 1799), cut short by his arrest on 14 September 1795 and a 39-month imprisonment, and asks the Princess to get him British half-pay as a former quartermaster.

t: An Orangist at Basle to William V, 17 August 1796 — the “non-decrypted” R2234 reads with its own key sheet
b: DECODE R2234, one page in the papers of Prince William V catalogued as an unread homophonic letter. The key sheet R2235 in the same file gives five alphabets, D, G, L, N and R; the letter changes alphabet on every line, starting from the capital that opens each section. Read that way, a correspondent at Basle asks for money and a decision on his lodging and reports on Salm’s hussars, Barthélemy, Degelmann and the French armies of Italy and the Rhine. Basle → William V in exile · five alphabets, one per line · 17 August 1796 · read An Orangist at Basle writes to the Stadholder, 1796 to William V Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V, inv. 339 (DECODE R2234, “non-decrypted”, “homophonic”). One page in letters, dated in clear “30 thermidor an 4 de la Rép. franç. / 17 août vieux style”. Read with the key sheet R2235 filed in the same inventory number. Daniel Bourdeau · read 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. DECODE lists R2234 as an unread homophonic letter from an unknown writer to William V. Its own note suggested that the seven capitals down the left margin match a key of five alphabets in the same file; that key, R2235, is a printed pair of tables ( Schrijf Tafel and Translateur Tafel ) with alphabets labelled D, G, L, N and R. The capital sets the alphabet of the first line of a section, and each following line moves to the next alphabet in the order D–G–L–N–R. With that rule the whole letter reads in French. The writer, living at Basle under Republican dating, asks for a letter by 4 September and a bill of 50 louis each quarter, reports that the Prince of Salm is raising hussars for Prussia on condition they pass to the Prince of Orange, fears the Prussian ministers are being lulled by the French, and passes on what Barthélemy’s secretary and Degelmann say about the armies of Italy and the Rhine. A few words stay doubtful because of my transcription, and the clear signature is not read. The pencil note “Tollius” on the leaf is an archival attribution I did not test.

t: An Orangist at Basle to William V, 17 August 1796 — the “non-decrypted” R2234 reads with its own key sheet
b: The head of R2234 (rotated): the section capital D, the date in clear, and the first lines. Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 339, via DECODE R2234. The key, R2235, has two sheets. The Schrijf Tafel (writing table) gives, for each of D, G, L, N, R, the cipher letter for each of the 25 plain letters a–z without j. The Translateur Tafel is the same five rows as inverses. The rows are built in pairs: D and R undo each other, G and N undo each other, and L is its own inverse, so the second sheet is the first with its labels swapped. DECODE R2235, the Schrijf Tafel : five enciphering alphabets. Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 339, via DECODE R2235. The letter uses the key in a way the tables do not state. The first line of the first section reads under D (“gasoez ma 12” = “depuis le 12”), but the second line does not. Trying all five alphabets on lines 2 to 5 showed that they read under G, L, N and R, in that order. Each line starts with a dash, and a new capital in the margin (D, G, L, N, R, D, G) restarts the cycle at that alphabet. Word division, figures and punctuation stay in clear. DECODE’s “homophonic” label is wrong: it is a five-alphabet cipher that changes alphabet line by line.

t: An Orangist at Basle to William V, 17 August 1796 — the “non-decrypted” R2234 reads with its own key sheet
b: The corrected French, one line of the letter to a line; the alphabet of each line is in brackets. […] marks words spoilt by my transcription. [D] Depuis le 12 juillet je n’ai pas reçu de vos nouvelles; quel silence! J’attends [G] sans faute une lettre pour le 4 septembre, […] ou à [L] renoncer ou à reprendre ma maison pour 3 mois, mon bail finissant le 4 octobre. [N] Il me faut aussi vers ce temps-là une nouvelle lettre de change de 50 louis, et cela de 3 en 3 [R] mois, pour subvenir à l’horrible cherté de ce séjour; et j’en suis aux derniers […] [G] […]. Un officier d’état-major venu à Bâle dit qu’il est [L] d’un régiment de hussards que le prince de Salm lève pour le roi de Prusse [N] sous condition de rentrer au service du prince d’Orange quand il retournera en [R] Hollande; c’est une imprudence d’en [parler] ici. Mandez-moi ce qui en est; je me recommanderais [L] pour y en faire autant. Par contre on assure que le prince aura Hambourg(?), le pays […] [N] de […] Osnabruck. Cela est-il vrai? J’ai peur que les ministres prussiens ne se laissent [R] endormir comme à l’ordinaire par les belles paroles des Français, qui n’ont pas le [dessein de] voir [N] autre chose que bien s’ancrer sur les 2 rives du Rhin. […] et Barthélemy [R] ne m’invite plus, depuis que l’on m’a mis, je ne sais pourquoi, dans la gazette de Hambourg du 5 [R] juillet, ou depuis 2 malles prises. Son secrétaire me disait hier que dans un mois on [D] s’attendait à la jonction de l’armée d’Italie à celle du Rhin par le Tyrol; cela ne ressemble [G] pas à la paix. Degelmann n’y croit pas et ne sait rien. [L] Il est venu hier un courrier français d’Italie; rien n’a transpiré: donc [N] mauvaise nouvelle pour eux. Ce qu’on écrit de Bâle de passages de courriers […] [R] d’envoyer des mensonges. Mais s’il y avait un congrès, je ne pourrais y rien faire sans [G] être aperçu. [in clear] Salut et fraternité [signature] In English, in brief. No letter since 12 July; he needs an answer by 4 September on whether to keep his house for three more months, the lease ending on 4 October, and a bill for 50 louis every quarter, Basle being ruinously dear. A staff officer at Basle says he belongs to a hussar regiment the Prince of Salm is raising for the King of Prussia, on condition that it pass into the Prince of Orange’s service when he returns to Holland. It is said that the prince will have Hamburg(?) and the country about Osnabrück. He fears the Prussian ministers will again be lulled by the French, who want only to hold both banks of the Rhine. Barthélemy, the French envoy, no longer invites him since he was named in the Hamburg gazette of 5 July; Barthélemy’s secretary expects the Army of Italy to join the Army of the Rhine through the Tyrol within a month, which does not look like peace; Degelmann, the Imperial envoy, does not believe it. A French courier from Italy has come and nothing has leaked, so the news is bad for the French.

t: Prince Frederick of Orange to his brother, 7 May 1795 — the “non-decrypted” R2242 reads with the R1892 key
b: DECODE R2242, four pages in the papers of King William I catalogued as an unread numerical substitution. The digit pairs are the square recovered for R1892, and it reads them unchanged; page 1 carries its own clear Dutch under the cipher, which confirms the key and a dozen word signs. The cipher pages report the scattered émigré troops, the Basel ratification and envoys sent to Paris. About twenty word signs remain unread. XVIII-3 (DECODE R2242), four pages: a short cipher with clear Dutch under it, a clear letter dated London 7 May 1795, and two pages of cipher. The digits are the same vertical pairs as in R1892, and that key reads them unchanged. Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 21 September 2026 read in part Summary. DECODE lists R2242 as a non-decrypted numerical substitution. Its own note guesses that the writer is Prince Frederick of Orange (1774–1799) writing to his elder brother, and that the cipher is linked to the “Rassemblement” letter R1892. It is. Each letter is again a pair of digits 1–6 written top over bottom, and the square recovered ciphertext-only for R1892 reads all three cipher pages without change. Page 1 checks the key independently: a contemporary hand wrote the clear Dutch under its four cipher lines, and it agrees word for word, giving the values of a dozen word signs as well. Pages 3 and 4 are one continuous Dutch text. It reports that the officers and troops are scattered with “geen de minste saamenhang”, that the ratification (of the Prussian Peace of Basel) was published before it had arrived, and that ministers and ambassadors were sent to Paris with it. It also says that “they” persist in not recognising the present government unless no “Robespierismus” is introduced. About twenty word signs on those pages stay unread, and the transcription from photographs of photocopies has doubtful pairs. Page 1. Four cipher lines, and below them the clear Dutch: “als deezen brief geleesen hebt, dan genoomen en gebraaden…”. Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Koning Willem I XVIII-3, p. 1, via DECODE R2242.

t: Prince Frederick of Orange to his brother, 7 May 1795 — the “non-decrypted” R2242 reads with the R1892 key
b: Read with the key; | marks an unread word sign, [ ] a restoration. … | onse alliansie met | geeft | ook verandering. Men heeft de officier[s] en de trouppes | wel | malkander gelegen … is | staat op veele der gedimitteerde offeciers te maaken; men zi[et] | niet veel | stellen. Ook is er geen de minste saamenhang tussen | [z]elve, zij [zijn] geheel verstrooijd … hooft … natuurlijk zoude | zig | zouden toonen hebben … de politiken ook | verslappen … op vertrouwen … men zig | niet te veel op[laten] … het point der coalitie met alle … men heeft de ratificatie ons met | gepubliceert, of schoon de ratificatie zelver nog niet gekoomen was … | Parijs | onse ministers … zijn nog | ambassadeurs gesonden om [de] ratificatie van onse | over te brengen … maar blijft persisteeren het tegenwoordig gouvernement niet te erkennen, dan zoo zij geen Robespierismus durven te introduceeren … zeer veel dispositie … is mijn respect … het geheele geselschap … groet mijn broe[der]. The news fits London in late April and early May 1795. Prussia had made peace with France at Basel on 5 April and ratified it that month; the Batavian Republic was negotiating the Treaty of The Hague (16 May); and the Orange émigré troops, dismissed or scattered after the flight of January, were the subject of R1892.

t: Prince Frederick of Orange to his brother, 7 May 1795 — the “non-decrypted” R2242 reads with the R1892 key

The transcription was made by a language model from photographs of photocopies. Several pairs are doubtful: p3 line 1 (“wat ze id men”), p4 line 8, and single letters in saamenhang , ministers and coalitie (grade C). The overall sense of pages 3–4 is H; individual clauses between signs are M. “Robespierismus” is clear (H); whose recognition of “the present government” is meant depends on an unread sign.

p: Informant to the Nevers household, June 1588
t: A Paris informant to the Nevers household, 6 and 9 June 1588 — read
b: BnF fr. 3976 ff. 133–134 (DECODE R3708), catalogued as an unknown sender to an unknown recipient, is the third letter of the court informant of ff. 62 and 131, with eighteen cipher runs and no decipherment. The key rebuilt for f. 62 read every run. Three weeks after the Barricades, the curés of Saint-André and Saint-Benoît are stirring up the people, La Chapelle carries the Hôtel de Ville’s decisions to Guise’s council, and the échevin Cotteblanche refuses to let the Arsenal’s guns go to Corbeil. His letter of 9 June (f. 139), glossed at the time, confirms the key run for run. Three pages of clear French with eighteen cipher runs and fifteen code numbers, and no decipherment. The informant is the one who wrote ff. 62 and 131 of the same volume, and the key rebuilt from those letters read all eighteen runs.
