Daniel Bourdeau · read 22 September 2026 read Informant to the Nevers household, 6 and 9 June 1588 — Read 7 δ g 5 ꝗ S t 9 1d 6 14 … → curez St André … · 19 k 1d 12 m 17 g 5 [ 7 ϙ → Montmorency · same key as f. 62 Paris → the household of the duc de Nevers · letter-and-figure homophonic cipher with code numbers · 6 June 1588 · read A Paris informant to the Nevers household, 6 and 9 June 1588 BnF Français 3976 ff. 133–134 (DECODE R3708, “unknown sender to unknown recipient”, not deciphered). Three pages of clear French with eighteen cipher runs and fifteen code numbers, and no decipherment. The informant is the one who wrote ff. 62 and 131 of the same volume, and the key rebuilt from those letters read all eighteen runs. His next letter, of 9 June (f. 139), is glossed by a contemporary decipherer. The same key reads it independently, and every gloss agrees. Daniel Bourdeau · read 22 September 2026 read Summary. DECODE catalogues these leaves as a non-deciphered letter of 6 June 1588 from an unknown sender to an unknown recipient. The hand, the monogram and the cipher are those of the court informant whose letter of 29 April 1588 (f. 62) was read here earlier the same day, with a key rebuilt from the glosses on his letter of 4 June (f. 131). That key read most of the runs at sight: Nevers , Nevers en court , ligueurs , pardonne , mutiner le peuple , Corbeil . The rest were re-transcribed at full resolution and read against the clear text. They extend the key by three signs: the y with a cross is y ( Montmorency ), the 4 with a cross is z ( curez , bruictz ), and a bracket-shaped sign is n. The letter describes Paris three weeks after the Day of the Barricades. The curés of Saint-André and Saint-Benoît are stirring up the people. The new prévôt La Chapelle carries every decision of the Hôtel de Ville to Guise’s council, where the archbishop of Lyon and the président de Neuilly sit. The échevin Cotteblanche has refused to let Guise take the Arsenal’s guns to Corbeil without the King’s leave. 226 of the 230 cipher signs read with certainty. The other four occur once each and are read from context. The same informant’s letter of 9 June (f. 139, not on DECODE) has a contemporary decipherment written over every run. The key read its 106 signs without change, and all six runs match the glosses. Its glossed code numbers identify 10 as Épernon, 38 as Garrault, 98 as la paix and 107 as the Grand Écuyer. Eight code numbers stay unidentified. The letter also corrects the earlier reading of a gloss on f. 131: code 24 is Nevers, not Navarre.

p: Informant to the Nevers household, June 1588
t: A Paris informant to the Nevers household, 6 and 9 June 1588 — read
b: Fr. 3976 is a volume of Nevers’s papers for 1588, on Gallica as btv1b9060548h . F. 133r is view 223, f. 133v view 224 and f. 134r view 225. The letter is dated at the head 6 de Juin 1588 and at the foot Ce 6. Juing a 10 heures du soir , and it closes with the cipher monogram of ff. 62 and 131. The cipher runs are set into the clear sentences, as on f. 62. The writer uses bare code numbers as well: 4, 9, 10, 11, 12, 23, 24, 25, 33, 79, 94, 102, 104, 105 and 106. Two of them, 9 and 106, stand inside a run and are underlined, like the code numbers in the clear text. F. 133v, lines 2–3: Il n’y a que les 7δg5ꝗ S t 9 1d 6 14 + 2t S t 8 s 1d 17 p 13 ε = curez St André et St Benoist , qui font rage de 19 11 ε p 1d s 14 n s 16 t 11 δ o s = mutiner le peuple . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3976 f. 133v, via Gallica (btv1b9060548h, view 224).

p: Informant to the Nevers household, June 1588
t: A Paris informant to the Nevers household, 6 and 9 June 1588 — read
b: A sign is one character, or the figure 1 (written like a dotted i) followed by a character. Several signs stand for more than one letter. The table of the f. 62 reading ( write-up , nevers1588/key.md ) was applied unchanged. This letter confirmed it and added three values. The y with a cross below (ϙ) is y : Montmorency , artillerye . The 4 with a cross below is z : curez , faulx bruictz , and Pichenaz for Pigenat. The f. 62 table had it as q. A bracket-shaped sign, and a long J-shaped sign, are n : nommé , conseil , Nevers en court , Nuilly . The J-shaped sign is p in prevost . z is a in Arsenac and Pichenat . 9 is r in artillerye and h in Pichenat and Cotteblanche . o is u once, in bruictz . The code numbers are identified from the context here and on ff. 62 and 131: code reading evidence 11 le Roy glossed on f. 131; “des deputez vers 11” 24 the duc de Nevers glossed nevers on f. 131; “24 se peult souvenir qu’estant a La Cassine” 102 Paris “102 renvoye des deputez vers 11” 9 the duc de Guise “9 voullant faire sortir l’artillerye de l’Arsenac pour aller a Corbeil” 12 Catherine de Médicis “chez 12 elle a resolu d’envoyer 79 vers 24” 104 a woman of the Nevers household, probably the duchess “l’ont supplié de les accompaigner d’un mot de lettre, ce qu’elle a faict” 10 the duc d’Épernon glossed Espernon on f. 139; “la survenue de 10 qui est maintenant absent” 38 Garrault glossed on f. 139 98 la paix glossed on f. 139: “par ce moyen l’on aura 98” 107 the Grand Écuyer glossed on f. 139: “107 s’insinue es bonnes graces de 9” 4, 23, 25, 33, 79, 94, 105, 106 not identified 4, 9, 24 and 94 are the names Paris offers the King “a son choix” The gloss over 24 on f. 131 was recorded as “Navarre” when f. 62 was read. Looked at again, it reads nevers , and Nevers fits every use of 24 here. The Nevers notes have been corrected.

p: Informant to the Nevers household, June 1588
t: A Paris informant to the Nevers household, 6 and 9 June 1588 — read
b: The clear text is given in modern word division. The cipher runs are in bold, and cuts are marked […]. F. 133r: 24 se peult souvenir qu’estant a n 9 7 2 13 f p 1d t = La Cassine , Nevers’s château in the Rethelois, 11 ne luy escripvoit qu’a force . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3976 f. 133r, via Gallica (btv1b9060548h, view 223). Je suis tres marry qu’aiez pris en mauvaise part ce qui a esté escript a 24 […] Mais parce qu’avant son partement il offroit a 11 de demourer s’il en estoit de besoing, on estimoit qu’il se portast encore mieulx qu’alors, et par consequent sans peril de sa personne il pouvoit s’approcher de Roy . Or nous avions bien consideré que si Nevers alloit veoir 11 sans estre mandé d’affection, il y pourroit recevoir quelque pire traictement […] Secondement, 24 se peult souvenir qu’estant a La Cassine 11 ne luy escripvoit qu’a force, et neantmoings apres qu’il fut venu il luy fit caresse et honneurs […] Tiercement, tout le monde desire Nevers en court beaucoup plus que l’on ne faisoit alors. Et non seulement ligueurs mais aussi les aultres […] Jusque la qu’il commence ja a courir ung bruit que 102 renvoye des deputez vers 11, avec charge entre aultres choses de le supplier que pour tesmoigner a 102 qu’il pardonne et n’a mauvaise volonté, il luy laisse pour 94 ou 4 ou 9 ou 24 a son choix. Ledit 102 n’a encore envoyé vers Nevers […] Il n’y a que les curez St André et St Benoist qui font rage de mutiner le peuple . […] Quant a l’eslection des prevost des marchans et eschevins, elle n’a esté aultrement faicte que je vous l’ay mandé, que j’avois entendue de Pichenat . […] Mais comme vous scavez, ce ne sont gens d’estat, de sorte que par ruses et faulx bruictz on leur faict tousjours passer quelque carriere, car si tost que quelque chose a esté resolu en l’hostel de ville, le prevost Chapelle ne fault de rapporter le tout au conseil de 9 et 106 pour adviser les moyens de rompre les deliberations qui ne leur plaisent, ou assistent tousjours 33 et de Bray, l’evesque de Lion, Nuilly . L’on m’a asseuré neantmoings que ces jours passez 9, voullant faire sortir l’artillerye de l’Arsenac pour aller a Corbeil , l’un des eschevins, nommé Cotteblanche, dist qu’il ne consentiroit jamais que cela se feist sans permission du Roy. [f. 134] Quant a 33, j’ay perdu tout ung jour pour cuyder le veoir, mais il fut toute l’apresdisnée chez 105, qui est logé au logis de Montmorency . Translation of the runs’ sense. Nevers was being urged to come to court, where everyone wanted him, the ligueurs included. Paris talked of asking the King, as a sign that he pardoned the city, to let it choose among four names. Only the curés of Saint-André (Christophe Aubry) and Saint-Benoît (Jean Boucher) were still inciting the people. The new municipality was steered by rumour, and La Chapelle-Marteau reported everything decided at the Hôtel de Ville to Guise’s council. With 33, “de Bray”, Pierre d’Épinac archbishop of Lyon and the président de Neuilly in attendance, that council undid whatever it disliked. When Guise wanted the Arsenal’s artillery for Corbeil, the échevin Cotteblanche refused without the King’s permission. F. 133v, lines 13–19: the runs for par ruses et faulx bruictz , le prevost Chapelle , conseil de 9 et 106 (the code numbers underlined inside the run), 33 et de Bray, l’evesque de Lion, Nuilly , l’artillerye de l’Arsenac , Corbeil , and nommé Cotteblanche . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3976 f. 133v, via Gallica (btv1b9060548h, view 224).

p: Informant to the Nevers household, June 1588
t: A Paris informant to the Nevers household, 6 and 9 June 1588 — read
b: Three days later the informant wrote again: BnF fr. 3976 f. 139, piece 74 of the BnF notice, “Lettre chiffrée avec déchiffrement contenant des nouvelles de Paris. Ce 9 juing 1588” . It is not on DECODE. The letter is one page with six cipher runs and code numbers, in the same hand and with the same monogram. Here a contemporary decipherer wrote the plaintext over every run and over most of the numbers. The key built from ff. 62 and 131 was applied to the six runs before the glosses were compared. It reads all 106 signs, and each reading matches the gloss. F. 139, lines 1–6: n s d t 5 6 5 v t l p s 14 13 glossed leuee de deniers ; 38 glossed Garrault ; 1d 17 12 9 p 14 5 13 notaires ; 9 14 r s 1d ε z g t l 12 s argent a rente ; and the long run glossed Nuylli Marcel prevost des marchans et eschevins . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3976 f. 139, via Gallica (btv1b9060548h, view 234). C’est chose veritable que le prevost des Marchans s’est retourné mettre en la Bastille. Je n’ay peu descouvrir au vray qu’il se face aucune levee de deniers . Mais bien m’a l’on asseuré, mesmement 38 [Garrault], que notaires cherchent argent a rente , dont Nilly, Marcel, prevost des marchans et eschevins respondent. Mais beaucoup ont faict difficulté d’en bailler, et de moy je m’estonne que Marcel y soit meslé. On dit que 107 [le Grand Escuyer] s’insinue es bonnes graces de 9 [Guise] et en presse. Son frere a aussi quitté 10 [Espernon]. […] L’on tient pour certain que 11 [le Roy] accorde a 9 la lieutenance generalle , et que par ce moyen l’on aura 98 [la paix]. 38 a plusieurs advis a donner a 24 [Nevers] quand il sera pres de 11 […] Ce 9 Juing. The League municipality was raising loans through the notaries on the guarantee of Neuilly, Claude Marcel, the prévôt and the échevins. The rumour that Henri III would make Guise lieutenant-general came true with the Edict of Union in July. The glosses also settle two things for the other letters. 24 is Nevers, the reading the f. 131 gloss gave once it was re-read. 10 is Épernon, which makes sense of “la ruyne de 10” on f. 62 and “la survenue de 10 qui est maintenant absent” on f. 133.

p: Informant to the Nevers household, June 1588
t: A Paris informant to the Nevers household, 6 and 9 June 1588 — read
b: The pages were cut into overlapping bands from the full-resolution Gallica images (4895 × 6460 px), and the eighteen runs were transcribed sign by sign ( r3708/ciphertext.txt ). Most runs read with the f. 62 key as it stood. The run after de sorte que did not: as first transcribed, its second half matched none of the 133,000 French word forms in the project’s corpora. A second pass at native resolution corrected the transcription to 16 9 14 9 δ 13 5 f 5 12 J z δ n c δ g o p 7 ε ꝗ = par ruses et faulx bruictz . The tail of the run after tousjours 33 was read the same way: J δ 1o n ϙ is Nuilly , the spelling the writer uses in clear on f. 133r ( le president de Nuilly ).

p: Informant to the Nevers household, June 1588
t: A Paris informant to the Nevers household, 6 and 9 June 1588 — read
b: curez St André et St Benoist : the sign + (e in André ) and the pair 2 t ( et ) occur only here. Read from context, grade C. Nuilly : the sign 1o (i) occurs only here. Grade H for the name, which is spelled the same way in clear on the same page. de Bray : the letters are read (the curly 8 is b, u or v), but the person is not identified. de vray (“indeed”) is possible, grade M. Pichenat : the last sign reads z ( Pichenaz ). The curé of Saint-Nicolas-des-Champs, François Pigenat, is meant. Grade H. Code numbers 4, 23, 25, 33, 79, 94, 105 and 106 are not identified. 79 is the Queen Mother’s messenger to Nevers; the gloss over it on f. 139 cannot be read. 105 lodged at the Hôtel de Montmorency. 33 attended Guise’s council and “faict semblant d’estre du tout sien” toward 4, who “n’ouvre encore ses yeulx”. The informant’s list of numbers has not been found. Who the letter is to. “Vous” took offence at what was written to 24, so the recipient is someone close to Nevers rather than the duke himself.

t: Catherine de Médicis to Villeroy, 7 February 1581 — the Queen Mother’s cipher read in full
b: DECODE R4157 (BnF fr. 15564 ff. 30–34), catalogued as an unknown sender to Villeroy, 5 February 1587, is Catherine de Médicis writing from Chenonceau on 7 February 1581, and is printed in her Lettres t. VII. Its eight cipher lines, on the prince Dauphin, the oath of the Low Countries to Anjou and the embassy to England, are read sign by sign with Tomokiyo’s reconstructed key, extended by twelve values. The last line he could not read is d’Angleterre and then padding. Chenonceau → Villeroy in Guyenne · homophonic cipher with a small nomenclator · 7 February 1581 · read Catherine de Médicis to Villeroy, 7 February 1581 from Catherine de' Medici → to Nicolas de Neufville, seigneur de Villeroy BnF français 15564 ff. 30–34 (DECODE R4157, catalogued as “unknown sender to unknown recipient, 5 Feb 1587”): a long clear letter of the Queen Mother with one block of eight cipher lines on f. 33r. The block is read here sign by sign, including the last line that the published key left unread. Daniel Bourdeau · read 22 September 2026 read Summary. The catalogue entry came from DECODE, which lists R4157 as a partly enciphered letter of 5 February 1587 from an unknown sender, with Villeroy in the title. The docket on the address leaf reads “Double de la lettre de la Royne mere du Roy à Mr de Villeroy du v[ii]e febvrier 1581”: the letter is Catherine de Médicis’s, written at Chenonceau on 7 February 1581 with a postscript of the 8th and an autograph postscript. It is printed in the Lettres de Catherine de Médicis , vol. VII (1899), pp. 349–353, where the cipher appears silently in clear, taken from a contemporary decipherment written in the margin and under the block. Satoshi Tomokiyo had reconstructed the cipher from this page, noting that the last line “cannot be read except for the first d”, without publishing a plaintext. With his key, corrected and extended by twelve values (among them 18 = dict , 4/b = nous , the codes for mais , la and Angleterre ), every one of the 289 signs is accounted for: 262 read as French and 27 are nulls. The unread last line is the code for “Angleterre” after the d’ , then twenty signs of padding. The cipher adds two words the edition lacks (“et non devant”, “ne laisserons de le nommer”).

t: Catherine de Médicis to Villeroy, 7 February 1581 — the Queen Mother’s cipher read in full
b: Villeroy, secretary of state, was in Guyenne with Bellièvre and the duc d’Anjou, carrying out the peace of Fleix (November 1580). Catherine writes from Chenonceau about the chamber of justice for Guyenne, the money for the troops, the handing back of Mende, the quarrel between the dukes of Montpensier and Nevers, and the embassy that was to go to England for Anjou’s marriage to Elizabeth. The cipher block is one sentence in that last part: why the court is not pressing the prince Dauphin, Montpensier’s son, to go to England. DECODE R4157, “Non-decrypted”, 9 pp., sender and recipient unknown, 5 Feb 1587 Actually Catherine de Médicis → Nicolas de Neufville, seigneur de Villeroy, Chenonceau, 7 (and 8) February 1581; BnF fr. 15564 ff. 30–34, Gallica views 40–44. DECODE image P7 (f. 38, “Madame…”) belongs to another letter. Cipher f. 33r, eight lines, 289 signs; deciphered at the time in the left margin and on three lines under the block In print Lettres de Catherine de Médicis , ed. Baguenault de Puchesse, t. VII (1899), pp. 349–353, “Orig. fonds français 15564, f° 30” The docket (f. 30 verso of the cover leaf, Gallica view 40): “Double de la lettre de la / Royne mere du Roy / a Mr de Villeroy / du v[ii]e febvrier 1581”. DECODE’s “5 Feb 1587” comes from this line. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 15564 f. 30v, via Gallica (btv1b9064027v, view 40).

t: Catherine de Médicis to Villeroy, 7 February 1581 — the Queen Mother’s cipher read in full
b: BnF fr. 15564 f. 33r, lower part (Gallica view 43): the clear text ends “se dizant par deçà qu’il”, then eight lines of cipher. A second hand wrote the decipherment in the margin (“doibt aller en flandres recevoir le serment de fidelite…”) and went on under the block (“et fera tout ce qu’ilz pourront pour le service…”). Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 15564 f. 33r, via Gallica (btv1b9064027v, view 43). The cipher is a homophonic substitution on Greek letters, digits and invented signs, one to three signs per letter, with special signs for mm and ss . A small nomenclator covers de, le, la, que, qui, pour, nous, mais, faire, tout, avec, dict, prince and Angleterre , and it is used for syllables as well: fi[de]lite , [de]mourer , Con[de] , [le]gation , mon[dict] . An overbar marks several of the codes. Nulls pad the start of the block, the end of line 4 and the end of the last line.

t: Catherine de Médicis to Villeroy, 7 February 1581 — the Queen Mother’s cipher read in full
b: One line per manuscript line; codes in brackets, nulls in braces. The clear text before the block is “car, à ce que j’entends, nous n’i gaingnerions rien, se dizant par deçà qu’il”. {3 nulls} DOIBT AL ER EN FLANDRES RECEUOIR [LE] SERMENT [DE] FI[DE]LITE [DE] CEULX [DE]S {null} PAIS BAS [POUR] MON FILZ ET [QUI]L Y DOIBT [DE]MOURER ET [QUE] [LE] [PRINCE] [DE] CON[DE]E DO IBT MENER [LE]S FORCES [QUI] S’ASSEMBLENT ET [FAIRE] [TOUT] CE [QUI]LZ [POUR]RONT [POUR] [LE] SERUICE [DE] MON[DICT] FILZ [QUI] SE [DICT] AUSSI Y [DE]BUOIR ALER {3 nulls} AU TEMPS [QUE] [NOUS] AUEZ ESCRIPT ET NON [DE]UANT [MAIS] [NOUS] NE LAISSER ONS [DE] [LE] NOMMER [AVEC] [LE][DICT] SIEUR [DE] MONPENSIER AU[DICT] POUOI(R) [DE] [LA] [LE]GATION D’[ANGLETERRE] {20 signs of padding} Normalised: “…se dizant par deçà qu’il doibt aller en Flandres recevoir le serment de fidélité de ceulx des Païs-Bas pour mon filz, et qu’il y doibt demourer, et que le prince de Condé doibt mener les forces qui s’assemblent, et faire tout ce qu’ilz pourront pour le service de mondict filz, qui se dict aussi y debvoir aller au temps que nous avez escript, et non devant; mais nous ne laisserons de le nommer avec ledict sieur de Montpensier audict pouvoir de la légation d’Angleterre.” In English: “…since it is said here that he [the prince Dauphin] is to go to Flanders to receive the oath of fealty of the people of the Low Countries for my son [Anjou], and to stay there, and that the prince of Condé is to lead the forces now gathering and do all they can for my son’s service, who says he means to go there too at the time you wrote to us, and not before. But we shall not fail to name him, with the said lord of Montpensier, in the commission for the embassy to England.” The contemporary decipherment and the 1899 edition give the same text, except that they lack et before non devant and de before le nommer . The edition also spells the name Montpensier where the cipher has Monpensier .

t: Catherine de Médicis to Villeroy, 7 February 1581 — the Queen Mother’s cipher read in full
b: The DECODE images are Gallica openings of fr. 15564 ff. 30–34 and a crop of the block. The docket and the content (Anjou in the Low Countries, Condé’s troops, “Chenonceau”) pointed to 1581. The letter is in volume VII of Catherine’s letters, not in volume IX where a 1587 date would have put it. The block was transcribed from the Gallica native scan, one label per sign. A first attempt without the key, aligning the signs with the printed text (one sign per letter plus nulls, by EM and annealing), failed. The printed passage turned out to be only half of the plaintext: the rest of the decipherment is on the lines under the block, which at first looked like the letter’s clear continuation. Tomokiyo’s reconstruction for “BnF fr. 15564, f.33” (Cryptiana, French ciphers during the reigns of Charles IX and Henry III ) read the block as soon as the labels were mapped onto it. A second pass at double magnification split signs that the first labels had merged: forked ψ = n and curled ɣ = t; filled ᴀ = z and Δ = f; ϖ = g, the looped u = s and the &-shape = z; ɦ = u and б = e; small v = e and capital V = tout ; bold ʒ = avec and barred Ʒ = e; ɤ = ss. Values missing from the published table were fixed from the text: 18 = dict (four times: mon[dict] filz , se [dict] , le[dict] sieur , au[dict] ); C̄σ = mais ; ß̄ = la ; ō = Angleterre ; 4/b = nous , not vous ( que nous avez escript , mais nous ne laisserons ); ℬ = p, ꝏ = u, ꝑ = t, F̣ = i, ϑ = l, d = x.

t: Catherine de Médicis to Villeroy, 7 February 1581 — the Queen Mother’s cipher read in full
b: After “[de] [la] [le]gation d” the last line has an overbarred ō and then twenty signs. The reading takes ō as the code for Angleterre and the twenty signs as padding: the contemporary decipherer, who had the key, ends at “de la legation d’Ang[leter]re” and writes nothing more; f. 33v opens in clear with the next sentence, “Nous adviserons, aiant oy ledict La Fin…”; the tail contains Tomokiyo’s declared null Z7 twice, and the same signs (Ʒ with a dagger, the double f, a small raised hook) that pad the start of the block before “doibt”; the few tail signs that have letter values give “a l mm a que”, which is not French. So Tomokiyo’s “the first d” is the d’ of d’Angleterre , and the rest was never meant to be read.

t: Catherine de Médicis to Villeroy, 7 February 1581 — the Queen Mother’s cipher read in full
b: ō = Angleterre occurs once and is fixed by the decipherer’s “d’Ang…re” and the edition, not by a second occurrence: grade M. The Latin e after the de code in Condé is either an e (for é) or a null: grade M. “pouoi” at the end of line 6 lacks its r. Either the encipherer left it out or the Z that opens line 7 was meant for both r and de . Everything else reads with a key value (H from Tomokiyo’s table, or C against the contemporary decipherment).

t: Two ciphers in the Strängnäs sequentiary of 1517
b: DECODE R4349 is the Dominican sequentiary Uppsala C 513. Its scribe dated it on f. 19v in a four-line colophon under chant notation, every vowel written as the next letter (a→b, e→f, i→k, o→p, u→x); the Uppsala catalogue printed the reading in 1992, checked here letter by letter. The “six symbols in a note” of DECODE are the close of an Old Swedish note to Anders Larsson pasted on f. 1r, transcribed here; too short to read. Strängnäs → Västerås · vowel shift and six signs · 1517 · colophon read, six signs too short Two ciphers in the Strängnäs sequentiary of 1517: a dated colophon and a six-sign signature Uppsala University Library, C 513, f. 19v: a paper book of sequences with square notation, written for the Dominicans of Västerås. DECODE catalogues it as R4349, a ciphered letter from Strängnäs with “six symbols”, sender and recipient unknown. The book holds two ciphers. On f. 19v the scribe dated it in a colophon in which each vowel is replaced by the letter after it. The Uppsala catalogue printed that reading in 1992, and it is checked here. On a slip pasted on f. 1r, a short Old Swedish note to one Anders Larsson closes with six signs. That is the note DECODE describes, and six signs are too few to read. Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 22 September 2026 read in part Summary. Catalogue entry 235 came from DECODE R4349, which has one placeholder image, a scan of two catalogue pages, and a note describing “a short ciphertext of six symbols out in a note”. The manuscript, Uppsala UB C 513, is a Dominican sequentiary with two ciphered pieces. The long one is the scribe’s dating colophon on f. 19v, four lines set under chant notation, with every vowel written as the next letter (a→b, e→f, i→k, o→p, u→x). Andersson-Schmitt, Hallberg and Hedlund’s catalogue of the Uppsala C collection (1992) gives the rule and the reading. Here the folio was found in the library’s Alvin scans, transcribed letter by letter (125 letters), and decoded to the printed reading word for word: the book was written in 1517 in the Strängnäs convent for the convent of Västerås. The short one is the piece DECODE’s note means. It is a paper slip pasted on f. 1r, a private note in Old Swedish sending herbs and cinnamon bark for Anders Larsson’s chest, which ends where a signature would stand with six signs, ÿ ɑ M ÿ u ꝺ . The colophon’s rule does not fit them, no shift of the alphabet gives a name, and six signs cannot fix a key, so they stay unread. Of 131 cipher tokens, 125 are read.

t: Two ciphers in the Strängnäs sequentiary of 1517
b: Uppsala UB C 513, f. 19v: the ciphered colophon under its staves. The red-stroked initial A is the only plain vowel. Image: Uppsala University Library, C 513 f. 19v, via Alvin (public domain). C 513 is a sequentiary of 84 paper leaves in one early-16th-century cursive hand. The owner’s entry on the front pastedown reads Liber conuentus insulensis ordinis predicatorum . f. 19v closes the sequence Benedicta sit celorum regina with “…in celesti patria Amen”. The scribe then carried on in the same hand, on four more text lines under notation, in what looks like a garbled language. A red catchword Corda manibus , the incipit of the next sequence, closes the page. Annp dpmknk mkllfskmp qxkngfntfsk- mp dfckmp sfptkmp prfsfns lkbfr sf- qxfnckpnbrkxs fst scrkptxs kn cpnxfntx strfngfnfnsk prp cpnxfntx knsxlfnsk The rule is the old scribal trick of writing each vowel as the next letter of the alphabet (i and j, u and v counting as one letter each): plain a e i o u written b f k p x Consonants stand for themselves, and word division and doubled letters are kept. The rubricated capital A of Anno is left plain. Because b and p are also ordinary consonants of the text, the written b in lkbfr is a real b ( liber ) and the written p in scrkptxs , prfsfns and prp is a real p ( scriptus, presens, pro ). Everywhere else they stand for a and o. Context always decides, and no word stays ambiguous.

t: Two ciphers in the Strängnäs sequentiary of 1517
b: Anno domini millesimo quingentesimo decimo septimo presens liber sequencionarius est scriptus in conuentu strengenensi pro conuentu insulensi. “In the year of the Lord 1517 this sequentiary was written in the convent of Strängnäs for the convent of Västerås.” Insulensis is the Dominican house of Västerås, the owner named on the pastedown. The catalogue adds a small irony. A later reader at Västerås, who evidently could not read the ciphered date, wrote on f. 20v that the book was the work of Frater Gudmundus Benedicti “circa annum 1520”.

stt: colophon read; six signs too short
t: Two ciphers in the Strängnäs sequentiary of 1517
h: The note on f. 1r and its six signs
b: Uppsala UB C 513, the slip pasted on f. 1r: a note to Anders Larsson. The last line ends liff oth sel and the six signs. Image: Uppsala University Library, C 513, slip on f. 1r, via Alvin (public domain). The catalogue notes only that a slip with a post-medieval Swedish text is pasted on f. 1r, and that “an Anders Larsson receives medicines”. Read from the scan (uncertain words marked ?): thetta skal wal[?] larens? andhers hess? lass son wara andhers y brygghe stuffuan … kære hertans brodher andhers larsson h[elsa]? sändher yagh edher littit örther til edher brysth kanelbark men yak ffruchthar ath han är gammal kære brodher edhra [w]älgärningar? är yak ffor ringa til at betala hwilket yak tager then effuige gudh til help then yak edher beffaller til liff oth sel ÿ ɑ M ÿ u ꝺ “…to Anders Larsson in the brewhouse. Dear brother Anders Larsson, I send you a few herbs for your chest, cinnamon bark, but I fear it is old. Dear brother, I am too poor to repay your kindnesses, which I leave to the eternal God, to whom I commend you in life and soul.” Then come the six signs, where the writer’s name would stand. The last line: liff oth sel , then ÿ ɑ M and ÿ u ꝺ . Image: Uppsala University Library, C 513, slip on f. 1r, via Alvin (public domain). The signs look like cursive letters of the same hand: ÿ as in yagh , and ꝺ the hand’s looped d, as in edher . They fall into two groups of three, each opening with ÿ, as a first name and a patronymic would. The colophon’s vowel shift does not apply, since none of b, f, k, p or x occurs. None of the 23 shifts of the alphabet on five readings of the signs gives a name or a formula, and nothing else in the book is in this hand. Six signs with one repeat cannot fix a substitution. They stay unread.

t: Two ciphers in the Strängnäs sequentiary of 1517
b: The DECODE record’s only image is a placeholder icon. Its attached PDF is the catalogue entry, which named the folio and the rule. A first pass took DECODE’s “six symbols” to be a garbled description of the colophon. All 175 Alvin images were then checked, and the slip on f. 1r turned up. The only other extra writing is clear pen trials on the back pastedown. Alvin’s scans of C 513 are public domain. f. 19v is attachment 42, and its full TIFF was cut into line crops and transcribed. The inverse rule was applied by a small script. It reads k as i and x as u (neither is a consonant in this text) and chooses a or b, e or f, and o or p by a beam search over the whole colophon under the project’s Latin n-gram model. A first pass word by word, with no context, took prp for oro . With the sentence as context, it chose pro , and the output matched the catalogue’s reading in every word.

b: The six signs closing the f. 1r note ( ÿ ɑ M ÿ u ꝺ ) are not read. Too short, with no key and no sibling in the same hand. Probably the writer’s name. The colophon: all 125 cipher letters have a value, and all 19 words read as sense (grade H). The note’s clear Swedish is a first reading from the scan; the words of its first line are uncertain. In the transcription, the minims after the initial A could be read m or nn. The rule requires nn ( Annp ), as the catalogue has it. In the first cpnxfntx the n is carried by a stroke over cp . The catalogue cites earlier literature on the book: Collijn (1917), Moberg (1927) and Hedlund’s plate of 1977. Whether any of these printed the decipherment before 1992 was not checked.

t: Stojan, a Serb prisoner, to the aghas, knezes and his kin — Cyrillic, not a cipher
b: DECODE R688, in the Chiffres 1664–1668 bundle of the Vienna Hungarian conspiracy files, is catalogued as a simple substitution in graphic signs. The signs are Cyrillic letters and the language is Serbian: a prisoner named Stojan greets the aghas, knezes and his Vlachs by name and begs them to get him out of the German prison. A slip on f. 31 holds a second, damaged note. Serb prisoner → aghas, knezes and kin · Cyrillic script, no cipher · 1664–68 (bundle span) · not a cipher Stojan's Letter from Prison ÖStA, Haus-, Hof- und Staatsarchiv, Ung. Akt. Spec. Verschwörerakten VII. Varia, Fasc. 327, Konv. D ( Chiffres 1664–1668 ), ff. 30–31 · DECODE R688, catalogued as a non-decrypted simple substitution in graphic signs The signs are Cyrillic letters. The pages hold a plea in vernacular Serbian from a man held in a Habsburg prison, and a short second note on a slip. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 22 September 2026 not a cipher Summary. DECODE R688 (three pages, "Non-decrypted", simple substitution, graphic signs, no language) entered the Unsolved Catalogue as item 270, a ciphered letter of an unknown sender to an unknown recipient in 1664. Both DECODE images were viewed here. Nothing on them is enciphered. The script is Cyrillic, in an untrained upright hand with Church Slavonic spellings, and the language is Serbian. The letter opens Сїи листь писа Стоянь , "this letter was written by Stojan". Stojan greets the aghas, knezes and odabaše , "small and great", and his Vlachs by name, and begs them to get him out of "the German prison". A slip on f. 31 carries four damaged lines of a second note of the same kind. The letter was probably bound with the ciphers because no clerk in Vienna could read it. The pages were transcribed line for line; about a quarter of the words stay doubtful because of blots, deletions and the torn slip.

F. 30r, lines 2–10: ѿ града … поклонь и животе здравїе агамъ кнезїамь … , the greetings and the list of names. Image: Österreichisches Staatsarchiv, HHStA, Verschwörerakten Fasc. 327 Konv. t: Stojan, a Serb prisoner, to the aghas, knezes and his kin — Cyrillic, not a cipher
b: The opening, with doubtful words marked [?]: ✝ Сїи листь писа Стоянь … ѿ града З[?]вачь поклонь и животе здравїе агамъ, кнезїамь, ѿдабашамъ[?] и маламъ и великимъ. И пакъ посло и животе здравїе влахомъ моема: Вуку, Гаврилу, Радонѣци[?], Вучиту[?], куму Продану, Мирку, Павлу, Димитру, Марку с всемь христианомь. … Братїа, да ми се смилуете, можите мене извадить из немачкий тамнице а ваше душе из пакле. "This letter was written by Stojan from the town of Z[?]vač: greeting, life and health to the aghas, the knezes, the odabaše [company commanders], to small and great. And again I send life and health to my Vlachs: to Vuk, Gavrilo, Radonja, Vučeta, my kum Prodan, Mirko, Pavle, Dimitrije and Marko, with all the Christians. … Brothers, have mercy on me. You can get me out of the German prison, and your souls out of hell." The rest of f. 30r is about groschen, money he lacks, pledges and "what is needed". The last line is struck through and blotted. On f. 30v he says to bring the money to the town of Bor[?], and "I know horses and men, we can get [me] out, and all be glad, amen". The letter was written for him by someone else: Писа намъ Младь Бакиі[?] у градъ Бор[у] . A postscript sends greetings to his wife and asks kum Prodan to go himself to the Magyar[?]. Most of this postscript stays uncertain. The slip on f. 31 begins Сїи лисъ писа Х[?]саань[?] у Пет… and sends life and health to the writer's mother and brothers. It is too damaged to read further.

t: Stojan, a Serb prisoner, to the aghas, knezes and his kin — Cyrillic, not a cipher
h: Why it was catalogued as a cipher
b: A letter in Cyrillic would have been as opaque to a Vienna chancery clerk as a cipher. It was bound in the Chiffres bundle, and DECODE described it from that bundle heading as a substitution in graphic signs. The same thing has happened to other items in this project. The DECODE record should read: not a cipher, cleartext Serbian (Cyrillic). This correction is queued with the transcription.

t: Stojan, a Serb prisoner, to the aghas, knezes and his kin — Cyrillic, not a cipher
b: The place names Z[?]vač and Bor[?] are uncertain readings. Settling them would help to place and date the letter. About a quarter of the words, mostly in the money passage and the postscript, are doubtful (grade M or I in the README Conventions scale). These are gaps in reading a rough hand, not cipher: a reader of early modern Serbian working from the original would close most of them. Why a Serb prisoner's plea sits among the conspiracy papers is not known. It may have been intercepted, or it may come from a prisoner held in the Habsburg border garrisons.

The catalogue listed R7707 as a ciphered letter between unknown correspondents, with DECODE’s volume span 1716–1836 as its date. The eight images show one cipher page, f. 37r: ten lines of invented cursive signs, 205 in all, each followed by a dot. The other leaves are a codebreaker’s worksheets. They hold frequency tallies, contact tables, a list of the signs that occur doubled, and the guess “l – vowel – e”. There is also an unrelated household bill, and a docket, “4 Aout 1728 / 31 Aout / 5 8bre”. The codebreaker never reached a reading. The signs were transcribed here, and the counts agree with his tally on f. 40r. The index of coincidence is 1.07, which is flat. That rules out a simple substitution in any language. Monoalphabetic annealing in seven languages failed. So did Vigenère and Beaufort at periods 5 and 10, and a Quagmire-type search with an unknown sign alphabet. Two hundred signs are too few to break a polyalphabetic system without the key. The letter stays unread.

t: A cipher of 1728 its codebreaker could not read
b: The transcription ( ct.txt ) uses arbitrary labels for the signs. Its counts match the 1728 tally within a few units for every sign: the commonest sign has 14 against his 14, and l has 13 against his 16. The “Duplicates” are simply the signs that occur doubled in the text. The index of coincidence is 1.07, where 1.0 is random. A monoalphabetic substitution of French or English would give 1.7–2.0. There is no repeated trigram in 205 signs. The periodic index rises slightly at periods 5, 10 and 15 (1.25, 1.34, 1.29). That hints at a five-alphabet system, but columns of about 41 signs are too short to prove it.

t: Burghley to Walsingham, 5 July 1572 — name codes in a clear letter, one read

t: Walsingham’s letter-book, November 1572 — name codes in clear letters, one read
h: What reads, and what was tried
b: [3] = the Queen. In all four places the code stands for a person English policy turns on: someone warned to look to Scotland, someone news may “touch”, someone France and Spain mean to “entertain with good words”. The Queen fits every time, and no other candidate fits all four. Grade C (consistent context, no key). [7], [9], H. [7] follows “Glasgow” (the Bishop of Glasgow, Mary Stuart’s ambassador) and is also the man who swore never to rest while the Reformed religion survived. That points to the Cardinal of Lorraine or the Duke of Guise, but a code that follows a name may mark a title rather than a person. [9] follows both “Florence” and “Rome” and then stands alone (“the [9]”). Its three uses do not settle on one person, so it stays open. The nine-sign run. It mixes digits, a letter and signs. Nine symbols of an unknown alphabet cannot be read without the key. What was checked: the sibling records from the same volume (R8357, R8363) have no key. The pages carry no glosses. Tomokiyo’s survey of Elizabethan ciphers (Cecil–Norris, Throckmorton, Stafford) has no Walsingham key of 1570–73. CSP Foreign vol. x does not calendar these letters. Digges prints them without deciphering the codes.

Baurleighs?” to an unknown recipient, dated 27 January 1572, “short parts encrypted only”. The image is f. 395r of Harley MS 260, the later fair-copy letter-book of Walsingham’s embassy in France. It is signed “Your assured frind William Baurleighe”, the copyist’s spelling of Burghley, and dated “from Westm the 24th of Januarie 1572”, which is 24 January 1573 in modern reckoning. Dudley Digges printed it in The Compleat Ambassador (1655). The page holds no letter cipher and no code numbers. It has only two boxed 9s, one after “Lyons” and one after “Roome”. In the other letters of this volume a box after a word marks that word as a cover-name, a place name that stands for a person, and the digit in the box varies. So every word of the letter reads, and there is nothing to decipher. Who the cover-names Lyons and Roome stand for is not stated anywhere in the letter-book, in Digges or in the Calendars.

t: Burghley to Walsingham, 24 January 1573 — a clear letter with two cover-name markers
b: Burghley writes that he is “sorie and ashamed” that he cannot yet send anything that settles Walsingham’s own case, his recall from France. He promises to keep working for it. He leaves news of Lord Worcester’s journey to the Secretary. Then he comes to the business of the cover-names: Glascoe Davison longeth to heare from Lyons [9] for that by your last tickett, I understand that Steward tould you that one should come from Roome [9], the shipp abode in the place appointed the space of 23 daies. And soe I end, trusting to see you here amongst your frinds within this sixe weekes at the leaste to bee revoked by that tyme. From Westm the 24th of Januarie 1572. Your assured frind William Baurleighe. “Tickett” is the separate slip on which Walsingham sent his secret news. The same plot about a ship, Steward, Glasgow and the Rome/Florence party runs through the letters of November 1572 and February 1573 in this volume ( R8361 , R8364).

t: Burghley to Walsingham, 24 January 1573 — a clear letter with two cover-name markers
h: Why the boxed 9s are not cipher
b: In the Harley 260 letters that Digges printed, boxed digits appear directly after a place name: Florence [9], Rome [9], Glasgow [7], and in February 1573 both “Glasco [9]” and “Glasco [g]”. The same cover-word takes different digits, so the digit does not encode a value. The box flags the word before it as a cover-name for a person. In R8362 both boxes follow place names, Lyons and Roome, and the sentence reads without them. The two tokens are explained. No other signs are on the page.

t: Burghley to Walsingham, early 1573 — the ship sent to St Valery, read in part
b: BL Harley MS 260 f. 419 (DECODE R8364), catalogued as an unknown sender’s letter of February 1572, is Walsingham’s letter-book copy of Burghley’s reply of early 1573 about the ship for the Archbishop of Glasgow’s gentleman. Its six-sign place name recurs in four letters printed by Digges and reads VALERY, the port where a French letter in Walsingham’s file asks for a ship to be kept waiting. A nine-sign run and four name codes need the 1571 key, SP 106/2 f. 141A, which is not online. Westminster → Paris · homophonic letter cipher and name codes in a clear letter · early 1573 · read in part Burghley to Walsingham, early 1573: the ship sent to St Valery from William Cecil → to Francis Walsingham BL Harley MS 260 f. 419r–v (DECODE R8364, catalogue 122), listed as “Unknown sender to …, Feb 1572”. It is a copy in Walsingham’s embassy letter-book of Burghley’s letter answering Walsingham’s of 20 January 1573. The letter is in clear English except for name codes and two short cipher runs. The six-sign run is a place name that Digges printed in four letters of the same winter. Compared across all five copies it reads VALERY, the Channel port of Saint-Valery-sur-Somme. Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 22 September 2026 solved in part Summary. DECODE R8364 is two pages of a fair-copy letter-book, not an original. The ciphered letter is Burghley to Walsingham, written late in January or early in February 1573. It answers Walsingham’s letter of 20 January 1573 (R8363) about a gentleman of the Archbishop of Glasgow, Mary Stuart’s ambassador in Paris, who was trying to cross to England. Dudley Digges printed the letter in The Compleat Ambassador (1655, p. 327) with the cipher left as signs. An earlier pass counted about 25 cipher signs here and closed the letter as too short. This time every cipher passage in Digges’s volume was found, about 45 of them over 1570–73. The same six-sign word turns up in two Burghley and two Walsingham letters about that ship, always six signs long, with the same first and third signs and changing signs elsewhere. Walsingham’s own file of these months, Cotton MS Vespasian F VI, holds “a French letter earnestly desiring that a ship might be kept in waiting at St. Valery” (11 Dec 1572). The word reads VALERY (grade M, probable). The rest stays open: a nine-sign run, three person codes and the cover-name markers. The key of 1571 survives at the National Archives (SP 106/2 f. 141A), and the sent letter is in Cotton Vespasian F VI. Neither is online.

t: Burghley to Walsingham, early 1573 — the ship sent to St Valery, read in part
b: Harley MS 260 is a later fair copy of Walsingham’s Paris correspondence of 1570–73, one letter after another with their addresses, under running heads by month. Folio 419r opens with the end of Walsingham’s own letter of 6 February 1572 (old style), in which he asks to be relieved. Then comes the address “To the right honorable Mr Fraunces Walsingham Esq, the Queenes Maiesties Amba[ssador] in Fraunce”, and the letter beginning “Sir I have receaved yor lres of the xxth of this month with the tickett after yor accustomed manner contayning [9]”. The copy breaks off at the foot of f. 419v with a struck-out “finis”. Digges printed it from another copy, with the rest of the letter (Worcester’s dishonour off Boulogne, the French libel against Burghley, Walsingham’s letters of the 24th), under the running head “The Lord Burleigh to Fr. Walsingham”. DECODE’s sender (“unknown”), recipient (“…”) and date (February 1572) come from the letter-book’s old-style year and the address line. The letter is Burghley’s, to Walsingham, of late January or February 1573.

t: Burghley to Walsingham, early 1573 — the ship sent to St Valery, read in part
b: Digges printed the cipher of Walsingham’s correspondence in cipher type, not as the figures the earlier pass assumed. A search of all 457 page images of his volume, first by the OCR’s word confidence and then by two page-by-page scans, found about 45 ciphered passages in the letters of 1570–73. Four of them are the same word, in letters about the one ship: Letter Context Digges Harley 260 Burghley, Westminster, 11 Nov 1572 (p. 301) “he hath required me to provide a passenger to attend at Harwich. Le the Port of …” 2 0 ǂ 6 ɔ Δ Walsingham, Paris, Nov 1572 (p. 303) “he desireth that the ship may stay at … 9 or 10 days” 2 ɔ ǂ 6 r y Walsingham, Paris, 20 Jan 1573 (p. 313; R8363 ) “a Gentleman of [9] departed hence to … with intention to imbarque there” 2 ) ⌘ Ꭾ ) 4 2 1 ⌘ ε 9 4 Burghley, early 1573 (p. 327; R8364) “by Davisons writing of a ship sent to …” 20 ǂ H Ꭾ ) 2 0 ‡ H 6 1 Every copy has six signs. The first is always 2 and the third always the same crossed sign (ǂ, ⌘ and ‡ are the founts’ and the copyist’s versions of it). The other four places change from copy to copy. That is what a homophonic alphabet gives when one word is written several times. The place is a French port where a ship waits for passengers bound for England, with Harwich on the English side. The Nov 1572 letter has Walsingham ask that the ship may stay there nine or ten days. Cotton MS Vespasian F VI, the volume of Walsingham’s letters and drafts of 1572–73, holds at f. 197 “A French letter; earnestly desiring that a ship might be kept in waiting at St. Valery. Dec. 11”. VALERY has six letters, and Digges’s copy of the Walsingham letter even ends in a plain “r y”: V = 2 · A = 0, ɔ, ), 1 · L = ǂ, ⌘, ‡ · E = 6, Ꭾ, H, ε · R = ɔ, ), r, Ꭾ, 9, 6 · Y = Δ, y, 4, ), 1 A few signs turn up under two letters (ɔ/) under A and R, 1 under A and Y). They are the places where Digges’s type and the letter-book copyist blur distinct manuscript signs, which the Digges and Harley copies of the same letters show. The reading does not depend on them. Dieppe, the other six-letter port, needs a different sign for each of its two Ps and two Es in every copy, and nothing in the sources points to it. Harwich, Dover, Calais and Dieppe are all written in clear elsewhere in these letters. Grade M (probable): the alphabet is not otherwise known, but the length, the fixed signs, the “ry” and the St Valery ship in Walsingham’s file point the same way. With it the passage reads: I see there was a great mistaking of our doings, for by Davison’s writing of a ship sent to [St] Valery, [tt] imagined that Hall had a meaning to provoke Glasgow to come hither; whereupon this last gentleman came to enquire of Hall some assurance, if [3] should so do, to enquire […]. This you must think must needs appear very strange. The same reading applies to Walsingham’s group of 20 January in R8363 , where the Glasgow gentleman “departed hence to [St] Valery with intention to imbarque there if the barque were not departed”.

h: What was tried for the rest
b: The key. Hsuan-Ying Tu’s thesis on Walsingham’s intelligence (York, 2012) cites the key itself: TNA SP 106/2 f. 141A, “Sir Francis Walsingham Cipher, 1571” . She gives the Harley 260 letters of 1570–73, among them f. 399 (R8363), as examples of its use. DECODE has eight keys from SP 106/2 but not f. 141A. The nearest in date, SP 106/2 f. 50 (R343), names Moray, Cardinal Châtillon, Dover, Dieppe and Calais and belongs to Norris’s embassy of 1568–70. Its homophones give neither VALERY nor sense in the Digges runs. SP 106 is online only in the subscription State Papers Online. The sent letter. Cotton MS Vespasian F VI holds Burghley’s originals to Walsingham of 14 October 1572 (“with many cyphers”), 3 and 7 November 1572, and, at f. 245, a letter of 1572–3 from Somerset House that is probably this one. It also holds Walsingham’s drafts in clear of his letters of November 1572 to February 1573. The volume is catalogued “partly in cipher” and is not digitised. The Calendar. CSP Foreign vols. ix and x were searched for letters “partly in cipher, deciphered” that could be paired with Digges’s cipher. Walsingham to Smith of 10 August 1572 (no. 527) is deciphered, but Digges prints that letter without its cipher sentence. Burghley’s letters to Walsingham are not in SP 70, and this one is not calendared. The nine-sign run. Of its signs only H is known (= E, from the place name). Cribs such as passport, safe conduct, “the Queene”, “the Regent” and “Lord Seton” do not fit the shape. The Burghley–Walsingham runs of 1572–73 in Digges give only about 80 signs, loosely typeset, and too few overlap with this run to fix it.

t: Raince to Montmorency, Rome, 1526 — the key was misread by one column
b: Eight ciphered despatches of the French embassy’s secretary at Rome sit in BnF fr. 2984; about 106 lines of them, the 13 May and 20 November 1526 letters to Montmorency, exist in no edition. The obstacle was never cryptanalytic. Tomokiyo published the key in 2020, but reading which glyph sits under which letter in his table by eye slips a column: l , m and n were each a place wrong, and every reading built on it was corrupt. Measured off the image instead — every ink blob within 15 px of a header column — the table resolves a control line glyph for glyph with nothing left over, and 86 of the 106 lines then read by hand from the microfilm. Nine days before the League of Cognac: the Castilians and the Bourguignons, le chemin de Valence , a capitulation for which ilz seront cause de la destruction , the plague in Rome, advices reaching the Imperials by their own people, and a man taken un jour, en plaine place pres du palais . Two months after the Colonna raid, a pontificate that seroit la cause de la totale ruine de sa maison . The clear close of 13 May, transcribed here, expects Andrea Doria at Civitavecchia within a day with six galleys. Rome → the Court · homophonic letter cipher with nulls and word signs · 1526 · read in part Nicolas Raince to Montmorency, Rome, 13 May and 20 November 1526 to Anne de Montmorency BnF Français 2984, pp. 29–31 and 105 · about 106 ciphered lines, 5,629 glyphs · in no edition · the nine days before the League of Cognac, and two months after the Colonna raid on the Vatican Tomokiyo published the key in 2020; the reading of it here had slipped a column. Re-measured off his table, verified glyph for glyph on the leaf, and 86 of the 106 lines then read by hand against numbered-token images Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 17 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read in part Summary. Nicolas Raince was the French embassy’s secretary at Rome, and BnF fr. 2984 (Béthune 8509) keeps eight of his despatches of 1526 in cipher. Tomokiyo published the key for them in 2020, DECODE holds two of the letters as decrypted, Mignet noted in 1886 that the one letter “entirely in cipher” has its clear duplicate eight leaves earlier in the same volume, and Bourrilly printed the ciphered passages of two more in 1901. What has never been read anywhere found is most of the 13 May 1526 letter to Montmorency and the lower part of the 20 November one: about 106 lines. The obstacle was never cryptanalytic. It was that the published key had been read off Tomokiyo’s table by eye and slipped one column, so that l , m and n were each a place wrong and every reading built on it was corrupt. Measured off the image instead, the table resolves a control line glyph for glyph, and 86 of the 106 lines have now been read by hand from the microfilm. The 13 May letter reports the Emperor’s side of the negotiation nine days before Cognac — someone qui estoit en la court de Savoye est party pour venir icy , the Castilians and the Bourguignons, a plan to prendre le chemin de Valence , a capitulation for which ilz seront cause de la destruction , the plague in Rome, and a named man taken un jour, en plaine place pres du palais . The 20 November letter turns on a pontificate that seroit la cause de la totale ruine de sa maison . Status: read in part. 86 of 106 lines read glyph by glyph, with gaps left as gaps; 20 lines carry only a machine decode and are excluded from the edited text. One glyph, occurring ten times and always at a clause boundary, is in no published table.

t: Raince to Montmorency, Rome, 1526 — the key was misread by one column
h: The key had been read off by one column
b: Tomokiyo set out the 1526 key in French Ciphers during the Reign of Francis I (2020) as an image: a header row of plaintext letters over up to four rows of cipher glyphs, the columns about 78 px apart. It is a monoalphabetic substitution with homophones, three nulls and three word signs. Reading which glyph sits under which letter by eye is the whole difficulty, and the first pass here slipped a column. Doing it by measurement instead settles it. Locating the white header letters in the magenta band, then labelling the ink blobs below and assigning each to the nearest header column, every blob falls within 15 px of a column centre — a fifth of the column spacing. The measured table is: Every glyph cut out of the key image and labelled by the column it measures into. Three homophones for a and u/v , four for e , three for i , two each for l , o , p , r and s ; no glyph at all for x ; three nulls. Image: Drawn here from S. Tomokiyo’s key table, Cryptiana, “French Ciphers during the Reign of Francis I” (2020). The correction. l is the 9 , not the round s ; m is the round s , not the long f ; n is the long f . The first pass had these one place to the left. H measures under s , not under r where it had been put. Why it matters. That single shift is what produced dongUeaent for longuement , egsembde for ensemble and SonseigEur for monseigneur in the first machine draft. Every file derived from the shifted table was discarded. Confusable pairs. p has a T and a circle with a dash to its right; r has a 4 and a dash then a circle. The two are near mirror images and are the easiest pair on the leaf to confuse. The most frequent single glyph, a circle at the foot of a barred stem, is an e . Word signs. A looped L with a tail = con ; two small circles joined by a curve underneath = l’empereur ; a cursive y with a descender = le pape . The letter y is E , so a y-shaped glyph is the word sign, not the letter. The control. With the measured table, p. 29 line 20 resolves glyph for glyph and leaves nothing over: ∧ λ n v ✕✕ 7 ∧ ℓ ꝛ I ℓ 7 f 9 o ⊡ ꝛ v 4 ℓ ϝ 7 ∧ o R ꝛ E ψ ny 7 ∧ ℓ T o 4 ℓ E T ꝛ v 4 R 7 f ✕✕ 4 I ⊡ E → s [null] qui estoit en la court de Savoye [null] est party pour venir icy The line uses a , c , d , three of the four e homophones, two of the three i , l , n , o , p , q , r , s , t , u/v , y , and two of the three nulls. That is the evidence the table is right.

b: The numbers written on successive Gallica views run 29, 31, 33, 35, 37 — two apart, not one. Read as folio numbers that would mean half the volume’s openings were never filmed, and every letter in it half missing. They are page numbers, written on odd pages only: view n shows pages 2 n −4 and 2 n −3, 85 views cover about 167 pages, and the digitisation is complete. So the 13 May letter is three consecutive pages, 29, 30 and 31, and the 20 November one is p. 105. The text settles it independently. Page 29 ends … et n’est possible … monstrer plus a[ffe]- and page 30 opens -ction . Both halves of that join were read glyph by glyph before it was noticed.

t: Raince to Montmorency, Rome, 1526 — the key was misread by one column
b: The film is legible at about 2× but the ink is grey and the hand is small, so the difficulty is not the cipher but the transcription. Three things made the reading possible. One image per manuscript line, cut into four overlapping quarters and stacked, so a whole line is read in one view without losing magnification. Numbered tokens. Connected-component segmentation gives 5,629 glyph tokens; drawing each token’s box on the line and numbering it means a hand reading is written as one character per token and lands aligned to the segmentation with no guesswork. Every line was checked against its token count before it was kept. A scaffold, not a reading. A classifier over the token images, combined with a space-free period-French 6-gram beam, proposes a letter for every token. It is right on about 85–90 % of them, which is enough to speed a hand reading and nowhere near enough to be one. p. 30 line 8 with every segmented token boxed and numbered. The hand reading of this line is [null] respondu à ce que ce qu’on a envoyé d’icy et de V[null]enise par deu- , running on into line 9 as -ers ledict seigneur . Token 39, a K , is a null standing inside the word Venise . Image: Annotated here on BnF fr. 2984 p. 30 (Gallica btv1b90598430). Where the ceiling is, measured. The hand readings double as training data, so the classifier can be scored honestly by leaving one hand-read line out at a time: training data leave-one-line-out per-token accuracy the map’s own confident tokens only 0.840 + hand labels, weight 1 0.856 + hand labels, weight 8 0.901 (peak, at 32 hand-read lines) + hand labels, weight 30 0.860 That is the whole argument for doing it by hand. At 0.90 per token a six-letter word survives at 0.53, which is why only about a third of the machine text segments into real French words however the decoder is tuned. The residual confusions are between glyphs that really are similar at this resolution — ψ (e) against 4 (r), the cursive ℓ (t) against 9 (l) against the lollipop (d), the caret (s) against the vee (u) against × (a) — not between glyphs the key leaves ambiguous. More labels will not fix that; better images would.

t: Raince to Montmorency, Rome, 1526 — the key was misread by one column
b: Nine days before the League of Cognac was signed. The clear close on p. 31, transcribed here for the first time, dates and signs it — De Rome, ce xiij jour de may, 15c xxvj … Nicolas Rainse — and reports that Rome expects Andrea Doria at Civitavecchia that day or the next, with six galleys and two brigantines . The three ciphered pages that precede it read, in part: … ne cessera jamais qu’il n’ayt destruict ledict seigneur … — and, a line later, d’autres propo[s] … ains de vert[u] et mensonges . … ont receu … de Castille, qu’ilz disent … ; ensemble … les bourguignons ; and, of a great lord, les castilliens li[sent] au (con)traire que lesdessusdict[z] sont … … delib-eré prendre le chemin de Valence … à ceste fin, et qu’il ne voul-oyent qu’il feust … si grant seigneur. … et qu’il[z] seront cause de la destruction, de la part d’avoir faic-t capituler avec … — the likeliest referent being the Treaty of Madrid of January 1526, though the letter does not name it. Ledict He[rr]er[a](?) doit partir de dans deux ou troys jours pour s’en retourner — the name is not settled —; and …s qui estoit en la court de Savoye est party pour venir icy. p. 30: (L’empereur) est esbay de ce que … n’a escript autrement, aucune part deça, depuis son retour … en son royaume; et m’en a parlé plusieurs fois . … que mondict seigneur l’Admiral luy av-oit dict que seroit celuy qui y tiendroit. J’ay tousiours respondu à ce que ce qu’on a envoyé d’icy et de Venise par devers ledict seigneur … … deux ou trois fois qui a[voit] deu venir à Rome … disant prendre tout pour le mieul[x] … Bien est vray, monsei-gneur… p. 31: … la peste qui est au logis … ; …s foys escript des advis qui viennent aux imperiaulx par leu[rs] … ; … es grant dommaige en toutes les sortes qu’on pourroit … ; [il] y ayt grant obligation pour les dommaiges qu’ilz disent ledict avoir… and, near the end, a named man: …t un jour, en plaine place pres du palais, un nommé Pietro Anthonio … secretaire ou serviteur dudict, qui estoit icy pour luy … followed by propos … quel estoit cause de tout le mal … deux ou trois fois .

b: Twenty lines of the 106 carry only the machine decode. They are kept, marked, in trans/reading.txt and left out of the edited text rather than dressed up as a reading. Gaps inside the 86. The edited text leaves … wherever the glyphs did not resolve. Nothing is supplied by conjecture; a wrong confident reading would be worse than a hole. One glyph is in no published table: a bold vertical stem crossed by two horizontal bars, the lower one longer and projecting right. It occurs ten times across all four pages and every occurrence falls at a clause boundary — between plaisirs and qu’il , between lectres and qui est , opening a sentence. It is not the barred-b g , not the barred-stem e , and not any of the three nulls. Most likely a point or a fourth null; it is written · in the edited text. The p. 29 / p. 30 join reads …monstrer plus a[ffe]- + -ctio?e , where the glyph after ctio measures as a plain triangle ( f ) rather than the n the sense wants. Left with a query. Two personal names are not settled: messire Ca?in , who appears twice on p. 30, and the agent read He[rr]er[a] on p. 29. What would finish it is not modelling but light. The Gallica item is a black-and-white microfilm; reader’s photographs of pp. 29–31 and 105 would let the segmentation run clean, and the measured ceiling above says that is worth more than any further training data.

t: Raince to Montmorency, Rome, 1526 — the key was misread by one column
b: Key measured, not read. Header letters located in the key image, ink blobs labelled and assigned to the nearest column, every assignment within 15 px of a column centre. Contact sheet of every labelled glyph kept. Verified on the leaf against a control line that resolves with nothing left over, using sixteen of the alphabet’s letters and two of its three nulls. Segmentation by connected components on a background-normalised binarisation, tokens assigned to lines by a y-histogram, x-overlapping components merged; 5,629 tokens over the four pages. Cluster-to-letter map hill-climbed against a space-free period-French 6-gram, with each cluster restricted to the letters its glyph shape allows. Restricting the moves is what stops the collapse into a degenerate map that defeats an unconstrained solver on a stream with this much segmentation noise. Hand reading line by line against numbered-token images, one character per token, length-checked against the segmentation. Honest scoring by leave-one-line-out over the hand-read lines, since a model trained on its own output otherwise scores itself. Everything is in the repository: the measured key and reading method in raince/CALIBRATION.md , the account in raince/NOTES.md , the hand labels in raince/gold/labels.txt , the edited reading in raince/trans/reading_edited.txt , the line-by-line text with each line marked hand or machine in raince/trans/reading.txt , and the clear close of 13 May in raince/trans/p31_clear_close.txt .

Catalogue item 44 grouped four DECODE records attributed to Ferenc Rákóczi II. Three of them address “Monseigneur” and “Votre Altesse”: they are reports sent to Rákóczi, like R902 ( Groffey to Rákóczi, 1707 ). A first pass on DECODE's text transcriptions read them in substance with the preserved key DECODE R639. A second pass went back to the fourteen page images. It re-transcribed every cipher page and read the key sheet itself, which corrected DECODE's copy of the table (45 = S, 47 = T, the Z line, and the two unnumbered “de” codes 173 and 174). R912 and R922 now read at 97% of groups. R852 turned out to carry its own contemporary clear copy: it is dated Danzig, 22 January 1706, and its word codes come from a different issue of the table. The fourth record, R483, is Rákóczi's own letter from Lwów, signed “Franciscus Princeps” on 27 June 1711, eight weeks after the Peace of Szatmár. Aligning its 2,531 groups with the clerk's interlinear rebuilds a 224-code syllabic key that reproduces 70% of the clerk's letters and settles several of his doubtful words.

t: Four letters “of Ferenc Rákóczi II”: three were written to him
b: Monseigneur, j’ay receu la lettre que V. A. m’a fait l’honneur de m’escrire le 26. X bre . Je feray passer au S r Groffey celles qui estoient pour luy … V. A. peut luy donner directement les ordres, outre que je vous respons encore une fois de sa fidelité … J’ay veu une ou deux fois un imprimé latin intitulé Mercurius hungaricus . Il seroit tres important pour le service de V. A. qu’on imprimast regulierement toutes les semaines une feuille de cet imprimé … il n’y a point de gazetier allemand ny hollandois qui ne detruise à son ayse le Roy me d’Hongrie … On croioit encore à Berlin qu’il n’y avoit plus de Hongrois depuis l’action. The ciphered page is followed by its clear copy, read here from the image, and by a short clear note offering to keep a register of M. de Bonnac's letters and bills of exchange. The writer is at Danzig and speaks of Groffey in the third person. The cipher's letters and syllables agree with R639, but its word codes do not: 144 is de and 254 is la , where R639 has beaucoup and jusque . It is an earlier issue of the table.

t: Four letters “of Ferenc Rákóczi II”: three were written to him
b: Monseigneur, je me suis privé pendant quelque temps de l’honneur d’escrire à Vostre Altesse … fait à Madame la Palatine de Belz … une copie authentique de cette vente au sieur Kray … autant qu’il a esté possible par mon credit et par mes avances … pour joindre le Roy de Pologne … l’avantage de luy continuer mes services à la Cour de Pologne … je suis avec tout le respect possible, Monseigneur. The letter concerns a sale for the Palatine of Belz (Elżbieta Sieniawska), orders for carbines, and the sieur Kray. On page 2 it turns to money and to someone who is a prisoner.

t: Four letters “of Ferenc Rákóczi II”: three were written to him
b: J’ay eu l’honneur de marquer à Vostre Altesse … le Roy Stanislas … le Palatin de Belz … le grand Général … la pacification … une nouvelle élection en Pologne … le Czar … escrite au maréchal Rehnskiöld … Monsieur le Palatin de Russie … avec un profond respect et un zèle parfait. A survey of Polish and Swedish politics that includes the Rehnskiöld affair of R902. It also covers a regiment asked of Rákóczi, which King Stanisław and the Germans hold against him, and Tököly.

t: Four letters “of Ferenc Rákóczi II”: three were written to him
b: This letter is signed in autograph “Franciscus Princeps” and dated in clear “Leopoli die 27. Junii Anno 1711”. It is addressed to a trusted envoy on his way to Holland. Cipher and clear alternate within the lines, and the clerk wrote the decipherment above every ciphered stretch. Rákóczi sends a copy of the “Tractatus sic dictae Pacis Carolianae”, the Peace of Szatmár, which he calls a fraud worked out in Vienna. He will not recognise a king proclaimed in the counties outside a free diet, contrary to the 1687 article of Pozsony: nos Regem extra dietam promulgatum, non deposito [juramento], agnoscere non posse sine … ruina [libertatum nostrarum]. He appeals to the Tsar and the Polish Republic to mediate. He offers to come to a free diet and recognise a lawfully crowned king if the confederates recover their estates. He calls the Allies' assurances a “diversio armorum” and asks for the war to go on. He also reports Pálffy's cannon before “arcem nostram Munkatsiensem”, the confederation in Poland and the Muscovite advance. A clear postscript concerns mathematical instruments ordered from Mangold. The key. Each cipher line was aligned with the Latin above it by hard EM, with each code taking up to four letters. The result is a syllabic cipher with homophones. Single letters have several values (190 and 430 s; 140 and 380 n; 60 and 300 e; 20 and 260 a), open syllables have their own codes (257 re, 428 ti, 68 se, 362 de, 96 no, 457 ri, 92 ce, 152 co), and a few words and names are coded whole. Of 224 codes, 156 occur at least twice. Decoding the letter with this key reproduces 70% of the clerk's letters. Where the clerk's handwriting is doubtful, the cipher usually decides the reading.

t: Philippe Groffey (?) to Ferenc Rákóczi II, 15 October 1707 — the catalogue had the direction backwards
b: The existing transcription is good enough to establish subject and argument, but not to print every sentence as diplomatic plaintext. The excerpts below distinguish H (direct table reading), C (secure contextual repair of an evident digit slip), and M (meaning recoverable but wording still provisional). Grade Reading Why it matters C J’ay aussi [eu] l’honneur [de] vous… The transcript has 142 where 192 gives eu , and 143 where 173 gives de . C … Monseigneur … les lettres de Monsieur Ráday au général Rehnskiöld … Identifies the report’s central diplomatic correspondence. C … à la Cour de Suède … Locates one field of the writer’s activity. C sur mon zèle à Votre [Altesse] Consistent with a report addressed to Rákóczi. H je me suis donné tous les mouvements The writer describes exerting himself on the recipient’s behalf. M … prendre les intérêts de la Pologne autant à cœur … se sacrifier … pour affranchir la liberté … opprimée par les Suédois en faveur du roi Stanislas States the political burden of the closing discussion; connectors remain vulnerable to transcription error. Other securely anchored names and phrases include the king of Poland, the king of Sweden, Russia, Prince Konstanty, Polish grandees and troops, the Emperor and Vienna, and English and Dutch actors. Taken together, the letter is an intelligence and lobbying report, not a private letter written by Rákóczi.

t: Philippe Groffey (?) to Ferenc Rákóczi II, 15 October 1707 — the catalogue had the direction backwards
h: The unsigned writer was probably Philippe Groffey
b: R902 has no open signature, so the attribution must remain qualified. Three independent clues converge: The exact key is headed De Monsieur de Bonac et Graffei . The letter reports Ráday’s approach to Rehnskiöld and activity at the Swedish and Polish courts. Contemporary scholarship identifies Philippe Groffey, also written Grophey or Graffei, as Rákóczi’s representative around those courts and as a contact of Ráday. This is strong historical attribution, not proof from a signature. The public title therefore retains the question mark.

t: Randolph to Sussex, 5 July 1570 — the cipher and its decipherment on the next leaf
b: DECODE R4931 (Cotton Caligula C II f. 277), catalogued as an unread Randolph letter of 1569, is Randolph’s despatch from Edinburgh of 5 July 1570. A crib attack from Boyd’s abstract read about 70% of the cipher before the next leaf, f. 278 (DECODE R4932), turned out to be its contemporary decipherment. Every cipher run is read: the Scottish Queen’s party’s distrust of Elizabeth, the stayed regency, Morton, the money, the soldiers’ pay, Grange. Edinburgh → the Earl of Sussex · word-divided homophonic substitution with name signs, inline with clear English · 5 July 1570 · read at the time Randolph to Sussex, 5 July 1570: the cipher and its decipherment on the next leaf to Earl of Sussex BL, Cotton MS Caligula C II f. 277 (DECODE R4931; catalogue item 99). DECODE dates it 1569 and gives no reading. It is Thomas Randolph's letter to the Earl of Sussex, "At Edenborowe the 5te of Julye 1570". DECODE offered R4930 as the key record, but that record is Burghley's notes on the Norfolk letters. The decipherment is f. 278, filed as its own "decrypted" record, R4932. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 21 September 2026 resolved Summary. Catalogue item 99 was a DECODE record of a Randolph letter to Sussex, "non-decrypted", dated 1569, with "what the cipher hides not known". The letter is dated at Edinburgh, 5 July 1570. It is clear English with five cipher runs, the longest about seventy words. Boyd's Calendar of Scottish Papers iii (1903), no. 339, abstracts Sussex's clear copy of it. Using that abstract as a crib, a language-model anneal read about 70% of the cipher words before any decipherment was found. It recovered "murtherers and traitors", "determined to have made a regent" and "whome nether by lawe, duetie or conscien they thinke them selves bounde unto". The next leaf in the volume, f. 278 (DECODE R4932), then turned out to be a contemporary decipherment: a clerk re-copied each cipher word and wrote the plaintext above it. That leaf confirms every value the anneal had found, and it closes the remaining gaps. The letter says the Scottish Queen's party "have litle confidens [in] the Q. of England, that so ofte changeth her course". The King's lords, who had "determined to have made a regent, dyd staye it" on hope of better comfort. They now fear being forced to join "murderers and traytors, bothe of kyng and regent". Randolph adds that he has spoken with Morton, that the soldiers' pay should be continued, and that Grange does not look for the Scottish Queen's "home cumming". The only doubt left is in three faint words of the clerk's first gloss line.

t: Randolph to Sussex, 5 July 1570 — the cipher and its decipherment on the next leaf
b: This is a word-divided substitution. Its signs are Latin letters, figures and invented marks, with two or three signs for the common vowels, and some signs stand for persons or phrases. The signs are ⊟ = "the S. Q. partie in Scotland", θθ = "the S. Queene", ΠΠ = "the Q. of England", and a struck +++ for the Earl of Morton. The values the glosses confirm include: = c, c u/v, D r, q s, ɛ n, δ t, ϙ o, Ӿ o, 4 d, # i, 8 e, ʒ a, 3 f, Π g, ⍏ n, U h, Ω t, ϖ m, λ m, ≡ i, Γ h. Tomokiyo's pages do not list this key. His Randolph ciphers are the 1559–60 Sadler–Croft ones.

t: Randolph to Sussex, 5 July 1570 — the cipher and its decipherment on the next leaf
b: The clear text is in roman type and the deciphered text in italics. The deciphered wording is the f. 278 clerk's, checked word by word against the cipher on f. 277. f. 277r, ll. 1–10. I have receaved your L. lre of the seconde of this present, and what maye answer some parte thereof your L. hathe I trust seen by myne wrytten from hens the same daye, wch in effecte as this. The S. Q. partie in Scotland wyl reke ther owne […] the S. queene handes […] fortefy, have litle confidens [in] the Q. of England, that so ofte changeth her course; and now of late of all, whereas they were determined to have made a regent, dyd staye it full sore agaynst their willes, upon hope of better comfort, and shall be forced to yeld [to] ennemies, and [be] conforted [with] murderers and traytors, bothe of kyng and regent, and to obbey her whome nether by lawe, duetie or conscien they thinke them selves bounde unto. This your L. shall reyde not spoken of my selfe, but this is a great parte of their greif, and all most everie mans speche, and preached in pulpet in playner wordes then I lyste to wryte. f. 277r, ll. 16–18. …to be sorte wth your L. it thinke utterlye undon , what so ever be come of us . I have spoken with therle of Morton , who is of that mynde that before I have wrytten, and in verie playne speche lamentethe the state of his countrie… f. 277r, l. 27. … the mony , whiche I knowe will marveylouslye discomforte him, as it dothe also some other… f. 277r, l. 29. …that the soldiars may be continewed in pay untill the Convention be ended. f. 277v, l. 14. I knowe he loketh not [for] the S. Q. home cumming .

t: Randolph to Sussex, 5 July 1570 — the cipher and its decipherment on the next leaf
b: The two images of R4931 are byte-identical to two of R4930's, so the "key" record was checked first and found to hold no key. Boyd's abstract, made from Sussex's clear copy, was lined up with the cipher runs. The runs were transcribed into sign tokens and annealed against an English n-gram model (en-1640s) with word divisions kept. With no crib pinned, the anneal already produced "murtherers and traitors", "regent", "whome … nor conscience they thinke them selves … unto". Pinning the crib words fixed about 70% of the text. The rest would not converge, because several signs that look alike on the page (plain, curly and barred x; 3 against a tailed ʒ) carry different values. A sweep of the DECODE records from the same volume then found R4932, the decipherment, one leaf on. Every value recovered earlier agrees with it.
