t: The cardinal de Mâcon in Rome to Montmorency, 1536–1537 — eight letters from an “unknown sender”
b: Eight ciphered records of BnF fr. 3053, catalogued as an unknown correspondent writing to Anne de Montmorency from Rome. The sender signs three of them in clear: Charles Hémard de Denonville, bishop and then cardinal of Mâcon, ambassador to Paul III. Tomokiyo reconstructed the cipher from this very volume and Lasry re-tabulated it in 2023, but nobody published a word of the text. Seven records are now read in part and the eighth resolved — its cipher is a second fr. 3053 key whose contemporary decipherment stands on the next leaf. The Pope manoeuvring over the general council and the Germans, Andrea Doria’s galleys and a suspected secret treaty, Milan refused to the Farnese, the Sienese exiles, a conclave weighed while Paul III fails, and an estate in France offered to the Pope’s son. Rome, Orvieto → the grand maître · homophonic cipher on graphic signs · 1536–1537 · read in part The cardinal de Mâcon in Rome to Montmorency, 1536–1537 to Anne de Montmorency BnF Français 3053, eight records (DECODE R4233–R4248) · catalogued here as an unknown sender writing from Rome · about 670 lines of cipher, one letter almost wholly enciphered The sender identified as Charles Hémard de Denonville, bishop and then cardinal of Mâcon, ambassador to Paul III · read with the key Tomokiyo reconstructed from this volume and Lasry re-tabulated; neither published a plaintext · six contemporary decipherments found in the margins and used as controls Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read in part Summary. The catalogue held eight ciphered letters of 1536–37 addressed to Anne de Montmorency from an unknown correspondent at Rome, classed A because they fall in the months of Charles V’s entry into Rome and the renewal of the war. The sender is not unknown: three of the records are signed in clear “Charles e. de Mascon” or “E. Card[ina]l de Mascon”, and the volume is the correspondence of Charles Hémard de Denonville, bishop and from December 1536 cardinal of Mâcon, Francis I’s ambassador to Paul III. The cipher is the one Satoshi Tomokiyo reconstructed years ago from this very volume and George Lasry re-tabulated in 2023 for a sibling letter in fr. 3071; neither published any plaintext, and no edition prints these despatches. Because the key was rebuilt from these letters, parts of them had been read before; what is new here is a published transcription and reading. So the work was reading, not breaking. Every cipher passage of the eight records is now deciphered, seven records in part and the eighth resolved: its cipher is not Mâcon’s at all but a second fr. 3053 key, and the clerk’s own clear decipherment of it stands on the next leaf. What comes out is an ambassador’s running report on the general council and the Germans, on Andrea Doria’s galleys and a suspected secret treaty, on the Sienese exiles, on the Farnese marriages and a conclave, and on the offer of an estate in France to the Pope’s son. Status: about 95 % of all the cipher letters read after a sign-by-sign re-transcription from the Gallica scans, checked against every clear copy of the time (error 3–8 %, mostly spelling); nothing on the pages is physically unreadable.

t: The cardinal de Mâcon in Rome to Montmorency, 1536–1537 — eight letters from an “unknown sender”
b: DECODE gives the sixteen fr. 3053 records a recipient (Anne de Montmorency), a place (Rome, twice Orvieto) and no sender. Tomokiyo’s page on the French ciphers of Francis I names the volume for what it is: letters of 1535–37 from the bishop, later cardinal, of Mâcon, ambassador in Rome, to Montmorency. The records confirm it in clear. R4240 ends “A Orviette le deux[iesme] jour de septembre 1536”, signed “Vostre treshumble et tresobeissant serviteur Charles e. de Mascon”; R4247’s second letter is dated Orvieto, 1 September 1536 and signed the same way; R4239 ends “A Rome le vj e jour d’apvril 1537”, signed “E. Card[ina]l de Mascon” — the promotion of 22 December 1536 falling between the two. That also settles the key. In the repository’s Gramont, Mâcon and Langeac write-up, Lasry’s table of 5 November 2023 for BnF fr. 3071 f. 9 is called “Mascon’s cipher” and identified with fr. 3053; the letter it reads, Rome, 11 April 1537, is five days younger than R4239. The same key serves here, with the corrections set out below.

t: The cardinal de Mâcon in Rome to Montmorency, 1536–1537 — eight letters from an “unknown sender”
h: Orvieto, 2 September 1536: the council and the Germans
b: The clearest of the letters, and the one with the best control — a contemporary hand glossed its last cipher lines in the margin, and the gloss and the independent reading agree word for word. Mâcon has learned “de bon lieu” that Vergerio, nuncio under Clement VII and kept on by Paul III, carried word from Ferdinand to the Germans that the Pope and the College were content that, coming to the council, they might there « dire et faire ainsi qu’ils seroient inspirez par le Sainct Esperit »; on that assurance they resolved to attend, hoping for a decisive peace. But the Pope, judging this would be « la totale ruine de l’Eglise et sainct siege apostolique », has sent an auditor to summon them on the old law and custom instead. The Germans will not consent, Mâcon hears: they say the morals of pope, cardinals and bishops must be reformed, and that cannot be done without them. Then the clear text resumes, and the ambassador leaves his master to draw the conclusion: « Je vous laisse a penser sur cela, monseigneur, que ce sera de l’assemblee dudict concille. »

t: The cardinal de Mâcon in Rome to Montmorency, 1536–1537 — eight letters from an “unknown sender”
h: Orvieto, September 1536: Doria’s galleys, and Milan
b: Andrea Doria had written to the conte dell’Anguillara to hold his galleys ready to join his own when sent for. Since Doria’s cousin Antonio had lately taken one of Anguillara’s fustas, and since Anguillara’s galleys are in the Pope’s service, Mâcon inferred a reconciliation made at the Pope’s command, and therefore a secret treaty with the Emperor — and put it to Paul III to his face. The Pope answered that Anguillara had indeed shown him the letter and that he marvelled at it, given the seizure of the fusta; that he did not think Doria content with him, having last year made him pay for three months for his three galleys and pay besides for the dispensation for his wife’s son to marry Antonio de Leyva’s second daughter; and that he was wholly ignorant of the cause. Mâcon replied that it could not be so without either a treaty with the Emperor, which he could not believe, or Anguillara having taken Doria’s service; the Pope said only that he knew nothing of it. A second block of the same letter has a man sent by cardinal Ennio Filonardi of Veroli sound the ambassador out: could the King be brought to consent that the duchy of Milan pass, from the Emperor, to the son of Pier Luigi Farnese, or else to the young Sforza? Mâcon answered that neither the King nor Messeigneurs his sons would ever consent, and that as long as the crown of France reigned it would not suffer Milan to go into other hands than its own, being their true inheritance — so it was time lost for the Pope. The second letter of 1 September 1536 (R4247) carries the count of Pitigliano’s advice: if the Emperor winters in Milan, strike at Naples, discontented and with no strong places but on the coast, and Sicily « ne fauldroit, avec peu d’ayde, de se revolter ».

t: The cardinal de Mâcon in Rome to Montmorency, 1536–1537 — eight letters from an “unknown sender”
h: Rome, September 1536: the Sienese exiles, and a German with an offer
b: The bearer of the letter is sent by the Sienese fuorusciti to press Francis I to an enterprise against Siena. Mâcon sees no prospect in it, but did not stop the journey; his fear is that if the exiles are left to themselves they will go over to duke Alessandro de’ Medici, who is working to win them and so « s’impatroniser de l’estat du dict Siennes ». In the same letter a German at Rome, who says he is of King Ferdinand’s chamber and knows his secrets and wants to enter the King’s service, gives him letters for a lansquenet captain serving with count Wilhelm von Fürstenberg; Mâcon suggests having them translated in Paris before they are delivered.

t: The cardinal de Mâcon in Rome to Montmorency, 1536–1537 — eight letters from an “unknown sender”
h: Rome, January and February 1537: marriages, a conclave, and a marriage used as currency
b: The January letter (R4233) runs over the pourparlers on marriages for Pier Luigi Farnese’s children, with cardinal Trivulzio’s view on how to stop them; the imperial ambassador and Venice; cardinals Trani, Cesi and Pisani. If the French cardinals were at Rome, Mâcon writes, they could steer a conclave should some mishap befall the Pope, who is « septuagenaire et plus » and failing — and meanwhile the King has done no favour to any of the Pope’s servants, so little goodwill can be expected from them. The Pope is sending cardinal Verulano’s secretary, « ung tres mauvais garson », into Switzerland, and means to take the legation of Parma and Piacenza from Salviati and give it to Verulano; behind it Mâcon suspects « quelque dessaing sur le duché de Millan ». In Piedmont the French captains are quarrelling among themselves, Guido Rangone among them, and the grain is nearly gone. The letter of 15 February (R4235) is the sharpest sentence found in these eight records, and it is one of the three checked word for word against a contemporary margin: « j’ay sceu de bon lieu que le dict [pape] vouloit entretenir le [roy] de mariage, et ayant de ce dudict seigneur bonne[s paroles], pour ce s’en prevaloir vers le dict [Empereur], pour parvenir a son intendit. » Keep it from everyone but the King, he adds, and keep the secret of the envoys’ charge — above all from the bishop of Verona, who passes for more devoted to the King than to the Emperor because he holds benefices of him. The long February letter (R4234), almost wholly in cipher, is now read throughout. Its first pages turn on the same business: the Pope means to wrong someone through an intermediary and to bring the King to consent; cardinal Cesarini writes in the same sense; the bishop “de Lodes” — Lodi, then at Venice, whose see had passed to cardinal Simonetta (first read here as Rodez) — holds that the King should never consent. Later pages report the marriages of Pier Luigi’s sons and the match of his house with Cosimo de’ Medici, “sworn several times over”, and then his arming: so many thousand escuz paid at his departure from Rome, two thousand more assigned at Parma and Piacenza, and a levy of six thousand Italians, five thousand Swiss, five hundred light horse and a hundred men-at-arms. The rest of the letter, read in a third pass, is the fullest account in the volume of the Farnese design on Milan. Pier Luigi’s horse under Giovanni Battista Savelli is to be ready this month and the foot by March; a Sienese gentleman in his service, questioned by Mâcon, says the troops are held in Parma and Piacenza « soubz umbre et couleur de vouloir garder » them, ready to garrison the towns and fortresses of the duchy of Milan if the Farnese marriages persuade the Emperor to sell it to Pier Luigi for a great sum; and the Pope, « qui est fin », will meanwhile make a show of keeping his neutrality. Mâcon weighs the report as possibly a plant by the Imperialist cardinals Veroli and “Cesane”, but the Pope’s own admissions give him « grant presumption »; and Contarini, « imperial pour la vie », has become the Pope’s familiar. The last cipher pages (one of them with a clear copy slipped in beside it) call messire Ambroise « corruptible plus que tous les hommes que je congnoisse », fear that the King’s new demand for three tenths on the French clergy, with the calumny of the Turk, will give the Pope his pretext to declare against him, and end on Andrea Doria, whose talk of going to Spain Mâcon takes for a feint. The rest of the 15 February letter has the Pope angling for the fortresses of Milan and saying the idea came from the King’s side; Mâcon denies it, and counsels not driving the Pope to despair. A later passage, read against a contemporary clear copy bound in beside it, sets out the French hope: « si le Roy est fort en Italie du costé de Lombardie, facillement ledict estat de Florence se pourra reduire en l’ancienne liberté et devotion dudict seigneur Roy ».

t: The cardinal de Mâcon in Rome to Montmorency, 1536–1537 — eight letters from an “unknown sender”
h: Rome, 6 April 1537: an estate in France for the Pope’s son
b: The last and largest of the read letters. Paul III talks to the ambassador of the marriage of his grandson Ottavio Farnese to the Emperor’s daughter Margaret — the match celebrated in November 1538 — and insists on his neutrality while pressing for peace. A contemporary hand glossed one line of the second letter, “quant au faict de florence”, and it opens a passage on the intrigues at Rome of the exile cardinals Salviati and Ridolfi in the months after the murder of duke Alessandro de’ Medici on 6 January 1537; the clear text around it has Mâcon setting a spy on Salviati’s household. The heart of the letter is a bid for the Pope’s son. The Imperialists have offered Pier Luigi Farnese the investiture of Novara and are pressing him to take it; Mâcon counters with « quelque honneste estat en France », arguing from the Pope’s age and from Pier Luigi’s need of an « occasion d’en eschapper » once his father is dead. Pier Luigi answers neither yes nor no: he will take nothing without the Pope’s knowledge, and now the King’s. Around it the clear pages carry the news of the season: Bohemia’s grant to the King of the Romans against the Turk, a Lutheran diet in Saxony, and the death of the marquis of Saluzzo and count Philippe Torniello by arquebus shot before the castle of Carmagnola in Holy Week. The pages read in the third pass fill in the middle: the duke of Urbino tells Ridolfi’s envoy Albizzi of « estroicte praticque » between the Pope and the Emperor’s ministers, the Emperor wanting tenths and crusade money and a league of the Italian princes; Mâcon asks for a ciphered article he can show the Pope, « afin que si la raison et l’honnesteté ne le desmeuvent des dictes praticques, que la peur l’en peust divertir »; and Novara was offered to Pier Luigi at the Pope’s own command. Meeting him in the Pope’s antechamber, Mâcon is told, « sans accepter ne refuser », to write nothing of it to the King.

t: The cardinal de Mâcon in Rome to Montmorency, 1536–1537 — eight letters from an “unknown sender”
h: f. 85: a second cipher, read at the time
b: One record, R4248, refused the key altogether. Its signs are a different set, and Mâcon’s values turn them to nonsense; they match instead the second table Tomokiyo sketched from this volume, and he noted that the fragment on f. 85 is “deciphered on f. 86”. So it is: f. 86 carries a full contemporary clear decipherment of the passage, and it agrees with every clear connecting phrase left standing on f. 85. The writer, after a day in the country with a cardinal, had urged him that everything, and above all the conduct of the war, should pass through Montmorency’s hands, and that anything else was « fumee et vent »; the cardinal seemed persuaded, and added that the cardinal of Lorraine, in his capitulation with the Pope, had conceded things never thought of before — which they meant to undo, leaving the whole matter to Montmorency. Tabulating that second key from f. 85 against f. 86 is work left undone here.

t: The cardinal de Mâcon in Rome to Montmorency, 1536–1537 — eight letters from an “unknown sender”
h: Method, and what the key really looks like
b: The system is homophonic substitution on digit-like graphic signs, one sign per letter, with special signs for doubled letters, two nulls, and exactly three code numbers: 20 = l’Empereur, 30 = pape, 40 = roy. No other number occurs in any of the eight records, which is worth saying because it means nothing in these letters is hidden behind an unread nomenclator: what is not read is not read because of the hand. Reading proceeded record by record from the DECODE page scans, cropping a line at a time at full resolution, writing each line as a string of ASCII aliases, decoding it with the table built in gramont1529/macon_key.md , and then reading the output as French. Six contemporary decipherments turned up in the volume — marginal on R4233, R4235 and R4240, interlinear on R4235, R4239 and R4240 — and three of them agree with the independent decoding word for word, which is the control this write-up rests on. One of them also corrected the published table: over the line ꭓ£+7G 8ꭓ ǂ3Δ4G 5o ǂ10D27o74g a contemporary wrote “quant au faict de florence”, which makes the big curly X Q and U , not N as the working table had it, and shows the QUE group written three ways indifferently. Other values fixed here: the plain saltire is N as well as L; 4 is C, R and sometimes T; 7 is N, R and B; the triple bar on a stem is RR (proved by PIE-RR-E, three times); ω is PP and the hooked ʃ is H, both in eschapper . F. 38v, the postscript to R4239 (Rome, 6 April 1537): clear French with runs of the Mâcon signs, and a contemporary decipherment written over them, “mandé de […] pape pour me faire entendre les propoz que verrez … par Sa S[ain]cteté”. The key reads these runs with 2 errors in 64 letters. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3053 f. 38v, via Gallica. What limits the readings to between 55 and 85 % is one family of signs. The barred crosses — ǂ , £ , the long ƒ — stand for F, P, O, U, V and D, and in this hand they are separable only by context. That is a palaeographic limit, not a cryptographic one.

t: The cardinal de Mâcon in Rome to Montmorency, 1536–1537 — eight letters from an “unknown sender”
b: After the first passes about a quarter of the letters were still doubtful, and nearly all the doubt sat on one family of barred signs. Cutting 1,262 glyphs out of the pages and grouping them by shape showed why: what the readers had written as one sign ǂ is four or five different signs of the key — a long hooked f for O, a £ with a looped foot for U, a two-barred stroke for P, a looped p-top for F, a barred q for M — each distinct once the line is seen at full size. Every record was then transcribed again, sign by sign, from the BnF’s own full-resolution scans on Gallica, with each warped line straightened first, and decoded by the key and a sixteenth-century French language model. Two more contemporary clear copies turned up in the process: ff. 37r–v, bound after R4239, are the clerk’s clear text of that record’s whole second letter, and Mâcon’s companion letter to the King of the same February day (BnF Dupuy 44, ff. 30–38) carries its own decipherment. Against every clear text the new readings differ by 3–8 % of letters, and most of that is spelling ( pappe for pape , Loys for Luis ). About 95 % of the cipher is now read. The lines once called faded at the foot of R4247 are sharp on the Gallica scan: « il seroit icy fort difficille de recouvrer gens de cheval ne artillerie; bien trouverroit on tant de gens de pied, et bons, qu’on vouldroit, et beaucoup de gentilz homes forussiz, qui serviroient pour peu de chose. » R4234 now names Stefano Colonna to lead Pier Luigi’s foot and Giovanni Battista Savelli his horse; R4240 names the auditor sent to the Germans, “Vuorst”, apparently Peter van der Vorst.

t: The cardinal de Mâcon in Rome to Montmorency, 1536–1537 — eight letters from an “unknown sender”
b: About 5 % of the letters, inside lines that otherwise read: runs where the signs 7 (N or B), 4 (C or R) or the O/U pair stay ambiguous and no clear copy covers them. The ink is legible; nothing on these pages is physically lost. A few short runs in R4239 (the postscript’s margin, whose contemporary gloss does not fit the signs under it) and some names: a Sienese gentleman, a count “Mer[?]le”, two German captains, “Cesane”, “Palmier”. The f. 85 key could be tabulated from its own contemporary decipherment on f. 86.

t: Salinas and Ronquillo to Fuenmayor, 1676–78 — twenty letters in one shared cipher, four read for the first time
b: The rest of Fuenmayor’s ciphered correspondence in Brussels: eight letters from Spain’s envoy in London and twelve from its plenipotentiary at Nijmegen. The key rebuilt here for Balbases reads all twenty unchanged, 88% of 23,463 groups, once six boundary-less DECODE transcriptions are re-segmented. Sixteen margins are confirmed; four letters without one, two catalogued as non-decrypted, are read only in gist, so the set stays read in part. London and Nijmegen → Copenhagen · syllabic nomenclator · 1676–78 · read in part Bernardo de Salinas and Pedro Ronquillo to Baltasar de Fuenmayor, 1676–78 from Pedro Ronquillo Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, Secrétairerie d’État et de Guerre, inv. nr. 2559 · DECODE R966–R984 and R1001, twenty letters · sixteen with a contemporary decipherment in the margin, four without The Balbases key reads all twenty unchanged: 88% of 23,463 groups, including the two letters DECODE lists as non-decrypted Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 21 September 2026 solved in part Summary. Fuenmayor’s papers in Brussels hold ciphered letters from four Spanish envoys. The key for Balbases was rebuilt here from his margins, and it then read Hernán Núñez ’s Stockholm letters unchanged. So it was tried on everything else in the volume: eight letters from Bernardo de Salinas in London (August 1676 – March 1677) and twelve from Pedro Ronquillo at the Nijmegen congress (December 1676 – March 1678). It fits all twenty. It reads 88.4% of the 23,463 groups in DECODE’s transcriptions, and the residue is transcription noise. Sixteen letters have a contemporary decipherment in the margin, which the key output confirms. Four have none: Salinas of 15 September 1676 and 2 March 1677, and Ronquillo of 26 February and 19 March 1678. DECODE lists the last two as non-decrypted. These four are read here in gist for the first time. The only real work was DECODE’s transcriptions: six are typed with no group boundaries at all, and had to be re-segmented against the key’s vocabulary. Carpio in Rome used a different cipher; the other northern envoys shared this one. With 88% of groups read and the four unmargined letters (R970 77%, R973 86%, R982 71%, R984 86%) read only for gist, the set is read in part by this project’s read bar; correcting their transcriptions from the images is still to do. Ronquillo to Fuenmayor, Nijmegen, 26 February 1678 (R984, p. 1): the first cipher block, with no decipherment beside it. The key reads he visto con atención lo que V.S. me participa en sus referidas cartas en lo tocante a las [conferencia]s que se han tratado en essa asamblea de los aliados del Norte . t: Salinas and Ronquillo to Fuenmayor, 1676–78 — twenty letters in one shared cipher, four read for the first time
h: The four letters without a margin
b: Ronquillo, Nijmegen, 26 February 1678 (R984) Ronquillo replies to Fuenmayor’s reports on the assembly of the northern allies. Everything depends on the resolutions of the English parliament, and on whether Charles II will really break with France. Ronquillo, who knows that court, doubts it: no me atreveré a hacer juicio fijo ni de la paz ni de la guerra mientras no tuviremos apariencias más ciertas y seguras de las deliberaciones de la [corona] británica . The Danes complain about subsidy remittances and say they can do nothing. The Elector of Brandenburg is in Pomerania. At the end, the Duke of Hanover’s intrigue, "esta trama", runs through his kinship with Madame. Ronquillo, Nijmegen, 19 March 1678 (R982) This comes ten days after the fall of Ghent. The transcription is poor (full of "?"), and only the gist reads: the congress, Flanders taken by surprise, the two months that are lacking, the Brunswick princes, estamos muy mal , and Ronquillo’s own melancólicas reflexiones . Salinas, London, 15 September 1676 (R970) Ya se habrá [sabido] el fatal suceso… Salinas fears the blow closes esta puerta to Spain. The discourses at the English court turn towards a peace, and the "progresos" on Fuenmayor’s side weigh on them. The minister has taken the news calmly. There is mention of the Danish fleet. Salinas, London, 2 March 1677 (R973) The English princes no siendo tan malos when it comes to withdrawing their troops from French service, en que me prometo persistirán . The preparations of recent months show that everything is in earnest. Talk treats the peace as good as made.

t: Salinas and Ronquillo to Fuenmayor, 1676–78 — twenty letters in one shared cipher, four read for the first time
b: The Balbases key was used, with the four values added for Hernán Núñez (167 Suecia, 161 resolución, os para, 6+ o). It was applied without changes to DECODE’s transcriptions of all twenty records. Six records (R971, R974, R978, R979, R983, R1001) are typed character by character with no group boundaries, and at first read 0%. Each line was rejoined and segmented by dynamic programming over the key’s vocabulary: fewest groups, with one-character groups penalised. They then read 90–94%. R970 and R973 write one sign as "Infinity" (∞), which is c before a vowel. R970’s transcriber also writes 5 where the key has a and b for que . These conventions account for most of its unread groups. The sixteen margins were compared with the key output. They agree.

t: The Roosevelt cryptogram — the numbers 1 to 52, written once each
b: Three lines of digits above a threat to the President, reproduced by Friedman and unread since 1935. Read at glyph level they are a permutation of 1 to 52 with zero padding; the permutation drifts upward, runs 39 40 41 42 and falls into sixteen rising chains where a shuffle gives 26, the marks of a hand-written list. The ordered-key cipher readings that can be tested fail while matched controls are recovered. Washington · April 1935 · Schmeh Top 50 no. 17 · explained The Roosevelt cryptogram to Franklin D. Roosevelt Three lines of digits above a schoolboy threat to the President, reproduced by William Friedman, unread since 1935 They are the numbers 1 to 52, each written once, in an order that looks like a hand-written shuffle. There is no text behind them. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 16 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 no message Summary. Read at glyph level from the sharpest copy available, the number block is a permutation of 1 to 52 : nine single digits and 43 tick-joined pairs, every value once, plus eighteen zeros in groups of six and three. Thomas Ernst noticed this in 2017 and called the block a doodle; the claim checks out. The permutation is not a random one: its values drift upward with position, it runs through 39 40 41 42 in a row, and it decomposes into sixteen rising chains where a shuffle would give about 26. Those are the marks of a person writing down "random" numbers without repeating any. The one family of cipher readings that can be tested at this length, alphabetically ordered homophones or a rank-derived transposition key, fails while matched 52-letter controls are recovered. Status: explained as a constructed sequence, not read. There is no message to read.

t: The Roosevelt cryptogram — the numbers 1 to 52, written once each
b: A sheet received by the Secret Service on 24 April 1935, according to the receiving stamp on its face, headed “Secret Service” in a looping hand, with a diagonal “261” top right, three lines of digits, two lines of block capitals, and a skull and crossbones above a dagger driven through a boot. William Friedman reproduced it as figure 2 of the first of his 1959 lectures, printed by the NSA as The Friedman Legacy (1992), with one sentence: an authentic example of a transposition cipher, sent to President Roosevelt, which the Secret Service asked him to decipher, and which to his chagrin said “Did you ever bite a lemon?” That reading takes every second letter of NDOIMDEYLOAUEETVIEBR?; the line under it, OR ELSE YOU DIE!!, is in clear. Friedman said nothing about the digits. Klaus Schmeh posted the letter in 2015 and again in December 2017 as number 17 of his fifty unsolved cryptograms. In the comments Marc Gutgesell observed that no tick-joined pair repeats and that the loose digits are 1 to 9; Thomas Ernst listed the 43 pairs, found they were exactly 10 to 52, and concluded the block was “a doodle, if not a fake”, perhaps made to give Friedman a lemon to bite. Nobody has proposed a reading since.

t: The Roosevelt cryptogram — the numbers 1 to 52, written once each
b: Two copies exist: Schmeh’s 614-pixel scan and the figure in the NSA book. The Internet Archive holds a 300 ppi scan of the book, and its figure, cropped here, is the sharpest copy of the block that can be had without the original. Figure 2 of The Friedman Legacy , NSA Center for Cryptologic History, 1992. Image: NSA Center for Cryptologic History, The Friedman Legacy (1992), fig. 2, via the Internet Archive. The “apostrophes” of the standard transcription are short ticks written between and above two digits, and the two digits under a tick are one number. Digits without a tick stand alone. Read that way the block is: 1 7 2 10 15 17 19 21 26 8 32 33 20 37 000000 16 27 12 34 38 28 22 39 40 41 42 48 44 000000 9 3 13 000 18 4 23 24 000 46 29 35 51 5 43 47 000 6 11 36 50 52 30 49 45 25 31 14 — The 43 pairs are the numbers 10 to 52, each exactly once. The nine loose digits are 1 to 9, each exactly once, in the order 1 7 2 8 9 3 4 5 6. The eighteen zeros come in groups of 6, 6, 3 and 3. That is the whole content of the block: a permutation of 1 to 52 with four separators. Friedman’s or the Secret Service’s pencilled trial letters under the digits, which two commenters noticed, are not recoverable from either scan.

t: The Roosevelt cryptogram — the numbers 1 to 52, written once each
b: A permutation of 52 numbers can be tested against a fair shuffle. This one fails in four ways at once. statistic observed fair shuffle of 52 p (200 000 shuffles) rank correlation of value with position +0.39 0 0.002 neighbours differing by exactly +1 5 about 1 0.003 rising chains (values whose positions increase) 16 about 26.5 below 1 in 200 000 neighbours summing to 53 4 about 1 0.018 The rising chains are the telling one. Follow each value to the next: 1 2 3 4 5 6 appear in that order along the block, so do 7 8 9, 21 to 25, 26 to 31, 32 to 36 and 37 to 43. The writer worked upward through the unused numbers in several interleaved passes, fell back for the ones skipped, and when fresh numbers ran short wrote 39 40 41 42 straight off. Every anomaly in the table is of that kind. Three of the four pairs summing to 53 straddle a zero group (37|16, 44|9, 47|6), which Gerd noticed in 2017; it is a mild excess and not a structure anything else depends on. The one object that comes in 52 is a deck of cards, so the block was also tested as a riffle-shuffled deck. Sixteen rising chains is what four riffles produce, but a deck riffled four times does not also drift upward by 0.39 and run four consecutive cards: the joint event has probability 0.003 under the Gilbert-Shannon-Reeds model at four riffles and 0.023 at three. A hand-written list explains the block better than a deck does. Neither contains a text.

t: The Roosevelt cryptogram — the numbers 1 to 52, written once each
h: The cipher readings that can be tested
b: A block in which every number appears once can be a cipher in only two ways: a homophonic substitution with 52 homophones each used once, or a transposition key derived from a 52-letter phrase by ranking its letters. With an unordered key either reading can produce any 52-letter text at all, so neither can be tested or refuted; one commenter demonstrated this by fitting an arbitrary sentence. With an ordered key, homophones assigned to the alphabet in order or the phrase recovered from the inverse permutation with letters nondecreasing along the ranks, the plaintext is fixed by 51 boundary choices, about 66 bits, against roughly 70 bits of redundancy in 52 letters of English. That is testable, just. The test: simulated annealing over nondecreasing maps from 1 to 52 onto the alphabet, scored by a character 5-gram English model, in six readings (sequence order and inverse permutation, alphabet forward and reversed, zero groups as word breaks or ignored), with 60 restarts of 60 000 steps each. The control: 52-letter passages of Dickens and Melville enciphered with ordered homophonic keys and attacked identically. reading best score, nats per letter best candidate sequence, alphabet a to z −3.02 abadefillbookofmdoomloorstsbadfallsnowassadovyouslod sequence, a to z, zeros as word breaks −2.70 abadefillbooko endoonloorsus dad falltoowast adovyouslod sequence, alphabet z to a −3.18 uttooooonsnnolonominoffeedertootooenlatedtoldandenno inverse permutation, a to z −2.63 derssteeretiryehereheissuehistwehisthinnootrustoutst inverse permutation, z to a −3.03 ttheeetsiteseatstetstreeatssedassseesspooneibeendeed controls, 8 passages −1.48 to −1.97 7 of 8 read at 88 to 100% of letters; one at 46% Nothing from the block comes within 0.6 nats per letter of a recovered control, and no candidate holds a run of English longer than a chance word. The block’s own structure works against an ordered key: under a forward alphabet the nine single digits must all become a, b or c, so every candidate opens “aba”. The ordered readings are excluded at the strength the controls allow; the unordered ones cannot be tested, and a block that is only consistent with an untestable key is not distinguishable from a doodle.

t: The Roosevelt cryptogram — the numbers 1 to 52, written once each
b: Ernst’s arithmetic is right, and the permutation carries the fingerprints of a hand that wrote 1 to 52 once each in a made-up order, then dressed the list with runs of zeros. The letter lines below it are a transposition so shallow that Friedman read it at sight; the number lines above are a cipher-shaped object with nothing inside. Whether the sender meant it as a hoax on the Secret Service, as Ernst suggests, or simply copied out what he thought a cipher looked like, the block cannot be read because it does not encode anything. An unordered one-time key remains possible in principle and is indistinguishable from a doodle. What would reopen the question: the original sheet in the William F. Friedman Collection at the NSA, whose reverse carries a typed text and whose face carries the pencilled trials, or a second message from the same hand.

t: Charles I to Prince Rupert, 29 April 1645
b: A holograph cipher letter of the King to his nephew, catalogued as undeciphered (BL Add MS 18983 f. 14, DECODE R4921). Read with George Lasry’s reconstruction of the King’s cipher with the Queen, applied unchanged: the King cannot convoy his artillery train and asks Rupert to march and fetch it. About twenty code groups stay open. Oxford → Prince Rupert · homophonic with nomenclator · 29 April 1645 · read “That in case I cannot bring my train of artillery to you”: Charles I to Rupert, April 1645 from Charles I → to Prince Rupert British Library, Add MS 18983 f. 14 (DECODE R4921): one holograph page marked “Duplicate”, with a clear opening and close and about 300 cipher groups between them. It was catalogued as not deciphered. Read here with George Lasry’s 2020 reconstruction of the King’s cipher with the Queen (TNA SP106-5, on DECODE R929), applied unchanged. Daniel Bourdeau · read 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 Summary. DECODE lists this letter of Charles I to his nephew Rupert as non-decrypted, and no decipherment of it turned up in print. Warburton’s Memoirs of Prince Rupert (1849) prints Digby’s letters of 27 and 30 April on the same business, but not this one. The cipher has a homophonic alphabet on the numbers 1–80 and a nomenclator of letter+digit groups (n1, n3, c5, h1…). A period frequency tally of the King’s cipher with the Queen (BL Add MS 32256 f. 5, DECODE R9116) uses the same group shapes. That pointed to the key Lasry rebuilt for the Queen’s letters of January 1646, and the key read the letter at once. The King, hemmed in at Oxford by Cromwell’s raids, says he cannot convoy his train of artillery to Rupert without horses. He has sent for Goring and asks Rupert to march speedily and fetch it. That is what Rupert did in early May, the march that ended at Naseby. About twenty code groups are still open, or read only from context. They do not change the sense.

t: Charles I to Prince Rupert, 29 April 1645
b: One page in the King’s hand, dated “Oxford 29 April 1645” and marked “Duplicate”, the second copy sent by another route. It opens in clear: “Nepueu, if you have receaved my two which were upon friday & sonday last this will be the lesse necessarye, howsoeuer it is fit to tell you that I very much like your opinion”. The cipher then runs almost to the foot, with a few clear words kept inside it (“I have”, “yett will”, “but what”, “order”, “assuringe you that”). It closes “upon the word of your loving Oncle & most faithfull frend, Charles R.” The dorse is endorsed “From the King, Oxford Ap. 29 1645, Cypher”. BL Add MS 18983 f. 14: the clear opening and the first cipher lines. Image: British Library, Add MS 18983 f. 14, via DECODE R4921.

t: Charles I to Prince Rupert, 29 April 1645
b: The letter uses Lasry’s “TNA SP106-5” key, reconstructed in 2020 from Henrietta Maria’s circle’s letters of January 1646 (TNA SP 106/10 f. 247). Its alphabet is homophonic: E = 1–5, A = 14–17, T = 78–80, and so on. Its nomenclator groups include a1 = and, a4 = be, c5 = for, e5 = in, f2 = it, h1 = no, k1 = of, n1 = to, n3 = the, p6 = which. It was applied without change. The key has no values for the groups 81–98. Most of them stand at the end of a phrase and act as nulls or stops. Two recur with a meaning fixed by context: 95 = my and 98 = artillery (“transport my artillery to you”, “bring my train of artillery”). Several letter+digit groups the key leaves blank read from context: c2 = do, b2 = can, k4 = nor, and 412 in “412-ant” = warr(ant). Before the key was found, two other ciphers were ruled out. The Duke of Richmond’s cipher, used in the sibling letter of 31 July 1645 (R4922), has letter values above 100. The Digby–Walsingham key (R8724) is a different system. A ciphertext-only homophonic solver on the numbers alone did not converge.

t: Charles I to Prince Rupert, 29 April 1645
b: Modernised spelling; groups still open and readings from context are in square brackets. Nephew, if you have received my two which were upon Friday and Sunday last, this will be the less necessary; howsoever it is fit to tell you that I very much like your opinion [61] for the present. Know [that] to [?thow] to follow it until I [211 186] enough to convoy, and draught [horses] enough to transport my artillery to you; to which [c1: end?] I have sent for Goring, who I hope (yet will not warrant) to be able to do both. But what [d4] can not [be done] if you do not [376] all our [148]s be in order: therefore I desire you to [327: march] speedily for my assistance, that in case I can not bring my train of artillery to you, you may come and fetch it; assuring you that no time shall be lost, nor pains spared for doing of this, if it be possible, upon the word of your loving uncle and most faithful friend, Charles R. It agrees with Digby’s letter of 27 April, printed by Warburton (iii 77–78): “since your Highness says, you cannot relieve the place without the train, and that it is not possible for the King to bring the train to Prince Rupert…”. It also agrees with Digby’s of 30 April, which asks Rupert for one hundred draught horses.

t: Nicolò Sadoleto to Ercole I d’Este, Pozsony 1482 — the Venetian counter-offer to Matthias Corvinus
b: Ferrara’s envoy at the Hungarian court in the first summer of the War of Ferrara wrote parts of his despatches in a sign cipher; they were never printed, and DECODE lists four as partly decrypted. The alphabet is rebuilt from two sibling letters filed with their contemporary clear copies, which also shows that two of the four targets were read at the time. The cipher of 16 July 1482, which has no clear copy, is read but for a few words under stains and the fold: Venice had offered Matthias Veglia, a fleet command for his natural son János Corvin and a hundred thousand ducats a year, and Sadoleto urged that the League match it. A faded block of 17 August gives fragments only. Pozsony → Ferrara · sign cipher, monoalphabetic with homophones · July–November 1482 · read in part Sadoleto at Pozsony, 1482: the Venetian counter-offer to Ercole I d'Este Archivio di Stato di Modena, Cancelleria, Ambasciatori, Ungheria b. 1/9 · four ciphered despatches of Nicolò Sadoleto, Ferrara’s envoy to Matthias Corvinus, catalogued in DECODE as partly decrypted (R1101, R1102, R1103, R1106) The key is rebuilt from two sibling letters that carry contemporary clear copies · two of the four targets turn out to have been deciphered at the time · the cipher of 16 July 1482 is read, a few words under stains and the fold apart · one faded block gives only fragments Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 19 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 solved in part Summary. In the spring of 1482 Venice attacked Ferrara, and Ercole I d’Este sent Nicolò Sadoleto to Matthias Corvinus to bring Hungary into the war on the side of the League (Naples, Milan, Florence, the Pope). His despatches from Buda and Pozsony were never printed: the nineteenth-century Hungarian copyists passed them over. DECODE lists four of the 1482 letters as partly decrypted. The images, on DECODE and on the Vestigia database, show a sign cipher with word divisions kept and clear words mixed in. Two sibling letters survive with the Ferrarese chancery’s clear copies beside them (Vestigia 1283 for 15 July and 1295 for 31 August 1482); aligning them sign by sign gives the alphabet, about twenty-five signs with homophones for the vowels and n , r . With it, two of the four DECODE targets turn out to be read already: 15 July has its clear copy (no. 7a) and 27 November has two sheets of decipherment (nos. 26a, 26b). The letter of 16 July 1482 has no clear copy. Its seven cipher lines are read here, along with further cipher on pp. 3 and 4 found in a second pass; a few words under stains and the binding fold stay unread. Sadoleto learnt in secret that the other side had written to Francesco Quirino at Matthias’s court offering the King Veglia, the command of the fleet for his natural son, and a hundred thousand ducats a year. Further down, Sadoleto urges Ercole that the League should match that sum. The faded four-line block of 17 August (the copy of his letter to King Ferrante) gives only fragments. The twelve 1483 letters DECODE also lists (R1107–R1118) all turn out to have contemporary decipherments, as copies or as slips pasted to the leaf.

t: Nicolò Sadoleto to Ercole I d’Este, Pozsony 1482 — the Venetian counter-offer to Matthias Corvinus
b: No Este key for this embassy is known. The archive’s Cifrario series holds a key “per corrispondere con Nicolò Sadoletti a Napoli tra 1479 e 1480”, rebuilt by nineteenth-century archivists (Cremonini 2017, n. 39), but it is not digitised. The key was therefore rebuilt from the letters. The cipher keeps word divisions, which makes alignment straightforward. The clear copy 7a of 15 July runs “… volesse unirse e pigliare questa impresa, e non lassasse pretermittere questa opportunità laquale mai più fo, né forse sera, e che lo facesse per lo amore …”, and the first lines of the cipher on the original’s second page match it word for word. The one-page letter of 31 August and its clear 13a confirm it: “epsa me dice che è certa che la liga non … perchè Millano et Fiorenza non voriano …”. One habit shows up at once: where 13a has perchè the original writes quid in ordinary letters, which works as a code word hiding in plain sight. t: Nicolò Sadoleto to Ercole I d’Este, Pozsony 1482 — the Venetian counter-offer to Matthias Corvinus
h: Pozsony, 16 July 1482: what Venice offered the King
b: The letter’s clear part is routine news of the court. The last seven lines are in cipher. Essendo in Buda per partire per venire a Posonia, sapi per gran secreto da […] Francesco como [X] haveva scripto ad Francesco Quirino, che è qua, fo[sse] a … gli fa[cesse] … como [X] voleva havere seco bona a[micit]ia, et voleva dargli Vegla, et voleva lo figlio (e bastardo) per loco capitaneo de la [arma]ta per mare, et gli voleva dare ogni anno cento milia. “Being in Buda about to leave to come to Pozsony, I learnt in great secret from […] Francesco that [X] had written to Francesco Quirino, who is here, […] that [X] wanted to have good friendship with him, and wanted to give him Veglia, and wanted his son (the bastard) as captain-general of the fleet at sea, and would give him a hundred thousand every year.” The anchors are words that could be nothing else: Buda , Posonia , Francesco twice, Quirino , Vegla , capitaneo , per mare , ogni anno , cento milia . The sense fits the moment. Veglia (Krk) had been taken by Venice from Count Giovanni Frankopan in 1480, and the count was at Matthias’s court that summer (13a: “le qui lo Conte Zohane da Vegla”). The “son, the bastard” can only be János Corvin, Matthias’s natural son and intended heir. The sum is the telling detail. Six weeks later, in the letter of 31 August, Sadoleto told Ercole that Matthias “per cento milia ducati ogni anno pigliaria la impresa”, that is, would enter the war for the League for a hundred thousand ducats a year. The cipher of 16 July shows where that price came from: it was the figure the other side had already put on the table. [X] is a five-sign group that occurs twice, after como both times, as the subject of haveva scripto and of voleva havere seco bona amicitia . It does not spell a word in the letter key, so it is a nomenclator entry, and the context makes it the Venetian side, most likely “la Signoria”. The informant’s title before Francesco is another three-sign group not yet read. Second reading, 20–21 September 2026 A second pass corrected the text above and found more cipher. The informant’s title spells out in the ordinary alphabet as dom , so the name is “dom Francesco”. Group [X] turns up again in the letter of 27 November, where the contemporary decipherment 26b renders it as the Signoria of Venice. A six-sign group K is aligned with the King of Hungary’s title in the 15 July clear copy. The doubtful end of line 3 and start of line 4 read fosse a [K] / gli facesse offerta . The sign for ss is checked against facesse and imparasse in the 15 July letter, and the sign for ff against affinita . The corrected seven lines: essendo in Buda per partire per venire a Posonia, sapi per gran secreto da dom Francesco como [la Signoria di Venetia] haveva scripto ad Francesco Quirino che è qua, fosse a [el Re di Hungaria] e gli facesse offerta como [la Signoria] voleva havere seco bona amicitia et voleva dargli Vegla et voleva lo figliolo (e bastardo) per loro capitaneo de l’armata per mare et gli voleva dare ogni anno cento milia The cipher does not stop there. The sentence continues on p. 3 (“… ducati. ma voleva potere soldare et cauare gente de questo regno. et questo l’aveva saputo sua [S.] per subtile via et non volse per cosa del mondo che io monstrasse saperne cosa alcuna”): Venice also wanted the right to recruit soldiers in Hungary, and the informant made Sadoleto promise to show no knowledge of it. Further down p. 3 comes a mixed passage of clear and cipher in which Sadoleto argues his own case to Ercole: per ogni modo disponerse ad dare a questo [Re] cento milia ducati ogni anno sino a sei o septe anni, che seri[a] questa suma che li domanda, et non seria gran suma alla liga, considerata la indubitata victoria che sua m[aesta] … — non scio percio se sua maesta atentasse(?) … monstra desiderare et haver piu bisogno in questo principio. ma … alla liga … tractare, et non e da perder tempo, et se vol[e]no spen[dere] dinari a questo tempo et fare la bona spesa … “… to make up [the League’s] mind at all costs to give this King a hundred thousand ducats a year for six or seven years, which would be the sum he asks, and it would not be a great sum for the League, considering the certain victory that His Majesty … he shows he wants it and needs it more at this beginning … there is no time to lose, and if they mean to spend money, now is the time to spend it well …” So the letter sets the Venetian counter-offer beside Sadoleto’s advice to match it: a hundred thousand ducats a year from the League. Page 4 carries one more cipher line, “se bene non la mandato a questo …”.

t: Nicolò Sadoleto to Ercole I d’Este, Pozsony 1482 — the Venetian counter-offer to Matthias Corvinus

b: DECODE lists twelve more Sadoleto letters of 1483 from Buda and Zagreb (b. 1/10, R1107–R1118), several as partly decrypted. None is open. The slips show on DECODE’s photographs; on Vestigia’s later ones they have been lifted, which is why the pages look unread. The 1482 key reads the cipher of R1118 in agreement with its slip (“ma come scripsi a V.S. non gli [s]panza questo accordo col turcho”).

t: Nicolò Sadoleto to Ercole I d’Este, Pozsony 1482 — the Venetian counter-offer to Matthias Corvinus
b: All images are 4320 × 3240 two-page spreads, fetched from DECODE with a logged-in session and from Vestigia, which needs no login. The cipher lines were cut into strips, glyphs segmented by connected components and numbered on the strip (the segmentation script is the one written for the Milanese letters of 1489, see Buda 1489 ), and read by eye against the clear copies. The pairs of signs most easily confused were settled on high-magnification crops: the two Δ forms ( p and q , which differ only in the loop at the apex), the stemmed and flat-topped sixes ( e and n ), and the long ſ against Γ.

t: Alonso Sánchez at Venice, 1522 — the cipher was already solved, and the catalogue entry was wrong
b: Twenty-nine DECODE records (RAH Salazar 9/23–9/26, R9593–R9657) held here as unread ciphertexts of the imperial ambassador at Venice. Satoshi Tomokiyo had reconstructed the cipher outright and published it in September 2025, a year before the entry was scored, so there is no break to be had. The entry is corrected instead: the run spans four volumes and not one, every record is dated 1522 so the treaty of July 1523 is not in it, nine of the letters are Lope Hurtado de Mendoza’s, and almost all carry a contemporary decipherment. The nomenclator turns out to be alphabetically ordered, which fills in the numeral run; three values so predicted are then confirmed in two letters outside Tomokiyo’s coverage, both read in part here: R9653 on the siege of Rhodes, and R9635, a whole page of cipher on the sums owed by the Signoria and the restitution of goods seized from imperial vassals. Lope Hurtado’s code groups take finals Sánchez’s key does not have — a third cipher, still unreconstructed. Venice → Charles V · homophonic alphabet with a three-letter nomenclator · 1522 · already solved by others; catalogue entry corrected, two letters read in part Alonso Sánchez at Venice, 1522 — the cipher was already solved, and the catalogue entry was wrong to Charles V Real Academia de la Historia, Salazar 9/23–9/26 · DECODE R9593–R9657 · the imperial ambassador at Venice reporting to the Emperor through the Italian War of 1521–26 Catalogued here as twenty-nine unread ciphertexts. The cipher had been reconstructed and published by Satoshi Tomokiyo in September 2025 · what is added here is the correction of the entry, the ordering rule of the nomenclator, the numeral series, first readings of parts of R9635 and R9653, and the separation of a second correspondent’s cipher Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 20 September 2026 · updated 21 September 2026 resolved Summary. The catalogue held this as a B-class target: twenty-nine ciphertexts of Alonso Sánchez, imperial ambassador at Venice, recorded in DECODE as Non-decrypted , with a note that Tomokiyo had reconstructed the cipher. The first thing to do was to find out what he had actually published. He had published the whole cipher — the substitution alphabet, a nomenclature of some 177 three-letter codes, and the deciphered opening lines of forty letters — on 6 September 2025, a year before this entry was scored. So there is no break to be had here, and this write-up says so. What is left is worth doing anyway, and four things came out of it. The catalogue entry is wrong in three ways : the run is spread over Salazar 9/23, 9/24, 9/25 and 9/26 rather than 9/24 alone; every record in it is dated 1522, so the negotiation ending in the treaty of July 1523 is not in this group at all; and nine of the records are not Sánchez but Lope Hurtado de Mendoza. Almost every record also carries a contemporary decipherment bound in with it, so these letters were never unread — they are unedited. The nomenclator turns out to be ordered : codes are consonant–vowel–consonant, and sorting them by first and third consonant puts the plaintext in alphabetical order, so an unassigned code is bracketed by its neighbours. That fills in the numeral run Tomokiyo left blank, and two of the values so predicted, cef = xxvi and cif = xxvii, are then confirmed in the text of R9653. Two letters outside Tomokiyo’s coverage are read in part here: R9653, a leaf mostly in clear on the siege of Rhodes with a ciphered paragraph at the foot reporting letters out of France; and R9635, a whole page of cipher on the sums owed by the Signoria and the restitution of seized goods, which attests a third predicted numeral, cab = xv. Finally, the Lope Hurtado letters use code groups with final p and z , which Sánchez’s key does not have — a third cipher of the same family , still unreconstructed. Status: found already solved, with the entry corrected and one letter read in part. The remaining twenty-seven records are transcription work, not cryptanalysis.

t: Alonso Sánchez at Venice, 1522 — the cipher was already solved, and the catalogue entry was wrong
h: What was already published, and when
b: Satoshi Tomokiyo, Correspondence in Cipher of Imperial Ambassadors Alonso Sanchez and Juan Manuel (1522) , posted on Cryptiana on 6 September 2025 and enlarged on 9 September, reconstructs the cipher outright. He worked from the contemporary decipherment attached to DECODE R9605, and describes the moment it opened: browsing R9613 he noticed that vog and xig were frequent and so likely common monosyllables, and that a q with a double bar was often affixed to a code and might be the plural -s ; he was then stuck on the handwriting of the decipherment. Turning to R9605 he saw vog veg near the end, two codes close together in an alphabetical listing and both frequent, and matched them to en el in the plaintext. After that, as he puts it, there was no real difficulty. The article gives the substitution alphabet as a hand-drawn table, the nomenclature, and the deciphered first lines of R9593–R9632, plus the whole of R9621 and the last paragraph of R9623. It also reconstructs the parallel cipher of Juan Manuel , imperial ambassador at Rome (DECODE R9499–R9529), which is built to the same design with different values. This is the answer to the contamination question the project records for every target: a full public reading of the system existed a year before the work, it was found before the attempt rather than after, and the reading below uses it.

t: Alonso Sánchez at Venice, 1522 — the cipher was already solved, and the catalogue entry was wrong
h: What the catalogue entry got wrong
b: The entry read “RAH, Signatura 9/24 (29 items)”, 1522–23, and justified its importance by the negotiation that brought Venice out of the French alliance and ended in the treaty of July 1523. Pulling the fifty-five DECODE record pages R9603–R9657 and tabulating them contradicts all three parts. The shelfmark. The run is spread over Salazar 9/23, 9/24, 9/25 and 9/26 . R9603–R9618 are in 9/24, R9619–R9632 in 9/25, R9633–R9657 in 9/26, and Tomokiyo’s list reaches back into 9/23. The dates. Every record carries a 1522 date — the last of them November 1522. Nothing in this group reaches 1523 , so the treaty of July 1523 is outside it. The letters belong to the year of La Bicocca, the loss of Genoa and the fall of Rhodes, not to the year of the Venetian realignment. The authorship. Nine records are by Lope Hurtado de Mendoza , not Sánchez: R9634, R9644, R9645, R9646, R9648, R9649, R9650, R9652, R9656. One further correction matters more than any of them. DECODE marks almost every record in the group Inline Cleartext: Yes , meaning a contemporary decipherment is bound with the ciphertext, and the Calendar of State Papers Spain, vol. 2, calendars many of these same letters with the note “Autograph in cipher. Contemporary deciphering”. These letters were never unread. What they lack is an edition. A status of Non-decrypted in DECODE records the state of the database, not the state of knowledge, and this entry read it as the latter.

t: Alonso Sánchez at Venice, 1522 — the cipher was already solved, and the catalogue entry was wrong
h: The cipher, and the rule that orders it
b: The system is the 1496 Ferdinand-and-Isabella type: a homophonic substitution alphabet, three nulls that letters open with, a q with a double bar for the plural -s , and a nomenclator of three-letter codes for common words, names and places. Word division is kept. The vocabulary is large for the date. Setting Tomokiyo’s table out as data shows the codes are not arbitrary. They are consonant–vowel–consonant over first position, sixteen consonants z y x v t s r p n m l h g f d c b , running backwards through the alphabet as the plaintext runs forwards; middle, the five vowels a e i o u ; third position, nine consonants b c d f g h l m n . That is 720 slots, of which about 177 were recovered. Sorting by (first consonant, third consonant, vowel) puts the plaintext in alphabetical order — zid zod zud | zef zif | zog zug | zel | zem zom | zen zun gives a(h)un, ahun, al, allende, algun, alla, alli, antes, aqui, aquell, arma, assi . The alphabetisation is the clerk’s own and is loose at the edges ( allende before algun , cosa before concorda ), so what the rule gives for an unassigned code is a range, not a point. Where the plaintext is a numeral series, the range collapses to a value.

t: Alonso Sánchez at Venice, 1522 — the cipher was already solved, and the catalogue entry was wrong
h: The numeral series, predicted and then confirmed
b: Tomokiyo has cob xviii, cub xix, cad xx through cud xxiv, and caf xxv, and leaves the rest of the block blank, with a query on cud and an uncertain “[xxviii?]” in his reading of R9598. The ordering rule fills the run: code cab ceb cib cob cub cad ced cid cod cud caf cef cif cof cuf value xv xvi xvii xviii xix xx xxi xxii xxiii xxiv xxv xxvi xxvii xxviii xxix The two in bold were predicted before they were seen, and then met in the foot paragraph of R9653 in a context that can only be a pair of dates — see the next section. That in turn resolves the uncertain “[xxviii?]” of R9598 as cof . The predicted values are carried in key_codes.tsv flagged as this project’s, separately from Tomokiyo’s.

t: Alonso Sánchez at Venice, 1522 — the cipher was already solved, and the catalogue entry was wrong
h: R9653: the fall of Rhodes, in clear, with a ciphered postscript
b: R9653 is Sánchez to Charles V, Venice, 20 November 1522, Salazar 9/26 f. 299–301. It is beyond the end of Tomokiyo’s list and has not been read before. Folio 299r is a mixed leaf: six lines of cipher at the head, some thirty lines in clear, two lines of cipher at the foot, then the signature. RAH, Salazar 9/26, f. 299r. The clear middle carries the news of Rhodes; what could not be said openly went into the cipher above and below it. Image: Real Academia de la Historia, Madrid, Salazar 9/26 f. 299r, via DECODE R9653. The clear middle, read from the image: A xiij del presente fue la postrera que escreui a v[uest]ra m[agesta]d y dixe las nueuas de Rodas que aqui hauia dicho vn patron de vn nauio; despues [vinie]ron cartas y los d’esta republica me embiaron vn sumario, cuyo traslado sera con esta. Esta manyana han houido otras cartas y son de Candia de su general de xx del passado, y las tenia el de Rodas de x del mismo. … Lo que dizen es que hasta x de octubre hauian dado los turquos cinco conbates muy rezios a Rodas por diuersos lugares, y baterias, y por debaxo de tierra por las minas y por debaxo de la agua, y siempre los hauian rebotado y muerto gran numero dellos — dizen xx mil. Pero vn secretario de la Señoria me ha dicho a mi que despues que el turquo esta sobre Rodas se le han muerto cinquenta mil hombres en las batallas y de dolencia; su armada de mar estaua muy mal en horden, y algunos hauisos hai que la persona del turquo se ha retirado y passado en tierra firme. … Dizen que los de Rodas esperan socorro con desseo, y que si les llegasen mil infantes ternian por muy cierta la victoria. No hai duda sino que ahora hauria buena disposicion de hazer muy gran daño al turquo y a su armada. Rhodes capitulated a month after this was written, on 22 December 1522. The foot paragraph. It opens with the three nulls every letter in this cipher opens with; the second line resolves cleanly. Image: Real Academia de la Historia, Madrid, Salazar 9/26 f. 299r (foot), via DECODE R9653. The second line runs yeh +plural xig tom xig cef y cif xel mog vuc xig … — “cartas de Francia de xxvi y xxvii del passado de …” : letters out of France of 26 and 27 October, the month in which Francis I’s position in Lombardy collapsed. It is this pair of dates that confirms cef and cif . The first line gives ta es , vam embaxa(dor) , vuc +plural, zid a(h)un , rug la , gub señor , vog en , around spelled-out letters not yet settled. A small corroboration from the other end of the group: Lope Hurtado’s letter of 9 November (R9648) opens in clear “La carta de V. M[agestad] recebi de xxvj de octubre” — the same post that Sánchez reports reaching Venice.

t: Alonso Sánchez at Venice, 1522 — the cipher was already solved, and the catalogue entry was wrong
h: R9635: a full page of cipher, read in part
b: R9635 is Sánchez to Charles V, Venice, 16 September 1522, Salazar 9/26 f. 20–22, calendared in CSP Spain vol. 2 p. 482 and also beyond Tomokiyo’s list. Folio 20r is the best ciphertext page in the group: about twenty-five lines of cipher, whole-page, in a clean well-spaced hand , with a contemporary decipherment written between the lines in lighter ink — but only in patches, so most lines have to be read from the key. RAH, Salazar 9/26, f. 20r. Each paragraph opens with three nulls, padded out with the meaningless clear words como and quien — which is what Tomokiyo’s “como quierr” note under the nulls column of his alphabet means. Image: Real Academia de la Historia, Madrid, Salazar 9/26 f. 20r, via DECODE R9635. cipher reading xof +s yeh +s xig dom pud das cartas de vuestra magestad pac +s xig vum gɣ lal los de esta republica xel gub rac del señor infante vud +s zef xig pac +s mud +s cob pol9 ducados allende de los otros xviii mil ped xig cab pol9 vud +s mas de xv mil ducados faf +s pac +s … pol9 vud +s pic xig vom todos los … mil ducados luego de esto interlinear gloss obligados … fuessen restituydas sus bienes The subject is money and reprisals: the sums owed by the Signoria under the capitulation — eighteen thousand ducats outstanding from a previous year, more than fifteen thousand in another reckoning — and, in the glossed lines, goods seized that were to be restored to their owners . That is the same business as the sequestrations of imperial vassals’ goods at Venice which fill R9638 (11 October 1522) entirely in clear, and the same reckoning of xx mil ducados allende de xviii mil that Tomokiyo read in the last paragraph of R9623. Two points of notation, which the page settles: pol9 is pol ( mi ) followed by the letter sign for l , giving mil — that sign is easily taken for a g in this hand; and gɣ lal is the spelled letters r-e followed by lal ( publica ), giving republica , the word these despatches turn on. This page also attests cab = xv , in mas de xv mil ducados — a third of the numerals predicted from the ordering rule, after cef and cif in R9653. None of the seven is contradicted.

t: Alonso Sánchez at Venice, 1522 — the cipher was already solved, and the catalogue entry was wrong
h: The letter alphabet, and the sign that was miscalled
b: Tomokiyo gives the substitution alphabet only as a hand-drawn table. Read off at high zoom it is about thirty signs over twenty-two letters (a b c d e f g h i l m n o p q r s t u x y z), most of them with two or three homophones: a = n , ʒf ; d = ∞ , 3 , ɸ ; g = bold ∞ , L ; n = ᶻ , ℞₄ ; and so on. Two things fall out of it. The “q with a double bar” is the letter s — not a separate plural marker. The plural ending is simply the letter s written after a code group, so Tomokiyo’s guess that it “may well be the plural ending -s” is right for the wrong reason. And r is a different sign , a q with a loop, easily confused with it in this hand. The map is carried in alpha.py and verifies on spelled runs taken from R9635 f. 20r: nx#gn = ahora , ttn#n = nada . It does not yet give the spelled runs continuously, and the reason is worth stating because it is the whole remaining obstacle. Tomokiyo transliterates the code groups with latin labels drawn from a set that includes v , which is not one of the twenty-two plaintext letters; the code labels and the alphabet therefore do not share one transliteration, and every sign has to be matched to both by eye. At the resolution DECODE serves, telling the homophone pairs apart — Ɋ (r) from ǂ (s), 9 (l) from Ɋ (r), ∞ (d) from bold ∞ (g) — is a judgement call at each occurrence, and getting it wrong silently produces plausible-looking Spanish that is not what the page says. So the runs are left marked rather than filled in. The way through is the one the glosses offer: collate the patchy interlinear decipherment on R9635 f. 20r word by word against the signs beneath it, which pins each homophone in this scribe’s hand; the unglossed lines and the rest of the group then follow. That is edition work against a published key, not cryptanalysis.

t: Alonso Sánchez at Venice, 1522 — the cipher was already solved, and the catalogue entry was wrong
h: R9605 gives ground truth, and it changes two things
b: R9605 (9/24 f. 39–44, 7 May 1522) is the record Tomokiyo broke the cipher from, and its images show why: the cipher and the clerk’s full contemporary decipherment sit on facing leaves . Aligned at the end of the letter, where the clear reads Plegue a Dios no lo yerre en el camino. De Venecia a vij de mayo 1522 : cipher plaintext how nuf no code pac lo code ɡɣβ4q4 yerre spelled vog veg en el code — Tomokiyo’s own way in, met here in situ zn·β·aɤ + nuf cami + no = camino spelled, then a code group used for the last syllable Two things follow that the key alone could not give. Code groups stand for syllables as well as whole words — nuf is no the adverb in one breath and the final syllable of cami-no in the next, so a reading that assumes one group is one word will mis-segment. And the lookalike signs separate : camino needs β = m , ahora ( nx#Ɋn , R9635 f. 20r) needs Ɋ = r , and the bold ∞ is g . All three are a “g”-shape at the resolution DECODE serves, and they are the single largest source of error in the spelled runs. Continuing the same passage against the clear “la venida del visorey con todas las postas , que despacho y escrivo” gives three more results. xel def = del visorey and ded + xof = veni + da = venida , verbatim. The spelled run for escrivo is seven signs for seven letters, fixing z = c, ɡ = r, aɤ = i, m = v , # = o with ground truth beneath them — the method working. And va = despacho , not “desponho” : Tomokiyo’s table gives a word that is not Spanish, where the clear reads que despacho y escrivo with ho = que and va in that slot. It also explains his puzzled “me desponho x-e-r-o-n que” in R9623. A correction to the published key. One check came out inconclusive and is recorded as such. The clear at “que fue a …” stands over the group cud , which Tomokiyo reads “xxiv?”; had the clear read xxv , the whole c-block series would shift by one and the values predicted here would be wrong. It does not settle it — the date is written over a correction and reads as something like xxv y xxvij , two dates rather than one, so it cannot be matched to a single group. cab , cef and cif do not depend on it: each was confirmed in its own context, independently of where the run starts. The same alignment runs from the very first word of the letter. Clear (f. 42): “Ya dixe a V. Mag. que el embaxador de Hungria fue respondido de los desta republica con buenas palabras…” ; cipher (f. 39r ll. 1–2): cig = ya ; vu ·o·ɣ = di +x+e = dixe ; dom pud ho veg = vuestra magestad que el; vam vuc ·ɡ = embaxa + do +r = embaxador ; n·℞·∞ ɡ·aɤ = Hun-gria, spelled across the line break; sa = fue ; ɡ·ɣ·q·ao·#·& vu vuc = r-e-s-p-o-n + di + do = respondido ; xig vum ɡ·ɣ lal = desta republica ; xa yuc ·n+s = con buenas . Nothing in that is a guess — the clerk’s plaintext stands over every group on the facing leaf. It fixes the sign table against ground truth rather than by eye: n =a, ɣ =e, ɡ =r, aɤ =i, o =x, # =o, q =s, ao =p, & =n, m =v, z =c, β =m, and the q-with-double-bar = s. ( q =s here against Tomokiyo’s alphabet column q =t: two similar glyphs, and the pair to watch next.) Carried to the unread page, though, the table does not by itself unlock it, and that corrects the diagnosis offered above. On R9635 f. 20r the first line is ‖ como ‖ quien ‖ deg ho feb ʒnɡ xof +s yeh +s xig dom pud . The tail is secure — das cartas de vuestra magestad — and the null padding matches R9605 exactly. But deg , feb and ʒnɡ resolve to nothing: none is in the nomenclator, and the last spells y-a-r , which is not a word. Sense wants recebi in that slot, whose code is hug — nothing like what is written. So the bottleneck is not the sign table but the step before it: turning the cursive shapes into labels. R9605’s hand and R9635’s differ enough that a shape read confidently as d in one is something else in the other, and a wrong label yields a code group that either does not exist or exists with the wrong value. The alignment has to be done on the image , glyph against the clerk’s word above it, building a picture-book of each sign as this scribe forms it — not by transcribing to labels first and resolving afterwards. That is slower, and it is the honest route. This is also why R9605 and R9613 are not additions to the reading: they were deciphered by the Emperor’s own clerk in 1522, on the facing leaves. Transcribing that clear text gives a continuous plaintext of those letters, but it is an edition of a 1522 decipherment, not a decipherment. The records that are genuinely unread have no such facing plaintext. The route through is now open and is the next session’s work: align the whole of R9605’s cipher against its decipherment — several hundred signs of ground truth — to fix each homophone in this scribe’s hand, then carry it to the unglossed pages.

t: Alonso Sánchez at Venice, 1522 — the cipher was already solved, and the catalogue entry was wrong
h: The edition pass: the model of the writing was wrong
b: The failure reported above came from a wrong model of the page, and correcting it is what opened it. Everything here is written in ordinary latin-looking cursive. The two systems are told apart by shape-length and context: three-letter latin trigrams are nomenclator codes ( xig , vog , dom , pud , lig , nuc ), read straight off Tomokiyo’s table; single letters and short runs between them are the substitution alphabet , where the letterform and the value differ — n =a, y =e, g =r, o / ✗ =x, # =o, ao =p, m =u/v, z =c, β =m, 9 =l, q-with-double-bar = s. Three nulls open each paragraph, padded with the clear words como and quien . Verified on R9605 f. 39r l. 1 against the clerk’s plaintext on the facing leaf: cig vu·o·y n dom pud ho veg = “Ya dixe a vuestra magestad que el” , with vu (di)+ o (x)+ y (e) = dixe . With that, the unread page reads. R9635 f. 20r ll. 2–3 run continuously: lig vog vom nuf gad lel ao-y-g- xig -g nuc … xa pac +s xig vum g-y- lal = “pues en esto no se puede perder nada … con los de esta republica” Two things in that sentence are new. lel = puede , a code Tomokiyo never recovered: it brackets between lal publica and lol pudi , and the sense fixes it. And perder is written p-e-r + xig ( de ) + r — a code group used mid-word for a syllable , the same pattern R9605 showed with cami + nuf ( no ) = camino . Line 9 then gives an independent check on the whole approach: nul ( obliga ) + vuc ( do ) + s = obligados — and obligados is precisely the word the 1522 decipherer wrote in the gloss above that stretch. Key, alphabet and gloss agree without being fitted to each other. Further down the page: pef pac ho zel xig a-h-o | r-a = me lo que antes de ahora ; yig ( capitula ) + c-i-o-n = capitulacion ; and ho hob hec ho pac +s = que quien Inglaterra que los , with hec = Inglaterra — the English ambassador at Venice being the running subject of these months. Lower on the page: vom +s cad pol-9 xig a-h-o-r-a = estos xx mil de ahora ; ao-# xig g pac suf -z-e-r lu - ho = poderlo hazer, porque ; and rug +s lul ta = las quales . Those last show the mirror of the stem-plus-ending pattern — codes run together to make one word : lu ( por )+ ho ( que ) = porque , lul ( qual )+ ta ( es ) = quales , suf ( ha )+z-e-r = hazer . The page closes with darian todos los …, no pude …, si no se … en …, and then opens a fresh paragraph with the same three nulls and pac +s xig vum r-e- lal = los de esta republica . One code there, cag , is unassigned in Tomokiyo’s table and sits at the end of the numeral run immediately before cig ( ya ); cag = xxx is the natural continuation and suits the sense, but it is one slot past where the run is attested and is left probable, not certain. Line 5 gives xof veg + p-r-i-m-e-r-o + xig ta = da el primero de es [te], which fixes β = m on this page independently of camino in R9605; and at high zoom the ending of capitulacion is the curly second form of c that Tomokiyo draws as a backwards 3, so that word is settled rather than inferred. Every line of f. 20r now carries a reading. Continuous or substantial: ll. 2–6, 9, 10, 11, 13, 15, 17, 18, 20, 22, 23, 25, with the passages at ll. 7 and 14; partial, with runs still unresolved: ll. 1, 8, 12, 16, 19, 21, 24. The page is read throughout in substance — subject, sums, parties and the drift of the argument — while a scatter of spelled runs inside partially-read lines stays open. It is not a word-perfect diplomatic edition and is not offered as one. (The crops were cut by dividing the written area into twenty-five equal bands, so the line numbers are approximate; the readings are anchored to their own words.) The remaining lines are the same work at the same zoom, cryptanalytically unremarkable, and are left untranscribed rather than filled in by inference. One token resists: gta , a dozen occurrences, cannot be a code (its middle position is not a vowel) and is most likely g ( y ) + ta ( es ), but that does not sit well everywhere and is left unresolved. The edition is in sanchez1522/edition/ . Folio 21 is two further full pages of cipher, denser than f. 20r, with the decipherer’s gloss obligados … fuessen restituydas sus tierras continuing across it. One paragraph on the right-hand leaf, marked A in the margin, is written entirely in the clear, and it names the English ambassador: M[icer] Ricardo Paceo, embax[ad]or de Inglaterra, me ha dado el incluso memorial y rogado que escriva a v[uest]ra m[agesta]d suplicandole por las cartas que dize para el Papa y para don Joan. Sup[li]co a v[uest]ra m[agesta]d muy humilmente, con primero las mande enbiar, pues es persona que merece toda buena obra de v[uest]ra m[agesta]d, por ser muy servidor suyo y aficionado &c. Richard Pace , Henry VIII’s envoy at Venice, has given Sánchez an enclosed memorial and asked him to press the Emperor for the letters he wants for the Pope and for don Juan — Juan Manuel, the imperial ambassador at Rome, whose own 1522 cipher Tomokiyo reconstructed in the same article. Sánchez seconds the request warmly. This fixes the identification behind hec = Inglaterra met on f. 20r, and it is the same Pace who opens R9631 in Tomokiyo’s list. The two leaves of f. 21 are not yet transcribed line by line.

t: Alonso Sánchez at Venice, 1522 — the cipher was already solved, and the catalogue entry was wrong
h: Lope Hurtado de Mendoza writes in a third cipher
b: The nine Lope Hurtado records bound in the same volumes look at first like more of the same: the same period, the same recipient, cipher mixed with clear inside the sentence, code groups of the same shape. They are not in Sánchez’s cipher. The test is the third position. Sánchez’s codes end strictly in b c d f g h l m n . Folio 260v of R9648 gives tep , tap , and groups ending in z — finals Sánchez’s key does not contain. Juan Manuel’s Rome cipher, by contrast, does use p r s t z as finals ( jap papa , jir , jus , boz , qat ). So Lope Hurtado’s key is a third member of the family. Whether it is Juan Manuel’s own key is not settled here. None of the groups legible on that leaf — ton , tep , tap , xul , xild , zar , xurzun — has a value in Tomokiyo’s Juan Manuel table either, but that table is itself a partial recovery, so their absence decides nothing. Several of these records carry contemporary decipherments, so the key is recoverable by the same route Tomokiyo took; they deserve a target of their own.

t: Alonso Sánchez at Venice, 1522 — the cipher was already solved, and the catalogue entry was wrong
h: What is open, and how good the reading is
b: The six-line head paragraph of R9653 f. 299r is not transcribed. Ink has bled through from the facing leaf and at the resolution DECODE serves the two hands cannot be separated reliably. Transcription, not cryptanalysis, is the obstacle. R9653 f. 300–301 and R9635 f. 21–22 have not been examined. On R9635 f. 20r the spelled-out letter runs between the code groups are only partly transcribed, so the page has continuous sense but is not yet a continuous text. Collating the patchy interlinear glosses line by line against the cipher would settle the letter alphabet in this hand and close it. The other twenty-seven records are untouched here. Most have a contemporary decipherment bound in, so the work is transcription and edition against the published key. Lope Hurtado’s key is unreconstructed. Grades. The resolved run of R9653’s foot paragraph is graded C — certain on the code groups, which are unambiguous against the published key and make continuous sense. The remainder of that paragraph and the whole head paragraph are I , incomplete. The clear middle is a reading of ordinary Spanish secretary hand and carries no cipher grade; two words in it are conjectural and marked with brackets above. cof xxviii, cuf xxix, cab xv, ceb xvi, cib xvii are predicted, not observed , and are flagged as such in the key file.
