t: Sir Thomas Smith to Cecil and the Queen, 1562–1566 — DECODE R9236, R9248–R9254
b: The first test passage, in the letter to the Queen of 17 January 1563, came out as chief … on the other side , and Forbes (ii 287) prints: “I do take yt marvelous necessary, that some man were sent to be with the admirall who now is chief on the other side.” In the letter to Cecil of 27 January all 32 stretches run with Forbes’s text in order: the rendering of Tankervill ; that is to have one on the other side with the admiral, and I have named him who, for th’acquaintance with the admiral and all of that faction, the knowledge of the countrey and all other respectes, is most fit. But you must dispach him streight ; you must not stic for honest allowance in tyme of service ; Monsieur Danville is to come over into England shortly ; such noblemen of Scotland as favoreth the religion and wold contynew the amytie between Scotland and us . The letter of 13 April is read in full, the Blois letter of 7 March in about half.

t: Sir Thomas Smith to Cecil and the Queen, 1562–1566 — DECODE R9236, R9248–R9254
h: 1563–1566: the passages the calendar only summarises
b: Arles, 24 November 1564 (“chiefly in cipher, deciphered”, CSP no. 815): “[The Cardinal of Lorraine] and the [Prince of Condé] have had conferens and familiar banketting togither at Soissons and at Nanteuil chasteau, which was the late [Cardinal] of Burbons’ … They of Guyse … complaine that all letters that come from the Cardinal … be opened, principally at Paris and Lyons … Madame de Guise … daily in great dispatches to and from Scotland … This bearer Hume is altogether a Lidington, whom you shall find double, I am afraid, or rather triple, having … pencions of all three princes.” Avignon, 4 October 1564 (CSP no. 714; Forbes’s heading had been taken as 27 October): the two designs of the French court, one of them of the papists, to bring “all again to the olde state” and “break the amity” of England and Scotland; “the Bishop of Glasgow is here greater, no embassador”; “the marriage of the Queen of Scots”, the Earl of Warwick, Lord Robert and the Prince of Spain, “two marriages for her”; “the house of Guise stronger, which is too stronge”; the Earl of Lennox’s practice “to marry his sonne”, and “they feare that she is enclined to this last offer of Lenox”. Valence, 1 September 1564 (CSP no. 642): the amity between England and Scotland, the Earl of Murray, “such lords and great men … be the great favourers of religion … to do some great enterprise”, Huntly “died and his sonnes were taken”, Lethington, the Bishop of Glasgow’s pension, and “to marry Lord Robert”. On 3 September the two ciphered words are names: Nanion Cocborne and Villeroy. 25 January 1564 (CSP no. 103): the Spanish ambassador reports the French making ladders at Étaples and Boulogne, to surprise a town in England or fall on the Low Countries; the King of Spain has made no league with the Pope and means nothing against the Queen of Navarre, but wants “to make himself rich”. The other letters are shorter. Arles, 20 November, on the bearer Adam Hume, runs almost word for word with the calendar up to “glad to be rid of him”. Narbonne, 7 January 1565, covers the posts out of Scotland, Beton and Hume going by land, and “the marriage between the Duke of Guise and the Queen of Scots”. From Bourbon-l’Archambault, 22 March 1566, come the ambassadors of Spain and Scotland with the Cardinal of Lorraine, the Bishop of Glasgow looking to be a cardinal, and a Scottish woman who is “the conveyor of [letters] out of Scotland to the [Lady] Lennox”. And 29 April 1566 names “Peter Clare … Almain captain … Albert de Rosemberg”, and the “continuation with the princes of Almain for the recovery of Metz and Calais”.

t: Sir Thomas Smith to Cecil and the Queen, 1562–1566 — DECODE R9236, R9248–R9254
b: A seventh record, R9236 (Add MS 4136 f. 140, catalogue 94), is another of Forbes’s leaves: the ciphered passages of Smith to Cecil of 15 October, 20 October and 15/17 December 1562, to the Queen of 4 November 1563, and of “Sir Thomas Smith’s advertisements from France, 31 Jan. 1562[/3]”. The clear words scattered through them (London, Lyn, Poole, Boston, Dover, Hastings, Garnesey) are the nulls of the same key, R9261, not R9262, which DECODE names as the nearest key. Readings, added 21 September 2026: 15 October 1562 , all six passages: the Scots, the Queen of Scots, “break with you and to make war”, “that the hostages which you have shall be convoyed”, Flanders, Rollet and Monsieur Vyllemort. These agree with Forbes, Full View ii 119. 15/17 December 1562 , all six: “I see, you must hold ferme and fast: Frenchmen will come to reason but compellid … to trust no Frenchman of what religion soever he be … the Prince of Condé, which I do not believe … as soon as ever they be able, they will thither [bend] all their force”. These agree with Forbes ii 238. 4 November 1563 , to the Queen, read in full and confirmed by the calendar (CSP Foreign vi no. 1366): “…de Montaigne … whose carte of La Rochelle … under another pretence. I have given letters to my Lord Robert and Mr Secretarie … from Rouen … wrote of that same matter … I thinke he can do. But this at this tyme is most necessarie.” 20 October 1562 , all four passages, with Forbes ii 122 as the check: [Newhaven] is not so strong as supposed; if it were summer they would attempt to afray our men thence “with a garden of chamillion upon the hill on this side”; things begun there by [France] be not perfit. 31 January 1562/3 , the advertisements: only passage (2), “the queen of Navarre”, is read; (1), (3) and the last line remain fragments, and no printed text was found to check them against. One variant appears on this leaf only: a double bar stands for i . Passage-by-passage readings are in smith1562/decipher_E.md .

t: Sir Thomas Smith to Cecil and the Queen, 1562–1566 — DECODE R9236, R9248–R9254
b: The six records and the Smith-series key records were fetched from DECODE. The first key record DECODE names, R9262, is Throckmorton’s third cipher. The record listing around it gave R9261, whose first page is Smith’s cipher and whose second is Sir James Croft’s. The passages were transcribed from the images and the key applied sign by sign. Forbes’s printed letters (vol. ii, from the archive.org text) and the calendar summaries were used only to confirm readings, and where they did not fit the signs the reading was left open. Readings added to the key: enos , listed at the top of the key, is “Ambassador”, not a null; a marginal gloss on the 20 November letter spells it out. M̅ and M̈ are marriage and marry, B: is Bishop, C̄ is Congregation, J̣ is is or are, ! is in or into. The doubled long-s signs are st, the small open v is l, and a looped kite with a stem is w. A variant of the England sign stands for Earl (before Murray, Lennox and Warwick). The flag sign, the key’s “Germany” or “the Emperor”, stands where the calendar names Archduke Charles. Forbes’s copying slips: a single dot for a colon, 4 for e, ⊔ for π.

t: Sir Thomas Smith to Cecil and the Queen, 1562–1566 — DECODE R9236, R9248–R9254
b: The hooked-T family of word signs (here, his, they, this, thing) is read from context; Forbes’s dots on it are inconsistent (C). Unread word signs: ẓ, ï, C·, F̄ and the ḧ-like sign in 1 September passage 2. t: Cardinal Soglia to the nuncio Viale Prelà — a nomenclator with an alphabetical code
b: Rome, 15 June 1848: a ciphered dispatch to the nuncio at Innsbruck, intercepted at Turin and printed by Mazzini’s L’Italia del Popolo with a prize for its reader, posted on Cipherbrain in 2014 as unsolved. 5 is the word break, pairs of the other eight digits are letters and syllables, 8XXX is a one-part code in alphabetical order; a nomenclator annealer, checked first on a synthetic control, gave the first words. A counter-order: stay with the Emperor, do not ask for your passports. The nuncio had left Innsbruck the day before. Eleven code groups stay open. Rome → Innsbruck · digit table with syllables and an alphabetical code · 15 June 1848 · read Cardinal Soglia to the nuncio Viale Prelà, Rome, 15 June 1848 from Cardinal Soglia → to Viale Prelà Intercepted in the post at Turin and printed by Mazzini’s L’Italia del Popolo , Milan, 30 June 1848, as 955 digits with “a prize of some size for the best interpreter of these figures” · posted on Cipherbrain in 2014 as unsolved 5 is the word break, pairs of the other digits are letters and syllables, 8XXX is a code in alphabetical order · read except eleven code groups: a counter-order telling the nuncio to stay with the Emperor, written the day after he had left Daniel Bourdeau · solved 18 September 2026 · updated 21 September 2026 solved Summary. On 30 June 1848 Mazzini’s Milan paper printed a letter and a ciphered dispatch of Cardinal Soglia, Pius IX’s Secretary of State, to Mgr Michele Viale Prelà, nuncio to the Emperor, who had fled Vienna for Innsbruck. The pair had been posted at Turin on 20 June and never reached him. The paper could not read the cipher and offered a prize; Rome reprinted it as a broadsheet; the government kept silent; Spada’s history (1868–69) gave only a paraphrase from “a most authoritative person”. Klaus Schmeh posted the broadsheet on Cipherbrain in December 2014, where it stayed unsolved. The system is a small nomenclator: the digit 5 separates words, two-digit groups from the other eight digits are letters with homophones and syllables, and four-digit groups beginning with 8 are a one-part code whose values run in alphabetical order. The dispatch is a counter-order. An earlier letter had told the nuncio, after the Austrian ambassador Lützow had been ordered to leave Rome, to ask for his own passports and go home or to Cologne; per nuove sopraggiunte circostanze the Pope now wants him to stay at Innsbruck with the Emperor, wherever he goes, and the order about the passports is suspended. The instruction is going by three different routes; Mgr Morichini is to be shown it. According to the Dizionario Biografico , the nuncio had left Innsbruck for Frankfurt and Cologne on 14 June, the day before it was written. Status: read. Ten code words are read from context and checked against the alphabetical order; eleven code groups, among them the date of the earlier letter, cannot be recovered from this one message.

t: Cardinal Soglia to the nuncio Viale Prelà — a nomenclator with an alphabetical code
b: The image Schmeh posted, which Tony Gaffney had sent him, is not the Milan paper itself but a Roman broadsheet: Dispaccio del Card. Soglia. Tratto dal giornale l’Italia del Popolo 30 Giugno , printed by Clemente Puccinelli in Via Lata. Commenters identified the paper within a day (Helmut Winkler, Hans Jahr: L’Italia del Popolo , the organ of Mazzini’s Associazione nazionale italiana, year I, no. 40). Its preface says what the editors knew: The broadsheet’s head and preface: “a faithful and most exact copy of a letter and a dispatch of Cardinal Soglia to Mgr Viale Prelà, apostolic nuncio to the Emperor of Austria at Innsbruck. The cipher is, for now, unknown to us, and we entrust it as it is to the curiosity of our readers … Letter and dispatch, though dated at Rome, were posted on 20 June at Turin, addressed to … Mgr Michele Viale Prelà, archbishop of Carthage, Innsbruck.” Image: Broadsheet Dispaccio del Card. Soglia (Rome, Tip. Puccinelli, 1848), image from Tony Gaffney via K. Schmeh, Cipherbrain (13 December 2014). Two documents follow. The first is a letter wholly in clear, no. 6235: the Pope has read the nuncio’s two letters of 27 May and approves his decision to follow the Emperor at the Austrian foreign minister’s invitation; “what the instructions are, you will learn from my contemporary dispatch in cipher”; the language of the Ministry is not to be confused with the Pope’s own will. The second is the cipher dispatch, which opens in clear (“having news of your departure from Vienna and of your removal to that city, where His Imperial Majesty now resides, I take the occasion to send you this dispatch there”), then runs fourteen lines of digits, breaks into clear for one sentence (“To save time you must at once make the present dispatch known”), ends with two more lines of digits, and is signed G. Card. Soglia , Rome, 15 June 1848. At the foot: Un premio non tenue è destinato al migliore interprete di queste cifre . The dispatch begins. The first line reads 37 34 46 8247 5 01 8734 8760 8904 8739 8413 5 , Con mio (foglio) del [date] … The vertical rules are fold lines of the sheet; the scattered dots above and below the digits are ignored, and the reading does not need them. Image: Broadsheet Dispaccio del Card. Soglia (Rome, Tip. Puccinelli, 1848), image from Tony Gaffney via K. Schmeh, Cipherbrain (13 December 2014). The transcription used is Joe’s, posted as the fourth comment under Schmeh’s article on 15 December 2014. It was checked line by line against the scan cut into strips, and it is right except in one place: on line 12 the printed …2251242496774740906… lost a 4 . Corrected, the block is 955 digits. The printer made one error of his own, taken up below. Where the print has a dot in the line ( 3099.7.39 , 67367.067 ), it is ignored likewise: the text reads without it.

t: Cardinal Soglia to the nuncio Viale Prelà — a nomenclator with an alphabetical code
b: Three things are visible in the digits before any key is guessed. 5 divides words. Split at every 5, the block falls into 102 non-empty runs, and 92 of them have an even number of digits. The ten odd ones are seven lone digits 1 to 4, one run that ends in such a digit, one print error and one stray 8. A lone 1 , 2 , 3 or 4 is punctuation: comma, semicolon, colon, full stop. The full stop 4 stands immediately before the printed clear sentence. The 5 is not written at every word boundary; short words are often run together ( conmio , oper , perdilui ). 8 marks a code group. The digit 8 never occurs as the second digit of a pair. Where it occurs it begins a four-digit group: 8247 , 8319 , 8620 . Pairs are drawn from the eight digits 0 1 2 3 4 6 7 9, which gives a table of 64 cells. The pairs are letters and syllables. 355 pairs in all, 56 distinct: more symbols than an alphabet needs, far fewer than a code. The table as read. Rows are the first digit, columns the second; a dash is a cell that does not occur in this message. 0 1 2 3 4 6 7 9 0 – del no k s ta al a 1 chi m in – ma c – p 2 gli e ne la n che – – 3 qu da – b mi t con d 4 de l di se e o al r 6 il f – per si st i te 7 v (u) ti g – z to b p 9 c f l d g m n s Homophones: e 21, 44; b 33, 77; c 16, 90; d 39, 93; f 61, 91; g 72, 94; l 41, 92; m 11, 96; n 24, 97; p 19, 79; s 04, 99; al 07, 47. The eight empty cells (00 13 17 27 29 32 62 73) are unused here, not unread. a has one cell, 09, and it is the commonest group in the text (38 times). 70 is u and v ; doubled, it is the w of 92 70 36 74 46 70 70 Lutzovv . Code words and stems. The 8XXX groups stand for whole words or for stems that letters complete: 40 20 8424 67 degli (ordin)i , 19 09 04 99 09 8446 67 passa(port)i , 41 21 8433 16 67 19 46 le (parte)cipo . Nine are fixed by their context beyond reasonable doubt, and their values rise with the alphabet: 8319 8340 8374 8422 8424 8429 8433 8446 8620 Imperatore istruzione Monsignor opportuno ordin- Padre parte port- Roma This is the design Kent Ramliden described in his comment of 7 January 2015 from the cipher of the Vienna nunciature at the Congress of 1814: dinomes for letters and syllables, a four-digit series for words and names, and 5 as a word divider. There, the word series began with 7 and the dinomes avoided 5 and 7; here it begins with 8 and they avoid 5 and 8. His parse, with 7 as the marker, could not work on this text; with 8 it does. The print error: the first passaporti is printed 19 09 0 5 99 09 8446 67 . A 5 inside it would cut the word in two. The second passaporti , later in the text, is 19 09 04 99 09 8446 67 , so the printer set a 5 for a 4. A lone 8 after si on line 1 is unexplained.

t: Cardinal Soglia to the nuncio Viale Prelà — a nomenclator with an alphabetical code
b: Simple substitution fails, and the failure is informative. With 5 taken as the word break, a one-letter-per-pair annealer with 5-gram models in Italian, French and Latin got nowhere, about −3.4 nats a character in each language. The same solver was run on a synthetic control: an Italian text of the same length, enciphered homophonically in 68 two-digit symbols with the same word breaks ( synth.py ). It read the control exactly. So the solver was sound, and the pairs could not all be single letters. A nomenclator annealer. The next solver let each pair stand for a letter or a common syllable, one value per pair, with the 8XXX groups held out as unknown words. Among its outputs, runs such as circostanze , intendendosi and indirizzata were whole Italian words of chancery prose that no chance key would give. Pinned words, then reading by hand. Those three words were fixed and the annealer rerun; after that the text was read by hand, word by word, one pair at a time, each value checked against every other occurrence of the pair. Lutzovv and Inspruck fell out of the letters. Morichini is spelled out in the last line. The code. Once the letters were known, the 8XXX groups could be parsed out and set in order: Imperatore 8319 before istruzione 8340 before Monsignor 8374, and so on to Roma 8620. A one-part code in alphabetical order lets the value of an unknown group be estimated from where it falls between known ones (§05).

b: The end of the dispatch. The period 4 closes the cipher before the clear A risparmio di tempo dovrà con ogni sollecitudine rendere ostensibile il presente dispaccio ; the cipher then resumes with 5 09 8374 5 , a (Monsignor) , and spells Morichini . Image: Broadsheet Dispaccio del Card. Soglia (Rome, Tip. Puccinelli, 1848), image from Tony Gaffney via K. Schmeh, Cipherbrain (13 December 2014). Spelling normalised (the cipher writes v for u and commeteva ); (…) a code word, read from context; [8xxx] a code group not read; the sentence in italics is clear on the print Con mio (foglio) del [8734][8760][8904][8739][8413] si le commetteva che in seguito degli (ordin)i dati a Sua Eccellenza il (Signor), [8227] di Lützow, di abbandonare (Roma), Ella si facesse del pari a richiedere i passa(port)i per restituirsi alla Dominante, o per condursi in (Colonia), che (è) (lontan)a della (guerra), (com)e [8704]e lo avesse creduto (opportuno). (Tuttavia) per nuove sopraggiunte circostanze Le (parte)cipo [8093][8102] del (Padre) che Ella rimanga in Inspruck presso l’(Imperatore) e ovunque egli fosse per recarsi; intendendosi sospesa la indicata delibera [8136] relativa alla domanda de’ passa(port)i: interessa [8131] a (Padre) (cotest)a nuova (istruzione), che Le viene indirizzata per tre diverse vie, (col fine di) assicurarne l’arrivo. A risparmio di tempo dovrà con ogni sollecitudine rendere ostensibile il presente dispaccio a (Monsignor) Morichini per di lui norma alle pratiche affidategli. English By my (letter) of […] you were instructed that, following the (orders) given to His Excellency the (Signor) […] Lützow to leave (Rome), you should likewise ask for your passports in order to return to the capital, or to go to (Cologne), which (is) (far) from the (war), (as) […] you thought (fit). (However), because of new circumstances that have arisen, I inform you […] of the Holy (Father) that you are to remain at Innsbruck with the (Emperor) and wherever he may go; the said decision […] about asking for the passports being understood as suspended. It matters […] to the Holy (Father) [that] (this) new (instruction), which is being sent to you by three different routes (so as to) make sure it arrives … To save time you must at once make the present dispatch known to (Mgr) Morichini, for his guidance in the negotiations entrusted to him. Every group outside the brackets is spelled in letters and reads without choice. La Dominante is the capital, Rome. The sentence beginning interessa is grammatically incomplete, with its verb in the open groups [8131] or after them; its sense is plain.

t: Cardinal Soglia to the nuncio Viale Prelà — a nomenclator with an alphabetical code
h: The code words, checked by rank
b: Ten code groups are read from context: foglio , Signor , Colonia , è , lontan- , guerra , com- , Tuttavia , cotest- , col fine di . Context is not proof, but an alphabetical code gives a test that does not depend on context. A straight line was fitted to the nine firm anchors, code value against rank in a sorted list of the 1,500 commonest words of a 19th-century Italian corpus (slope about 0.47 code values per word; rankfit2.py ). The anchors themselves scatter about the line by 10 to 60 values, so that is the tolerance. Each context reading then gets a predicted value from its own rank: Code Reading Predicted Off by 8110 col (fine di) 8114 −4 8116 Colonia 8117 −1 8120 com(e) 8122 −2 8122 cotest(a) 8145 −23 8211 è 8199 +12 8247 foglio 8245 +2 8310 guerra 8289 +21 8346 lontan(a) 8339 +7 8632 Signor 8596 +36 8737 Tuttavia 8665 +72 Firm anchors against the same line: Imperatore +24, istruzione +21, Monsignor −14, opportuno −10, ordin- −11, Padre −10, parte −18, port- −41, Roma +60. Four readings land within five values of prediction, five more within the anchors’ own scatter, and one, Tuttavia , beyond it. The two largest residuals, Signor and Tuttavia , both lie beyond Roma , the last firm anchor, and both are positive, as is Roma ’s own: the late alphabet is denser in this code than in the word list, and the line extrapolates past it. The readings also come out in the right order among themselves ( col < Colonia < come < cotesta < è < foglio < guerra < lontano ) and in the right places among the anchors, which context alone would not guarantee. The order also rules things out. The obvious reading of con mio [8247] del is dispaccio , but a d -word cannot sit above è at 8211; foglio , predicted at 8245, can. Conte for [8227], before di Lützow , would have to fall between come (8120) and cotesta (8122), and the firm anchors alone put it near 8133; 8227 is in the e – f range. Both exclusions lean on the context readings nearest them, so they are as good as those readings.

t: Cardinal Soglia to the nuncio Viale Prelà — a nomenclator with an alphabetical code
b: The Emperor Ferdinand had left Vienna for Innsbruck on 17 May 1848. The nuncio followed him there, at the invitation of the Austrian foreign minister, and wrote to Rome on 27 May; the clear letter printed with the cipher is the Pope’s approval of that. Rome and Vienna were near rupture: papal volunteers were fighting the Austrians in the Veneto, and Count Lützow, the Austrian ambassador, had received his passports in the first days of May (the Rome Gazzetta of 9 May announced them) and left Rome on the evening of 16 May, according to the diary of Prince Agostino Chigi. The earlier instruction the cipher refers to, whose date is in the open groups, was the papal answer: the nuncio should likewise ask for his passports and go home, or to Cologne, away from the war. The cipher countermands it. What the nuove sopraggiunte circostanze were, it does not say. Carlo Luigi Morichini, archbishop of Nisibis and until April the Papal States’ finance minister, had left Rome on 27 May as extraordinary apostolic delegate to the Emperor and to Charles Albert and reached Innsbruck on the night of 10 June (Chigi); the Pope wanted his nuncio to stay beside the Emperor while Morichini negotiated, and wanted Morichini to see the order. It came too late on both counts. The Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani says that on 14 June the nuncio left Innsbruck and went as papal delegate to Frankfurt and to Cologne, returning to his post at Vienna in September. The dispatch is dated the 15th. A copy was posted at Turin on the 20th and never reached him; Chigi heard that it had been intercepted at Turin or Milan. It was printed in Milan on the 30th and posted up in the streets of Rome on 5 or 6 July. On 8 July Chigi noted that the feared ministerial crisis would not come of it, and that the Pope was said to have had no difficulty in showing the Ministry the part in cipher. The published guesses fare unevenly against the reading. Spada’s informant said the cipher contained the Pope’s approval of the nuncio’s conduct in keeping on good terms with the court and avoiding the scandal of his dismissal. The approval is in the clear letter; the cipher is an order, and the rupture it heads off was one that Rome itself had ordered. Il Labaro of 7 July, as summarised on Cipherbrain in 2016, guessed at a departure from the court and a role for the bishop of Nisibis, which is nearer to the truth, though in the reverse direction.

t: Cardinal Soglia to the nuncio Viale Prelà — a nomenclator with an alphabetical code
b: Eleven code groups occur once each and are not fixed by their context. The alphabetical order gives each a window: its place between the known values, converted to a stretch of the sorted word list ( windows2.py , piecewise between all anchors; roughly ±15 words). Code Window Context 8734 8760 8904 8739 8413 tr–tu / venti–vo(lgente) / beyond v / tu–u / n–o the date of the earlier letter: con mio foglio del … , probably an early-June date such as tre volgente with a reference 8227 ess–età–ex–fa il Signor, […] di Lützow ; Chigi calls him ex-ambasciatore 8704 te–ti come […]e lo avesse creduto opportuno 8093 8102 ch–ci / ci–co Le partecipo […] […] del Padre 8131 8136 cr–da / da–dar interessa […] al Padre ; delibera […] relativa Scoring every candidate in these windows with the character model picks only function words ( ciò , da , esse ), which is no reading. 8904 lies above every word in the list, which in a code of this kind may be z -words or an appendix of numbers or names. Filling these needs the 1848 papal codebook or other messages in the same code: the Secretariat of State and the Vienna nunciature archive in the Vatican, or Austrian intercepts in the Haus-, Hof- und Staatsarchiv, which Ramliden pointed to in 2015.

t: Cardinal Soglia to the nuncio Viale Prelà — a nomenclator with an alphabetical code
b: The eleven groups above, and so the date of the earlier letter and the exact wording of three clauses. The ten context readings are checked by order, not proved. The weakest are guerra (8310, only nine values below Imperatore at 8319, so nearly all h - and i -words would have to fit between them) and lontan- (8346, six above istruzione , leaving five values for everything from istr - to lon -). Both fit the sentence and the order, but a code this sparse there would be unusual. Tuttavia is furthest from its prediction, for the reason given in §05. della guerra where dalla guerra is expected, and the stray 8 after si on line 1, are as printed; whether they are the cipher clerk’s or the Milan compositor’s cannot be told from a reprint. The broadsheet is a Roman reprint of the Milan paper. The Milan issue itself (on repubblicaromana-1849.it) was not collated digit by digit.

t: Lope de Soria to Charles V, Genoa, 1523 — two ciphers, one broken from a court decipherment and one with no key at all
b: Eleven DECODE records (RAH Salazar A-28, R9488–R9498), none deciphered before: five despatches of the imperial ambassador at Genoa, June to August 1523, with their duplicates. The later cipher was rebuilt from a Soria letter that carries the court’s decipherment. The earlier one had no key or crib and fell to a substitution solver scored on Castilian of the 1520s. The letters read on the Venetian league, the French descent, a plan to seize Bergamo and Brescia, Siena, Beaurain’s mission and Andrea Doria’s first approach to the Emperor. Genoa → Charles V and Gattinara · two ciphers: letter signs with a small code, then a homophonic alphabet with a large code · June–August 1523 · read in part Lope de Soria to Charles V, Genoa, 1523 — two ciphers, one broken from a court decipherment and one with no key at all to Charles V Real Academia de la Historia, Colección Salazar y Castro A-28 (9/28) ff. 248–584 · DECODE R9488–R9498, eleven records, all Non-decrypted · five letters and their duplicates Key B rebuilt from DECODE R9844, a Soria letter of December 1523 with the court’s decipherment · key A broken ciphertext-only by a hill-climbing solver Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 19 September 2026 read in part Summary. DECODE lists eleven ciphered letters of Lope de Soria to Charles V, 1523–24, as not deciphered. They are five despatches from Genoa, June to 13 August 1523, most in two or three copies; one is to the chancellor Gattinara. Bergenroth calendared only the letter of 13 August, from its clear parts. The letters use two ciphers. Soria switched in late July: the letter of July has its body in the first and its post data in the second. The later cipher (key B) was rebuilt by aligning a Soria letter of December 1523 (DECODE R9844) with the court’s decipherment filed beside it. The earlier cipher (key A) had no key and no crib. About a thousand signs were transcribed, and a simulated-annealing substitution solver scored on Castilian state papers of 1520–21 recovered its alphabet from random starts. The three copies of the June letter then confirmed the homophones. The letters report the league with Venice being closed, the French king’s expected descent on Italy, a proposal to open war on the Venetians in the Bergamasco and Bresciano, Siena’s government, Beaurain’s mission to Bourbon, money for the Swiss, and Andrea Doria offering his galleys to the Emperor. Status: read in part. The June and July letters read nearly throughout. The key-B passages read in substance, but some code groups stay open, among them rip, pur, qed and mul in key A and a dozen groups in key B.
