t: Lope de Soria to Charles V, Genoa, 1523 — two ciphers, one broken from a court decipherment and one with no key at all
b: Key B (from late July 1523) is a homophonic alphabet of Latin-looking letters and signs, with two to four signs for the commoner letters, and a large code of three-letter lower-case groups: sub que, zog de, yed en, xab Francia, soc rey, zic principe, pic tab su Magestad, pup tab V. Magestad. The same cipher is in DECODE R9844 (BRAH 9/30 ff. 34–37), Soria to Gattinara, 30 December 1523. Its decipherment is on ff. 36r–36v, and aligning the two gave the first thirty groups and most of the letters. The Genoa letters then added the rest. Key A (June–July 1523) has about twenty-five graphic signs (ʒ, crossed ʒ, ⊖, α, ε, φ, π, ꜑, the tt ligature, the figures 2 3 7 9) and a handful of lower-case code words. The writer kept the word divisions. Its values: plain signs plain signs a 9, ꜑ n c o α, ꝓ (alone = que ) s ε, π e ʒ, crossed ʒ t ꜩ d c+ꜩ ligature l 2 u/v 3 i (b) 7 c ⊖ g (a) ꜑ with double bar r small o, L, Y m ∂ p б y φ f ♀, long-stemmed hook x m-sign Code words: cap que, lod de, leh en, luc duque, lih Milan, cip Venecia, mos infanteria, lim mil, sig lod saq Rey de Francia, rap Italia. The copies of the June letter spell out uenecia , infanteria and mil where another copy uses the code word, and that fixes three of them.

t: Lope de Soria to Charles V, Genoa, 1523 — two ciphers, one broken from a court decipherment and one with no key at all
b: The key-A block of the July letter (f. 444r–445v, 32 lines) was transcribed into ASCII names for the signs, with the code words set apart. The counts pointed to a near-monoalphabetic cipher. There were few signs; one sign stood alone ten times, which had to be y ; and one pair, c before the tt ligature, never separated, so it was a single sign. A simulated-annealing search over sign-to-letter maps was scored with a character 4-gram model of Danvila’s edition of Castilian state papers of 1520–21. It returned la liga general , cinco mil infantes , exercito and con la esperança from random starts in a few seconds. The remaining values, the homophones for a , o and e , and the code words were then fixed by hand. They were checked against the two other copies of the June letter and the duplicate of the July letter, which use different homophones in the same places. The work took one session; the model was given the images and nothing else for this cipher.

t: Lope de Soria to Charles V, Genoa, 1523 — two ciphers, one broken from a court decipherment and one with no key at all
b: … escriven de Milan como tenian nueva que era arrivado en Venecia un secretario del duque de Milan, el qual avia traido el mandado del Infante para concluir la liga con los venecianos, y que por esto el duque de Milan avia prometido al dicho Infante diez y ocho mil ducados, y que con esto tenian por cierto que se concluiria la dicha liga, y por esto se partia con diligencia el protonotario Caracciolo para ir a Venecia. Y ansi mismo escriven de Milan como aviendose [comen]çado de amotinar la infanteria … les avian enviado una paga … an escrito el duque de Milan y el señor Prospero al duque [de Genova] que quiera esforçarse de ayudar con alguna suma de dineros, y el respondio que no puede dar dineros, pero que tomara quinientos infantes de los del exercito para que esten aqui y los pagara por un mes … de manera que nadie atiende sino a su propio interese. The league of Venice with the Emperor was signed on 29 July and published on 15 August 1523. Here it is still being bought, with Milanese money on the Archduke Ferdinand’s mandate.

t: Lope de Soria to Charles V, Genoa, 1523 — two ciphers, one broken from a court decipherment and one with no key at all
b: […] de Leon escriven a los veinte y tres del mes pasado como lo esperavan, que vendria muy presto el Rey de Francia para pasar en Italia; pero hasta agora no se juntava gente de guerra para que puedan pasar tan presto con exercito. Podria ser que pensasen de pasar con solo la gente d’armas, con esperança que calaran los [qed], y con la esperança de los venecianos, y pensando valerse de los cinco mil infantes que tiene en Provença … Y creo que los dichos [rip] usaran con [pur] los tratos que uso Otaviano Campofregoso quando se fizo la liga general y pasava este Rey de Francia en Italia, que una vez nos deçia que querria entrar en la liga y otras veçes dava palabras por dilatar, fasta que paso el dicho Rey, y a la ora el se declaro nuestro enemigo … fuera bueno començarles luego la guerra. Desto se seguirian dos buenos efetos: lo uno, que se desgravaria el estado de Milan del aposiento del exercito y estaria mejor alojado en el Bergamasco y Bresano; y lo otro, que luego seria tomado Bergamo, de donde podrian sacar dineros para alguna paga a la infanteria. Y no seria milagro que se tomase presto Bresa o Verona. The [rip] can only be the Venetians or their government, still undecided a fortnight before they joined the league. Soria recalls how Ottaviano Fregoso, Doge of Genoa in 1515, strung the league along and then declared for France once Francis I had crossed the Alps. The closing and the post data of this letter are in key B. They report that Monsieur de Beaurain has arrived; Adrien de Croÿ, sieur de Beaurain, was the Emperor’s envoy to the Duke of Bourbon that summer.

t: Lope de Soria to Charles V, Genoa, 1523 — two ciphers, one broken from a court decipherment and one with no key at all
b: A long paragraph on Siena. The Sienese “comunidades” might be freed from their “tiranos” and governed as a republic. Soria argues that things voted by many are hard to carry through where opinions are divided, and that the Emperor would be better served by one man governing “de mano de su Magestad”. Y al cabo creo que avra de venir a esto, porque los seneses, de la condicion que son, que cada qual querra ser señor, y los otros no piensan sino solo en su propio interese. The first seven lines keep several open groups. A short passage names Beaurain again, at Turin.

t: Lope de Soria to Charles V, Genoa, 1523 — two ciphers, one broken from a court decipherment and one with no key at all
b: Beaurain carries this letter. Three days earlier a Piedmontese courier left by land for the Abbot of Nájera. Soria asks that the Emperor provide twenty-eight thousand escudos to a doctor at Constance to pay certain Swiss who have agreed to descend on France, and twelve thousand to a treasurer. The names of the doctor and the treasurer are not read.

t: Lope de Soria to Charles V, Genoa, 1523 — two ciphers, one broken from a court decipherment and one with no key at all
b: Andrea Doria and the Prince of Salerno are discontented with the King of France. He had promised them the enterprise of Genoa and then gave it to the Bastard of Savoy. Jeronimo Doria, a kinsman of the leading men of the city, told Soria on Andrea Doria’s behalf that if the Emperor would take him into his service with his galleys, he would serve “de muy buena voluntad”; the same was offered for the Prince of Salerno. A second passage: Soria has pressed Antoniotto Adorno to make the republic pay what it owes under the capitulation [made in the time of Pope Leo]. Adorno has asked Martin Centurion to take it up with the Emperor. Andrea Doria came over to Charles V only in 1528, so this is an early approach.

t: Lope de Soria to Charles V, Genoa, 1523 — two ciphers, one broken from a court decipherment and one with no key at all
b: Key A code words not fixed: rip (3x, the Venetians, graded C), pur (3x, the Emperor’s side, M), qed (2x, the Swiss, M), mul , dus , cop , and the opener TZ . Key B groups still open or guessed: yac , fob , taf , tu , pel , pug , zib , sib , xif , sab , 7 pes , per ; guessed: paf tiempo, tin papa, sud respuesta, xa hasta (M). Readings of R9491 lines 1–7, the personal names in R9494, and the number of Doria’s galleys are graded M. The rest of the key-B passages are C, and the June and July key-A texts H/C. Not collated sign by sign: R9490 (spot checks only), R9493 (checked at the doubtful words), R9496, R9498.

t: Lope de Soria to Charles V, Genoa, 1523 — two ciphers, one broken from a court decipherment and one with no key at all
b: Real Academia de la Historia, Salazar y Castro A-28 (9/28), via DECODE R9488–R9498; Salazar A-30 (9/30) ff. 34–37, DECODE R9844 (the key-B crib). G. A. Bergenroth, Calendar of State Papers, Spain , vol. 2, no. 586 (13 August 1523), on British History Online . Language model: A. Rodríguez Villa / M. Danvila, Historia crítica y documentada de las Comunidades de Castilla (Memorial histórico español 37), the text used in adrian1521/ . No page images are reproduced here: the scans are the Academy’s, served through DECODE to registered users. Transcriptions, both keys with their evidence, and the solver are in the repository folder soria1523/ .

t: Sormano and de Vaulx to François I, February 1529 — the duke of Ferrara declines the crown of Naples
b: Three ciphered despatches of the French agents at Ferrara, BnF fr. 3096 nos. 63, 65 and 66, listed unread beside two glossed siblings. Lasry’s key holds; the leaves add a null, a nomenclator for the duke and four letter forms. Eighteen thousand signs segmented from the Gallica scans, clustered and classified, then every line read on review sheets; the duplicate pair, which enciphers different stretches, checks itself. Alfonso d’Este will not take the kingdom or the captaincy of the French army, and the agents call his difficulties pretexts, eight months before Cambrai. Ferrara → the Court · homophonic symbol cipher with a nomenclator · February 1529 · read Sormano and de Vaulx to François I, Ferrara, February 1529 to Francis I BnF Français 3096, nos. 63, 65 and 66 · ten page sides, some 18,000 signs · catalogued with two deciphered siblings and no reading of their own · the duke of Ferrara asked to lead the French army on Naples, eight months before Cambrai Lasry’s key verified on the glossed sibling no. 62 and applied at glyph level; nos. 65 and 66 read end to end, no. 63 as far as its leaves go · the published table gains a null, a nomenclator for the duke and four letter forms Daniel Bourdeau · read 17 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. In February 1529 François I sent Joachim de Vaulx to join his resident Gaspare Sormano at Ferrara with an instruction for Alfonso d’Este: take the captaincy of the French army for the enterprise of Naples, and with it, if he would, the kingdom. Three letters report what followed, two of them the same despatch written twice (no. 66 is docketed duplicata ) and the third the sequel a few days later. The cipher is a homophonic substitution of some forty geometric signs whose key George Lasry reconstructed in 2023 from the two siblings in the volume that carry a contemporary decipherment; the three target letters carry no decipherment. The work here was transcribing them from the scans and applying that key; they are now read. The duke, after long audiences, risolutamente concluse per cosa dil mondo non voler per sé alcunamente accettare il regno et manco far l’impresa a suo nome ; he would accept only whatever settlement the King negotiated for him with the Pope, and pleaded the want of provisions. Sormano writes that this confirmed “what I always doubted”, that the duke never meant to take the command. The agents judge his difficulties pretexts and fall back on his son Ercole and on the marshal Trivulzio, expected on his way to Venice. Status: nos. 65 and 66 read end to end; no. 63 read in its clear and in its shorter cipher runs, the long runs on ff. 115v–116r only in patches; no. 63’s last leaf is not in the volume where it should be.

t: Sormano and de Vaulx to François I, February 1529 — the duke of Ferrara declines the crown of Naples
b: BnF fr. 3096 is a volume of original letters to François I and Montmorency of 1528–29. Nos. 62 to 67 are the Ferrara file: Sormano’s letters of March 1529 (no. 62, f. 113) and his doppio (no. 67, f. 124) carry a decipherment written between the lines by a contemporary hand; nos. 63 (ff. 115–116), 65 (ff. 119–120) and 66 (ff. 121–122) do not. Tomokiyo’s cryptiana page prints Lasry’s key for the glossed pair and lists the other three as undeciphered. On cryptiana that means no interlinear or nearby deciphered copy, not unsolved. Gallica has the volume at full resolution (btv1b9060015d, views 117–127), 8,660 pixels across a two-page spread, which is about 44 pixels per sign. What this page does and does not add. The key came from the same volume: Lasry found it, and it serves the glossed and the unglossed letters of fr. 3096 alike. Checking whether letters in one collection share a key, mostly by eye, is standard procedure, so this is not a key found elsewhere. The same cipher is also used in BnF fr. 3045 f. 28 and fr. 3034 f. 154 (Lasry, personal communication, 21 September 2026); those leaves are not read here. The main contribution is the transcription of some 18,000 signs, plus the null, the nomenclator sign and the letter forms it added to the table. Fr. 3096 f. 121r, the head of no. 66: duplicata in the upper right, the clear opening, and the first cipher runs. The large double circle after si douea and after Don Hercole is the sign for the duke. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3096 f. 121r, via Gallica (btv1b9060015d, view 125). The three letters are one negotiation. No. 65 and no. 66 both open Zobia passata Io Joachin gionsi qua , both subscribe Da Ferrara alli XXIII febraro 1529 , and no. 63 opens Il xxIII del presente per nostre duplicate lettere a vostra Maestà al lungo scrivessimo ciò che havevamo negociato con questo Signor Duca . So 65 and 66 are the duplicate pair sent on the 23rd and 63 is the follow-up. The catalogue’s “28 February” for no. 63 is not on the leaves that survive: the letter breaks off mid-sentence at the foot of f. 116v ( difficilmente crederemo … ), and f. 117 is a different paper in another hand, wholly unciphered, so its end and its date are elsewhere or lost. Both agents write. The narrative voice moves between Io Joachin and Io Sormano in the same letter, and the passages each man puts in cipher are those about his own audiences.

t: Sormano and de Vaulx to François I, February 1529 — the duke of Ferrara declines the crown of Naples
h: The cipher, and what the published key lacks
b: One continuous alphabet of geometric signs written on the line with the clear Italian, no word breaks, cipher and clear alternating mid-sentence. Common letters have three or four homophones: a V υ п 3, e ϰ k Γ 7, i Y ⊙ ρ 4, o Ц 1 ƌ, u/v T α γ H, s Ŧ ⊐; single signs for the rest, Δ c , ▽ q , π n , Q r , x t , 6 p , S g , E h , ϙ l , ꝑ m ; and two doubled letters, ⊡ ll and ≠ cc . That is Lasry’s table, and it is right: the first glossed run on f. 113r, ꜿ f T π Δ V 6 ρ x υ π Γ 1 ⊐ α 4 Δ 7 Q ƌ Δ E ϰ ⊐ , reads de vn capitaneo suicero che s[i] under the gloss d’un capitaneo suizari ch’si , sign for sign. The control, f. 113r (no. 62): a cipher run with the decipherer’s gloss above, de vn capitaneo suizari ch’si domanda … . The crossbarred long-s in second place sits under the e of de . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3096 f. 113r, via Gallica (btv1b9060015d, view 117). Four things on the leaves are not in the table, and each costs a reading until it is seen: A null. A tall sign with a large loop and a long descender curling left (ɧ) occurs in all three letters and twice in the second glossed run of no. 62, and carries no letter. H 1 Ǝ x ɧ Q п is vostra ; Δ E ɧ k is che ; Δ ɧ 1 π ſ ʈ Q x ʒ is conforto . The old note “no nulls observed” is struck. A nomenclator. The large double circle ◎ is not the i sign ⊙ written big. It reads duca everywhere it stands: con questo ◎, fusimo col deto ◎, andai dal deto ◎, circa le cose dil regno ◎ rispondesse . It often falls where the clear hand resumes, which is why it looks like a terminator at first. The fourth e is a crossbarred long-s. It reads as an f to the eye and is the commonest letter form on the page; f proper is the double loop ſſ ( offerta , sufficientissime ). Taken as f it corrupts one letter in twelve. ꝓ, the p with a curled tail, is d ( desiderio , dubitai , dal deto ), not an i homophone; and the open C-shaped boxes that the segmenter produced by the hundred are the left half of the r sign Q cut at its tail, not a sign.

t: Sormano and de Vaulx to François I, February 1529 — the duke of Ferrara declines the crown of Naples
b: No. 66 is not a copy of no. 65. The two were drafted independently from the same notes, and they encipher different stretches . Where no. 65 puts a sentence in cipher, no. 66 very often has it in the clear hand, and the reverse: no. 65, f. 119r (cipher, read here) no. 66, f. 121r (clear on the leaf) maiestà. fata la reuerentia a madama Rainea et al signor don Hercole fatta che hebbimo la reuerentia a Madama Rainea et al s[ignor] Don Hercole suadesimo, confortassimo et instantemente esortasimo et pregasimo suadessemo, confortassemo et instantementi essortassemo et pregassemo nel modo et condicioni in la deta instrittion contenune [sic] nel modo et condition in la ditta instruttion cõtenuti ringratiandola della cosi grande et honorata offerta che gli era piaciuto fargli ringratiandola della cosi grande et honorata offerta che gli era piaciuto fargli The right column was read off the leaf before the left was decoded, and neither was used to produce the other. It is an independent check on the key and on the glyph reading, and it settles most of what one copy leaves doubtful. It also means that any future reader with the two leaves side by side can recover most of the pair without a key at all.

t: Sormano and de Vaulx to François I, February 1529 — the duke of Ferrara declines the crown of Naples
b: Ten page sides at 40–60 signs a line and 35 lines a side is too much to read glyph by glyph from a screen at the resolution Gallica serves, and an earlier pass had stalled at a few lines. The route that worked treats the leaf as a character-recognition problem and keeps the reading with the eye: Segmentation. Line bands from the row-ink profile of each side (337 lines, one physical line once split, none missed), then column-ink valleys inside each band, with runs wider than one sign cut at their thinnest points. 18,273 boxes, each cropped to a fixed 100-pixel height about the line’s x-height centre so that ascenders and descenders keep their place. Clustering. Per-line Otsu threshold, blur, 16×22 raster plus width and ink, PCA to 70 dimensions, k-means with 700 centres. Cluster montages ordered by centroid similarity were labelled by eye, letter or “clear hand”, 212 of them automatically from a coarser 340-centre pass, the rest by hand: two sittings of about forty montages. Classification. A k-nearest-neighbour classifier on the labelled glyphs (raster plus gradient-orientation histograms) reassigns every box, including the ones in mixed clusters; five-fold cross-validation on the labelled set gives 90 % letter accuracy, most of the remainder being cipher signs against fragments of the clear cursive rather than sign against sign. A five-glyph majority window then marks each line into cipher and clear runs. Review. For every line a sheet: the magnified strip in two segments, and below it each segmented box with its index and the classifier’s letter. 170 sheets, read in order with the Italian in mind, correcting the letter where the shape or the word required. Every reading on this page comes from that step, not from the classifier alone. Fr. 3096 f. 119r, lines 4–7 of no. 65: ch’ tenir si douea [con questo ◎] / [acioche conclusion si facesse secondo il desiderio di vostra] / [Maiestà. fata la reuerentia a Madama Rainea et al signor don] / [Hercole, fusimo col deto ◎] et presentato le lettere di vra M[aes]tà di credenza . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3096 f. 119r, via Gallica (btv1b9060015d, view 123). The pipeline’s value is in the sheets, not in the decoded string: the classifier’s own line for f. 119r line 4 is acioc*econclvsmns*facesc*so*ondoili… , readable only because one already knows what it should say. Where the segmenter merges two signs or the hand writes one over a descender, the sheet shows it and the eye fixes it; where the signs run for a whole side without a clear word to anchor them, as on no. 63 ff. 115v–116r, the errors compound and the reading thins to patches.

t: Sormano and de Vaulx to François I, February 1529 — the duke of Ferrara declines the crown of Naples
b: Clear text roman, cipher in brackets, spelling of the leaf kept; (?) a word read from doubtful signs; {…} a ciphered stretch that resists reading; ◎ the duke Zobia passata Io Gian Joachino gionsi qua et dritto me ne veni al logiamento del Ambassator messer Gaspar Sormano, nel quale mi truovo, et a lui comunicata l’intention et comission di vostra Maestà et mostratagli l’instruttion et mandato di quella, et tra nui al lungo divisato et preso ordine dil modo che tenir si dovea [con questo ◎ acioché conclusion si facesse secondo il desiderio di vostra Maestà. Fatta la reverentia a Madama Rainea et al signor don Hercole fusimo col detto ◎], et presentato le lettere di vostra Maestà di credenza con quelle conveniente parole che ci parve convenire, esponessimo la nostra credenza et in nome di vostra Maestà [suadesimo, confortassimo et instantemente esortasimo et pregasimo sua Signoria voler accettare quello che lei, come suo buon et affectionato figliolo, ferisse(?) et deliberasse: far l’impresa di Napoli nel modo et condicioni in la detta instruttion contenute]; et qui con molte efficacissime ragion al lungo rimostrassimo [il stabilimento de sua Signoria, suo stato et posterità, l’honor et l’utile che l’une … riportare, et la satisfaction di vostra Maestà, et finalmente il bene, et con gran gloria di sua Signoria, la finale liberatione et quiete de l’Italia]; né gli fu taciuta la grande buon’opera che in beneficio della [sua persona, stato, casa et successione vostra Maestà haveva fatto … et la quasi ferma speranza che lei riteneva in tutto ridure sua Santità … accordi et condicion che … si dicevano et sua Excellentia poteva desiderar], et le qual tutte cose, volendo lei, al lungo gli furon narrate. Sire, benché in quello ragionamento, che fu assai lungo, [circa le cose dil regno ◎ rispondesse di sorte] che dall’hora haressimo possuto scriver quello che hora se dirà, nientedimanco concludendo lui che la cosa [per ◎ … grande ma sua … ricercava tempo per meglio pensarvi, presimo aspettar la sua final risposta, et in sto mezzo fussimo di novo con signor don Hercole et fattogli intender che hora era il tempo di operare in servicio di vostra Maestà et che la sua casa … stato ni toccava tanto … {five lines on Ercole’s own interest, read in patches}] … [avisassemo che io Sormano solo andasse, sì come andai, dal detto ◎ per rimostrargli … dì seguente dimandati fusimo da sua Signoria ◎ … et dipoi molte ragioni che a noi parsero sufficientissime, … solo per rimoverlo da ogni per lei preallegato sospetto, … ma etiam per disponerla a l’accettar di … bon animo quanto per vostra Maestà se gli offeriva]: finalmente, ringratiandola della [così grande et honorata offerta che gli era piaciuto fargli, risolutamente concluse per cosa dil mondo non voler per sé alcunamente accettare il regno et manco far l’impresa a suo nome]; et il parlar suo fu di sorte che [io Sormano mi parvi quasi chiarito di quello che io sempre dubitai, cioè che sua Excellentia, anchora che havesse dato orecchie et risposto] nel modo che io scrissi a vostra Maestà, veramente non havesse [animo d’intendere al capitaneato, del qual già molti giorni haveva ricercato]. Ben disse non solo contentarse ma con ogni instanza pregar vostra Maestà che la volesse [trattar tra lei et lei l’apontamento et accordo, circa el qual disse accettar quanto vostra Maestà facesse, persuadendosi che da quella non serà astretta far se non cosa conveniente et ragionevole]. Sire, per il gran desiderio che noi habbiamo che [questo signor Duca satisfacesse alla espettation de vostra Maestà], et in questo non volendo noi pretermetter alcun’opera et officio né lassar alcuna cosa intentata, non ostante [questa sua detta risposta, da capo fossimo col prefato signor don Hercole, veramente desideroso far servicio a vostra Maestà, … rimostrandogli che tal risposta poco concedeva(?) in alcun suo profitto; del che et lui con noi dolendosi della qualità et risposta del padre, si mostrò poco satisfatto; lo instassimo esser di novo con sua Excellentia, sperando che la non volesse perdere questa che dal tempo et da la liberalità di vostra Maestà se gli offeriva così bella occasion, come qual altra offerirse gli potesse … il suo stato … con suo poco et picolo pericolo … la sua casa et sua successione … Italia, et per satisfar a vostra Maestà] … [per conclusione si confirmò in la sopra scritta fatta risposta, et così mal satisfatto ritirandome … signor don Hercole, che con dir mi come el signor Duca in alcun modo intendere non … per sé, et quanto al capitaneato, non ostante ciò che nel sopra scritto primo ragionamento et poi era stato detto et … risposto, disse che sua Excellentia persisteva in la … forma et modo della risposta a questi dì data a me Sormano … così poco … risoluto et poco chiaro come la … fu data, toccando … accordo … componere le cose sue col …]. Sire, dalli soprascritti ragionamenti havuti con questo signor Duca pare di poter concluder che [non si possa far … fondamento che in effetto el … voler intrar o accettar el capitaneato, sul quale … provisione, circonstance et sue dependentie dal canto di sua Excellentia se … le difficultà, et a nostro giudicio … la cosa insieme con le sue provision … dependentie così difficile che paia … di difficultà, et non la volontà sia … quel che non lo facino accettar … questa nostra per aventura vana opinion] a vostra Maestà non c’è parso tacere. Io Joachin aspettarò qua il signor Marechial Triulzo, et siamo d’openione che sua Signoria, [dal prefato signor Duca molto stimata, a beneficio di questa cosa con sua Excellentia s’adoperi], il che per ben di questo negocio et servicio di vostra Maestà siamo certi farà ben volentieri. Da Ferrara alli XXIII febraro MDXXVIIII. English Last Thursday I, Jean Joachim, arrived here and went straight to the lodging of the ambassador messer Gaspare Sormano, where I am staying; I gave him your Majesty’s intention and commission and showed him your instruction and mandate, and having talked it over at length we settled how to proceed [with this Duke so that a conclusion might be reached as your Majesty wishes. Having paid our respects to Madame Renée and to Don Ercole we went to the Duke], presented your Majesty’s letters of credence with such fitting words as seemed right, set out our credence and in your Majesty’s name [urged, encouraged and most insistently exhorted and begged his Lordship to accept what he, as your good and affectionate son, should resolve upon: to make the enterprise of Naples in the manner and on the conditions contained in the instruction]. We showed him at length [the securing of his Lordship, his state and his posterity, the honour and the profit that would follow, your Majesty’s satisfaction, and finally, with great glory to his Lordship, the final liberation and quiet of Italy]; nor was he left ignorant of the great good that your Majesty had done [for his person, state, house and succession … and the nearly firm hope you held of bringing his Holiness wholly round … to terms and conditions that … his Excellency could desire]; all of which, since he wished it, was told him at length. Sire, although in that conversation, which was very long, [on the matters of the kingdom the Duke answered in such a way] that we could have written then what will now be said, still, he concluding that so [great] a matter needed time for reflection, [we resolved to await his final answer, and meanwhile went again to Don Ercole and let him know that now was the time to act in your Majesty’s service, and that his house … and his state were so much concerned …]. [We agreed that I, Sormano, should go alone, as I did, to the Duke, to show him … The next day we were summoned by his Lordship the Duke … and after many reasons which seemed to us more than sufficient, … not only to remove every suspicion he alleged, … but also to dispose him to accept with good will what your Majesty offered him]: in the end, thanking you for [so great and honourable an offer, he resolutely concluded that for nothing in the world would he in any way accept the kingdom for himself, nor make the enterprise in his own name]; and his manner of speaking was such that [I, Sormano, thought myself almost certain of what I had always doubted, namely that his Excellency, though he had lent an ear and answered] as I wrote to your Majesty, never truly [meant to take up the captaincy, which he had been asked for many days before]. He did say that he would not only be content but would beg your Majesty with every insistence [to treat between yourself and him the appointment and accord, and said he would accept whatever your Majesty did, being persuaded that you would bind him to nothing but what is fitting and reasonable]. Sire, out of our great wish that [this Duke should satisfy your Majesty’s expectation], leaving nothing untried, notwithstanding [this answer we went back to Don Ercole, who truly wishes to serve your Majesty …, showing him how little such an answer served his own profit; and he, grieving with us over the nature of his father’s answer, showed himself ill satisfied; we pressed him to go again to his Excellency, hoping he would not let slip so fair an occasion as your Majesty’s liberality and the times offered him … his state … at small and little risk … his house and his succession … Italy, and to satisfy your Majesty]. [In conclusion the Duke confirmed his earlier answer, and I, Sormano, withdrew ill satisfied … Don Ercole telling me that the Duke would in no way take it on for himself, and that as to the captaincy, whatever had been said and answered before, his Excellency held to the form of the reply given me some days ago, … as little resolved and as little clear as when it was given, touching on … an accord … to settle his affairs with the Pope …]. Sire, from all these conversations with the Duke it seems we may conclude that [no reliance can be placed on his in fact meaning to enter or accept the captaincy; on which, as to the provisions, circumstances and dependencies, on his Excellency’s side the difficulties … and in our judgement … the thing, with all its provisions and dependencies, is so difficult that it seems … it is difficulty and not want of will … that keeps him from accepting; this our perhaps vain opinion] we thought it right not to hide from your Majesty. I, Joachim, shall wait here for the marshal Trivulzio, and we are of opinion that his Lordship, [much esteemed by the Duke, will exert himself with his Excellency for this business], which for the good of the affair and your Majesty’s service we are sure he will do very willingly. From Ferrara, 23 February 1529. Madama Rainea is Renée de France, Louis XII’s daughter, married to Ercole d’Este in 1528; questo signor Duca is Alfonso I d’Este; il Marechial Triulzo is Teodoro Trivulzio, marshal of France and governor of Genoa. The capitaneato is the command of the French army in the kingdom of Naples after Lautrec’s death before the city in August 1528, when the King was looking for an Italian prince to carry the war; the crown of Naples was the bait. Alfonso’s refusal here, dressed in the want of provisions, is the first sign of the turn that ended with his abandonment of the French alliance and his accommodation with the Emperor at the Peace of Cambrai (August 1529) and the settlement of 1530.

t: Sormano and de Vaulx to François I, February 1529 — the duke of Ferrara declines the crown of Naples
b: No. 66 tells the same story in the same order, with the clear and ciphered stretches swapped as described above, and a fuller close: non mancaremo continuamente sollicitar sua Excellentia, et se da quella altro potremo haver se dirà . Its reading is in the repository ( sormano/n66_reading.md ) and its cipher runs are transcribed line by line beside those of no. 65; nothing in it changes the account. No. 63 is the sequel and the hardest of the three: four sides, three of them almost solid cipher, no sibling. What reads is enough for the sense. The duke had given una poco chiara et risoluta risposta on the captaincy and repeats it; he says he cannot see that the King and his confederates are making the provisions the enterprise needs, un esercito in campagna , money for Swiss, Spaniards and Genoese, and that all should be furnished before he commits, et tanto più hora, che già siamo — così disse — nel buon tempo . Two things he asks the King to remember, one about the Naples enterprise itself and one about the command. Dal canto suo disse non dover mancare ; the agents say they have omitted nothing in their power, judge from the duke’s nature that the matter debba esser non poco difficile , and put their hope in Trivulzio: Sire, con tutto che per le ragion dette siamo in … poca speranza che questo signor duca … intendere … capitaneato, pur in questa causa non volendo noi pretermetter alcuna natura d’opera et d’ufficio, se’l signor Marechial Triulzo andando a Vinetia passarà per qua … pensiamo operar che sua Signoria …; et in sto mezzo per tri o quatro giorni anchora Io Joachin qui l’espettarò . The letter stops at the foot of f. 116v in the middle of a clause. The full reading with the unread runs marked is sormano/n63_reading.md .

t: Sormano and de Vaulx to François I, February 1529 — the duke of Ferrara declines the crown of Naples
b: In no. 65 about a dozen words are marked (?) or left in braces: the five lines on Ercole’s interest at the foot of f. 119r, three lines at the foot of f. 119v, and the run on f. 120r where the duke’s answer is repeated. All are places where the segmenter merged or split signs in a dense run; the glyph strings are in the transcription and can be re-read. No. 63 ff. 115v–116r: roughly half the cipher lines read only in patches. The transcription gives the classifier’s string for each; a cleaner segmentation, or a copy of the letter in another volume, would finish it. The b sign (τ) was not securely identified on any leaf; the few b ’s in the text fall in words read from context ( buon , bene , bella ). The dates: 23 February 1529 is on the leaves for 65 and 66; no. 63 carries no date on ff. 115–116, and its last leaf has not been located.

t: Sormano and de Vaulx to François I, February 1529 — the duke of Ferrara declines the crown of Naples
b: BnF, Français 3096, ff. 113, 115–116, 119–122, 124: Gallica btv1b9060015d , views 117–127. G. Lasry, key to the Sormano cipher (2023), published as an image on S. Tomokiyo, “French Ciphers during the Reign of Francis I” ( cryptiana ). Context: the Naples campaign and Ferrara in 1528–29 in the standard accounts of the war of the League of Cognac; Renée de France’s marriage (June 1528) and the Este–papal quarrel over Modena and Reggio, which is the accordo … col Papa the duke wanted the King to make for him. Transcriptions ( n63 , n65 , n66_transcription.md ), readings, the key notes with the corrections ( KEY.md ), and the segmentation, clustering, classification and review-sheet scripts are in the repository ( sormano/ ). Page images are not committed.

t: Sormano and Passano from Ferrara — eight failures, a published key, and two corrections
b: Three ciphered letters of François I’s agents at Ferrara, February 1529. Eight independent methods failed on a 1960s microfilm that will not separate thirty-six symbol forms — and then George Lasry’s 2023 key, published all along on a page I had not searched, read them. It also graded the attempt: 20 of the 22 values derived here were right, and the two wrong ones were exactly what had blocked it. The Duke’s answer comes out as “risolutamente concluse per cosa dil mondo non voler … se alcunamente accetare il regno” — Alfonso d’Este refusing the kingdom for nothing in the world. With the documentary findings from the failure: no. 63’s lost third sheet, the duplicate that cribs its twin, and Passano identified. The page also records two things this write-up previously got wrong. Contributed by Arya Sanketbhai Patel. Ferrara → France · homophonic symbol alphabet with nomenclator · 23 and 27 February 1529 · key supplied, substance read Sormano and Passano from Ferrara — eight failures, a published key, and two corrections to Francis I BnF Français 3096 nos. 63, 65 and 66 · three ciphered letters of François I’s agents at Ferrara · eight methods failed on the microfilm; George Lasry’s 2023 key then read them and graded the attempt 20 of 22 The Duke’s answer: per cosa dil mondo non voler … se alcunamente accetare il regno · two earlier claims corrected on the page itself Arya Sanketbhai Patel · read in part 18 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read in part Summary. Three letters of 23 and 27 February 1529 from François I’s agents at Ferrara, BnF Français 3096 nos. 63, 65 and 66, in a symbol cipher. Two siblings in the same volume carry contemporary decipherments, so this was billed as an afternoon’s alignment. It was not: eight independent methods failed, because the hand uses some thirty-six forms for about twenty values and the 1960s microfilm does not separate them. I recorded that as a documented negative — and was then handed George Lasry’s 2023 key , which had been published all along on a page I had not searched. It reads the letters. It also grades my own work: 20 of the 22 values I had derived independently were right , and the two that were wrong were exactly the ones blocking me. With the key, the Duke’s answer comes out: “risolutamente concluse per cosa dil mondo non voler … se alcunamente accetare il regno” — he resolutely concluded that for nothing in the world would he in any way accept the kingdom. Alongside that stand the documentary findings that came out of the failure: the lost third sheet of no. 63, the duplicate that cribs its twin, and the identity of the second signer. Status: partly read. The key is verified end to end; a complete transcription of all three letters remains. This page also records two things I got wrong.

t: Sormano and Passano from Ferrara — eight failures, a published key, and two corrections
b: This write-up previously said two things that were false, and they are worth stating plainly rather than quietly editing away. “No published Lasry key for this manuscript could be found.” Wrong. It is published, on Tomokiyo’s French Ciphers during the Reign of Francis I , under the heading “Sormano’s Cipher”, with an exemplar table provided by George Lasry and built from this volume’s own glossed control, f. 113 . I had searched the Henri IV page and some journal indexes, failed, and reported the failure as an absence. A failed search is not evidence that a thing does not exist. “The claim that Alfonso refused the kingdom of Naples is not supported.” Also wrong. I had established from the King’s own letters that the errand was a proposed Italian league, found no source attesting a Neapolitan offer, and concluded the claim was unsupported. With the key, the cipher says he refused the kingdom. The right conclusion at the time was the narrower one: that I could not read it, and that the instructions described a different errand.

t: Sormano and Passano from Ferrara — eight failures, a published key, and two corrections
h: The documents, and a sheet that was not lost
b: Gaspare Sormano, a Milanese jurist whom the King kept “resident aupres de mon cousin le duc de Ferrare”, and a colleague who signs himself simply Ioachin , wrote to François I from Ferrara in February 1529 while France was losing Italy. Their letters sit in a Fontanieu recueil, digitised from a black-and-white microfilm of double-page openings; canvas equals folio plus four, fixed on two foliated leaves. The catalogue’s description needed correction at three points. Piece Letter Leaves Cipher 62 Sormano → the King, 22 March 1529 f. 113 short runs, interlinear decipherment 63 Sormano and Ioachin → the King, penultimo February ff. 115, 116 and 123 four sides, dense; one gloss 64 Langeac and Ioachin → the King, Venice, 6 May ff. 117–118 none 65 Sormano and Ioachin → the King, 23 February ff. 119–120 three sides, dense 66 the same, docketed “duplicata” ff. 121–122 three sides, dense 67 Sormano’s copy of his letter to the Duke of Urbino f. 124 four lines, marginal decipherment No. 63 is complete, and its last sheet is f. 123. The letter breaks off mid-sentence at the foot of f. 116v, and the target description said only that its final leaf was not where the catalogue implied. It is f. 123, bound out of order after the duplicate: numbered “3” at the foot where ff. 115 and 116 are numbered “1” and “2”, continuing the broken sentence, ending with the subscription and the signatures “Sormano, Joachin”, and dated “Da Ferr[ara] p[en]ultimo de Febraro M D XXVIIII” . Its blank verso carries the address docket, written sideways, “…et Sormano / de penultimo febraro 1529”. So the letter is dated after all, and penultimo February 1529 is the 27th, not the 28th the catalogue gives. No. 64, grouped with the rest, has no cipher at all, and f. 116v carries a third, unrecorded decipherment: the words “de Venetiani” written above a two-glyph group, which shows the cipher had a nomenclator.

t: Sormano and Passano from Ferrara — eight failures, a published key, and two corrections
h: The duplicate that cribs its twin
b: No. 66 repeats no. 65 almost word for word and is docketed “duplicata”, but the two clerks enciphered different stretches. Where no. 66 reads in clear “fatta che hebbimo la reverentia a Madama Rainea et al Sr Don Hercole”, no. 65 has that inside a cipher run; where no. 66 gives “per la grandezza sua ricercava tempo per meglio pensarvi, presimo aspettar la sua final risposta, et in sto mezzo col Sr Don Hercole di nuovo fossimo, et fattogli intender”, no. 65 ciphers it; and conversely no. 65 gives in clear “et presentato le lre di vra Mta di credenza … et in nome di vra Mta” where no. 66 ciphers. Four matched passages were checked. The consequence is that the pair supplies its own cribs, in the clerk’s own spelling rather than a later paraphrase, and that the union of the two clear texts recovers most of the letter of 23 February without touching the cipher.

t: Sormano and Passano from Ferrara — eight failures, a published key, and two corrections
h: The key, and how far it is verified
b: BnF Français 3096, f. 124r — Sormano’s copy of his letter to the Duke of Urbino. Four lines of cipher, tied by a double-crossed reference mark to a decipherment written down the left margin in a contemporary hand: “un cappitaneo suizzeri nominato calzolite ch al p[rese]nto si retrovava ne l’aquila…”. 161 letters of plaintext against about 161 glyphs. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3096 f. 124r, via Gallica (btv1b9060015d). The cipher is a homophonic symbol alphabet, letter for letter, with three or four forms for each common vowel and one or two per consonant, plus a nomenclator, a stop mark and a tie mark. Sormano says as much in clear in no. 62: he is writing “ in la mia cifra ”, at Ioachin’s request. The chain of recovery is short and checkable: Line 1 of the f. 124r crib reads glyph by glyph. At high magnification it is exactly 13 glyphs, and the margin gives exactly 13 letters for them, “n capitaneo sui”. That fixes twelve distinct glyphs. Line 2 confirms four of them independently , spelling nominato with the same forms for n, a, t and o in a different word, and adding e, r, i, o, m. The interlinear gloss on f. 113r spells capitaneo with the same glyphs again, five weeks earlier. An independent letter confirms the key without the 1529 decipherer at all. No. 66 reads in clear “il parlar suo fu di sorte ch Jo Sormano mi parue quasi”, and no. 65 ciphers that same sentence from “Jo” onward, so the twin supplies the plaintext. Applied to those 21 glyphs the key returns i o s ? r m a n o m i p a r u ? ? ? a s i — 17 of 21 letters, in words the crib never contained. Three of the four gaps then resolved, and the six glyphs immediately after “quasi” read chiaro with nothing prompting them, giving h. That stretch is enciphered in both copies, so “il parlar suo fu di sorte che Jo Sormano mi parue quasi chiaro” had not been read before. Twenty-two values, thirteen of them fixed twice over, with the homophone structure mapped. And then it stops.

t: Sormano and Passano from Ferrara — eight failures, a published key, and two corrections
h: Why it stops, measured eight ways
b: The obstacle is not the cipher. It is that this hand uses several forms which differ by less than the film records — two rho-like shapes separating i from l , a triangle against an alpha, a chi against a hooked 4, a plain stroke against a tailed 4. Every method tried runs into the same pairs. Approach Result Binary mask overlap (Jaccard) on segmented glyphs ranks wrong pairs closest Blurred, shift-tolerant mask cosine, tuned on a known line margin 0.017; 40 % clustering Nearest-template classification, line 1 onto line 2 26 % correct Grayscale NCC patches, leave-one-out 11 % correct Reading by eye, plaintext known in advance 17 of 21 letters Reading by eye, plaintext not known not Italian Language-model Viterbi decoding fluent invented Italian Automated boxes plus human identification at 7× legible, still contradictory Two escape hatches were closed rather than assumed. The IIIF service reports the master at 8657 × 5876 for a whole opening, about 4,300 pixels per page, so the magnified crops used above are interpolation of a 50-to-60-pixel glyph and no further detail exists. And the volume contains no key sheet. The seventh line is a warning, and it is the reason this page exists. The correct technique for a noisy substitution is to treat the glyph reading as probabilistic and decode under a language model, and these letters helpfully supply 7,194 characters of clear text in exactly the right orthography to train one. Done properly — nearest-exemplar emission scores from 161 labelled crib glyphs, an Italian character 4-gram model, Viterbi — the ciphered conclusion of no. 65 comes out as: echeretantacontaracherarandetolandicheretrarerararen onerarererarereranetarenenondendetonderiochera raralentanererenetondiondereteneranecherandeta That is fluent-looking Italian and it is entirely invented. Below about 40 % emission accuracy the language model stops correcting the shape model and begins generating from the corpus’s commonest patterns — che , tanta , ra , onde — assembled into nothing. A reader who did not check it against the glyphs would file it as a decipherment. Any claimed reading of these particular passages should be asked for its per-glyph evidence.

t: Sormano and Passano from Ferrara — eight failures, a published key, and two corrections
b: Everything here comes from passages in clear, or from outside the volume. Nothing is decoded. The embassy. Ioachin reached Ferrara “Zobia passata” (last Thursday), went straight to Sormano’s lodging, showed him the King’s instruction and mandate, and the two settled their line. They made their reverence to Madama Rainea — Renée de France, married to Ercole d’Este the year before — and to Don Hercole, presented their credentials, and put the King’s proposal to Duke Alfonso I with “molte efficacissime ragion”, reminding him of “la grande opera che in beneficio della sua persona, stato, casa et successione vra Mta havea fatto”. The Duke thanked them for “la cosi grande et honorata offerta”, said he was not only content but begged the King to be pleased to [cipher], and would not answer: “la cosa per la grandezza sua ricercava tempo per meglio pensarvi”. They waited on his final reply and worked meanwhile through Don Hercole, “veramente desideroso far servicio a vra Mta”. Their fallback is Marshal Trivulzio , named three times: his “auttorita et credito” with the Duke “assai conferira et servira”, he is expected through Ferrara on his way to Venice, and the letters of 23 February end waiting for him. Who Ioachin was. The catalogue’s “Joachim de Vaulx” and the Genoese negotiator Gian Gioacchino de Passano, seigneur de Vaux are one man, whom the French called simply Jean Joachim. Three confirmations: François I writes to Jean du Bellay of “Monsr de Vaulx, Jean Joaquin”; David Potter’s inventory notes that Passano “fut envoyé a Ferrare d’où il écrit le 23 février (BnF, fr. 3096, fo. 119-121)”, which is no. 65; and Molini prints the Venice letter in which the writers speak of “le lettere … da Ferrara per il Sig. Gaspar Sormano et per me Ioachin”. What was actually offered. The King’s letter to du Bellay of about 30 January 1529 states the charge Passano carried: “A ceste cause expedie icelluy de Vaulx avec pouvoir de proposer aux Venitiens, Fleurentins, duc de Millan et de Ferrare [et autres] afin si faire se peult une si saincte salut[aire alliance]” — a general Italian league against the Emperor, headed by the Pope, with France and England as contracting parties, “moyen de rompre les desseings et entreprinses de l’Empereur et d’avoir toute l’Ytallie contre luy”. That is the “instruction et mandato” the letters describe, and it is what the “cosi grande et honorata offerta” must concern. The target description for this item asserted that Alfonso “refuses the kingdom of Naples for himself and the captaincy of the French army”. The King’s instructions describe the league, not a kingdom, and François I held his Neapolitan claim only until Cambrai that August, so an offer was possible but unattested in the sources consulted. From that I wrongly concluded the claim was unsupported. The cipher settles it in the claim’s favour — see the next section. The league was the errand; the kingdom was evidently on the table as well. No. 67, which the margin note lets us read. A Swiss captain named Calzolari was at L’Aquila with 1,200 foot, Swiss and landsknechts, who wanted to come over “al beneficio de la lega”. Sormano judged this “nõ de picolo momento a beneficio della lega et damno d’inimici”; the Venetians would pay only their own share, no money was to be had at Ferrara, and rather than wait for the King’s answer and let the thing spoil he pledged his own credit to the Duke of Urbino, promising a good bank bill at Ferrara or Florence and that the King would pay. Molini’s print of the Venice letter of 6 May shows the operation this belongs to: the league buying the imperial mercenaries out of the Kingdom of Naples — “quelli Alamani che si leveranno dal servicio de gli nemici … al soldo de la lega si conduchino” — while the enemy “per meglio asicurarssi de l’Abruzo, et maxime de l’Aquila” threw up a fortress there.

t: Sormano and Passano from Ferrara — eight failures, a published key, and two corrections
h: With the key: the cipher reads
b: Sormano’s cipher, broken by George Lasry in 2023 — the exemplar table built from BnF Français 3096 f. 113, the glossed control in this very volume. Four forms for a , four for e , four for i , three for o , four for u/v , two for s , plus doubled cc and ll : about thirty-six forms for some twenty values. Ten exemplars per value is what makes them separable, and the absence of that is what defeated eight methods. Image: Table by George Lasry (2023), built from BnF fr. 3096 f. 113, via S. Tomokiyo, Cryptiana. The reconstruction scored 20 of 22. Checked against the table, the values I had derived independently from the two contemporary decipherments — n, c, a twice over, p, i three times, t, o twice, s, u/v twice, e, r, m, q, h — all agree. Two were wrong: the figure 4 is i , not e , and the figure 3 is a , not o . Those two errors are precisely the contradictions that had made calzolite unreadable and sent me round in circles. The table also supplies what I lacked (figure 9 = l , square-with-dot = ll , double f = f , capital S = g , crossed bars = cc ) and corrects a guess: the dotted circle I had filed as a stop mark is the letter i . The key verifies end to end. On the one stretch of no. 65 whose plaintext its twin supplies in clear, it returns the twin’s own words: glyphs S2 oo 9 al x u1 M r1 n1 x r1 D oo n1 D 9 H2 S2 r1 key s o l v t a m e n t e c o n c l v s e [ri]solutamente concluse And it reads the passage the whole item turns on. In no. 65’s account of the audience, immediately after those words, the cipher gives “per cosa dil mondo non voler … se alcunamente accetare il regno, né [ta]manco far …”. With the clear text either side: “… finalmente ringratiandola della cosi grande et honorata offerta che gli era piaciuto fargli, risolutamente concluse per cosa dil mondo non voler … se alcunamente accetare il regno, né [ta]manco far … et il parlar suo fu di sorte che [Jo Sormano mi parue quasi chiaro]…” He thanked them for so great and honoured an offer, and resolutely concluded that for nothing in the world would he wish in any way to accept the kingdom, nor even to … — the clause where the captaincy of the French army would stand, consistent with it and not yet read with confidence. Ferrara’s refusal is therefore in the cipher, in the emphatic per cosa dil mondo , and the sentence carrying it is controlled two words earlier by the twin’s own clear text. What remains is ordinary work. A complete transcription of all three letters. My eye still confuses some of the four i forms with the three o forms, several being round with a central mark, so individual words need checking; the readings above are secure where the twin controls them or where the Italian is unmistakable. The procedure in the method section — automated glyph boxes, then identification by eye against Lasry’s exemplars at about seven times — is the way to finish it.

t: Sormano and Passano from Ferrara — eight failures, a published key, and two corrections
h: The crib I went looking for, now superseded
b: Molini’s Documenti di storia italiana II prints other letters of these agents with their contemporary decipherments , and says so: of Sormano’s letter from Ferrara of 13 April 1529 he notes “Alcune espressioni sono in cifra, con sopra l’interpretazione di carattere sincrono, e sono quelle impresse in corsivo” — the ciphered phrases set in italics from the interlinear reading. That letter is in Sormano’s own cipher, the “mia cifra” of ours. Using it required resolving Molini’s ancien volume numbers. The offset is 5525: anc. N = Français (N − 5525) , confirmed four times — anc. 8621 = fr. 3096 from its own notice, anc. 8499 = fr. 2974 (“formerly catalogued as 8499”), anc. 8525 = fr. 3000 and anc. 8530 = fr. 3005 — and independently by Potter citing fr. 3000 fo. 69 for the letter Molini calls 8525 c. 69. The practice was then verified on the leaves: fr. 3000 fo. 74 carries its cipher and a full interlinear decipherment whose glosses match Molini’s italics word for word. Its glyphs are a different cipher, mixing digits — the Venice cipher of Langeac and Passano, not Sormano’s. So one document would break these letters: BnF Français 2974, folio 94 , Sormano to Montmorency from Ferrara, 13 April 1529, in Sormano’s cipher, carrying a contemporary interlinear decipherment whose text Molini already printed. Aligning that printed plaintext against those glyphs gives a long crib in the right cipher and should yield the whole alphabet with several exemplars per form, which is exactly what this attempt lacked. Of the five Sormano letters Molini prints, only this one carries the cipher note; the others he calls simply “È autografa”. And it is the one manuscript of the group the BnF has not digitised: microfiche only, reproduction matrix S 39769 . Molini does not print nos. 63, 65 or 66, so those remain unprinted as well as unread.

t: Sormano and Passano from Ferrara — eight failures, a published key, and two corrections
h: Method, and the procedure to use next
b: Because no imaging libraries were available, the pipeline is pure Python: sips -s format bmp writes an uncompressed BMP which is parsed directly, then thresholding, connected components, text-band detection from the horizontal ink profile, cleanup that splits run-together glyphs and absorbs fragments, shape clustering, and crib alignment by iterated Needleman–Wunsch. On the f. 124r crib it finds 4 of 4 text lines and 161 components against 161 letters, which is itself independent proof that the passage is letter-for-letter with no syllable groups. The best procedure found — and found last — is a hybrid: take the glyph boxes from the automated segmentation, which is reliable, and identify each glyph by eye from a word-level crop at about seven times. Reading whole lines by eye mis-segments; classifying automatically mis-identifies; the hybrid does neither, and produces sharp legible words. It is what a reader with the fr. 2974 crib should use.

t: Sormano and Passano from Ferrara — eight failures, a published key, and two corrections
b: BnF Français 3096, ff. 113–124 (Gallica, ark btv1b9060015d); Français 3000 f. 74 (ark btv1b9060027m); notices cc49559v, cc49428t, cc494576, cc494626. Giuseppe Molini, Documenti di storia italiana copiati su gli originali autentici e per lo più autografi esistenti in Parigi , II (Florence, 1837). David Potter, Inventaire des lettres missives de François Ier , 1529 (cour-de-france.fr, consulted via the Internet Archive). Christophe Justel, Preuves , p. 241, for the King’s letter to Alfonso of 27 January 1529. Unvalidated: every reading here is from a microfilm image or a printed edition, and the ciphered passages of nos. 63, 65 and 66 are not read. Not checked: the originals in Paris, fr. 2974 fo. 94.

t: A codebreaker’s file — the Italian intercepts of TNA SP 106/10
b: DECODE lists seven anonymous, undated, partly decrypted ciphertexts in State Papers 106 box 10. They are one case: the working file of a Jacobean codebreaker, with his solutions between the lines. The key he reconstructed is catalogued three records away as a key rather than a ciphertext, and so fell outside the target list; it sets out a two-figure cipher in which a bar or a tick over the group switches it from a letter to a word of one of two lists. Its vocabulary — Marques Inichiosa, Palatinato, C. Barberino, Il Principe — dates the file to 1623–24, against the catalogue’s 1558/1625. The file holds three different ciphers, not one, and about forty-five values of the three-figure code were rebuilt from the codebreaker’s own interlinear syllables. London · Italian nomenclator, three-figure syllabic code, letter-and-figure syllabary · c. 1623–24 · the file explained and dated, the letters read in part A codebreaker’s file: the Italian intercepts in TNA SP 106/10 The National Archives, State Papers 106, box 10 · DECODE R657, R660, R664, R704, R720, R721, R722, with the key record R725 · catalogued as seven separate anonymous ciphertexts, “1558/1625”, sender and recipient unknown They are one man’s working file · the key sheet he wrote out survives two records away from them · its vocabulary dates the whole group to the Spanish Match and the Palatinate, 1623–24 Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 20 September 2026 · updated 21 September 2026 read in part Summary. DECODE holds seven records for TNA SP 106/10 as separate ciphertexts by an unknown sender to an unknown recipient, dated only by the volume’s span, 1558 to 1625. They are not seven problems. They are the working file of one English codebreaker: intercepted Italian letters with his own solutions written between the lines, his scratch worksheets, and — catalogued three records away, as a key rather than a ciphertext, and so outside the target list — the fair copy of the cipher he reconstructed . That sheet, DECODE R725, is transcribed here in full. It explains the system in the codebreaker’s own words: two-figure groups that are read as a single letter, or as a word from one list, or as a word from a second list, according to whether the figure carries no mark, a bar or a dot. Its recovered nomenclature — Palatinato , Il Principe , Re d’Inghilterra , Papa , Nuncio , C. Barberino , Imbassiatore di Venetia and above all Marques Inichiosa — dates the file to 1623–24 , sixty years narrower than the catalogue. Working through all twenty-two ciphertext pages then shows that the file contains three different ciphers , not one, and that DECODE has one worksheet filed with the wrong letter. Of the second cipher, a three-figure syllabic code, about forty-five values were rebuilt by aligning the codebreaker’s interlinear syllables against his groups, enough to read phrases straight off the page. A further catalogue entry (62) held seven more records of the same box; they are his worksheets, and one of them is his own grid of the three-figure code of two of the letters, the code another sheet calls “the Venetian Cifer”. It rebuilds that code as a systematic syllabary of 117 values and corrects four of the values first rebuilt here. Status: the case is explained and dated, the key of the first cipher transcribed, the second read in fragments. No sender or recipient is yet named, and neither of the two long letters is yet read through.

t: A codebreaker’s file — the Italian intercepts of TNA SP 106/10
h: What the catalogue says, and what is actually there
b: The seven records are all headed TNA_SP106/10_UND_(…) — UND for undated — and all carry the same span, 1558 to 1625, which is simply the date range of the volume. The cataloguer had, however, already seen what the file was, and said so in a note on the first record: “This is clearly the worksheet of a codebreaker. This can be derived, not only from the fact that the lines of code are only partly decrypted, but also from the various code-sequences scribbled in the margin with identical codegroups in the middle. The handwriting seems to indicate that this document is probably late Tudor or early Stuart in origin, but except for Thomas Phelippes who worked for Walsingham, no other codebreakers from this period are known.” DECODE shelfmark stub pp. what it is R657 ff. 128–138 9 worksheets, two-figure system R660 ff. 139–140 2 intercept, 15 lines, solutions above the groups R664 ff. 167–169 3 intercept, ~500 groups in 45 numbered lines R704 ff. 186–187 2 intercept, 46 numbered lines, ~700 groups R720 ff. 188–189 2 worksheets R721 ff. 190–192 3 intercept, 26 lines, ~300 groups R722 ff. 193–195 3 intercept, like R704 and R721 R725 ff. 202–203, 205 3 the key: “Alphabet of Letters and Wordes” R725 is catalogued as a key , not a ciphertext, which is why it falls outside the seven and why the seven look unsolvable on their own. It sits eleven folios after the last of them in the same volume, in the same hand, and it is the answer to them.
