h: The key sheet, and the cipher in the codebreaker’s own words
b: DECODE R725 p. 3 (SP 106/10 f. 205), the fair summary: four headed columns — the letter alphabet, the letters that stand for whole words, the barred word-list, and the dotted word-list. Image: The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 f. 205, via DECODE R725 (p. 3). The third page of R725 is a fair copy in four headed columns. The first is “Alphabet of Single Letters” : A 10, 11 · B 31 · C 41 · D 25 · E 20, 90 · F 21 · G 51 · H 71 · I 30 · L 81 · M 91 · O 40 P 42 · Qu 72 · R 22 · S 94 · T 92 · V 50 · Z 93 · (X blank) The rougher draft on p. 1 of the same record gives D as 29, V as 90, and adds the line “X. Z. & serve to bee Nulles” ; p. 3 is the corrected state. R725 p. 1 (f. 202), the draft: “The Alphabett of Single Letters”, the run A–T with its figures, and the note that X, Z and & serve to be nulls. Image: The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 f. 202, via DECODE R725 (p. 1). The second column, “Alphabet of letters that are woordes” , is a second device of the same cipher: a written letter , not a figure, standing for a whole word. a = per · c = di · d = da · f = dal · g = il · h = in · n = ma · p = se q = et · r = con · t = non · v = chi · x = si · z = che The third column is headed Literarum resolutio , and under it the codebreaker writes the sentence that is the whole solution of the system: “It seemes there are numbers of woordes expressed by this difference of — over the figures whereof in this Cifar.” That is: a bar over a two-figure group makes it a word rather than a letter. The values he had recovered for the barred list are 11 tanto , 16 lettere , 18 relatione , 20 spedditione , 26 V. Signoria , 27 V. Paternità , 29 Sua Signoria , 30 uno , 37 Re d’Inghilterra (the draft writes Re di Britania ), 42 Padre , 52 liga . The fourth column is headed “An Alphabet of Characters thus marked 10′ 11′ etc. In these letters encountred” — a third reading of the same two figures, marked this time with a tick: The dotted series: 22 Il Principe, 23 Marques Inichiosa, 24 Imbassiatore di Venetia, 28 Imbassiatore, 32 Roma, 34 Palatinato, 80 perche, 82 in cio. Image: The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 f. 205, via DECODE R725 (p. 3). 22 Il Principe · 23 Marques Inichiosa · 24 Imbassiatore di Venetia · 28 Imbassiatore · 32 Roma · 34 Palatinato 49 Cattholico · 50 Stato · 57 Negocio or Occasione · 66 acciocche · 67 C. Barberino · 69 Governo 71 havere · 73 habuto · 77 mento · 80 perche · 82 in cio · 84 questo or questa · 85 quello or quella · 89 tutte · 90 Papa · 91 Nuncio So one two-figure group has three possible meanings, selected by a diacritic: bare, it is a letter; barred, a word of the first list; ticked, a word of the second. It is a compact and genuinely awkward system, and the codebreaker worked it out from the intercepts alone.

t: A codebreaker’s file — the Italian intercepts of TNA SP 106/10
h: The vocabulary dates the file to 1623–24
b: DECODE dates these records “1558–1625”, which is no date at all. The words the codebreaker recovered date them closely, because they are the words of one year: Marques Inichiosa — the Marqués de la Inojosa, Spain’s ambassador extraordinary in England from the spring of 1623 until he was recalled in the summer of 1624. C. Barberino — Francesco Barberini was made cardinal in October 1623, the nephew of the Pope elected that August. Il Principe and Re d’Inghilterra — Prince Charles and James I, with the Prince distinguished from his father, as he was in every despatch of the Spanish Match. Palatinato , liga , Papa , Nuncio , Imbassiatore di Venetia , Stato , Governo , Cattholico . That is the London of 1623–24: the Prince back from Madrid, the Spanish embassy under suspicion, the Palatinate unrecovered, the papal dispensation and the Venetian ambassador at the centre of the traffic. The intercepts are Italian letters passing through or out of that embassy world, and the file is the English government’s attack on them. That also puts the codebreaker outside the frame the DECODE note suggested: Phelippes died in 1625 and had long been out of favour; this is his successors’ work.

t: A codebreaker’s file — the Italian intercepts of TNA SP 106/10
h: The file holds three ciphers, not one
b: Going through all twenty-two ciphertext pages shows three distinct systems, which the catalogue does not separate: system records form A. two-figure nomenclator R657 worksheets; key R725 10 11 31 41 … , bare / barred / ticked B. three-figure syllabic code R660, R664; worksheets R720 533 359 515 … , inline with clear Italian C. letter-and-figure syllabary R704, R721, R722 Z6 n54 m56 g42 … b41 b33 One correction to the catalogue follows. DECODE files R720 as “worksheets of a codebreaker, possibly related to the intercepted letter in R704”. R704 is written in system C, with letter-and-figure groups; R720’s worksheet is covered in three-figure groups and trial Italian word-lists. R720 belongs with R660 and R664, not with R704.

t: A codebreaker’s file — the Italian intercepts of TNA SP 106/10
b: R660 and R664 are letters written half in clear and half in code — the writer enciphers what matters and leaves the Italian connective tissue open, which is exactly what let the English reader in, and what lets a reader in now. One whole line of R664 stands in the clear, and it is about the cipher itself: “potrete continuare nel modo cominciato, osservando però il [mutamento … alle volte … col … numeri suppositi]” The codebreaker wrote his solutions above the groups, syllable by syllable. Aligning those syllables against the figures gives the code back. About forty-five values were fixed this way, each anchored on a word that admits no other division: 111 al · 145 nume · 146 nu · 151 ra · 152 re · 153 tri · 154 ro · 165 che · 211 del · 240 et · 245 si 252 se · 253 si · 254 so · 260 ta · 261 te · 262 ti · 263 to · 316 ta · 319 cu · 320 in · 340 lettere 344 el · 356 i · 357 l · 359 n · 366 col · 411 que · 430 a · 433 la · 434 le · 436 lo · 456 o · 459 r 461 ve · 463 volte · 468 quello · 515 da · 516 de · 518 do · 535 mi · 536 mol · 537 mu · 542 quan · 544 gua · 560 za · 568 vostre R664 f. 1, line 38: 211 433 436 154 253 319 152 560 … with del·la·lo·ro·si·cu·re·za written above — “della loro sicurezza”. Image: The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 f. 167, via DECODE R664 (p. 1). Line 38 then deciphers straight off: 211 433 436 154 253 319 152 560 ·312· 359 518 ·367· 433 del la lo ro si cu re za ? n do ? la and lines 41–42, with a word running over the line break: 240 | hoggi terzo giorno | 468 434 516 146 456 461 252 359 → 560 et (in the clear) quel le de nu o ve se n za “et hoggi terzo giorno quelle de nuovo senza…”

t: A codebreaker’s file — the Italian intercepts of TNA SP 106/10
h: Method, and the check that the alignment is sound
b: The whole of this rests on reading the codebreaker’s interlinear syllables against the right groups, and a one-group drift would produce plausible nonsense. The alignment produced one apparent contradiction and then resolved it, which is the reason to trust the rest: group 252 read sen in one line and se in another, and 359 read za in one line and n in two others. Both resolve if the word senza runs over the end of line 41 — 252 se + 359 n closing the line, 560 za opening line 42 — which is what the manuscript shows. After that correction no value in the table above conflicts with any other across lines 34–45. The images came from DECODE with the project’s login; all of them are written across the page and had to be rotated before anything could be read. No solver was used and none was needed: this is a case where the archive did the cryptanalysis four hundred years ago and the work is to find the sheet on which it is written down.

t: A codebreaker’s file — the Italian intercepts of TNA SP 106/10
h: A fourth letter: the “Venetian cifar” dossier (R703 and six siblings)
b: Catalogue entry 66, DECODE R703 (ff. 184–185), turned out to belong to this file, and it is not a letter. Its second page is a positional index headed linea : every group from 200 to 399 with the lines where it stands ( 280. 2.6.9.20 ) and notes such as “201 is a finall sillable after an entire word”. Its first page, half upside down, carries glossed fragments ( l.2 280 367 464 432 , l.7 245 510 Almeno , l.14 297 506 395 e che quello , l.46 540 464 ) and grids of trial syllables. The fragments come from a three-figure letter of 46 numbered lines that the first two sessions took to be missing from the DECODE images; it is R722 (section 08b). It is not R664 or R660: in R660, 540 is Spagnoli , and the index does not list the lines where R664 uses 211. The same lost letter is worked on six more records that DECODE lists separately: R661, R667 (tally grids of every group 200–599), R684, R701, R702 (with an Italian–English word list copied from a dictionary) and R720. R701 names the system in the codebreaker’s hand: “Wordes marked wth letters in the Venetian Cifar” (369º nostro, 467º questo, 420 i altri, 233 r esser). System B is therefore the Venetian cipher , and a superscript letter on a group marks it as a whole word. His partial key for the letter is on R701 p. 3. It is a syllabary in which the last digit steps through the vowels: 209 va · 210 ve · 211 vi · 212 vo · 213 vu · 231–235 sa se si so su · 244 ra · 245 re 333–336 cha che chi cho · 366–370 la le li lo lu · 375–378 da de di do This key does not carry the fragments to a reading. It values four of the 28 groups quoted on R703, and the codebreaker’s own glosses contradict it (R702 glosses 244 as ta ). He had not broken this letter when the file stops. R703 is explained, not read. The intercept itself was found on 21 September 2026: it is R722 (below).

t: A codebreaker’s file — the Italian intercepts of TNA SP 106/10
h: The rest of the file: the codebreaker’s own table of “the Venetian Cifer”
b: DECODE lists seven further records from the same box as another set of anonymous ciphertexts (R658, R661, R663, R667, R684, R701, R702; catalogue item 62). None is an intercept. All are in the same hand as the rest of the file: count grids, syllable drills, Italian–English dictionary trawls, and one English political draft in clear (on cutting off “that supply of treasure that the K. of Sp. hath for the Indies”) reused as scrap paper. Two of them matter. R701 heads a list of word groups “Wordes marked with letters in the Venetian Cifer” : 369° nostro , 467° questo , 430 a passata . The same words stand in the side column of R658, and R658 is the codebreaker’s table of the three-figure code of R660 and R664: every group from 136 to 565, with a count of its occurrences below it and his value above it. R658 (SP 106/10 f. 125, turned the right way up), groups 251–565: sa sca stra sta over 251–551, se sce stre ste over 252–552; te ti to tu over 261–264, tre tri tro tru , ve vi vo , ze zi zo zu ; 165 che , 465 quel ; at the right 467 questo , 568 vostro , 440 Spagn… Image: The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 f. 125, via DECODE R658 (rotated here). The grid shows how the code was made. Each consonant takes five consecutive rows in the order a e i o u , and each hundreds column a different consonant: 151–155 ra…ru , 251–255 sa…su , 351–355 sca…scu , 551–555 sta…stu ; 260–264 ta…tu , 360–364 tra…tru , 460–463 va…vo , 560–564 za…zu ; 433–437 la…lu , 142–146 na…nu , 242–246 pa…pu , 442–446 pra…pru , 542–545 qua…quo ; the row x56 holds the bare vowels, x57–x59 single consonants (357 l , 359 n , 459 r ), and a handful of groups are whole words (339 liga , 340 lettere , 439 per , 165 che , 465 quel ), their ending given by a superscript letter. With the table, the code is rebuilt at 117 values, 102 of them written by the codebreaker and 15 predicted by the pattern. The check is R702, where he wrote out group strings with his own glosses. Every one of its 46 groups is in the table, and every string decodes to his gloss: 356 318 436 143 435 → i·co·lo·ne·li “i colonelli” · 341 433 436 154 → del·la·lo·ro 252 359 518 253 → se·n·do·si “sendosi” · 167 252 459 253 → con·se·r·si “conservarsi” 165 245 556 253 156 526 445 534 261 459 → che·po·s·si·a·mo·pro·me·te·r “che possiamo prometter” The same sheet glosses di 24 di maggio , del campo , per nome suo , sono capitate and efficacia : the letter he was working on was written in late May and spoke of a camp and of colonels. The table also corrects four values of section 05, which came from aligning glosses on R664 alone: 260 is ta , 262 ti , 263 to and 459 r (they had been read as mento , to , ti and v ), and 316 ta does not fit the ca…cu run it stands in. This is a different table from the one the codebreaker was building for the lost 46-line letter of section 07 (R701 p. 3: 244 ra , 245 re , 366–370 la…lu ; on R658 244 is pi , 245 po , 433–437 la…lu ), though it is built the same way. The words R701 lists under “the Venetian Cifer” are the words of R658’s side column, so on the sheets’ own evidence the name belongs to the code of R664 and R660; the lost letter is in a second table of the same kind, perhaps a later key of the same correspondence. R701 also carries a five-line text in a letter cipher ( Esg frp rohxog x rygo fa ombhpeip … ), which a substitution solver run against five languages did not break.

t: A codebreaker’s file — the Italian intercepts of TNA SP 106/10
h: The “lost” letter was imaged all along: R722, a Venetian secretary’s letter of 1625
b: Catalogue entry 58 grouped four more anonymous SP 106/10 records (R656, R662, R722, R931). R722 had been filed with the letter-plus-figure records of system C, following DECODE’s pointers, and nobody had looked at it. It is in fact the 46-line letter of section 07 : its first line ends 540 212 una di questi matine , the fragment R703 quotes as l.1 540 212 una che , and five more worksheet fragments stand in it verbatim ( 280 367 464 432 , 340 367 misciandosi , 245 510 Almeno , 297 506 395 … e che quello , 313 541 377 238 254 ). It has 48 numbered lines, half in clear Italian and half in three-figure groups, with the codebreaker’s trial syllables between the lines. The endorsement reads “Cypher of a Venetian Secretary to the Embassador of that nation in …” , with “1625” on the fold. The clear passages give its matter: Parmi che … , Io mi credo che questi siano … , Ho visto chiaramente che V. E. … , proposito che ella procurasse , di satisfattione con honor di … , il Spinola sotto Breda , di Bruselles si è inteso … , di Roma . Spinola besieged Breda from August 1624 until 5 June 1625, so the letter is of the first half of 1625, from a Venetian secretary to the Venetian ambassador in England. R722 is read in part : the clear text and the endorsement, not the code, which neither the codebreaker nor this project has broken yet. With the whole intercept in hand, every fragment on the worksheets can now be checked against its line. The other three records: R656 is the back of an English Exchequer draft (a sheriff’s answer naming Nosse, Rowley, Sherborne and Franke) used by the codebreaker for more line fragments of R722, e.g. l.12 313 541 377 238 254 . R662 is a torn strip of his English memorandum on how the code is built (“series of sillables beginning …”, “the vowels a.e.i. for every consonant”, “the most frequent … di”). R931 does not belong to the case: it is an English royalist letter of September 1645 in a numerical code of about 260 values (“(1) septembre 1645”, “earnestly”, “reasons” in clear). None of George Lasry’s 1645–46 SP 106 keys, the Goring key of the next record, or the Charles I–Culpeper key of 1645 fits it, and it stays open.

t: A codebreaker’s file — the Italian intercepts of TNA SP 106/10
h: What is uncertain, and what remains
b: The letter values of system A are C (from the codebreaker’s own fair copy, and internally consistent); the draft’s D 29 / V 90 against the fair copy’s D 25 / V 50 is the one place he corrected himself, and the fair copy is followed here. The system B values listed above are C where a whole word fixes them ( della loro sicurezza , senza , quelle de nuovo , che , et , volte , lettere , vostre ) and M for the single-syllable values seen only once (245, 316, 344, 356, 357, 459, 544). Groups seen but not valued on R664 f. 1: 233, 312, 367, 439, 477, 534, 551, 556, 560 in its second sense, 566. Several dozen more stand on ff. 2–3. The dating is C : it rests on Marques Inichiosa together with C. Barberino , and no single one of the names would carry it alone. The Venetian-code table (section 08) is H for the 102 values the codebreaker wrote and M for the 15 predicted from the pattern; 440 Spagn… and the value of 556 ( s in R702, unclear on the grid) are M . Which of the two three-figure tables R701’s heading names is C . Open from catalogue 62: the short letter cipher on R701 and the English draft on R661 (not identified). Not done: the gloss-alignment pass over R664 ff. 2–3, R660 and the R720 worksheets, which should carry system B to a full reading of both letters; the same treatment of system C on R704 and R721; the second three-figure code of R722, now that the intercept is found; R931 (1645), for want of a key; R657’s nine pages against the R725 key; and the identification of the correspondents and of the codebreaker.

t: The Stosch–Walton cipher instructions — not a letter but how to use the code
b: TNA SP 106/7 f. 33 (DECODE R597), catalogued as a partly decrypted French nomenclator letter with lines unsolved. It is an English instruction sheet for the cipher used with Baron Stosch, the British spy on the Stuart court who wrote as John Walton: three-digit syllable groups in two keys, 371 to change key, no separators, nulls 110, 220 and all above 900. The worked example carries its syllables and reads in full; the “unsolved” lines are the same example run together. Secretary of State's office → a correspondent of Stosch · syllabic code, two keys · c. 1731 · read (instruction sheet) “To puzzle it more”: the instructions for the Stosch–Walton cipher TNA State Papers 106/7, f. 33 (DECODE R597). DECODE lists it as a partly decrypted French letter in a nomenclator of letter pairs, with some lines unsolved. It is not a letter. It is an English sheet of instructions sent with a cipher that “serves only to correspond with Baron Stosch and Mr Walton”, and every group of its worked example has its syllable written above it. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 resolved Summary. The rule-scored catalogue took R597 for a ciphered letter from an unknown sender to an unknown recipient. The two DECODE images show an instruction sheet in English, one folio and its facing page, covering a cipher to be used with “Baron Stosch and Mr Walton who reside at Rome”, where “Rome” is corrected to Florence. Philipp von Stosch spied on the Stuart court for the British government from 1722 and signed his reports “John Walton”. He moved to Florence in 1731, so the sheet dates from about then. The system is a syllabic code of three-digit groups from 100 to 999 in two keys, A in black ink and B in red, used alternately. Group 371 means “changement de clef”. The groups are written without separation. The nulls are 110, 220 and so on, plus every group above 900. The worked example is Les Adherens du Pretendant se donnent beaucoup de mouvement à Rome , written first in key A and then again with a switch to key B after “donnent”. The writer put the syllable over every group. The “unsolved lines” DECODE mentions are that same key B example written as one unbroken string, to show what a real letter looks like. The whole sheet reads. Three figures are doubtful, and keys A and B themselves are not on the record.

t: The Stosch–Walton cipher instructions — not a letter but how to use the code
b: DECODE R597 (“TNA_SP106/7_Anne_(0091-0092)”) has two images. Its date, 1702–1837, is the span of the volume. Its metadata give cleartext English and plaintext French, cipher type nomenclator, symbols numerical, status “Partially decrypted”. The record note reads: “Part of letter with instructions for operating the Cipher with Baron Stosch and Mr. Walton … there are also lines unsolved. The nomenclature in question could not yet be identified.” Image 2 is f. 33 and holds the start of the text. Image 1 is the bifolium opened out, with the rest of the text on the left leaf (upside down in the scan) and the paragraph on nulls on the right. SP 106/7 f. 33: the worked example in key A, with the syllables over the groups and the sentence in clear beneath. Image: The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/7 f. 33, via DECODE R597.

t: The Stosch–Walton cipher instructions — not a letter but how to use the code
b: Transcribed from the images. The interlinear syllables are the writer's own. [?] marks a doubtful figure. In the inclosed Cypher (which serves only to correspond with Baron Stosch and Mr Walton who reside at Rome Florence) is to be perceived one in Numbers consisting of 3 Figures each as follows, Le s ad her en s du Pre te nd 316|509|139|134|435|509|702|593|506|408| an t se don ne nt be au co up de 440|204|236|503|508|306|446|447|342|702?|439| mo uv em en tà Ro me 612|501|535|435|106|392|413|—— Les Adherens du Pretendant se donnent beaucoup de mouvement à Rome. Or to puzzle it more after having made use of the Key A. in black Ink, as far as [Donnent] inclusive, which answers 371. which denotes [Changement de Clef] that the Key alters, and then put the Remainder of this Sentence into the Cypher B. the Numbers in red Ink and it will stand thus. — be au co up de mo uv em 371|436|433|342|218|446|678|417|553| en tà Ro me 453|023?|620|477| The chief art of this Cypher consists in the Numbers running on without distinction till a distribution of them is made as above, by three in a parcel, by the person who deciphers, and that you make use of two Keys alternately at pleasure. [When you write you put no Stops, as in our Ordinary Cypher, but write thus, 371436433342218446670 4175534530236208477.] You have several Nulls to intermix as 110. 220. &c and all above 900 are so. You make use of no Numbers under 100 or above 999. The example sentence means “The Pretender's adherents are very busy in Rome”. That is the kind of news Stosch sent home about the court of James Francis Edward Stuart.

t: The Stosch–Walton cipher instructions — not a letter but how to use the code
b: Code. Three-digit groups stand for syllables and letter pairs (le, s, ad, her, en, du, pre, te, nd …). DECODE's “letter pairs rather than words” is right. A repeated syllable keeps its group within one key (s = 509 twice, en = 435 twice in key A). Two keys. Key A and key B give different groups for the same syllable (be 446 / 436, au 447 / 433, mo 612 / 678). The writer switches at will, and 371 announces the switch. No separators. The groups run on and the decipherer cuts them into threes. This is the point where the sheet contrasts the method with “our Ordinary Cypher”, which used stops. Nulls. The round hundreds-and-tens groups 110, 220 and so on, and every group from 901 to 999.

t: The Stosch–Walton cipher instructions — not a letter but how to use the code
b: In key A, 702 appears for both “du” and “up”. One of the two is probably a slip by the writer or a misreading (grade C). In key B, the group for “tà” reads 023, which falls below the stated range of 100–999 (C). The run-on demonstration does not match the separated groups digit for digit (…446670… against 446|678, and …6208477 against 620|477). The writer copied it loosely (C). Only the 30 groups of the example are known. Keys A and B are not on the record. Whether one of the 16 SP 106 key records on DECODE is one of them has not been checked. The writer and the recipient are not named. The date c. 1731 is inferred from the Florence correction.

t: The SP 106/10 pigpen letter — a French letter in a homophonic “masonic” cipher
b: TNA SP 106/10 ff. 241–243, catalogued in DECODE as an undeciphered letter in the masonic alphabet. The textbook dotted-pigpen key pencilled on its flap reads nothing. The cipher is homophonic: cell shape plus dot count, several signs for common letters. A hand transcription of the last page let a quadgram solver find French, and the last page now reads almost in full: a client condoling to a patron over a gentleman’s marriage and begging the continuance of his goodwill. The first page is read in fragments; writer and recipient are unnamed. Unknown writer → “Monsieur” · homophonic pigpen, French · undated (17th century) · read in part The SP 106/10 pigpen letter: a French letter in a homophonic “masonic” cipher The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 ff. 241–243 (DECODE R927), described as an “undeciphered letter in the masonic alphabet, say 800 codegroups”. It had no key, sender, recipient or date. It was transcribed by hand and solved without a crib. Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 19 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read in part Summary. The letter is written in tic-tac-toe (pigpen) cell shapes, each followed by one to three dots. A later hand pencilled the textbook dotted-pigpen key on a flap ( akt · blu · cmw / dnx · eoy · fpz / gq · hr · is ). That key reads nothing, in any orientation or dot order. The cipher is actually homophonic : the sign is the cell shape plus its dot count (sometimes with an inner stroke), and common letters have several signs. An automatic transcription with about 25% errors defeated every solver. A full hand transcription of the last page (450 signs) led the solver to French, and fixed words (“monsieur”, “de vostre”, “croire que je vous honnore”) completed the key. The last page reads almost in full. It is the end of a letter from a client to a patron, condoling on or reacting to “the marriage of this gentleman”, and it closes et vous supplie tres humblement, monsieur, me continuer l’honneur de vostre bienveuillance . The first page is read only in fragments. Writer, recipient and date are still unknown. The foot of f. 243 turned to the writer's orientation. The last lines read … et vous supplie tres humblement, monsieur, me continuer l’honneur de vostre bienveuillance et croire que je vous honnor[e] . Image: The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 f. 243, via DECODE R927 (rotated here).

t: The SP 106/10 pigpen letter — a French letter in a homophonic “masonic” cipher
h: The document and the false key
b: There are three images: f. 241 (the first page), and f. 243 photographed twice, once with a paper flap folded over it and once with the flap lifted. The archive photographed the text sideways. Turned 90° anticlockwise, it runs in horizontal lines with word spaces. The flap carries a pencil grid, the standard dotted pigpen (a–i one dot, k–s two, t–z three). Applied to the letter it gives oeaeydakdorsefekdoi… , with g/q at 16% of the text and t almost absent. None of the 48 rotations, reflections and dot orders, and none of the 9! reassignments of shapes to cells, gives any language.

t: The SP 106/10 pigpen letter — a French letter in a homophonic “masonic” cipher
b: Each sign is one of the nine cell shapes, followed by one, two or (rarely) three dots, and sometimes with an inner stroke. The shape does not fix a group of letters: e is ◻·, ◻ with an inner mark, and one or two rarer forms; s has five or six signs; i three. Working key (shape named by its open side; the digit is the dot count): a ⊔1 b ⊓1 c ⊏1, ⊏ with bar 1 d Γ1 e ◻1 (+ inner-mark forms) f/q L1 g ⊔2 h ⊏-bar 2 i ◻2 (+ variants) l ⊏2, ⊏3 m ¬1 n ⌟1 o ⊐1 p ◻3 q L2 r Γ2, Γ3 s ⊓2 (+ variants) t ⊐2, ⊔2 u/v ⌟2 y ¬2 L1 serves for both f ( affection , effets ) and q ( que ). It is either a true polyphone or a variant not separated in transcription. Two circle or “9”-shaped signs and a few stacked composites are unresolved. They stand where names or abbreviations are expected.

J’escris a [&] ce que ce gentilhomme alloit faire par dela, et vous supplie tres humblement, monsieur, me continuer l’honneur de vostre bienveuillance et croire que je vous honnor[e] … Translation: “… I could not have received a keener sorrow than on learning that, from the marriage of this gentleman, … to the prejudice of the entire affection I have vowed to your service … I say nothing until occasions arise to show you its effects. I am writing to [&] about what this gentleman was going to do over there, and I beg you most humbly, sir, to continue me the honour of your goodwill, and to believe that I honour you …”

t: The SP 106/10 pigpen letter — a French letter in a homophonic “masonic” cipher
b: The glyph boxes and dots were segmented automatically, then corrected by eye from enlarged crops. The solver is simulated annealing over a homophonic key, scored by French, English, Latin and nine other quadgram models, with a letter-frequency penalty. It was tested first on synthetic homophonic text, with and without 10% noise. On the automatic transcription every language failed (best −4.5/char, unreadable). On the hand transcription French stood alone (−4.39), and the solver surfaced que dun , de la part de , plus . The key was then fixed from whole words and solved again.

t: Van Spaen to Van der Goes, 14–15 January 1808 — transcribed, no key survives online
b: DECODE R1941 holds a letter and its annex in a plain numerical code reaching at least 1339: 303 groups, 222 distinct. The archive inventory places it with the commissioners for the districts ceded around Zevenaar, writing from Düsseldorf in the Grand Duchy of Berg. No key is on DECODE, Croiset’s 1803 book does not fit, and Colenbrander does not print it. Düsseldorf → The Hague · numerical code · 14–15 January 1808 · attempted, not solved Van Spaen to Van der Goes, 14 and 15 January 1808 to Maarten van der Goes Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 2.01.08 Ministerie van Buitenlandse Zaken 1796–1810, inv. nr. 281, DECODE R1941: a letter of two pages and a one-page annex, both in figures between clear Dutch openings and closings. Both items were transcribed from the DECODE images and the archive inventory was checked for who sent them. Every key reachable online was tested and none fits. The code has to come from the archive. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 key not found Summary. DECODE catalogues R1941 as a letter from G. C. van Spaen tot Voorstonden, “ambassador at the Court of Westphalia”, to Maarten van der Goes, partly decrypted: its note says the small annex of 15 January was solved but the letter was not. The four images hold two items. One is the letter of 14 January (228 groups). The other is the annex of 15 January (75 groups), photographed twice. No decipherment is written on either, and no reading is attached to the record. The code is a plain run of numbers from 15 to 1339 with no series marks, so it is not one of Croiset’s marked books. The Nationaal Archief inventory describes inv. 281 as the letters of J.F.G. van Spaen and G. van Riemsdijk, commissioners for taking over the districts ceded around Zevenaar (1806–09). Düsseldorf was the capital of the Grand Duchy of Berg, the other party to that exchange. DECODE holds no key for this code, and Croiset’s 1803 codebook (R1035) gives word salad. Colenbrander’s Gedenkstukken V does not print the letters. With 222 distinct groups out of 303, most groups occur once, and the letter cannot be read without the codebook. Status: not solved. What would open it is the DECODE owner’s reading of the annex, which would give about 70 values, or the 1806–09 code of the ceded-districts commission in the Nationaal Archief.

t: Van Spaen to Van der Goes, 14–15 January 1808 — transcribed, no key survives online
b: R1941, the letter of 14 January 1808 (DECODE image P3, from a photocopy): the docket, the clear salutation and the first five rows of figures. Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 2.01.08 Buitenlandse Zaken 1796–1810 inv. 281, image P3 (from a photocopy), via DECODE R1941. The letter is docketed “Exh 14 january 1808” and opens in clear, “Hoog Edel Gestrenge Heer,”. Nineteen rows of figures follow. It closes in clear, “Ik heb de eer met de volmaakste hoogachting te verblijven, … Uwer Excellentie’s ootmoedige gehoorzame Dienaar”, with a signature read as “G. C. van Spaen”. The annex is headed “Dusseldorf den 15 January 1808” and filed as “136. Exh 18 january 1808”. It has seven rows of figures and the same closing. DECODE’s images P1 and P2 are two photographs of this one annex page. The archive inventory changes the attribution. In NA 2.01.08, inv. 281 is “Missiven van J.F.G. van Spaen en G. van Riemsdijk, commissarissen voor de overname der gecedeerde districten, de Lijmers, Huyssen, Malburgen en Zevenaar, jul 1806 – mei 1809”. G. C. van Spaen’s own letters as envoy in Berlin are inv. 244–248. The Düsseldorf letters therefore come from the Dutch commission for the territorial exchange with the Grand Duchy of Berg. Their subject is very probably that handover. A J.F.G. reading of the signature is not ruled out from the photocopy.

t: Van Spaen to Van der Goes, 14–15 January 1808 — transcribed, no key survives online
b: Each group is a number of one to four digits, separated by dots. A few groups are followed by a dash, which may mark a word boundary, and a few carry a small superscript letter ( 729 t , 793 s ), probably a clear ending as in other Dutch codes of the period. groups distinct letter, 14 Jan 228 181 annex, 15 Jan 75 69 both 303 222 Values run from 15 to 1339. The most frequent groups are 493 (six times), 297 (five), and 441, 424, 269 and 709 (four each). The sequence 602 441 373 occurs twice in the letter and once in the annex, and is probably a recurring name or title. Twenty-eight groups are shared between the two items. The transcription is spaen1808/transcription.txt . In this hand 3 and 5 are hard to tell apart.

t: The Sperantio file: King John of Hungary and an agent at Buda write to the dukes of Bavaria
b: Two ciphertexts catalogued on DECODE as Cornelio Sperantio’s letters are letters to the dukes of Bavaria sent under cover to him. King John Zápolya’s Latin letter of 6 February 1534, on the Hungarian gold and silver mines, reads 96% from its own interlinear decipherment; the same key reads a German newsletter from Buda of 8 February on Werbőczy’s everlasting peace with the Turk to 95%. The key is the one rebuilt here for R9415, so the file and R9415 are one correspondence. Buda → Munich · homophonic sign cipher · February 1534 · read in part The Sperantio file: King John of Hungary and an agent at Buda write to the dukes of Bavaria from John Zápolya → to Wilhelm IV, Duke of Bavaria Bayerisches Hauptstaatsarchiv, Kurbayern Äußeres Archiv 4591, ff. 248 and 250–251 (DECODE R9411, R9412; catalogue 163). DECODE lists both as letters of Cornelio Sperantio to an unknown recipient. They are letters to the dukes of Bavaria, sent under cover to Sperantio. The Latin letter carries a contemporary decipherment between the lines; the key was rebuilt from it and read the German letter too. It is the key rebuilt earlier for R9415 in the same volume. DECODE lists both as letters of Cornelio Sperantio to an unknown recipient. They are letters to the dukes of Bavaria, sent under cover to Sperantio. The Latin letter carries a contemporary decipherment between the lines; the key was rebuilt from it and read the German letter too. It is the key rebuilt earlier for R9415 in the same volume. Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 22 September 2026 read in part Summary. The catalogue entry was two DECODE records, “Cornelio Sperantio to …”, partially decrypted, 5 pages, in a volume of Bavarian cipher keys. The cover on f. 251v reads “Cornelio Sperantio etc. domino observandissimo”: Sperantio, the dukes’ man at Buda, received the packet. R9411 is a Latin letter of King John Zápolya to the dukes of Bavaria, Buda, 6 February 1534, about the Hungarian gold and silver mines and his servant Nicolaus Freiberger. It has an interlinear decipherment of the time over every line; the key was fixed from it by constrained annealing and the letter reads to 96% of its words. The same key, refitted for German, reads R9412, a newsletter from Buda of 8 February 1534 on Stephan Werbőczy’s embassy to the Porte and the everlasting peace with the Turk, to 95% of its words (89% counting only what the cipher yields, without the editorial supplies). The key agrees sign for sign with the one rebuilt in this project for R9415, King John’s side to the dukes in April 1533, so the Sperantio file and R9415 are one correspondence. Two sessions worked the target independently on the same day and are merged here. What stays open is illegible: blotted signs and five names in R9412, thirteen short gaps in R9411.

b: Record Folios Date Language What it is State R9411 248r–v Buda, 6 Feb 1534 Latin King John (Zápolya) of Hungary to the dukes of Bavaria; interlinear decipherment of the time read, 96% of words R9412 250r–251r, cover 251v Ofen (Buda), 8 Feb [1534] German, Latin passages in clear an agent at Buda to a duke of Bavaria, under cover to Cornelio Sperantio read in part, 95.0% (89% without supplies) The cipher is a homophonic substitution on the graphic sign set of the volume (↓ ω π 4 8 ÿ …), written without word division, with clear Latin passages left standing in the cipher (“Ceterum”, “Misimus nunc”, “Et primo” … “Quarto”). t: The Sperantio file: King John of Hungary and an agent at Buda write to the dukes of Bavaria
h: R9411: King John to the dukes, Buda, 6 February 1534
b: From the reading ( sperantio1534/r9411/reading_r9411.txt ), in the original Latin, with gaps as […]: Salutem et omne bonum. Illustrissimi principes domini ac fratres carissimi. Accepimus literas Vestre et ea quae […] etiam intelleximus quae […] secretarium suum scripserunt. Vestre ita sibi persuadere velint, quidquid nos in rem commodum et dignitatem earum et fratrum atque amicorum suorum id facere possumus, id semper libentissimo animo facturi sumus. […] videtur tamen esse res communicanda cum illustri domino regni nostri gubernatore, qui propediem hic apud nos futurus est. Videtur enim nobis esse satius de hac re capere consilium ipsius quam si ex abrupto apud potentissimum Turcarum imperatorem rem tentaremus. … Ceterum Vestre medio magnifici […] capitanei et consiliarii nostri … ex parte minerarum auri, argenti et aliorum metallorum, quae res nobis vehementissime fuit cordi, … cum Dei auxilio rem aggredi. … Misimus nunc hunc servitorem nostrum Nicolaum Freeberger ad Vestras … Bude sexta Februarii, anno etc. xxxiiii. In English: King John will do whatever he can for the dukes, whom he addresses as brothers. Their request must first go to the governor of his realm (Lodovico Gritti), who is expected shortly: better to take his counsel than to try the matter abruptly with the Turkish emperor. The news his adversaries spread is false. Through his captain and councillor he has begun on the gold, silver and other mines, a matter very close to his heart. He sends his servant Nicolaus Freiberger to the dukes, invites them to take on the working of such mines, and asks for masters skilled in them. A postscript asks for the Bavarian mining ordinance (“ordinacionem rerum montanarum”) by a sure messenger.

t: The Sperantio file: King John of Hungary and an agent at Buda write to the dukes of Bavaria
h: R9412: a newsletter from Buda, 8 February 1534
b: German, no gloss. It opens by repeating what the writer sent on 22 December by an unsure messenger. That date, in line 1, belongs to the earlier letter; this one is dated at its foot, “Datum Ofen, des achten Februarii”. From the reading ( sperantio1534/r9411/reading_r9412.txt ; […] unread, braces supplied from sense, capitals in clear on the page): wie erstlich, was der canczler herr Stephan Werbeczi bei dem Turcken hab ausgericht. ET PRIMO: so hat er dem Ungerland mit dem Turcken einen ewigen frid gemacht und angestossen. SECUNDO: das alle stett und flecken … als nemlich Peterwardein und […], mit Titil, Salmaulack {Salankamen} … TERTIO: … die zwitrachten, als von wegen des titels der kunig … QUARTO: … SED TAMEN PER MAXIMOS SUOS CONATUS NIHIL ALIUD IMPETRARE POTUIT QUAM ILLUD QUOD … The chancellor Stephan Werbőczy has obtained at the Porte an everlasting peace between Hungary and the Turk. The Danube places are named: Peterwardein (Petrovaradin), Titel, Salankamen. The dispute over the kings’ titles and the frontier towns is to be settled, and the writer has sent a copy of the Sultan’s letter. Then come plans against Transylvania and the mines. Fridrich Schmalcz has made himself head of the mining business and sends men skilled in mining to Pest; his factor at Nuremberg is named, and “herr Caesar” at Vienna. A bishop sends the duke his greetings in clear Latin. The b/w and d/t pairs share signs, so “beczi” is Werbeczi.

t: The Sperantio file: King John of Hungary and an agent at Buda write to the dukes of Bavaria
b: Both letters transcribed sign by sign from full-resolution line crops of the DECODE images (R9411 2,040 signs, R9412 2,725), in four passes on R9411 and three on R9412. R9411: a homophonic annealer on the la model, seeded with values from the interlinear gloss and fixed to it ( r9411/solve.py , run7.txt ); read by hand against the gloss. R9412: the R9411 key refitted on the de-1500s model, with pair and digraph signs set from context. After that, an interpretive pass (84% → 89%) and a gap audit (89% → 95.0%). Rejected, because each raised its own score while making the German worse: two automated look-alike repairs ( confuse.py ) and two key optimisers driven by a lexicon measure ( lexopt.py , lexopt2.py ). Control: a second, independent transcription of all five pages (4,745 signs) with the R9415 key and a Viterbi word fit ( fit.py ) gives R9411 at 91% without the gloss.

t: Thomas Spinelly to Henry VIII, Brussels, 1 February 1517
b: BL Cotton MS Galba B V ff. 40–41 (DECODE R8416), catalogued as a letter of Spinelly to an unknown recipient, London 1516, not decrypted. It is Spinelly’s clear despatch to the King from the court of Charles at Brussels, with five lines in a substitution of invented signs and no decipherment. A crib from the clear text (“audensier”) gives the alphabet: the Audiencier and Luigi Marliano expect the King’s entry into Brussels, and the Emperor at Cambrai about the 15th. Letters and Papers had only summarised the Cambrai clause. Brussels → Henry VIII · substitution of invented signs · 1 February 1517 · read Thomas Spinelly to Henry VIII, Brussels, 1 February 1517 to Henry VIII British Library, Cotton MS Galba B V ff. 40–41 (DECODE R8416, “Thommas Spynelly to unknown recipient”, 1516, non-decrypted). A clear English despatch with five lines in cipher. The cipher is a simple substitution with a few word signs; the passage is read in full. Daniel Bourdeau · solved 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 solved Summary. The Unsolved Catalogue (item 100) listed this DECODE record as a ciphered letter of “Thommas Spynelly” to an unknown recipient, London, February 1516, not decrypted. The four images show Spinelly’s own despatch to Henry VIII (“Please it your hyghnes”), written at Brussels on 1 February “M.D.XVJ”, old style, so 1517. It reports the Emperor Maximilian and King Charles at Lier and Mechelen, the French embassy at Vilvoorde and the handing over of Verona to Lautrec. All of it is in clear except five lines on f. 40v. There is no contemporary decipherment. The cipher is a substitution of invented signs with word division kept. A repeated nine-sign word fits “audensier”, spelled that way in clear on the same page, and gives the rest of the alphabet. Deciphered, the passage says that the Audiencier and Luigi Marliano expect the King’s entry into Brussels at the end of the week, and the Emperor at Cambrai about the 15th. Letters and Papers II no. 2862 (1864) already summarised the Cambrai clause. It gave no text of the passage and does not mention Marliano or the entry. Two word signs are read from context: the star is the Emperor, and one sign is probably the King. f. 40v: the cipher passage, after the clear words “and of this opinion is the”. t: Thomas Spinelly to Henry VIII, Brussels, 1 February 1517
b: DECODE imaged four pages. In the order of the leaves they are P1 f. 40r, P3 f. 40v, P4 f. 41r and P2 f. 41v, which carries the end of the letter and the subscription “your most humble and … seruant Thommas Spynelly”. The dating clause reads “Written at Methlyn Bruxells the fyrst day of february M.D.XVJ”. The old foliation 33–34 is the one used by Letters and Papers . So DECODE’s place (London) and recipient (unknown) are wrong: the letter was written in Brussels to the King. The year is 1517. Spinelly was Henry’s resident agent in the Low Countries. The despatch reports the meetings of Maximilian and Charles with Chièvres, the Chancellor, the Audiencier and Hans Renner, the French embassy, and the cession of Verona to Lautrec under the treaty of Brussels. It also covers Cardinal Schiner’s anger at that cession and the Emperor’s intention to keep his amity with England.

Word division is kept, and a few signs stand for whole words. plain sign plain sign plain sign a φ i, y e r c b τ k λ s ʃ c 4 l triangle v; σ (?) t k d ʒ m y u (w = δδ) δ e o n b p q h ρ o 7 Word signs: ϑ = of ; ꝁ = this ; w with a bar = that ; a star with a superscript = the Emperor ; and a small sign after “the” at the end of line 2, probably the King .

t: Thomas Spinelly to Henry VIII, Brussels, 1 February 1517
b: The clear text runs into the cipher mid-sentence (“and of this opinion is the”): Audensier and misser Loys de Merlien. The whiche Audensier saythe that the [King] in the laterende of this wicke shall make his entree in to this town, and [the Emperor] about the xv day of the present monethe so to Cambray. The Audiencier is the head of Charles’s chancery secretariat, named only by office throughout the letter (probably Philippe Haneton). “Misser Loys de Merlien” is Luigi Marliano, Charles’s physician and councillor, later bishop of Tuy. The clear postscript on f. 41v, written after the King came back from Vilvoorde and the Emperor went back to Mechelen, says that the coming of “his magestye” into this town is put off because he “loke[th] for certeyn princes oute of Almayne, the which he wol have at his entree”. “His majesty” there may be the Emperor, which leaves open whose entry the cipher means (see section 05). The Emperor did go to Cambrai, where the treaty with France was signed on 11 March 1517.

t: Stafford to Walsingham, Paris 1586 — Read
b: DECODE R8503, catalogued as a cipher letter of Sir Edward Stafford to an unknown recipient, is his holograph despatch from Paris to Sir Francis Walsingham of 19 September 1586 (BL Harley MS 1582 ff. 74–75). Its four short cipher runs were deciphered between the lines at the time. Re-read sign by sign here, they check exactly: a null 6 , homophones for i , l and e , and codes 47, 59 and 74 for Navarre, Condé and Guise. Paris → Sir Francis Walsingham · sign cipher with name codes, English · 19 September 1586 · read (deciphered at the time; key values rebuilt) Stafford to Walsingham, Paris, 19 September 1586 British Library, Harley MS 1582 ff. 74–75 (DECODE R8503). DECODE lists it as a letter of Sir Edward Stafford to an unknown recipient, partially decrypted. It is his holograph despatch to Walsingham in clear English, with four short cipher runs on f. 74v. Each run was deciphered between the lines when the letter arrived. We re-read every sign of the runs and rebuilt the letter values of the key from them. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 resolved Summary. DECODE catalogues R8503 as a two-page cipher letter from Sir Edward Stafford to an unknown recipient, dated London, 19 September 1586. The four images show something else: a holograph despatch in clear English, dated “Paris this 19th of September 1586”, signed by Stafford and addressed on f. 75v to Sir Francis Walsingham, Principal Secretary. Only four short runs on f. 74v are in cipher, 28 signs in all. A contemporary hand has written the decipherment above each run: “villequier”, “K. Navar”, “Kyll him and ye P. of Condé”, “D. Guise”. Read together, they give a warning that men of the Duke of Guise’s guard had sworn to kill the King of Navarre and the Prince of Condé. We checked the glosses sign by sign. Run 1 spells villequier across a line break once the null 6 is dropped, and run 3 spells kyll with the same letter signs, so the glosses are exact. 47, 59 and 74 are name codes. The letter is not in the Calendar of State Papers, Foreign , because Harley manuscripts fall outside the State Papers. Nothing stays open.

t: Stafford to Walsingham, Paris 1586 — Read
b: DECODE R8503 has four images: f. 74r, f. 74v, f. 75r (blank) and f. 75v (address leaf). The address, written upside down, reads “To the right honorable Sir Francis Walsingham knight, her Majesty’s principal secretary”, and the endorsement reads “19 Sept. 1586. From S r Edw: Stafford”. So DECODE’s “unknown recipient” is Walsingham. Its “London” is where the manuscript is kept: the letter was written in Paris, where Stafford was ambassador. The despatch is Stafford’s news of the court, a month after the Babington plot was uncovered. F. 74r covers the stir in England over a false report, the King of France and the Queen of Scots, Mendoza, and “that vile traitor Charles Paget”, who went to the Capuchins to speak with the King. F. 74v covers the copy of a letter about Épernon, a plot against Navarre, and the Queen Mother’s new powers to treat with the King of Navarre on the point of religion.

t: Stafford to Walsingham, Paris 1586 — Read
b: Stafford mixed an alphabet of letter forms and graphic signs with two-digit codes for persons. The glosses give these values: Letters, with homophones: v = D; i/y = x, ⊕; l = ◇, h; e = Δ, ꟷ; q = Ɗ; u = X; r = ʃ; k = M. Null: 6 . Dropping its four occurrences from run 1 leaves exactly v-i-l-l-e-q-u-i-e-r , with the line break after the second ◇. It then follows kyll in run 3, where it also reads as nothing. ⊗ closes run 1, as a final s (“Villequier’s”) or a stop. · is a separator. ω ʒ ϖ = “and”. It could be three letters or one word sign; we did not split it. Codes: 47 = the King of Navarre, 59 = the Prince of Condé, 74 = the Duke of Guise. Run 3 confirms the values from run 1 independently: the same x and ◇ stand for the y and l of kyll , and 47 recurs there as “him”, meaning Navarre. No key sheet for Stafford’s cipher with Walsingham has been found. S. Tomokiyo’s survey of Elizabethan ciphers ( Cryptiana ) notes only that Stafford used different ciphers with Walsingham and with Burghley, and that he sent Walsingham names to add to his.

There is a sixth, R7771, in the same run. They are letters to the Lord Treasurer, Burghley, among the papers of Thomas Edmondes, Elizabeth’s agent with Henri IV. The writer reports what the King told him in person, and dates from Tours, Blois and the camp before Laon. In each letter a few lines are written in invented signs inside the clear English. The signs are a simple substitution of English, keeping word divisions, with a few homophones and single signs for persons. The key was broken from the words the , of and to , and the same key serves all six letters, in two hands. Every passage reads except four lines on f. 59. Among them: the King breaking off his sister’s marriage to [Soissons?], Montmorency’s demand for custody of the young Prince of Condé, a would-be purchaser told “that his faith is not vendible”, and [Guise?]’s designs on Champagne and Reims in 1594. Butler’s Edmondes Papers (1913) has not been checked and may print some of these letters. t: Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire, 1916–17 — the intercepts the Foreign Ministry could not read
b: The Ministry of Communications copied every telegram to or from Sun Yat-sen’s people for the Japanese Foreign Ministry, which filed them unread. Fifty-six condenser telegrams of March–May 1916 read under five more keys of the Swatow telegram’s family, each accepted only when it read telegrams it was not fitted to, with rhyme-day dates as an independent check. They cover the monarchy cancelled, money wired via Taiwan, the price of a Wuhan rising, Chen Qimei’s murder, and the Foreign Ministry’s own advice relayed back to Sun. Also a Hankow +111 telegram and Sun ↔ Dai Jitao, March 1917. Shanghai ↔ Tokyo · telegraph code + code condensers · March 1916 – March 1917 · read Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire, 1916–17 to Sun Yat-sen The copies the Ministry of Communications made for the Japanese Foreign Ministry of every telegram to or from Sun’s people · JACAR, Gaimushō 1.6.1.4-2-1-2, 特定人ノ発受郵便物取調, vols 2–4 · no decodes in the files Fifty-six condenser telegrams of March–May 1916 read in whole or in part under five further keys of the Swatow telegram’s family and two tentative ones; a Hankow digit telegram; and Sun ↔ Dai Jitao, March 1917, in another key of the family Daniel Bourdeau · solved 18 September 2026 · updated 21 September 2026 solved Summary. The Swatow telegram of 3 April 1916 ( read here earlier ) turned out to be one sheet from a much larger intercept. Through 1916 and 1917 the Communications Bureau of the Japanese Ministry of Communications sent the Foreign Ministry a copy of every telegram and letter to or from Sun Yat-sen’s circle. The Foreign Ministry filed them and could not read the ciphered ones: there are no decodes in the files, and the analysts’ kana worksheets on one stream break off with pencilled guesses. Almost every condenser telegram of March–May 1916 in the files decodes under a key of the same systematic family as the Swatow telegram, with one key for each pair of correspondents. A key was accepted only when it stood at z ≥ 6 on one long telegram and then read others that played no part in finding it. Rhyme-day date codes in the signatures agree with the dates on the forms. Read in date order, the telegrams follow Sun’s party through the end of Yuan Shikai’s monarchy: 帝制取消 on 25 March, money raised in Manila and wired by way of Taiwan, a Shanghai rising that needs two weeks more, the price of a rising at Wuhan, and then, on 19 May, 英士昨下午在山田家被兇[轟?]斃 (“Yingshi was shot dead by assassins yesterday afternoon in the Yamada house”). A week later Tokyo tells Sun that Huang Xing reports the Foreign Ministry’s view that he should put off going to Qingdao. The Foreign Ministry was sent a copy of that telegram too, and could not read it. Status: read. Most long telegrams keep a few unread groups, marked [?]. Sun’s own six-vowel 文密 code of July 1916 onward, and the June 1917 telegrams, are not in the family and are not read.

t: Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire, 1916–17 — the intercepts the Foreign Ministry could not read
b: The series is 各国内政関係雑纂／支那ノ部／革命党関係（亡命者ヲ含ム）／特定人ノ発受郵便物取調, Gaimushō 1.6.1.4-2-1-2, volumes 2 to 4, on JACAR as B03050088300, B03050088400, B03050089100, B03050090000, B03050090100 and B03050090200. Each batch comes under a covering note headed 特定人發着郵便物等取調ノ件 (“inquiry into mail etc. sent and received by specified persons”), from the Director of the Communications Bureau (逓信省通信局長 田中) to the Director of the Foreign Ministry’s Political Affairs Bureau (政務局長 小池, Koike Chōzō). A typical note, 秘第八?之一號 of 25 May 1916, received the next day, reads 別紙寫電報及左記郵便物有之候: “attached are copied telegrams and the postal item noted below”. The telegrams are copied onto the Imperial Telegraphs’ own forms. Outgoing messages from Tokyo are on “Forwarded” forms, signed 中山 (Nakayama, Sun’s Japanese alias) or, in May, with the handler’s name 林蔚陸 (“Linwailuk”). Incoming messages are on “Received” forms addressed to “Rosamonde Tokio” (Soong Ching-ling), to “Linwailuk Tokio”, or to Nakayama at 109 Harajuku, Aoyama. The correspondents are Yamada Junzaburō in Shanghai (“Junzaburo Shanghai”), “Konglipo” in Manila, Kayano Nagatomo and Ju Zheng’s men at Qingdao (Seitō), “Youngchina” at San Francisco, Honolulu, Hankow, and the Shanghai leadership: Chen Qimei, Xu Chongzhi and the rest. Some of the traffic is in clear English (“2000 through Shokinginko”), and some is in plain telegraph code. Most of it is in ten-letter condenser words. The files hold no decodes. The Foreign Ministry did try. In B03050089100, frames 0076–0078 are a notebook copy of a long romanised kana stream (126 ten-letter groups, ending owari ), and frames 0079–0081 are the analysts’ worksheets on it. They copy the stream into katakana, divide it with slashes into groups of two or three, and pencil kanji guesses beside the groups, often with a question mark: 事, 先生, 國, 電, 軍, 謀. No continuous sense comes out of them, and the stream is not read here either.

t: Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire, 1916–17 — the intercepts the Foreign Ministry could not read
b: The system is the one described on the Swatow page . Twenty consonants (no w ) and five vowels give a hundred syllables numbered 01…99, 00, and two syllables make one four-figure group of the standard Chinese telegraph code. The syllables run on across ten-letter words without regard to the word breaks, and there is no additive. Every table in the family is a rule: the alphabet rotated or reversed, the vowels in some order, the numbers filled vowel by vowel. What changes between correspondents is the rotation and the vowel order: key row for 01 vowel order used on swatow1916 l e a i o u “Tanaka”, Swatow → Rosamonde, 3 April 1916 ( the Swatow telegram ) shanghai1916 z (alphabet reversed) i o a e u Sun ↔ Yamada Junzaburō, Shanghai; Shanghai (Chen Qimei, Xu Chongzhi …) → Rosamonde, March–April 1916 manila1916 g o e u a i Sun ↔ Konglipo, Manila; one Shanghai telegram signed by Xu Chongzhi seito1916 m u i e o a Qingdao (Ju Zheng; Kayano Nagatomo) ↔ Tokyo, March–April 1916 sanfran1916 x o e u a i Tokyo → “Youngchina”, San Francisco yamada1916 q e u i o a Tokyo (Xie Chi, “Linwailuk”) ↔ Junzaburo, Shanghai, May 1916 shanghai1917 k a e u o i Sun ↔ Dai Jitao, March 1917 ( below ) “Row for 01” is the consonant that takes 01 with the first vowel; the next consonant in the alphabet takes 02, and so on. The key names are those in famtest.py . Two more keys are tentative, each resting on one short telegram: Honolulu (alphabet reversed, filled consonant by consonant, vowels e a o u i ; z 4.9) and Manila in May (row for 01 d , vowels e u a o i ; z 4.4). Finding and accepting a key. The whole family, 57,600 tables counting the fill orders, origins and the ±111 additive, was run on each telegram, and each table was scored with a Chinese character model. The z figures on this page are that score measured against the whole family. A short telegram can put a wrong key on top by chance, so a key was accepted only when it reached z ≥ 6 on at least one long telegram and then read other telegrams it had not been fitted to. For example, shanghai1916 was found on a long Shanghai → Rosamonde telegram and then read Sun’s own outgoing telegrams to Yamada at z 7–10. The May key yamada1916 reads every telegram that carries the clear prefix word “Thirtyseventh”. Some short telegrams read under their pair’s key although another table scores slightly higher on them alone. They are counted as read because the text makes sense and the key is fixed elsewhere, not because of their own score. The dates check themselves. Chinese telegrams give the day of the month by a rhyme-category character (韻目代日). Where a signature carries one, it agrees with the date on the Japanese form: 支 4, 元 13, 篠 17, 皓 19, 號 20, 箇 21, 漾 23, 有 25, 宥 26, 豔 29. The one exception is a Shanghai telegram handed in on 22 May that ends 馬, the 21st. The date characters come out of the decryption and the key search never looked at them, so the agreement is an independent check. The clerks. These are copies made by Japanese telegraph clerks, copying letter strings that meant nothing to them, and they make the same mistakes throughout: g ↔ q by far the most often, then x written like d or s , h ↔ k ↔ n , e ↔ c , a ↔ o , and a dropped pair of letters now and then. Every emendation is a single letter of one of these kinds, justified by the sense and usually by a clean occurrence of the same group elsewhere. Examples are gequ → qequ 款 (“funds”), which recurs across the Manila traffic, and dunu → xunu 東. The transcriptions give the letters as written and list each change. A telegram with a pair dropped reads as noise until the pair is restored. The 25 May telegram from Tokyo scores z 4.1 as written and 6.8 once the missing ge of its first word is put back.

t: Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire, 1916–17 — the intercepts the Foreign Ministry could not read
h: March–April 1916: the monarchy cancelled, the money, the Shanghai rising
b: Conventions: [?] = group read as written but doubtful; a character in brackets = the reading after a one-letter emendation, where the notes mark it; □ = unread. Frame numbers are JACAR frames of B03050088300 unless stated. Yuan Shikai announced the end of his monarchy on 22 March 1916. At that point Sun Yat-sen was in Tokyo and his party was planning a rising in Shanghai. 25 March, Shanghai → Rosamonde (fr. 0468; z 6.7) 帝制取消，馮、朱等當漸觀望。滬異派力弱，於我略可從容佈置。海軍[?]發策較萬全，然猶急備未懈… “The monarchy is cancelled. Feng [Guozhang], Zhu [Rui] and the others will now wait and see. The opposing faction in Shanghai is weak, so we can make our dispositions at some leisure. A plan launched by the Navy … is safer, but we are still preparing urgently without slackening …” There is no signature. 26 March, Sun → Yamada (fr. 0465; z 7.4) 京信□□□策：袁暫退，使黎代；俟歐戰終，乃借英力[復]出。故滬事當發於袁退之前乃可。文 “The Peking letter … plan: Yuan to step down for now, with Li [Yuanhong] acting; when the European war ends, he comes back with British support. So the Shanghai action must be launched before Yuan withdraws. — Wen.” The same evening a 38-word telegram from Shanghai signed 美 (Chen Qimei; z 9.2) asked for arms to be shipped and a handover procedure, and closed: 穆日當局允暗濟械，已有接洽否？ (“The authorities have agreed to supply arms secretly: has contact been made?”). 穆 occurs twice with the same letters and is probably a cover word. 27 March, Sun → Konglipo, Manila (fr. 0462; manila1916) 滬電乃崇智所發，勿疑。文 “The Shanghai telegram was sent by [Xu] Chongzhi. Do not doubt it.” Earlier that day Manila had asked who was using the code to send telegrams from Shanghai, calling it 萬可疑, “most suspicious”. Xu Chongzhi’s own telegram of the 26th, signed in clear Shuichunchee , is in the Manila key, not the Shanghai one. 30 March – 4 April: money Much of the traffic is fund-raising. Tokyo asks the Fujian merchants in Manila to 盡力向閩幫籌[款?] (“do their utmost to raise funds from the Fujian guild”); Qingdao asks for fifty thousand, 惟需五萬元，懇速電匯 (“only we need 50,000 yuan; wire it urgently”); Manila reports what seems to be four thousand sent through the Hongkong Bank (a four-word telegram, weakly scored), and Tokyo acknowledges [四?]千圓. From Shanghai on 31 March (z 8.2): 田在滬交五千，到漢匯八千。近[又?]索三萬，無力應之 (“田 [a person] handed over 5,000 in Shanghai, 8,000 to be remitted on reaching Hankow. Lately another 30,000 is demanded; we have no means to meet it”). On the same day Sun warns Yamada (fr. 0485; z 7.9): 北方來電，帝制取消，軍心益振。而[滬?]反[?]觀望。恐前聯絡之人皆多不實，故托此爲辭，[?]得款耳。望兄詳察，勿受其欺。孫文 “Telegrams from the north: the monarchy is cancelled and the army’s spirit rises. But [Shanghai?] is … waiting to see. I fear the people we contacted earlier are mostly not genuine and use this as an excuse to get money. Look into it carefully and do not be taken in. — Sun Wen.” 4 April, Sun → Yamada (fr. 0494; z 9.8, no emendation) 由臺灣電六百金，請交寶昌路寶康里一八三號張宗海，往甘費。聞西林赴南寧組政府，定設法破之。文 “600 gold wired by way of Taiwan: please give it to Zhang Zonghai, 183 Baokang-li, Baochang Road, for the journey to Gansu. I hear Xilin [Cen Chunxuan] is going to Nanning to form a government: I will find a way to break it. — Wen.” This is the cleanest telegram in the files: forty characters and not one letter to change. Two more went out that afternoon. One ends 山東消息甚佳，月內當動。孫文。支 (“news from Shandong is very good; it will move within the month. — Sun Wen, the 4th”). The other, to Kayano at Qingdao (fr. 0492; seito1916, z 7.4), reports fifty thousand sent through the Yokohama Specie Bank, and arms to be shipped under the name of the Qingdao military administration (以寄青島軍政官名義). 13 April, Hankow → Sun (B03050088400 fr. 0517) This telegram is in digits, not condenser letters. It uses the +111 code that Consul Segawa described to the Foreign Ministry that May: each four-figure code group has 111 added, here without the digit reversal. A search over every additive and both digit orders puts −111 175 log-points clear of the next candidate, and the telegram then reads with no emendation: 武漢發動事，日人謂非念五萬不辦。迭電陸參兩部，桐以軍械運輸困難且爲時久。刻人心已熟，海陸均有七分以上把握，三萬可行。機不可[失]，望速決電示。元 “On the Wuhan rising: the Japanese say it cannot be done for under 250,000. [We] have wired the Army Ministry and the General Staff again and again; 桐 says the arms and their transport are difficult and would take a long time. Opinion here is ripe; army and navy are both more than seventy per cent sure; 30,000 would do it. The moment must not be missed. Decide quickly and wire. — the 13th.”

t: Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire, 1916–17 — the intercepts the Foreign Ministry could not read
b: By May, Sun was in Shanghai, where he arrived at the start of the month, and the Tokyo end was run by Xie Chi (謝持), who signs 持 and dates with rhyme characters. Every Tokyo–Shanghai condenser telegram of that month that reads at all reads under one key, yamada1916 (frames of B03050089100). 19 May, Shanghai → Linwailuk, Tokyo (fr. 0066; z 6.0) 英士昨下午在山田家被兇[轟?]斃，捕兇[一?]人，關係者數人。 “Yingshi was shot dead by assassins yesterday afternoon in the Yamada house; one assassin and several accomplices arrested.” Chen Qimei (陳其美, courtesy name Yingshi) was murdered in Shanghai on 18 May 1916 in the house of Yamada Junzaburō, the addressee of most of the Tokyo traffic. Tokyo replied the same day in two telegrams (both signed 持皓, the 19th): 英士被刺，傷[勢?]如何？盼覆 (“Yingshi stabbed: how are the wounds? Please reply”), and then 電悉。英士捐軀，極堪慟悼。主使爲誰？盼覆。先生[?]在滬[?]，務處處戒備。持皓 “Telegram received. Yingshi has given his life; we mourn him deeply. Who was behind it? Please reply. The Master … in Shanghai … must take every precaution. — Chi, the 19th.” Others asked the same question in other ways. From Kobe, 英士君遭難確否乞覆 came in plain code. From Manila, received on 23 May, 聞陳英士死確否？請覆 came to Tōyama Mitsuru in a key of its own. The Shanghai answer of 22 May (z 8.2) gives the instigator as 遣之暗殺主謀爲[政?]府, “the government”, and says that the pistols have been entrusted to Miyazaki to bring back. 23–25 May: arms and the students Tokyo on 23 May (z 8.2): Wu Feiji, back in Shanghai at 26 Rue Joffre, has ordered 300 Type-30 rifles and 100 Browning pistols through the Ōkura company at Dalian, with 2,000 taels already paid as deposit. Tokyo and Shanghai also wire back and forth about 席、趙兩處學生事, the business of Xi Zhengming’s and Zhao’s students at Tianjin, which had been demanding money for a rising. On 22 May Shanghai orders it stopped; on 24 May it says 學生事暫擱 (“shelve the students affair”); on 25 May Tokyo asks which of the two it means. 26 May, Tokyo → Yamada (fr. 0092–93; z 9.6) 克強言外務省意先生宜緩赴青島。又軍械事能得青木一電參謀本部較更有力云云… 宥 “Keqiang [Huang Xing] says the Foreign Ministry’s view is that the Master should put off going to Qingdao. Also, on the arms, a telegram from Aoki [probably Lt-Gen. Aoki Nobuzumi] to the General Staff would carry more weight … — the 26th.” Here Sun’s Tokyo office passes the Japanese Foreign Ministry’s own advice to Sun, and the Foreign Ministry was being sent a copy of the telegram. It had no means of reading it. Earlier that morning Tokyo had asked 報載先生昨[潛?]離滬，確否？ (“the papers report that the Master secretly left Shanghai yesterday; is it true?”). 29 May, Tokyo → Yamada (fr. 0113–14; z 6.6) 據譚根云，岑有軍[火]船四艘由神戸回粤，今遣彼來東運機[?]二臺，交該船載[?]…謝持 豔 “According to Tan Gen, Cen [Chunxuan] has four military steamers going from Kobe back to Guangdong, and has sent him to Japan to ship two machine[-guns?] on them … — Xie Chi, the 29th.” Cen Chunxuan is the “Xilin” whose government at Nanning Sun had promised on 4 April to break.

t: Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire, 1916–17 — the intercepts the Foreign Ministry could not read
h: After the condensers: Cai E and Huang Xing
b: From July the ciphered traffic changes to a code that is not in the family ( below ), but some telegrams in the later volumes are in plain telegraph code. Two of them belong to the same story. 10 July, Luzhou → “Ilchang Tokio” (B03050090000 fr. 0417) 宥電敬悉。承念甚感。久罹喉病，軍中失調，醫治漸痊，幸釋綺注。鍔叩。蒸 “Your telegram of the 26th received with respect. I am most grateful for your concern. I have long suffered from a throat illness, made worse by life with the army; treatment is gradually curing it; please set your mind at rest. — E, the 10th.” This is Cai E (蔡鍔), who led the Yunnan rising against the monarchy. The throat illness killed him in Fukuoka on 8 November 1916. 13 September, Tokyo (中田) → Huang Xing, Shanghai (B03050090100 fr. 0471) 閱報憂悚。接[?]電，母[恙?]稍安。請靜養。現如何？ “Alarmed to read the papers. […] telegram received; your mother is a little better. Please rest. How are you now?” Huang Xing was already ill, and he died on 31 October 1916, eight days before Cai E. The Japanese clerk’s own kanji glosses on this form differ from the codebook at two groups (4443 and 3225).

t: Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire, 1916–17 — the intercepts the Foreign Ministry could not read
b: B03050090200 (vol. 4, item 5, frames 0503–0513) holds three condenser telegrams of late March 1917. Two are from Sun in Shanghai, signed Sunwen in clear, to “Toi c/o Kikuchi Rioichi” in Tokyo. The third is the reply to “Sun yatsen Shanghai”, signed Tenkiutai (天仇, Dai Jitao). “Toi” is therefore Dai Jitao (戴季陶), staying with Kikuchi Ryōichi (菊池良一). The key is a seventh member of the family: row for 01 k , vowels a e u o i , no additive. It was found by running the family on the 23 March telegram alone, where it scores −321.6 against a population mean of −556.4 and s.d. 25.8, about nine standard deviations up; the next unrelated key is 124 points behind. The Swatow key gives nonsense. The 25 and 26 March telegrams played no part in finding the key, and both read in it at once. Dai Jitao to Sun, 26 March 1917 (JACAR B03050090200, frame 0506). The last word, written zimucuzaku , ends in zahu = 1359 宥 with the clerk’s h → k slip. 宥 is the rhyme code for the 26th, the date on the form. Image: Diplomatic Archives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan, Gaimushō 1.6.1.4-2-1-2, via JACAR B03050090200, frame 0506. 23 March, Sun → Dai (fr. 0504) 前電云三日後商妥□□□□□後音。此間必俟前約取消，始可致電北京照辦。各約已取消否？速覆。公司抄件瑞士尚未辦妥。文 “My previous telegram said that after three days [the matter] would be settled by agreement … [further] word. Here we must wait until the former contract is cancelled before we can wire Peking to act accordingly. Have the contracts all been cancelled? Reply at once. The company copy … [瑞士?] not yet settled. — Wen.” Words 4 and 5 as copied, pixaqaqe eianakerele , have 19 letters where 20 are needed, and ei is not a syllable. The clerk misplaced the word break and lost or misread at least two letters. pi completes 妥, and the last code of the damaged run, lebe 接, reads as written, so “…接後音” (“received further word”) is likely. The five codes between cannot be recovered with confidence. A search allowing one insertion and up to two substitutions finds nothing clean. 瑞士 needs an x / m change and is the least certain emendation. The telegram’s last word, qixapfete , has nine letters; read qixa pi ne te it gives 辦妥 and 文, Sun’s signature character, which also closes the 25 March telegram. 25 March, Sun → Dai (fr. 0507) 函悉。約取消後，當□□□能否。取消卽覆。文 “Letter received. After the contract is cancelled, [whether] … is possible. Reply as soon as it is cancelled. — Wen.” 能 needs zubo → xubo ; three codes do not read, and no one-letter variant makes sense of them. 26 March, Dai → Sun (fr. 0506) 本定今日赴熱海。□□來云：彼等須先□定，約三日回。□公司事如何？電示。宥 “I was to have gone to Atami today. … came and said that they must first settle …; [I shall be] back in about three days. How stands the company matter? Wire me. — the 26th.” 公司 has the same qabo for 司 that reads cleanly on 23 March. The two characters before 來云 do not read. 小池 (Koike Chōzō, who had left the Foreign Ministry’s Political Bureau in 1916) is two letters away and is no more than a guess. Together the three telegrams show Sun, in the last week of March 1917, waiting for “the former contract” to be cancelled before he can wire Peking, pressing Dai for news, and Dai asking after “the company matter”. They do not say what the contract or the company was. That needs the Chinese record for March 1917, which has not been consulted.

t: Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire, 1916–17 — the intercepts the Foreign Ministry could not read
b: Sun’s 文密 code. From July 1916 (B03050090000 fr. 0416: Tokyo → 中華新報 Shanghai, and Tokyo → 軍務院 Zhaoqing with the prefix 文密 ) to June 1917, some of Sun’s traffic uses ten-letter words with y as a sixth vowel and w as a consonant. It is not in the five-vowel family. A six-vowel version of the family, about 200,000 tables, finds nothing above z 4.1. The prefix names it as a separate code, probably one built on a table that is not a rule. The June 1917 telegrams between Sun and Dai (B03050090200 fr. 0509, 0511) are in that system, and they also contain clusters that are not consonant–vowel pairs ( myzoasdoke , liriopen ). Transcribed, not read. Late May 1916. Five Tokyo → Junzaburo telegrams have no “Thirtyseventh” prefix. Three are eight words long, and one survives as a typed copy, so misreading is ruled out. The pair statistics say the text is structured, but no key in the family reads them, and yamada1916 fails with every additive from 0 to 9999. Two Shanghai → “Ylchang Tokio” telegrams of 29–30 May use w as a consonant. These are probably early 文密. The kana stream of B03050089100 fr. 0076–0078, which the Foreign Ministry’s analysts worked on, is not read here either. The Swatow original. Every Latin-letter form in B03050088300 and B03050088400 was read, and none is from Swatow. The copy in B03050738800 is still the only one found, and its three garbled tail groups stay lost. Unread groups. Most long telegrams keep a few groups marked [?]: names that are not in the model, codes one letter from several readings, and supplementary-code characters. The two tentative keys (Honolulu; Manila in May) rest on one short telegram each. The March 1917 lacuna and the identity of the contract and the company are open.

t: The Swatow telegram to Sun Yat-sen — a systematic code condenser
b: Twenty consonants, five vowels, ten-letter words: a code condenser over the standard Chinese telegraph code. The family of systematic tables is small enough to brute-force, and one key reads 41 characters: Mo Qingyu’s independence at Chaozhou and Sun’s men ordered out of the Swatow garrison headquarters, 3 April 1916. China / Japan · telegraph code + code condenser · 1916 · solved "Tanaka" at Swatow to Sun Yat-sen to Sun Yat-sen Swatow, 3 April 1916, 6.05 pm, to "Rosamonde Tokio" · intercepted by the Japanese Foreign Ministry · JACAR B03050738800 (Gaimushō 680682) The condenser table recovered from 177 letters by brute force over the family of systematic tables; 41 of about 44 characters read Daniel Bourdeau · solved 15 September 2026 · updated 21 September 2026 solved Summary. In April 1916 the Japanese Foreign Ministry secretly obtained a 22-word telegram from a "Tanaka" at Swatow to "Rosamonde Tokio" — Soong Ching-ling's English name, so Sun Yat-sen's household — and could not read it. S. Tomokiyo listed it as unsolved in 2021 after trying the two code condensers known from Sun's Japanese supporter Yamada Junzaburō. The letters are the 20 consonants and 5 vowels of exactly such a condenser, and both known tables are systematic (alphabetical consonants, permuted vowels, filled row- or column-wise). That family is small — 57 600 keys with additives — and one of them, scored against a Chinese character model, stands eight standard deviations above the rest. The plaintext, in the standard telegraph codebook, is a field report from the revolutionaries' side at Swatow: 潮城由莫擎宇獨立。我軍亦光復汕頭。後莫率大隊來，令我退出鎮守府。我軍力薄，暫由翼□支持。文慧返…… "Chaozhou city has been declared independent by Mo Qingyu. Our force too has recovered Swatow. Then Mo came with a large body and ordered us out of the garrison headquarters. Our force is weak; for now we are supported by 翼□. 文慧 is returning …" — which is precisely what happened between 27 and 30 March 1916. Status: solved; three codes at the end are garbled in the received copy, and one name is unresolved. Sequel: the same family of keys reads some sixty more telegrams of Sun’s circle from the Ministry of Communications’ intercept files, 1916–17 — Sun Yat-sen’s circle on the wire .

t: The Swatow telegram to Sun Yat-sen — a systematic code condenser
b: JACAR B03050738800 is a Foreign Ministry file of 29 April – 11 May 1916 on Sun Yat-sen's cipher telegrams. It contains (i) five telegrams from Sun in Tokyo to a policeman of the Hankow consulate, in four-figure groups — the "+111" code that Tomokiyo has already read; (ii) a despatch, 機密送第一號, from Foreign Minister Ishii to the acting consul at Swatow, himself named Tanaka, asking who this "Tanaka" was, why he wired Sun, whether he was misusing the consul's name, and "if at all possible" to decode the telegram; (iii) the telegram; and (iv) the Hankow consul-general's report of 11 May on Sun's next scheme (five-figure groups, digits reversed, 111 subtracted). Nothing in the file reads the Swatow telegram. The first sheet of the telegram (JACAR B03050738800, frame 680682; crop by S. Tomokiyo). Station from Swatow, No. 1507, 22 words, 3/4/16 6.05 pm; address "Rosamonde Tokio". Image: Diplomatic Archives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan, via JACAR B03050738800, frame 680682; crop by S. Tomokiyo, Cryptiana. Twelve baxuxupeja qicijinati bemigasiqi jakebiqoye kufohemige tuxaboboba gedocijiga poyevayoxa leyoleveke biromapesa vorobenife xikebiqoye qekufiyaqa tijaqixiqo xitonatula xopavajejo ropezpo ngobunibai tanaka As read from the form. Tomokiyo's transcription has gedoeijiga and xitohatula ; the handwriting is c and n , and the decipherment requires exactly that. "Twelve" is the table indicator (Yamada's telegrams begin "Sixtyfour" for his 六十四號 table).

t: The Swatow telegram to Sun Yat-sen — a systematic code condenser
b: Alphabet. Consonants b c d f g h j k l m n p q r s t v x y z (twenty, no w) and vowels a e i o u — the 20 × 5 = 100 syllables of a two-digit code condenser: each syllable stands for a pair of digits, two syllables for one four-figure codebook group, and the syllables are run together and cut into ten-letter "words" to be charged as one word each. 177 letters → 88 syllables → 44 groups, one letter lost. Vowel u is rare (7 of 89 syllables against ~20 each for the others). In a column-major table each vowel owns a block of twenty numbers; the block 81–99, 00 is almost never a page number in the codebook (which stops in the 80s), so u is the high block. That already fixes the layout type. Known condensers. Yamada's Guoshiguan table runs x y z b c … v across rows and u o i e a down, numbered 01–99, 00 row by row; his Michigan table runs b … z alphabetically and o u a e i, numbered column by column from 00. Both are pure rule tables. The natural hypothesis for "table twelve" is another member of the same family: a rotation (or reversal) of the alphabetical consonants, a permutation of the vowels, either fill order, either origin, perhaps an additive as in Sun's own telegrams.
