b: Codebook = 電報新編 / 明密碼電報書 numbering (identical to the modern standard telegraph code for these characters). Dotted = emended letter · red = unresolved ba xu · xe pe · ja qi · ci ji · na ti · be mi · ga si · qi ja · ke bi · qo ye · ku fo · ne mi · ge tu · xa bo · bo ba · ge do 3390 1004 3945 5459 2348 1342 3747 4539 2053 6511 0076 0342 1788 3073 7333 1775 潮 城 由 莫 擎 宇 獨 立 我 軍 亦 光 復 汕 頭 後 ci ji · ga po · ye va · yo xa · le yo · le ve · ke bi · ro ma · pe sa · vo ro · be ni · fe xi · ke bi · qo ye · qe ku · fi ya 5459 3764 1129 7130 0171 0109 2053 6622 0427 6966 1343 1650 2053 6511 0500 5631 莫 率 大 隊 來 令 我 退 出 鎮 守 府 我 軍 力 薄 qa ti · ja qi · xi qo · xi to · na tu · la xo · pa va · je jo · ro pe · [zpo ngobunibai] 2548 3945 5065 5068 2388 2170 2429 1979 6604 暫 由 翼 □ 支 持 文 慧 返 … 潮 城 由莫擎宇獨立。我軍亦 光 復汕頭。後 莫 率大隊來，令我退出鎮守府。我軍力薄，暫由 翼□ 支 持。 文慧 返 …… The events. On 26 March 1916 Mo Qingyu (莫擎宇), a regimental commander at Chaozhou under Long Jiguang's Chao-Mei garrison, was won over by Chen Jiongming, Lin Hu, He Haiming and the local revolutionaries; on the 27th he occupied Chaozhou city and wired the provincial authorities "率師占領潮城，宣布獨立" — 潮城 , the very word of the telegram. On the 30th the Swatow guard troops declared for him and he formally proclaimed independence with his headquarters at Swatow. Sun's own Chinese Revolutionary Party men had meanwhile taken the town's garrison headquarters (鎮守使署); "Tanaka", one of the Japanese adventurers serving with them, reports on 3 April that Mo, arriving in force, has ordered them out, that they are too weak to resist, and that someone is returning — presumably to Tokyo to report. The Ministry's suspicion that the sender was trading on the Swatow consul's name is a nice irony: the consul was also a Tanaka.

t: The Swatow telegram to Sun Yat-sen — a systematic code condenser
b: 城. The form reads baxuxupeja → 90 04 , and no codebook has page 90. One vowel-stroke away is xe pe = 1004 城, which the history all but dictates (潮州 1558, 潮梅 2734 and 潮汕 3073 are unreachable from the letters). The second u is probably an e. 翼□ (5065 5068). Both syllables of 翼 are confirmed elsewhere; the second group's to is not, and 5068 (翿) is not a word. A name or a unit that "supported" the revolutionaries once Mo displaced them — the Swatow guard? a ship of Tang Tingguang's squadron? — is expected here. 文慧 (2429 1979). Sent as read; presumably a person who "returns". 文 is also Sun Wen's signature character. The tail. After 返 the form has zpo ngobunibai : a seven-letter "word" cannot occur in this system, and ng , ai are not syllables. An exhaustive search of all strings within three plausible edits (h/n, u/n, c/e confusions, dropped letters) yields no decoding into valid codes. Roughly three characters — a place or a request — are lost unless the second sheet of frame 680682 can be read at higher resolution. The two h syllables of the transcription ( he , ha ) both decode as nonsense and both read as n on the form (光, 支). The h row of the table is therefore unattested, but the layout leaves it no other place.

t: The Swatow telegram to Sun Yat-sen — a systematic code condenser
b: The JACAR file was read page by page (the archive's image server refuses automated access; the PDF was supplied by hand) for context and to check the letters. Syllable statistics: the 20 + 5 alphabet and the deficit of u pointed to a systematic, column-major condenser. Brute force over the whole systematic family (57 600 keys) with a character-unigram score over the standard codebook (Unihan telegraph tables; the 1916 numbering verified on Tomokiyo's decoded Sun telegrams). Four doubtful groups examined by one-letter alternatives; the readings 光復, 支持, 莫, 潮城 chosen by sense and then found in the handwriting. Edit-distance search over the garbled tail (negative). Historical check against the 26–30 March chronology of Mo Qingyu's rising.

t: Van Swieten to Cobenzl from Bonn, 1757–59 — an alphabetical syllabary rebuilt from the ciphertext
b: Three despatches of the young Gottfried van Swieten to Count Cobenzl, catalogued on DECODE as non-decrypted. The 1757 passage carries its own decipherment and shows the system: an alphabetical list of letters and syllables. No key survives for the 1759 table, so it was rebuilt from 553 groups by annealing a code map held in alphabetical order against a French language model, then corrected from the clear text round each run. Read at 96%: the Gueldre convention, Moers, and a frank verdict on Soubise’s army and its generals. Bonn → Brussels · numerical syllabary, two tables · 1757–1759 · read Van Swieten to Cobenzl, Bonn 1757–1759 from Gottfried van Swieten → to Count Cobenzl ARA Brussels, Secrétairerie d’État et de Guerre, inv. 1236, ff. 141, 327–328, 344–345 · DECODE R955–R957, “non-decrypted” · letters in French with ciphered passages in three-digit numbers The 1757 passage is deciphered in clear on its own page · the 1759 table rebuilt from 553 groups with no key or crib beyond the surrounding clear text · 96 % of the groups read Daniel Bourdeau · solved 22 September 2026 solved Summary. Gottfried van Swieten, later Mozart’s and Haydn’s patron in Vienna, began as a diplomat under Count Cobenzl, the Empress’s minister plenipotentiary in the Austrian Netherlands. From Bonn, the court of the Elector of Cologne, he reported to Cobenzl on the French armies in Germany during the Seven Years’ War, putting the sensitive sentences into numbers. DECODE holds three of these letters as non-decrypted. The undated one (R955) has the decipherment written under the numbers: the magistrates of Hanau debated neutrality in case the French left. It shows the system, an alphabetical list of letters and syllables with a few homophones. The two letters of January and February 1759 use a new table in the same style, with numbers 100–442. No key for it survives. It was rebuilt from the ciphertext by annealing a code-to-syllable map that must stay in alphabetical order, scored by a French language model. One random start in eight came out as French. The rest was corrected by hand against the clear text round each passage. The letters report the convention that left the revenues of Prussian Gueldre to the French while keeping the Empress’s sovereignty, the principality of Moers handed to a prince without asking her, and a sharp judgement of Soubise’s army. That army lived on Gueldre’s contributions and planned no magazines, and among its generals only Broglie was competent. Status: read. About 21 of 553 groups in the 1759 letters stay open, nearly all proper names.

t: Van Swieten to Cobenzl from Bonn, 1757–59 — an alphabetical syllabary rebuilt from the ciphertext
b: The 1759 numbers do not fit the 1757 values, but if the new table was built the same way, it has a strong constraint: a higher number never stands for an alphabetically earlier syllable. The solver ( msolve.py ) keeps one inventory index per observed number, sorted, and allows at most two numbers per syllable. It anneals the boundaries against a French character model ( fr-1750-nospace , added to the shared lang/ registry), with a small bonus per decoded letter. As a control, a 274-group French passage encoded with a random alphabetical table was recovered verbatim. On the real 491 clean groups, one start in eight gave “la nouvelle convention on laisse le revenu… en réservant la souveraineté… l’impératrice”, and the other seven did not. The key was then corrected by hand, run by run, against the French sentence each run sits in. For example, “avant que les campagnes soient garnies, on ne songe pas à faire des magazins , si ce n’est aux dépens des États de l’Empire qui sont entièrement épuisés”. The end of the table falls into place: x 438/439, y 441, z 442. So do word entries filed in their alphabetical slot: nous, pour, qui, roi, comte. R956, f. 344: runs of unseparated digits inside the clear text (“le grand principe paroît être de faire 392 135 133 389 385 403…” = subsister l’armée du roi y sans qu’il en coûte un sou ). Image: Archives générales du Royaume, Brussels, Secrétairerie d’État et de Guerre inv. 1236 f. 344, via DECODE R956.

t: Van Swieten to Cobenzl from Bonn, 1757–59 — an alphabetical syllabary rebuilt from the ciphertext
b: … de l’administration; la nouvelle convention laisse les revenus à la [G…] en réservant la souveraineté à l’Impératrice. On promet de toujours [?] de la part des François. Dans cette supposition, sans que nous ayons aucun ordre de la cour à ce sujet, et cela cause beaucoup de mésintelligences. On vient de la part de la [G…] de mettre en possession de la principauté de Meurs le prince de Con[…] […] qui vous formez des prétensions sans prévenir seulement l’Impératrice, qui en est souveraine. The Prussian lands on the Lower Rhine (Gueldre, Moers) were in French and Austrian hands from 1757. The passage records a convention that left their revenues to one party and the sovereignty to Maria Theresa. It also reports a grant of Moers made without informing her.

t: Van Swieten to Cobenzl from Bonn, 1757–59 — an alphabetical syllabary rebuilt from the ciphertext
b: Il est constant que l’armée du Prince de Soubise est dans le meilleur état qu’on puisse imaginer … avant que les campagnes soient garnies, on ne songe pas à faire des magazins si ce n’est aux dépens des États de l’Empire qui sont entièrement épuisés; le grand principe paraît être de faire subsister l’armée du roi y sans qu’il en coûte un sou . La campagne passée en fait la preuve, aussi le prince [name] a-t-il avoué que les contributions de la Gueldre avoient suffi à l’entretien de son armée , et qu’on avoit même transmis assez d’argent à l’armée de Contades pour subvenir aux frais du traitement des troupes pendant l’hiver , et que toutes les opérations de l’année passée n’avoient eu d’autre but. Le prince pense bien, mais le reste est malintentionné ; outre cela il n’y a pas un officier général entendu à cette armée, excepté le duc de Broglio; le major général (?) des Liégeois de Vaut est intéressé et ignorant, et non l’intendant nécessaire pour mettre en œuvre le système que j’ai détaillé ci-dessus … D’ailleurs, homme non violent , je n’ai pas besoin de parler de Dumesnil ; il est universellement connu pour être prussien, […] le prince Camille … Parmi les maréchaux de ce[…] il n’y a que [name] qu’on estime . Comme de notre côté nous ne pouvons pas résister aux plaintes fondées des États , et que les ordres de la cour nous obligent de faire des représentations … on a pris occasion de former des plaintes contre le comte de Pergen comme s’il n’agissoit pas conformément aux intérêts de la cause commune.

t: Throckmorton to the Regent Moray, 20 July 1569 — the Norfolk marriage letter, read
b: DECODE R8348 (BL Add MS 33531 ff. 79–80), catalogued with no sender and dated 26 July, is Sir Nicholas Throckmorton’s letter to Moray from Greenwich, 20 July 1569. It was deciphered between the lines at the time and summarised by Bain, but a water stain has faded half of the old decipherment. Every cipher passage is read again from the cipher with Tomokiyo’s key: the council’s plan for the Queen of Scots’ restoration and marriage, and a plea to send Lethington. Greenwich → the Regent of Scotland · letter-substitution with a few name signs, inline with clear English · 20 July 1569 · read at the time, text recovered Throckmorton to the Regent Moray, 20 July 1569 — the Norfolk marriage letter, read from Nicholas Throckmorton → to Regent Moray BL Add MS 33531 ff. 79–80 (DECODE R8348; catalogue item 83). DECODE lists it under an unknown sender and dates it 26 July. It is Sir Nicholas Throckmorton's letter to the Regent Moray, "At Grenew. the 20th of July 1569". A contemporary decipherment was written between the lines, and Bain calendared the letter in 1900. A water stain has faded much of that decipherment. Every cipher passage is read again here from the cipher itself. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 21 September 2026 resolved Summary. Catalogue item 83 was a DECODE record with no sender, a date of 26 July 1569 and the status "partially decrypted". The letter itself is signed in cipher "N. Throkmorton", dated at Greenwich 20 July 1569, and addressed to the "Lorde Regent of Scotlande". Bain's Calendar of Scottish Papers ii, no. 1103, summarises it as "in cipher deciphered". The Scottish recipients wrote a decipherment over every cipher line, and Satoshi Tomokiyo has reconstructed the key; both were known before this work. What was missing is the text. Bain gives two sentences, and the old decipherment is half washed out by a stain across ff. 79r and 80r. The cipher ink survived, so every cipher passage was deciphered again with Tomokiyo's key and checked against the gloss wherever it can still be read. The letter presses Moray to accept what the English council had "intended and resolved" about the Queen of Scots: her restoration and her marriage, the Norfolk match. It warns him that the "protestants your frendes" here have come round, and that "not one, no, not one" of any moment disallows the plan. It urges him to send Lethington to London at speed, because refusing would leave him "incombred both from hence, from thence, and from all other places". A few name signs and a handful of words stay uncertain.

t: Throckmorton to the Regent Moray, 20 July 1569 — the Norfolk marriage letter, read
b: This is a letter-for-letter substitution that uses Latin-looking letters as cipher signs, so the ciphertext looks like gibberish English. It has homophones for a, b, e, i, o and u (w is written as two u-signs) and single signs for persons: N = the Queen of Scots, W = the Queen of England, L = your Lordship, and a few others (Z, M, La, ⊔) whose referents the gloss does not preserve. Plain → cipher: a q/ħ, b r/K, c B, d ε, e α/ε, f a, g б, h c, i ∂/4, l f, m g, n ɧ, o 7/i, p k, r m, s n, t o, u p/Δ, x y, y x. The key is Tomokiyo's, and it held without change on every word read here.

t: Throckmorton to the Regent Moray, 20 July 1569 — the Norfolk marriage letter, read
b: The clear text is in roman type and the deciphered passages in italics. [?] marks a word not securely read, and a sign in brackets is a name sign. The page order is ff. 79r, 79v, 80r, 80v. f. 79r. What was intended and resolved here concerning the [N, Queen of Scots] [?] for her restauration, as for the disposition of her in marriage, your [L, Lordship] … thoroughly understand by Mr John Woodes narration. Since which time you did hear also by a letter sent from me to the Lord of Liddington in your [?] of the same matter absolutely and breefly … How your frendes which here aforesaid were of a contrarie minde for the whole, were violently constrained and by great necessitie urged to condescend and thereunto . So as now my good Lord the matter is not in state of deliberation, but rather requires expedite [?], having good opportunitie for execution . With further by all convenient means I doe wishe that you should concurre with your frendes [Z] here, who see so far into your case , and are so content for the same, as they desire nothinge so earnestlie as your Lordship's pr[ocuring] in that matter , and that to be donne in suche sorte, both for the [sign] and good affection, as it may not appear after [signs] to the [N] or to such as have interest in her , that you will doe nothinge frendly but compulsorilie, whereby the frendship, good affection borne you and thestimacion of you shalbe changed into worse conceiptes, and so gradatim your happines, tranquillitie, and anie good else, shalbe turned into turmoile, calamitie, and division, and the prosperitie of your neighbours and frendes eyther converted into greate dissention, or into a miserable transformation. Now (as matters have ben used and conducted) the protestants your frendes have credit and meanes to assure all things there and here in good termes . And suche may be your impugninge or [double?] proce[edinge] … f. 79v. … as yours and ours adversaries shall [sign] possess the instrument [?], and all other circumstances to the ruine of Religion, you, and your countrey also, and to worke the lyke effectes amongest us moost dangerouslye. You may perhaps amongest other perswasions be moved to thinke, that as you find a faction there to impugne their designe , so there shall not want Instrumentes and a party here to runne the same course . My Lorde I will not dissemble with you, and if I would you can gesse at the truthe. Some there be [sign] graunt which will to their [Z] power withstand this matter . Others will geve the lokinge on; and some will cary twoe faces in a hoode, lokinge which way the matter is lyke to wende. [M] Of all these sortes that will the end , to hasten apace, not to be lefte alone, [sign] when they shall see the ablest and the greatest runne and concurre together in the favour of the [N, M, La] for the purposes aforesaid . And albeit you may thinke [W, the Queen of England] will not so hastily favour her promotion , yet youre experience paste dothe teache you that [W] could never accord her overthrow , or be contented to see her lyfe dispossessed of her state. For I graunt, if her majestie would have runne the direct course against her, perhaps the same would have taken good successe , but this neutralitie can not stande as the worlde standeth. Some light you maye see and thereby conjecture the reste by her majesties letter written to you [sign] at that time , whereby also you may be resolved of what affections they f. 80r. they be in this matter which have the principall credit about her . [signs] I can assure your lordship there is not one, no, not one , which are of moment, that dothe not allow of this case, and maketh hast to shew his gratitude , leste he might be demed slowe. If I could by anye other course espye anye other thinge than your owne overthrowe, I would not write so peremptorilie unto you, neyther perswade you to geve place where peradventure your conscience may be combred, and some question of overprecise objections may arise to calle your honor in dowbte. We see so far to the beginninge, the middeste and the endinge, and doe forsee all dangers and eventes, as I thinke you can not, but [?] yourself to concurre with your frendes . Therefore settinge aside argumentacion, [Z, La, sign] wishe you should with speed [?] send hither the Lord of Liddington, who undoubtedly is both the wysest and the sufficientest man you may send to provide for you and all the reste substancyally and assuredly. And when you shall leave to be advised by him and to truste him, you shall procure unto yourselfe greatteste perill, and to the whole state of your countrey the grettest hazarde. No mans frendship will be more imbraced than yours, no mans estimacion more preserved. [sign] Contrarywise, if you desist or become an adverse party, you will be so incombred both from hence, from thence, and from all other places, your neighbours, as no man can advise you what to doe. Therefore God send you to directe your course for the beste. And so I commit you and all yours f. 80v. to almighty Gods counsell. At Grenew. the 20th of July 1569. Your L. to use and commande, N. Throkmorton . Address: "Lorde Regent of Scotlande".

t: Throckmorton — archived key and published plaintext
b: Twenty DECODE records in BL Add MS 4136 lead to Forbes and CSP. The archived third cipher reads two short samples, 42 tokens in all. A record-to-edition concordance separates the published counterparts from full token verification; composite material remains to be checked. France → Cecil, Elizabeth I and the Council · Homophones and nomenclator · 1560–63 · Prior solution verified Throckmorton: the key survives, and the text was printed from Nicholas Throckmorton → to William Cecil Twenty records catalogued as non-decrypted in BL Add MS 4136 lead to surviving keys, Forbes's eighteenth-century edition and the Calendar of State Papers. Two samples verify the connection. Daniel Bourdeau · resolved 20 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 Summary. The proposed target was a group of twenty DECODE records, R9220–R9234, R9242–R9245 and R9255. All 54 image references were obtained; they represent 39 distinct photographs because adjacent records share leaves. Four nearby key records add 17 photographs. R9262 supplies the archived “Third Cipher” and reads a complete numbered extract on R9220, matching Forbes I, p.355. A second, shorter check on R9230 matches Forbes II, p.12. A twenty-record concordance identifies published counterparts, most by date and addressee. These are 42 verified tokens, not twenty complete decryptions . Tomokiyo had already identified the printed texts and surviving keys; this result confirms that route and corrects the target description.

t: Throckmorton — archived key and published plaintext
h: A key test on the first leaf
b: R9220, f.110, begins in the middle of a letter. Its first complete numbered extract, (6), reads: all be it i be revoked or the warr breake In modern English: “albeit I be recalled, or war break out.” Throckmorton is asking Cecil to obtain permission for Mr Jones to remain abroad and gain experience, even if the ambassador is recalled or war begins. Forbes prints the phrase in volume I (1740), p.355, within the 7 March 1559/60 despatch. The same leaf includes the 8 March continuation and the separate letter to the Queen of 9 March. R9220, f. 110: below Throckmorton’s signature, the numbered extracts (6) and (7) in his third cipher. Extract (6) reads “all be it i be revoked or the warr breake”. Image: British Library, Add MS 4136 f. 110, via DECODE R9220. The 27 transcribed cipher tokens include two nulls. The alphabet on R9262 image P1 supplies the letters: dotted 4, 5 and 6 all represent r ; plain 4 represents o ; colon-marked 6 represents u/v . P3 gives the marked A for all and marked b for be . P4 gives the suffix -ed , and P9 gives the curved T for the/to . Thus the reading tests the alphabet, word signs, suffixes and nulls together. The final word before breake is warr , with two different r homophones, not wars . R9230, f.133, offers a second check at the opening of extract (1): orleans or burges These fifteen alphabet tokens agree with Forbes II (1741), p.12. CSP Foreign V, no.425, paragraph 11 summarizes the surrounding warning: the apparent preparations against Orleans or Bourges may conceal an attack on Rouen, Newhaven (Le Havre), and Dieppe. No.426 describes a separate decipher of the ciphered passages. The rest of that sentence has not been transcribed token by token here. Both checks have grade H : values read from the archived key. Spacing and capitalization are editorial. The printed counterparts were available during verification, so these are known-plaintext checks, not blind decipherments. The token labels and values are preserved in control.json and control_9230.json , with a replay script. The script verifies substitution of those labels; inspection of the images establishes the glyph identifications.

t: Throckmorton — archived key and published plaintext
h: Prior work and the misleading target description
b: Satoshi Tomokiyo's Elizabethan cipher study already identifies the Add MS 4136 ciphertexts as largely extracts, cites Forbes, reconstructs three Throckmorton ciphers, and records the archive keys in a November 2024 note. This is not a newly discovered key or first publication of the plaintext. DECODE's “Non-decrypted” status describes the record and cannot by itself establish that the text is unread. t: García de Toledo to Philip II, 16 July 1565 — a relief of Malta waved off by the Grand Master’s fires
b: The duplicate of the viceroy of Sicily’s ciphered despatch from Messina, two months into the Great Siege, AGS Estado leg. 1394 no. 247: clear Spanish with every sensitive word in two-digit figures, and no decipherment on the leaf or in PARES. Two runs beside clear words, seiscientos soldados and en tiera , gave eleven letters; the figures 12–43 run through the alphabet in order, so the rest was predicted and confirmed, and all 1,930 groups read. The Piccolo Soccorso got into the Borgo; a second run of galleys turned back four miles out on La Valette’s signals, as Mosiur de Lenni reported; and Sicily cannot pay for the war. Messina → Philip II · homophonic figure cipher in alphabetical order · 16 July 1565 · solved García de Toledo to Philip II, Messina, 16 July 1565 from García de Toledo → to Philip II AGS Estado leg. 1394 no. 247, the duplicado of a ciphered despatch from the viceroy of Sicily two months into the Great Siege of Malta · four pages of Spanish with every sensitive word in two-digit figures · no decipherment on the leaf or in the catalogue Broken from two runs beside clear words; the key is the alphabet in order on the figures 12–43, so the rest was predicted and then confirmed · 1,930 groups read end to end Daniel Bourdeau · solved 18 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 solved Summary. On 16 July 1565 Don García de Toledo, viceroy of Sicily, wrote to Philip II from Messina with news from besieged Malta. The copy at Simancas is the duplicado : clear Spanish with the names, numbers and intelligence replaced by runs of two-digit figures, and nothing on the leaf or in the PARES record to say what they mean. The cipher is a homophonic substitution in which the figures 12 to 43 run through the alphabet in order, three figures for each vowel and one for each consonant, with no nulls and no code words. Two runs standing beside clear words, seiscientos soldados after los and en tiera after puso , gave eleven letters; the order of the table predicted the rest. The letter reports that the 600 soldiers Don Juan de Cardona landed entraron en el burgo a saluamento ; that the Grand Master wept for joy; and that a second run of galleys toward the harbour turned back when La Valette made them las sennales del fuego clarissimas para que no entrassen . The rest is money and fortification: El estar sin galeras me destruye , and in the kingdom there is nothing si no infinitas deudas . Status: read end to end; a handful of words are doubtful in sense, none in their figures. The original despatch, which could carry a contemporary decipherment, has not been found.

t: García de Toledo to Philip II, 16 July 1565 — a relief of Malta waved off by the Grand Master’s fires
b: The Archivo General de Simancas, Estado, legajo 1394, no. 247, is catalogued on PARES as Duplicado de carta cifrada de García de Toledo, capitán general del Mar, a Felipe II, rey de España , 16 July 1565. It is two leaves: four pages of text (ff. 1r–2v) and an address leaf, sealed and inscribed En manos del señor Franco de Erasso , for the King’s secretary Francisco de Eraso. The first page is docketed Dupp.do in the upper left. A duplicate was a second copy sent by another route in case the first was lost, and this one is a clerk’s copy: it carries copying slips that the original presumably does not ( quesido for querido , puddo for puedo , lonze for onze ). PARES serves the six images (four text pages and the address leaf twice) as plain JPEGs about 915 pixels wide. That is the largest size the viewer gives; asking for any zoom other than the default returns a smaller image. At that size the figures are legible when a line is cropped and enlarged two and a half to five times, which is how every figure here was read. F. 1r, lines 1–3: Llevo tan [ ruyn ] . [ nueua ] a V. Mag. el correo passado que no me ha parescido detener este para que [ en parte ] la mejore. los [ seiscientos / soldados ] que don Juan de Cardona puso [ en tiera ] fue . The run after los and the run after puso are the two cribs that broke the cipher. Image: Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 1394 no. 247 f. 1r, via PARES (image 1). The letter is written in running Spanish, and the figures stand in the line wherever a word was thought sensitive: the relief, the Grand Master, the galleys, the signals, sums of money, place names, the enemy. Figure runs are written without word breaks, so a run such as 3618243616241829 is one or several words run together.

t: García de Toledo to Philip II, 16 July 1565 — a relief of Malta waved off by the Grand Master’s fires
b: A homophonic substitution on two-digit figures, in which the values 12 to 43 are assigned to the letters in alphabetical order. The five vowels and u/v have three figures each, every consonant one: letter figures letter figures letter figures a 12 13 14 i 24 25 26 r 35 b 15 l 27 s 36 c 16 m 28 t 37 d 17 n 29 u / v 38 39 40 e 18 19 20 o 30 31 32 x 41 f 21 p 33 y 42 g 22 q 34 z 43 h 23 The alphabet has no j , k or w , and u and v are one letter, as in the clear hand. The table uses exactly the thirty-two values from 12 to 43, and no figure outside that range occurs in the letter: no nulls, and no code groups for names or words. Names are spelt out letter by letter, Caragoca (Syracuse), Augusta , Cabo Bono , Argel , Maltta , Mecina , Mosiur de Lenni . The homophones are not used evenly. Of the three a figures, 13 occurs about 140 times, 14 about 95 and 12 about 50; of the e figures, 19 is used twice as often as 18 and nearly four times as often as 20; of the o figures, 31 about a hundred times against 40 for 30 and 13 for 32. The clerk had favourites. The overall letter frequencies are ordinary Spanish: a and e first, then s , r and o . Four things about the hand need to be known before the decode reads cleanly. ñ is written nn ( sennales , Espanna , campanna ). Double letters are sometimes written single ( en tiera ) and sometimes doubled where the word has one ( spantaado , quinta[a]les ). The duplicado has its own copying slips, listed above. And the confusable pairs in this hand are 17/19 , 35/36 , 35/38 (a long-tailed 3 against a dotted 8) and 13/14 .

t: García de Toledo to Philip II, 16 July 1565 — a relief of Malta waved off by the Grand Master’s fires
b: Two cribs from the clear text. The second line of f. 1r has los followed by the run 36 18 24 36 16 24 18 29 37 30 36 and, on the next line, 36 30 27 17 13 17 31 36 . Eleven figures with the first repeated at the fourth and eleventh places, standing after an article, fit seiscientos , and the next run then reads soldados . A few words on, the run after don Juan de Cardona puso is 19 29 37 25 19 35 14 , en tiera , “put ashore”, spelt with one r . Together these fix a c d e i l n o r s t , with two figures each for a , e , i and o . The table closes itself. Set out by value, the recovered figures were already in alphabetical order: 13 14 a , 16 c , 17 d , 18 19 e , 24 25 i , 27 l , 29 n , 30 31 o , 35 r , 36 s , 37 t . Once that was seen the gaps did not need solving. Each could be predicted from its position and then checked on a word: 21 f , 41 x , 42 y and 43 z were filled that way and confirmed on 18212118373136 effetos , 15124119271836 baxeles , 42151329 yban and 332712431935 plazer . Transcribe, decode, correct. The whole letter was then transcribed digit for digit with the clear text around the runs, and decoded by script. Nonsense in the output points to a misread figure, almost always one of the confusable pairs above, and every correction to the transcription was found that way rather than by re-reading at random. The audit. All 1,930 figure groups fall inside 12–43; all thirty-two values occur; no run has an odd number of digits. An out-of-range value or an odd run would be the mark of a transcription error, and none is left.

t: García de Toledo to Philip II, 16 July 1565 — a relief of Malta waved off by the Grand Master’s fires
b: A key built from the clear text could in principle only reproduce what the clear text already implies. The check is a name the clear text does not contain. On f. 1v, after the Grand Master’s signal not to enter, the clear hand writes y ansi lo dize and then the run 2830362539 35 1719 271929 2925 , which decodes to Mosiur de Lenni : Monsieur de Leinì, that is Andrea Provana di Leinì, the Savoyard commander whose galleys sailed in the relief squadron, and exactly the man who would report whether the signals were made. Nothing in the clear text points to him. F. 1v: millas del [ puerto ]. el [ maestre ] les hizo [ las senna / les ] del [ fuego clarissimas ] para que no [ entrassen ] / y ansi lo dize [ Mosiur de Lenni ] y todos los demas y dentro de . The run after dize is the check on the key. Image: Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 1394 no. 247 f. 1v, via PARES (image 2). The rest of the ciphered matter is consistent in the same way: Don Juan de Cardona’s 600 soldiers, the pilot Don Juan Çanoguera , the Conde de Módica serving at his own cost, Gian Andrea Doria’s claim on the viceroy’s funds, and the fortification of Syracuse and Augusta.

t: García de Toledo to Philip II, 16 July 1565 — a relief of Malta waved off by the Grand Master’s fires
b: Clear text roman, figures in italic ; spelling of the leaf kept ( nn = ñ, u / v as written); word division inside a figure run is editorial, since the cipher writes none; square brackets are editorial f. 1r Llevo tan ruyn nueua a V. Mag. el correo passado que no me ha parescido detener este para que en parte la mejore. Los seiscientos soldados que don Juan de Cardona puso en tiera fue Dios servido de guiallos tanbien que todos entraron en el burgo a saluamento . Dizeme este que ha salido que fue tan grande la alegria del maestre , abracando la gente sin podello hablar, que lloraua de plazer ; y tanbien dize que otro dia salio la misma gente a dar en los Turcos y que mataron mas de dozientos, aunque estas salidas en ningun caso queria que las hiziese , y por muchas letras se lo tengo scripto con mucho encarescimiento. Del maestre no tengo carta , que estoy spantado [ms. spantaado ] dello, pero no tengo por mala seña olvidarse de mi, aunque no creo que tardara a dos o tres dias a venir; y conforme a lo que scriuiere uere de proueer lo mas que por el se pudiere . El estar sin galeras me destruye , porque se po- f. 1v -drian hazer algunos effetos en baxeles suyos que van y vienen, pero trayendo las que aca ay ocupadas en iuntar la gente no se puede proueer a todo . Si [u]iniessen las de Spanna me darian mucha ayuda . Las galeras que yban a entrar por el puerto llegaron a quatro millas del, con muy buena orden y gran determinacion , y aquella noche , que sera lunes , vna hora antes que amaneciesse , viniendo el martes , entro a saluamento la uarqueta que yo hauia embiado para auisar al maestre de las sennales , con la qual tuuo auiso de lo que hauia de hazer ; y tornando las galeras el martes en la noche a otras quatro millas del puerto , el maestre les hizo las sennales del fuego clarissimas para que no entrassen , y ansi lo dize Mosiur de Lenni y todos los demas; y dentro de la hora sennalada las continuo la segunda vez, y las galeras se tornaron a meter a la mar por no ser descubiertas , y han llegado aqui esta mannana . El don Juan Çanoguera, que es el que las guiaua , lo hizo muy bien , y todos los demas. Y este no sabe que[r]ido [ms. quesido ] el maestre aceptar estas galeras ; aunque podria ser por parescelle la entrada muy dificultosa , no dexo de tenella por buena senal . Dizen todos los nuestros que, en acabando de hazer el maestre las sennales , vieron y oyeron vna gran cantidad de arcabuzeria, y que juzgauan ellos que sera salua para mostrarnos que nuestra gente sera dentro . Este ombre que es venido salio del burgo el mismo lunes a los diez y nueue, y no trae nueua de la uarqueta que entro , porque no sera aun llegada ; la qual puso el que yo embie a do le mande, y de alli f. 2r hauia de yr a nado hasta el burgo , y ansi llego saluo , como a la clara se ve por las sennales ; y la ciudad hizo el mismo fuego , que tanbien es indicio que llego el que por aquella parte embie con el duplicado . Los tiempos son tales y las necessidades tan grandes, que aunque se tuuiesse mucho dinero no osaria deshazerme de vn rreal para pagar deudas ; y aunque es justissimo lo que V. Mag. manda de Juan Andrea, se podra hazer poco con el, pero lo que se pudiera no se dexara de hazer como V. Mag. lo manda, que cierto yo desseo dalle toda satisfacion, y el solo sera en este tiempo el que de mi cobrara alguna quantidad. Es necessario poner luego mano en comencar a fortificar , por todo lo que podria suceder , la fruente que Caragoca tiene en tierra firme , y en leuantar vn cavallero en la mar que corresponde —çierto es secanos donde podria ser assaltada . Tanbien es necessario comencar al fin de octubre la fortificacion de Augusta , por que la ocasion no mostrasse a los enemigos el segundo salto. Para estas casas es menester dinero , y en este reyno no ay si no infinitas deudas . V. Mag. mande echar quenta de los ytalianos que se han de leuantar , y de los spannoles que se han de pagar, y del sueldo de las naues, que cada mes importa quarenta mil escudos sin dos mesadas que se les deuen; y vease tanbien el uizcocho que de nueuo es menester hazer, que aunque despues se desquente a las galeras su parte, todavia este dinero sale del que V. Mag. me ha embiado. Hanse comprado quinientos quintales de artilleria de peso f. 2v de Espanna , mucha xarcia y madera para las yaretas [jaretas]; y aunque esta xarcia y madera puede seruir para las galeras que se huuieren de hazer, y lo del metal es dinero que no se pierde , todavia cuesta buen pedaço. Tanbien se haze armamento para las ocho galeras que vienen de Espanna , y otros gastos de botas, barriles, murriones y coracinas que no se pueden escusar. Y si se quenta esto, y se añade el sueldo de la ynfanteria , contando tanbien el gasto de [l]onze galeras que se arman de nueuo, vera V. Mag. que la prouision echa no basta para tantas casas, ni yo pu[e]do [ms. puddo ] sustentar con ella los gastos que V. Mag. apunta en su carta , tanto mas si esto se fuesse nada alargando . Y los quarenta y ocho mil ducados que venieron para las galeras ya estaua comido la mitad , y otra buena parte se deue a la gente. Y considerado esto, suplico a V. Mag. mande proueer como mas se paresciere que conuiene a su seruicio, y en el gastallos se terna el miramiento que V. Mag. manda. Dize este que ha salido que todos los turcos que estan en tierra , demas de los bastiones a do tienen sus baterias , estan todos circundados de trincheas siete, ocho y diez palmos altas , assi a la parte de los nuestros como a la parte de la campanna ; y que quando el partio no hauia otros que no las tuuiessen si no mil y quinientos turcos que estauan al agua . Confirma que hauian perdido mucha gente , y que en el campo corrian dolencias de que morian . Por essos auisos vera V. Mag. los nauios que hallo sobre Cabo Bono el baxel que yua con uino a la Goleta . Tengo por cierto que son los de Argel que se uienen a iuntar con la armada ; y esto creo por no saber que de Maltta aya salido cantidad dellos , porque dize este que del armada no se hauia desmandado nauio ninguno quando el partio , ni tan poco lo escriue el gouernador de la ciudad , como vera V. Mag. por su carta original que yra con esta. Cuya vida guarde Nuestro Señor por tan largos años como sus criados y vassallos desseamos y la christiandad ha menester. De Mecina , a XVJ. de Julio 1565. Postscript (entirely in the clear) Ya tengo scripto a V. Mag. por otras quan bien le sirue el conde de Modica, y a su costa; y hauiendole agora scripto el almirante su padre la muerte de la duquesa su madre, y llamandole que vaya a España, no obstante que esto le ymporte mucho, no ha querido hazello ni yrse deste reyno hasta ver el sucesso de las cosas de aca. Hame parescido muy justo auisar dello a V. Mag., para que tenga entendido su voluntad y el seruicio que haze en ello a V. Mag. English García writes from Messina on 16 July 1565, about two months into the siege and some days after the relief known as the Piccolo Soccorso reached the Borgo (Birgu) at the start of July. Everything below that is in italics in the Spanish was in figures. The relief got in. He had sent the King bad news by the last courier and writes now to soften it: the six hundred soldiers Don Juan de Cardona put ashore all entered the Borgo safely. A man just out of the Borgo says the Grand Master embraced them, unable to speak, and wept for joy; and that the next day the same men sortied against the Turks and killed more than two hundred, though García had written many times that there were to be no sorties. He has no letter from the Grand Master himself and expects one within two or three days. A second run turned back. The galleys meant to enter the harbour came within four miles of it, in good order. That night, an hour before dawn on Tuesday, the barqueta he had sent ahead to arrange the signals with the Grand Master got in. On Tuesday night the galleys came again to four miles off, and the Grand Master made the fire-signals, very clear, that they were not to enter, and repeated them within the appointed hour, as Monsieur de Leinì and all the others report. The galleys put back out to sea so as not to be seen, and reached Messina this morning. Çanoguera, who guided them, did it very well. Nobody knows why the Grand Master would not take the galleys in; perhaps the entry looked too hard, but García takes it for a good sign. As the signals ended the galleys heard a great volley of arquebus fire, which they judged a salute to show that the men were inside. The messengers. The man who left the Borgo that Monday has no news of the barqueta , which had not arrived when he left. The barqueta landed García’s messenger where it was ordered, and from there he was to swim to the Borgo; the signals show he arrived. La ciudad , Mdina, made the same fire, a sign that the man sent by that route with the duplicate had arrived too. Money. Even with money in hand he would not dare part with a real to pay debts. He will do what he can for Gian Andrea Doria, as ordered, and Doria will be the only one paid anything. He asks the King to reckon the Italians to be raised, the Spaniards to be paid, and the ships, which cost forty thousand escudos a month with two months’ pay already owed; biscuit to be baked; five hundred quintals of artillery by Spanish weight, cordage and timber for the jaretas ; fitting out the eight galleys coming from Spain and eleven more being armed; casks, barrels, morions and cuirasses; and the infantry’s pay. The provision sent does not cover it: half the 48,000 ducados sent for the galleys is already spent and much of the rest is owed to the men. “Being without galleys ruins me.” Fortification. Work should begin at once on the landward front of Syracuse and on a cavalier facing the sea, where the ground would let it be stormed; and on the fortification of Augusta at the end of October, so that the occasion should not show the enemy “the second leap”. For this money is needed, and in this kingdom there is nothing but infinite debts. The besiegers. The man from the Borgo says all the Turks ashore, besides the bastions where they have their batteries, are ringed with trenches seven, eight and ten palms high, facing both the Christians and the open country; when he left, only fifteen hundred Turks at the water were without them. The Turks have lost many men, and sickness is killing men in their camp. At sea. The ships that a vessel carrying wine to La Goleta found off Cape Bon, García is sure, are the Algiers squadron coming to join the fleet. No ship had left the fleet at Malta when his man came away, and the governor of la ciudad says none either, as his original letter, sent with this one, will show. Postscript, in clear. The Conde de Módica serves well and at his own cost; summoned to Spain by his father the Admiral after his mother’s death, he will not leave Sicily until he sees how things end here. The letter was written during the worst of the siege, while García was still gathering the force that landed on Malta as the Gran Soccorso on 7 September; the siege was raised days later. In July he had few galleys to spare, and this letter shows what they could do: put small parties into the Borgo by night and watch for the Grand Master’s fires.

t: García de Toledo to Philip II, 16 July 1565 — a relief of Malta waved off by the Grand Master’s fires
b: yaretas (f. 2v, line 1): the figures are unambiguous, 42 12 35 20 37 14 36 . It is read as jaretas , the netting rigged over a galley’s deck; with the 41/42 confusion it could be xaretas , the same word. secanos (f. 2r): “çierto es secanos donde podria ser assaltada ” is taken as shoals or dry ground that would let the sea-facing cavalier be stormed. The figures read; the sense is a guess. “salio del burgo el mismo lunes a los diez y nueue”: taken as the hour, not the day of the month, since 19 July is after the letter’s date. Which duplicate went by way of Mdina (f. 2r, el que por aquella parte embie con el duplicado ) is not said; it is presumably a second copy of García’s own message to the Grand Master. The original despatch, which this is the duplicate of, and the Mdina governor’s letter that went with it have not been found on PARES; a search for the ciphered Toledo letters of 1565 returns only this item. The original could carry a contemporary decipherment in the secretariat’s hand, and that would be the independent check on this reading. Until it is found, the check is internal: the self-consistency of the table, the audit, and the names. No published text of the letter was found in web searches for the document and for editions of the Simancas Malta correspondence (18 September 2026). That is not the same as a search of the printed literature on the siege, and an edition may exist that the searches missed. The table was rebuilt here from two cribs in the clear text, not taken from a published source. Toledo’s cipher was not on anyone’s unsolved list, and the alphabetical-order key is easy to recover, so it may well have been recovered before, by Tomokiyo or from other material. The claim is a reading of this letter, not a first break of the cipher.

Tomokiyo, cryptiana , which marks the Malta cipher letters of 1565 as undeciphered. In Tomokiyo’s usage that means there is no interlinear decipherment or nearby deciphered copy. It does not mean unsolved; unsolved material from cryptiana is listed on its unsolved page (G. Lasry, personal communication, 21 September 2026). The key may therefore already be known from other material. Context: the Great Siege of Malta (18 May – September 1565), the Piccolo Soccorso of late June and early July and the Gran Soccorso of September, in the standard accounts of the siege. The digit-for-digit transcription ( transcription.txt ), the key ( key.json ), the decode and render scripts, the raw and edited readings and the notes are in the repository ( toledo1565/ ), with the six PARES images in toledo1565/img/ .

t: Toulon to Van Hogendorp, 30 July 1803 — the code identified, its book offline
b: DECODE R2034: a one-page letter from the Batavian foreign ministry’s cipher clerk to the envoy in Russia, in Croiset’s six-series Correspondentiecijffer, which survives only as a physical booklet (NA 2.21.045/34313). The three decrypted 1801 Berlin dispatches in the same code were transcribed and aligned: they fix 3 of its 67 words, and nine values claimed earlier are withdrawn. R1035, R1038 and R1891 do not fit. The Hague → St Petersburg · numerical word code, six series, Dutch · 30 Jul 1803 · attempted, key not digitised Toulon to Van Hogendorp, 30 July 1803 — the code identified, its book offline from Lodewijk van Toulon → to Dirk van Hogendorp Nationaal Archief, 1.02.13 Legatie Rusland, inv. 208; DECODE R2034. A single page from the Batavian foreign ministry’s cipher clerk to the Republic’s new envoy in Russia, in clear only at the date, the salutation and the signature. Its code is Croiset’s Correspondentiecijffer , which survives only as a physical booklet in the Nationaal Archief. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 22 September 2026 attempted Summary. Lodewijk van Toulon was the clerk in charge of the ministry’s codes. On 30 July 1803 he wrote to Dirk van Hogendorp in 110 code groups. Only “Den Haag 30 July 1803”, “Burger Minister!” and “Heil en Hoogachting! L. van Toulon” are in clear. A start control (430~) and an end control (763~) enclose 67 text groups, and 41 padding groups follow. The Nationaal Archief describes the key: a Correspondentiecijffer made by S. E. Croiset, used from 1799 and annotated for Hogendorp at St Petersburg in 1803. It is inv. 34313 of the Croiset papers (2.21.045) and has not been digitised. The same code carried three dispatches from Berlin in 1801 (DECODE R1944–R1946), and each survives with its contemporary solution. All three were transcribed and aligned here. They fix three of Toulon’s 67 words: handen , brengen and niet . The code’s series are not alphabetical and it has homophones, so the other 64 groups cannot be recovered from so little. An earlier pass had claimed nine values, and it had also rejected two digitised keys on the strength of them. Those values did not survive the full transcriptions and are withdrawn here. The 5 August 1803 codebook (R1035) and the 1765 St Petersburg key (R1038) were tested again and neither fits. A scan of the six written pages of inv. 34313 would make the letter read mechanically. R2034, the first five rows. Each group carries its series mark above it: a wave (430, 336, 51), a caret (120, 526, 307), a double stroke (897, 230, 934), a bar (528, 451, 877) or a plus (1, 518, 616). Unmarked groups are a sixth series. Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 1.02.13 Legatie Rusland inv. 208, via DECODE R2034.

t: Toulon to Van Hogendorp, 30 July 1803 — the code identified, its book offline
b: DECODE’s cataloguer notes that a cipher clerk seldom wrote in his own name to an envoy, and that such a short message “can only pertain to matters of encryption”. The date fits: six days later, on 5 August 1803, the ministry signed a new and much larger codebook for the St Petersburg legation (DECODE R1035). Hogendorp’s own ciphered dispatches of 5 July 1803 (R1942) were written in the older code, the one Toulon uses here. The code has six series of numbers from 1 to 992: unmarked, and marked with a wave, a caret, a double stroke, a bar or a plus. The same number under a different mark is a different word. The 1801 solutions show that common words have several equivalents ( Heer is 453̅ and 370~), and that the words in each series are not in alphabetical order (in the wave series 297 is Men , 370 Heer , 500 dat , 580 de , 733 zeer ). A number therefore says nothing about the word it stands for, and without the book only a word already seen in a solved letter can be read. The transcription was checked against the image at full zoom. Ten groups differ from the first transcription of 20 September: 336~, 897″, 880^, 859~, 528̅, 145^, 616+, 215̅, 625̅ and 188̅.

t: Toulon to Van Hogendorp, 30 July 1803 — the code identified, its book offline
h: The 1801 letters in the same code
b: The key’s annotation says it was used “in anno 1801” with the Batavian ministers abroad. Three dispatches of the chargé d’affaires Étienne Bourdeaux from Berlin survive with their solutions: R1946 (no. 20, 7 February 1801): 202 groups against a 158-word solution that opens “De Heer van Haugwiz en de Heer van Krudner, die intime vrienden zijn, zyn zeer en peine over het envoy van Kalitscheff naar Parys”. After the start control 357″ it runs strictly one group per word as far as niet (word 150). That fit is confirmed where 153̅ falls on Paul and 222̅ on niet . R1944 (no. 16, 31 January 1801; its solution is misfiled as R1946’s third image): 115 groups against 77 words. The subject is a stolen cipher. Rosencrantz believes a servant copied his cipher, the bureau that held it was broken into, and a courier is being sent to St Petersburg with a new one. 927+ is Cyffer three times, but two runs of the cipher have no counterpart in the solution. R1945 (3 February 1801): 187 groups against 152 words. The alignment drifts, so no value can be fixed from it. Every group of R2034 was looked up in all three, and in Hogendorp’s unsolved R1942. A value counts only if the number and the mark both match: Group Word of R2034 Value From Grade 394 5 handen R1946, word 111 H 58 28 brengen R1944, its last word M 222̅ 51 niet R1946, word 150 H 934″ · 907^ 18 · 50 wonderlijk · zoo Sillem’s paraphrase of R1942 I Three padding groups also turn up in R1946 (205̅ gantschelyk , 458+ ook , 239″ antwoord ). This confirms the code is the same but adds nothing to the text. J. A. Sillem’s 1890 biography of Hogendorp quotes “zo wonderlijk” from the ciphered dispatch no. 12 of 5 July 1803. The adjacent pair 907^ 934″ in R1942 is a plausible match, but nothing in the print fixes where the phrase falls, so the pair is kept only as a conjecture.

t: Toulon to Van Hogendorp, 30 July 1803 — the code identified, its book offline
h: What was tried and ruled out
b: The nine values of the first pass. The 20–21 September pass put 51~ = van , 279 = en , 153 = Paul , 43~ = zyne , 304~ = wegens and 380~ = de . It took them from partial alignments of R1944 and R1946 that were never saved as transcriptions. The full transcriptions do not contain those groups where the table put them. In R1946 van is 444̅ or 957~ and wegens is 564~. Paul is 153̅ with a bar, while R2034’s 153 has none. These values are withdrawn. The 5 August 1803 codebook, R1035. Van Kampen’s reconstruction (HistoCrypt 2026) has 1,849 entries in seven series. R2034 was decoded with every assignment of its five marks to R1035’s six. The best assignment gives no more hits than random marks do (22% of groups under the natural mapping, 28% at random), and the words it produces do not connect. Its one striking run, “met Zijne Keizerlijke Majesteit”, is a single phrase entry between two empty cells. Hogendorp’s R1942 of 5 July is also at chance against R1035, as it should be for a dispatch written a month before that book. The 1765 St Petersburg key, R1038, and Schimmelpenninck’s key, R1891 (Croiset papers inv. 34312). R1038 has no entry for niet , handen or brengen . Both mark single digits rather than whole groups, so they belong to different systems. The other Batavian records on DECODE. R1926 (Schimmelpenninck, London, 28 February 1803) and R1896 use digit marks. R1947 and R2053 (Van Dedem, 1789) use four-digit groups. R1033 (Six van Oterleek, 1808) is in the R1035 book. None is in this code. Print. Sillem’s Dirk van Hogendorp (1890), the 1943 edition of Hogendorp’s letters to his brother, Colenbrander’s Gedenkstukken IV, Tomokiyo’s Cryptiana and Van Kampen’s paper give no decipherment of this letter.

t: Urquhart’s Cyphral Octastich — a book cipher on his own Jewel, read without the plaintext
b: Eight lines and a “Decagram” of numbers on the last leaf of The Jewel (1652), Schmeh’s Top 50 no. 28. Number k indexes a word on physical page k of the book, and Urquhart took the first word of the initial he needed: a habit checkable without any plaintext. The public transcription was thirteen numbers short; the 1983 edition’s photographs on the HCPortal give 285, which decode straight with 238 of 284 first-occurrence hits against 0.43 for shuffled and random-page controls, into a royalist prayer for Charles II. Vals AI published the rule in August 2026 as a Claude Fable 5.1 result; the companion distich claim does not reproduce. London · book cipher on the author's own printed book · 1652–53 · octastich read Thomas Urquhart’s Cyphral Octastich and Distich from Thomas Urquhart The Jewel (1652), final leaf · eight lines and a “Decagram”, 285 numbers to 201 · Logopandecteision (1653), “The Cyphral Distich”, 64 numbers to 70 · Schmeh’s Top 50, no. 28 The octastich is read in full from the EEBO-TCP text of The Jewel and a fresh transcription of its 285 numbers from the 1983 edition, without using the plaintext published by Vals AI on 31 August 2026; 238 of 284 numbers are first-occurrence hits against 0.43 for both controls. The distich rule does not reproduce. Daniel Bourdeau · solved in part 16 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 solved in part Summary. Urquhart printed a verse under the octastich saying the key was “gather’d out of my Exskybalorum” and that he loved “an aphaeresified treason”: the cipher takes word-initials from the book it is printed in. The k -th number, counting straight through the poem, is a word index into physical page k of the 1652 Jewel , and Urquhart took the first word on the page that began with the letter he wanted. That habit makes the rule testable without any plaintext: whether number n on page k is the first word of its own initial is a fact about the page. The public transcription (Schmeh, 2015) turned out to be short by thirteen numbers; the 1983 Jack and Lyall edition, photographed on the HCPortal record, gives 285. Decoded one number per page against the TCP text, 238 of 284 are first-occurrence hits, against 0.43 for the same numbers shuffled and 0.44 for random pages, and the poem reads: Great Lord, mantaine that regal familie, / Whereof King Charls the second is the head, / And grant that he may beare the supreme sweigh / Where English, Scots and Irsh are borne and bred; / And […] this usurp’d authoritie / Reigne in his royal predecessors stead: / Let him be our sole Cesar, Artur, Hector, / Our Emperour, King, Monarch and Protector. / Amen, so be it. Vals AI published this rule and plaintext on 31 August 2026 as a Claude Fable 5.1 result; here it is reached from the text and the numbers alone, and their two caveats are traced to defects of the digitised copy. The distich claim, i -th number into the i -th Proquiritation, gives 34 of 64 first-occurrence hits, chance for texts that short, and no English. Status: octastich read, ten letters of line 5 excepted; distich open.

t: Urquhart’s Cyphral Octastich — a book cipher on his own Jewel, read without the plaintext
b: The distich stands under the heading “THE CYPHRAL DISTICH” after the thirty-two Proquiritations that close Logopandecteision , followed by six lines promising that “an honest skilful man” will find in it “his own heart’s wishes, and the Author’s minde”. Reticuli Labs showed on 1 September 2026, and the 1834 Maitland Club reprint confirms, that this page is in the 1834 Works (p. 417) and not in the British Library’s 1653 copy. The octastich stands on the last leaf of The Jewel (1652), a leaf missing from every digitised copy; its public transcription is Klaus Schmeh’s, from a scan sent him in 2014, and the HCPortal record holds a scan with the verse beneath it, which a reader quoted in 2019: To this Octastick if you will subjoyn / A Decagram of this same stuff of mine, / All gather’d out of my Exskybalorum, / You’ll find a Rule by which, with great decorum, / You may most comfortably regulate / Your actions, thoughts and speeches; and know that / I love an aphaeresified treason / Better then any prosthesized reason. Aphaeresis is the loss of a word’s first letter. Urquhart says, in his way, that the cipher is made of initials taken out of his own book. The octastich as reprinted in 1983: the first line and the start of the second. Read as word indexes into the pages of The Jewel , line one gives “Great Lord, mantaine that regal familie” and line two “Whereof King Charls the second is the head”. Image: Urquhart, The Jewel, ed. Jack and Lyall (Scottish Academic Press, 1983) p. 212, photograph via the HCPortal record.

t: Urquhart’s Cyphral Octastich — a book cipher on his own Jewel, read without the plaintext
h: A test that never sees the plaintext
b: A book cipher of this kind is normally judged by whether the letters it yields make sense, which invites the objection that a determined reader can make sense of anything. Urquhart’s habit removes that objection. If he scanned each page from the top and stopped at the first word beginning with the letter he needed, then for the right page the number he wrote is the index of the first word of its own initial. That is a property of the number and the page alone. For a wrong page, or a wrong rule, it holds at the base rate, which in this book is about 43 % for a random page and index because small indices are common and the first few words of any page are first occurrences by construction. The EEBO-TCP transcription of The Jewel was parsed into word lists per page. The 1652 printer numbered pages 34–35, 38–39, 42–43 and 46–47 twice and skipped 60 and 110, so pages are counted physically from p. 1, and three duplicated page breaks that the TCP carries for re-shot images are removed. Schmeh’s 272-number transcription, the only one in circulation since 2015, omits the run-over lines of stanzas 2 and 6, one figure, and misreads one; a dynamic-programme alignment that may skip pages still placed it at 231 first-occurrence hits in 267 and read five lines. The photographs of the 1983 edition on the HCPortal record give the full 285, which then decode straight, one number per page. Run First-occurrence rate The 285 numbers, one per physical page 0.838 (238/284) Same numbers shuffled, 200 trials mean 0.434, max 0.491 Numbers in order, pages randomly permuted, 200 trials mean 0.436, max 0.509 Schmeh’s 272 numbers, aligned with page skips 0.865 (231/267), vs 0.686 shuffled and re-aligned Distich, i -th number into i -th Proquiritation 0.53 (34/64), no English Distich, shuffled, against pages of The Jewel , 100 trials mean 0.50, max 0.62 Line 1 alone makes the case: 28 of its 33 numbers are exactly the first word of the needed initial on physical page k , and the other five are one word off (25 for 26, 18 for 17, 23 for 22, 75 for 74) or a TCP variant, which is the size of difference one expects between a modern tokenisation and a 1652 page.

t: Van Reede from Berlin, 1787–1793 — the Grand Chiffre despatches read, the 1793 code open
b: DECODE lists three ciphered letters of the Dutch envoy at Berlin as non-decrypted. The French despatches of December 1787 and March 1788 are in William V’s Grand Chiffre of 1782 (DECODE R1024), confirmed on a control letter with known plaintext; the digits the DECODE transcription left under one catch-all sign were resolved with a French language model. They report the King of Prussia’s refusal to guarantee the Dutch possessions overseas in the 1788 alliance, and Russian and Austrian moves in the Turkish war. The 1793 letter to the Secret Committee is in another, marked three-digit code and stays unread. Berlin → The Hague · one-part numerical code-nomenclator · 1787–1793 · read in part Van Reede from Berlin: the Prussian alliance and the possessions overseas to Van de Spiegel Nationaal Archief 3.01.26 (L. P. van de Spiegel) inv. 190 · DECODE R1026 (29 Dec. 1787, two pages) and R1027 (4 Mar. 1788, one page); Nationaal Archief 1.01.02 (Staten-Generaal) inv. 6695 · DECODE R1893 (24 Mar. 1793, four pages). The two French despatches are in the 1782 Grand Chiffre of Stadholder William V (DECODE R1024). A control letter with its plaintext on DECODE confirms the key; the digits the DECODE transcription could not place were resolved with a French language model. The 1793 letter is in another code and is not read. Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read in part Summary. Arend Willem van Reede, the Dutch Republic’s envoy in Berlin after the Prussian restoration of the Stadholder in 1787, wrote to the Grand Pensionary Van de Spiegel in a numerical code. DECODE holds three of his letters as non-decrypted and suggests the code is William V’s “Grand Chiffre”. It is: the key of 1782 (DECODE R1024, 4,732 entries from 1 to 5000, in alphabetical order) reads an undated Van Reede letter whose plaintext DECODE also gives (R1028) word for word. Applied to R1026 and R1027 it at first gave broken text, because the DECODE transcriber wrote J+ for a sign they could not place, and that sign does not stand for one digit. Each such group was tried with all ten digits and the reading chosen by a French character model; 105 groups were settled that way and both despatches now read. 452 of 472 groups have a value. They concern the treaty of alliance Prussia signed with the Republic in April 1788: the King “could not guarantee our possessions overseas”, and the article was reworded to cover only an attack by a European power. The 1793 letter to the Secret Committee of the States-General is written in marked three-digit groups (696 groups, 513 distinct forms), for which no key has been found; it stays open.

t: Van Reede from Berlin, 1787–1793 — the Grand Chiffre despatches read, the 1793 code open
b: R1026 (29 December 1787) and R1027 (4 March 1788) are Van Reede’s own despatches to Laurens Pieter van de Spiegel, in dot-separated groups of one to four digits with clear French at the head and foot. R1026 carries an interlinear gloss over its first groups, dites … avant hier , which is the first check on any key. The two letters share 49 groups. R1893 (24 March 1793, to the Secret Committee, in Dutch) is different to look at: three-digit groups with strokes, carets, tildes and dots above single digits. R1026, first page: the gloss dites … avant hier above the first groups. Image: Nationaal Archief, The Hague, 3.01.26 inv. 190, first page, via DECODE R1026. The key is DECODE R1024, the “Grand Chiffre” of William V (Koninklijk Huisarchief A29, inv. 301, dated 1782): a one-part French code in which the numbers run with the alphabet, up to 5000. Whole words, names ( le Comte de Finkenstein , Monsieur de Herzberg ), syllables and letters all have values, so rare words are spelt out: ul·er , simple·ment .

t: Van Reede from Berlin, 1787–1793 — the Grand Chiffre despatches read, the 1793 code open
b: R1028, an undated Van Reede letter headed Chiffre de Mr de Reede , has its plaintext written out on DECODE. Its groups, read with R1024, give la reponse A donner au [Roi] à la communication que Sa Majesté vient de faire A leurs haut Puissance les voici le Ministre d’Angleterre A ajouter dans son rapport qu’on esperer·oit ic[i] qu’on approuver·oit A Londres… , matching the clear version word for word. The key is right and complete enough. The same key on R1026 read cleanly in some lines ( il doit y avoir ce matin … une conference à ce sujet ) and made nonsense in others. Every nonsense word came from a group containing DECODE’s J+ , which the transcriber defined as “a sign that is not represented by other signs” and used 136 times in the two letters. The first pass read it as 3. It is not one digit: 275J is 2750 dites , as the gloss says; JJ8J is 1181 le Roi ; 375J in ce matin à … heures is 3751 dix . The writer’s hand has several forms of some figures, and the transcriber put the doubtful ones under one symbol.

t: Van Reede from Berlin, 1787–1793 — the Grand Chiffre despatches read, the 1793 code open
b: resolve_j.py reads the DECODE transcription, keeps plain digits as written and treats each J+ as unknown. For each group it lists every digit filling whose number is in the key, and a beam search (width 40) chooses among them with a six-character French model built from eighteenth-century diplomatic correspondence (the Politische Correspondenz text already in the repository). Groups without J+ are never changed. 79 groups in R1026 and 26 in R1027 were resolved this way. The model can choose a wrong but grammatical word, and it cannot repair a plain digit the transcriber misread; both kinds of error remain in the passages marked below.

Square brackets are groups with no value; [?] marks stretches that stay garbled. dites [1250] … avant hier les deux Ministres ont proposé au Roi le projet de l’alliance tel que vous l’avés, Monsieur [?] … j’ai prié Monsieur de Herzberg de détail[ler] séparement les sentiments dans le rapport et de motif[s] [?] la réponse … hier au soir [?]. Il doit y avoir ce matin à dix heures une conférence à ce sujet encore entre le Roi et ses deux Ministres; j’espère qu’il n’y aura pas de changement. Le seul [point] jusqu’ici dont il soient [?], c’est que le Roi a dit [qu’il] ne pouvoit pas garantir nos possessions d’outre-mer. Je ne l’ai pas demandé, mais bien qu’au cas [que nous] fussions attaqués [?] par une [puissance de] l’Europe [?] fournir en argent [?]; peut-être Sa Majesté entend[-elle] par garantir fournir [?]; mais quand cela seroit [4433] le Prince d’Anhalt-Schaumbourg [?] … ce point, l’article [?] que j’ai eu l’honneur de vous [?] l’Angleterre [331] à la réquisition du Comte de Finkenstein, Monsieur de Herzberg [?] le Traité [?] fixer [?] jusqu’à présent [?] a été arrêté hier, et ce que j’ai eu l’honneur de vous […] [clear:] Depuis que ceci a été chiffré, Monsieur, j’ai [appris] au sortir d’une conférence que les deux ministres ont eu avec le Roi … … il est à craindre que [?] a été décidé dans la conférence de [ce] matin, que sans article ul·térieur le mot de possessions d’outre-mer on dir·oit simple·ment que si la République étoit attaquée par une Puissance [européenne] … lui fourn·iroit les secours [?] … si leurs Hautes [Puissances] … ordonne·nt [?] d’après la manière dont ceci m’a été dit [?] [2800] [3160] [clear:] Si j’ai bien compris, je n’ai pas [lieu de] m’attendre à d’autres changements. J’ai l’honneur d’être avec un très profond respect … In English. Two days ago the two ministers, Finckenstein and Hertzberg, put the draft alliance to the King as Van de Spiegel had sent it; a further conference between the King and the ministers is set for ten this morning. The only point raised so far is that the King said he could not guarantee the Republic’s possessions overseas. Van Reede had not asked for that, only that if they were attacked in Europe the King would help with money or supplies. After the conference he adds that the article is to drop the words possessions outre-mer and say simply that if the Republic is attacked by a European power the King will furnish the aid; he expects no further change. This is the defensive treaty signed at Berlin on 15 April 1788, which guaranteed the stadholderate and the Republic’s territory in Europe; the Anglo-Dutch treaty of the same day covered the possessions overseas.

t: Van Reede from Berlin, 1787–1793 — the Grand Chiffre despatches read, the 1793 code open
b: [3660] [2800] les nouvelles de Russie … [ce] matin port[ent] que mes[sieurs] [?] sont fort [?] de ce que l’Impératrice doit avoir [?] la triple alliance. Monsieur de [?] n’a point [2637] encore de réponse et ne croit la recevoir qu’après que l’Impératrice aura celle qu’elle attend de Vienne à la demande qu’elle a faite à l’Empereur, s’il étoit résolu [?] … à ce qu’on croit … l’Empereur a fait la déclaration [de guerre] à la Turquie. Monsieur de [?] croit encore que l’[?] voudra attendre le retour du premier courier [50] expédié à Londres, qui a été suivi de deux autres, avant de s’expliquer sur les propositions du [?] [3153] [2751] [3660]. [clear:] N’y ayant rien de plus, Monsieur, qui puisse mériter votre attention, j’ai l’honneur de vous présenter mes respects … [A. W. van] Reede In English. News from Russia; the Russian side is anxious about the proposed triple alliance of Britain, Prussia and the Republic. The Russian envoy has no answer yet and expects none until the Empress has Vienna’s reply to her question to the Emperor; Joseph II has made his declaration of war on Turkey (9 February 1788). A courier has gone to London, followed by two more, before anyone will declare on the proposals.

t: Van Reede from Berlin, 1787–1793 — the Grand Chiffre despatches read, the 1793 code open
b: Groups with no value. R1026: 1250, 2142 3068 (two groups run together), 331, 308?9, 2637, 2800, 3160; the corrected 4433 over 4 4 3 8 reads, though its value is uncertain. R1027: 3660 (twice), 2800, 3?089, 2637, 1?1021, 50, 3153, 2751. 2637, 2800 and 3660 recur in both letters and are probably names added after 1782. Garbled stretches. Where DECODE misread a plain digit, the key gives a real but wrong word ( comme ils mauvais oyent à différer , Monsieur de L L nr , probably the Russian envoy Alopeus). A new transcription from the images would clear most of them; the scans on DECODE are 1290 px wide and the hand’s variant figures are hard to separate at that size. Grades. The readings are not graded group by group. The structural sentences quoted in English (the conference, the refusal to guarantee the overseas possessions, the reworded article, Joseph II’s declaration) rest on runs of groups without J+ and are certain; words chosen by the model are probable. R1893, 24 March 1793, to the Secret Committee: not read. Three-digit groups whose single digits carry one of five marks, 696 groups in 513 distinct marked forms. That is a code of several thousand values, not the Grand Chiffre. The Fagel-family keys on DECODE (R2846, R2848, R2850, R2851) and the decrypted control R2243 do not fit it, and there is no crib. With far fewer groups than code values, a ciphertext-only attack is not feasible; it needs the Secret Committee’s key or a deciphered copy from the States-General’s secret files.

t: Van Reede to William V, 1792 — the lemon-juice letter
b: A one-page letter in William V’s Grand Chiffre, catalogued on DECODE as partially decrypted with its contents unknown. Read in full with the 1782 key R1024. It is a cover note: the Prince’s secretary Larrey is told that the enclosure’s four blank half-pages carry writing in lemon juice, and that the figures after the message are nulls. Berlin → The Hague · one-part numerical code-nomenclator · 4 February 1792 · read Van Reede to William V, 1792: the lemon-juice letter to William V Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 205; DECODE R1057, one page, “partially decrypted”. Read end to end with the Stadholder’s Grand Chiffre: the cipher is a cover note pointing to a despatch in invisible ink. Daniel Bourdeau · read 21 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read Summary. The Unsolved Catalogue listed this letter (item 217) from the DECODE record: a numerical nomenclator, partially decrypted, contents unknown. DECODE’s own note already named the code as William V’s “Grand Chiffre”, and the key survives as DECODE R1024; it had just read two other Van Reede despatches ( Van Reede 1787 ). A contemporary hand glossed the first eight lines between the figures, but DECODE’s transcription of that gloss is garbled (“monsieur de Raney eal avenant… blanc he de ci r cle”) and no one had put the letter together. Decoded with R1024, all 62 message groups read at once, with one transcription correction (4204 → 4202, tro ). The letter tells M. de Larrey that there is citron , lemon juice, on the four blank half-pages of the enclosure, and asks him to warn the Prince of Orange and hand him the letter. It ends: “les chiffres suivants sont des non-valeurs”. The 21 groups after it are nulls. The enclosure, which carried the actual news, is not on the record. The letter, with the contemporary pencil gloss over the figures (“tro n sur le(s) … demi”, “blanc he de l i n clu”). The last three rows carry no gloss: they are the nulls. Image: Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 205, via DECODE R1057 (rotated here).

t: Van Reede to William V, 1792 — the lemon-juice letter
b: Berlin, 4 February 1792, Van Reede to “Monsieur”, in clear except for eleven lines of figures separated by dots, signed “A. W. van Reede”. 83 groups in all. The key is the 1782 one-part French Grand Chiffre of William V (KHA A29 inv. 301, DECODE R1024, values 1–5000), the same one that reads R1026, R1027 and the control R1028.
