t: Del Vasto to Charles V and a letter to “Garbino”, 1527–28 — one read in part by others, one read 98 %, one without its key
b: Three imperial ciphers in BnF fr. 3022, listed with no decipherment. Del Vasto’s letter from Ischia of 27 September 1527 had been read in part by George Lasry and Satoshi Tomokiyo, with 47 of its 1,146 words still queried. The anonymous “report” is del Vasto’s own letter of December 1527: with Lasry’s key, code groups identified here from context and his syllable signs corrected, it reads 98.0 % of 1,680 cipher signs, measured, as his plan to march on Siena, Perugia and Urbino; ten code groups stay open. The Madrid letter to “Garbino” is in Hieronimo Ranzo’s initial-letter code. Its numbering is not alphabetical, and without the table only its function words come out. Ischia, Rome and Madrid → Charles V and “Garbino” · letter cipher with code groups; initial-letter code · September 1527 – April 1528 · partly read Del Vasto to Charles V, and a letter to “Garbino” from Madrid, 1527–28 from Alfonso d'Avalos → to Charles V Bibliothèque nationale de France, français 3022 nos. 6, 10 and 20 · imperial papers that reached French hands during Lautrec’s campaign in Italy · catalogued with “no decipherment noted” One of the three had already been read in part by others. One is read here, 98 % of its cipher measured, with George Lasry’s key extended; ten code groups stay open. The third is in a code whose key does not survive, and it stays unread. Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 18 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 read in part Summary. The catalogue grouped three pieces as one target: a letter of the Marquis del Vasto to Charles V from “Ysola” (Ischia), 27 September 1527 (no. 10); an anonymous “Rapport … à l’empereur” (no. 6); and an Italian memoir from Madrid, 11 April 1528 (no. 20). The first thing to check was whether anyone had read them already. No. 10 had been read : George Lasry in 2023, text edited by Satoshi Tomokiyo in 2026, though 47 of its 1,146 words are still queried and it was not reworked here. No. 6 is del Vasto’s own letter of early December 1527. Lasry had its letter layer but not its code groups, and some of his syllable signs are paired wrongly. Code groups identified here from context, and syllable signs corrected against the manuscript, bring it from 92.6 % with Lasry’s key alone to 98.0 % of 1,680 cipher signs, measured . It reads as del Vasto’s plan for moving the army out of Rome. No. 20 is a letter to “Garbino” in the code of Hieronimo Ranzo, a kinsman of the Chancellor Gattinara. All 1,315 of its groups were transcribed, with about 2,600 more from Ranzo’s own letters. Without the key, only its function words can be recovered. Status: partly read. No. 10 read by others, 47 words queried; no. 6 read 98.0 % measured, with ten code groups (11 signs) and nine short stretches (23 signs) open; no. 20 not read. No. 20 needs Ranzo’s code table or a clear copy of one of his letters.

t: Del Vasto to Charles V and a letter to “Garbino”, 1527–28 — one read in part by others, one read 98 %, one without its key
b: Français 3022 is a sixteenth-century recueil of originals and copies, mostly imperial correspondence of 1527–28 that came into French hands. There are about twenty letters of Juan Pérez, the imperial secretary in Rome, several of them in clear. There are three letters of the Marquis del Vasto (Alfonso d’Ávalos), who commanded the imperial infantry after the Sack of Rome. There are Spanish “avertimientos” of 1528 from Fuenterrabía and Bayonne, and a small bundle of Italian espionage papers. The notice’s folio numbers run about three higher than the ink foliation. Below, folios are the ink numbers and “views” are Gallica’s (ark btv1b90601558). No. Folios (views) What it is Outcome 10 ff. 26–28 and loose f. 39 (51–55, 76–77) Del Vasto to Charles V, “de Ysola”, 27 September 1527 Read in part by others (Lasry 2023, Tomokiyo 2026); 47 of 1,146 words queried; not reworked or measured here 6 ff. 16v–17v (32–34) Catalogued as an anonymous report; actually del Vasto to Charles V, Rome, early December 1527 Read, 98.0 % of 1,680 cipher signs measured; 10 code groups and 9 short stretches open 19 ff. 40–43 (78–85) Del Vasto to Charles V, Rome, 6 November 1527 (not in the target, same key as no. 6) Lasry’s letter layer for f. 40; ff. 41r–41v searched here for contexts; ff. 41–43 not transcribed; content summarised in CSP Spain 20 ff. 44–46v (86–91) Italian letter to “Garbino”, Madrid, 11 April 1528 Transcribed; not read 20bis, 21 ff. 48–50v (94–98) A jargon, a code-name list and an “Aditione nel zifra” Read; they explain the design of no. 20’s code

t: Del Vasto to Charles V and a letter to “Garbino”, 1527–28 — one read in part by others, one read 98 %, one without its key
h: Checked first: who had read them
b: The catalogue says “no decipherment noted”, and the obvious place for a French decipherment was checked first. The eighteenth-century Clairambault copies were searched. Clairambault 327 ff. 279–280 copies no. 20 as “Lettre non signée écrite au seigneur Garbino du 11 d’avril 1528 … partie en chiffre, partie non”, with the cipher copied and nothing deciphered. Clairambault 314 f. 337 copies the addition sheet. Neither carries a decipherment, and none turned up in the neighbouring français volumes. The decipherments are modern. Tomokiyo’s cryptiana pages record that George Lasry sent him a solution of no. 10 in 2023. In 2026 Tomokiyo edited it into a Spanish text and published it as “Gasto–Charles V Cipher 1”. That text is not complete: of its 1,146 words, 47 carry a query, 19 of them a bare “?” for an unread group, and a few stretches are garbled; Tomokiyo still asks for someone to finish it. He also published Lasry’s preliminary letter-level decryption of a second cipher, used in no. 6 and in no. 19, asking for someone who knows Spanish to finish that too. No. 10 is therefore counted here as read in part by others. It was not reworked, and since only an edited text exists and no sign transcription, it is not measured. BnF fr. 3022 f. 26r, no. 10: del Vasto from Ischia, 27 September 1527. The cipher letters are disguised Latin letters with word divisions kept, which is why it fell to Lasry’s solver. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3022 f. 26r, via Gallica (btv1b90601558, view 51).

t: Del Vasto to Charles V and a letter to “Garbino”, 1527–28 — one read in part by others, one read 98 %, one without its key
b: The piece catalogued as an anonymous report opens in clear: “A seis de noviembre escrivi a V. M. muy largo y tanbien a xxvij de setiembre, cuyos duplicados van con esta”. The clear first page reports the agreement with the Pope for “la libertad suya y de los cardenales” (the capitulation of 26 November) and says that del Vasto is still in Rome only because the Prince of Orange, “el qual se espera que verna de aqui a tres dias”, has not yet arrived to take the command. That puts it in the first days of December 1527. f. 16v: “y por otros se sabe como han buelto sobre Mylan”, then cipher. The first cipher words, dʃfp nnbt qʃftxp , read creo mas presto . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3022 f. 16v, via Gallica (btv1b90601558, view 32). The cipher is a Caesar shift of one place over a 21-letter alphabet, with homophones, plus a nomenclator of three-letter groups beginning with b , c or d . Lasry’s decryption has the letter layer right; it checks against the f. 16v ciphertext word for word. It leaves the groups as [doz] , [deh] and so on. His key also pairs a row of syllable signs two to a label (al, con, de, el, es, la, lo, no, para, por, qve, sin), and checked against the glyphs these pairings merge different signs: boz is esto , not “fin” (“y por esto pienso”, “en estos tiempos”); bab is mas ; bar is tan (“tan adelante”, “tan cerca”); bop is como ; bopt , Lasry’s “con s”, is ellos (“porque ellos no tienen gente”); bie is el , not “al”; bis is de ; and bep is es in some places and en in others. Two of his cipher words are not text at all: at stands at every boundary between clear and cipher, going in and coming out, and quia stands before the cipher on f. 17r and f. 41r. They are switch markers. The barred sign ≡ is a stop. The code groups were identified by taking every occurrence of each across nos. 6 and 19 and reading the Spanish around it. All are grade I (inferred from context); none is confirmed by a key or a clear copy. Group Reading Deciding context doz Lautreque “piénsase que [doz] será para ir sobre el reino” deh la Marca “su camino es por la [deh], porque traen su artillería por agua hasta Ravena” bog buelta “camina la [bog] del reino”; “la [bog] de Perosa” ceg hombre “no quieren ser más [ceg]s d’armas” daf quiere “para caminar un exército se re[daf]n” (requieren) dor para “[dor] ir sobre el reino”, “[dor] caminar” baf primero “mi parecer es [baf] que salga el exército” dnd qual “Siena, la [dnd] es muy devota de V. M.” dnb dinero “alguna manera de [dnb] o de hazelles la guerra” biq , boq duque, estado “al [biq] de Urbino”; “el [boq] de Urbino y tomallo” cef gente “esta [cef] ha venido en un número tan poco” dod , don , dum , cez , raq quando, si, su, ni, mi “por vía de [dum] Santidad”; “no se puede mover [cez] dar un paso” bet dello(s) “no quedando en Lombardía exército [bet]s tan pujante”; no. 19 f. 41v “el poco cuidado que [bet] he” da otro (not “liga”) “no[da]s” = nosotros; no. 19 “no hiziesen [da] fruto” dop tiempo (not “invierno”) “si el [dop] que ya entra fuerte no lo estorva”; “en estos [dop]s” dab , das tiene(n) “porque ellos no [dab]n gente” <37> final(mente) “y [<37>]mente no podrían”; in no. 19 “y [<37>]mente yo veo” The rest of the table (di mandado, coy Italia, der poca, bim empresa, cip mil, cac Florencia, bag rica, det he, bad basta(ra), bas deve or puede, and others) is in n6_codes.json and n6_reading.md . The measure is taken on n6_signs.tsv , which keeps Lasry’s decryption as a list of cipher signs, adds five signs seen on the image that his list leaves out, and gives each run a reading and a status; n6_measure.py checks it reproduces his stream exactly. State of the key Cipher signs read Fraction Lasry’s key as it stands 1,555 / 1,680 92.6 % with the code readings of 18 September 1,595 / 1,680 94.9 % with the 22 September corrections and additions 1,646 / 1,680 98.0 % With these the cipher of ff. 16v–17v reads as a strategic proposal. Del Vasto wants the army out of Rome and moving north before Lautrec settles the matter in Lombardy. His plan: secure Siena, “la qual es muy devota de V. M.”; threaten Florence so that the League must come to its aid; take Perugia, “una tierra del Patrimonio muy rica y muy gruesa”, and the state of Urbino, “en el qual se hallará poca resistencia”; and pass into the Marche, “donde no pueden faltar vituallas”. It ends with a warning that runs through all his letters of that winter: “que el exército por lo de advenir no se puede sostener desta manera”, and that with so many shortages “es imposible que el servicio de V. M. se haga como sus fieles vasallos deseamos”.

t: Del Vasto to Charles V and a letter to “Garbino”, 1527–28 — one read in part by others, one read 98 %, one without its key
b: Every code value above is grade I, read from context. The 34 signs still unread are these. Ten code groups, eleven signs. Each has one or two contexts, and none fits a single value. Blocker: open codes; more contexts are in no. 19 ff. 41–43, which are not yet transcribed. dnh : “porque según la [dnh] no la seguirán en venir tan adelante”. Roma, suggested on 18 September, does not fit. bnq : “dificultoso el bolver y que mas el quedar y [bnq] y finalmente no podrían”. rar (twice): “es ganar en el camino a [rar] y ponella debaxo el mando de V. M.”; “si no los suyços se acogieren [rar]”. Florencia or Luca are candidates; neither is settled. car : “sera poner espanto a [car] y ocasión a estos enemigos”. cny : “en esta empresa servirá … mil [cny]”. bny : “de hazelles hazer [bny] un movimiento”. beb : “podrase ir más fácilmente a socorrella [beb] porque es mejor el camino”. bnc : “podrase tomar apuntamiento [es bnc]”. ge+ : after “como si se estuviese el exército dentro”; possibly a stop. der at 17va.2: “la principal de [der de] país”. Elsewhere der = poca , which does not fit here. Nine short stretches, 23 signs besides the codes. The signs are transcribed, but the syllable values that make sense elsewhere make none here, most likely because Lasry’s labels merge different glyphs, as they do for es/en and con/tan/ellos. Blocker: open codes; they need a glyph-level retranscription of these words. the head of f. 16v, “[y y por] [mq] creo mas presto”; “[en de las los] que más se ha de trabajar”; “el duque de Urbino [es de] otro exército está en Narni y Todi”; “servirá [que de con] mil [cny]”; “irá [que l] camino”; “la principal de [der de] país”; “si caminara en [cnt] parte” ( ninguna or otra ); “se puede esperar [es] más ventaja”; “apuntamiento [es] [bnc]”. A third letter in the same key would settle most of them. No. 19 is one. Lasry decrypted its first leaf; ff. 41r and 41v were searched on the images for the open groups, which gave bet = dello and the switch markers, but ff. 41–43 have not been transcribed in full. CSP Spain III.2 no. 233 summarises its content from a copy in the Salazar collection, not its words, so it gives no crib.

t: Del Vasto to Charles V and a letter to “Garbino”, 1527–28 — one read in part by others, one read 98 %, one without its key
h: No. 20: the Garbino letter and Ranzo’s code
b: f. 44r, no. 20: “R. de […] S. r da poi de haverni scripto per piu l[ette]re”, the dates of letters received (23 November, 3 and 28 December, 4 February), then the code. Every group is a small letter with a number above it. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3022 f. 44r, via Gallica (btv1b90601558, view 86). No. 20 is an Italian letter, dated at Madrid on 11 April 1528, endorsed on the back to “Garbino”. It alternates clear and code. The clear passages report that the Chancellor was ill with gout, that fifty galleys were being fitted out, that a million ducats had been raised in Castile and 500,000 more were expected from the Cortes of Aragon, and that the Empress was in the seventh month and the prince would be sworn heir. The coded passages, about two thirds of the letter, are what it was sent for. The design is explained by the sheets bound after it. On f. 48 is a jargon, with more on f. 49: cover letters signed “Antonio de Cosenza” to “Andrea Romano in Valencia”, news disguised as the price of grain, and a list of cover names. On f. 49v the Emperor is “Joan Jacobo”, del Vasto “portolano de Gergenti”, Garbino himself “antonio petra”. On f. 50 is an “Aditione nel zifra” that shows how the code works. f. 50, the “Aditione nel zifra”: apresso a 327 , al garbino a 330 , Defensione d 308 , havendo h 106 , perilche p 400 . Syllables ( ar , are , an , exne ) have groups too. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3022 f. 50, via Gallica (btv1b90601558). Each code group is the initial of the word with a number: apresso is a 327 , Cartagenia c 327 , Garbino g 215 , soa santità s 395 , and common syllables get groups of their own. The addition continues each letter’s list from where the base table stopped (a1–326, b1–156, c1–326 …). The same code is used in the signed letters of Hieronimo Ranzo in BnF fr. 2988 ff. 2 and 9–10 and fr. 3019 f. 73. Poggio mandata per il Montepulciano” — the last cipher with Poggio, sent by way of Montepulciano. The right people, the right courier, the right years. Neither key fits, and that is checked below.

Meister's key of 1539–42 spells the convention out: “pongasi la nulla al fine di ogni parola” , put the null at the end of every word. This scribe did not. There are 482 nulls where the text needs about 1300 word ends, so the stretches between them average 12.6 digits — far too long to be words, which misled two earlier passes here. The chancery instruction quoted in section 04 resolves it: the null marks the end of a letter or syllable carrying an abbreviation, not the end of a word. the vowels three independent tests The vowel-bearing digits are {7, 0, 3} Italian ends about 97% of its words in a vowel, so word-final enrichment separates the classes. Over the 482 stretches: 1: 1.79 7: 1.76 3: 1.52 0: 1.49 against 6: 1.01 9: 0.64 2: 0.58 5: 0.25 8: 0.08 . Digit 8 ends a word at one twelfth of its overall rate. The frequency masses agree independently, to three decimals: {7,0,3,1} carries 0.476 of the text where all five Italian vowels carry 0.479. And a third line, new this session, agrees again — every string enriched immediately before a null ends in one of those digits. the word endings new Two units carry a third of all word endings Scanning every n-gram for enrichment before a null gives an extremely sharp answer. unit occurrences immediately before a null p 27 265 86 7.4 × 10 −33 80 349 82 4.2 × 10 −21 73 222 38 9.8 × 10 −7 37 73 17 1.7 × 10 −5 27 and 80 together end 35% of the marked words. For comparison, the commonest two-letter ending in real Italian takes under 5%. Word endings this concentrated are single codes, not letter pairs. structure new Two-digit units, and a real phase The stretches between nulls prefer even lengths, 278 against 202, chi-squared 12.0 on one degree of freedom. An earlier pass here looked at exactly this and recorded “no preference”; that was an error, and it cost two attacks. Inside those stretches the digit distribution at even offsets differs from the one at odd offsets: chi-squared 39.4 against a null of 8.3 ± 4.1 built by shuffling each segment, z = +7.6 . Digit 9 sits at even offsets 1.60 times as often as odd. Every doubled digit is suppressed, some severely — 00 occurs 6 times against 117 expected, 44 twice against 35, 99 twice against 21. Four hundred shuffles of the same digits produce a mean of 0.01 such suppressed pairs and never more than one.

t: The Farnese letter — Simon Klee’s solution reviewed
b: Antonio Elio (1506–1576), known in his own lifetime as Antonio delle Zifre , was cipher secretary to Paul III — the pope whose cardinal-nephew and Secretary of State, Alessandro Farnese, wrote this letter. He is credited with inventing the polyphonic cipher, and he trained the Argenti brothers who followed him. In 2025 Lasry, Simonetta and Biermann published a reconstruction of one of his designs. It has four properties: Syllabic. Most symbols encode consonant-vowel syllables, with a few for clusters or short words. Polyphonic. Every syllable symbol carries two meanings, and the second is chosen by a dot on the preceding symbol . The dots are applied inconsistently, so even a secretary holding the key is often guessing. Compound symbols. Some elements are encoded by pairs, so any symbol may be stand-alone or half of a pair . h and every doubled letter are dropped before encryption. Each of those makes a prediction, and this cryptogram satisfies all four. measured here Elio's design all ten doubled digits suppressed — 00 occurs 6 times against 117 expected doubled letters dropped before encryption dotted digits are 7, 2, 0 and the digit after a dot is 2/0/7/5 the dot sits on the antecedent and selects the alternate meaning word-final units are two digits, 27 and 80 , at p < 10 −20 consonant-vowel syllables as units unsupervised units come out 15% one digit, 32% two, 29% three; the even-length preference is real but only 58/42 any symbol may be stand-alone or half of a compound consonant runs three times too long for letters the level is syllables, not letters The doubling rule is not an inference. Meister prints the Farnese chancery’s own written instruction: “Scrivasi stretto et senza duplicare le consonanti quando occorrono dittioni che la ricerchino” — write tightly, and without doubling the consonants where the words call for them. The same instruction says other names may be abbreviated “con il segno della nulla in fine della lettera o sillaba” , with the null at the end of a letter or syllable. That reframes digit 4: it is an abbreviation and syllable marker, not a word separator — which is why the stretches between nulls average 12.6 digits and never did look like words.

h: What the specialists say about breaking it
b: Lasry, Megyesi and Kopal worked this exact corpus for Cryptologia in 2021. Two of their sentences govern everything here. On the one published key that names Poggio — the one whose title matches this letter’s own courier — “attempts to decipher the ciphertexts using that key did not produce any result.” And on the cipher itself: “The scheme appears to be a variable-length polyphonic cipher , which is a unique case in the Vatican collections … The ciphertexts in the second part (IA-2) seem to belong to another key.” Their phrase for the scheme, variable-length polyphonic , is what the run-length, phase and compression work on this page arrived at from the other direction, without having read it. The 2025 paper is blunter. “Ciphertext-only cryptanalysis for such a cipher would be extremely difficult and nearly impossible, even with modern computing, without prior knowledge of the principles of its complex design.” And with matching plaintext in hand, recovering the key of a sibling took three expert cryptanalysts two full days to make initial inroads, and many hours more to finish.

t: The Farnese letter — Simon Klee’s solution reviewed
h: The plaintext is unpublished — but its neighbours are not
b: No edition, calendar or regesta prints this letter. The Spanish nunciature of the period has no published series at all: Monumenta Hispaniae Vaticana stops at 1486, Olarra’s index begins in 1556, Serrano covers 1566–72. Nuntiaturberichte aus Deutschland I/7 prints Poggio but jumps from December 1541 to July 1543, its editor noting that the 1542 correspondence survives only in fragments. Concilium Tridentinum IV prints Farnese to Poggio on 5 February and 4 June 1542 and has nothing from April; its two April letters go to the nuncio in France instead. Pastor prints exactly two Farnese–Poggio letters, February 1541 and August 1542. Three manuscripts would settle it, and none is digitised: Naples, Archivio di Stato, Carte Farnesiane 723 — a Farnese to Poggio letter of 12 April 1542 , three days before this one and in the same courier cycle. AAV, Lettere de’ Principi 14 A — the Farnese to Poggio register copies, running to 4 June 1542. This is where the printed editions took their texts. BAV, Chigi L III 65 — the originals, 348 folios. Calibrating from dated letters in the editions puts 23 November 1541 at f. 153 and 29 June 1542 at ff. 191–195, so 15 April 1542 should sit at roughly ff. 165–190 . These registers are repeatedly described as carrying contemporary interlinear decipherments. A clear copy may simply be sitting there.

Compare the two transcripts as they are distributed. transcript single spaces between digits double spaces Portugal IA-1 — Part 4, solved 7603 3210 Spain IA-2 — Part 5, this one 6412 6 The Portugal transcript carries the spacing of its page; the Spain transcript is one undivided stream. When this section was first written it read the difference as a transcriber’s omission that the images would repair. That was wrong. George Lasry, who set the challenge, confirmed on 16 September 2026 that the Part 5 documents carry no visual separators at all — no dots, commas or wider spaces between tokens — and that recognising the variable-length tokens is the point of the challenge and the reason it is rated Level X. t: The Farnese letter — Simon Klee’s solution reviewed
b: If the text sat on a fixed two-digit grid it could be cut into units and attacked as a substitution over about a hundred symbols with three thousand tokens. That is tractable, and it is the one thing that would make this cryptogram breakable. So it was tested directly, in the three ways the null could behave. phasing chi-squared, even vs odd shuffle null z null counted, absolute index 6.8 9.0 ± 4.2 −0.53 null deleted, global index 4.3 8.0 ± 4.0 −0.93 null deleted, per cleartext run 4.3 8.0 ± 4.0 −0.93 All three sit below their shuffle nulls. There is no fixed two-digit grid anywhere in the text. The only phase signal is a local one that restarts at each null, and it is modest. That is the final piece, and it is exactly what Elio’s compound symbols predict — any symbol may be stand-alone or half of a pair. Without a segmentation there is no unit inventory; without a unit inventory there is no substitution to attack; and the polyphony doubles every unit’s meaning on top of that.

t: The Farnese letter — Simon Klee’s solution reviewed
b: The cipher is a variable-length syllabic code : mostly two-digit units, some of one digit, over vowel-bearing digits {7,0,3} and consonant-bearing {8,5,2,6,9}, with 27 and 80 as the dominant word-final units and 4 as an intermittent word null. The arithmetic is consistent — 6068 non-null digits at about two per unit is some 3000 units, at about 2.3 units per word some 1300 words of four to five letters, which is ordinary Italian for four folios. Against a shuffle of its own digits the text has 441 repeated 7-grams where the shuffle gives 5 , and 244 repeated 8-grams where the shuffle gives none. Unsupervised byte-pair encoding separates it from both controls: compression gain +1.6% for the cipher, −8.2% for genuine Italian pushed through a polyphonic single-digit cipher, −14.0% for a shuffle. It is a codebook, and it recurs because the same words recur. What would open it is the key from Chigi M II 49, or a matching plaintext in the Farnese correspondence of April 1542, or more ciphertext in the same key. Not another search. Five model classes have now been tested here, two of them against matched synthetic controls that the same code solves correctly. Working files in vatican5/ : vc.py and vc_syn.py (the constrained search and its matched control), phase.py (parity and phase), escape.py (suppressed pairs), units2.py (unit inventory), bpe.py (unsupervised units with controls), cvtest.py (the vowel/consonant run test).

h: The manuscript images, and the sibling letter
b: On 18 September 2026 the DECODE records behind the challenge were opened with a registered account: record 92, the eight 400 dpi page images of this letter with its transcription and address leaf, and record 91, the letter bound just before it in the same volume (ff. 62v–66v, catalogued as Spain IA-1). There is only one transcription DECODE’s transcription of record 92 is byte for byte the text MysteryTwister distributes. The images are the only new evidence. The address leaf confirms the reading of the frame: Al Rev.mo mons. come fratello il vescovo di Tropea, Nuntio di N.S. (Poggio was bishop of Tropea), endorsed Roma 1542, dal Card.le Farnese ; the last page closes Da Roma alli XV di Aprile 1542 … Come fratello, Il Car. Farnese . No hidden decipherment Faint writing runs between the cipher lines of 70v. Mirrored, it reads dar notitia … circa la materia della … and per questa causa principali è stato mandato : the cleartext of 70r showing through the leaf. There is no interlinear decipherment on any page. An image-verified transcript Every cipher line of 70r–73r was re-read against the images, digit by digit. The transcript proves sound, but not perfect: 151 digit positions change (2.3%), 62 by substitution, 39 by insertion, 22 by deletion. The largest single fault is on 71v, where the transcriber copied four groups twice ; on 72v and 73r the scribe struck digits through, and those are now marked. Of the 202 dots in the transcript nearly all sit over the digit given; about 20 missed dots were added, for 222. The commonest confusion is the scribe’s flat-topped 3 against his z-shaped 2 and barred 7. About 90 small dots also stand on the line between digits, all on 71r–73r. The digit before one is most often the null 4. At one per seventy digits they are far too sparse to divide words — Lasry is right — and look like clause punctuation. No structural statistic moves. Doubled digits, the dotted digits (7, then 2 and 0), the digits that follow a dot (7, 2, 0, 5), the vowel set and the unit inventory are what the earlier sessions measured. The sibling letter is another key this letter (IA-2) Spain IA-1 Portugal IA-1 (Part 4, solved) digits 6552 2956 10934 doubled digits, against chance 0.30 0.88 0.57 share of digit 1 3% 16% 16% IA-1, a December letter on the Diet of Nuremberg and Buda, repeats digits freely and leans on digits this letter hardly uses. Lasry, Megyesi and Kopal called IA-2 “another key” than IA-1; the numbers agree, and nothing transfers. Record 91’s four document images are cleartext Farnese letters of summer 1542, with no key sheet. A new exclusion: no renumbering of the Farnese keys fits A doubled digit stays doubled however a key is renumbered, so the rate of doubled digits belongs to the key’s design, not its numbering. Italian, written in the chancery’s own orthography (no h, no doubled letters), encoded with each printed key: encoding doubled digits against chance Meister key 1, data a Monsig. Montepulciano 9.7% 0.82 Meister key 2, ultima con Mons. Poggio 7.8% 0.63 any polyphonic single-digit key 6.4% 0.48 this letter 3.6% 0.30 Key 2 would put about 510 doubled digits into 6552; the letter has 233, some twelve standard deviations short. So neither printed Farnese key, under any relabelling of its digits , is this letter’s key. This one was built so that the same digit almost never has to be written twice. Only 7, 5 and 8 double at all, which is what a syllabary gives when most digits serve only as the first half of a unit or only as the second. DECODE holds nothing further The public catalogue has no other record from Paul III’s chancery: nothing under Poggio, Montepulciano, Tropea or Chigi, Farnese only from 1579, and no papal item among the records of 1538–1548. The four undated papal keys of the Camera Apostolica (records 23, 202–204) were fetched as a last check. They are the Avignon keys of Gabriele de Lavinde, about 1379: symbol alphabets and letter-pair nomenclators, 160 years too early. So the images did what Lasry said they would: they settle the dots and the doubtful digits, and nothing more. The routes in are the ones in section 09 — the key, the clear copy, or more of the Spagna 1A ciphertext — and all three need an order from the archive. Working files in vatican5/ : IA-2_reread.txt (the image-verified transcript), decode/reread/ (the page-by-page readings with every disagreement listed), decode/build_reread.py . The images themselves are the Vatican’s and are not redistributed.

t: Ferdinand the Catholic to Jerónimo de Vich, 1511–12 — Ravenna, Milan and a spiritual war on Louis XII
b: Three letters of Ferdinand the Catholic to his ambassador at Rome, AHN Estado 8715 N.45, N.57 and N.60 (April 1511 to September 1512), written wholly in cipher and filed without the decipherment their siblings carry. The nomenclator, a homophonic alphabet with 153 code groups for words and syllables, was rebuilt by lining two deciphered siblings up with the clerk’s text, and then read the three letters it was not built from. Julius II’s cardinals and Venice, Ferdinand’s account of how his army was pushed into Ravenna, the Sforza restoration in Milan. The 1515 letter is another system. Terrateig’s 1963 edition, not seen, may already print them. Seville, Burgos, Logroño → Rome · nomenclator with homophones and syllabic code groups · 1511–12 · read Ferdinand the Catholic to Jerónimo de Vich, 1511–12 from Ferdinand the Catholic Archivo Histórico Nacional, Estado 8715 N.45, N.57 and N.60: three letters of the King of Aragon to his ambassador at the court of Julius II, written wholly in cipher, with no decipherment on the leaves or in PARES The key rebuilt from two siblings that do carry the clerk’s decipherment, N.46 and N.52BIS, then used to read the three letters it was not built from · about 22,500 signs and groups, 153 code groups recovered · the 1515 letter N.73 is another system and stays unread Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 18 September 2026 · updated 22 September 2026 3 of 4 read Summary. The Vich family papers in the Archivo Histórico Nacional hold Ferdinand the Catholic’s letters to Jerónimo de Vich, his ambassador at Rome from 1507. Most of the ciphered ones were filed with a clerk’s decipherment; three of 1511–12 were not. The cipher is a nomenclator: a homophonic alphabet of figures and marked letters, and about 150 three-letter code groups that stand for whole words ( pef que , mix papa , sap venecianos ) and for syllables inside spelt-out words. Lining up two deciphered siblings with their decipherments gave the alphabet and the common groups; the three cipher-only letters were then read with it. N.45 (Seville, 4 April 1511) is a long complaint against Julius II, who published new cardinals and absolved the Venetians sin dezirme ni comunicarme , and a programme of three points: the papal army in a safe place, the Emperor–Venice concord, and Ferrara. N.57 (Burgos, 5 June 1512) is Ferdinand’s account of how his army was pushed into the battle of Ravenna against his written orders: las cosas de guerra es muy peligroso for those absent from them, and to do it again would be echar la soga tras el caldero . N.60 (Logroño, 1 September 1512), written during the Navarre campaign, sets out the restoration of Massimiliano Sforza in Milan, resists the Pope’s claims to Parma, Piacenza, Modena and Reggio, and asks for las armas espirituales against Louis XII as a protector of schismatics. Status: all three read in substance; by the notes’ estimate about 5, 7 and 14 per cent of the text of N.45, N.57 and N.60 is still unread or doubtful. The Barón de Terrateig’s 1963 edition of this correspondence prints Ferdinand’s letters from this legajo and was not seen; the three letters may already be printed there.

t: Ferdinand the Catholic to Jerónimo de Vich, 1511–12 — Ravenna, Milan and a spiritual war on Louis XII
b: Jerónimo de Vich, a Valencian noble, was Ferdinand’s ambassador at Rome through the pontificate of Julius II and into that of Leo X. His family’s papers passed to the Archivo Histórico Nacional and are catalogued with the Estado section, legajos 8714 and 8715. A PARES search for Vich cifrada lists the ciphered items. Most of them have a contemporary decipherment on the leaves that follow the cipher, written out in clear by a clerk at Rome; three of 1511–12 do not, and neither does one of 1515. Signature Date Place State 8714 N.12 30 Sept 1508 cipher and decipherment 8714 N.26 28 July 1509 cipher and decipherment 8714 N.39 13 May 1510 Monzón cipher and decipherment 8715 N.41 22 May 1510 cipher and decipherment; same key as below 8715 N.45 4 Apr 1511 Seville cipher only — read here 8715 N.46 5 July 1511 cipher and decipherment — key source 8715 N.52BIS 1 Mar 1512 cipher and decipherment — key source 8715 N.57 5 June 1512 Burgos cipher only — read here 8715 N.60 1 Sept 1512 Logroño cipher only — read here 8715 N.73 26 Oct 1515 Pedrezuela cipher only; a different system, not read 8715 N.74 30 Jan 1519 Charles I; cipher and decipherment in a third system 8715 N.79 “1500” “Clave de cifra”: a plain letter-to-sign table, not the key to any of these The letters are long. N.45 runs to thirteen pages of cipher (378 lines), N.60 to thirteen (432 lines), N.57 to one page and three lines. Apart from the heading date, the closing dateline and the royal signature, everything is in cipher. N.46, 5 July 1511: the first lines of the cipher (above) and of the clerk’s decipherment filed after it (below), Con beltran de cordona que partio de Sevilla a xvj de junio respondi a vuestras letras y scrivi todo lo que mas me ocorria; despues no he recebido vuestras … In the cipher, sal has pef is todo lo que , fid despues , mik no , par recebido , sub vuestras . Pairs like this gave the key. Image: Archivo Histórico Nacional, Estado 8715 N.46, images 1 and 3, via PARES; the two strips set together here.

t: Ferdinand the Catholic to Jerónimo de Vich, 1511–12 — Ravenna, Milan and a spiritual war on Louis XII
b: One key serves N.41, N.45, N.46, N.52BIS, N.57 and N.60, from May 1510 to September 1512. It has two parts. A homophonic alphabet. Each letter is written with one to three signs: figures, and letters with bars, loops or dots added. The labels below are the ASCII names used in the transcriptions, not the shapes themselves. letter signs letter signs letter signs a to 7 b h O p P SS mt b B i e Z r 40 tt E c ch l c s d eh d oo ll 7o t X g 9 e 4h 3 m q u 3t f gh n 11 W v V g o o ah T y / z 8 / p Code groups. Lowercase groups of two to five letters, most of three, stand for words: pef que , diz de , dih con , fak el , hor la , has lo , raf por , rif porque , mix and mye papa , fef emperador , sap venecianos , fio Ferrara , fuq Francia , dur / dox / dux duque , hib guerra , gup batalla , mak Nápoles , hel Ingalaterra . Some are syllables used inside words that are otherwise spelt out: pob si in si-t-io , flart me in pri-me-ras , mik no in me-no-r , plort al in c-al-dero . The groups are not in alphabetical order of their meanings, but related words often share an initial: f for el, en, es, esta, estado, emperador, Ferrara, Francia, franceses , m for mucho, muy, mil, manera, Nápoles, no, nos , p and r for que, quiere, quales, por, para, parte . Several words have two or three groups. In all 153 groups have been recovered; the full list is in vich1511/key.md . Traps. fug is señor and fuq Francia , and the two differ by a tail. plart mi and plort al differ by one letter, and the transcribers of N.45 and N.60 read the second differently; its value al is supported by c- plort -dero in N.57. The barred q is m in most places and a in a few: on the leaf there seem to be two similar signs, m with two bars and a with one, which the transcription has merged. In N.60 a tailed 8 reads i / j , and P serves for j and y as well as p .

t: Ferdinand the Catholic to Jerónimo de Vich, 1511–12 — Ravenna, Milan and a spiritual war on Louis XII
b: Nothing here was broken cold. N.46 (5 July 1511) and N.52BIS (1 March 1512) are in the same key and each has the clerk’s decipherment on the leaves after the cipher. Both were transcribed sign by sign from the PARES images, and the cipher was lined up with the decipherment word by word, as in the figure above. That gave the alphabet and the commoner code groups. The three cipher-only letters were then transcribed in the same labels and decoded by script ( decode.py ). Where the decode left a group unread, its value was fixed from the sense of the surrounding Spanish and accepted only when it read the same way elsewhere; fio Ferrara , dur duque , fuq Francia , gib franceses and sum tierra were added this way. The key went from the groups the two siblings supply to 153.

t: Ferdinand the Catholic to Jerónimo de Vich, 1511–12 — Ravenna, Milan and a spiritual war on Louis XII
b: Built on two letters, read on three others. The alphabet and the core groups come from N.46 and N.52BIS alone. They read N.45, N.57 and N.60, which contributed nothing to them, as running Spanish. The datelines. Each letter’s place and date are written in clear at the foot, and they agree with the catalogue: Seville, Burgos, Logroño. The contents fit the dates. N.45 complains of Julius II’s publication of new cardinals, which fits the promotion of 10 March 1511, less than four weeks earlier. N.57 turns on a battle lost after the Pope’s side and Vich pressed the viceroy to fight, which fits Ravenna (11 April 1512). N.60 starts from bulls para lo de Navarra and puts Massimiliano Sforza into Milan, which fits the Navarre campaign of summer 1512 and the Sforza restoration agreed that August. None of this is in the clear text. A proverb spelt out. In N.57, echar la soga tras el caldero (to throw the rope after the bucket) is spelt out sign by sign except for el , and for al in c-al-dero , which are code groups. A spelt-out proverb that comes out right is hard to get by accident. N.57, lines 26–28: … que seria ec- / -har la soga tras el caldero. Lo que en este caso de la / guerra toca hazer a vos … es procurar que el papa y venecianos cumplan . On the middle line, hor is la , fak el , and plort the al of caldero ; on the last, hib guerra , mix papa , sap venecianos . Image: Archivo Histórico Nacional, Estado 8715 N.57, image 1, via PARES. N.57, the end: the last three lines of cipher ( … y la de Ferrara … que la trateys … sin que la sienta el papa … hazedme lo saber ), the dateline in clear, en burgos a v de junio de dxij , and the royal signature. Image: Archivo Histórico Nacional, Estado 8715 N.57, image 2, via PARES.

t: Ferdinand the Catholic to Jerónimo de Vich, 1511–12 — Ravenna, Milan and a spiritual war on Louis XII
b: Quotations are the decode with word division and spelling normalised lightly; […] marks groups not read A long complaint against Julius II, then instructions. It opens with the news Vich had sent: the publication of the new cardinals, la publicacion de los nueve cardenales que crio el papa , which Ferdinand takes as proof that the Pope will not follow his counsel. The Pope has absolved the Venetians and treated with them sin dezirme ni comunicarme ; he has not kept his promise over the priory of San Juan; and because he would not follow Ferdinand’s advice to keep his army out of danger, there followed la rota que dezis . The business is the Emperor and Venice. Ferdinand gives draft terms for their concord: Padua and Treviso to stay with Venice in fief against a tribute, Verona, Vicenza, Riva, Rovereto and Peschiera to go to the Emperor; yo estoy muy determinado de ser perpetuamente unido con el emperador . France is offering him a separate perpetual alliance without the Emperor, which he will not take, and a rupture would wreck his war against the Moors. Orders go to Fabrizio Colonna under an enclosed letter of credence. Near the end he sums up the three points Vich is to press: la primera, que la gente del papa este en lugar seguro y donde no se aventure … la segunda, que apreteys muy vivamente la conclusion de la concordia del emperador y de los venecianos; y la tercera, la concordia de Ferrara, todo esto de la manera que de suso [es] dicho. “First, that the Pope’s troops stay in a safe place where they are not put at risk; second, that you press very hard for the conclusion of the concord between the Emperor and the Venetians; and third, the settlement of Ferrara, all in the way set out above.”

t: Ferdinand the Catholic to Jerónimo de Vich, 1511–12 — Ravenna, Milan and a spiritual war on Louis XII
b: The aftermath of Ravenna, where on 11 April 1512 the French destroyed the army of the Holy League under Ferdinand’s viceroy of Naples, Ramón de Cardona. Ferdinand reconstructs how his army came to fight. Vich’s letters, and the papal side, pressed the viceroy, saying que si no la hazian, el papa no compliria la paga y que se concertaria con Francia , if they did not fight the Pope would not meet the pay and would come to terms with France; and this against Ferdinand’s repeated written orders not to risk a battle. por cierto que las cosas de guerra es muy peligroso […] los que estan absentes della; que siempre se ha de remitir a los que las tienen presentes. “Truly, in matters of war it is very dangerous for those who are absent from it [to decide]; they must always be left to those who have them in front of them.” Do not do it again, he says, for it would be echar la soga tras el caldero , to lose the rope after the bucket. What is left to Vich is to procurar que el papa y venecianos cumplan their share of the pay, to bring the Emperor’s business to a conclusion, and to treat the Ferrara business secretly, sin que la sienta el papa , and report back, que yo dare orden como se efectue .

t: Ferdinand the Catholic to Jerónimo de Vich, 1511–12 — Ravenna, Milan and a spiritual war on Louis XII
b: Written from the Navarre campaign, the longest and least complete of the three. Its parts, in order: Reproach to Julius II (pp. 3–5). Vich had sent the bulls para lo de Navarra , and word that the Pope was acting against what had been agreed. Ferdinand recites what he has spent por tierra y por mar to rescue the Pope, the Church and Italy, and the Pope’s ingratitude in not paying his troops as the League requires. He traces it to the Pope’s suspicion que el Emperador y yo nos […] de Italia, no siendo assi la verdad (the notes supply hemos de apoderar , “mean to seize Italy”), and tells Vich to remove it. Milan (pp. 6–8). The Emperor and Ferdinand agree that Massimiliano, fijo del duque Ludovico , be put into the duchy by the Emperor’s hand, so that Pope and Venice lose the suspicion that Milan is being taken for the Emperor; possession of the state and its fortresses is to be taken at once in Massimiliano’s name. A marriage is in view for el infante don Fernando , Ferdinand’s grandson, with la fija de la duquesa de Milan . Venice and the papal claims (p. 9). Venice should not be stopped from recovering the towns it held before the war, or it will not pay. The Pope is trying to take Parma, Piacenza, Modena and Reggio, against the capitulation of the League, under which no member is to act en perjuizio de otra ; that is to wait until Milan is secured. Spiritual war on Louis XII (pp. 10–11). Ferdinand wants the Pope to use las armas espirituales : to deprive the King of France of his crown and of Guyenne and Normandy, as principal fautor i receptador […] cysmaticos i heretycos , to absolve his subjects of obedience and grant a crusade against him, as was done against the Emperor Frederick and King Pedro. Money, and Milan before Ferrara (pp. 12–15). Pensions of cinquenta mil ducados de pension cada año , shared among the members of the League, to hold an Italian power to it, que es muy sustancial ; if the Pope insists on beginning with Ferrara, Vich is to insist on finishing the French in the state of Milan first, and on a mutual guarantee of each member’s state in Italy.

t: Ferdinand the Catholic to Jerónimo de Vich, 1511–12 — Ravenna, Milan and a spiritual war on Louis XII
b: N.73, from Pedrezuela on 26 October 1515, is in another system. It is 124 lines, 3,177 tokens of 197 kinds, mostly three-letter code groups ( sin 151 times, sud 97, no 93, zre 89) with a smaller set of signs. None of the 1511–12 values carries over. No deciphered sibling is known: the nearest, N.74 of 1519, is Charles I’s and in a third system ( sex papa , sin de ), and N.79, filed as a clave de cifra , is a simple letter table that fits none of these letters. Annealing against a Spanish five-gram model, with the code groups treated as runs of letters, as whole units, and as breaks between runs of signs, gave nothing: scores well below Spanish and seeds that disagreed. The sign runs are short (median three), so a letter model has little to hold on to. This letter needs a crib or a deciphered sibling. Its clear text is the docket a 26 de octubre 1515 , the opening videlicet iterum , and the dateline en Pedrezuela a xxvj de otubre de dxv .

t: Ferdinand the Catholic to Jerónimo de Vich, 1511–12 — Ravenna, Milan and a spiritual war on Louis XII
b: Possibly. The Barón de Terrateig, Política en Italia del Rey Católico 1507–1516. Correspondencia inédita con el embajador Vich (CSIC, Madrid 1963, 2 vols.), edits this correspondence, and it was not seen for this reading. What could be found out about it without the book (web searches and Google Books snippets, 18 September 2026): Volume II prints Ferdinand’s letters to Vich as numbered documents with AHN Estado references; a snippet shows a letter dated Logroño a XXVI días de octubre 1512 followed by Documento n.° 89, A.H.N. Estado , and later historians cite 1512 letters in vol. II from p. 206 on. The book has plates of ciphered letters and prints Descifrado de la carta que figura en la lámina … beside them, and its index has many entries under Rávena, batalla de . No snippet, review or citation was found that quotes or cites the letters of 4 April 1511, 5 June 1512 or 1 September 1512, or says whether Terrateig printed cipher-only letters in clear. So it is open whether Terrateig printed N.45, N.57 and N.60, and if so whether he printed a decipherment of them. Given that his volume II prints Ferdinand’s 1512 letters from this legajo, it should be assumed until checked that he may have. PARES itself records no decipherment for these three items.

t: Ferdinand the Catholic to Jerónimo de Vich, 1511–12 — Ravenna, Milan and a spiritual war on Louis XII
b: Unread text. Of the tokens transcribed, about 2.6 % in N.45, 3.5 % in N.57 and 7.5 % in N.60 are groups the key does not yet have. The notes put the share of text still unread or doubtful higher, about 5, 7 and 14 %, because some stretches decode letter by letter without yet making sense. The four other deciphered letters in the same or the earlier key (N.41 and the three in 8714) were not used and would close many of the gaps. Look-alike signs. The q sign for m and a , and the group pairs plart / plort and flart / flort , need one careful pass against the images before they are trusted. Single-context values. Some groups were fixed from one or two contexts in the three letters. fer , for instance, is keyed as dio(s) , but it also stands where Fer- of Fernando is wanted; it may be a syllable group, not a word. Readings the notes supply. In N.60, the words after que el Emperador y yo nos are unread, and hemos de apoderar is the sense, not the decode. Guyenne and Normandy are in the decode, but whom they are to go to sits in unread groups; the notes’ “assigned to England” is an inference. The duquesa de Milan whose daughter is proposed for the infante is presumably Isabella of Aragon, widow of Gian Galeazzo Sforza, and the daughter Bona; the letter as read does not name them. A nearby line reads el fijo del duque Ludovico que mato a su padre , whose sense in context is not settled. Prior publication. See section 09. The three letters may already be in print in Terrateig 1963, which was not consulted. N.73 is unread, and nothing here bears on its content.

t: Ferdinand the Catholic to Jerónimo de Vich, 1511–12 — Ravenna, Milan and a spiritual war on Louis XII
b: Archivo Histórico Nacional, Estado, leg. 8715: N.45, PARES 12751390 ; N.46, 12751391 ; N.52BIS, 12760824 ; N.57, 12751402 ; N.60, 12751405 ; N.73, 12751418 ; also N.41 (12751386), N.74 (12751419), N.79 (12751424), and leg. 8714 N.12, N.26, N.39 (12751356, 12751370, 12751383). Barón de Terrateig (J. Manglano y Cucaló de Montull), Política en Italia del Rey Católico 1507–1516. Correspondencia inédita con el embajador Vich , 2 vols., CSIC, Madrid 1963. Not consulted; see section 09. Context: the Holy League of 1511, the battle of Ravenna (11 April 1512), the conquest of Navarre (July 1512) and the restoration of Massimiliano Sforza (1512), in the standard accounts. The sign-by-sign transcriptions ( n45_pp03-09.txt , n45_pp10-15.txt , n57_transcription.txt , n60_pp03-09.txt , n60_pp10-15.txt ), the decodes ( *_decoded.txt , n57_decode_v3.txt ), the key ( key.md , decode.py ), the N.73 transcription and solver attempts, and the notes are in the repository ( vich1511/ ). The PARES images are not committed; pares.py re-fetches them.

t: The duc de Nevers to Robert de La Vieuville, 30 September 1587
b: A copy of a clear letter from Nevers in the king’s camp to the new governor of Mézières, with code numbers and three short runs of figures and letter-signs set in (BnF fr. 3975 ff. 101–102, DECODE R4289). The key is Nevers’s cipher no. 16 of 1587, read here from the key book. Its code numbers fit: 42 et 43, eschevins et maire de ville; 63, La Vieuville. The runs and the letter text stay unread, because the only images are a microfilm on which the hand is too poor. Saint-Aignan → La Vieuville · code numbers and letter runs in a clear letter · 30 September 1587 · not read Nevers to La Vieuville, 1587 from Duke of Nevers BnF Français 3975, item 34, ff. 101r–102v (DECODE R4289; Gallica btv1b90605473 , views 185–188). A copy of a letter from the duc de Nevers, written at Saint-Aignan in the king’s camp on the Loire, to the new governor of Mézières, with cipher set into the clear text. The key is Nevers’s cipher no. 16 of 1587, which Tomokiyo lists; its code numbers fit. The letter itself stays unread: the only images are a black-and-white microfilm, and the hand is too poor on it. Daniel Bourdeau · attempted 22 September 2026 not read Summary. The catalogue entry said that what the cipher hides is not known. The BnF notice calls the item a “letter with cipher and decipherment”, but the two leaves carry no decipherment. They are a copy, about 110 lines in a very hasty hand, of a letter in clear French with the cipher set into it: code numbers on f. 101v and f. 102v, and three short runs of figures and letter-signs. Tomokiyo’s Nevers key no. 16 (BnF fr. 3995 f. 32v), which I read in full from the sheet, gives the code numbers sense: a 42 et 43 de is “to the eschevins and the maire de ville”, 63 with a bar is La Vieuville, 48 is the château and 30 the artillery. The same key reads a phrase of Nevers’s letter of 31 August 1587 to the same man. The three letter runs (33 signs) do not read under it: every reading the key allows, scored inside its clear context, is nonsense. The letter text I can read only at 30–40% on the microfilm, and a noise control shows a solver needs about 80% glyph accuracy. The letter is not in Gomberville’s edition of Nevers’s Mémoires (1665), and none of the neighbouring leaves deciphers it. Status: attempted, not read. A colour scan or the original at the BnF would unblock it.

t: The duc de Nevers to Robert de La Vieuville, 30 September 1587
b: f. 101v, lower half: … 42 et + run A + pour … a 42 et 43 de … , then de pouvoir + run B + vous entretenir . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3975 f. 101v, via Gallica (view 186). Item 34 of fr. 3975 is ff. 101–102: three written pages and a third, with the endorsement Nevers 1587 30 sept. / Mr de La Vieuville on f. 102v. The BnF describes it as a copy. It is in the same hasty hand as the next item (f. 103, Nevers to the Queen Mother, 1 October 1587) and as Nevers’s letter of 31 August to La Vieuville in fr. 3416. Most of it is clear French: words like possible avant , la campagne , garnison , vous entretenir , faudra and adieu can be picked out. Robert de La Vieuville had been named governor of Mézières by the duc de Guise on 29 July 1587 (fr. 3975 item 27). Nevers was with Henri III’s army facing the German reiters. The code numbers fit that: the towns of Nevers’s Champagne government (Rethel, Reims), the town officers of Mézières, the château and the artillery.

t: The duc de Nevers to Robert de La Vieuville, 30 September 1587
b: Tomokiyo lists the Nevers ciphers in the key book BnF fr. 3995. Key no. 16 (1587, f. 32v) has a homophonic alphabet of digits and letter-forms ( a 8 9 , e 7 6 , i 5 4 , l 3 2 , s i 5 , t g f , u e d , r ſ k , qu n m …). It also has plain code numbers 10–100 for offices and places (42 eschevins, 43 maire de ville, 48 château, 50 Rethel, 51 Mézières, 64 Reims) and barred numbers 1–81 for provinces and persons (2 Rethelois, 25 Roy, 36 Nevers, 63 La Vieuville). Two things tie it to this letter. First, its code numbers make sense in the clear context. Second, it reads the one enciphered phrase Tomokiyo transcribed from the 31 August letter (fr. 3416 f. 53v), d r h f K 6 x 8 4 t = vostre main , which he had tried with key no. 11 without result. Keys 11 and 12 do not fit this letter.

t: The duc de Nevers to Robert de La Vieuville, 30 September 1587
b: f. 102v, the end of the letter: 63̅ (La Vieuville), 42 et 40 , run C k 7 n 6 2 9 7 before faudra , 40 et 50 , and adieu . Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3975 f. 102v, via Gallica (view 188). About 31 code numbers are legible, all on f. 101v and f. 102v; f. 101r and f. 102r have only clear amounts such as 1200. Graded as in the site conventions : number no. 16 grade 42 et 43 eschevins et maire de ville H 63̅ (three times) La Vieuville H 2̅ Rethelois C 48 château (“Chau”) C 30 artillerie C 50, 64, 15 Rethel, Reims, garnison M 33 et 35 et 34 barred: Conty, Montpensier, Soissons (three princes of the blood); plain: menées, menaces, surprise M 40 huguenotz M 28, 29, 36, 80 no bar visible: levée / Reine de Navarre, deniers / Roi de Navarre, paix / Nevers, Guise / ? t: The duc de Nevers to Robert de La Vieuville, 30 September 1587
h: What was tried on the rest
b: The three runs. A ( 5 i 7 f Z r d 6 5 i 8 t h 6 ♁ 7 2 5̅ , after eschevins et ), B ( 5 i 7 ♁ 6 2 9 v , between de pouvoir and vous entretenir ) and C ( k 7 n 6 2 9 7 , before faudra ). I enumerated every reading no. 16 allows, with the unclear glyphs expanded (9 as a or as the tailed t ; the Z-sign as m , r , l or g ; h , which the key does not use, as any letter). Each was scored with the period French model, alone and inside its clear context. None is French. The best are si et rou essance de si , sie de lan and requelae ; C gives requeste only if two of its digits are misread. The digits that decide them (2 or s, 9 or t, 6 or b) cannot be told apart on the microfilm. The letter text. A glyph-by-glyph transcription of 19 lines of f. 101r (about 900 glyphs) was about 60% sure per glyph. Scored as French it fails. Run through a homophonic substitution solver, in case it was letter cipher, it fails too. A control with real French enciphered and degraded shows the solver recovers text at 20% glyph error but not at 40%, and the transcription scores like the 40% case. So the problem is legibility, not the method. A printed text. Gomberville’s Mémoires de M. le duc de Nevers (1665), both parts, searched for Vieuville, Vieville, Vieuuille and Aignan: not there. The other Vieuville letters in the BnF notices (fr. 4715, fr. 4716) are of 1589. DECODE holds no transcription. The neighbouring leaves. f. 103 (to the Queen Mother, 1 October) and f. 127 (to La Vieuville, 23 October 1587) are Nevers letters of the same weeks. Neither deciphers this one.

t: The duc de Nevers to Robert de La Vieuville, 30 September 1587
b: The letter text, ff. 101r–102v, about 110 lines: unread. It is illegible on the microfilm, the only images there are. Runs A, B and C, 33 signs: unread. Key no. 16 applies, but the digit forms cannot be read with certainty. Code numbers 28, 29, 33–35, 36 and 80: plain or barred cannot be decided. What would finish it: a colour scan of fr. 3975 ff. 101–102, or a reading of the original at the BnF. With a sure transcription, key no. 16 should read the runs directly.

t: Galeazzo Visconti to Montmorency from the camp at Landriano, 30 August 1528
b: BnF fr. 3034 f. 154 (DECODE R4223), catalogued as from an unknown sender and not deciphered. The cipher is Galeazzo Visconti’s, and George Lasry had published its key in 2023 but not the text. Read here in part, 1247 of 1337 signs, with his key extended on the letter: a council of war at Landriano on marching to Milan or Pavia, which Visconti lost to a scheme of “Francesco” and the Venetian officers. Two signed sibling letters show the crossed sign is the figure 4, so the name codes 48, 4θ and 4r are numbered codes with no surviving key. Campo a Landriano → the grand maître · invented-sign substitution with numbered codes · 30 August 1528 · read in part Galeazzo Visconti to Montmorency from the camp at Landriano, 30 August 1528 to Anne de Montmorency BnF Français 3034 f. 154r–v, no. 68 (DECODE R4223, catalogue item 177, “unknown sender”). Thirty-nine lines of cipher in Italian, read with George Lasry’s 2023 key for Visconti’s cipher, extended on the letter and checked on two signed sibling letters. Daniel Bourdeau · read in part 22 September 2026 read in part Summary. DECODE lists R4223 as a two-page cipher letter from an unknown sender to Anne de Montmorency, “Non-decrypted”. It is unsigned, but the cipher is Galeazzo Visconti’s: Satoshi Tomokiyo’s cryptiana lists the leaf with two letters Visconti signed, and George Lasry’s key table of 5 November 2023 is headed “BNF Francais 3045f28 and 3034f154 – Italian”. Only the key had been published, not the text. The 39 cipher lines were transcribed sign by sign from the Gallica images and read with Lasry’s table, which the letter itself extended. 1247 of 1337 cipher signs read as sense (93.3%). Visconti describes a council of war held the day before at Landriano on whether the League army should march on Milan or on Pavia. He argued for Milan and lost: a scheme of “Francesco”, whispered to the Venetian officers, swung the Duke of Urbino and the proveditor to Pavia, and Visconti was interrupted when he spoke. The sibling letters show that the crossed sign is the figure 4, so the name groups 48, 4θ and 4r are numbered codes. No list of them survives, and they stay open with a few one-off signs.

t: Galeazzo Visconti to Montmorency from the camp at Landriano, 30 August 1528
b: Français 3034 is a volume of original letters to Montmorency. No. 68, f. 154, opens with three words in clear, Poco scritti le lre , then runs in cipher for thirty lines on the recto and nine on the verso. The close and date are in clear: pregando n[ost]ro S[ign]or Dio dona a V. S. bona e longa vitta. Da al Campo a Landriano ali XXX d’aust . Landriano, south of Milan, was the camp of the League army in the late summer of 1528, after the collapse of Lautrec’s expedition to Naples. f. 154r, lines 1–6: the clear Poco scritti le lre , then “Il consiglio de heri fu per tirare queli capitanei che erano lì a la opinione …”; line 5 ends with the code 48. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3034 f. 154r, via Gallica (view 243). The cipher replaces each letter with an invented sign. The signs include a tau for A, a round d for D, a bold k for R, a psi for I, a sign like ne for S and one like me for L, and a sign written like the word far for CHE. E has three forms and A two. Lasry’s table gave most of the letters. The letter added the values for ne , me , the small y (N, with a bent-arm form for B), θ (G), plain p (M), far and fu , and fixed q as H, or F in Francesco . It also showed that the long thin diagonal strokes under the lines are later word dividers, added by someone who worked on the letter. They are not parts of signs.

t: Galeazzo Visconti to Montmorency from the camp at Landriano, 30 August 1528
b: Final pass. [..] is an unread sign, (?) a reading whose sense is not established, [48], [4θ], [4r], [peu] are code groups. f. 154r Poco scritti le lre. Il consiglio de heri fu per tirare queli capitanei che erano lì a la opinione che no fuse andase a Milano, perché era la mia(?) tuto causato comtagio. Scrito questo, s’è chiarito questa mane, ha esendo venuto il duca d’Urbino a casa de [48], per deliberare o a Milano o a Pavia. Ove erano asciilati(?) tuti li capitanei o nostri che [..] sono, molti, et a quesi de la Signoria che sono ascicsai pui(?). [qq] uolse(?) [48] che il duca d’Urbino tirase tuti li so[..] da uno canto et lui li lo[..] da uno altro, aciò dito ognuno sua opinione, lui do[..] deliberaseno [..]. E questa fu inventione de Francesco, dita in secreto ha queli de la Signoria, erano tropo, aciò che se vincese la opinione de andare a Milano. Rex. Il che [..] è [..] parso al duca d’Urbino providitore et maiore parte de loro dal canto nostro. Io era solito sempre esere chiamato il primo per aprire il camino ali altri, et questa volta ha comenciato a Francisco, poi ali altri pochi, poi a me [..] acuvante(?) se; dicese nula, [4θ] dise che ere da andare a Pavia. Io comenciai a dire quelo agio scrito de andare a Milano. Pensate che Francesco il primo a interompere, poi qualche uno altro che mi vergogno dirlo, [4r] sapendolo dissimulare. Rex: il fine mi lasoren[o](?) dire cum fatica, s[e] non(?) fisse. Si va a questo modo se harà uno pastone de mala digestione. Io vedo asai cose, ma che è in mia posa [..] a provederli; e sapiate che tuti li f. 154v nostri, dico tuti, comenciando al capori, [..] e ga[..] Dio ch’io scriva al [peu] et a vostra S. provedase da li che per me ie sono d[..]cuspaeo(?) n[..]ita(?) [..] celaro(?); però mai de dire il servicio dil [peu], e vaglia quanto potrà. Tuta volta certifico em(?) che havem [..] si ne [..] dito il duca d’Urbino providitore, et a io che se andarà per o s[..]u[..]o(?) a traversat[..] il camino tra Milano e Pavia, e don[..]de i ni spire[..]rà(?) poi il resto, [clear] che ca fin de questa ma[teria], pregando n[ost]ro S[ign]or Dio dona a V. S. bona e longa vitta. Da al Campo a Landriano ali XXX d’aust. In English Visconti writes that the council held the day before was meant to bring the captains present round to the view that the army should not go to Milan. That morning the Duke of Urbino came to the lodging of [48] to decide between Milan and Pavia, with all the captains, many of them, and the officers of the Signoria of Venice. It was arranged that each should give his opinion in turn. This, he says, was a device of Francesco’s, whispered to the Venetian officers, so that the vote would go against Milan, and the Duke of Urbino, the proveditor and most of the captains came down against Milan. Visconti was usually called first, “to open the way for the others”. This time Francesco was called first, then a few others, then Visconti. [4θ] said the army should go to Pavia. When Visconti began to argue for Milan, as he had written, Francesco was the first to interrupt, then others he is ashamed to name, and in the end he was let speak only with difficulty. “If it goes on this way we shall have a stew of bad digestion.” He sees much and can do little to remedy it. He asks Montmorency to see to matters for all the captains, in the service of [peu], perhaps the King. The Duke of Urbino and the proveditor have said that the army will go to cut the road between Milan and Pavia, and he will write the rest later. “Francesco” may be Francesco Maria Sforza, the League’s duke of Milan, who wanted Pavia. The letter does not say so.

t: Galeazzo Visconti to Montmorency from the camp at Landriano, 30 August 1528
b: The two pages are Gallica views 243 and 244 of btv1b90600370. They were deskewed and cut into line strips at full resolution. The line centres drift by up to 90 pixels across the page, so each strip was placed by measurement. A first rough transcription of 1344 tokens showed at once that Lasry’s table reads Italian. Each line was then transcribed again sign by sign against the table, and every value the table lacked was fixed from words that already read. A second pass redid the verso and retried every open spot on the recto. Two other Visconti letters in the same cipher were then opened: Visconti to Angelo Bolano, Alessandria, 15 October 1528 (fr. 3045 f. 28), and Visconti to Francis I, in campo in la pieve de Loccate , 15 June 1529 (fr. 3096 f. 91). The key reads both (“mal tratamento”, “che disperat-”). In both, the crossed sign appears in numeral pairs, 42 and 48, so it is the figure 4. The name groups of this letter are therefore numbered codes, and 48 appears in the letter to the King as well. The groups rr and qq also recur there as units. None of these codes has a value anywhere.

t: Galeazzo Visconti to Montmorency from the camp at Landriano, 30 August 1528
b: Numbered codes , no key material: 48 (twice; the host of the council), 4θ (the captain who spoke for Pavia), 4r (before sapendolo dissimulare , and again in v03), rr (r21), qq (r09, before uolse ), peu (twice; perhaps the King). Only a surviving nomenclator could fix them. The final sign pair of so··, lo··, do·· (r10–12): the same pair each time. The sense suggests soi , loi , doi , one I value for the pair. That is a proposal only (I). It does not occur in the siblings. One-off signs : [Y r] in r12, a small sign and a blot in r16, [v b] in r30, Π in v08 and v09. The lines read without them, so they may be nulls. That is not proved (M). Illegible : only the blotted sign and the flourished ſt ligature in v01. A third pass (22 September 2026) enhanced the other spots on the Gallica native (autocontrast, unsharp mask, threshold, 2×): the middle of v03 is legible, and its ǂ-r pair is the numbered code 4r of r25, so that gap is a code; the r21 rr carries an overbar, so it is the code rr; fuo is Lombard fu , as in the letter to the King. The count is now 1247 of 1337 signs (93.3%). Values read, sense open (M): la mia (r03), asciilati (r07), ascicsai pui (r09), acuvante (r21), lasoreno and se non (r26–27, C), and in v03 and v07 the runs marked (?).
